Chapter Five: The Tathāgata’s Radiance and Awakening From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Radiance and Awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from the wheels upon his two feet.
It universally illumined the trichiliocosm: ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Pūrvavidehas,
ten billion Aparagoyāṇīs, ten billion Uttarakuru-dvīpas, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Vajra-perimeter mountains,
ten billion births of bodhisattvas, ten billion renunciations of the household life by bodhisattvas, and ten billion...
The Buddha’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; ten billion Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma;
ten billion Tathāgatas entering parinirvāṇa; ten billion Sumeru Kings of Mountains; ten billion heavens of the Four Great Kings;
ten billion heavens of the Thirty-three Gods; ten billion Yāma heavens; ten billion Tuṣita heavens; ten billion Nirmāṇarati heavens.
Ten billion Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, ten billion Brahmā heavens, ten billion Ābhāsvara heavens,
ten billion Śubhakṛtsna heavens, ten billion Bṛhatphala heavens, and ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens—
all that exists within this world appeared therein.

Thus he saw the Buddha seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; it was likewise so in ten billion Jambudvīpas.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, in each of the ten directions across all ten billion Jambudvīpas, a great bodhisattva was seen, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, coming to where the Buddha was.

They were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bodhirāja Bodhisattva, Vasumitra Bodhisattva, Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva, Guṇaśrī Bodhisattva, Netraśrī Bodhisattva, Vīryaśrī Bodhisattva, Dharmaśrī Bodhisattva, Jñānaśrī Bodhisattva, and Bhadraśrī Bodhisattva.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come are the Golden World, the World of Joyful Colors, the World of Flower Colors, the World of Campaka Flower Colors, the World of Blue Lotus Colors, the World of Gold Colors, the World of Jewel Colors, the World of Vajra Colors, the World of Crystal Colors, and the World of Reality Colors.
Each of them, in the presence of the Buddhas of their respective lands—

namely, Acalamati Buddha, Jñānāgni Buddha, Viśuddhajñāna Buddha, Vinayajñāna Buddha, Uṣabhijñāna Buddha, Niṣṭhājñāna Buddha, Anuttarajñāna Buddha, Vaśitājñāna Buddha, Brahmajñāna Buddha, and Arivijayajñāna Buddha— purely cultivated the brahma-faring.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
“If there is one who perceives the Perfectly Awakened One as being liberated and free from all outflows,
yet remains unattached to any world, he does not possess the eye of pure vision.”
If there is one who knows the Tathāgata, Observing that nothing exists,
And knows the characteristic of the dispersal and extinction of dharmas, That person will swiftly become a Buddha.
Able to see this world As being unattached in all places.
The body of the Tathāgata is likewise; such a person will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
If, within the Buddha-dharma, their mind accords with equanimity and enters the gate of non-duality, that person is inconceivable.
If one perceives me and the Buddha as abiding in the mark of equality, that person dwells in non-dwelling and is far removed from all existence.
Form and sensation have no number; perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
One who can know in this way is a Great Muni.
There is nothing that sees, nor is there any dharma that is seen;
having clearly understood all dharmas, such a one can illuminate the world.
In a single thought-moment one sees all Buddhas appearing in the world, yet in reality there is nothing that arises; such a person possesses great renown.
There is no self and no sentient beings, nor is there any destruction.
If one can transform such signs, that person is a superior man.
Within the one, they understand the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, they understand the one.
These successive arisings are not real; the wise have nothing to fear.
Just as Mañjuśrī spoke these verses in this place, so it was in all places.

At that time, the light passed beyond this world and shone everywhere throughout ten Buddha-lands in the eastern direction; likewise, it did so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Within each of those worlds, everything from ten billion Jambudvīpas up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens was fully manifested.

Thus he saw the Buddha seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury World, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; in each of those worlds, there were likewise ten billion Jambudvīpas, all of which appeared in the same manner.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he saw that in each of the ten directions there was a great bodhisattva, accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, who had come to the Buddha’s presence—namely, Mañjuśrī and others, up to Bhadramukha.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come range from the Golden World up to the World of Reality-like Color; in each of their respective native lands, they have purely cultivated the brahma-faring under Buddhas ranging from Immovable Wisdom Buddha to Subduer-of-Enmity Wisdom Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, being present in all places, spoke in verse:

"Seeing sentient beings oppressed by suffering, Enveloped by delusion and pierced by the thorns of craving and desire, They constantly seek the unsurpassed path; Such is the nature of all Buddhas’ Dharma."
Free from the two extremes of annihilation and permanence, seeing that the reality of phenomena does not shift—
this wheel, never before turned, you now turn, this unsurpassed wheel.
For inconceivable eons, you have donned the armor of great vows and virtue.
To deliver beings from birth and death, such is the Dharma of the Great Sage.
The Guide subdues the multitudes of Māras; his valor and strength are invincible.
With words of loving-kindness, he dispels all fears—this is the unsurpassed Dharma of compassion.
Having attained profound wisdom within, they are able to destroy all afflictions;
in a single thought they perceive all things, manifesting sovereign displays.
They can beat the drum of the True Dharma, its sound shaking the lands of the ten directions.
Causing them to attain the unsurpassed path, they personally realize that the nature of phenomena is thus.
Without destroying the immeasurable realm, they are able to travel through countless lands;
grasping at nothing within all existence, they are as sovereign as a Buddha.
With incomparable joy and mindfulness, the Buddhas are ever pure;
the Tathāgatas are equal to space, for they have fulfilled their vows.
For the sake of each and every sentient being, even within the Avīci Hell,
Though scorched and boiled for immeasurable eons, their minds remain as pure as the Most Victorious One.
Not begrudging body or life, they constantly protect all Buddha-dharmas;
fully practicing patience, they shall attain the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the light passed beyond ten worlds and illuminated a hundred worlds in the eastern direction; likewise, it did so for all directions up to the zenith.
Within each of those worlds, everything belonging to the ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to the ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens, was fully manifested.

Thus he saw the Buddha seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury World, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; in each of those individual worlds, there were likewise ten billion Jambudvīpas, all of which appeared in the same manner.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he saw in each of the ten directions a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, approaching the Buddha’s presence—namely, Mañjuśrī and others, up to Bhadramukha.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come range from the Golden World up to the World of Reality-like Color; in each of their respective native lands, they have purely cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of Buddhas ranging from Immovable Wisdom Buddha to Subduing-Enemy Wisdom Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī of all places spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has awakened to all phenomena, Which are like illusions and like empty space;
With a pure mind free from obstruction, He tames the various classes of sentient beings.”
Some see him at the time of birth, his wondrous form like a mountain of gold;
dwelling in this final body, he illuminates all like the full moon.
Some see him when walking in meditation, gathering immeasurable merit.
Perfectly endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, the Lion among Men is a teacher who practices illumination.
Sometimes he is seen with clear and pure eyes, observing and illuminating the ten directions;
at other times he is seen laughing and playing, for the sake of the inclinations and desires of sentient beings.
Some see him roar like a lion, his pure and peerless body manifesting his final birth; whatever he speaks is nothing but truth.
Some see him at the time of renouncing the world, liberated from all fetters.
Cultivating the practices of all Buddhas, one should always joyfully contemplate quiescence.
Sometimes seeing them seated at the site of enlightenment, they perfectly awaken to all phenomena,
cross to the shore of all merits, and extinguish the darkness of ignorance and afflictions.
Sometimes one sees the Honored One among gods and humans, fully endowed with a heart of great compassion;
sometimes one sees him turning the wheel of Dharma, delivering and liberating all living beings;
or one sees him roar with fearlessness, his dignified appearance most subtle and wondrous.
Subduing all worlds, his spiritual powers are unimpeded.
Some see him with a mind of tranquility, the lamp of the world forever extinguished;
others see the Honored One of Ten Powers, manifesting the sovereign Dharma.
At that time, the light passed beyond a hundred worlds and illuminated a thousand worlds in the eastern direction; likewise, it did so for all directions up to the zenith.
Within each of those worlds, everything belonging to ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens, was fully manifested.

Thus he saw the Buddha seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury World, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; in each of those worlds, across ten billion Jambudvīpas, it was likewise so.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he saw in each of the ten directions a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, approaching the Buddha’s presence—namely, Mañjuśrī and others, up to Bhadramukha.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come range from the Golden World up to the World of Reality-like Color; in each of their respective native lands, they have purely cultivated the holy life in the presence of Buddhas ranging from Immovable Wisdom Buddha to Subduer-of-Enmity Wisdom Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī of all places spoke in verse, saying:
“The Dharma of the Sugata is profoundly deep; It is without marks and without existence.
Because sentient beings are subject to inversion, Everything appears in succession.”
Without "I" or "mine," their realm is empty and tranquil;
the body of the Sugata is pure, self-awakened and free from all dust.
Perfectly enlightened, luminous, and liberated, they are immeasurable and beyond counting.
Within boundless worlds, arising through the conjunction of causes and conditions,
there are no aggregates, elements, or sense bases; forever free from the suffering of birth and death,
and not reckoned among the worldly, he is thus called the Lion of Men.
Liberated both internally and externally, fundamentally and eternally empty by nature, all things are free from falsehood; such is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Having abandoned craving and all afflictions, the long-flowing stream never turns back again.
The Perfectly Awakened One understands all phenomena and delivers immeasurable sentient beings.
In a single thought-moment, he perceives no duality; he contemplates the Dharma of quiescent extinction with a mind free from attachment—the Buddha’s sovereignty is immeasurable.
Thoroughly knowing the law of causes and conditions, karmic retribution, and sentient beings,
his most supreme and unimpeded wisdom is profound and inconceivable.
He universally beholds the realms of the ten directions and adorns and purifies all Buddha-fields.
The Tathāgata is free from falsehood and delivers immeasurable multitudes.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like refined gold; regarding all that exists and does not exist, he teaches the pure Dharma according to those who are to be transformed.
At that time, the light passed beyond a thousand worlds and illuminated ten thousand worlds in the eastern direction; likewise, it did so for all directions up to the zenith.
Within each of those worlds, everything contained—from ten billion Jambudvīpas to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens—was fully manifested.

Thus he saw the Buddha seated upon a lion throne in the Lotus Treasury, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; in each of those worlds, within ten billion Jambudvīpas, it was likewise so.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he saw that in each of the ten directions there was a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, coming to where the Buddha was—namely, Mañjuśrī and others, up to Bhadramukha.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come—ranging from the Golden World to the World of True Color—each of them practiced the pure conduct of brahmacarya in their respective homelands before Buddhas ranging from Immovable Wisdom Buddha to Subduer of Enmity Wisdom Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, being present in all places, spoke in verse:
"Detached from the pleasures of gods and humans, Always practicing the mind of great compassion,
Rescuing and protecting all living beings— This is his pure and wondrous karma."
Always placing faith in the Tathāgata, their minds do not regress;
never abandoning mindfulness of the Buddhas—this is their pure and wondrous karma.
Forever leaving the ocean of birth and death, they do not retreat from the flow of the Buddha-dharma.
Abiding well in the wisdom of cool serenity— this is their pure and wondrous karma.
Amidst the four modes of physical deportment, contemplating the Buddha’s profound virtues day and night without interruption— this is their pure and wondrous karma.
Knowing the immeasurability of the three periods of time, one does not give rise to a mind of indolence;
constantly seeking the merits of the Buddha—this is that pure and wondrous karma.
Contemplating the body according to its true mark, one sees that all things are utterly quiescent.
Free from attachment to self and non-self— this is that pure and wondrous karma.
Observing the minds of sentient beings and remaining far removed from false conceptions,
thereby accomplishing the realm of reality— this is that pure and wondrous karma.
Able to weigh immeasurable lands, And drink the entirety of all oceans;
Having accomplished the wisdom of supernormal powers— Such is their pure and wondrous karma.
They calculate the number of all Buddha-lands, Whether they possess form and characteristics or lack them.
All things, without exception, are exhausted; this is their pure and wondrous karma.
The atoms within immeasurable Buddha-lands, with each atom representing a single Buddha— to be able to know their number entirely; this is their pure and wondrous karma.
At that time, the light passed beyond ten thousand worlds and illuminated a hundred thousand worlds in the eastern direction; it was likewise so for all directions up to the zenith.
Within each of those worlds, everything contained—from the ten billion Jambudvīpas up to the ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens—was fully manifested.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, being present everywhere, spoke in verse:

“If one seeks to see the Tamer of Men By means of the great supernatural power of form-nature, This is the inverted vision of one with cataracts; Such a person does not recognize the most supreme Dharma.”
The physical color, form, and marks of the Tathāgata’s body cannot be beheld by anyone in any world;
even if one were to attempt to measure them for billions of nayutas of kalpas, his wondrous color and majestic power would never reach their limit.
One does not take the marks and signs as the Tathāgata; The dharma of nirvana is signless and free from signs.
Possessing all-encompassing wondrous realms, He manifests them all according to what is appropriate.
The true Dharma of all Buddhas is immeasurable; none can analyze or describe its characteristics.
The true Dharma of all Buddhas neither joins nor disperses; its nature is fundamentally and eternally quiescent.
One does not regard the aggregates as the Tathāgata; far removed from grasping at signs, one observes reality.
Having attained the power of mastery and the definitive vision, the path of speech is cut off and the sphere of activity ceases.
Equally observing that body and mind have no distinct characteristics, All things, internal and external, are entirely liberated;
For immeasurable billions of eons, there is no dualistic thought; The Sugata is profound and far-reaching, free from all attachment.
Universally emitting wondrous light, It shines throughout the realms of the world.
With pure eyes and all-encompassing wisdom, The profound and vast meaning is sovereign.
The one can become the immeasurable, And the immeasurable can become the one.
Knowing the natures of all sentient beings, they accord with them in every place.
Their bodies come from nowhere and go nowhere;
they are illusory and not real, yet they manifest in various forms.
All worlds arise from false conceptualization;
these phenomena of false conceptualization have never had an inherent nature.
Such is the true mark, which only a Buddha can fully realize.
"If one can know in this way, then one sees the Teacher.

Within each of those worlds, everything from the ten billion Jambudvīpas up to the ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens was manifested in its entirety.

The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come—ranging from the Golden World to the World of True Color—each purified their brahma-conduct in the presence of Buddhas, from Immovable Wisdom Buddha to Subduer of Enmity Wisdom Buddha, within their respective native realms.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, being present everywhere, spoke in verse:
"The Most Victorious One, the Self-Awakened, transcends the world; Independent and extraordinary, none can surpass him.
The Great Sage transforms and delivers all beings, Fully endowed with pure and wondrous merits."
His mind is unstained and without location; He dwells eternally in non-conceptuality, without dependence.
Forever abiding in auspiciousness, he cannot be destroyed— The majestic, venerable, and Great Teacher.
From primordial purity and luminosity, all darkness is extinguished; Forever free from all defilements, it is without dust or impurity.
Tranquil and unmoving, it is free from the perception of extremes; This is called skillfully entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Desiring to enter the profound Dharma-ocean of the Sugata, One should distance oneself from the false imaginings of body and mind;
Understanding the true nature of all phenomena, One shall never again follow a mind of doubt.
The realm of all Tathāgatas throughout all worlds is able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
yet within the self-nature of phenomena there is nothing to be turned—thus the Unsurpassed Teacher teaches through skillful means.
Thoroughly understanding all phenomena without doubt, forever free from the delusions of existence and non-existence,
giving rise to no conceptual thoughts of differentiation, they correctly contemplate the Buddha’s bodhi with right intention.
When discerning all phenomena with clear understanding, they lack intrinsic nature and are spoken of as mere conventional designations;
following the true teaching of the Buddhas, phenomena possess neither a single characteristic nor many.
Among the manifold dharmas there is not a single characteristic; within a single dharma there are likewise no many.
If one can thus comprehend all dharmas, this is knowing the immeasurable virtues of the Buddhas.
Observing all phenomena and sentient beings, The world of lands is entirely quiescent;
With a mind that has no dependence and is free from conceptualization, This is called the right mindfulness of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Sentient beings, all phenomena, and the lands— To discern and understand them as being without distinction,
And to skillfully observe them as they are in their true nature, Is to understand the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, being present everywhere, spoke in verse:
"Great wisdom is immeasurable; The wondrous Dharma is peerless.
It is ultimately able to deliver others Across the great ocean shore of birth and death."
His lifespan has no end, and he is forever free from the blazing fires of affliction;
having accomplished great merit, this is the power of skillful means.
Regarding the profound Dharma of all Buddhas, he awakens to it in accordance with its very nature.
Constantly contemplating the dharmas of the three periods of time, they do not give rise to thoughts of contentment;
thoroughly understanding the objects of perception, they never give rise to deluded imaginings.
That joy is inconceivable—this is the power of skillful means.
He constantly delights in observing sentient beings, yet has no perception of a "sentient being";
he manifests the pursuit of physical forms, yet is forever free from the perception of any realm of existence;
within, he constantly delights in meditative stillness, yet has no perception of attachment.
That mind is without attachment; this is the power of skillful means.
Skillfully observing with wisdom, one clearly understands the characteristics of all phenomena;
with focused mindfulness and right reflection, one constantly practices the nature of nirvana.
Delighting in the path of liberation, endowed with impartial wisdom,
and abiding in the dharma of cessation— this is the power of skillful means.
Following the Tamer of Men, one attains the most supreme Buddha-enlightenment.
Embracing all-knowledge, as vast as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
skillfully entering the true reality and teaching and transforming all living beings—
that they achieve the most supreme intention is the power of skillful means (upāya-bala).
The Buddha has taught the profound meaning of the Dharma; they are able to understand it in full accordance with it.
Entering deep and vast wisdom, they eliminate all obstacles.
Regarding the paths that lead to every destination, they are able to reach them all.
Practice is the path of self-awakening; this is the power of skillful means.
The mind is like the realm of empty space, and also like the nature of transformative manifestations.
It is the fundamental nature upon which all things depend; these characteristics are, in truth, no characteristics at all.
Practicing within the nature of nirvāṇa, which is like the characteristic of empty space, one is able to reach the profound and wondrous realm; this is the power of skillful means.
Constantly maintaining mindfulness day and night, one counts the days, the new and full moons, and the passage of the sun and moon.
The divisions of years, seasons, and kalpas, as well as the characteristics of the beginning,
end, formation, and destruction of all worlds, he knows through observation;
he understands them all with perfect clarity— this is the power of skillful means.
All classes of living beings, according to their karma, undergo birth and death—
whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception;
he knows with perfect clarity the names and titles of each, and the destinies to which they go.
To attain this inconceivable state is the power of skillful means.
Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present,
one should follow what the Buddha has taught, observing them with right mindfulness and careful discernment.
"Awakening to the equality of the three periods of time,
just as their true nature is— this is the profound and wondrous path, possessed of peerless power of skillful means. At that time,
the light passed beyond one hundred million worlds, illuminating ten billion worlds in the eastern direction, and likewise throughout the zenith.

"Upholding the dharma of difficult practices, Firm and never regressing,
Always diligent day and night, Never giving rise to weariness."
Having already crossed the sea that is so difficult to cross, I let out the great lion’s roar:
"All classes of sentient beings, I shall now deliver them all.
They are tossed and driven upon the current of birth and death, sinking and wallowing in the ocean of craving and desire."
Delusion and confusion form a heavy web; in the darkness there is great terror.
The steadfast man who is free from pride can completely sever them all.
With transcendent valor he becomes a Hero of the World—this is the realm of the Buddha.
Those in the world who are heedless remain long deluded and intoxicated by the five desires;
their unreal proliferation of false conceptions forever constitutes an obstacle to great suffering.
Diligently cultivate heedfulness and practice all the teachings of the Buddhas.
The great vow can deliver others; this is the realm of the Buddha.
The wise extinguish the primal limit through immeasurable and hard-to-perceive kalpas.
Sentient beings rely on the self and revolve in endless birth and death.
Causing them to enter the dharma of quiescent extinction, And practicing the most supreme teaching;
vowing to proclaim this wondrous dharma— This is the realm of the Buddha.
Seeing those suffering sentient beings, Orphaned, destitute, and without protection,
Forever submerged in the various evil realms, The three poisons constantly blaze;
In the Avīci hell, where there is no rescue, They are perpetually consumed by fire day and night.
Vowing to deliver them from such suffering— This is the realm of the Buddha.
Deluded and having lost the true path, they practice various deviant ways;
seeing those multitudes of living beings dwelling long in great darkness,
he manifests the lamp of wisdom so that they may see all the Buddha-dharmas.
I vow to be able to provide illumination; this is the realm of the Buddha.
Within the ocean of the three realms of existence, deep and vast without limit or bottom, I see those multitudes of sentient beings drifting and drowning, unable to find rescue.
For their sake, he diligently applies skillful means, constructing the ship of the True Dharma to universally rescue all who are to be saved; this is the realm of the Buddha.
Lacking any vision of fundamental reality, they constantly abide in dependence upon ignorance.
Sunk in the abyss of birth and death, their minds bewildered by ignorance,
the wise perceive this suffering and construct for them a bridge of Dharma;
through great compassion they expound the teaching— this is the realm of the Buddha.
Beholding that prison of birth and death, its agonizing torments beyond measure,
where throughout the long night of old age, sickness, and death, the three sufferings compete to assail and oppress;
having personally awakened to the profound and wondrous Dharma, one should single-mindedly cultivate the wisdom of skillful means.
Vowing to deliver these beings from suffering—this is the realm of the Buddha.
Hearing the Buddha’s most profound Dharma, they possess faith free from doubt;
filling the lands of the ten directions, they universally traverse all realms of phenomena.
"Observing the dharma of emptiness and stillness, his mind is free from fear;
manifesting in forms identical to all beings—he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

Following and discerning with knowledge, They thoroughly comprehend the aspect of suchness.

was able to enter profound meditative concentrations, and observed the true meaning of reality.
Causing all the multitudes to rejoice and turn toward the Tathāgata,
the Bodhisattva practices this Dharma and swiftly attains the Unsurpassed Way;
able to inquire of the Buddhas of the ten directions, his mind remains ever serene.
With faith in the Buddha, one does not regress; all dignified deportments are fully perfected.
Regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, one thoroughly realizes them to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Observing correctly in this manner, one is able to see the true Buddha.
With a mind of immeasurable purity and bliss, pervading the realms throughout the ten directions,
you are able to expound the true meaning within all lands;
having extinguished the afflictions and hardships of the multitudes, you abide securely in the Dharma of equality.
If one can transform others in this way, such a person is equal to the Tathāgata.
Hearing the Buddha’s wondrous voice, they attain the unsurpassed Dharma;
they constantly turn the pure wheel of Dharma, which is profoundly deep and difficult to perceive.
The Dharma taught by the Most Victorious One is fully endowed with the meaning of the seven factors of enlightenment;
through such unsurpassed contemplation, one constantly beholds the bodies of all Buddhas.
One does not perceive the Tathāgata as empty, for his quiescent extinction is like an illusion.
Though seeing, there is nothing seen, like a blind person facing the five colors;
those who grasp at signs through delusion do not see the Buddha.
Only when one is entirely free from attachment does one behold the True Tathāgata.
The various karmas of sentient beings are difficult to distinguish and know;
Their bodies, internal and external throughout the ten directions, appear in all manner of infinite forms.
The Buddha’s body is likewise: it fills all the ten directions.
One who can know that which is difficult to know is a Great Guide.
Just as immeasurable lands abide supported by space,
neither coming from the ten directions nor going anywhere when they depart.
Whether the world is formed or destroyed, it fundamentally has nothing upon which to rely;
the Buddha-body is likewise, filling the entire realm of empty space.

Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva’s Clarification of Difficulties *The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva’s Clarification of Difficulties At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Bodhisattva Vijñānottama:
“O Son of the Buddha!
The nature of the mind is one; how can it produce various karmic retributions, such as leading to the happy realms or leading to the evil realms?”
Some possess all their faculties while others do not;
some are born in favorable realms while others are born in unfavorable realms;
some are handsome while others are ugly; and they differ in their experiences of suffering and happiness.
Karma does not know the mind, and the mind does not know karma;
sensation does not know retribution, and retribution does not know sensation;
the mind does not know sensation, and sensation does not know the mind.
"Because the cause does not know the condition, and the condition does not know the cause;
because wisdom does not know phenomena, and phenomena do not know wisdom?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment replied in verse:
“Because you seek to transform sentient beings, you are able to inquire about this meaning:
the true nature of all phenomena as it is. Listen attentively as I explain it to you.
All phenomena lack self-mastery; when sought for their reality, they cannot be found.”
Therefore, among all phenomena, the two are mutually unaware of one another.
Just as a swift-flowing stream flows on and on without ceasing,
yet the two [aspects of the flow] are mutually unaware of each other, so too are all phenomena.
Just as the flame of a bright lamp flickers on and on without a moment's pause,
yet these two do not know one another, so too are all phenomena.
Just as a long wind arises, fanning and sweeping to produce the power of movement, so it is with all things.
The two do not know each other; all phenomena are likewise so.
Just as the deep and vast earth supports one another through mutual dependence, yet the two do not know each other, so too are all phenomena.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties—through these various sufferings are produced, yet in reality there is nothing produced.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without production; it is through manifestation that production appears.
In that state, there is no manifestation, and what is manifested has no existence.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties— their nature is entirely empty and quiescent; they are false and devoid of reality.
Observing with right reflection, one sees that what exists is non-existent;
such a vision is not inverted because the Dharma-eye is purified.
Whether it be false or not false, real or unreal—
"Both the mundane and the supramundane are nothing but provisional designations.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Vasumitra Bodhisattva:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

All sentient beings are, in truth, not sentient beings; how then does the Tathāgata teach and transform them according to their time, their lifespan, their bodies, their conduct, their inclinations, their vows, their intentions, their skillful means, their reflections, their deliberations, and their perceptions?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhanaśrī replied in verse:
“The realm of the mind of clear wisdom Is always joyful in the practice of quiescence.
I shall now speak according to reality; O virtuous one, listen well and attentively.”
Contemplating the internal body through analysis, one asks: "What does my body possess?
If one can contemplate in this way, they will realize the existence or non-existence of the self.
Examining every part of the body, one finds that nothing exists as a basis for support.
One who clearly understands this body has no attachment to the body.
Being able to comprehend the body as it truly is, they penetrate all phenomena with clarity;
knowing that all phenomena are entirely illusory, their mind remains unstained.
Body and life follow one another, revolving in mutual dependence like a whirling firebrand; their beginning and end cannot be known.
The wise are able to observe that all things are impermanent.
All phenomena are empty and selfless, thus free from all marks.
Actions arising from causes and conditions are without self, like a dream;
their nature as karmic retribution is quiescent, with no difference between before and after.
All phenomena of the world have the mind alone as their master;
those who grasp at signs according to their desires are entirely in error.
All phenomena that exist in the world are entirely false and illusory.
One cannot understand that all phenomena Are truly without duality.
All phenomena of arising and ceasing Arise entirely from conditions;
moment by moment they swiftly return to extinction, Without any difference between their beginning and end.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Since the four great elements of all sentient beings are entirely neither 'I' nor 'mine,' why is it that sentient beings experience suffering or pleasure, perform evil or good deeds, are beautiful within or without, receive small or great retributions, and have retributions either in the present life or in future lives, while the nature of all phenomena is neither good nor evil?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī replied in verse:
"Whatever karma one performs, The fruit and retribution received will likewise be so.
There is no agent who creates it; Thus have all Buddhas taught."
Just as a bright and clear mirror reflects the image of a face according to its presence, yet possesses nothing within or without, so too is the nature of karma.
It is also like seeds in a field; each remains distinct and does not know the others.
Spontaneously acting as a cause, the nature of karma is likewise so.
Just as a great illusionist at a crossroads manifests various forms, the nature of karma is likewise so.
Just as a craftsman constructs a wooden figure that can produce various sounds,
yet it has neither a self nor a non-self, so too is the nature of karma.
It is also like various species of birds, which produce different calls upon emerging from their shells.
It can produce various kinds of sounds, and the nature of karma is likewise.
Just as through the convergence of proximate causes and conditions one undergoes birth yet there is no one who comes,
and the various faculties are each distinct, so too is the nature of karma.
Just as in the great hells, sentient beings undergo suffering and affliction;
yet this suffering has no place of origin, and the nature of karma is likewise so.
It is also like a universal monarch who has perfected the seven supreme jewels.
They come from nowhere, and the nature of karma is likewise.
Just as all worlds undergo formation or destruction,
yet in their formation and destruction there is no coming or going, so too is the nature of karma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Śrīmatī, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata awakens to only a single dharma; how is it that he speaks of immeasurable dharmas, such that his voice pervades immeasurable worlds, is able to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings, produces immeasurable sounds, manifests immeasurable bodies, thoroughly knows the mentalities of immeasurable sentient beings, displays immeasurable sovereign powers of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*), reveals immeasurable and boundless worlds, manifests immeasurable and supreme adornments, and displays immeasurable varieties of realms—yet in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such distinctions are truly unobtainable?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Virtue Chief answered in verse:
“The Son of the Buddha is able to inquire Into this most profound and subtle meaning;
If the wise should understand this, They will always delight in seeking merit.”
Just as the nature of earth is one, yet can support all manner of things without discriminating between unity and difference, so too are the qualities of all Buddhas.
Just as the nature of fire is one, yet can burn the things of the world...
The nature of fire is without discrimination; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as when the waters of a hundred rivers pour into the great ocean, their taste remains no different; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as the nature of wind is one, Blowing and moving all things,
yet the nature of wind is without discrimination— Such is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Just as when a dragon’s thunder rolls, It rains everywhere upon the earth;
As raindrops are without discrimination, so too are the dharmas of all Buddhas.
Just as the great earth is one, yet can produce various kinds of sprouts,
while the nature of the earth remains without distinction, so too are the dharmas of all Buddhas.
Just as the sun, unobscured by clouds, Is able to illuminate the ten directions universally,
And its radiance possesses no diverse nature, So too are the dharmas of all Buddhas.
Just like the moon in the sky, There is none in the world who does not see it.
Not reaching every single place, such is the nature of all Buddhas' dharmas.
Just as the Great Brahmā King universally manifests throughout the great trichiliocosm,
yet his body remains without distinction, such is the nature of all Buddhas' dharmas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Since the Tathāgata’s field of merit is equal and without distinction, why do the fruits and rewards of giving differ?"

There are various complexions, various dispositions, various lineages, various faculties, various wealths, various wonders, various retinues, various sovereignties, various merits, and various wisdoms; yet the Tathāgata is impartial toward them all, having neither enemy nor friend?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mūrdhaja replied in verse:
"Just as the great earth, though one, Can produce all manner of sprouts,
Without partiality toward enemy or friend— So too is the Buddha-field of merit."
Just as water has but one taste, yet differs according to the vessel,
so the field of merit of all Buddhas is one, yet appears diverse because of sentient beings.
Just as a great master of illusions can cause the multitude to rejoice, so too do the Buddhas manifest various forms for the sake of beings.
The Buddhas are the holy field of merit; according to one's vows, they cause joy to arise.
Just as the King of Eloquence can bring delight to the multitude, so too do the Buddhas, the holy field of merit, cause all sentient beings to rejoice.
Just as a clear and bright mirror reflects various images according to what is before it,
so do the Buddhas— the holy field of merit— appear differently according to sentient beings.
Just as the Great King of Medicines eliminates all poisons, [so does the Buddha eliminate all afflictions].
The Buddhas are the holy field of merit, capable of extinguishing the afflictions of suffering.
Just as when the sun rises, it can dispel all darkness,
so too do the Buddhas, the holy field of merit, universally illuminate the realms of the ten directions.
Just as the pure full moon universally illuminates the four continents,
The Buddhas, the holy field of merit, are impartial and free from partiality.
Just as the Vairambha wind shakes all the earth,
The holy field of merit of all Buddhas can shake the existence of the three realms;
like when the fire of the kalpa arises, there is no heaven or earth that is not consumed by it.
The holy field of merit of all Buddhas can burn away all forms of existence.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Jinshou:
"Son of the Buddha!
Do sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata as teaching the severance of all afflictions?"

Is it by knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; and delusion and craving, that one severs all afflictions?

If one knows form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, delusion, and craving, and thereby severs all afflictions, what increase or decrease would there be in the Tathāgata’s teaching?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jinshou replied in verse:
"O Son of the Buddha, listen well and attentively as I explain the meaning according to reality:
there are those for whom there is a swift path to liberation, and there are those for whom liberation is difficult to attain."
If one wishes to eliminate immeasurable faults and evils,
one should at all times exert great and courageous diligence.
Just as a tiny fire is extinguished when the firewood is wet, [so too are faults quenched by such effort].
Within the teachings of the Buddha, so it is with those who are indolent.
It is like a person drilling for fire; if they rest several times before the fire has emerged, the heat will cease and the fire will be extinguished—so it is with the indolent.
Just as one who seeks fire from a pure fire-gem While remaining apart from its conditions will never find it,
So too is the case with the indolent. Just as one might close their eyes while seeking to see forms In the bright, clear sun, [so too is the case with the indolent].
Within the teachings of the Buddha, so it is with those who are indolent.
It is like a man without hands or feet who wishes to shoot arrows across the great earth;
his intent will never be fulfilled, and so it is with the indolent.
Just as one might seek to exhaust the waters of the great ocean with a single drop from a hair,
so too are those who are indolent regarding the Buddha’s teachings.
It is like wishing to extinguish the conflagration at the end of an eon with a mere handful of water.
Within the teachings of the Buddha, so it is with those who are indolent.
It is like a person who, seeing the empty sky, says, "My body fills it.
Within the teachings of the Buddha, so it is with those who are indolent.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Dharmottara:
"Son of the Buddha!

As the Buddha has taught, those who hear and receive the Dharma are able to sever their afflictions (*kleśa*). How is it that sentient beings, upon hearing the True Dharma, are unable to sever these defiled states—namely, following lust, anger, and ignorance; following pride, attachment, resentment, stinginess and jealousy, hatred, and crookedness—and yet these various impurities do not leave their minds, and while their minds have no [wholesome] activity, they are able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*)?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmottara replied in verse:
"O Son of the Buddha, listen well and attentively to the true meaning of what you have asked.
It is not merely by accumulating much learning that one can enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata."
It is like a person being swept away by water, who dies of thirst while fearing drowning;
so it is with much learning when one cannot practice as taught.
It is like a person who gives great gifts of all kinds of delicacies.
One who does not eat and starves to death—so it is with one who has heard much.
It is like a skilled physician who thoroughly knows all prescriptions and medicines, yet cannot cure his own illness; so it is with one who has heard much.
Just as a poor man, day and night counting another's treasures, possesses not even half a coin for himself; so too is it with much learning.
Just as a prince of a universal monarch ought to enjoy boundless bliss, [so should the one who has realized the Dharma].
Due to karmic obstructions, one suffers in poverty; so it is with those who have heard much [but lack realization].
Like a deaf person who skillfully performs various melodies—pleasing others but not hearing them for themselves—so it is with those who have heard much.
Just as a blind man, though unable to see for himself, can paint because of his prior training;
so too is it with those who have heard much. Just as a sea captain can ferry across immeasurable multitudes, so too is it with those who have heard much.
To rescue others while unable to save oneself—much learning is also like this.
It is like a person standing in a great assembly who eloquently speaks of sublime and wondrous matters, yet within possesses no true virtue; much learning is also like this.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī, saying:
"Son of the Buddha!

Within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is foremost. For what reason does the Tathāgata sometimes praise for the sake of sentient beings the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, prajñā-pāramitā, as well as loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā)—each of these individual dharmas being unable, on its own, to attain unsurpassed bodhi?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī replied in verse:
"That which is difficult to know, yet can be known, In accordance with the minds of sentient beings—
Regarding the meaning of what the Son of the Buddha has asked, Listen attentively as I now explain."
In the past and future ages, as well as among the present Guides,
none have ever attained the Unsurpassed Way by means of even a single dharma.
The Tathāgata knows the inherent nature and the practices cultivated by sentient beings.
For those who are well-suited for deliverance, he preaches the pure and wondrous Dharma:
to the stingy, he praises giving; to those who violate the prohibitions, he praises upholding the precepts;
to the angry, he praises patience; and to the indolent, he praises diligence.
To praise meditative concentration while the mind is distracted; To praise wisdom while one is ignorant and deluded;
To praise loving-kindness while lacking benevolence; To praise great compassion while harboring anger and malice;
To praise sympathetic joy while filled with sorrow and grief; To praise equanimity while still bound by hatred and attachment.
One who practices in this way gradually understands all phenomena.
Just as when constructing a palace, one first establishes a firm foundation,
so too are generosity and ethical discipline the basis for all the practices of a bodhisattva.

Just as a firm and solid city defends against all enemies and hardships, so too do patience and diligence protect all bodhisattvas. Just as a king of great power brings peace to the world through his majestic virtue, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva bring peace to the world through his majestic virtue. Just as a powerful physician dispels all diseases, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dispel all afflictions. Just as a great leader guides all beings to safety, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva guide all beings to the safety of Nirvāṇa. Just as a great ship carries many people across the sea, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva carry many beings across the ocean of birth and death. Just as a great cloud rains down upon the world, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva rain down the Dharma upon the world. Just as a great wind blows away all dust, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva blow away all the dust of afflictions. Just as a great fire burns away all grasses and trees, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva burn away all the grasses and trees of afflictions. Just as a great flood washes away all mud and filth, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wash away all the mud and filth of afflictions. Just as a great mountain is immovable and stable, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva immovable and stable in the presence of all afflictions. Just as the great ocean contains immeasurable jewels, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contain immeasurable roots of goodness. Just as the great earth supports all living beings, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva support all living beings. Just as the great sun illuminates the world, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva illuminate the world with the light of wisdom. Just as the great moon cools the world, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cool the world with the light of compassion. Just as the great Brahmā King rules over the heavens, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva rule over the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples. Just as the great Śakra King protects the gods, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protect all sentient beings. Just as the great Māra King rules over the realm of desire, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva rule over the realm of all dharmas. Just as the great Nirvāṇa extinguishes all fires, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva extinguish all the fires of affliction. Just as the great Dharma-realm is vast and boundless, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva vast and boundless in his practice of the path. Just as the great Samādhi is profound and tranquil, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva profound and tranquil in his mind. Just as the great Prajñā is sharp and penetrating, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sharp and penetrating in his wisdom. Just as the great Liberation is free from all bonds, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva free from all bonds of affliction. Just as the great Tathāgata is the supreme among all beings, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva the supreme among all bodhisattvas. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of these various skillful means, brings peace to the world, dispels all afflictions, and leads all sentient beings to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Dhyāna and wisdom are likewise; they bring peace and security to all bodhisattvas.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch fully enjoys every pleasure, so too do the four immeasurables bring peace and happiness to all bodhisattvas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha:
"O Son of the Buddha!
All Buddhas attain liberation from birth and death through the Single Vehicle alone; why then do we now see that all Buddha-fields differ in every respect?"
That is to say:

the world, sentient beings, the teaching of the Dharma, the transformation of others, lifespan, radiance, spiritual powers, assemblies, the Buddha-dharma, and the duration of the Dharma—all such matters are entirely different; yet there is none among them who does not possess all Buddha-dharmas and is able to achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse:
“The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is always thus: The Dharma-King has but a single Dharma.
All those who are unimpeded Transcend birth and death by means of this one path.”
The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body;
their single mind and single wisdom, as well as their powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise one.
According to the fundamental practices of sentient beings, they seek unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha-fields and their assemblies, and the teachings they proclaim, are all different.
Yet all Buddha-fields are equally and universally adorned and pure;
it is because the karmic actions of sentient beings differ that what they perceive varies from one to another.
The Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma cannot be seen by sentient beings;
so too it is with the assemblies of the Dharma-body in the Buddha-fields and their preaching of the Dharma.
Their original practices were vast and pure, fully accomplishing all vows.
That person perceives reality, a wise one possessing clear insight and vision.
In accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, they cause each to perceive reality regarding all karmas and their retributions; this is due to the sovereign power of the Buddha.
The Buddha-fields have no differing characteristics, and the Tathāgata has neither hatred nor affection;
according to the conduct of those sentient beings, they themselves obtain such a vision.
It is not the fault of all Buddhas, nor of the Teacher who dwells in peace.
In immeasurable worlds, various manifestations appear differently.
In all worlds, those who are ready to be transformed always behold the Hero among Men; such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma.
At that time, the bodhisattvas said to Mañjuśrī, “Son of the Buddha!
We have each explained what we understand. Your eloquence is profound; it is now your turn to expound: what is the realm of the Buddha?”
What is the cause of the Buddha’s realm?
What is that which enters the Buddha’s realm?
What is that which is delivered within the Buddha’s realm?
What is the knowledge that accords with the Buddha’s realm?
What is the dharma that accords with the Buddha’s realm?
What is the discerning knowledge of the Buddha’s realm?
What is the consciousness that perceives the Buddha’s realm?
What is the definitive knowledge of the Buddha’s realm?
What is the illumination of the Buddha’s realm?
"What is the vastness of the Buddha’s realm?
At that time, Mañjuśrī replied in verse:
"The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space."
All sentient beings enter it, yet in truth there is nothing entered.
This cause of the Tathāgata’s realm can only be discerned by a Buddha;
even throughout immeasurable kalpas, others could not exhaustively expound upon it.
In accordance with sentient beings, they enter all worlds;
their wisdom is ever tranquil, unlike what is perceived by the world.
To deliver all living beings, they accord with the faculties and minds of those beings.
Proclaimed and expounded without end, this is solely the realm of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata’s omniscience is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time;
the wondrous realm of all Buddhas is entirely like empty space.
The Dharma-realm has no marks of difference; it is taught in accordance with sentient beings.
If one wishes to analyze it in full detail, that is solely the domain of the Buddha.
Throughout all worlds, there are immeasurable varieties of sounds.
He fully understands all things according to their timing, yet in reality there is no discrimination.
It cannot be known by consciousness, nor is it the domain of the mind;
its self-nature is truly pure, and he is able to reveal it to all living beings.
Neither karma nor afflictions, Tranquil and abiding nowhere;
Without ignorance and without activity, They move through the world with equanimity.
The minds of all sentient beings Pervasively exist throughout the three periods of time.
"In a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata fully and clearly understands all things.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the sentient beings of this Sahā world saw all the sentient beings in this buddha-field: their practiced dharmas, their performed karmas, their worldly conduct, their conduct according to their bodies, their conduct according to their faculties, the places where they were born as a result of their karma, whether they upheld the precepts or violated them, and the fruits of their preaching the Dharma—all such matters within this world, they saw them all completely.

In this way, throughout the hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds in the eastern direction—worlds that are immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, peerless, boundless, limitless, and unspeakably vast as space and the dharma-realm—one sees all of them, even unto the fruits of their preaching of the Dharma;
and it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Five;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: On Pure Conduct.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!

How does a bodhisattva possess bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are unstained; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are non-harming; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are non-deluded; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are non-regressive; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are immovable; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are praiseworthy; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are pure; bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are free from afflictions; and bodily, vocal, and mental actions that accord with wisdom?
What are the bodhisattva’s accomplishments regarding place of birth, lineage, family, physical marks, mindfulness, wisdom, course of rebirth, fearlessness, and awakening?

What is the bodhisattva’s foremost wisdom, supreme wisdom, excellent wisdom, most excellent wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, incalculable wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, and ineffable wisdom?

What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of causes, the power of intention, the power of skillful means, the power of conditions, the power of the objective sphere, the power of the faculties, the power of tranquility and insight, and the power of meditative concentration?

How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; skillfully know the law of dependent origination; skillfully know the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; and skillfully know the past, future, and present?
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?

How does a bodhisattva fulfill the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?

How does a bodhisattva attain the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible; the power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma in the past, future, and present; the power of knowledge regarding the various faculties; the power of knowledge regarding the various dispositions; the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations; the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations; the power of knowledge regarding the defilement and purification of dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; the power of unimpeded knowledge regarding past lives; the power of unimpeded knowledge regarding the divine eye; and the power of knowledge regarding the severing of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies?
How is it that a bodhisattva is constantly protected, revered, and made offerings to by the various celestial kings;

and how is he protected, revered, and made offerings to by the dragon kings, the ghost kings, the gandharva kings, the asura kings, the garuḍa kings, the kiṃnara kings, the mahoraga kings, human kings, and Brahmā kings?
How is it that a bodhisattva serves as a shelter for sentient beings, as a rescue, as a refuge, as a destination, as a torch, as illumination, as a lamp, as a guide, and as an unsurpassed guide?
How is it that a bodhisattva is the foremost among all sentient beings, the greatest,
the most excellent,
and the supreme?
Is it unsurpassed?
Is it unequaled? Is it equal to the unequaled?
At that time, Mañjuśrī replied to the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
O Son of the Buddha!
You have asked about such a meaning for the sake of great benefit and great peace, out of compassion for the world, to bestow advantage upon all, and to bring happiness to gods and humans.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes the actions of body, speech, and mind, they are able to attain all supreme and wondrous merits;
regarding the True Dharma of the Buddha, their mind is free from all hindrances.
They are able to turn the wheel of Dharma turned by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present in accordance with it;
they do not abandon sentient beings, clearly penetrating the true mark of reality;
they sever all evils and are fully endowed with all virtues.
Their physical forms and appearances were foremost, being entirely like those of the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
they had accomplished the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes and attained complete mastery over all phenomena, serving as the second honored guides for sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What kinds of actions of body, speech, and mind can bring about all supreme and wondrous merits?
'When a Bodhisattva is at home, they should wish that all sentient beings abandon the hardships of the household life.'"
Entering into the dharma of emptiness, one serves one's parents with filial piety; may all beings provide protection and nourishment for all, forever attaining great peace.
When gathering with one's wife and children, one should wish that all sentient beings may escape the prison of craving and be free from longing and attachment.
When obtaining the five desires, one should wish that all sentient beings may abandon greed and delusion,
becoming fully endowed with merit.
If among music and entertainment, may all beings attain the joy of the Dharma and perceive all phenomena as like illusions.
If in a private chamber, may all beings enter the stage of the noble ones and forever leave behind the defilement of desire.
When putting on precious necklaces, one should wish that all beings cast off their heavy burdens and cross over from the shores of existence and non-existence.
When ascending a multi-storied pavilion, one should wish that all beings ascend the hall of the Buddha-Dharma and attain the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
When giving away what is most cherished, one should wish that all sentient beings relinquish everything, their minds free from greedy attachment.
When in a gathering, one should wish that all sentient beings achieve ultimate liberation and reach the abode of the Tathāgata.
If one is in peril or distress, one should wish that all sentient beings may have mastery over their own will and be free from all obstructions.
Having left the home life out of faith, one should wish that all sentient beings may abandon worldly affairs and have no attachments in their minds.
If entering a monastery, one should wish that all sentient beings may be in complete harmony,
their minds free from all obstructions.
When approaching teachers, whether great or small, one should wish that all sentient beings may open the gate of skillful means and penetrate deeply into the essential teachings of the Dharma.
When seeking the method of leaving the household life, one should wish that all sentient beings attain non-retrogression and have minds free from obstruction.
When casting off secular clothing, one should wish that all sentient beings understand the Way and cultivate virtue,
never again succumbing to indolence.
When shaving off the beard and hair, may all sentient beings sever their afflictions and attain ultimate quiescence.
When donning the kashaya robe, may all sentient beings cast off the three poisons and their minds find joy.
Upon receiving the dharma of renunciation, may all beings, like the Buddha’s renunciation,
guide and enlighten all.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings penetrate deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings lead and govern the great assembly,
free from all obstacles.
When upholding the pure precepts, one should wish that all beings fully cultivate and train in all precepts.
When practicing the prohibitions of the Path, one should wish that all beings be fully endowed with the precepts of the Path and practice deeds according to reality.
When first requesting an upādhyāya, may all beings attain the wisdom of non-arising and reach the other shore.
Upon receiving full ordination, may all beings attain the supreme, wondrous Dharma and perfect skillful means.
When entering a room or dwelling, one should wish that all beings ascend the unsurpassed hall and attain the dharma of non-retrogression.
When spreading out a bed or seat, one should wish that all beings spread the seat of wholesome dharmas and perceive the true mark of reality.
Sitting upright with body straight, one should wish that all beings sit beneath the Bodhi tree, their minds free from dependence.
Sitting in the full lotus posture, one should wish that all beings have firm roots of goodness and attain the Immovable Ground.
In the meditative absorption of samādhi, may all beings turn toward the gates of samādhi and attain ultimate concentration.
In observing all phenomena, may all beings see the reality of dharmas without any hindrance.
When relinquishing the cross-legged posture, one should wish that all sentient beings realize the nature of all conditioned phenomena, which ultimately dissolve and perish.
When placing the feet upon the ground after descending from the seat, one should wish that all sentient beings tread the path of the sages,
attaining unshakable liberation.
When first lifting the feet, may all beings transcend birth and death and be fully perfected in wholesome dharmas.
When putting on clothes, may all beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and always know shame and remorse.
Adjusting the robes and tying the sash, one should wish that all beings examine themselves and cultivate the Way,
never destroying wholesome dharmas.
Next, putting on the upper garment, one should wish that all beings attain superior roots of goodness and reach the ultimate, supreme Dharma.
When putting on the saṃghāṭī robe, one should wish that all sentient beings be shielded by great compassion and attain the dharma of immovability.
When holding a willow branch in hand, one should wish that all sentient beings have their minds attain the True Dharma and be naturally pure.
When chewing on a willow branch at dawn, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the taming tusks to devour all afflictions.
When attending to the calls of nature, one should wish that all sentient beings eliminate filth and impurity, becoming free from lust, anger, and ignorance.
Having approached the water, one should wish that all beings turn toward the unsurpassed path and attain the supramundane dharma.
Washing away impurities with water, one should wish that all beings be fully endowed with pure patience and be ultimately free from defilement.
Washing the hands with water, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain most excellent hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Rinsing the mouth and cleansing the teeth, one should wish that all sentient beings turn toward the gates of pure Dharma and attain ultimate liberation.
Holding a mendicant’s staff, may all beings establish pure assemblies of giving and perceive the Path as it truly is.
Carrying an alms bowl, may all beings become perfected vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans.
Setting out upon the path toward the Way, may all beings aspire to the Bodhi of the Buddha and attain ultimate liberation.
If already upon the path, may all beings accomplish the Way of the Buddha, with nothing further to be practiced.
When traveling along a road, one should wish that all beings tread upon the pure Dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction.
When seeing a high road, one should wish that all beings ascend the unsurpassed path and transcend the triple world.
Seeing a downward path, may all beings be humble and gentle, entering the profound Dharma of the Buddha.
Seeing a perilous road, may all beings abandon the evil paths and eliminate false views.
If one sees a straight road, one should wish that all beings attain a mind of central correctness,
such that their bodies and speech are without crookedness.
If one sees a road where dust is stirred up, one should wish that all beings forever leave behind defilement and impurity, becoming ultimately pure.
Seeing the path free from dust, they should wish that all beings be permeated by great compassion, their minds and intentions supple and moistened.
Seeing deep pits and ravines, they should wish that all beings turn toward the true Dharma-realm and eliminate all hardships.
Upon seeing a hall for hearing lawsuits, may all beings wish to expound the most profound Dharma so that all may be in harmony.
Upon seeing a great tree, may all beings wish to be free from the mind of contention and devoid of anger and resentment.
If one sees a grove of trees, one should wish that all sentient beings be honored by all with prostrations,
as the Teacher of Gods and Humans is revered.
If one sees a high mountain, one should wish that all sentient beings attain supreme goodness, such that no one can see its summit.
If one sees thorns and brambles, one should wish that all sentient beings may pull out the thorns of the three poisons and have no heart of malice or harm.
Seeing a tree with lush foliage, one should wish that all sentient beings may shade themselves with the Way and enter the samādhi of dhyāna.
Seeing beautiful flowers on a tree, one should wish that all sentient beings open with purity like these flowers, fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks.
Seeing abundant fruit on a tree, one should wish that all sentient beings initiate the practices of the Bodhi-tree and achieve the unsurpassed fruit.
Seeing flowing streams, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the flow of the True Dharma and enter the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
If seeing pond water, one should wish that all sentient beings fully attain the indestructible True Dharma of all Buddhas.
If one sees a bathing pool, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, their questions and answers being inexhaustible.
Seeing a person drawing water from a well, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the eloquence of the Tathāgata,
which is never-ending.
If one sees a spring of water, one should wish that all beings have inexhaustible roots of goodness and unsurpassed realms.
Seeing mountain streams and waters, one should wish that all beings wash away their defilements and attain the purity of mental liberation.
If one sees a bridge, one should wish that all beings construct the bridge of Dharma,
ferrying across people without ceasing.
If one sees the cultivation of gardens and orchards, one should wish that all beings weed out defilement and evil, so that the roots of desire do not arise.
Upon seeing the Aśoka grove, one should wish that all sentient beings attain joy in their hearts and forever eliminate sorrow and affliction.
Upon seeing a beautiful garden and pond, one should wish that all sentient beings diligently cultivate all manner of goodness and become fully endowed with Bodhi.
Seeing a person in fine adornment, one should wish that all beings adorn themselves with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Seeing a person in plain white clothing, one should wish that all beings ultimately reach the further shore of *dhūta* (ascetic purification).
Seeing those who delight in their aspirations, one should wish that all beings find joy in the pure Dharma and take pleasure in the Way.
Seeing those who are sorrowful and anxious, one should wish that all beings develop a sense of weary detachment toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Seeing those who are joyful, one should wish that all beings attain supreme bliss, serene and free from affliction.
Seeing those who are suffering, one should wish that all beings eliminate all miseries and attain the wisdom of the Buddha.
Seeing those who are strong and healthy, one should wish that all beings obtain a vajra-body, free from decay and senility.
Seeing those who are ill, one should wish that all beings realize the body is empty and quiescent, and be liberated from all suffering.
Seeing a person of handsome appearance, one should wish that all beings joyfully revere all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Seeing a person of ugly appearance, one should wish that all beings distance themselves from base and evil, adorning themselves with virtue.
Upon seeing one who repays kindness, one should wish that all beings always mindfully remember the Buddhas and the benevolent virtues of the Bodhisattvas.
Upon seeing one who betrays kindness, one should wish that all beings always behold the worthy sages and refrain from committing any evil.
If one sees a śramaṇa, one should wish that all beings be tranquil and subdued, reaching ultimate perfection without remainder.
If one sees a brāhmaṇa, one should wish that all beings attain true purity and be free from all evil.
If one sees a seer, one should wish that all beings turn toward the path of true correctness and attain ultimate liberation.
If one sees an ascetic practicing austerities, one should wish that all beings be firm and diligent, never retreating from the Buddha-way.
Seeing those clad in armor, one should wish that all beings vow to don the dharma-armour and attain the teacherless Dharma.
Seeing those without armor or weapons, one should wish that all beings remain far removed from all evils and draw near to wholesome dharmas.
Seeing those who engage in debate, one should wish that all beings attain supreme eloquence and subdue the heterodox.
Seeing those who live by right livelihood, one should wish that all beings attain a pure livelihood, their dignified conduct never wavering.
If you see a sovereign king, you should wish that all beings attain the status of a Dharma King and turn the unimpeded wheel.
If you see a prince, you should wish that all beings tread the path of the Buddha’s sons and be born through transformation within the Dharma.
If you see an elder, you should wish that all beings forever leave behind craving and desire, and deeply understand the Buddha-dharma.
If you see a great minister, you should wish that all beings always attain right mindfulness and cultivate all manner of goodness.
If one sees a city wall, one should wish that all beings attain a vajra-body, their minds indestructible.
If one sees a royal capital, one should wish that all beings be clear-sighted and far-reaching in their illumination, with mastery over merit and virtue.
If one sees exquisite forms, one should wish that all beings obtain supreme and wondrous forms,
praised by devas and humans.
When entering a village to beg for food, one should wish that all beings enter the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), their minds free from obstruction.
Upon entering a person’s gate, one should wish that all beings enter the gate of *dhāraṇī* and behold the teachings of all Buddhas.
Upon entering a person’s hall or chamber, one should wish that all beings enter the Single Buddha Vehicle and clearly comprehend the three periods of time.
When encountering those who find it difficult to uphold the precepts, one should wish that all beings do not abandon any good deeds and forever cross to the other shore.
When seeing those who have forsaken the precepts, one should wish that all beings transcend all hardships and deliver themselves from the three evil realms.
If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all beings have a mind so pure it is empty of afflictions.
If one sees a full bowl, one should wish that all beings be fully endowed with and perfected in all wholesome dharmas.
When obtaining food, one should wish that all beings may make offerings of the Dharma, their resolve fixed upon the Buddha-way.
When not obtaining food, one should wish that all beings may remain far removed from all unwholesome actions.
Seeing those with a sense of shame and remorse, one should wish that all beings practice right conduct with shame and remorse, and bring their faculties under control.
Seeing those without shame or remorse, one should wish that all beings leave behind shamelessness and immodesty, and universally practice great compassion.
When obtaining fragrant and delicious food, one should wish that all sentient beings know moderation and have few desires,
their minds free from attachment.
When obtaining unwholesome food, one should wish that all sentient beings fully accomplish and perfect the *asaṃskāra-samādhi* (the concentration of wishlessness).
Upon obtaining soft and delicate food, one should wish that all sentient beings be permeated by great compassion, their minds and intentions becoming supple and gentle.
Upon obtaining coarse and harsh food, one should wish that all sentient beings forever distance themselves from worldly cravings and flavors.
When swallowing food, may all sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their nourishment and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
Regarding the various flavors of what they eat, may all sentient beings obtain the supreme flavor of the Buddhas, which is transformed into nectar.
When the meal is finished, may all sentient beings be filled with virtuous conduct and achieve the ten powers.
When preaching the Dharma, may all sentient beings attain inexhaustible eloquence and penetrate deeply into the Buddha-dharma.
When withdrawing from one's seat and leaving the hall, one should wish that all beings deeply enter the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.
When entering water, one should wish that all beings deeply enter the Buddha-way and equally penetrate the three periods of time.
When bathing the body, one should wish that all sentient beings have no defilement in body or mind, and possess immeasurable radiance.
