How much more so to receive and uphold it with right mindfulness, to practice according to the teaching, and to attain true understanding!
Even if one were to carry the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system upon one’s head for an entire kalpa without the body moving, [it would not be as difficult as this].
What that person has done is not difficult; it is far more difficult to have faith in this Dharma.

Even if one were to provide all manner of pleasant requisites for as many sentient beings as there are motes of dust in the great trichiliocosm for the duration of an eon, their merit would not be superior; having faith in this Dharma is truly preeminent.
If one were to hold ten Buddha-fields in the palm of their hand and remain suspended in mid-air for an eon, such an act would not be difficult;
far more difficult is it to have faith in this Dharma.
If one were to provide all manner of delightful offerings for as many beings as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields throughout an entire eon, their merit would not be superior;
rather, it is the one who has faith in this Dharma who is truly preeminent.
If one were to reverently make offerings for an entire eon to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields,
the merit of one who can receive and uphold this chapter would be far superior to that.
When the Worthy One had finished preaching this chapter, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways;
the palaces of all Māras became like heaps of ink, while light illuminated the ten directions and the evil realms were extinguished.
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions appear universally before Bhadrapāla;
each extends his right hand to stroke his crown—Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva’s virtue is immeasurable.
Having rubbed the crown of his head with his right hand, all the Tathāgatas praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, true son of the Buddha! It is well that you have so eloquently expounded this Dharma; we rejoice in it.”

Chapter Nine: The Buddha Ascends the Summit of Mount Sumeru At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority, throughout all the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, in every one of the four continents and in each Jambudvīpa, there was a Tathāgata sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, none of whom failed to manifest themselves.
Each of those bodhisattvas, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expounded various teachings.
Each of them thought to themselves:
"I am in the presence of the Buddha."
At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual authority, he rose from this seat and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, proceeding toward the palace of Śakra.
Then, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, Śakra immediately prepared a lion throne made of various jewels within the Palace of Sublime Victory.
It was adorned with ten thousand varieties of miscellaneous jewels;
ten thousand kinds of jeweled canopies covered it from above;
and it was interlaced and draped with ten thousand nets of precious gems.
Above that were ten thousand kinds of exquisite jeweled canopies, with celestial silks and various gems forming hanging streamers;
they were adorned with ten thousand kinds of necklaces and garlands,
and ten thousand kinds of precious robes were spread upon the seats.
Ten thousand devaputras stood in attendance before him;
ten thousand Brahmās surrounded him;
and ten thousand rays of light shone upon him.
At that time, Śakra, having adorned the lion throne for the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
I pray only that you will compassionately accept my invitation to dwell in this palace."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted his invitation and ascended to the Sublime Palace;
it was likewise so throughout all the ten directions.
At that moment, the immeasurable musical sounds of Śakra became silent and ceased, due to the Buddha’s spiritual power.
He immediately recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke in verse:
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata, endowed with great compassion, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things.
That Buddha once entered this place; Therefore, this ground is most auspicious.”
The wisdom of Konāgamuni is unimpeded; among all auspicious things, it is supreme.
That Buddha once came to enter this place; therefore, this ground is most auspicious.
The body of Krakucchanda Buddha was like a mountain of gold; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
That Buddha once came to enter this place; therefore, this ground is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Anupamapatra is free from the three stains; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
That Buddha once came to enter this place; therefore, this site is most auspicious.
Śikhin Tathāgata was ever tranquil, the most supreme among all that is auspicious;
that Buddha once came to enter this place, and for this reason this ground is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was like the full moon, the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this place, and therefore this ground is most auspicious.
Puṣya has realized the ultimate truth, the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this place, and therefore this ground is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Tiṣya possesses unimpeded eloquence, the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once came to enter this place, and for this reason this ground is most auspicious.
Padmottara Buddha is pure and stainless, the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this place, and for this reason, this ground is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara’s radiance shines universally; he is the most supreme among all that is auspicious.
That Buddha once entered this place; therefore, this ground is most auspicious.
Just as Śakra here praised the merits of the ten Buddhas with verses through the Buddha’s spiritual power,
so too did the Śakras of the ten directions each recollect the roots of goodness they had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and praise them in verse in the same manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One ascended the lion throne and sat in the full lotus posture.
Once seated, the palace suddenly became as vast and expansive as the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; it was likewise so throughout all the ten directions.

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas Assembling in the Sublime Victorious Hall to Recite Verses, Part One of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. At that time, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in a hundred Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions—ten such worlds in every direction—the names of these worlds were: Indra, Lotus, and Jewel-Heap. Next is named Utpala; next is named Sucarita;
next is named Sukṛta.
The next is named Joy;
the next is named Constellation;
the next is named Insatiable Compassion.
The next is named Ākāśa (Space).
His Buddha is named Avikāra-candra (Unchanging Moon);
the next is named Akṣaya-candra (Inexhaustible Moon).
Next is called the Moon of Immovability;
next is called the Moon of Fragrant Wind;
next is called the Moon of Sovereign Heaven.
Next was named Moon of Purity;
next was named Moon of the Unsurpassed;
next was named Moon of the Constellations.
The next was named Moon of Non-Decay;
the next was named Moon of Infinite Sovereignty.
The Bodhisattva there was named Dharma Wisdom.
Next is named Sarvajñāna; next is named Vijayajñāna;
next is named Guṇajñāna.
Next is named Vīryamati; next is named Sumati;
next is named Prajñāmati.
Next is called True Wisdom;
next is called Unsurpassed Wisdom;
next is called Firm Wisdom.
These bodhisattvas each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas within their own lands, had purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, each of those bodhisattvas, accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-world, came to the place where the Buddha was, paying him respectful homage and prostrating themselves.
Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he manifested lion thrones made of precious jewels; sitting upon them in the full lotus posture, they filled the ten directions.
Just as the Bodhisattvas had gathered like clouds upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in this world, so it was in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrously colored light from his two big toes, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions—the four continents, the foot of the Bodhi tree, the summit of Mount Sumeru, and the Palace of Supreme Victory—where the great assembly of Tathāgatas was clearly revealed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Teacher of Gods and Humans appears everywhere, In all adorned and pure lands;
Upon the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, In the wondrous and supreme palace of Śakra.”
Moved by compassion, they accepted the invitation of the Heavenly King;
thus they dwelt within his palaces, each with ten [attendants], praising the Buddha with auspicious verses.
These were the great retinues of the Buddhas, the assembly of pure Bodhisattvas.
They have come from the ten directions, sitting upright in the full lotus posture.
Each bears a name identical to their own, just like my assembly of bodhisattvas;
having left their original lands, they have gone to visit the various Buddhas.
The World-Honored Ones of our own land all share the same name;
each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas, has purely cultivated the bodhisattva practices.
O children of the Buddha, you should know that this is through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
In all worlds, each thinks, "The Buddha is before me.
Now we see the Buddha seated in the Śakra-vijaya Palace;
it is likewise in the ten directions—such is the Tathāgata’s power of mastery.
In all worlds, those who resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood first establish pure vows and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
Through these pure bodhisattva practices, they train for immeasurable and incalculable eons.
Unimpeded within the dharma-realm, there is no one able to measure it.
It universally illumines the ten directions, extinguishing the darkness of ignorance;
nothing can equal it, and for this reason, none can know it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvajñāna, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“Though one may constantly behold the Tathāgata throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons,
Within this True Dharma, one has still not yet seen the reality.”
Through deluded conceptualization, one grasps at all phenomena, increasing the net of ignorance and confusion.
Wandering in the cycle of birth and death, one remains blind and dark, failing to see the Buddha.
Though one may contemplate all phenomena, one has still not seen the true mark (*dharmatā*).
All phenomena arise and perish; they are merely attached to as provisional names.
All phenomena are without arising; all phenomena are without ceasing.
If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas will always be manifest before one.
Without grasping and without view, empty and still, devoid of reality;
all Buddhas are primordially empty, beyond the reach of thought.
If one understands that all phenomena are thus inconceivable, [one realizes the truth].
Regarding those various afflictions, their minds remain unstained.
To falsely grasp at the characteristics of phenomena is itself the darkness of delusion;
for this reason, they do not see the Buddha, nor do they attain reality.
The Muni transcends the three periods of time; He is fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence.
Abiding yet without a place of abiding, The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is entirely pure.
Through causes and conditions, phenomena arise; Through causes and conditions, phenomena cease.
Observing the Tathāgata in this way, one ultimately leaves behind delusion and confusion.
The Wisdom of Dharma has already expounded the pure and subtle Dharma;
having heard it from that Victorious One, I realize that Bodhi is inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānavatī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The wisdom of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep; No one at all can fathom it.
Not knowing the true Dharma, The world is entirely deluded.”
The ignorant child contemplates thus, falsely grasping at all phenomena;
for this reason, he does not see the Buddha, who is fully endowed with pure marks.
With a mind deluded by folly, he falsely grasps at the characteristics of the five aggregates.
Failing to realize true reality, one therefore does not see the Buddha.
All phenomena, when analyzed, are entirely devoid of true reality;
by understanding all phenomena in this way, one then beholds Vairocana.
Because of the first five aggregates, the subsequent aggregates arise in succession;
by understanding the five aggregates in their proper order, one perceives the Buddha, who is inconceivable.
Like a treasure in a dark place, it is not seen because of ignorance.
In the ultimate truth there is no speaker; though one possesses wisdom, none can behold it.
Just as when the eyes are not clear and pure, one does not see subtle forms, so too, with an impure mind, one does not see the Buddha-dharma.
Just as the bright, pure sun cannot be seen by those without eyes,
so too one whose mind is deceitful and crooked will never behold the Buddhas. Therefore,
one should purify the eye of wisdom and observe the characteristics of all phenomena.
The characteristics of phenomena are seen with clarity, Just like images within a mirror.
All the wisdom previously taught, The pure and subtle Dharma—
Having heard it from that Victorious One, I beheld the Buddha Vairocana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are empty and lack reality, yet people falsely grasp at them as having solid characteristics.
For this reason, the ignorant and deluded constantly turn the wheel of birth and death."
Unwholesome states are not supreme dharmas, yet one falsely conceives them as having the characteristics of supreme dharmas;
for this reason, obstacles arise, and through delusion, one perpetually wanders in saṃsāra.
Without knowing the Eightfold Noble Path, how can one know one’s own mind?
Due to those inverted perceptions, they increase all manner of evil.
Failing to see that all phenomena are empty, they constantly undergo immeasurable suffering;
such people do not achieve accomplishment because they lack the pure Dharma-eye.
If you wish to know all minds, you must first seek the Dharma-eye;
as I have taught, one who can see the true Buddha will have a mind free from attachment.
If there is one who sees the Buddha, their mind shall have no point of clinging.
They perceive reality as it is taught by the Buddha;
seeing the Great Wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body—
because they are able to see the Tathāgata, they possess the pure eye.
Only through non-seeing can one see all truly real dharmas;
if one has a view regarding dharmas, that person sees nothing at all.
How wondrous is the truly real dharma, by which the Buddha guides sentient beings!
Within all states of existence, there is neither birth nor death.
This sublime wisdom was previously taught by the Victorious One as the pure and subtle Dharma;
having heard it from that Victor, I have deeply understood the path of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vigorous Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Because they practice with various false conceptions, Their eye of wisdom is not purified;
Ignorance and wrong views increase, And thus they never see the Buddhas."
If one can perceive the false and deceptive, as well as the true Dharma, and discern with clarity what is real and what is unreal, then one sees the pure Buddha.
To see is itself a defilement; therein, there is nothing to be seen.
The Buddhas are free from that which is seen; therefore, their vision is pure.
The dharmas of worldly speech are false and lack reality;
knowing that the world arises from conditions, one can leave behind the afflictions of birth and death.
The world and that which is not the world— observing them both as entirely equal,
knowing the reality of both— is what is called a true seer.
If one can contemplate in this way, the outflows are exhausted and one attains mastery.
Neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the non-dual view.
Neither false nor not false, this is not the teaching of the Buddhas;
for the true reality is without dual characteristics, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure.
The nature of phenomena is inherently pure, Formless like space;
nothing can be predicated of it— Thus do the wise contemplate.
They joyfully observe all phenomena As quiescent and non-existent.
Knowing also that there is nothing to be cultivated, one is able to see the Honored Muni.
One who sees the Buddha in this way possesses immeasurable merit;
all their practices are tranquil, empty, and signless.

The Second Part of the Tenth Chapter: “Verses Spoken by the Two Bodhisattvas Assembled at the Sublime Victorious Palace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Good Wisdom (Sudhi), empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“How wondrous are the Buddha, the World-Honored One, And the immeasurable Tathāgatas!”
Through liberation from a harmful mind, one delivers oneself and can deliver others.
With right view, the lamp of the world, seeing reality as it is without inversion,
one beholds the Buddha because of the merit accumulated over immeasurable and incalculable eons.
All conditioned phenomena are empty and lack reality; Ordinary beings call them ultimate truth.
All things lack intrinsic nature; They are all entirely equal to space.
This is what the one of inexhaustible wisdom has taught: The teacher has nothing to teach.
Fully knowing that all existence is non-existent, one thus attains that which is inconceivable.
Expounding the inexhaustible as inexhaustible, because sentient beings are empty and quiescent,
one who knows their true nature beholds the One of Great Renown.
To say that non-viewing is viewing, and to speak of sentient beings through the doctrine of no-self—
both this view and these sentient beings are entirely non-existent.
When the viewer has nothing to see, this viewing does not destroy the true nature of phenomena.
This is called the true Dharma, as taught by all Buddhas.
One who can know the true Buddha and that which the Buddha has taught will see all worlds everywhere, just like the Buddha Vairocana.
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has skillfully explained the pure and luminous path;
the Bodhisattva Vīryamati expounds the immeasurable Dharma.
Regarding the characteristics of all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—one should cultivate them as equal within the single characteristic.
"In this way, one is able to see the Buddha, abiding securely in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Having heard the most supreme teaching, the light of pure wisdom immediately arose."
Universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, one perceives all Buddhas.
To reckon that there are sentient beings is the most difficult state;
the Dharma has no true master, existing only as provisional verbal designations.
The deluded and confused are unable to know the true nature of their own selves;
since the Tathāgata is not to be grasped through signs, therefore they do not see the Buddha.
When the dust and defilements obstruct the eye of wisdom, one does not see the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
For immeasurable and incalculable eons, one wanders through the ocean of birth and death.
Wandering is birth and death; non-wandering is nirvana.
Both birth and death and nirvana are ultimately unattainable.
Those who speak with falsehood and delusion claim that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are different;
they are confused regarding the Dharma of the noble ones and do not recognize the unsurpassed path.
Such people who grasp at signs say that there is a Buddha who has attained perfect enlightenment.
With inverted views and lack of right mindfulness, one does not see the Buddha.
If one can know this true Dharma, the mark of the quiescent *tathatā*,
then one sees the Most Perfectly Awakened One, who transcends the path of language.
All phenomena are spoken of as illusory; in reality, phenomena do not exist at all.
Though one seeks them with diligence, none can be found by any of the World-Honored Ones.
They clearly understand the past, as well as the future and the present.
"Ultimately and eternally quiescent, Therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva True Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Better to undergo immeasurable suffering Than to fail to hear the voice of the Buddha."
They do not experience any happiness, yet they do not hear the name of the Buddha.
Thus, for immeasurable kalpas, they have endured these manifold sufferings and afflictions,
wandering through birth and death because they have not heard the name of the Buddha.
By means of the non-substantiality of all phenomena, the Perfectly Awakened One distinguishes the true from the false;
because there is no characteristic of combination, this is called Bodhi.
The manifest Buddha does not arise from the conjunction of conditions, and the same is true for those of the past and future.
All phenomena are signless; this is the true nature of the Buddha.
If one can contemplate the profound meaning of all phenomena in this way, one will see immeasurable Buddhas and the true mark of the Dharma-body.
Knowing reality as it truly is, and knowing the unreal as unreal, he has thoroughly understood the limit of reality;
therefore, he is called the Perfectly Awakened One.
That the Awakened One has nothing to awaken to—this is the Buddha’s true and wondrous Dharma.
The Buddhas cultivate in this way: neither as one nor as two.
Knowing that the single dharma is manifold, and knowing that manifold dharmas are one;
since dharmas have no place of dependence, how could they be joined through conditions?
The agent and the action—both are non-existent;
if one can understand them thus, they cannot be found when sought.
This state that cannot be found is that upon which all Buddhas rely.
“Dharmas have nothing upon which they rely; the Awakened One has nothing to which he clings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Unsurpassed Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Unsurpassed Mahāsattva Is far removed from the marks of sentient beings.”
The supreme aspect is non-existent; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.
The subtle is non-existent, and the coarse is likewise non-existent.
That which is attained by all Buddhas is neither sought nor created.
This Dharma is beyond calculation; it is the realm of all Buddhas.
It is also free from the non-numerous; this is called the true Dharma of the Buddha.
The sun of wisdom shines upon the ten directions, extinguishing all darkness and obscurity.
Nor is there anything illuminated, nor is there anything unilluminated.
Always delighting in the dharma of tranquility, forever free from any basis of reliance,
liberated from a place of dependence, they are unstained by any phenomena.
The great wise ones who see well abide in reality;
if there are no two dharmas, one should know that even one does not exist.
Without one and without two, all things are utterly quiescent.
The threefold world is empty; this is what the Buddhas perceive.
The Buddhas teach sentient beings to abide securely within the True Dharma;
by understanding that there is no place of abiding, one shall behold the true body.
That which is not the body is itself the body; it does not turn and cannot be seen.
Without turning and without seeing, this is called the Unsurpassed Body.
It is that which is expounded by true wisdom—the infinite teachings of all Buddhas.
"Whoever hears this Dharma shall always attain the pure eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Wisdom (Dṛḍhamati), empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Sentient beings do not know gratitude; yet the Tathāgata gives rise to compassionate wisdom."
Appearing in the world, he shines universally to dispel all darkness.
Arousing great compassion, he surveys all living beings who undergo immeasurable suffering and are eternally bound within the three realms of existence.
Except for the Perfectly Awakened One, the Most Victorious and Honored Teacher,
among all gods and humans, there is no one to whom refuge can be sought.
If the world were without the Buddha and the assembly of worthy sages, [there would be no refuge].
Those various classes of sentient beings possess not a single kind of happiness.
The Tathāgata and his assembly of noble sages appear in this world to open the eye of pure wisdom and cause them to attain eternal peace and joy.
Those who behold the Tathāgata obtain the greatest benefit;
those who hear the Buddha’s name with joy are true stupas of the world.
We have gained excellent benefit, having come before to pay homage to the Tathāgata.
Having heard this subtle and wondrous Dharma, all shall surely attain the path of Buddhahood.
Regarding the brilliant liberation of the three periods of time and its most profound realms,
all the bodhisattvas have purified and opened their eyes of wisdom.
We are filled with profound joy, beholding the Buddha Vairocana,
whose immeasurable and boundless wisdom is inexhaustible in its exposition.
His supreme intelligence is firm and steadfast, as is that of all the sons of the Buddhas.
"Throughout countless billions of eons, The virtues of the Buddha could be expounded without end.

Chapter Eleven: The Ten Abodes of Bodhisattvas From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "The Ten Abodes of Bodhisattvas," Chapter Eleven. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond as many Buddha-lands as there are motes of dust in a thousand Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, he beheld as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust in a thousand Buddha-worlds; all these Tathāgatas were named Dharmamati.
At that time, those Buddhas addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Noble son! You are indeed able to enter this bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means. Noble son!"
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-fields, empower you with their spiritual might; thus, you are able to enter this samādhi of right reception.

Furthermore, it is by the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha, by his majestic spiritual power, and by the power of your own roots of goodness; and because he wishes to cause you to expound the Dharma extensively, to nurture the wisdom of the Buddhas, to open up and understand the Dharma-realm, to discern the realms of sentient beings, to eliminate hindrances, to enter the unimpeded sphere, to enter the *dhāraṇī* of all-knowledge through peerless skillful means, to awaken to all phenomena, to skillfully know the various faculties [of beings], and to maintain the teaching of the Dharma—namely, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva.
“Good son! You should now, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

At that time, all the Tathāgatas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dharmamati unimpeded wisdom, non-abiding wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, non-deluded wisdom, indestructible wisdom, non-evil wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, non-lax wisdom, and non-retrogressive wisdom.
Why is this? Because the nature of the Dharma is such through the power of that samādhi.
At that time, each of the Buddhas extended his right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
Having rubbed their heads, he arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of the Buddha!
The lineage of the bodhisattvas is profoundly deep and vast, equal to the dharma-realm and space; all bodhisattvas are born from the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
O Sons of the Buddha!
The ten stages of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas' practice have been taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten?

First is called the Initial Resolve; second, the Cultivation of the Ground; third, the Practice of Cultivation; fourth, Birth into Nobility; fifth, Fulfillment of Skillful Means; sixth, the Upright Mind; seventh, Non-retrogression; eighth, the Youthful Truth; ninth, the Prince of Dharma; and tenth, the Consecration.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
These are called the ten abodes of the Bodhisattvas, as taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
O Sons of the Buddha!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dwelling of the first production of the thought of awakening?
This bodhisattva sees the Buddha endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his wondrous form complete, revered and difficult to encounter;

or they behold a supernatural transformation, or hear the preaching of the Dharma, or listen to instructions, or see sentient beings undergoing immeasurable suffering, or hear the Tathāgata extensively expound the Buddha-dharma, whereby they produce the thought of bodhi, seek all-knowledge, and never turn back.
Because this bodhisattva has attained the initial resolve, they obtain the factors of the ten powers (*daśabala*). What are these ten?
They are as follows:

The knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the defilement and purification of karmic retribution; the knowledge of the faculties; the knowledge of inclinations and desires; the knowledge of natures; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the arising and purification of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments; the unimpeded knowledge of past lives; the unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows throughout the three periods of time—these are the ten.
O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: learning to reverently honor and make offerings to all Buddhas; praising all bodhisattvas and protecting the minds of sentient beings; drawing near to the wise and virtuous; praising the non-retrogressive Dharma; cultivating the merits of a Buddha; extolling and admiring them; being born before all Buddhas; skillfully practicing the samādhi of tranquility; praising the departure from the cycle of birth and death; and acting as a place of refuge for suffering sentient beings.

Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause the bodhicitta to become increasingly firm and steadfast, thereby accomplishing the unsurpassed path; such that whatever Dharma is heard is immediately understood through self-awakening, without relying on the realization of others.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Dwelling of Purifying the Ground?
In this dwelling, the Bodhisattva gives rise to ten kinds of mind toward all sentient beings."
What are the ten? They are:

the mind of great loving-kindness, the mind of great compassion, the mind of joy, the mind of peaceful abiding, the mind of rapture, the mind of delivering sentient beings, the mind of protecting sentient beings, the mind of "mine," the mind of a teacher, and the mind of a Tathāgata. These are the ten.
O Sons of the Buddha!
That bodhisattva should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: first, one should diligently study and single-mindedly seek extensive learning; cultivate the concentration of detachment from desire; draw near to virtuous friends and do not contravene their instructions; know well when to speak; train in fearlessness; clearly understand profound meanings; thoroughly comprehend the True Dharma; know the practice of steadfast dharmas; abandon the darkness of ignorance; and abide securely and immovably.
Why is this? Because they wish to increase great compassion for all sentient beings;
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, without relying on the awakening of others.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s dwelling of practice?
This Bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas in ten ways.”
What are the ten? They are as follows:

contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and lacking sovereignty; that all phenomena are not to be relished; that all phenomena have no accumulation or dispersal; that all phenomena lack solidity; that all phenomena are false and illusory; and that all phenomena lack diligent application, conjunction, or stability. These are the ten.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: training in the analytical knowledge of all realms of sentient beings; the analytical knowledge of all dharma-realms; the analytical knowledge of all world-systems; the analytical knowledge of the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; and the analytical knowledge of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Why is this? Because they desire to increase their clear and pure wisdom regarding all phenomena;
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, without relying on the awakening of others.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Dwelling of Noble Birth?
This Bodhisattva is born from the correct teaching of all the noble dharmas and cultivates ten kinds of dharmas.”
What are the ten? They are as follows:

indestructible faith in the Buddha; ultimate mastery of the Dharma; a tranquil and concentrated mind; discerning sentient beings; discerning buddha-fields; discerning worlds; discerning various karmas; discerning retributions; discerning birth and death; and discerning nirvana. These are the ten.
O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
studying the discernment of the Buddhadharma of the past, future, and present; practicing the Buddhadharma of the past, future, and present;
fulfilling the Buddhadharma of the past, future, and present; and impartially observing all Buddhas.

Why is this? It is because one desires to bring about clear understanding of both worlds through equal contemplation, so that whatever Dharma is heard is immediately understood by oneself, rather than awakening to it through another.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dwelling that is fully endowed with skillful means?
This bodhisattva should hear and practice ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten?

All the roots of goodness practiced are for the purpose of: rescuing and protecting all sentient beings; benefiting all sentient beings; bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings; having compassion for all sentient beings; bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment; causing all sentient beings to abandon all hardships; pulling all sentient beings out of the suffering and affliction of birth and death; causing all sentient beings to rejoice and be happy; causing all sentient beings to be tamed; and causing all sentient beings to attain nirvana—this is called abiding in the perfection of skillful means.
O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should train in ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: learning that sentient beings are boundless; knowing that sentient beings are incalculable; knowing that sentient beings are inconceivable; knowing the various forms of sentient beings; knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable; knowing that sentient beings are empty; knowing that sentient beings lack autonomy; knowing that sentient beings are not real; and knowing that sentient beings possess nothing.
Why is this? It is because one desires their mind to be free from any defilement or attachment;
such that upon hearing the Dharma, they immediately attain understanding for themselves, without relying on the awakening of others.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Abiding in the Right Mind?
This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings and attains a mind of certainty."
What are these ten? They are as follows:
hearing praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, one’s mind remains fixed and unshakable regarding the Buddha-dharma;
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, their minds remain steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of bodhisattvas, their minds remain steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of the practices performed by bodhisattvas, their minds remain steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that sentient beings are finite or infinite, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that sentient beings are defiled or undefiled, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that sentient beings are easy to deliver or difficult to deliver, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that the dharma-realm is finite or infinite, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that the dharma-realm is subject to formation or destruction, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that the dharma-realm exists or does not exist, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma.
These are the ten.
O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study these ten dharmas.

What are these ten? They are as follows: studying that all phenomena are signless; all phenomena are without intrinsic nature; all phenomena cannot be cultivated; all phenomena are non-existent; all phenomena lack reality; all phenomena are like space; all phenomena lack self-nature; all phenomena are like illusions; all phenomena are like dreams; and all phenomena are like echoes.

Why is this? It is because they desire to attain the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; thus, whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, awakening to it without depending on others.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s dwelling of non-retrogression?
When this Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, their mind becomes firm and remains unshakable.”
What are the ten? They are as follows:
hearing that there is a Buddha or that there is no Buddha, one does not regress from within the Buddha-dharma; hearing that there is Dharma or that there is no Dharma...
Not regressing from the Buddha-dharma whether there is a bodhisattva or no bodhisattva;
not regressing from the Buddha-dharma whether there is the practice of a bodhisattva or no practice of a bodhisattva;
and not regressing from the Buddha-dharma whether the practice of a bodhisattva transcends birth and death or does not transcend birth and death.
Whether there is a past Buddha or no past Buddha, one does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
whether there is a future Buddha or no future Buddha, one does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
whether there is a present Buddha or no present Buddha, one does not regress from the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-knowledge exists.

Exhaustion and non-exhaustion; not regressing from the Buddha-dharma; the dharmas of the three periods of time being of one mark and yet not of one mark—these constitute the ten [non-regressions] within the Buddha-dharma.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: knowing that the one is the many, and the many are the one; knowing the meaning according to the flavor, and knowing the flavor according to the meaning; knowing that what is non-existent is existent, and knowing that what is existent is non-existent; knowing that what is not a characteristic is a characteristic, and knowing that what is a characteristic is not a characteristic; knowing that what is not a nature is a nature, and knowing that what is a nature is not a nature.

Why is this? Because they desire to be fully endowed with skillful means regarding all dharmas; whatever dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, awakening to it without depending on others.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Abiding in Youthful Purity?
In this regard, the Bodhisattva establishes his mind in ten kinds of dharmas.”

What are the ten? They are: purity of bodily conduct, purity of verbal conduct, purity of mental conduct; taking birth according to one's will; knowing the minds of sentient beings; knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; knowing the various natures of sentient beings; knowing the various karmas of sentient beings; knowing the formation and destruction of worlds; and possessing unimpeded mastery over supernormal powers. These are the ten.
O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: learning to know all buddha-fields; shaking all buddha-fields; sustaining all buddha-fields; contemplating all buddha-fields; visiting all buddha-fields; reaching everywhere throughout all worlds; being skilled in posing questions regarding immeasurable sublime dharmas; manifesting immeasurable bodies through supernatural transformations; being skilled in understanding immeasurable sounds and voices; and reverently making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas within a single thought-moment.

Why is this? Because they wish to produce skillful means within all dharmas and achieve them fully; whatever dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, awakening to it without depending on others.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Dwelling of the Dharma Prince?
This Bodhisattva is skillfully proficient in ten kinds of dharmas."

What are these ten? They are: skillfully understanding the destinies of sentient beings; skillfully understanding all afflictions; skillfully understanding all habitual tendencies; skillfully understanding the wisdom of expedient means; skillfully understanding the differentiation of immeasurable dharmas; skillfully understanding all modes of deportment; skillfully understanding the differentiation of all worlds; skillfully understanding the past, future, and present; skillfully explaining the conventional truth; and skillfully explaining the ultimate truth. These are the ten.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Those Bodhisattvas should study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: learning to well know the dwelling place of the Dharma King; well knowing the majestic deportment practiced by the Dharma King; well knowing how to establish the station of the Dharma King; well knowing how to skillfully enter the domain of the Dharma King; well knowing how to discern the domain of the Dharma King; well knowing the consecration with the nectar of the Dharma King; well knowing how to receive and uphold the teachings of the Dharma King; well knowing the fearless dharmas of the Dharma King; well knowing the unattached dharmas of the Dharma King; and well knowing how to praise the dharmas of the Dharma King.

Why is this? Because they wish to attain unobstructed wisdom regarding all phenomena, such that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on others for enlightenment.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Stage of Empowerment?
This Bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of abidings in wisdom."
What are these ten? They are: being able to shake all immeasurable worlds;

being able to illuminate all immeasurable worlds; being able to sustain all immeasurable worlds; being able to travel throughout all immeasurable worlds; being able to purify all immeasurable worlds; knowing the mental activities of all immeasurable sentient beings; knowing the conduct of sentient beings according to their minds; knowing the various faculties of all immeasurable sentient beings; being able to skillfully deliver all immeasurable sentient beings; and being able to subdue all immeasurable sentient beings. These are the ten.
O Sons of the Buddha!
That Bodhisattva’s body is unknowable;
his bodily actions possess supernormal power, and he is sovereign in his supernormal powers.
The knowledge of the past, the knowledge of the future, the knowledge of the present, the knowledge of purifying all Buddha-fields, the realm of the mind, and the realm of wisdom are unknowable;
they cannot be known by any sentient beings, nor even by Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Princes.
“O sons of the Buddha!
Those bodhisattvas should study ten kinds of knowledge. What are these ten?

That is to say: the wisdom of learning regarding the three periods of time; the wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom of non-obstruction within the dharma-realm; the wisdom of the immeasurable and boundless dharma-realm; the wisdom that fills all worlds; the wisdom that universally illumines all worlds; the wisdom capable of sustaining all worlds; the wisdom that discerns all sentient beings; the wisdom of all modes of knowledge; and the Buddha’s immeasurable and boundless wisdom.

"Why is this? It is because they wish to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), so that whatever Dharma they hear, they shall immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the awakening of others.

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*), worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners. Heavenly jewel-flowers, heavenly powdered incense, heavenly jewel-garlands, heavenly mixed incense, heavenly jewel-robes, heavenly jewel-clouds, and heavenly ornaments rained down. Heavenly exquisite music resounded spontaneously without being struck, further producing the sound of fearlessness.

Thus, upon the Palace of Sublime Victory atop Mount Sumeru in this world-system of four continents, through majestic spiritual power and transformations, the Dharma of the Ten Abodes was preached; and so it was likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, there were great bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms in ten buddha-fields, filling the ten directions. They came to this land and spoke these words: "Excellent! "
Excellent! Son of the Buddha, you have well expounded this Dharma. We, all of us, share the same name: Dharmamati;
the lands from which we have come all share the same name: Dharmamegha.
Those Tathāgatas all share the same name, "Wondrous Dharma";
in the presence of our Buddhas, they likewise teach the Ten Abodes.
As for the names, phrases, and syllables of their great assemblies and retinues, they are identical and without difference.
"Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
Empowered by the spiritual authority of the Buddha, we have come to this land to bear witness for you.

Just as these great Bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms within ten Buddha-worlds, came to bear witness here when the Dharma of the Ten Abodes was preached upon the Palace of Sublime Victory atop Mount Sumeru in this four-continent world, so it is likewise in all the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and all dharma-realms, and spoke in verse:
“I behold the subtle and wondrous body of the Honored One of Great Wisdom, Whose marks and signs are perfectly complete and majestic.
Most supreme and venerable, exceedingly difficult to encounter— The courageous Great Being has now first resolved his mind [upon enlightenment].”
Beholding the peerless and great supernormal transformations, hearing the exposition of the sublime Dharma and its instructions,
and observing the immeasurable sufferings of the five realms of existence, the fearless Great Being first resolved his mind upon enlightenment.
Having heard that the Tathāgatas, the Honored Ones of Universal Wisdom, are fully endowed with immeasurable merit,
and understanding that the nature of the Buddha’s mind is like space, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves to attain enlightenment.
Able to know what is possible and what is impossible, as well as such matters as self and non-self;
desiring to understand the true meaning of equality, the bodhisattva for this reason first generates the mind of enlightenment.
Regarding all karmic retributions, whether good or evil, throughout the past, future, and present worlds—
desiring to observe them all with perfect equanimity, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
Regarding the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations, they accord with right concentration and remain unattached;
wishing to skillfully discern the arising of defilement and purity, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves their mind on enlightenment.
According to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, and their various powers of diligent cultivation and vigor,
desiring to fully comprehend and discern them all— thereby, the Bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The various desires of all sentient beings, and their hearts' fondness for and attachment to all manner of hopes—
wishing to fully comprehend and discern them all, the Bodhisattva therefore first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The various natures of all sentient beings, Immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—
Desiring to fully comprehend and discern them all, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
To all destinations reached by every path, And the Noble Eightfold Path leading toward the unconditioned—
Desiring to fully comprehend and know their true reality, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
Seeing all classes of sentient beings throughout all worlds, wandering through the ocean of birth and death in the five realms of existence,
and desiring to attain the divine eye that perceives all with clarity, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Regarding all matters of the past, with their inherent natures and all their characteristics,
desiring to follow and comprehend them through the knowledge of past lives, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
All the afflictions of the world, And all their fetters and residual habitual tendencies—
Desiring to fully awaken to and exhaust them completely, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
All worldly phenomena of conventional truth, the paths of names, discourses, and language—
desiring to clearly comprehend the meaning of these conventional truths, the Bodhisattva thereby first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
All phenomena are beyond the reach of language; they possess no intrinsic nature, being like space.
Desiring to clearly realize the meaning of ultimate truth, the bodhisattva thus first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
Shaking all Buddha-worlds, overturning and surging through the great oceans—
desiring to fully comprehend the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
From a single hair-pore he radiates immeasurable light, Universally illuminating all lands throughout the ten directions;
Desiring to awaken to all-encompassing enlightenment within a single ray of light, The Bodhisattva thereby first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Immeasurable Buddha-fields, inconceivable in number, He can place them all within the palm of one hand;
Desiring to understand that all things are like illusions and transformations, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind [on enlightenment].
All sentient beings throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields, he places them all upon the tip of a single hair;
desiring to fully comprehend that they are all utterly quiescent, the Bodhisattva thereby first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The waters of all the great oceans throughout the ten directions— If one were to exhaust them drop by drop with a single hair until none remained,
And desired to discern and know the number of those drops, It is for this reason that the Bodhisattva first resolved his mind on enlightenment.
All the inconceivable buddha-fields, Were ground into fragments like fine dust;
Desiring to discern and know their total number, The bodhisattva thereby first resolved his mind [on enlightenment].
Throughout immeasurable eons of the past and future, Regarding the signs of the formation and destruction of all worlds,
Desiring to thoroughly penetrate their ultimate limits, The Bodhisattva therefore first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
All the Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three periods of time, As well as all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—
Desiring to discern the paths of the three vehicles, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind [on enlightenment].
All immeasurable and boundless worlds, he is able to lift up entirely with a single hair;
wishing to know the true nature of existence and non-existence, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
Mountains of Vajra-enclosures, beyond measure in number, can all be placed upon the tip of a single hair;
wishing to know how the greatest can possess the mark of the smallest, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, one is able to fill them completely with a single voice;
desiring to fully understand and comprehend this pure and wondrous sound, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
The languages and dharmas of all sentient beings— He expounds them all in a single word without exception;
Desiring to fully understand this pure and subtle sound, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
The Tathāgata’s pure and subtle voice fills all worlds throughout the ten directions;
desiring to attain the mark of a perfect tongue-faculty, the Bodhisattva for this reason first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, He sees all that undergoes formation and destruction;
Desiring to understand that all are entirely illusory, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
In all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, The infinite Tathāgatas therein—
Desiring to fully comprehend the Buddha’s True Dharma, The Bodhisattva, for this reason, first resolves his mind [on enlightenment].
Universally able to manifest immeasurable bodies, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds,
desiring to fully comprehend them all as being like illusions and transformations— by this, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
In the past, future, and present worlds, To fully comprehend, in a single thought-moment, All the infinite and boundless Tathāgatas—
For this reason, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind [on enlightenment].
Desiring to fully expound even a single phrase of the Dharma for incalculable eons without end,
and wishing that their eloquence never be interrupted— for this reason, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions, with their shifting and changing marks of birth and extinction—
desiring to fully comprehend them all in a single thought-moment, for this reason the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
With pure and wondrous conduct of body, speech, and mind, They traverse the ten directions without obstruction;
Desiring to realize that the three periods of time are entirely empty and quiescent, The Bodhisattva thereby first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

Once the Bodhisattva has thus resolved their mind, they should learn to offer complete respect and worship to all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions; such is the teaching spoken by those who do not regress.
The Bodhisattva relinquishes all manner of pleasures, yet does not weary of saṃsāra in seeking bodhi;
by means of this exhortation, joy, and praise, one who speaks thus teaches the non-retrogressive path.
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, whatever sages and worthies dwell therein, the Bodhisattva should constantly praise them;
one who speaks thus teaches the non-retrogressive path.
Supreme, most excellent, and peerless, The profound, subtle, and pure Dharma— By means of this, Bodhisattvas transform sentient beings; To speak thus is the teaching of non-retrogression.
The unsurpassed, pure, and wondrously virtuous Dharma cannot be destroyed by any demons;
the Bodhisattvas revere and constantly praise it—such is the teaching that causes no regression.
All excellent merits whatsoever, the Honored One among gods and humans has fully accomplished;
by means of these he establishes all bodhisattvas—he who speaks thus is the King among Men.
Through skillful means they teach and transform, beholding Buddhas immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable;
those who can employ such skillful means to transform others are speakers of the non-retrogressive teaching.
All the most profound samādhis, he teaches to all sentient beings without exception;
the Bodhisattva discerns and fully guides them—such a speaker is one whose teaching is non-retrogressive.
Able to utterly destroy the wheel of birth and death, Fully turning the wondrous Dharma-wheel of the Noble Path,
Unattached to anything in all the worlds— The Buddhas have prophesied such a one as a Bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva sees immeasurable multitudes revolving in birth and death and undergoing all manner of suffering,
and acts as their protector and refuge, they are a bodhisattva prophesied by all Buddhas.
This describes the Bodhisattva’s dwelling of the initial resolve, single-mindedly seeking the unsurpassed path;
as I have taught this subtle and wondrous Dharma, so do all Buddhas.
The second stage, the Ground of Refinement, belongs to the true sons of the Buddha; first, they should resolve their minds and form this thought:
"May all classes of living beings follow and practice the teachings of the Buddhas."
The mind that seeks to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; The joyful mind that never abandons sentient beings;
The mind of great compassion that seeks to rescue and protect them as one's own; The mind that gives rise to the heart of a Great Teacher, the Tathāgata.
Having generated such sublime and wondrous thoughts, One should diligently study and seek extensive learning;
With a tranquil mind and right reflection, One should always keep close to virtuous friends.
Following and practicing in accordance with his teachings, gentle in speech and free from negligence,
he is well able to discern all times and attains the profound meaning of the Dharma without fear.
One who clearly understands the profound meaning and realizes the True Dharma, Is then freed from all darkness of ignorance;
having abandoned folly and dwelling with a settled mind, Such a person is called a true son of the Buddha.
They are also called Bodhisattvas who Purify the Grounds, single-mindedly and firmly seeking awakening;
having thus well trained in the teachings of all Buddhas, they are truly named sons of the Buddha.
The third is the true child of the Buddha in practice; they should contemplate all phenomena in this way:
as impermanent, suffering, empty, and lacking solidity; as selfless, without a master, and not independent.
All phenomena are not to be delighted in; they are unconditioned, deceptive, and unreal.
They neither accumulate nor disperse; one who observes them thus is a bodhisattva.
Discerning and observing the realm of sentient beings, one should likewise understand the realm of all phenomena;
skillfully employing the observation of expedient means, one perceives immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Within all the lands of the ten directions, The four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, And the realms of desire,
form, and formlessness— He is able to observe, discern, and know them all.
Skillfully and clearly penetrating all realms, reaching the ultimate truth without exception—
those who accord with such teachings of the true Dharma are Bodhisattvas.
The fourth is the noble son of the Buddha by birth, Born from the true Dharma of all the sages and saints;
Unattached to the existence or non-existence of all phenomena, He abandons birth and death and transcends the triple world.
Faith in the Buddha is firm and indestructible; with a ultimately pure mind, one never regresses.
Clearly observing the profound Dharma, one realizes that all sentient beings lack true reality.
The worlds of karmic activity and all Buddha-fields, Birth-and-death, retributive fruits, and nirvāṇa—
If a Son of the Buddha can contemplate them thus, He is said to be born through the Tathāgata’s Dharma-transformation.
In the past, future, and present worlds, The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and the True Dharma—
Seeking the ultimate through immeasurable skillful means, They have accomplished all the dharmas of the Great Sages.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time Observe with equanimity, without marks of difference;
Since distinctions and differences cannot be found, Those who observe in this way penetrate the three periods of time.
Those whom I have thus praised are called Mahāsattvas dwelling in the four stages;
if one can practice and study in this manner, one will swiftly attain the unsurpassed Bodhi of a Buddha.
The fifth is the Bodhisattva, the true son of the Buddha, Who dwells in the perfection of subtle skillful means;
Deeply entering pure and clever expedients, He brings all deeds of merit to ultimate completion.
All the immeasurable merits you have cultivated, you dedicate entirely to being a refuge for all;
with great compassion that brings benefit, peace, and happiness, you take pity on and deliver all living beings.
To eliminate all hardships for all beings in the world, To forever uproot birth and death and bring them joy,
To subdue all classes of living beings, And, endowed with merit, lead them to Nirvana.
Universally for the sake of all living beings, He analyzes and expounds the pure Dharma;
This is called the fifth Mahāsattva, Who accomplishes skillful means to deliver sentient beings,
Possessing all merits and virtues, And expounding the pure and wondrous Dharma of the five abodes.
The sixth is the true son of the Buddha with a rectified mind; understanding the true Dharma, he is free from delusion.
Among all the devas and humans in the world, through right mindfulness and reflection, he extinguishes all that is false and illusory.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, or of all the paths practiced by Bodhisattvas,
or of sentient beings being finite or infinite, their minds remain unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Sentient beings may have defilements or be free from them; some are easy to deliver, while others are difficult to deliver.
The dharma-realm may be finite or infinite; worlds may come into being or undergo destruction.
Whether they hear that the Dharma-realm exists or does not exist, throughout the past, future, and present,
the Bodhisattva remains unmoved in mind as they observe all these phenomena in profound stillness.

Contemplating all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature or characteristics, their meaning is truly like space, just like a magical illusion or what is seen in a dream; such a person possesses true understanding of the Dharma.

The seventh is the non-retrogressive true son of the Buddha: whether hearing that there are dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or hearing that there are no dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they emerge from neither and do not retrogress.
Whether all Buddhas of the past, future, and present exist or do not exist;
whether dharmas arise and cease or do not arise and cease; whether they possess a single characteristic or diverse characteristics.
If one is many and many are one, Their meanings and flavors are quiescent and entirely equal;
Far removed from the inverted marks of oneness and difference— This is called the Bodhisattva’s stage of Non-retrogression.

Whether there be the mark of phenomena or the absence of marks, whether there be the nature of phenomena or the absence of nature—both are devoid of reality and equal to space; one who knows thus will surely reach the ultimate end.
The eighth is the stage of Youthful Innocence, the true son of the Buddha; His conduct of body, speech, and mind is fully perfected;
Subtle, wondrous, pure, and undefiled, He manifests spontaneously according to his will.
He fully knows the minds of all sentient beings, And is skillfully able to observe the nature of their various desires;
He understands that the phenomena of sentient beings are without distinction, As well as the signs of formation and destruction throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Swiftly attaining all sublime supernatural powers, they travel to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
moving with sovereign ease and without hindrance, they hear the preaching of the wondrous Dharma and receive and uphold it all.
Causing all lands to quake in six ways, He is able to sustain all worlds;
With a Brahma-voice filling the realms of the ten directions, He delivers and liberates immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings.
The inquiries concerning the Buddha’s meaning are incalculable, and his manifestations of form are immeasurable;
he expounds the words of the Dharma according to those who are to be transformed, exactly as the Buddha has taught, without any difference.
The ninth prince, Mahasattva, is fully able to discern all classes of sentient beings;
well-knowing their various afflictions and behaviors, he delivers them through skillful means according to what is appropriate for each.
Skillfully discerning and knowing the characteristics of all phenomena, Clearly penetrating the prior and subsequent limits of the world,
Expertly understanding conventional truth and the ultimate truth, Fully endowed with skillful means without exception.
They are well able to thoroughly understand the station of the Dharma King; they accord with the majestic deportment of the Dharma King;
they skillfully know how to peacefully enter the rank of the Dharma King; and they skillfully know how to discern the realm of the Dharma King.
The tenth is the true son of the Buddha who has received empowerment;
skillfully upholding all dharmas, he accords with the Dharma to enter its profound meaning, and is able to analyze and explain it all to the ultimate end.
They deliver all sentient beings without exception, yet they do not grasp at the marks of those beings;
remaining tranquil and unmoving, they train in right mindfulness, ever present before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Bodhisattvas who have received empowerment are true sons of the Buddha; they are fully able to bring all supreme dharmas to ultimate perfection.
Throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, they are able to cause them all to tremble and illuminate them universally with light.
Able to sustain all worlds in the ten directions, Purifying the minds of all sentient beings,
Fully knowing the faculties of all beings, He proclaims the Brahma-voice, filling the ten directions.
Taming and transforming all sentient beings, causing them all to cultivate the bodhicitta;
universally entering the buddha-fields of the ten directions, observing the entire dharma-realm without exception.
The consecrated form-body and its physical activities, The inconceivable mastery of supernormal powers,
And the wisdom that observes the Buddha-lands of the three times— These are beyond even the comprehension of the Prince.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Buddha-dharma, They discern and know them all without obstruction;
The dharma-realm is immeasurable and boundless, Filled entirely with Buddhas and śrāvakas.
Throughout all worlds, they are able to sustain them all with light that shines everywhere;
for all classes of sentient beings, they proclaim the wisdom of ultimate, perfect enlightenment.

Thus, these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, all born through transformation from the Tathāgata’s Dharma, manifest according to their skillful means and spheres of activity; no devas or humans can comprehend them.
Having first resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, filling the ten directions without exception,
thoroughly comprehending the characteristics of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time, they fully accomplish all-knowledge.
Boundless Buddha-fields and worlds, Innumerable and countless classes of sentient beings,
Afflictions, karmic retributions, and the bodhicitta— In all such things, there is no attachment whatsoever.
When first seeking the Buddha-way, one gives rise to a single thought;
Neither the sentient beings of the world nor those of the Two Vehicles can know it— How much less so the other merits of a Bodhisattva?
All worlds throughout the ten directions, they can lift up entirely with a single hair;
knowing that the Bodhisattva’s practices are complete, they shall swiftly attain the All-Knowledge of the Tathāgata.
The waters of all the great oceans in the ten directions, one could exhaust them drop by drop with a single hair;
to know their number entirely within a single thought—such a practitioner is a true child of the Buddha.
If all worlds were ground into dust, one could distinguish and know their total number;
the conduct of a Bodhisattva is equal to the number of those atoms—one who acts thus is called a true son of the Buddha.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, And all the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas,
Could not fully explain and analyze The merits of a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind.
When a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, it is vast, immeasurable, and boundless;
with great kindness and great compassion, it covers all beings—how much more so the other merits of a bodhisattva!
Chapter Twelve: The Brahma Conduct. At that time, the Devaputra Samyaksmṛti addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

In all worlds, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, out of faith, leave home for the homeless life to study the Way; they cast off worldly adornments and don the dharma robes. By what skillful means do these bodhisattvas cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), fulfill the ten stages of the bodhisattva path (*bodhisattva-daśabhūmi*), and swiftly achieve unsurpassed, equal enlightenment?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati replied to the Devaputra Samyaksmṛti: "Virtuous One!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, seeking exclusively for unsurpassed enlightenment, must first distinguish ten kinds of dharmas."
What are the ten? They are:
the body, bodily action; speech, verbal action; the mind, mental action; the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts. One should contemplate them in this way:
Is the body the holy life? Or, up to: is morality the holy life?
If the body were the holy life, one should know that the holy life would not be pure.
One should know that the holy life is contrary to the Dharma;
one should know that the holy life is turbid;
one should know that the holy life is foul and evil.
One should know that the holy life is defiled;
one should know that the holy life is a stain;
one should know that the holy life is crooked and deceitful.
One should know that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) consists of eighty thousand families of worms.
If bodily action constitutes the holy life, one should know that the four modes of deportment of the body constitute the holy life;
looking to the left and right, lifting the foot, and setting it down constitute the holy life.
If the mouth is the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should know that vocal sound is the holy life;
one should know that speech is the holy life;
one should know that mental contact is the holy life.
One should know that the movement of the tongue is the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
one should know that the union of lips and teeth is the holy life.
If vocal action (*vākkarma*) is the holy life, one should know that speech itself is the holy life.
One should know that what has been described as action and non-action, praise and blame, defamation and renown, constitutes the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

If the mind is the holy life, one should know that applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), non-forgetfulness, reflection (*manasikāra*), illusions, dreams, and so forth, are all the holy life.
If mental action were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should know that perception (*saṃjñā*) is the holy life;
designation (*prajñapti*) is the holy life;
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, suffering, pleasure, sorrow, and joy—all these are the holy life.
If the Buddha is one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), is it form (*rūpa*) that is the Buddha?
Is it feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) that is the Buddha?
Or is it the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics that are the Buddha?
Are all supernatural powers and karmic retributions the Buddha?
If the Dharma is that which is pure conduct, is the Right Teaching the Dharma?
Or is it cessation and detachment from nirvana that is the Dharma?
Is this dharma something that arises or does not arise?
Is it something real or unreal?
Is it something false or illusory?
Is this dharma one of conjunction or disjunction?
If the Saṃgha consists of those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya), is it the Saṃgha that is directed toward the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala)?
Or is it the Saṃgha that has attained the fruit of stream-entry?
Is it those who are heading toward the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat* who constitute the Saṅgha?
Or is it those who have already attained the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat* who constitute the Saṅgha?
Is it the Sangha who possesses the three knowledges and six supernormal powers?
Is it the Sangha who is liberated at the proper time?
Or is it the Sangha who is liberated independent of time?
If precepts constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*), is the boundary of the precepts (*sīmā*) the precepts?
Is the assembly of ten persons the precepts?
Or is it the inquiry into purity and impurity that constitutes the precepts?
Is the preceptor who confers the precepts the precept?
Is the upādhyāya who performs the threefold karmavācanā the precept?
Or are the shaving of the hair, the dharma robes, and the practice of begging for food the precept?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate these ten dharmas in this way:

"Furthermore, one knows that the past has nowhere to go, the future is nothingness, and in the present there is no agent, no knower, and no experiencer of retribution; this world does not pass over to that world, nor does that world pass over to this world."
What are the phenomena that constitute the holy life?
Where does the phenomenon of the holy life reside?
Who possesses this phenomenon of the holy life?
Is this dharma of the holy life existent?
Is it non-existent?
Is it a material phenomenon?
Is it a non-material phenomenon?
Is it the phenomena of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Or is it not the phenomena of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses right mindfulness free from obstruction; he observes and discerns that all phenomena of the three periods of time are equal, like empty space, without dualistic characteristics.
One who observes in this manner possesses wisdom and skillful means without any obstruction.
They do not grasp at signs regarding any phenomena, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
they observe all Buddhas and all Buddha-dharmas with equanimity, as if they were like space.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful cultivation of pure brahmacarya.
Furthermore, one cultivates ten superior dharmas. What are these ten?

They are: the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the retribution of all karmas of the past, future, and present; the knowledge of the arising of all meditative absorptions, samādhis, and states of meditative attainment, as well as their defilement, purity, and emergence; the knowledge of the faculties of sentient beings; the knowledge of their various inclinations and pleasures; the knowledge of their diverse natures; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the unobstructed knowledge of past lives; the unobstructed knowledge of the divine eye; and the knowledge that severs the habitual tendencies. These are the ten.

Thus observing the ten powers of the Tathāgata as profound and immeasurable, they fully cultivate a heart of great compassion; they discern all sentient beings yet do not abandon them, nor do they abandon quiescent extinction;
they perform unsurpassed deeds without seeking karmic retribution;
and they contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, lightning, echoes, and transformations.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, they will swiftly attain all the merits of the Buddhas through minimal effort.
It is entirely possible that they will constantly delight in observing the non-dual nature of phenomena.

At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening; knowing the true nature of all phenomena, one is fully endowed with the body of wisdom, having realized it through no other means.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Eight;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: The Merits of Bodhisattvas Who Have First Aroused the Mind of Enlightenment.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
How many treasuries of merit does a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind for enlightenment accomplish? Dharmamati replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!
This matter is profound!

It is difficult to know, difficult to believe, difficult to understand, difficult to explain, difficult to penetrate, and difficult to discern. Nevertheless, relying upon the Buddha’s spiritual power, I shall fully expound it.”
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were a person who provided all manner of articles of pleasure to the sentient beings in *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the eastern direction for as long as one kalpa; thereafter, they instructed them to purely cultivate the five precepts.
