The same applies to the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
O Son of the Buddha! What do you think?
Would the merit of that person be considered great?
Śakra said: "O Son of the Buddha!
With the exception of all the Tathāgatas, no one else can measure the merit of that person."
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said to Śakra:
“O Son of the Buddha!

Even a hundredth part of the treasury of merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment cannot be matched by the merit of that person; nor can it be matched by a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a billionth part, a hundred-billionth part, a trillionth part, a hundred-trillionth part, a hundred-nayuta part, a thousand-nayuta part, a hundred-thousand-nayuta part, a billion-nayuta part, a hundred-billion-nayuta part, a trillion-nayuta part, a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta part, or even by any incalculable, incomparable, or ineffable part—the merit of that person does not equal even one such fraction.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy:

suppose there were someone who provided all manner of articles of pleasure to the sentient beings in ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in each of the ten directions for as long as a hundred eons, and thereafter instructed them to purely cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action;”

Having taught the ten wholesome paths of action, he further provided all manner of articles of enjoyment for up to a thousand kalpas, and only then instructed them to purely cultivate the four dhyānas.
Having taught the four dhyānas, he again provided all manner of articles of enjoyment for up to a hundred thousand kalpas, and only then instructed them to practice the four immeasurable minds.
Furthermore, he provided all manner of articles of enjoyment for up to a billion kalpas, and only then instructed them to practice the four formless attainments.
Furthermore, one might provide all manner of articles of enjoyment for a hundred billion kalpas, and only thereafter instruct them so that they attain the fruit of Srotāpanna;
furthermore, one might provide all manner of articles of enjoyment for a thousand billion kalpas, and only thereafter instruct them so that they attain the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin;
furthermore, one might provide all manner of articles of enjoyment for a hundred thousand billion kalpas, and only thereafter instruct them so that they attain the fruit of Anāgāmin.
Furthermore, one may provide all manner of articles of enjoyment for as many as a hundred billion nayutas of kalpas, and thereafter instruct them so that they attain the fruit of Arhatship;
furthermore, one may provide all manner of articles of enjoyment for as many as a thousand billion nayutas of kalpas, and thereafter instruct them so that they all become Pratyekabuddhas.
O Son of the Buddha! What do you think?
Would the merit of that person be considered great?
Śakra addressed him, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
As for that person’s merit, none but the Buddhas can know it; all others are entirely unable to do so.”
Dharmamati said: "O Son of the Buddha!

Compared to the treasury of merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind, the merit of that person does not equal even one part in a hundred, one part in a thousand, nor even an incalculable, incomparable, or ineffable fraction thereof."
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

When all Buddhas first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, it is not for the sake of providing all the articles of pleasure for the sentient beings within ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in each of the ten directions, nor for the sake of [remaining] for a hundred eons up to a thousand *koṭi-nayuta* eons, that they appear in the world; rather—

Nor do they appear in the world for the sake of teaching so many sentient beings to purely cultivate the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions, the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, or the path of the pratyekabuddha; rather,
they resolve upon bodhicitta because they wish to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed,
and they resolve upon bodhicitta because they wish to fill all worlds throughout the ten directions.
They resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully deliver all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully know the formation and destruction of all worlds;
they resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully know the arising of defilement and purity among the sentient beings within all worlds.
They resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully know the intrinsic purity of the nature of all worlds;
they resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully know the false afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds on enlightenment because they wish to fully know the death here and birth there of all living beings.
They resolve their minds on Bodhi because they wish to fully know the skillful means regarding the faculties of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds on Bodhi because they wish to fully know the thoughts and mental activities of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds on Bodhi because they wish to fully discern all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
“Because they wish to fully know the equal realm of all Buddhas, they resolve their minds on Bodhi.
‘O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, let us set aside this analogy:”

Suppose there were a person who, in a single moment of thought, could pass through immeasurable worlds to the east. By means of such sovereign supernatural power, even if that person were to travel eastward for immeasurable, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they still could not reach the limit of those worlds.

Furthermore, suppose there were a second person whose supernatural power was sovereign, able in a single moment of thought to pass through all the worlds traversed by the former person during immeasurable, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; even if this second person were to travel eastward from here for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they still could not reach the limit of those worlds.

Furthermore, suppose there were a third person whose supernatural power was sovereign, able in a single moment of thought to pass through all the worlds traversed by the former person during immeasurable, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the fourth person possesses sovereign spiritual power; in a single moment of thought, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the former person during immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the fifth person possesses sovereign spiritual power; in a single moment of thought, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the former person during immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the sixth person possesses sovereign spiritual power; in a single moment of thought, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the former person during immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the seventh person possesses sovereign supernatural power; in a single moment, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the previous person over immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the eighth person possesses sovereign supernatural power; in a single moment, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the previous person over immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the ninth person possesses sovereign supernatural power; in a single moment, he can traverse the worlds traversed by the previous person over immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Furthermore, the tenth person possesses sovereign supernormal power such that, in a single moment of thought, he can traverse worlds further than those traversed by the preceding persons over immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

That tenth person, by means of this most excellent and sovereign supernormal power, travels eastward for immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, yet still does not reach the limit of the worlds; the same applies to the worlds of the ten directions.

If one were to continue in this manner until there were a hundred such persons, using their most excellent and sovereign supernormal powers to travel through the ten directions for immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it might still be possible to know and reach their limits; however, the treasury of merit of a Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment cannot be known. Why is this?
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment does not limit themselves by saying they do so only for the sake of sentient beings in such-and-such a world;

rather, they resolve their mind on enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, desiring to discern and know all worlds,
and desiring to know that a subtle world is itself a great world, and that a great world is itself a subtle world.
They know that few worlds are identical to many worlds, and they know that many worlds are identical to few worlds;
they know that vast worlds are identical to narrow worlds, and they know that narrow worlds are identical to vast worlds;
they know that a single world is identical to immeasurable and boundless worlds, and they know that immeasurable and boundless worlds are identical to a single world.
They know how to enter a single world from within immeasurable and boundless worlds, and they know how to enter immeasurable and boundless worlds from within a single world;
they know that defiled worlds are precisely pure worlds, and they know that pure worlds are precisely defiled worlds;
within a single pore, they discern and know all worlds, and within all worlds, they discern and know the nature of a single pore.

Knowing that one world gives birth to all worlds, and knowing that all worlds are like empty space, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because they desire to know all worlds in a single thought-moment, leaving nothing out.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy:

suppose there were a person who, in a single thought-moment, could discern and know the total number of formations and disintegrations in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds in the eastern direction; and suppose this person, through diligent skillful means, proceeding step by step in every thought-moment for immeasurable, countless, and incalculable eons, desired to calculate and fully know the number of formations and disintegrations of the worlds in the eastern direction—even then, they would still be unable to know it.

Furthermore, suppose there is a second person who, within a single thought-moment, is able to fully comprehend the number of world-systems formed and destroyed throughout the immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the first person. Even with such diligent application and successive moments of thought, this person would still be unable to exhaustively know the number of world-systems formed and destroyed in the eastern direction over immeasurable and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
and so it continues in this manner, progressing through to the tenth person.

That tenth person can, within a single thought-moment, fully comprehend the number of world-systems formed and destroyed over immeasurable, boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as calculated by the ninth person. Yet, despite this person’s diligent application and successive moments of mindfulness, even over immeasurable, boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they cannot exhaustively know the number of world-systems formed and destroyed in the eastern direction; the same applies to all ten directions.

While the number of world-systems formed and destroyed throughout the immeasurable, boundless worlds of the ten directions may still be known, the treasury of merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*) cannot be known. Why is this?

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind does so without limitation, because they resolve upon bodhicitta out of the knowledge of the number of kalpas and the formation and destruction of that many worlds;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva resolves upon bodhicitta because they desire to fully understand the number of kalpas and the formation and destruction of all worlds;
and because they desire to know that a long kalpa is itself a short kalpa, and a short kalpa is itself a long kalpa.
They know that one eon is identical to incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, and that incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* eons are identical to one eon;
they know all eons in which there is a Buddha,
and they know all eons in which there is no Buddha.
They know that within the kalpa of one Buddha there are immeasurable Buddhas, and they know that within the kalpas of immeasurable Buddhas there is one Buddha;
they know that within different kalpas there are non-different kalpas, and they know that within non-different kalpas there are different kalpas;
they know that kalpas with an end are kalpas without an end, and they know that kalpas without an end are kalpas with an end.
They know that immeasurable eons are but a single thought-moment, and they know that a single thought-moment is immeasurable eons;
they know that all eons enter into the non-eon, and they know that the non-eon enters into all eons.

Desiring to fully comprehend the number of eons and the formation and destruction of all worlds throughout the past, future, and present limits, they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s first great vow-adornment, namely:
the illumination of wisdom that fully knows all kalpas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Setting this analogy aside for a moment:

suppose there were a person who, within a single thought-moment, could fully know the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds; yet, even if such a person applied diligent skillful means, proceeding sequentially from thought-moment to thought-moment, they would be unable to exhaustively know the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings in the eastern worlds throughout immeasurable, countless, and incalculable eons (*kalpa*).

In this manner, the succession continues until it reaches the tenth person. This tenth person, through diligent application for immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas, is able to fully comprehend in a single thought-moment the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings known by the ninth person. Yet, despite such diligent application, proceeding step by step through every thought-moment for immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas, this person still cannot exhaustively know the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings in the worlds of the eastern direction;

the same applies to the ten directions. While the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings in the immeasurable, boundless, and asankhyeya worlds of the ten directions might still be comprehended, the treasury of merit of a Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind toward enlightenment cannot be known.
Why is this? Sons of the Buddha!

It is not because they wish to know the various inclinations and desires of sentient beings in only so many worlds that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved their minds on enlightenment give rise to the bodhicitta; rather, it is for the sake of knowing them all.
They resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because they wish to fully know the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions;
because they wish to know that these various and immeasurable desires and inclinations are, in essence, a single desire, yet without destroying the distinct nature of each individual desire;
because they wish to fully know the ocean of desires and inclinations of all sentient beings; and because they wish to know the desire of even a single sentient being...
This is the aspiration of all sentient beings: they desire to fully know the various desires and pleasures of all sentient beings—past, future, and present;

they desire to fully know similar desires and dissimilar desires; they desire to know that all desires are one single desire, and that one single desire is all desires; they desire to attain such complete fulfillment as this.
They come with the power of various desires and pleasures: desiring to know superior desire and unsurpassed desire;
desire with remainder and desire without remainder; equal desire and unequal desire; desire with a basis and desire without a basis;
common desire and uncommon desire; finite desire and infinite desire; and wholesome desire.
Unwholesome desire, worldly desire, supramundane desire, the desire for great wisdom,
pure desire, superior desire, the desire for unimpeded knowledge, the desire for the liberation of an unimpeded-knowledge Buddha,
pure desire, impure desire, extensive desire, narrow desire, subtle desire, coarse desire; therefore, one generates the [aspiration for awakening].
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
desiring to fully know all sentient beings—specifically that each and every sentient being possesses ten kinds of desire, namely:

desire born of suffering, desire for means, desire for hope, desire for attachment to flavors, desire arising according to causes, desire arising according to conditions, exhausted desire, and universal desire—a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to analytically understand and fully comprehend this web of desires gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy:

suppose there were a person who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the various faculties of sentient beings throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds; and by means of this wisdom and diligent skillful means, proceeding sequentially from thought-moment to thought-moment, they were unable to exhaustively know the various faculties of all sentient beings in every world of the eastern direction—even extending to the full knowledge of every single sentient being, each of whom possesses ten kinds of faculties—throughout immeasurable, countless, and incalculable eons.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy:

suppose there were someone who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the various aspirations of sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds in the eastern direction—and to speak extensively, even to the point of knowing that every single sentient being possesses ten kinds of aspiration.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment:

suppose there were someone who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the various skillful means of sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds—and to speak extensively, even to the point of knowing that every single sentient being possesses ten kinds of skillful means.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment:

suppose there were someone who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the mental states of every single thought of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds—and to speak more broadly, suppose they could fully know that every single sentient being possesses ten kinds of mind.
O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment:

suppose there were a person who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the various karmas of sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds, and so forth, until they fully knew that every single sentient being possesses ten kinds of karma.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy:

suppose there were a person who, in a single thought-moment, could fully know the various afflictions of all sentient beings in the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the eastern direction. Even if this person applied diligent skillful means, proceeding through each successive thought-moment for immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable eons, they would still be unable to know all the various afflictions of every sentient being in the eastern direction.”
In this manner, it is passed on successively until reaching the tenth person.

This tenth person, regarding the various afflictions of sentient beings known by the ninth person over immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, can distinguish and know them all within a single thought-moment. Yet, through diligent application and successive moments of mindfulness, even over immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this person still cannot fully know all the various afflictions of all sentient beings; this remains true even when extending to the ten directions.

While the various afflictions of all sentient beings in that many worlds may still be known, the treasury of merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*) cannot be known.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind does not limit themselves to wishing to know only the various afflictions of sentient beings within such-and-such worlds; rather, they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They resolve their minds on bodhicitta because they desire to fully discern and understand the various afflictions of all sentient beings;
that is to say:
they desire to fully know light afflictions, heavy afflictions, afflictions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and afflictions of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
The immeasurable afflictions of each and every sentient being; the various kinds of discursive thoughts and afflictions of all sentient beings;
afflictions based on ignorance; afflictions associated with craving; the affliction of the unwholesome root of greed;
the affliction of the unwholesome root of hatred; the affliction of the unwholesome root of delusion; and the afflictions of equal proportions.
All afflictions— fundamental afflictions, afflictions of "self" and "mine," afflictions of pride,
afflictions arising from false recollection and delusion, afflictions such as the sixty-two views born of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
afflictions of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and afflictions of obstructions— he desires to fully understand all these for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because they are born into the net of afflictions and delusions, yet possess great kindness, great compassion,
and all-encompassing wisdom, they resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment:

suppose there were a person who, within a single thought-moment, could see all the present Buddhas and all sentient beings in the infinite and boundless worlds of the eastern direction; and suppose this person were able to revere, prostrate to, honor, praise, and contemplate them with a single mind, making various offerings of immeasurable superior flavors of food and drink, incense, flowers, necklaces, silken banners, flags and canopies, exquisitely adorned palaces, curtains, jeweled nets spread as coverings, and lion-thrones decorated with many jewels; and suppose this person, through diligent skillful means, were to offer such a multitude of wonderful requisites to these Buddhas in every successive thought-moment for immeasurable, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.”

Furthermore, he exhorted and instructed those sentient beings to use such various and wondrous offerings to make offerings to the Buddhas for immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. After those Tathāgatas had entered *parinirvāṇa*, he further built stupas made of immeasurable jewels as offerings for each and every Tathāgata. These stupas were so high and vast that each one completely filled immeasurable and boundless worlds; moreover, they were adorned with the most exquisite and precious jewels. Within each stupa were immeasurable and innumerable images of the Tathāgatas, the radiance of which shone universally throughout immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds. Furthermore, he exhorted each and every sentient being to erect jeweled stupas for the Tathāgatas, making them as magnificent and beautiful as before, and it was likewise so in the worlds of the ten directions.
"O Son of the Buddha! What do you think?
Is the merit of that person not indeed great?"
Śakra replied: "The merit of that person is known only to the Buddha; no one else is capable of fathoming it. Dharmamati replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!

The treasury of merit of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind toward enlightenment is such that the merit of those other persons does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, nor even a fraction that is incalculable, incomparable, or indescribable.”
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were a person who, regarding the first person and the sentient beings he exhorted, applied diligent skillful means, moment by moment in succession, throughout immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and was able to produce within a single thought-moment all the meritorious deeds and articles of offering performed during those times. Such diligent application of skillful means by this person, moment by moment in succession throughout immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of merit from making offerings, is described at length as before;
and so it continues in turn up to the tenth person, described at length in the same manner.

The treasury of merit of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment is such that the merit of that other person does not equal even one part in a hundred, one part in a thousand, nor even an incalculable, incomparable, or ineffable fraction thereof. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha!

That bodhisattva does not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of making offerings to a limited number of Tathāgatas; rather, he resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because he desires to make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time throughout the worlds of the ten directions, equal in extent to the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.

Having generated this mind, they attain the unobstructed wisdom of all Buddhas throughout the limits of the past; they attain faith in the merits of all Buddhas throughout the limits of the future; and they attain knowledge of the wisdom taught by all Buddhas throughout the limits of the present. All the merits of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas entirely believe in, incline toward, uphold, and cultivate them, attaining realization through personal experience and becoming equal to all the merits of all Buddhas. Why is this?
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind does so because they wish not to sever the nature of all Buddhas;
because they wish to cause the mind of loving-kindness and compassion to fill all worlds so that no sentient beings are left behind;
and because they wish to fully deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
Because they wish to fully know the formation and destruction of all worlds;
because they wish to fully know the arising of the defilement and purity of sentient beings in all worlds;
and because they wish to cause all sentient beings within the three realms of existence to attain complete purification.
Because they wish to fully know the mental activities, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
because they wish to fully know the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings as they pass from this life to that;
and because they wish to fully know the faculties and skillful means of all sentient beings.
Because they wish to fully know the mental activities of every sentient being;
because they wish to fully know all sentient beings of the three periods of time;
and because they wish to fully know the complete merits of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because they wish to fully know the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
because they wish to fully know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time are endowed with pure dharmas;
and because they wish to fully know the mark of equality in the dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because they wish to fully know the purity of the causes and conditions for the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
because they wish to fully know the power of the wisdom cultivated by all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and because they wish to fully possess the dharmas of fearlessness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because they desire to fully possess and adorn the unique qualities of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
because they desire to fully attain the equal and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, which is as vast and boundless as the dharma-realm;
they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment is himself a Buddha;

he is equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, equal to the realm of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and equal to the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. He attains the single body and the infinite bodies of the Tathāgata, and the sentient beings transformed by the equal wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are all entirely equal to him.

They are able to shake all worlds; they are able to universally illumine all worlds; they are able to bring rest to the sufferings of the evil realms in all worlds; they are able to adorn and purify all worlds; they manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in all worlds; they cause all sentient beings to attain joy; they cause all sentient beings to understand the profound Dharma-realm; they are able to protect and maintain the lineage of all Buddhas; and they fully attain the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.

That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment is never separated from the Buddhas of the three periods of time and their Dharmas; nor is he separated from all Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and the dharmas they practice; nor from mundane and supramundane dharmas, nor from sentient beings and the dharmas pertaining to sentient beings. He single-mindedly seeks the unimpeded wisdom of Bodhi.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and by the force of the treasury of merit of bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment, worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways. A rain of celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial garlands, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments fell;
naturally, subtle and wondrous musical sounds were produced, and the roar of the lion’s voice resounded, emitting great radiance that universally illuminated the ten directions.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, all named Dharmamati. Each manifested his own body, appeared before the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, and addressed him, saying: "Excellent!
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!

You have well expounded the treasury of merits of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind. We Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand buddha-fields, likewise all proclaim this treasury of merits of a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind; and so it is for all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

When the Bodhisattva Dharmamati spoke these words concerning the treasury of merit of the Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment], sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-worlds all attained the treasury of merit of the Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds and gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

We now bestow upon them all the prediction [of their future Buddhahood]: in a future age, each shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood throughout the ten directions, all sharing the same name of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Pure Mind (*Vimalacitta*). We shall all protect and uphold this Dharma for the sake of all future Bodhisattvas;
just as in this Sahā world, in Jambudvīpa among the four continents, beneath the Bodhi tree, at [the place of] Śākyamuni...
Upon the summit of Mount Meru, in the Palace of Sublime Victory, he expounded this Dharma and transformed sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—
thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds that are immeasurable,
incalculable, inconceivable, boundless, and inexpressible, equal to the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
Furthermore, it is said that they teach this Dharma to transform sentient beings; those who preach the Dharma are all named Dharmamati (Dharma-Wisdom).

This is due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, the power of the Buddha’s original vows, the manifestation of the Buddha-Dharma, the universal illumination of the light of wisdom, the understanding of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the suchness of the Dharma, and the joy of all Bodhisattvas.
“Because of joy; because of praising the merits of all Buddhas; because of fully knowing the equality of all Buddhas;
and because of understanding that the Dharma-realm is without duality.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati surveyed the ten directions, surveyed the entire great assembly, surveyed the realm of empty space, and surveyed the realm of sentient beings who have attained accomplishment. He did not contradict the retribution of karma, which is as pure as the realm of empty space. Desiring to uproot the defilements of sentient beings within the three realms of existence, desiring to cause sentient beings to attain vast liberation, desiring to know their various faculties, observing the three periods of time equally as they rightly tend toward Nirvana, and wishing to manifest his own profound and pure merits, he, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, spoke in verse:
"With a heart of great kindness and great compassion, filling the realms of the ten directions,
distinguishing all Buddha-fields, the Buddha-dharma, and the three periods of time;
desiring to possess the merits of a Buddha and the ocean-like treasury of the Bodhisattva teachings,"
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they first resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Desiring to discern and know all categories of living beings, as vast as space and equal to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
as well as all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma, they set forth.
Desiring to attain the state of all Buddhas, the power of reaching the destination of all paths,
and the accomplishment of non-retrogression for the benefit of all living beings,
one should always give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Distant from thoughts of anger, One cultivates a mind of benefit.
With the light of loving-kindness illuminating the ten directions, One acts as a refuge for all beings;
All Buddhas protect and keep one in mind— Such merit is inconceivable.
Desiring to know them all in detail— the Buddha-fields of all Buddhas,
the wondrous Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, which is profoundly deep and inconceivable,
a treasury of immeasurable merit, with wisdom both profound and vast—
Because of this initial resolve, they single-mindedly seek the Bodhi of the Buddhas;
desiring to discern and know all categories of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, their wisdom is without obstruction.
Whether coarse or subtle, all worlds— be they narrow, vast, or immeasurable—
the Bodhisattva knows the one within all, and knows all within the one.
Practicing therein with diligence and without negligence, he remains ever heedful.
Neither wearying of nor attached to suffering or pleasure, for the sake of delivering sentient beings;
all Buddhas appear before them, whom they joyfully contemplate without satiety,
as they enter entirely into the profound Dharma, the ocean of immeasurable merit.
Toward all beings in the five realms, he feels compassion as for an only son;
may they be cleansed of all defilements and become fully endowed with the pure Dharma.
Desiring that the lineage of the Buddhas never be severed, he brings it to ultimate continuity.
Subduing all māras, Destroying them without remainder;
Contemplating the Tathāgata with equanimity, And the characteristics of all dharmas of the three periods of time—
The profound and subtle Dharma— One should constantly practice it without negligence.
The Bodhisattva always delights in contemplating the realm of all Buddhas;
therefore, the Tathāgatas confer upon them the empowerment of nectar-like wisdom.
Their faith is indestructible, as firm and solid as a diamond.
Toward all Tathāgatas, one recognizes their kindness and repays it.
This most supreme state, the light of immeasurable wisdom, is self-realized and not derived from another;
this is the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind.
He is fully able to discern and know the desires of sentient beings in the five realms,
their various karmic retributions, and all the movements of their minds.
He knows the sharpness or dullness of their faculties and their immeasurable, innumerable natures.
The supreme realm of all things is the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve for awakening.
This bodhicitta is immeasurable, equal to the pure dharma-realm;
it is unattached and without dependence, untainted like space.
Having accomplished the wisdom of the Buddha, their minds are without obstruction;
they clearly realize the limit of reality, which is quiescent, extinguished, and free from falsehood.
They thoroughly understand the minds of sentient beings, yet they harbor no conception of "sentient beings."
Through the skillful analysis of dharmas, they ultimately reach the other shore;
throughout immeasurable and innumerable kalpas, they are able to discern and know them all.
They travel to the various Buddha-fields, clearly understanding the most profound Dharma.
If one can discern and know the immeasurable teachings of all Buddhas,
the treasury of the pure Dharma-realm, understanding them truly without doubt;
and if one deeply comprehends the faculties of sentient beings, reaching the ultimate further shore—
Contemplating all phenomena with equanimity, one is then equal to the Tathāgata.
With a pure and immeasurable mind, always standing before the Buddhas,
one reveres and honors them, making offerings to the Lions among Men.
They behold all Buddhas with joyful vision, never wearying of it;
those Tathāgatas protect and keep this bodhisattva in mind.
Regarding all profound and wondrous dharmas, they discern them without obstruction.
Without attachment and without dependence, his mind is pure like space.
That Lion among Men, whose ocean of wisdom is profound and vast,
enters meditative absorption in stillness, perceiving the three periods of time without obstruction.
Firm and unshakable, nothing can destroy it;
Dedicated to the unsurpassed path, never has it been interrupted.
Leaving darkness for the light of rectitude, He resolved to study all wholesome dharmas.
Always joyfully contemplating quiescence, one is fully endowed with true nature.
Silent and beyond the path of speech, viewing all things with equanimity and without distinction, one does not discriminate among phenomena; this is that which arises from Suchness.
They are able to discern and know, The profound realms of all Buddhas;
Tranquil, they enter into meditative absorption, With the three types of supernormal knowledge free from obstruction.
Within the worlds of the ten directions, In all the Buddha-fields,
Through the Bodhisattva’s power of mastery, in a single thought-moment they pervade all;
possessing immeasurable and incalculable skillful means,
they travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions— such a one is called a true son of the Buddha.
Fully endowed with the mind of great compassion, Cooling and removing the thirst of craving;
With great loving-kindness mindful of all beings, Unimpeded like space.
Toward those classes of sentient beings, He does not give rise to the notion of "sentient beings."
Having completely abandoned all falsehood, they wander pure throughout the ten directions.
To all those living beings therein, they constantly bestow fearlessness;
such is their practice of truth, and thus they are equal to the Tathāgata.
Constantly preaching the most profound Dharma, pure and free from all attachment,
for this reason the Buddhas of the ten directions all protect and keep them in mind.
Throughout the past and future worlds, across immeasurable and innumerable kalpas.
Recalling them all in successive order, he possesses complete discerning knowledge.
Within the present, throughout all worlds in the ten directions,
the Bodhisattva is able to pervade everywhere, delivering all living beings.
With profound wisdom and correct observation, he understands clearly without obstruction;
he fully knows that all things arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and that they are subject to decay and lack any inherent solidity.
For all classes of sentient beings who possess doubts and difficulties, [he provides resolution].
The Bodhisattva completely eliminates [all afflictions] and dwells securely within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
With the power of fearlessness, the Bodhisattva subdues all Māras and is able to extinguish the darkness of ignorance for the sake of all sentient beings.
Whether the world is forming or decaying, one understands all through discernment;
if one can contemplate in this way, there will be no doubt regarding the realm of the Buddha.
By observing the phenomena of the three periods of time, the net of doubt is forever removed.
Toward all Tathāgatas, one’s pure faith is indestructible.
Abiding securely through the power of faith, one achieves the power of wisdom;
because wisdom is purified, one attains definitive understanding of reality.
Until the very end of the future, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
I desire to cause all multitudes to ultimately attain liberation.
Amidst the boundless cycle of birth and death, I shall apply myself with diligence, never wearying.
In all places of the hells, he undergoes suffering for the sake of sentient beings;
as a treasury of merit and wisdom, he fully accomplishes all perfections.
He is able to skillfully discern the faculties of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, they are able to discern and know the various karmas of sentient beings;
according to those karmas and their respective remedies, the Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma for them,
acting in accordance with worldly ways through a heart of great compassion.
Regarding all phenomena, they have fully realized emptiness and selflessness;
within each and every sound, they expound immeasurable teachings.
The Bodhisattvas emit great rays of light in various subtle and wondrous colors.
Universally illuminating the realms of the ten directions, It extinguishes all darkness.
At the tip of each ray of light, Upon pure jewel-flower seats,
Bodhisattvas are seated, all of them Expounding the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Within a single pore, one universally beholds the lands of the ten directions,
their wondrous adornments, and the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
at the abode of each and every Tathāgata, they are surrounded by immeasurable multitudes.
With pure and wondrous wisdom, they clearly understand the minds of sentient beings.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in immeasurable Buddha-fields, Bodhisattvas,
by the power of their spiritual penetrations, reach them all in a single thought-moment.
Out of reverence and to benefit all sentient beings, he made offerings to the Buddhas;
at the abode of each and every Teacher, he inquired about and resolved the most profound meanings.
Toward all World-Honored Ones, he first conceived the thought of them as his compassionate fathers.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they distinguish the practices of bodhisattvas.
With clear and pure, sharp wisdom, they penetrate the profound treasury of the Dharma;
giving birth to immeasurable knowledge, their realization of the Buddha-dharma is unimpeded.
Though one were to analyze and expound the dharma-realm for immeasurable and incalculable eons,
those eons might reach their end, yet the dharma-realm would never be exhausted.
Contemplating all phenomena with equanimity, the mind remains unstained.
Without weariness toward the suffering of birth and death, their wisdom is free from obstruction.
This is the unsurpassed lineage of the Buddhas, the royal house of the Dharma of the three periods of time;
all the dharmas of the Tathāgatas are born from this Bodhisattva.
The pure and wondrous Dharma-body manifests in various forms,
Just like a great illusionist, whose desired manifestations are seen by all.
Sometimes dwelling among sentient beings, he brings them to the ultimate fulfillment of bodhisattva practice.
Or again, manifesting his initial birth, Renouncing the world to practice the Way;
Or, beneath the King of Trees, Spontaneously attaining perfect enlightenment;
Or, for the sake of sentient beings, Manifesting entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Abiding now in the profound and wondrous, The immeasurable and sovereign Dharma,
Neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas, Nor any others, can fathom it. The body, speech,
and mind of the Bodhisattva Are quiescent and devoid of the mark of arising.
Universally responding to all worlds, there is no skillful means that is not manifested.
Such true sons of the Buddha possess realms that are profoundly deep and wondrous;
if sentient beings were to attempt to conceive of them through thought, their minds would become confused and driven to madness.
Fully endowed with all [perfections], they dwell securely in unimpeded wisdom;
they universally manifest all Tathāgatas and their immeasurable powers of mastery.
The treasury of the Bodhisattvas' merit is peerless in the world.
How much more so for the Most Victorious Honored One, Immeasurable and inconceivable!
Although the Bodhisattva has not yet attained The perfection of all-knowledge,
Through immeasurable gateways to the Dharma, He has reached the ultimate further shore.
All supreme and wondrous dharmas are already fully perfected;
seeking exclusively for bodhi, they have reached the ultimate path of the One Vehicle.
Regarding all those sentient beings, they skillfully know the proper and improper times.
For the sake of benefiting [beings], he manifests great supernormal powers;
his single body completely fills all buddha-fields,
emitting pure radiance that shines with peerless brilliance.
Illuminating the realms of the ten directions, He extinguishes all darkness;
Universally raining down the sublime Dharma, He is like a great dragon king of the ocean.
Observing all phenomena, He sees them as false and illusory.
Due to the power of afflictions and karma, beings constantly revolve in the cycle of birth and death.
With a heart of great compassion, you universally shelter all living creatures;
through pure and wondrous skillful means, you deliver immeasurable multitudes.
The power of the Bodhisattva’s merit is equal to that of all Tathāgatas;
his ocean of immeasurable wisdom is as pure as space.
Having fully cultivated the Bodhisattva practices throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, he has attained this state.
With diligent application of skillful means, they desire to deliver all sentient beings.
They are able to discern and know the various conducts of living beings,
causing them to cultivate pure karma and aspire to seek the unsurpassed path.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing this supreme and wondrous Dharma,
is certain not to regress, as they clearly contemplate all-knowledge.
All worlds are immeasurable and inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva is able, within a single thought-moment, to pervade them all.
Having distanced himself from false conceptualizations, his mind is like space;
as the one pure Dharma-body, he universally responds to all worlds.
Tranquil and eternally unmoving, manifesting throughout the ten directions,
they discern all phenomena without grasping at the characteristics of any dharma.
Thoroughly understanding all dharmas, their minds remain unstained.
He delivers all sentient beings, yet there is no one who is liberated.
All classes of living beings, with their various hopes and aspirations—
whether dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate— are quiescent like empty space.
In accordance with the various classes of beings and their diverse desires and inclinations,
he possesses immeasurable powers of mastery and is able to manifest transformations for them all.
Just as a master illusionist can manifest various forms, [so too does the Buddha appear].
The sovereign power of the Bodhisattva fills the realms of the ten directions.
The Bodhisattva’s pure Dharma-body is immeasurable and equal to space;
according to the desires and inclinations of sentient beings, there is nothing that does not manifest.
The mind is unstained, true and without falsehood;
the dharmas of affliction are pure and entirely non-existent.
Whether in liberation or non-liberation, the mind remains unstained.
Universally bestowing upon suffering sentient beings the unsurpassed bliss of nirvāṇa;
throughout all worlds, possessing wisdom and fearlessness,
and fully endowed with the various marks and signs, they have perfected the unsurpassed path.
In a single thought, they discern all the characteristics of phenomena throughout the past, future, and present; yet when sought, these are found to be non-existent.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the prior limit and thoroughly understands the past.
The characteristics of the future limit are likewise ultimately such.
They discern and fully know all Buddha-worlds;
having eliminated all afflictions, they are replete with every merit.
Always delighting in contemplating tranquility, they ultimately proceed toward nirvāṇa;
rejoicing in the samādhi of non-contention, their minds have no point of reliance.
The Bodhisattvas are equal to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); there is nothing that can equal them.
Having perfected the firm practice, they are definitively non-retrogressive.
Cultivating all supreme practices, they dwell in tranquility without dependence;
their minds are ever-abiding, as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
The pure and wondrous conduct of Bodhisattvas fills all dharma realms;
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know them completely and distinctly.
Those who wish to seek the wisdom of the Teacher and reach the ultimate, most supreme path [should study this].
The profound all-knowledge, the unsurpassed king of liberation—
With courageous and diligent perseverance, swiftly arouse the bodhicitta.
Desiring to seek the most supreme bliss, one should quickly sever all outflows (*āsrava*).
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first gives rise to the pure mind,
the treasury of merit within that mind cannot be fully described.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they praise the conduct of the Tathāgata.
Listen with single-minded attention to the path practiced by the Most Victorious One:
Even if all immeasurable Buddha-fields were ground into the finest dust,
and one mote of dust were placed in each field, one could discern and know them all.
Within all these buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas of every realm have been expounding this treasury of primary merit, yet it remains inexhaustible.
They skillfully discern sentient beings, yet they harbor no conception of "sentient beings."
Skillfully understanding all languages, yet having no conceptualization of speech;
possessing profound and unimpeded wisdom, they discern all worlds;
skillfully understanding the formation and destruction of kalpas, yet having no conceptualization of formation or destruction.
With a pure and vast mind, like the nature of space,
you clearly understand the phenomena of the three periods of time and all worlds.
You have eradicated all afflictions, exhausting them forever without remainder.
The unimpeded contemplation of tranquil extinction— this is the True Dharma of the Buddha.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, at the abodes of all Tathāgatas,
he reaches them all in a single thought-moment, yet his mind remains unstained.
Skillfully understanding the non-arising nature, The suchness of the limit of reality,
All various kinds of marks Are entirely devoid of true reality.
Immeasurable and incalculable, All the Tathāgatas—
Together with their pure retinues, they all went to pay homage and make offerings.
They constantly delighted in questioning the Tathāgata regarding the profound and subtle Dharma;
all these bodhisattvas were dedicated to the practice of pure vows.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
All the Teachers are seen in a single thought-moment, Yet the mind has no point of reliance.
Within all the three realms of existence, There are the most supreme and wondrous merits.
By means of these pure practices, they adorn all Buddha-fields.
With the unobstructed eye of wisdom, they skillfully understand all sentient beings;
they discern that nothing exists, remaining far removed from and untainted by attachment.
Skillfully understanding the faculties of sentient beings, their afflictions and habitual tendencies,
and the various desires of living beings, they thoroughly comprehend the inconceivable.
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas first know the minds of sentient beings.
According to those who are to be delivered, the wise one preaches the Dharma.
Skillfully knowing the proper and improper times, as well as the pure and impure conduct of sentient beings,
he gradually causes them to become purified until they ultimately attain liberation.
Immeasurable nayutas of profound samādhis, The Bodhisattva, through the power of mastery,
can enter them all in a single thought-moment. Regarding the characteristics of entering,
arising from, and abiding in these samādhis, He thoroughly discerns and knows them all.
Regarding immeasurable realms, you have well understood the conditions for their abiding and arising.
Such wisdom as this is entirely and fully perfected;
before long, you shall attain Bodhi, free from all obstacles.
Constantly acting for the benefit of sentient beings, they rightly proceed toward the light of wisdom;
they are able to bestow upon sentient beings the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Man.
They are fully capable of skillfully discerning the length of all kalpas.
Day and night, as well as months and years—these too he observes skillfully.
With right mindfulness and without negligence, he thoroughly understands all worlds;
he discerns the various Buddha-fields, which in reality are without distinction.
Able to skillfully discern and know all worlds,
yet within those lands of the ten directions, they harbor no conceptual discrimination.
Observing correctly in this manner, they perceive the worlds of the ten directions.
He purifies all lands, yet his mind remains unattached.
Having perfected the power of wisdom, he is equal to all Tathāgatas;
through the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, he discerns and knows all sentient beings.
He fully knows the various classes of sentient beings and the retributions for their good and evil deeds;
regarding the past and future worlds, he is clear-sighted and unimpeded.
He knows all worlds and the diverse natures of sentient beings.
Within those three realms of existence, they are able to discern and know them all.
Regarding all classes of sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern and know their faculties— whether superior, middling, or inferior.
The various classes of all sentient beings— their superior, middling,
and inferior desires and pleasures, whether pure or impure— he is able to discern and know them all.
Having discerned and known these sentient beings, he knows all the paths leading to every destination.
Having forever severed the continuity of conditions, they have ultimately transcended the three realms of existence.
Regarding all samādhis, meditative attainments, dhyānas, and liberations—
whether arising from defilement or purity— they are able to discern and know them all.
To know successive past lives, and to experience the suffering and pleasure therein—
such discernment as this is the power of the Tathāgata.
Regarding all that is wholesome and unwholesome, and the afflictions and karma of sentient beings:
Distinguishing the births within the five realms, one ultimately attains nirvāṇa.
If all outflows are not yet exhausted, one is able to proceed to birth in various places;
once the habit-energies of afflictions are extinguished, one reaches the ultimate, unsurpassed path.
Using skillful means to deliver sentient beings, extinguishing defilements and perfecting the pure path—
the wise one who can discern this is truly a hero among men.
Endowed with the ten powers, the light of his wisdom dispels all darkness.
Abiding in the most supreme power, all doubt is utterly extinguished.
Within each and every pore, immeasurable Buddha-fields and all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are clearly seen.
Whether defiled or pure, with all their various wondrous adornments,
he knows them all distinctly according to the karmic actions of those beings.
Within each and every atom, there are all the Buddha-fields.
The Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas— All the sons of the Buddha see them all.
All lands do not accumulate, Neither chaotic nor crowded;
All enter into a single land, Yet there is nothing that enters.
The lands of the ten directions, equal to space and the dharma-realm,
he can fully discern and know within a single pore;
he universally beholds all the most supreme ones throughout the realms of the ten directions.
The subtle, pure, and magnificent adornments of all Buddha-fields, all Tathāgatas, and their purified lands—
the wise perceive them all within a single pore.
The differentiated characteristics of the three periods of time, And all realms of phenomena;
The continuity of seasons and years— By discerning these, one attains liberation.
Such a true son of the Buddha Is fully endowed with fearlessness.
These are called heroes among men, those of clear understanding and wisdom;
such profound Dharma gates as these, the wise discern them all.
Toward the Tathāgata, they maintain immeasurable reverence and joy.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, he has nurtured a treasury of merit.
To make offerings to all Buddhas and to deliver sentient beings,
he manifests various forms through his immeasurable power of mastery.
The realm of his wisdom is equal to that of all Tathāgatas;
in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, he has fully accomplished all that he studied.
Regarding the treasury of the profound and tranquil Dharma, he delights in it entirely without ever being satiated.
With a heart of reverence and respect toward all Teachers,
they practice the bodhisattva path and constantly drink the nectar of the Dharma;
being able to discern it all well, they nurture the qualities of wisdom.
With unimpeded eloquence regarding Bodhi and profound samādhis,
their faith is immovable like Mount Sumeru;
they nurture all sentient beings as a treasury of all meritorious virtues.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with immeasurable great compassion,
universally mindful of all sentient beings, has a mind free from attachment.
Bestowing the joy of the knowledge of all modes upon all living beings, he practices such giving.
Desiring to rescue the entire world, To forever leave behind the defilements of affliction,
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Great compassionate heart is immeasurable;
Regarding the Buddha, themselves, and all sentient beings, They view them as equal, without distinction.
One contemplates the mark of tranquil extinction; all phenomena are like space.
The wise contemplate them thus as the true nature of all things.
The Bodhisattva’s initial resolve is a profound treasury of merit.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, it could not be fully described.
It is for the sake of the birth of all Tathāgatas, the joy of the seclusion of the Pratyekabuddhas,
the assembly of autonomous Śrāvakas, and all worthy sages.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in all the boundless Buddha-fields,
may all classes of sentient beings make offerings for immeasurable eons;
furthermore, may they be taught to cultivate the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the four dhyānas.
The four immeasurables, the formless attainments, And the peaceful liberations;
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable eons, Providing all manner of requisites for their comfort;
Moreover, teaching them the supreme Dharma, Until their outflows are exhausted and they become Arhats.
Such various merits as these may still be measured;
But the treasury of merit from generating the resolve for enlightenment is beyond analogy and ineffable.
Furthermore, if one transforms immeasurable multitudes, Causing them all to become pratyekabuddhas—
The samādhi of tranquility and its profound, manifold virtues—
compared to the treasury of the first resolve, that person’s mass of merit does not equal even one hundredth part, nor even what can be expressed in words.
Immeasurable and boundless, as numerous as atoms are the Buddha-fields;
even if a person possessed of supernatural power could traverse them all in a single thought,
such power of the divine feet, though practiced throughout immeasurable eons, [would never reach the end].
Those lands may still be counted, but the treasury of those who have resolved their minds is difficult to know.
Throughout the kalpas of the past, future, and present— immeasurable and without limit—
even such kalpas as these might have their numbers known.
When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they become a treasury of immeasurable merit;
like the realm of empty space, its boundaries cannot be known.
Throughout the past, future, and present, across all the reckonings of kalpas—
Because the Bodhisattva is able to discern everything in a single thought-moment;
The jewel of the Bodhisattva’s resolve desires to reach the past, future, and present,
Understanding them all clearly in one thought-moment, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, The beings in immeasurable lands—
All their desires and aspirations, He discerns them all in a single thought-moment.
Knowing the faculties and skillful means, And the movements of the mind in every thought,
Even space may yet be measured, But the bodhicitta is difficult to know.
The reason it cannot be measured Is that great compassion is immeasurable;
It bestows universal happiness upon all, Filling the realms of the ten directions.
Desiring that all may attain the Buddha’s joy of liberation within the treasury of Dharma, they first give rise to the mind of the precious treasury; the power of their merit is immeasurable.
Whatever desires and hopes sentient beings have, and whatever thoughts they seek through skillful means—
According to those various faculties, And the actions of body, speech, and mind, One is able,
within a single thought-moment, To fully awaken to each and every one of them;
Desiring to attain all-knowledge, One resolves the mind for bodhi.
All classes of sentient beings, with their immeasurable afflictions and karma,
because of these bound karmic deeds, undergo various states of existence in every realm.
Even the limits of such retributions for bound karma might still be known.
The treasury of merit from generating the mind of awakening is inconceivable.
It is inconceivable because one is able to give rise to the supreme vow,
making offerings to all Buddhas and forever departing from all afflictions.
Simultaneously eliminating the afflictions and karmas of all classes of sentient beings,
rescuing them from the sufferings of the three periods of time, and perfecting the mind of great compassion;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the infinite and innumerable Buddhas—
In a single thought, they make offerings to all, while simultaneously exhorting sentient beings.
They are perfumed with exquisite incense; with precious banners, various pennants, and canopies;
with celestial robes and rare, wondrous delicacies; and with the finest flavors of ambrosial nectar.

According to the season, there are various palaces and pavilions, with beds, couches, and articles of adornment, as well as pure grounds for walking meditation; these provide a place to settle the body and accord with the mind of the Way.
All such articles of offering are adorned with immeasurable jewels.
The radiance emitted by mani-jewels is entirely a cause of happiness.
Thus making offerings to the Buddha, while also exhorting sentient beings,
one constantly performs such offerings throughout inconceivable eons.
These various merits may yet be fully described,
But the treasury of merit from generating the mind of awakening is beyond all analogy.
All possible analogies, as extensively analyzed before, [Are insufficient.]
Compared to the initial generation of the mind of awakening, immeasurable [virtues] do not equal even one part of it.
The state of being the Honored One among men throughout the three periods of time, all meritorious deeds and activities,
and the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi— all arise from the initial generation of the mind.
Throughout countless billions of kalpas, you have practiced the unsurpassed path;
it has been incalculable and immeasurable, exceeding all measure.
Having perfected all-knowledge, its power is unfathomable.
Reaching that shore of enlightenment, they ferry across the realms of all living beings.
When first generating the bodhicitta, it is as vast as space;
giving birth to all merits, its characteristics are identical to the dharma-realm.
Equally contemplating the nature of all phenomena, As they truly are, without differing marks,
Forever transcending all existence, Their nature is like that of a steadfast hero.
Into the profound and true nature of reality, Sublime wisdom enters in accordance.
Infinite Buddha-lands, in a single thought-moment, they pervade them all.
Regarding all that is known by the All-Knowing One, there is nothing they do not observe universally;
the boundless realms of the Buddhas, they comprehend with unimpeded penetration.
Constantly cultivating sublime merit, peerless among all;
Fully endowed with subtle and wondrous precepts, pure and free from blemish.
Bestowing everything both internally and externally, giving to all with an impartial mind.
Constantly practicing giving at all times, Diligent and never regressing;
Single-mindedly cultivating the correct reception [of precepts], The treasury of merits of all dhyānas;
Always practicing subtle and wondrous wisdom, Profound, vast, and without limit or bottom.
In this most supreme ground, the true sons of the Buddha achieve the attainment of suchness-wisdom and practice the profound equanimity.
All Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present—
All are protected by majestic spiritual power; The initial aspiration for bodhicitta,
Profound samādhis, And immeasurable dhāraṇīs,
Through the sovereign powers of all Buddhas, Adorn this initial aspiration.
All the worlds throughout the ten directions, None are able to calculate their number;
Immeasurable and boundless, They are like the realm of empty space.
The first arousal of the bodhicitta Is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
All those who are lions among men arise from the first resolve for enlightenment.
The Tathāgata’s ten powers, the fourfold eloquence, the fearlessnesses,
and all immeasurable virtues— all arise from the first resolve for enlightenment.
All the Teachers, with their eighteen unique qualities and such supreme wisdom,
all arise from the initial resolve for enlightenment.
The wondrous form-bodies of the Buddhas, adorned with various marks, [also arise therefrom].
Ultimately free from falsehood, the pure and true Dharma-body,
Worthy of offerings by devas and humans, with profound and unimpeded wisdom—
All such merits as these arise entirely from the initial resolve for enlightenment.
All pratyekabuddhas and the immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas—
all such worthy sages— arise entirely from the initial aspiration for enlightenment.
The four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the most profound samādhis likewise stem from that same source.
All these immeasurable joys arise from the initial resolve of the mind. Throughout the past,
future, and present, for all beings among gods and humans in the worlds of the ten directions,
whatever joy they experience in their births within each realm of existence—
Through skillful means and diligent vigor, they have fully disciplined all their faculties;
these immeasurable joys all arise from the initial resolve. Why is this so?
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, by virtue of their initial resolve, are endowed with the six pāramitās;
they transform all classes of sentient beings, causing them to abandon the heterodox and enter the right path.
Thus, they are able to cause those within the three realms to receive these various kinds of bliss.
The Bodhisattva’s profound and wondrous wisdom penetrates all things without obstruction;
he guides and instructs all sentient beings, purifying and cultivating sublime deeds.
He extinguishes all afflictions and every unwholesome action.
Cultivating the path to nirvāṇa, he delivers all beings.
With the light of immeasurable wisdom, like the radiance of the pure sun,
and endowed with pure and white conduct, he is like the full moon.
An inexhaustible treasury of boundless merit, Like the oceans of the ten directions, Stainless and untainted, Pure as the void.
The initial resolve of a Bodhisattva Is beyond all praise; it can never be fully extolled.
May all sentient beings be caused to fully experience every kind of happiness.
For immeasurable and innumerable eons, they shall extensively cultivate great vows and constantly practice meritorious deeds for the sake of taming sentient beings.
Immeasurable and beyond counting, His pure vows are inconceivable;
All are fully and perfectly fulfilled, Causing all beings to attain purity.
Universally observing all phenomena, He sees them all as empty, signless, and wishless.
By virtue of the power of his vast vows, his mind is pure and free from fear.
He understands the true nature of phenomena, which is as pure as space;
both concentration and distraction are equal to him, for they are quiescent and devoid of intrinsic existence.
The profound and wondrous dharmas, immeasurable and inconceivable,
he constantly expounds for the great assembly, his mind free from attachment.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all the Tathāgatas—
That Buddha constantly praises the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve;
With immeasurable, wondrous merits, he adorns that initial resolve.
Reaching the shore of ultimate purity, his nature becomes identical to all Tathāgatas.
If all classes of sentient beings, throughout immeasurable and innumerable kalpas,
were to praise the initial resolve [to attain enlightenment], their merit would never be exhausted.
This treasury of the merits of all Buddhas is from which Bodhisattvas are born.
Among all the three realms of existence, it is supreme and without peer.
If you wish to obtain the bright and pure lamp of wisdom of all Buddhas,
you should establish great vows and swiftly generate the bodhicitta.
Among all merits, the bodhicitta is supreme;
it can attain unimpeded wisdom and is born through transformation from the Buddha-dharma.
The minds of all sentient beings can all be discerned and known.
The atoms of all lands may still be counted;
The realm of empty space in the ten directions may even be measured with a single hair;
But the initial resolve of a Bodhisattva is ultimately unfathomable.
Because of the initial bodhicitta, the Buddhas of the three times are born;
all sentient beings obtain every kind of supreme and wondrous happiness.
The merits praised by the Buddhas are all fully possessed because of this.
Within the realm of the Buddha, their minds are free from doubt.
If one can forever distance oneself from all doubts and uncertainties,
then one can extinguish the immeasurable obstacles of sentient beings.
By means of the initial bodhicitta, one adorns and purifies all Buddha-fields,
causing all sentient beings everywhere to be fully endowed with subtle and wondrous wisdom.
Desiring to see the lands of the ten directions and all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
Furthermore, if one wishes to attain an immeasurable, profound treasury of merit,
and if one desires to extinguish the immeasurable suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.
"You should establish firm vows and swiftly give rise to the bodhicitta. —
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Nine.
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Ten, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Fourteen: The Exposition of the Dharma. Chapter Fourteen: The Exposition of the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryamati addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind upon enlightenment accomplishes such an immeasurable treasury of merit, adorns themselves with great adornments, mounts the vehicle of omniscience, enters the bodhisattva’s path of non-retrogression, remains far removed from the world, and aspires to seek perfect awakening."
All those who dwell where the Buddhas dwell have attained abiding and will certainly achieve unsurpassed bodhi.

How does that bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate merit so that it becomes increasingly superior, causing all Tathāgatas to rejoice; how does he fulfill the merits upon which bodhisattvas abide and their pure conduct; how does he bring his great vows to fulfillment and obtain the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; how does he transform and deliver beings according to what is appropriate for them; how is he able not to abandon the various pāramitās; how does he liberate all sentient beings who request his help; how does he cause the Three Jewels to flourish so they never cease; and how do all his roots of goodness, spheres of activity, and skillful means of practice become entirely non-empty?
“Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
Please expound this Dharma for us; we wish to hear it with joy.”

Just as the merits cultivated by all bodhisattvas eliminate the darkness of ignorance, subdue all demons, restrain all non-Buddhists, and remain free from defilements; they fully accomplish all virtues and ultimately and forever leave behind the hardships of the evil realms.
They are fully endowed with pure and profound wisdom, the merits of all the bodhisattva stages, the various pāramitās, samādhis, and dhāraṇīs;

the six supernormal powers, the three insights, and the dharmas of purity; they adorn all buddha-worlds, possess the primary and secondary marks, and have subtle and wondrous voices; they are pure in mind and conduct, and are endowed with the powers, fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Tathāgatas.

Endowed with a Buddha-field, maturing sentient beings according to their needs, at the appropriate times, and according to their faculties, they fully perfect immeasurable Buddha-activities, the immeasurable merits of all bodhisattvas, the true Dharma of bodhisattvas, the practices of bodhisattvas, the path of bodhisattvas, and the realms of bodhisattvas, thereby swiftly attaining the state of a Tathāgata.
They are able to protect all the immeasurable Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas;

they analyze and expound them extensively, revealing and manifesting them such that they cannot be destroyed by any demons or non-Buddhists; they uphold the True Dharma without end, and are able to proclaim it throughout all worlds.

The Deva Kings, Nāga Kings, Yakṣa Kings, Gandharva Kings, Asura Kings, Garuḍa Kings, Kiṃnara Kings, Mahoraga Kings, Human Kings, Brahmā Kings, and all the Buddhas, the Dharma Kings, shall all protect this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
He is revered, honored, respected, and praised by all the world, and is constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.

All Bodhisattvas likewise love and revere him; he attains the power of roots of goodness and increases pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). He is able to open the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, adorning himself with the Great True Dharma, and sequentially expounding the practices of Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramati, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

“Excellent! I pray you will explain the Mahāyāna Dharma— The various merits accomplished by Bodhisattvas, Their profound entry into vast and immeasurable practices, And their perfection of pure, teacherless wisdom.”
If there is a bodhisattva who first resolves their mind, Accomplishing the vehicle of merit and wisdom,
Entering the supramundane path of certainty, They will surely and swiftly attain the Buddha’s bodhi.
How may one, within the True Dharma of the Buddha, cultivate merit so that it ever increases and excels,
causing all Tathāgatas to rejoice, and come to dwell upon the stages where the Buddhas abide?
With pure conduct and fulfilled great vows, possessing the treasury of bodhisattva wisdom,
you are able to deliver all beings, yet remain unattached to any sentient being?
Never abandoning any of the perfections, all their deeds and practices are entirely non-in vain;
they are able to deliver all sentient beings who are invited, causing the Buddha-dharma to flourish and never cease.
With the unobstructed realm of pure vision, you possess all merits while seeking the Buddha-way;
what is the pure path practiced by the Hero among Men? Please explain it in its entirety and with full distinction.
Having extinguished all the darkness of ignorance, Subduing the hosts of Māras and restraining the non-Buddhists,
With stainless merits fully accomplished, How did you attain the wondrous wisdom of the Honored One among Men?
Forever free from the sufferings of the various difficult realms and evil paths, Fully endowed with pure wisdom,
Possessing immeasurable and profound great merits, How can one accomplish the most supreme powers of all paths?
Having attained the most excellent and wondrous wisdom among humans, you deliver beings according to their needs;
throughout inconceivable Buddha-fields, you perform the work of a Buddha with sovereign and immeasurable ease.
All supreme and profound practices, Discerning the treasury of merits of the Bull among Men,
Constantly able to protect and uphold the most excellent Dharma— What worldly hardships can ever destroy such a one?
How is it that you are fearless like a lion, Endowed with merit like the full moon,
