Like a lotus flower unsullied by water, And pure in virtue like the Most Victorious One?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati addressed the Bodhisattva Vīryamati, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

O Son of the Buddha, because you bring great benefit, great peace, and great welfare to the world, out of compassion for all devas and humans, you are able to inquire about such profound and pure conduct of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!

You abide in profound and true wisdom and the power of great diligence; practicing with single-minded devotion, you have attained non-retrogression and transcended the world. Your mastery in what you inquire about is equal to that of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Listen now with focused attention and reflect well upon it.
I shall, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, speak to you briefly."
O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having already attained the treasury of merit from generating the mind of enlightenment, should depart from the darkness of delusion, diligently guard it, and extinguish all negligence.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten dharmas by which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain non-negligence. What are these ten?
First, maintaining pure ethical discipline;
second, distancing oneself from ignorance and purifying the bodhicitta;
third, abandoning flattery and crookedness while feeling compassion for sentient beings.
Fourth, they diligently cultivate roots of goodness and attain non-retrogression;
fifth, they always delight in tranquility, remaining far removed from all ordinary persons, whether lay or ordained;
sixth, their minds do not yearn for or take pleasure in worldly delights.
Seventh, to single-mindedly and diligently cultivate all superior and wholesome deeds;
eighth, to abandon the two vehicles and seek the bodhisattva path;
ninth, to constantly practice meritorious virtues with a mind free from defilement.
Tenth, they are skillfully able to discern and know their own bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of practices by which a bodhisattva dwells in heedfulness.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Having already been able to abide in this dharma of heedfulness, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further correctly practices ten kinds of pure dharmas. What are these ten?
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices according to what has been taught; having perfected mindfulness and wisdom, he abandons all frivolous and negligent conduct, abiding securely in the profound, subtle, and excellent Dharma. He constantly delights in seeking the Dharma with a mind that knows no satiety;
according to the teachings he hears, he attains true contemplation and fully gives rise to skillful wisdom, enabling him to enter the sovereign mastery of the Buddhas.”
The mind is always tranquil and concentrated, never distracted; hearing good or evil, the mind feels neither sorrow nor joy, just as the great earth regards all sentient beings with equanimity;
regarding those of superior, middling, and inferior classes, one regards them all as Buddhas.
Reverently make offerings to one's preceptors, teachers, spiritual friends, bodhisattvas, and Dharma masters,
maintaining this sequence of mindfulness at every thought as if they were the Omniscient One.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure dharmas of a bodhisattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus diligently practices mindfulness and awareness, does not abandon skillful means, and cultivates the profound dharma with a mind that relies on nothing, they enter into non-contention."
They thoroughly understand all the immeasurable, boundless, profound, and wondrous Buddha-dharmas, causing all Tathāgatas to be entirely delighted.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to cause all Buddhas to be delighted."
What are the ten? First, practicing with diligence without ever turning back;
second, not begrudging one's own body or life.
Third, not seeking gain or offerings;
fourth, cultivating all dharmas as being like empty space;
fifth, through skillful means and wisdom, observing that all dharmas are identical to the dharma-realm.
Sixth, to discern all phenomena with a mind that has no dependence;
seventh, to constantly give rise to great vows;
eighth, to achieve the light of pure patience and wisdom.
Ninth, they skillfully know all dharmas that cause harm or benefit;
tenth, the dharma-gates they practice are entirely pure.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas that a bodhisattva practices, which are able to bring joy to all Buddhas.
"Sons of the Buddha!
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas in which a bodhisattva dwells securely, which are able to bring joy to all Buddhas."
What are the ten? They are:
abiding in heedfulness; and abiding in the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Abiding in great loving-kindness;
abiding in great compassion;
abiding in the fulfillment of all the pāramitās.
Abiding in the pure conduct of a bodhisattva;
abiding in the fulfillment of immeasurable great vows;
abiding in skillful means.
Abiding in all powers; abiding in all phenomena;
like space, having no point of dependence.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas in which a bodhisattva abides, enabling them to bring joy to all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!"
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice ten kinds of dharmas, they can swiftly accomplish all the stages (*bhūmi*). What are these ten?
First, their minds always delight in performing all meritorious deeds.
Second, practicing the path of the great adornments of the various pāramitās;
third, possessing clear and penetrating wisdom that does not follow the words of others;
fourth, never being separated from true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Fifth, they constantly cultivate diligence without ever regressing;
sixth, they skillfully grasp the Buddha’s intent and uphold all dharmas;
seventh, they practice all roots of goodness with minds free from sorrow or distress.
Eighth, they adorn themselves with the adornments of the Mahāyāna, the brilliant light of their sharp wisdom universally illuminating all;
ninth, they dwell securely in the dharma-gates of all stages;
tenth, they share in the roots of goodness and the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas that a bodhisattva practices to swiftly accomplish all the stages.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Once those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have established themselves in the various stages (*bhūmi*), they should first cultivate skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

In accordance with the Dharma-gates of the stages they have attained, in accordance with the profound wisdom they have attained, in accordance with their activities, in accordance with the fruits upon which they rely, in accordance with their spheres of activity, in accordance with their masteries, in accordance with their manifestations, and in accordance with their discrimination of the various supreme Dharma-gates—having attained these supreme Dharma-gates—they thoroughly discern them all and remain unattached to any phenomena (*dharma*).
All phenomena are created by the mind.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva can clearly observe in this manner, they will be able to fulfill all the stages (bhūmis).
That bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"I should swiftly accomplish all the stages (bhūmi). Why is this?

When I practice according to the teachings regarding these stages, I shall attain immeasurable treasuries of merit; having attained these immeasurable treasuries of merit, I will gradually reach the stage of Buddhahood; and having reached the stage of Buddhahood, I will be able to perform the work of a Buddha."

Therefore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly and diligently practices, does not abandon skillful means, and remains free from sorrow and distress; thus attaining great adornment, they abide in the dwelling of a bodhisattva.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice ten further dharmas, they are able to completely purify all bodhisattva practices. What are these ten?
First, to relinquish everything entirely so as to fulfill the wishes of all sentient beings;
second, to maintain pure ethical discipline without any transgression;
third, to be fully endowed with patience that is inexhaustible.
Fourth, they diligently cultivate skillful means without falling back;
fifth, they are free from delusion and maintain right mindfulness, remaining constantly in samādhi without distraction;
sixth, they discern and clearly comprehend all phenomena.
Seventh, they fully accomplish and perfect all practices;
eighth, their reverence for merit is as steadfast as the king of mountains;
ninth, they act as a pool of coolness for all sentient beings.
Tenth, causing all sentient beings to be identical with the Buddha-dharma.
Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas through which a bodhisattva practices, whereby they are able to completely purify all bodhisattva deeds.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice such pure conduct in this way, they further attain ten kinds of increasingly superior and wondrous dharmas. What are these ten?
First, all Buddhas of the other directions will protect and keep them in mind;
second, they will cultivate and nurture superior roots of goodness;
third, they will dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s skillful and secret expedient means.
Fourth, they always delight in drawing near to and relying upon spiritual friends;
fifth, they dwell securely in diligence and practice non-negligence;
sixth, they discern all phenomena as being neither collective nor individual.
Seventh, they dwell securely in the perfection of unsurpassed great compassion;
eighth, they give rise to wisdom by contemplating phenomena as they truly are;
ninth, they are able to skillfully practice through ingenious expedient means.
Tenth, they contemplate the power of the Tathāgata through all skillful means.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure, increasingly superior, and wondrous dharmas of Bodhisattvas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure vows. What are these ten? They are:
the vow to bring sentient beings to maturity, with a mind free from sorrow or distress;”
May I nurture and increase my roots of goodness and adorn and purify Buddha-fields;
may I reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas;
and may I, without begrudging body or life, protect and uphold the True Dharma.
May they, through various gateways of wisdom, cause all sentient beings to be born in the buddha-fields;
may all bodhisattvas enter the dharma-gate of non-duality and enter the dharma-gates of the Buddha to discern all phenomena;
and may all who wish to see the Buddha behold him in full.
May all future kalpas, until the end of time, be as brief as a single moment;
may I fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
and may I purify the gateway to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure vows of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice ten dharmas, they are able to fully satisfy all their vows. What are these ten?
First, they give rise to great adornment, with minds free from sorrow or distress;
second, they turn toward superior vows and keep all bodhisattvas in mind.
Third, to aspire to be reborn in all the adorned and purified Buddha-fields heard of in the ten directions;
fourth, to reach the ultimate limit of the future;
fifth, to ultimately bring all sentient beings to fulfillment and to perfect one's great vows.
Sixth, dwelling through all kalpas without perceiving their length;
seventh, regarding all suffering as not being suffering;
eighth, having no defiled attachment in the mind toward any pleasure.
Ninth, they thoroughly and skillfully discern the liberation that is equal to the unequaled;
tenth, they attain great nirvana, which is without distinction.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully satisfy all vows;
once the bodhisattva mahāsattva has fulfilled these vows, they attain ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries of Dharma. What are these ten?

They attain the inexhaustible treasury of beholding all Buddhas; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of *dhāraṇī*; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of discerning the Dharma; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of the great compassionate mind that protects all beings; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of all *samādhis*; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of merit that fulfills the intentions of sentient beings; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of profound wisdom that understands the reality of phenomena; they attain the inexhaustible treasury that gives birth to the various supernormal powers and distinguishes all jewels; they attain the inexhaustible treasury of being protected by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas; and they attain the inexhaustible treasury of the wisdom that discerns immeasurable and boundless worlds.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten inexhaustible treasuries attained by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through which he accomplishes a treasury of immeasurable and boundless merit.
Endowed with pure wisdom, he transforms and delivers beings according to their needs.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva transform sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them?
This Bodhisattva knows the expedient means suitable for each of those sentient beings.”
He knows the various causes and conditions of all sentient beings;
he knows the thoughts and mental activities of all sentient beings;
and having known their thoughts, he teaches them the remedial dharmas.
For those with an abundance of greed, teach the contemplation of impurity;
for those with an abundance of hatred, teach the contemplation of great compassion;
for those with an abundance of delusion, teach them to discern all phenomena.
For those with equal proportions of the three poisons, he teaches the dharma-gate of complete and supreme wisdom;
for those who delight in birth and death, he teaches the three kinds of suffering;
and for those attached to the various realms of existence, he teaches the dharma-gate of emptiness.
For sentient beings who are indolent, they teach the practice of diligence;
for sentient beings who are arrogant, they teach the contemplation of equality;
for those whose minds are deceitful and crooked, they teach that the bodhisattva-mind is tranquil and non-existent.
Regarding all such afflictions and maladies, he teaches immeasurable methods of counteraction.

He fully expounds the meanings and flavors in their proper sequence, distinguishing wisdom through the contemplation of the equality of phenomena, such that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

He expounds the nature of all phenomena as being subject to disintegration, yet within the dharma-realm there is nothing that is scattered or extinguished; he cuts off doubt and causes all to rejoice;
according to their various faculties, he teaches them to enter the ultimate truth and instructs them in all merits so they may enter the ocean of the Tathāgatas;
he speaks of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) to destroy all marks.
Teaching the Dharma-treasury by revealing the Dharma-realm;
teaching that all things depend on the mind and are free from defilement;
and teaching the equal mindfulness of all Buddhas with reverence and intimacy.
Teaching with a gentle voice that is free from attachment;
teaching with all sounds without distinction;
teaching the sublime Dharma that is without peer.
He is fully endowed with the body of the equal wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
In this way, the bodhisattva is constantly able to transform and deliver all sentient beings, yet his mind remains tranquil and concentrated, never becoming distracted.
Not forsaking any of the pāramitās, one fully adorns the six pāramitās for the sake of all classes of sentient beings.
Being able to relinquish everything internal and external, yet never giving rise to a mind of stinginess—this is called the pure dāna-pāramitā.
Furthermore, because one does not give rise to the mark of maintaining precepts, one is without attachment to them; this is called the pure *śīla-pāramitā*.

Being able to endure all sufferings, and having neither sorrow nor joy in the mind upon hearing the good or the evil, remaining as unshakable as the great earth—this is called the pure *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

Through courageous diligence and skillful cultivation, their minds are firm and non-retrogressive, ultimately accomplishing the gateway to the Buddha’s wisdom; this is called the pure *vīryapāramitā*.
Having relinquished all desires, they enter into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) with a pure sequence of joy and bliss born of seclusion, remaining undefiled;
they incinerate and extinguish afflictions (*kleśa*), giving rise to immeasurable concentrations and great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

through successive transcendence, they enter immeasurable gateways of samādhi, entering immeasurable samādhis within a single gateway, fully knowing the spheres of all samādhis, and gradually perfecting the stages of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This is called the pure dhyāna-pāramitā.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, one receives and upholds it; one reveres and draws near to spiritual friends with a tireless mind;
and one always delights in hearing the Dharma without ever feeling satiated.
Regarding all dharmas they have heard, they are able to observe them correctly and enter into true samādhi, thereby abandoning all inverted and false views;
through skillful means, they discern and understand that the ocean of the characteristics of all dharmas lacks intrinsic nature, and they cultivate the gate of the Tathāgata’s profound wisdom;
endowed with all the powers of wisdom, they ride upon the wisdom of the universal gate and are able to enter all gates of wisdom.
This is called the pure Prajñāpāramitā.
It manifests all worldly modes of conduct to teach and transform sentient beings while remaining free from sorrow or distress in mind.
It manifests its body according to what is appropriate for each being, and in all its actions, its mind remains unstained by attachment.
They manifest the conduct of both the ignorant and the wise;
they manifest the gates of birth-and-death and liberation, being skillfully able to discern all practices of expedient means;
they manifest immeasurable matters of adornment, are able to enter into all realms of rebirth, and fully comprehend the conduct of all sentient beings.
This is called the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) that is utterly pure. It is the ultimate accomplishment of all sentient beings;

the ultimate purification of all worlds; the ultimate making of offerings to all Tathāgatas; the ultimate understanding and penetration of the reality of all phenomena without obstruction; the ultimate cultivation that fulfills the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the ultimate dwelling through future kalpas as if it were a mere moment; the ultimate perception of future kalpas as being like a single thought-instant; the ultimate understanding and penetration of all formation and destruction; the ultimate manifestation of all Buddha-fields; and the ultimate attainment of the wisdom of all Buddhas. This is called the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) that is fully endowed.
Through the power of self-mastery and rectitude, one is free from all afflictions; through the power of being fully endowed with purity, one is able to correctly guide others.
Fully accomplished and perfected, one cannot be defeated by any.
With the power of great compassion fulfilled and the power of great loving-kindness impartial, one is able to provide shelter and protection for all sentient beings.
The power of dhāraṇī can sustain the meaning of all skillful means;
the power of sublime eloquence causes all sentient beings to rejoice;
the power of the various pāramitās adorns the Mahāyāna; and the power of great vows has never been interrupted.
The various supernormal powers give rise to immeasurable Buddha-powers that protect and shelter all beings;

this is called the *pāramitā* of the power of purity. Knowing the increase of greed, knowing the increase of hatred, and knowing the increase of delusion; furthermore, knowing the stages of training through the analysis of equal proportions (*sabhāga*); within a single thought-moment, fully knowing the mental activities of the minds of all sentient beings; being able to know all the hopes and aspirations of sentient beings; being able to know the reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*); understanding and penetrating the profound power of the Buddhas' wisdom; and universally knowing all the gateways to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
This is called the perfection of pure wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus purify all the perfections, fulfill all the perfections, and do not abandon any of the perfections, they ride upon the Great Adornment and are able to deliver all sentient beings who have been invited."
He teaches and transforms all beings to cultivate wholesome conduct, causing them all to forever leave the evil realms behind and diligently practice with vigor to transcend all hardships.
To those with much greed and desire, he teaches the contemplation of detachment;
to those with much anger and hatred, he teaches the contemplation of equanimity.
To those with much wrong view, teach the contemplation of causes and conditions;
to sentient beings of the desire realm, teach the abandonment of desire, ill will, and unwholesome states;
to sentient beings of the form realm, teach the superior contemplation.
For sentient beings in the formless realm, he teaches subtle wisdom;
for those who delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he teaches the practice of tranquility;
and for those who delight in the Mahāyāna, he teaches the adornment of the Mahāyāna with the ten powers.

Just as when first generating the mind of enlightenment, seeing sentient beings fallen into the various evil realms, one lets out a great lion’s roar: "I shall know their mental afflictions and deliver them by means of all the Dharma gates."
When Bodhisattvas are endowed with such wisdom, they are able to deliver all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they are able to cause the Three Jewels to flourish and ensure that they never cease."

Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta, they are thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted;
because they reveal and expound the profound and wondrous treasury of all dharmas, they are thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted.
By fully upholding and practicing the teachings on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.
Furthermore, by being able to praise all great vows, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted;
by analytically explaining the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
By practicing the six points of harmonious respect, one is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.

Furthermore, by planting the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings to produce the sprouts of perfect enlightenment, one is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted;
by not sparing one's own body or life to protect and uphold the True Dharma, one is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted.
Skillfully guiding the great assembly with a mind free from anxiety or affliction, he is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.
Not contradicting the teachings of the True Dharma spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, he is thus able to ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.

In this way, the Bodhisattva does not interrupt the Three Jewels; all his actions are without anything that is not wholesome, and he is able to perform every act of dedication, ultimately and decisively attaining unsurpassed Bodhi.

When a bodhisattva has thus established themselves in pure actions of body, speech, and mind, they employ various skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings through the roots of goodness they proclaim; their words are never in vain, and they are able to cause all sentient beings to attain joy.

In all that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice, there is not even a single thought of error; all such profound and wondrous deeds are sustained by wisdom and skillful means, and they are entirely able to dedicate them toward unexcelled bodhi.
"When a bodhisattva thus abides in the pure dharmas free from delusion, they fully produce ten kinds of adornments in every moment of thought. What are these ten?"
The adornment of the form-body is manifested according to the needs of beings;
the adornment of speech removes the doubts of the multitude and causes them all to rejoice;
the adornment of mental activity enters into all meditative absorptions within a single thought-moment.
The adornment of the Buddha-field eliminates all traces of affliction;
the adornment of radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions;
the adornment of the retinue is able to gather superior assemblies, causing them all to rejoice.
With the adornment of spiritual powers, they manifest with mastery according to what is appropriate;
with the adornment of the Buddha’s teachings, they are able to gather in all those of keen wisdom;
with the adornment of the ground of nirvana, they manifest the fulfillment of attaining enlightenment in a single place throughout all ten directions.
Adorned with the Dharma, they preach the Dharma according to the assembly, the time, and the capacity of the listeners.

Having thus brought forth these ten kinds of adornments in every thought-moment, the Bodhisattvas’ actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure; they are forever free from delusion, and their wisdom is perfected.

If there are sentient beings who associate with, revere, follow, and leave the household life alongside such a bodhisattva to hear and receive his Dharma teachings, or who rejoice in them, remember them, or even merely see or hear of him, these beings will certainly and ultimately attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the agada medicine: when sentient beings see it, all their illnesses are completely eliminated.

When Bodhisattvas achieve such an immeasurable treasury of Dharma, sentient beings who behold them have all their afflictions and diseases cured, and they attain mastery over their minds regarding pure and white dharmas.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains such skillful means and abides in this Dharma, they eliminate ignorance.
Because they are fully endowed with wisdom, they subdue all Māras;”
By virtue of great compassion, he subdues all non-Buddhists;
by virtue of being fully endowed with the power of wisdom and merit, he eradicates all mental impurities and afflictions;
and by entering the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), he is fully possessed of roots of goodness and his mind is free from sorrow or distress.
By virtue of the power of the merits cultivated in the presence of previous Buddhas, they are able to leave behind all the hardships of the evil realms;

because their pure wisdom is fully perfected, they give rise to the pure stages of a bodhisattva, the various pāramitās, all samādhis, the six superknowledges, the three clarities, and the four fearlessnesses; by the power of sequential skillful means and wisdom, they purify buddha-fields and adorn them with the marks and signs of excellence;
and by the power of the pure and white dharmas of body, speech, and mind, they attain the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas.

With wisdom and discernment, they swiftly understand all phenomena; through the power of their great vows and the Tathāgata’s spiritual power and great wisdom-power, they manifest various Buddha-fields in accordance with sentient beings.
Adapting to those who are ready for transformation, they turn the Great Dharma Wheel and deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice in this way, they cultivate the immeasurable treasury of Dharma and gradually attain the state of a Tathāgata.

They perform the bodhisattva practices across immeasurable lands, uphold the True Dharma as great Dharma masters, and protect and maintain the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas. Having accomplished the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), they eloquently expound the profound Dharma amidst the great assemblies; their physical marks are dignified and majestic, and their preaching of the Dharma is comprehensive and complete."

Possessing the four analytical knowledges and endowed with immeasurable, skillful means, they are able to attain inexhaustible gateways of wisdom. Their voices are sublime and exquisite; by expounding a single word of the Dharma, they can gladden all beings, guiding them according to their needs and capacities so that they may achieve understanding and enter the gateways of wisdom.
By means of such immeasurable skillful means, the Bodhisattva universally expounds the treasury of the Dharma for all sentient beings, never giving rise to a mind of indolence;
amidst the great assembly, he is fearless, and none in any world can defeat him;
fully endowed with the supreme Prajñāpāramitā, he sequentially discerns the characteristics of all phenomena without interruption.
With the four supreme and wondrous analytical knowledges, he expounds all dharmas through various parables that are inexhaustible.
Endowed with great compassion, he is able to bring all beings to a state of refreshing coolness and joy.
He cultivates great loving-kindness, which pervades the ten directions.
Seated upon the lion throne, he extensively expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

With the sole exception of a Tathāgata, there is none who can surpass him, none who can see the crown of his head, none who can scrutinize him, and none who can humble him; it is impossible for anyone to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse through debate.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have accomplished such sublime and wondrous dharmas, the great assemblies filling boundless worlds—each and every body therein being as vast as a trichiliocosm—[are thus transformed].”
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva stands amidst that assembly, his body is so extraordinary that it outshines the entire gathering until they all become invisible.
With a heart of great compassion, he universally covers all beings.
With profound wisdom, they discern that mind;
having achieved fearlessness and being fully endowed with eloquence, they extensively expound the Dharma, causing all to rejoice.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished immeasurable pure wisdom; because they have accomplished immeasurable skillful means; because they have accomplished immeasurable power of right mindfulness; because they have accomplished inexhaustible skillful means; because they have accomplished the dhāraṇī for discerning all phenomena; because they have accomplished the profound wisdom for discerning all phenomena; because they have accomplished the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas; because they have accomplished the true wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they have accomplished the pure skillful means of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they have accomplished the extensive exposition and the protection and maintenance of the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; and because they have accomplished the power of the wisdom of the great vows of Bodhisattvas—the supreme and wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Dharmamati had finished speaking this "Treasury of Increasing Merit," desiring to reiterate this meaning, he, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke in verse:
"When a Bodhisattva dwells in the first stage, They nurture the treasury of merit;
Cultivating heedfulness, The light of their wisdom illuminates the ten directions."
When Bodhisattvas guard their bodhicitta and never forget it,
all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions rejoice in their hearts.
Diligently practicing with vigor, their power of right mindfulness remains firm and unshakable.
Their conduct is non-retrogressive, and they do not cling to the world.
Always delighting in the profound Dharma, they achieve the concentration of non-contention;
all the Most Victorious Ones of the ten directions are filled with joy.
The Buddhas, having rejoiced, have perfected the stage of vigor and accomplished a treasury of merit and immeasurable, profound wisdom.
All their practices are pure, and they are fully endowed with all the stages (bhūmis).
The original vows of the Buddhas of the ten directions are all fully and completely fulfilled.
Thus is wisdom perfected, and one attains the treasury of all profound dharmas.
Having attained this treasury of dharmas, one acts in accordance with the world.
Having accomplished skillful means, they discern the minds of sentient beings;
according to what is appropriate for their transformation, they expound the Dharma for them.
Having already been able to extensively teach the Dharma, they do not abandon their own practice.
Fully endowed with the pāramitās, they have accomplished great merit.
Having perfected the pāramitās, all those sentient beings originally invited from the immeasurable ocean of birth and death have been completely delivered across.
Thus constantly practicing, day and night without rest or indolence,
one causes the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to flourish, ensuring they never cease.
The immeasurable practices cultivated are pure and fully perfected.
All have reached the ultimate end, Having accomplished the most supreme stage.
That which the Bodhisattvas practice Is true and without deception;
They deliver all classes of sentient beings, Freeing them from the defilements of affliction.
Having accomplished such dharmas, they eliminate the darkness of ignorance,
subdue all māras, and ultimately attain bodhi.
The sons of the Buddha who practice in this way are fully endowed with the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
They are able to analyze and expound upon the profound treasury of all Buddhas.
If one can expound in this manner, they are the foremost among Dharma-preachers;
for the sake of all sentient beings, they universally rain down the nectar of the Dharma.
With boundless great compassion, filling the realms of the ten directions,
he is able to discern and know the minds of all sentient beings.
Having understood the minds of sentient beings, as well as their various other mental activities,
For their sake, he expounds the profound Dharma, immeasurable and beyond counting.
His every movement is ever calm and composed, like that of a great elephant king;
as majestic and fierce as a lion, no one can harm him.
"Immovable like Mount Sumeru, Wisdom like the great ocean,
Raining down the water of nectar everywhere, To extinguish the heat of afflictions.
After the Bodhisattva Dharmamati had spoken this verse, the Tathāgata expressed his approval, and the great assembly practiced accordingly.

15. Chapter on the Sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s Ascent to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. *The Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vaipulya*, Chapter Fifteen: The Tathāgata’s Ascent to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, throughout all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and in every single Jambudvīpa within the four continents, there was not one where the Tathāgata was not manifest, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
Each of those bodhisattvas, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, expounded various teachings, each of whom considered themselves to be in the presence of the Buddha.
At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, without leaving the Bodhi tree or the palace of Śakra, he proceeded toward the Jewel-Adorned Hall in the Yāma Heaven.
At that time, the celestial king, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, immediately prepared a precious lion throne within the palace known as the Lotus Treasury;
it was adorned with a hundred thousand varieties of jewels,
and a hundred thousand jeweled canopies completely covered it above.
A hundred thousand jeweled nets served as necklaces;

above them were a hundred thousand canopies of various exquisite jewels, further adorned with a hundred thousand celestial flower-canopies, heavenly silks, and miscellaneous gems hanging down as pendants;
and it was further embellished with a hundred thousand strings of pearls.
A hundred thousand precious robes were spread upon it;
a hundred thousand devaputras stood in attendance before him;
and a hundred thousand Brahmās surrounded him.
One hundred thousand bodhisattvas offered praises before him;
one hundred thousand rays of light shone forth as illumination;
and one hundred thousand kinds of music spontaneously resounded.
One hundred thousand sounds of the joy of the True Dharma;
one hundred thousand manifestations of the wondrous marks of the roots of goodness;
and the protection and sustenance of the majestic spiritual power of one hundred thousand Tathāgatas.
He nurtures it with a hundred thousand treasuries of merit;
he purifies it with a hundred thousand samādhis;
and he makes it pure through a hundred thousand treasuries of vows.
One hundred thousand extraordinary and unprecedented sublime signs were manifested;
one hundred thousand wondrous dharmas appeared before him;
and one hundred thousand sovereign powers were universally displayed everywhere.
A hundred thousand marks of excellence and subtle characteristics arose simultaneously;
a hundred thousand sounds proclaimed all dharmas.
At that time, having adorned the lion throne of the precious lotus-womb, the Heavenly King joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will compassionately accept this palace.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation and immediately ascended the jeweled palace; it was likewise so for all the Yāma heavens throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the celestial king’s immeasurable music became silent and still; he then recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata of Renowned Fame is heard throughout the ten directions, The most supreme among all auspicious things.
He has entered this palace adorned with mani-jewels; Therefore, this place is the most auspicious.”
The Tathāgata Jewel King, Lamp of the World, supreme among all that is auspicious, has entered the Palace of the Supreme Flavor of Ambrosia; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Prāmodyarāja possesses immeasurable wisdom; Among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
Having entered the Hall Adorned with Various Jewels, Therefore, this place is most auspicious.

The Tathāgata Prajñācakṣus, the lamp of the world, The most unsurpassed among all auspicious things, Has entered this extraordinary and most excellent palace; Therefore, this place is the most auspicious.
The Tathāgata’s benefit for beings is immeasurable; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
Having entered this pure palace of the jewel mountain, this place is therefore most auspicious.
The Teacherless Tathāgata, Honored One of the World, supreme among all that is auspicious, has entered this subtle and wondrous chamber of precious incense; therefore, this place is most auspicious.

The Honored One among devas and humans, the Lamp of the World, The Unsurpassed among all auspicious things, has entered this light and subtle fragrant palace; Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Aśoka, the Lion of Debaters, supreme among all auspicious things, has entered the Palace of the Pure Universal Eye; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Upholding the discernment of the Tathāgata’s virtues, supreme among all auspicious things, you have entered this Palace of Playful Adornment; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Duṣkaracaryā benefits the world; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
Having entered the Hall of Universal Radiance of Equal Color, this place is therefore most auspicious.
Just as the King of the Yāma Heaven here, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, recalled the past Perfectly Enlightened Ones and praised them with verses,

so too did the Kings of the Yāma Heavens in all worlds throughout the ten directions each recall the roots of goodness they had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and praise them with verses in the same manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One ascended the jeweled palace and sat cross-legged upon a lion throne within a treasury of precious lotuses.
At that moment, the jeweled palace suddenly became vast and expansive like the realm of the Yāma Heaven, and the worlds of the ten directions were likewise transformed.

16. Chapter on the Bodhisattvas’ Verses Spoken in the Palace of Yāma Heaven. *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Great Vaipulya*, Chapter Sixteen: The Bodhisattvas’ Verses Spoken in the Palace of Yāma Heaven. At that time, in each of the ten directions, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-lands, there were worlds named Immeasurable Wisdom, next named Banner Wisdom, next named Earth Wisdom, next named Supreme Wisdom, next named Lamp Wisdom, next named Vajra Wisdom, next named Peaceful Wisdom, next named Sun Wisdom, next named Pure Wisdom, and next named Brahma Wisdom.

That Buddha was named Constantly Abiding Eye; next, Immeasurable Eye; next, True Eye; next, Immovable Eye; next, Celestial Eye; next, Pure Eye; next, Tranquil and Certain Eye; next, Radiant Mark Eye; next, Unsurpassed Eye; and next, Pure Luster Eye.

The names of those bodhisattvas were: Forest of Merit, next Forest of Wisdom, next Forest of Victory, next Forest of Fearlessness, next Forest of Shame and Remorse, next Forest of Diligence, next Forest of Accomplished Power, next Forest of Firmness, next Forest of the Tathāgata, and next Forest of Knowledge.
These bodhisattvas each practiced the pure life of brahmacarya in the presence of the Buddhas in their respective lands.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, those bodhisattvas, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-world, came to the place where the Buddha was, paying him respectful homage and prostrating themselves before him.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, in each direction from which they had come, there were manifested lion thrones made of precious jewels; upon these they sat cross-legged, filling the ten directions.
Just as the Bodhisattvas had gathered like clouds in the Yāma Heaven of this world, so it was likewise in all the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrously colored light from his two toes, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions, all the four continents, the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Lotus Treasury Jewel Lion Throne in the Yāma Heaven palace, the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, and the entire great assembly, so that they were all clearly manifested.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“Universally emitting pure light, It shines throughout the realms of the ten directions;
All beings behold the Buddha, Pervading all without obstruction.”
The Buddha dwells in the palace of Yama, upon a precious lotus throne;
throughout all worlds, this is a marvel never before seen.
He praises the ten Tathāgatas, and all sentient beings hear it.
The World-Honored One’s great assembly—there is not one who does not see it all.
Throughout the realms of the ten directions, he proclaims the unsurpassed Dharma;
likewise, they all share the same name, just as my own assembly of bodhisattvas.
Each from the worlds of the ten directions, they have come to this place;
those noble beings have purely cultivated the holy life.
Those Tathāgatas, likewise, each bear the same name.
They behold the Buddha’s pure lands and his sovereign power of supernatural transformations.
They see the Tathāgata everywhere— among humanity or at the site of enlightenment—
and they further see the World-Honored One dwelling here in this palace of Yama.
Throughout all worlds, none can conceive of the Buddha;
yet according to the vows of sentient beings, he appears to all.
When sentient beings behold the Tathāgata, they perceive his immeasurable power of mastery.
The Great Seer who has transcended the world possesses an immeasurable treasury of merit.
Traveling through the realms of the ten directions, he encounters no obstacles whatsoever;
his single body becomes infinite, and his infinite bodies become one.
"Their merit is profoundly wondrous; none can fathom it.
Unattached and without dependence, they are as pure as space.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"In inconceivable kalpas, a Teacher of Gods and Humans is difficult to encounter;
likewise, great beings free from defilement are rare to meet in this assembly.
They are all possessors of omniscience, and their light of wisdom shines everywhere."
He expounds the profound and wondrous Dharma, bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
All worlds are perpetually shrouded by the darkness of ignorance;
the Tathāgata, the lamp of light for the world, is able to extinguish them all.
Generosity, precepts, patience, and diligence, The treasury of dhyāna and samādhi, And the cultivation of profound, wondrous wisdom— These shine universally upon all things.
The Tathāgata has no equal; How much less could there be one superior to him?
Grasping at all phenomena through inversion, one therefore does not see the Buddha.
With sovereign supernormal powers, immeasurable and inconceivable,
neither coming nor going, he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If there are those who hear or behold the Pure Teacher of Gods and Humans,
they will forever emerge from all evil realms and remain far removed from all suffering.
Having cultivated and sought awakening for immeasurable and innumerable eons, [they shall attain it].
Upon attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, one extensively delivers all living beings.
Throughout inconceivable eons, one makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
yet if one can understand this meaning, one's merit shall surpass theirs.
"Though one were to give away immeasurable lands, filled with all manner of precious jewels, if one cannot understand this meaning,
one shall ultimately not attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Victorious Forest, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as in the month after spring, when the sky is free from clouds and mist, the sun shines with pure radiance, illuminating everything without exception.
Its light is immeasurable; none in the world can count it."
Those with eyes do not yet know this; how much less so those who are blind and ignorant?
The Tathāgata is likewise: his light of merit is immeasurable, and throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, none can discern or know it.
The radiance has no place from which it comes, Nor does it go anywhere when it departs;
Neither born nor extinguished, It is empty, quiescent, and devoid of existence.
Of all future phenomena, None whatsoever have ever come into being.
There is no arising and no present; therefore, there is no past.
All phenomena are without arising, and likewise they are without cessation.
One who can understand it in this way beholds the Tathāgata.
Because all phenomena are unarisen, one should know they are non-existent;
knowing through such discernment, this person penetrates the profound meaning.
Since all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, there is nothing that can be known.
If one can understand in this way, there is then nothing to be understood.
That which is said to have "arising" should be known as arising from that which is produced;
by understanding their true nature, one will then be free from doubt.
"All that is born, Right contemplation is likewise so;
When a bodhisattva contemplates thus, They are fully endowed with all-knowledge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless Forest, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"This place is boundless, as vast as the Dharma-realm;
there is nowhere it does not reach, serene and immutable.
If one hears such a teaching and responds with reverence, faith, and delight,"
Forever free from the three evil realms and all hardships and sufferings,
they travel to immeasurable and incalculable worlds,
hearing this most profound Dharma and recollecting it with faithful upholding.
Having heard and received the pure, profound, and wondrous Dharma from the Great Sage,
they single-mindedly seek bodhi and ultimately attain the unsurpassed path.
With deep faith in the Buddhas of the past and the teachings of all those Buddhas, they proceed.
The Lamp of All Worlds, who extinguishes the darkness of all delusions—
whosoever hears of the Buddha’s immeasurable power of mastery and develops resolute faith and inclination,
they shall be fully endowed with the qualities of a Hero among Men.
If one can believe with single-minded devotion in all the Buddhas of the present,
who have attained equal and perfect enlightenment and reveal immeasurable meanings—
this Dharma is extremely difficult to encounter throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons.
If there are those who hear it, they should know it is through the power of the original vow.
Such profound Dharma of the Buddha can be fully and skillfully received and upheld, and explained extensively for the sake of sentient beings; such a person is inconceivable.
"Therefore, through diligent vigor, practicing the great adornment and hearing and upholding this true Dharma, one shall ultimately attain Bodhi. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Having heard the Dharma of True Reality, so extraordinary and unprecedented,
those who rejoice with faith and delight shall have all their doubts extinguished.
The One of All-Knowledge and All-Vision himself proclaims this profound and wondrous Dharma."
The Buddha’s wisdom shines upon all without exception; therefore, it is inconceivable.
It does not arise from wisdom, nor does it arise from a lack of wisdom;
having thoroughly realized all phenomena, it extinguishes the darkness of the world.
Material phenomena and non-material phenomena—these two are not one;
so too it is with the foolish and the wise, for their natures are each distinct.
Birth-and-death and nirvana—both of these are entirely illusory.
So it is with the foolish and the wise: neither possesses any reality.
When the world first comes into being, there is no sign of its decay;
so it is with the foolish and the wise: the two are mutually contradictory.
The Bodhisattva’s initial resolve and his final mind—fools and the wise are likewise; these two are both non-corresponding.
Just as the consciousnesses of the six sense-faculties function alternately and are not identical, so it is here.
The same is true for the foolish and the wise: ultimately, they do not harmonize.
Just as the *gadhā* medicine eliminates all poisons, so too does wisdom destroy all the darkness of delusion.
"The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, is supreme and none can surpass him;
all that he speaks is true and real, and for this reason, he is difficult to encounter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are without distinction; only the Buddha discerns them through knowledge.
There is nothing he does not penetrate, for his wisdom has reached the further shore.
Just as gold and its golden color are in their nature without distinction,"
Thus, dharma and non-dharma— Their nature is without distinction.
Sentient beings and non-sentient beings— Both are devoid of reality.
Thus, dharma and non-dharma— Their nature is non-existent.
Just as in the future world there is no characteristic of the past, so it is with all phenomena: they have no characteristic of reality.
Just as past phenomena have no characteristic of arising, [so too are all things].
All phenomena are likewise; they are entirely devoid of characteristics.
Nirvāṇa cannot be grasped, though it is spoken of in two ways;
all phenomena are likewise, without any distinct characteristics.
Just as various numbers are all merely numerical phenomena, so too are all dharmas; their nature is without distinction.
Just as the number ten increases by one until it reaches the immeasurable, so it is with all things.
All these are originally but numbers; they are distinguished only by wisdom.
Just as all worlds may be destroyed at the end of an eon by the conflagration, yet space remains undiminished, so too is the wisdom that is without a teacher.
"The ten directions are empty and without difference, yet sentient beings give rise to discrimination;
thus they perceive the Tathāgata, and in their delusion, they do not see the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Accomplished Power, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All classes of sentient beings are entirely encompassed by the three periods of time;
all sentient beings of the three periods are, in turn, encompassed by the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
The five aggregates arise from karma, and all karmas arise from the mind."
Mental phenomena are like illusions, and sentient beings are likewise so.
The world is not made by itself, nor is it made by another;
because they do not know its true nature, the wheel of birth and death turns constantly.
What is called the turning of the world is entirely the turning of suffering;
because sentient beings do not know this, the wheel of birth and death turns constantly.
Both "the world" and "non-world" are neither real.
Because sentient beings are deluded, they falsely grasp at the characteristics of all phenomena.
The five aggregates (*skandha*) throughout the three periods of time are called the "world";
these exist through falsehood, yet when they are absent, that is the "transcendent world."
What are these five aggregates? What are the characteristics of the five aggregates?
Not seeing the disintegration of the five aggregates, one falsely grasps them as being permanent.
The five aggregates are illusory phenomena; in reality, they do not exist at all.
Emptiness and stillness are unchanging; ultimately, they are free from all marks.
Since the world is empty and tranquil, so too are the Buddha and the Dharma.
These three dharmas are such that their nature is non-existent.
"Having eliminated all inversions, Clearly perceiving the reality,
The one who possesses all-knowing vision Is ever present before me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavana, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as the nature of the earth element, Its own-being is non-existent;
The sovereignty of all Buddhas, Its nature is likewise so.
All the worlds together Unanimously praise the Buddha."
Seeking that praised dharma, one finds no place of origin throughout the ten directions.
Sentient beings grasp at it through delusion, claiming it to be real;
yet when analyzed apart from sentient beings, the nature of karma cannot be found.
The nature of karma is non-existent; the bodies of sentient beings are not real.
With their various and immeasurable forms, they likewise have no place of origin.
All shapes and colors—the nature of karma is inconceivable.
Though they are seen, they are non-existent; the nature of consciousness is likewise so.
The bodies of all Buddhas are thus, inconceivable and beyond grasp;
with immeasurable and wondrous form-bodies, they appear universally in all lands.
The immeasurable body is not the Buddha; the Buddha is not the immeasurable body.
The pure and wondrous Dharma-body has ultimately crossed to the other shore.
If there is one who can behold this pure and wondrous Dharma-body, [they shall likewise attain liberation].
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, such a person’s mind is free from delusion and confusion.
Observing all past phenomena as equal to nirvana,
that person beholds the Tathāgata and dwells forever in ultimate peace.
"Cultivating right mindfulness, Clearly seeing the Perfectly Awakened One, Signless and non-existent— This is called a Dharma Prince. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-vana, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as a skilled painter distributes various pigments,
Taking on different colors through delusion, The four great elements are without distinction.
The four great elements are not the pigments, And the pigments are not the four great elements."
Apart from the substance of the four great elements, there are no separate colors;
the mind is not the color of a painting, nor is the color of a painting the mind.
Apart from the mind there is no painted color, and apart from painted color there is no mind.
That mind does not abide permanently; it is immeasurable and inconceivable.
It manifests all forms, yet each does not know the other.
It is like a skilled painter who cannot know the mind that paints.
Know that all phenomena are likewise in their nature.
The mind is like a master painter, painting the various five aggregates;
within all worlds, there is no phenomenon it does not create.
As is the mind, so too is the Buddha; as is the Buddha, so too are sentient beings.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
All Buddhas fully understand that everything evolves from the mind.
If one can understand in this way, that person sees the True Buddha.
The mind is not the body, and the body is not the mind;
yet they perform all the works of a Buddha with unimpeded mastery never before seen.
"If anyone wishes to know all the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate in this way: the mind creates all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
That which is grasped cannot be grasped; that which is seen cannot be seen;
that which is heard cannot be heard; that which is thought cannot be thought.
Regarding the finite and the infinite, one should not impose limitations.
Regarding the finite and the infinite, neither is to be grasped.
To speak what should not be spoken is self-deception;
one’s own purpose will not be accomplished, nor can one bring joy to sentient beings.
If there were one who could praise all the Tathāgatas of immeasurable number for inconceivable eons, their merit would never be exhausted.
It is like the wish-fulfilling jewel, which can manifest infinite colors.
This form is not true form; the Buddhas are likewise so.
Like the purity of space, it is not form and cannot be seen, yet it can manifest all forms, while its own nature remains invisible.
Such a person of great wisdom manifests immeasurable forms;
they are not what consciousness perceives, and no one can behold them.
Though one hears the voice of the Tathāgata, that sound is not the Tathāgata.
Apart from sound, one does not know the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This state is profoundly subtle; if one can discern and know it, one adorns the unsurpassed path and remains far removed from all delusions.
All Tathāgatas have no teaching of the Buddha-dharma;
according to those who are to be transformed, they expound the Dharma for them.
*The Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Eleven, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: The Ten Practices of the Bodhisattva Puṣpakūṭa; Part One. Chapter Seventeen, Part One: The Ten Practices of the Bodhisattva Puṣpakūṭa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Forest of Merit, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "Skillful Subjugation.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, he beheld Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-worlds;
all these Tathāgatas were named Forest of Merit.
At that time, those Buddhas said to the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to enter this Samādhi of Skillful Subjugation.

It is because the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-lands, have empowered you with their spiritual strength that you are able to enter this Samādhi of Skillful Subjugation.

It is by the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha, by his majestic spiritual power, and by the power of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas; because he desires to cause you to extensively expound the profound Dharma, to nurture all-knowledge, to discern the natures of all sentient beings, to leave behind all obstacles and enter the realm of non-obstruction, to accomplish all skillful means, to accomplish all-encompassing wisdom, to awaken to all phenomena, to skillfully know the various faculties [of beings], and to hear and retain all teachings.
These are the ten practices of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
You should now, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound this sublime Dharma in detail.

At that time, those Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha the dharma of non-obstruction, the dharma of peaceful abiding, the dharma of teacherlessness, the dharma of non-delusion, the dharma of non-confusion, the dharma of purity, the dharma of immeasurability, the dharma of supremacy, the dharma of stainlessness, and the dharma of non-retrogression.
Why is this? It is due to the power of that samādhi.
At that time, each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
Having rubbed their crowns, he immediately arose from meditative concentration and addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The practices and deeds of bodhisattvas are inconceivable; they are as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as empty space."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the dharmas practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
There are ten practices of a bodhisattva, proclaimed by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. What are these ten?

First is the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others; third, the practice free from anger and resentment; fourth, the inexhaustible practice; fifth, the practice free from delusion and confusion; sixth, the practice of sublime manifestation; seventh, the unattached practice; eighth, the practice of reverence; ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas; and tenth, the practice of reality.
These are the ten practices.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s practice of joy?
This Bodhisattva acts as a great donor, capable of relinquishing all that he possesses, bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings with an impartial mind.
Having given, he feels no regret; he does not look for karmic retribution, nor seek fame, nor seek rebirth in superior realms, nor seek profit and sustenance.

He desires only to rescue and protect all sentient beings, to gather in all sentient beings, to benefit all sentient beings, to study the original practices of all Buddhas, to correctly recollect the original practices of all Buddhas, to attain the purity of the original practices of all Buddhas, to uphold the original practices of all Buddhas, to manifest the original practices of all Buddhas, and to extensively expound the original practices of all Buddhas, so as to cause all beings to leave suffering and attain happiness. This is called the Joyful Practice of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When a bodhisattva practices the conduct of joy, all sentient beings feel joy, love, and respect for them; wherever there are lands with poverty, the bodhisattva vows to be reborn there.
Noble, wealthy, and of great riches, his treasures were inexhaustible.
In every moment of thought, immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable sentient beings would come to the Bodhisattva’s abode and say:
"O Benevolent One!"
"We are poor and destitute, having nothing to sustain us; we pray that you will grant us compassionate rescue so that we may preserve our lives.
The Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, fulfilled all their needs, and there was none who did not rejoice.

The Bodhisattva does not give rise to anxiety or distress through the burden of seeking and searching; rather, they simply give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great compassion, practicing giving without weariness, desiring that [beings] may always come.
Having arrived, he felt redoubled joy and celebration, thinking thus:
"I have gained a great benefit.

These sentient beings are my field of merit and my virtuous friends; without being invited or requested, they have come of their own accord to instruct me and inspire my mind to practice the Buddha-way."

I should now train myself in this way so that all sentient beings may universally attain joy; through the merits I have cultivated throughout the three periods of time, may I swiftly accomplish the pure Dharma-body and sovereign spiritual powers, so that all sentient beings may obtain whatever they require and find complete satisfaction.
By this merit, may all sentient beings fully attain perfect enlightenment and deliver immeasurable beings, leading them all ultimately to *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

I shall first cause all sentient beings to fulfill their various aspirations, and only thereafter shall I attain equal and perfect enlightenment. I shall be free from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of "mine," the notion of a life span, notions of diversity, the notion of a *pudgala*, and the notion of an agent. The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings are empty and without distinction;

they are free from the dharma of desire, the dharma that is not real, the dharma of non-existence, the dharma that is not solid, the dharma that is not to be relied upon, and the dharma that is not something produced.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, he perceives no giver, no recipient, no material wealth, no field of merit, no karma, no retribution, no fruit, no great fruit, and no small fruit.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the three periods of time and gives rise to this thought: "Alas!

Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and entangled by afflictions; they constantly flow within the ocean of suffering of the cycle of birth and death, failing to attain stability amidst unstable phenomena."

I shall fully learn all that the Buddhas have learned, to benefit sentient beings and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment; I shall awaken all and cause them to be pure, following along with cessation and contemplating the dharmas of the three periods of time.
"This is called the first practice of joy of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the second practice of benefit of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?"

This bodhisattva maintains pure ethical discipline; regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, his mind is free from defiled attachment, and he extensively expounds the dharma of non-attachment for the sake of sentient beings.

They do not seek rebirth in the superior realms of humans or devas, nor in noble families; they do not seek gain and offerings, nor physical beauty, nor the status of a sovereign; they simply maintain the pure precepts with steadfast resolve.
One should form this thought:

"I maintain the pure precepts, free from all entanglements, the blazing fires of affliction, and the suffering of grief and lamentation; I do not betray sentient beings, and the Buddhas rejoice in me, so that I may ultimately achieve unsurpassed bodhi."

"When a Bodhisattva maintains pure precepts in this manner, if within a single day there were immeasurable, countless, asaṃkhyeya great Māras, each of whom brought with them immeasurable, countless, asaṃkhyeya hosts of celestial maidens— all of whom were upright and beautiful, with exquisite countenances and seductive charms that could bewitch the human heart—
and furthermore, if they brought all manner of musical instruments and delights, desiring to come and disturb the Bodhisattva’s resolve for the Way."
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"These five desires are dharmas that obstruct the Path; they are capable of hindering unsurpassed bodhi."
Therefore, a bodhisattva does not give rise to even a single thought of desire; his mind is as pure as that of a Buddha.

Except for employing skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, he never internally departs from the bodhisattva’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). With firm and correct mindfulness, he does not, for the sake of the conditions of the five desires, give rise to a single evil thought to afflict or disturb sentient beings.
"I would rather sacrifice my own body and life than inflict evil upon others; it is impossible that I should ever inflict evil upon others.
Since I first beheld the Buddha, I have never once given rise to a single thought of desire, much less acted upon it."
If one were to engage in such activities, it would be impossible [to attain liberation].
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Sentient beings have dwelt for a long night within birth and death, recollecting the five desires, craving the five desires, delighting in the five desires, their minds constantly wandering among the five desires, and being forever submerged in the realms of the five desires, unable to emerge from them. I should now train myself in this way:"
They cause all the Māra kings, their retinues of celestial maidens, and all sentient beings to establish themselves in the unsurpassed precepts;

having established them in the pure precepts, they further instruct them so that they attain the stage of non-retrogression, achieve equal and perfect enlightenment through all-knowledge, and even reach ultimate nirvana without remainder.
Why is this? This is my own karma; all Buddhas have likewise trained in this way.
They have abandoned all improper conduct, the conceit of a self, and ignorance.
Contemplating the profound and equal Dharma of all Buddhas, they attain omniscience and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, thereby severing perversions.
There are no perversions apart from sentient beings, nor are there sentient beings apart from perversions;
within perversions there are no sentient beings, and within sentient beings there are no perversions.
Perversion is not the sentient being; the sentient being is not perversion.
Perversion is not an internal phenomenon;
perversion is not an external phenomenon.
Sentient beings are not internal phenomena; sentient beings are not external phenomena. All dharmas are merely illusory and lack reality;
they do not abide for even a moment and possess no solidity.
"Just as an illusion deceives the foolish, one should realize that all phenomena are like dreams and like lightning.
One who understands in this way can reach the ultimate bodhi at the end of birth and death.
To deliver those who have not yet been delivered;
to liberate those who have not yet been liberated;
and to bring to subjugation those who have not yet been subjugated.
To those who have not attained tranquility, may they attain tranquility;
to those who have not attained peace, may they attain peace;
to those who have not been freed from defilement, may they be freed from defilement.
Those who have not yet attained purity, may they attain purity;
those who have not yet attained nirvana, may they attain nirvana;
those who have not yet attained happiness, may they attain happiness.
I shall renounce all worldly affairs so as to bring joy to all Tathāgatas.

Fully accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas, I shall abide in the unsurpassed and most supreme Dharma, impartially and correctly contemplating all sentient beings, discerning and understanding all phenomena, remaining far removed from all evils, forever abandoning falsehood, extinguishing all afflictions and habitual tendencies, achieving the sublime and wondrous skillful means of transcendence, attaining immeasurable and boundless eloquence, and perfecting profound wisdom of emptiness and stillness.
This is called the second beneficial practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the third practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the practice free from anger and resentment?"
This bodhisattva is always able to cultivate the dharma of patience, being humble and respectful, with a serene countenance and loving speech;
they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, nor do they harm both;
they do not exalt themselves, do not exalt others, nor do they exalt both.
Not considering oneself right, nor considering others wrong, nor considering both to be right;
not praising oneself, but forming this thought:

"I shall constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to leave all evil behind and sever greed, hatred, delusion, arrogance, pride, a distracted mind, stinginess, envy, and crookedness."
"They are established through the dharma of great patience.
When a bodhisattva has thus accomplished this pure dharma of patience, suppose there were immeasurable and countless sentient beings, each with immeasurable and countless retinues;
and each sentient being had immeasurable and countless emanated heads.
Each head has immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya tongues;
from these tongues issue immeasurable and innumerable evil sounds;
from these sounds issue immeasurable and innumerable insults.
With vulgar and filthy speech, they reviled and insulted the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, each of these sentient beings possessed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya hands;

in their hands they held immeasurable and innumerable blades and staves, with which they beat, struck, crushed, humiliated, and harmed the Bodhisattva, continuing without rest for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
When a bodhisattva encounters such bitter suffering, they reflect thus:

"If, because of this suffering, I give rise to a mind of anger, then I shall not be self-subdued, nor self-guarded, nor self-clarified, nor self-serene, nor one who has cultivated meditative concentration, nor one who is truthful, nor one who does not cherish their own body; how then could I cause others to give rise to a heart of joy and attain liberation?"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Because of this body and mind, I have endured all manner of suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable kalpas;
therefore, I shall earnestly exhort myself to gladden the mind and skillfully discipline and regulate it."
"Why is this? Because I shall abide in the unsurpassed Dharma, desiring to enable all sentient beings to likewise attain this Dharma.
He then reflected further:
"This body is empty and quiescent; it is without self or what belongs to a self, and lacks any true nature.
It is empty and non-dual. Whether suffering or pleasure, neither exists, for all phenomena are empty."
"I shall understand this and explain it extensively for others.
Therefore, although I now encounter bitter suffering, I must endure it.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, for their benefit, for their peace and security, for their inclusion, and so as not to abandon them—and desiring to cause sentient beings to attain non-retrogression and the ultimate accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi—I shall practice the Dharma practiced by the Buddhas."
This is called the third inexhaustible practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva: the practice of being without anger or resentment.
"Sons of the Buddha!
What is the fourth inexhaustible practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

This bodhisattva diligently cultivates vigor, supreme vigor, most excellent vigor, foremost vigor, great vigor, subtle and wondrous vigor, superior vigor, unsurpassed vigor, unequaled vigor, and vigor equal to the unequaled.
That bodhisattva is not disturbed by sensual desire;
nor is he troubled or disturbed by anger, delusion, pride, malice, stinginess, envy, resentment, deceitfulness, lack of shame, or lack of remorse.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"I do not wish to afflict sentient beings, nor even wish to afflict a single sentient being; therefore, I diligently cultivate vigor.
It is solely because I wish to abandon all afflictions that I practice vigor."
One practices diligence because one desires to destroy all fetters;
one practices diligence because one desires to abandon all habitual tendencies;
one practices diligence because one desires to fully discern all sentient beings.
One practices with diligence because one desires to know the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings;
one practices with diligence because one desires to know the afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
one practices with diligence because one desires to know the various aspirations of all sentient beings.
They practice with diligence because they wish to know all the spheres of experience of all sentient beings;
they practice with diligence because they wish to know all the faculties of all sentient beings;
they practice with diligence because they wish to know the minds and mental activities of all sentient beings.
They practice with diligence because they wish to know the realm of all phenomena;
they practice with diligence because they wish to know the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
they practice with diligence because they wish to know the equal Dharma of all Buddhas.
They practice diligence because they wish to know the equality of the three periods of time through skillful means;
they practice diligence because they wish to know the pure and equal Dharma;
and they practice diligence because they wish to attain all the Buddha-dharmas.
They practice diligence because they wish to know all Buddha-dharmas through a single gateway of skillful means;
they practice diligence because they wish to know the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable nature of all Buddhas;
