and they practice diligence because they wish to know the great wisdom and excellent skillful means of all Buddhas.
"Because one wishes to know all Buddha-dharmas and to analyze them sentence by sentence for the sake of sentient beings, one practices with diligence.
When a Bodhisattva has accomplished such diligence, if someone were to say:

"For the sake of each and every sentient being in immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya worlds, you are able, throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas, to fully undergo the sufferings of the Avīci Great Hell so that those sentient beings may ultimately attain Nirvāṇa;"

Furthermore, there have appeared in the world immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya Buddhas who caused immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya sentient beings to experience various kinds of happiness; yet you still continue to undergo the sufferings of the great hells—only after that shall you attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I am able to undergo the sufferings of the hells for every single sentient being in all those worlds;
when the Buddhas appear in the world and sentient beings experience happiness, I shall likewise undergo suffering, and only thereafter will I attain the Unsurpassed Way."
Furthermore, another person said:
"If you were able to take a single hair-tip and drain all the waters of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) great oceans until they were completely exhausted?"
Could one take infinite, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds and grind them into atoms, and know their total number?
And likewise, could one maintain the bodhicitta at every successive moment of thought, never abandoning or forgetting it?
When a bodhisattva hears these words, they do not retreat nor do they regret; instead, they leap for joy with great exuberance and diligently cultivate vigor, thinking:
"I have attained a sublime benefit."
"Because of me, may the sentient beings of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds forever be freed from all suffering.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:

"I shall undergo all sufferings on behalf of all sentient beings, universally causing them to leave behind all suffering and attain the ultimate Nirvana without remainder; only then shall I realize the Unsurpassed Way."
This is called the fourth inexhaustible practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the fifth practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion?
This bodhisattva achieves the foremost right mindfulness, which is never distracted, firm and indestructible, supremely excellent, pure, and immeasurable;

having abandoned the darkness of delusion, they discern right mindfulness and are well able to receive and uphold the worldly and world-transcending sūtras and śāstras, the sūtras and śāstras on material phenomena and non-material phenomena, and the sūtras and śāstras on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

There is no delusion or confusion in dying here and being born there; there is no delusion or confusion in entering or emerging from the womb; there is no delusion or confusion in abiding in the bodhicitta; there is no delusion or confusion in drawing near to spiritual friends; there is no delusion or confusion in studying all the Buddha-dharmas; there is no delusion or confusion in awakening to the works of Māra; there is no delusion or confusion in distancing oneself from the works of Māra; and there is no delusion or confusion in practicing the bodhisattva conduct for immeasurable eons.

Having accomplished such immeasurable and innumerable firm and correct mindfulness, for immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, [the bodhisattva] hears and receives the true Dharma from all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

That is to say: the profound Dharma; the subtle and wondrous Dharma; the adorned Dharma; the variously adorned Dharma; the Dharma of various collections of names, phrases, and syllables; the Dharma that adorns bodhisattvas; the unsurpassed Dharma that adorns all Buddhas; the Dharma of pure right aspiration; the Dharma of non-attachment to all worlds; the Dharma of discerning all worlds; the vast Dharma; the immeasurable Dharma; the Dharma of abandoning the darkness of delusion and discerning the world; the common Dharma; the uncommon Dharma; the Dharma of the sphere of bodhisattva wisdom; and the Dharma of mastery over all-knowledge.
Having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva never again regressed or forgot it for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Why is this? Because when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva originally practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas, he never troubled or disturbed sentient beings; he maintained right mindfulness and samādhi, did not sever the True Dharma, did not sever his roots of goodness, and did not sever his wisdom.
This bodhisattva cannot be disturbed by immeasurable kinds of sounds, namely:
loud sounds, harassing sounds, sounds that cause terror, subtle and exquisite sounds, unpleasant sounds, and sounds that distract the six sense faculties.

When the Bodhisattva hears such immeasurable and innumerable sounds—whether pleasant or unpleasant—he remains undisturbed in right mindfulness, undisturbed in samādhi, undisturbed regarding his objective sphere, undisturbed in entering the subtle and wondrous Dharma, undisturbed in the Bodhisattva practice, undisturbed in cultivating the bodhicitta, undisturbed in the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, undisturbed in observing the true Dharma, undisturbed in the wisdom that transforms sentient beings, undisturbed in maturing sentient beings, undisturbed in the pure wisdom that establishes sentient beings, and undisturbed in observing the profound meaning.
Because they do not engage in unwholesome karma, they have no obstruction of unwholesome karma;
because they do not engage in afflictions, they have no obstruction of afflictions;
because they do not engage in disrespect, they have no obstruction of disrespect.
Because they do not practice the slandering of the Dharma, they have no obstruction of slandering the Dharma.

Such immeasurable kinds of sounds—each and every one of these voices—pervade the infinite, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds of the ten directions; throughout infinite, boundless, and incalculable eons, they never cease. They are able to agitate and disorder the faculties of sentient beings, causing them to go mad, yet they cannot disturb this Bodhisattva’s profound samādhi.

Within samādhi, the bodhisattva contemplates and discerns the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of all sounds; he skillfully discerns and knows the nature of their arising, abiding, and ceasing.

He also skillfully observes those who hear sounds: when hearing pleasant or unpleasant sounds, their minds are free from hatred or love, their right mindfulness remains undisturbed, and they skillfully grasp the characteristics of those sounds without becoming stained or attached to them.
One knows that all sounds are non-existent, lacking true reality; they have no creator and no original limit, being no different from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This bodhisattva accomplishes the tranquil conduct of body, speech, and mind, never again regressing;
they dwell securely in the various dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis.
Having awakened to all dharmas, their wisdom is perfected, and they attain the Samādhi of Detachment from All Sounds, with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) gates of samādhi as its retinue.
Nurturing great compassion in every thought-moment, they are able to attain immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis and ultimately achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having heard this sound of the great evil that destroys the faculties, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in pure right mindfulness."
"Regarding all-knowledge, they attain non-retrogression and ultimately achieve nirvana without remainder.
This is called the fifth practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: being free from delusion and confusion.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the sixth practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Practice of Excellent Manifestation?
This Bodhisattva accomplishes the pacification of the actions of body, speech, and mind;”
There are no bodily, verbal, or mental actions that are non-existent or non-manifest;
there are no bodily, verbal, or mental actions that are bound or liberated.

Being neither bound nor liberated, all manifestations have no basis and no dwelling, abiding in accordance with the mind in the nature of immeasurable minds and the like, as well as the nature of all phenomena.
It is devoid of the characteristics of intrinsic nature; it manifests as signless, its characteristics being profoundly deep and bottomless.

Suchness-nature is free from karmic retribution; through skillful means, it gives rise to that which is free from birth—neither arising nor ceasing, quiescent, and nirvana-like. It is not existent, yet it is spoken of as existent; the path of language is cut off.

Detached from all worlds and dwelling nowhere, they nurture the roots of goodness arising in Bodhisattvas; they enter the dharma-gate of being free from falsehood, unbound, and unattached; they enter the dharma-gate of reality; they enter the dharma-gate of transcending the world; and they discern all worldly dharmas.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"All sentient beings have non-nature as their nature;
all dharmas have the unconditioned as their nature."
All Buddha-fields have non-characteristic as their characteristic;
ultimately, all three periods of time are entirely devoid of self-nature;
the path of language is cut off, and there is no dependence upon any phenomena.

The Bodhisattva understands such profound dharmas as these: he understands that all worlds are entirely quiescent; he understands the profound and wondrous dharmas of all Buddhas; he understands that there is no difference between the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas, such that worldly dharmas enter the Buddha-dharma and the Buddha-dharma enters worldly dharmas;
yet the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas do not become confused, nor does the worldly dharma destroy the Buddha-dharma.

The true dharma-realm is indestructible; it abides in the impartiality of the True Dharma throughout the three periods of time. Furthermore, one does not abandon the bodhicitta nor the mind that transforms sentient beings, but rather increases the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion, desiring to deliver all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If I do not bring sentient beings to maturity, who shall?
If I do not discipline sentient beings, who shall?"
If I do not bring peace to sentient beings, who shall?
If I do not cause sentient beings to rejoice, who shall? If I do not purify sentient beings, who shall?
The Bodhisattva further reflected:

"Having understood this profound Dharma, I see that sentient beings undergo great suffering and affliction, treading upon perilous paths and being entangled by various defilements. They are like those with grave illnesses, constantly tormented by pain and bound by the ties of affection within the prison of birth and death;
they never leave the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or King Yama, unable to eternally extinguish the immeasurable mass of suffering and remaining separated from the three obstacles."
Constantly dwelling in the darkness of ignorance, they do not see the light of reality; they undergo endless birth and death and fail to attain the path of liberation.

Circling through the eight difficulties, they are afflicted by folly and defiled by various impurities; submerged in a boundless and deep sea of afflictions, deluded by false views, they do not behold the true path.
The Bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"It would be improper for me to abandon sentient beings if they are not yet matured while seeking my own perfect enlightenment.

I shall first teach and transform sentient beings; throughout immeasurable kalpas, I shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices, instructing those who are not yet matured to reach maturity, instructing those who are not yet tamed to become tamed, and instructing all those who have not yet crossed over to attain liberation."

When this bodhisattva dwells in this practice, the devas, worldlings, Māras, Śakras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, gandharvas, and others, upon seeing this bodhisattva, rejoice and look up to him with reverence.

If there are sentient beings who revere, make offerings to, respect, and prostrate before [this], or even merely see or hear it, all such acts shall not be in vain; they will certainly and ultimately attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the sixth practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Practice of Good Appearance.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the seventh practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Practice of Non-Attachment?"

With a mind free from attachment, this bodhisattva is able, in every thought-moment, to observe incalculable worlds and to purify incalculable Buddha-fields, remaining without any defiled attachment toward those Buddha-fields.

They went to the abodes of incalculable Tathāgatas to pay homage and show reverence, making offerings with incalculable flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, various jewels, flower garlands, celestial robes, miscellaneous gems, jeweled parasols, banners, and all manner of ornaments—each in incalculable quantities—while their minds remained free from attachment.
They practice incalculable skillful means yet perform no action; they possess incalculable thoughts yet abide in the dharma of non-thought.
In every moment of thought, they behold immeasurable Buddhas, yet their minds have no attachment toward those Buddhas;
their minds have no attachment toward the marks and signs of the Buddhas.
Regarding the radiance of the Buddha, their minds have no attachment;
regarding the buddha-fields, their minds have no attachment;
hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, their minds have no attachment.
Their minds have no attachment toward the worlds of the ten directions;
their minds have no attachment toward the assembly of Tathāgatas;
their minds have no attachment toward the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Hearing the Dharma with joy, their minds are free from attachment;
they broaden their correct minds, restrain their thoughts without distraction, practice the bodhisattva deeds, and remain unattached even to the Buddha-dharma.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in each and every Buddha-field throughout the ten directions, for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, reveres, prostrates to, and makes offerings to the Buddhas without ever feeling weary or satisfied;
upon seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma, his mind remains free from attachment;
and upon seeing the Tathāgatas and the great assemblies of bodhisattvas as a magnificent adornment, his mind remains free from attachment.
When seeing impure lands, their minds feel no aversion.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena through the lens of quiescent equanimity.

All phenomena are without defilement, without purity, without darkness, without light, without discrimination, without non-discrimination, without falsehood, without reality, without security, without danger, without the right path, and without the wrong path.

"In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and enters into the nature of sentient beings; they teach, discipline, and bring sentient beings to maturity, yet their mind has no attachment toward those beings.
They uphold all phenomena, yet their mind has no attachment toward those phenomena.
Without abandoning the bodhicitta, they abide where the Buddhas abide, yet their mind has no attachment toward that which the Buddhas abide in."
They enter into various paths of speech, yet their minds have no attachment to these paths of speech;
they enter into the paths of sentient beings, yet their minds have no attachment to these paths of sentient beings;
they discern and are able to enter all samādhis and meditative attainments (samāpatti), yet their minds have no attachment to them.
They travel to immeasurable, boundless, and unspeakable Buddha-lands; beholding those Buddha-lands, their minds are free from attachment;
and when departing from those Buddha-lands, their minds have no lingering longing.
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in all Buddha-lands, with a mind free from attachment, understands the true teaching of the Buddhas;
they encounter no obstacles regarding the Unsurpassed Way;
and they have already attained firm establishment in the correct teaching of the Buddhas.
Fully endowed with the bodhisattva practices, securely dwelling in the bodhisattva mind, and accomplishing the bodhisattva’s liberation of tranquil extinction;
without conceptualizing or clinging to the bodhisattva’s conduct, abiding in the pure path of the bodhisattva, one receives the prophecy of truth.
Having received the prediction of enlightenment, he reflected thus: "Ordinary people are foolish and ignorant;

they do not know the True Truth, nor do they see the True Truth. They are dull-witted and lack faith; their minds are not sincere, and they constantly act with defiled attachment. They wander through birth and death, failing to see the Buddhas, being separated from spiritual friends, and straying from the Right Path. Deluded by false views, they do not seek the Teacher who tames, nor do they revere the King of Ten Powers. Unaware of the Bodhisattvas' kindness, they associate with evil associates. Hearing that all phenomena are empty, their hearts are filled with great terror. With improper reflection, they slander the True Dharma, abandon the Right Path, and delight in following deviant ways. They enter the net of Māra, remain far removed from the Buddhas, and are constantly attached to the various realms of existence, undergoing manifold sufferings."
At that time, having seen those sentient beings undergoing various sufferings, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion increased; he contemplated all roots of goodness with a mind free from attachment.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva formed this thought:

'For the sake of each and every sentient being throughout the ten directions, I shall remain for immeasurable, boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to bring sentient beings to maturity, without weariness or fatigue in my mind.'"
They dwell together constantly, never wishing to abandon one another or depart.
Just as with the tip of a hair, they use a single hair-tip to measure throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
for the sake of a single sentient being, they each remain at every point on a hair-tip for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
"As it is for one sentient being, so it is for all sentient beings.
With this mind of great compassion, he proceeds through every thought-moment in succession without ever ceasing;
yet, toward sentient beings, his mind remains free from attachment.
Upon each and every tip of a single hair, they fully cultivate all the practices of the bodhisattvas throughout the entirety of the past and the future.

They do not cling to the body, nor to phenomena, nor to mindfulness, nor to vows, nor to samādhi, nor to practice, nor to tranquility, nor to spheres of experience, nor to the teaching and maturing of sentient beings, nor to entering the profound realm of reality (dharmadhātu).
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva observes in this way:
"The entire dharma-realm is like an illusion."
The dharmas of all Buddhas are like lightning;
the practices of bodhisattvas are like dreams;
the teachings heard are like echoes.
All worlds are like transformations;
they arise from the retribution of karma.
Like the emanations of Māṇibhadra, one knows that all sentient beings are like painted images, their various and diverse forms all being drawn by the mind.
All dharmas thus expounded are identical to the limit of reality;
within a single thought-moment, they pervade the ten directions.
Cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva, they are as vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate like empty space.

Within a single thought-moment, they fully know the definitive skillful means of all Buddhas; they understand that the characteristics of the mind revolve with extreme rapidity, yet they remain unstained by and unattached to this mind.
The Bodhisattva thus contemplates non-self.
Seeing the Buddha transform and deliver all sentient beings, he attains immeasurable joy within the Buddha-dharma;
giving rise to great compassion, he protects and rescues all, his mind free from sorrow and affliction, and he attains the vow of joy.
Those who are immature, he shall bring to maturity;
those who are unsubdued, he shall subdue.
Remaining detached from the world, yet he is able to accord with all the world.

If I hear the sounds of sentient beings in all directions and lands, their various karmas, their designations, their aggregations, their cycles of rebirth, their various activities, their spheres of experience, their various stages, and their arisings, I shall, by the power of my great vows, go everywhere to those places; I shall never abandon my vast aspiration to teach and transform sentient beings, nor shall I give rise to even a single thought of defiled attachment.
Why is this? Because by being without attachment, they benefit themselves and others, achieving pure fulfillment.
This is called the seventh practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the Practice of Non-attachment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the eighth practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Practice of Reverence?

This Bodhisattva accomplishes roots of goodness that are reverent, indestructible, supreme, inconceivable, inexhaustible, non-retrogressive, incomparable, tranquil, and the roots of goodness of all Buddha-dharmas.”
When this bodhisattva practices these deeds, his mind always delights in the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas;
he single-mindedly and exclusively seeks unsurpassed enlightenment, never for a moment abandoning the great vows of a bodhisattva;
and while practicing the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons, he does not dwell on the various sufferings encountered, nor does he give rise to distress.

They cannot be destroyed by any demons; they are all protected and remembered by all Buddhas; they constantly practice the various pure conducts of Bodhisattvas; they diligently cultivate all the immeasurable ascetic practices of Bodhisattvas without ever becoming weary; and they attain the non-retrogressive, great Mahāyāna vow.

Once this bodhisattva has established themselves in and honored the bodhisattva practices, in every moment they are able to transform the birth-and-death and the hardships of incalculable eons, thereby nurturing the immeasurable great vows of a bodhisattva.

If there are sentient beings who revere, make offerings to, or even merely see or hear [this], they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression and be certain to ultimately realize unsurpassed bodhi.
That bodhisattva observes sentient beings and realizes they do not truly exist, yet does not abandon them.

It is like a river that does not reach the opposite shore, nor does it come from this shore; it does not cease in the middle of the stream, yet it can ferry sentient beings across from one shore to the other because its flow continues uninterrupted.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: he does not tend toward saṃsāra, nor does he tend toward nirvāṇa; yet, without dwelling within the middle current of saṃsāra, he is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the other shore—the place of peace, fearlessness, and freedom from sorrow and affliction.
Regarding the number of sentient beings, his mind has no attachment.
He does not abandon one sentient being while becoming attached to many,
nor does he abandon many sentient beings while becoming attached to one.
The realm of sentient beings does not increase, nor does it decrease;
the realm of sentient beings is not born, nor does it perish;
the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, nor does it grow.
The realm of sentient beings is not non-existent; the realm of sentient beings is non-dual. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva deeply understands that the realm of sentient beings is like the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and there is no duality between the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.

Within the non-dual dharma, there is no increase and no decrease, no arising and no cessation; the true nature of dharmas is real, neither coming nor going, without any basis for attachment, and not forming dualistic marks.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva understands that all dharma-realms are characterized by non-duality.
In this way, through skillful means, the bodhisattva understands the profound dharma-realm.
Abiding in the signless and abiding in pure, wondrous signs, they adorn their bodies.
They are skillfully able to discern all signs, decisively reaching the ultimate further shore, and fully discerning and knowing the number of sentient beings.

They are able to manifest their bodies in all buddha-fields, yet their minds remain unattached to those fields; they penetrate deeply into the Buddha-dharma without being defiled by it, discerning its meanings and flavors, and expounding them extensively for others.
Regarding all phenomena, they remain at the limit where all desires are transcended, yet they do not sever the bodhisattva path nor abandon bodhisattva conduct.
They practice inexhaustible merit and enter the pure dharma-realm.

Just as fire produced from a fire-jewel can never be exhausted, so too the treasury of merits of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible, and their work of teaching and transforming sentient beings is likewise inexhaustible.
Yet the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is neither ultimate nor non-ultimate;
neither free from grasping nor not free from grasping;
neither dependent nor independent.
It is neither a worldly dharma nor a Buddha-dharma;
it is neither an ordinary person nor one who has attained the fruit.
Thus, the bodhisattva accomplishes a mind of reverence, cultivates the bodhisattva practices, and does not teach the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
He does not teach the Buddha-dharma, nor does he teach worldly dharmas;
he does not teach sentient beings, nor does he destroy sentient beings;
he does not teach the right path, nor does he destroy the right path.
They do not teach defilement, nor do they teach purity. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure.
One knows that all phenomena are without reception, without transformation, and without retrogression.
When practicing this profound dharma of quiescence, one does not give rise to the thought:
"I am now practicing this dharma," "I have already practiced this dharma," or "I shall practice this dharma."
He has never entertained the thought that there are any aggregates,
elements, or sense bases— whether the internal world, the external world, or both— that constitute great vows or the various *pāramitās*.

Why is this? Within all dharmas, there is no inclination toward the vehicles of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, or Buddha; nor is there any inclination toward the realm of ordinary beings, nor any inclination toward the realms of defilement and purity, or birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-dual, yet there is no "non-duality" [to be grasped].
It is like space: though one searches for it throughout the ten directions, there is no differentiation, yet it is not that space does not exist.
When a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena in this way, they find them to be entirely without distinction.
It is not that they fail to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment;
rather, that which is most true does not contradict right practice, universally manifests the conduct of a bodhisattva, and yet never abandons their immeasurable great vows.
They tame sentient beings, turn the great wheel of Dharma, do not destroy cause and effect, and do not contravene the dharma of the contemplation of quiescent equality.

These Bodhisattvas are entirely equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; they do not sever the Buddha-nature, do not damage the True Dharma, and cause the True Dharma to flourish. Their eloquence is inexhaustible, and regarding all dharmas, their minds are without attachment. They dwell securely in the Hall of Dharma, discerning the profound teachings, abiding in fearlessness, and never abandoning the dwelling of the Buddhas. They do not contravene worldly laws, manifesting universally throughout the world while remaining unattached to the mind of the world.

When a bodhisattva thus accomplishes the cultivation of bodhisattva practices through the attainment of honored wisdom, they cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind the evil realms and various hardships of the world;
they teach, mature, and establish them within the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, remaining firm and unshakable.
Having taught them thus, he further thought:

"All sentient beings do not recognize kindness or righteousness; they continue to kill and harm one another; their false views increase and flourish; they are deluded regarding the right path; they are filled with afflictions and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance."
Even if there were spiritual friends filling the world, all of whom were thoroughly enlightened and fully endowed with wisdom, I would not practice the bodhisattva path for their sake alone.
Why is this? Among those who are virtuous or evil, I do not seek gain or support, nor do I pursue fame or reputation, even for so much as a single thread or a single word of affection.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, while practicing the bodhisattva path, he did not give rise to a single thought of seeking his own peace; rather, he desired only to subdue all sentient beings, purify all sentient beings, and deliver all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.

One should not seek gain or offerings, nor dwell upon the faults of others; one should always practice the bodhisattva path with an impartial mind, viewing enemies and kin with equality and without distinction, desiring to lead them ultimately to the other shore and to fully accomplish unsurpassed bodhi.
This is called the eighth practice of honoring by the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the ninth practice of wholesome dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
This Bodhisattva serves as a pool of the Dharma that brings cooling relief to all sentient beings, including devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, and others.
They protect the true Dharma so that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of purity;
they preach the Dharma without obstruction, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of meaning;
their eloquence regarding meaning is inexhaustible, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma.
The analytical discernment of phenomena is inexhaustible because one has attained the dhāraṇī of correct speech;
the analytical discernment of expression is inexhaustible because one has attained the unobstructed dhāraṇī;
the analytical discernment of the meaning and flavor of the teachings is inexhaustible because one has attained the Buddha’s dhāraṇī of the consecration of ambrosia.
They cause sentient beings to rejoice with inexhaustible eloquence, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of self-awakening;
their shared eloquence is inexhaustible, because they have entered the *dhāraṇī* of shared eloquence;
they explain various meanings, names, phrases, and syllables inexhaustibly, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of correct speech.
Their immeasurable eloquence is inexhaustible because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable praise;
throughout the trichiliocosm, they manifest bodies like those of Buddhas, fully endowed with wondrous voices.
Regarding all phenomena, they perform the Buddha-work without any obstruction.

According to those who should be transformed, according to the sounds by which they are understood, and according to the faculties of sentient beings, they preach the Dharma at the appropriate time with their broad and long tongues and pure voices, never departing from great compassion.
According to what is appropriate for each, from every single word they produce immeasurable sounds, causing all to rejoice.

Suppose there were sentient beings who fully knew the laws of immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya languages; who knew immeasurable karmas; and who knew immeasurable retributions—such immeasurable and countless asankhyeya sentient beings filling immeasurable, boundless, and asankhyeya worlds, serving as the retinue of the Bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva is present in this assembly and utters a single word of Dharma, it causes all these sentient beings to attain understanding and liberation.
It is likewise with the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great multitudes who serve as the retinue of such bodhisattvas.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva again thought:
'Suppose that upon the tip of a single hair, within a single moment of thought, there were to assemble an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) multitude;
and suppose that in this manner, moment after moment in succession, such multitudes continued to assemble throughout all past and future kalpas, yet they would still not be exhausted.'"
"The various members of that great assembly speak with different voices and their questions are each distinct.
Upon hearing all such inquiries and challenges, the Bodhisattva felt no fear in his heart and thought to himself:
"Even if all sentient beings were to come and pose difficult questions, I would resolve their webs of doubt with but a single word, causing them all to rejoice."
When the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, his words are not false or vain.
In every single word, there is the adornment of immeasurable and boundless wisdom, accomplishing an infinite treasury of all merits.
The light of wisdom universally illumines all things; all dharmas are fully perfected, and the knowledge of all modes is accomplished.
Having established themselves in the practice of wholesome dharmas, these bodhisattvas are able to purify themselves and also bring benefit to all sentient beings.
In this way, throughout this trichiliocosm, and even across immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds, he transforms his own body into the color of pure gold, endowed with wondrous sounds.
Regarding all phenomena, they perform the work of a Buddha without any obstruction,
transforming and delivering sentient beings through immeasurable and boundless gates of pure Dharma.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has ten kinds of bodies:
the body that enters the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-realm, for the purpose of eliminating all worlds;”
The future body, because it gives rise to all realms of existence;
the non-arising body, because it deeply delights in the equality of the non-arising of dharmas;
the non-ceasing body, because all dharmas are beyond the reach of verbal expression.
The non-substantial body, because it is suchness in its true reality;
the body free from delusion and falsehood, because it manifests according to needs;
the body without coming or going, because it is free from dying here and being born there.
The indestructible body, because the nature of the dharma-realm is indestructible;
the single-characteristic body, because the path of verbal expression is severed throughout the three periods of time;
the signless body, because of the skillful discernment of the characteristics of all dharmas.
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished these ten kinds of bodies are able to act as a shelter for all sentient beings, because they nurture their roots of goodness;
they act as protectors for all sentient beings, because they bestow great fearlessness;
they act as a refuge for all sentient beings, because they cause them to dwell in great peace and security.”
He is the honored guide for all sentient beings, because he reveals the gateway to the unsurpassed path;
he is the teacher for all sentient beings, because he employs skillful means to lead them into the true Dharma;
he is the lamp for all sentient beings, because he enables them to see the retribution of karma.
They are the illumination for all sentient beings, because they have attained the most profound Dharma;
they are the torch for all sentient beings, because they cause them to leave behind ignorance and understand the true Dharma;
they are the light for all sentient beings, because they cause them to attain the stage of clarity.
To serve as a lamp for all sentient beings in every realm of existence, by manifesting the sovereign power of the Tathāgata—
this is called the ninth practice of wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Once this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is established in the practice of wholesome dharmas, he becomes a cooling pool of Dharma for all sentient beings, because he has reached the profound depths of all the Buddha’s teachings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the true practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva accomplishes the foremost speech of truthful reality;”
As they speak, so they act; as they act, so they speak.

This bodhisattva studies the true speech of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, enters the nature of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and becomes equal to the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This bodhisattva accomplishes all such roots of goodness, studies the non-dual speech of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and accords with the all-encompassing wisdom of the Tathāgatas.
This Bodhisattva accomplishes the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
the knowledge of all karmic retributions—past, future, and present—of sentient beings;
and the knowledge of whether the faculties of sentient beings are complete or incomplete.
The knowledge of the various natures of sentient beings;
the knowledge of the various inclinations of sentient beings;
and the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations for sentient beings.
The wisdom that discerns the impurity, purity, arising, timely, and untimely transformation of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments;
the wisdom regarding the formation and destruction of all past worlds;
and the unobstructed divine eye-wisdom.
The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows;
yet they do not abandon any of the practices of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
It is because he wishes to bring all sentient beings to subjugation and purification.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:

"I see sentient beings undergoing immeasurable suffering; it would be improper for me to attain perfect enlightenment before I have delivered them. I shall fulfill my great vows and only then become a Buddha."
I cause all sentient beings to resolve to seek Bodhi and ultimate Nirvana without remainder. Why is this?

It is not because sentient beings requested me to resolve my mind on Bodhi and practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva; rather, I have resolved my mind of my own accord for the sake of all sentient beings, desiring to cause them ultimately to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, I am the most preeminent among all things because I do not cling to sentient beings;
I have attained supremacy over all things because I discipline sentient beings;
I am free from all darkness because I understand the limit of non-existence regarding sentient beings.
I have attained what was to be attained, because my original vows are fulfilled;
I am skilled in transformations, because I am adorned with the merits of a bodhisattva;
I possess skillful gathering, because I am protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon his original vow, he attains entry into the adornment of unsurpassed wisdom.

According to what is appropriate for all sentient beings, he is able to transform and deliver them; having fully satisfied their original vows according to each, he attains sovereign wisdom regarding all dharmas, causing all sentient beings to attain purity."
In every thought-moment, they are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
in every thought-moment, they are able to go to immeasurable Buddha-lands;

in every thought-moment, they see immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas and their adorned lands, manifesting the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas, reaching the ultimate limits of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. Their bodies are infinite, appearing in accordance with needs; they are immeasurable and unimpeded, yet without any dependence.
Within one's own body, Buddha-fields are universally manifested; all sentient beings, all dharmas, and the Buddhas of the three periods of time are all clearly revealed.
"This Bodhisattva knows the various perceptions and various desires of sentient beings, as well as the purity of their karmic retributions;
according to what is appropriate for each, he manifests his body to them and thereby tames them."
They understand that all phenomena are like illusions, like transformations, and like lightning;
sentient beings are like dreams.

These Bodhisattvas possess inexhaustible bodies of meaning and flavor, maintain pure right mindfulness, and definitively know all phenomena. They enter various samādhis and supreme wisdom, tranquilly observing the stage of non-duality.
All sentient beings rely upon two dharmas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, dwelling in a mind of great compassion, cultivates such profound and wondrous dharmas, reaching ultimate tranquility.
Having attained the ten powers of a Buddha, they enter the Indra-net Dharma-realm with mastery and achieve the Tathāgata’s unimpeded liberation.
As a hero among men, they let out the great lion’s roar and attain fearlessness;
as a Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma, they are able to turn the unimpeded, pure wheel of the Dharma.
They have accomplished wisdom and liberation, thoroughly understanding all the activities of the world;
they have severed the revolving stream of birth and death and entered the great ocean of wisdom;
they are able to benefit all sentient beings, protect and uphold the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and exhaustively master the ocean of all Buddhas' skillful means.
This is called the tenth true practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Once this bodhisattva is established in this true practice, they are able to cause all devas and humans, the eight classes of beings, and immeasurable sentient beings to become pure and joyful.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Part Two of the Seventeenth Chapter, "The Ten Practices of the Bodhisattva Guṇakusumasaṃcaya.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways; such is the natural law of the Tathāgata’s majestic majesty:

there rained down clouds of celestial flowers, clouds of celestial incense, clouds of celestial powdered incense, clouds of celestial garlands, clouds of celestial robes, clouds of celestial jewels, and clouds of celestial ornaments.
Furthermore, the music of celestial maidens spontaneously resounded, and wondrous celestial light shone everywhere, producing the subtle and exquisite voices of the devas.

As the Ten Practices were thus proclaimed in the Yāma Heaven palace within this four-continent world system, so too did it occur throughout the worlds of the ten directions by the Buddha’s spiritual power.

At that time, from each of the ten directions, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields who filled the ten directions and came to this land.
Having arrived, he spoke to the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, saying: "Excellent,
Son of the Buddha!
You are thus able to expound upon the practices of all bodhisattvas.
All of us bodhisattvas who have come here share the same name, Guṇakūṭa;
our worlds are all named Guṇadhvaja, and our Buddhas are all titled Samantaguṇa.
In our Buddha-field as well, we teach the ten practices, the sequence of meanings of names, phrases, and syllables, and the assembly of followers is likewise, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

We have come to this land by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness for you. Just as we have come to bear witness to the teaching of the Ten Practices in the Palace of Jewel Adornments within the Yāma Heaven of this four-continent world system, so it is likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed all dharma-realms and their retinues throughout the ten directions. Desiring to ensure that the lineage of Buddhas would never be severed; desiring to purify the seed-nature of Bodhisattvas; desiring to prevent the turning back of the seeds of Bodhisattva vows; desiring to ensure that the seeds of practice were not interrupted; desiring to encompass the seeds of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; desiring to analyze and explain the seeds of sentient beings’ roots of goodness; desiring to observe the timing and faculties of all sentient beings; desiring to understand the types of conduct arising from the defiled or pure minds of beings; and desiring to universally illumine the seeds of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he spoke in verse:
"With a reverent heart, I prostrate at the feet of the Honored One of Ten Powers, Whose pure, stainless wisdom is unimpeded."
The realm is profound and far-reaching, beyond compare; its Way is pure as empty space.
The most supreme among men, free from all obstructions, With immeasurable merit and fearlessness,
With non-dual wisdom, peerless and equal to none, All his actions are utterly pure.
The present Guides of the ten directions, who understand the true meaning and are fearless,
possessing peerless merit and free from all evils— they shall swiftly reach the ultimate, unsurpassed path.
All Tathāgatas, heroes among men, have already fully given rise to great compassion;
with minds dwelling within the pure Dharma-realm, they act for the benefit of all living beings.
Peerless throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, the self-existent Perfectly Awakened One has extinguished the darkness of ignorance;
all Buddha-dharmas are entirely equal, and his merit is indestructible.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, they are able to behold all Tathāgatas;
regarding these Tathāgatas, they harbor no falsehood, and their practice is non-regressive.
If one perceives the pure true dharma-realm, The profound, subtle, and supreme ultimate truth, One cannot be deluded by any ignorance or falsehood; Such practice can accomplish the treasury of merit.
Skillfully knowing the various types of sentient beings, they enter the true and wondrous Dharma-realm;
awakening spontaneously without depending on others, their conduct is like space.
Observing that all infinite and boundless worlds are ultimately and entirely quiescent,
and that all phenomena are without obstruction— the conduct of such a person is superior to that of a Muni.

Endowed with firmness that cannot be turned back, Accomplishing the most supreme and revered Dharma, With pure vows fulfilled, they have reached the other shore; Listen attentively to all the practices of the Bodhisattvas.
Throughout all infinite and boundless stages, his wisdom is clear and penetrating without obstruction;
taking the profound and subtle as his sphere of activity, this is called the conduct of a fearless master of discourse.
He analyzes every sentence in detail and penetrates deeply into sublime wisdom.
Truly understanding all phenomena, that one practices as a Great Muni.
Far removed from all evil, always able to benefit sentient beings—
that person is a treasury of merit, equal to all the Teachers of Men.
To all living beings everywhere, he constantly bestows fearlessness;
pure and free from attachment, his conduct is beyond compare.
His mind is pure and unattached, tranquil and free from verbal faults.
Endowed with wondrous merit, they cultivate the most supreme practice;
having ultimately realized the profound meaning, their merit is certainly inexhaustible.
They cultivate the practice of immortality, and all Buddhas constantly protect and mind them.
Free from the mind of self and anger, with sublime voice filling the ten directions,
dwelling securely in the teachings of the True Dharma, his conduct is beyond compare.
Having reached the further shore through giving, he is naturally adorned by a hundred blessings.
That wisdom is supreme, able to bring joy to the multitude.
Having skillfully entered the stage of profound knowledge, they abide with a mind unmoving.
Their practice is like a vajra, firm and indestructible.
Entering fully into all dharma-realms, Following them to reach the other shore,
Ultimately attaining sovereign mastery— Such is the course of the Sun of Dharma.
The Peerless Muni, Cultivating the non-dual dharma,
The mind always delights in tranquility, and wisdom is without obstruction.
Within subtle and minute worlds, it accommodates vast universes;
there is no realm not understood as it traverses the mountain-king of wisdom.
Throughout all worlds, their minds are pure and free from attachment;
having reached the further shore through upholding the precepts, they practice the conduct of purity.
Their wisdom is immeasurable, equal to space and the dharma-realm.
Deeply entering and fully endowed with wisdom, this is the supreme Vajra practice.
Wisdom completely fills the Dharma-realm of the three periods of time;
with a mind ever free from indolence, one enters the most excellent state.
The path leading to all destinations, The discernment of the Dharma of the Ten Powers,
Physical conduct free from obstruction— This is the sphere of supreme wisdom.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, Among the infinite classes of sentient beings,
The Bodhisattvas provide universal protection and deliverance; this is the conduct of those free from delusion.
Cultivating all Buddha-dharmas with diligent effort and without indolence, they cause the entire world to be purified; this is the conduct of the Great Dragons.
Fully knowing the faculties of all beings, Thoroughly understanding their various desires,
Comprehending their immeasurable natures, And practicing with equanimity;
Throughout the realms of the ten directions, They have long endured immeasurable suffering.
His mind is free from sorrow and affliction; he practices with joy.
He emits nets of radiant light that universally illumine all worlds;
endowed with the clarity of wisdom, he skillfully cultivates the practice of insight.
They are able to shake all the infinite realms of the ten directions;
they constantly benefit all beings without causing them any fear.
Skillfully understanding the methods of language, they distinguish the path and reach the other shore.
The radiance of stainless wisdom is the practice of the Immovable One.
Skillfully understanding the realms of rising and falling, he distinguishes the way to reach the other shore;
having accomplished the stage of the inexhaustible, this is the practice of the most supreme wisdom.
With immeasurable virtues, he constantly practices seeking enlightenment;
having reached the shore of those merits, his great renown is of inexhaustible conduct.
He is the unsurpassed supreme master of treatises, the most excellent lion’s roar.
Causing all beings to be completely purified, this is the practice of those free from defilement.
Receiving the consecration of the Buddha’s nectar and being granted the prophecy of a Dharma King,
this is the practice of the Great Mind that culminates in the methods of skillful means.
Discerning all multitudes, their minds are free from attachment;
Resolutely upholding the treasury of the Dharma—this is the practice of the Dharma King.
Within each and every word, he is able to produce immeasurable sounds.
Sentient beings each have their own understanding, yet this is the sphere of unimpeded wisdom.
Having reached the ultimate limit of the dharma of language, they discern and fully comprehend it all;
far removed from all falsehoods, they practice according to the vision of reality.
Abiding securely in the ocean-seal of the Dharma, He skillfully seals all phenomena;
Realizing that phenomena have no substantial characteristic, This is the conduct of his body of skillful means.
Within each and every land, Throughout immeasurable and innumerable eons,
Exhausting the practices throughout all kalpas, their minds feel neither sorrow nor weariness.
Seeing within a single pore countless Tathāgatas, each with a different name,
is the practice of those who have skillfully cultivated.
Just as on the tip of a single hair, one universally sees immeasurable Buddhas;
so too does one see the Buddhas in all worlds.
An immeasurable and incalculable number of eons can be made to last for the duration of a single thought-moment.
Neither long nor short, this is the practice of those who have attained liberation.
To see it is entirely not in vain; all that is cultivated is truly real.
These karmic practices cannot be destroyed; such is the practice of the Most Victorious One.
For immeasurable and incalculable eons, He contemplates the Buddha without weariness;
Able to bring joy to all beings— This is the practice of unimpeded wisdom.
For immeasurable and incalculable eons, He observes the realms of sentient beings.
Sentient beings and non-sentient beings—this is the conduct of the steadfast hero.
Possessing the treasury of wisdom, a cool pool of merit, he benefits all multitudes; this is the conduct of the foremost person.
The Dharma-realm is without limit, Immeasurable like empty space;
With no attachment to speech, This is the practice of the fearless master of debate.
Within a single samādhi, He enters immeasurable samādhis.
Ascending that unsurpassed hall, the Master of Treatises, Pure Moon, practices.
Having reached the ultimate shore of patience, he endures the dharma of tranquil extinction;
far removed from a mind of malice, he is one who acts with immeasurable wisdom.
Without leaving a single world, Without rising from a single seat,
They universally manifest throughout the lands of the ten directions, The conduct of immeasurable bodies.
Immeasurable Buddha-fields Can enter into a single world.
The Buddha-fields neither increase nor decrease; such is the inconceivable sphere of his activity.
Distinguishing between what is possible and what is impossible, he enters the various powers with thorough discernment.
Having accomplished the unsurpassed powers, this is the sphere of the foremost power.
Regarding all karmic retributions of the past, future, and present, their wisdom is non-retrogressive; this is the practice of the wise.
Skillfully knowing the timely and the untimely, they subdue all beings.
Teaching and transforming others without missing the proper time, he well knows what should be practiced according to the occasion.
His physical conduct is entirely virtuous, and so too are his verbal and mental actions.
He is unattached to anything; his mental activities proceed from pure wisdom.
With wisdom that skillfully discerns, the eloquence of Dharma is inexhaustible;
its sphere of activity is equal to reality as it is—this is the conduct of the Tathāgata.
A treasury of unimpeded merit, he delights in the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Deeply entering all dharma realms, they follow the conduct of those who have entered therein.
They are equal in mind to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, without any divergent thoughts;
their single mark is without distinction, as they practice within the unimpeded realm.
Deeply entering the ocean of wisdom, They eliminate all darkness of delusion;
Able to grant the pure eye, It is the sphere of activity for those with the pure eye.
All the Teachers always practice The Dharma of non-duality.
With mastery over supernormal powers, they fulfill all that is to be practiced.

Throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, they universally rain down the rain of the sublime Dharma, causing all beings to understand the true meaning; such is the activity of the Cloud of Dharma.
Universally toward all Buddhas, they have attained firm faith;
in the liberation of omniscience, their training is entirely perfected.
Within a single thought-moment, they fully know the minds of all sentient beings.
Having thoroughly realized the nature of the mind, he dwells in the sphere of that nature which is devoid of intrinsic being.
Within inconceivable worlds, he manifests immeasurable transformation bodies;
traveling everywhere without equal, he is peerless among all who practice.
In immeasurable worlds, before all the Tathāgatas currently residing there,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly appears in the presence of those Buddhas.
When the Bodhisattva enters samādhi, sentient beings perceive him as a single body.
The Bodhisattva emerges from samādhi, and the multitude beholds his immeasurable bodies.
His conduct is profoundly subtle and wondrous; he has never committed a verbal transgression.
With immeasurable joy in his heart, he causes all beings to rejoice.
Having attained unattached wisdom, he discerns and knows all faculties;
his mind is unstained, and his conduct is the supreme discipline.
Through skillful means he distinguishes the dharmas, and he has attained mastery over all phenomena.
Throughout all worlds, they constantly perform the deeds of the Buddhas.
The subtle and wondrous conduct of the Bodhisattvas is as vast as space;
who that hears of this would not have their heart rejoice?
That wisdom has no equal; with the eye of insight, he sees all things.
His skillful means are peerless; such is the practice of incomparable wisdom.
With inexhaustible, sublime merit, he is able to extinguish all evils.
Having reached that pure shore, the sphere of peerless practice,
they accomplish the dharma of adornment and abide securely in non-retrogression;
they deliver immeasurable multitudes, yet harbor no notion of a "sentient being."
Practicing the conduct of non-contention, possessing the subtlety of omniscience,
transforming sentient beings through the True Dharma, acting with pure vision,
revering all Buddhas, and being fully endowed with ultimate wisdom.
Having achieved fearlessness, acting through the wisdom of skillful means,
they are able to universally enter all worlds and all phenomena,
as well as the various classes of sentient beings, delivering and liberating immeasurable multitudes.
Throughout the realms of the ten directions, He beats the unsurpassed drum of the Dharma.
Constantly bestowing immeasurable teachings, The practice of the Immortal One,
Sitting cross-legged in a single body, He fills immeasurable lands.
Sentient beings are not oppressed; by the power of the pure Dharma-body, within a single flavor and a single meaning, they distinguish infinite meanings.
Their preaching is inexhaustible; this is the sphere of activity of boundless wisdom.
Cultivating the liberation of the Buddhas, With wisdom free from obstruction;
Accomplishing fearlessness and Immeasurable virtues of skillful means,
They comprehend the oceans of all worlds And the oceans of all Buddha-fields.
The ocean of Dharma, the ocean of wisdom, Delivers and liberates the ocean of sentient beings.
Some see the Bodhisattva Entering the womb and being born;
Some see him attaining perfect enlightenment And his immeasurable meritorious deeds.
In every buddha-field, he manifests parinirvāṇa;
yet in truth, there is no nirvāṇa, for the Fearless Teacher abides eternally.
His vajra-body is without change, appearing to sentient beings according to their needs.
Reality is without distinction, the sphere traversed by the single body.
The equal dharma-realm is one, yet it is fully endowed with immeasurable meanings.
One should constantly and joyfully contemplate the three periods of time as the single mark of the signless dharma.
Reaching those various shores of upholding, they establish sentient beings in the True Dharma;
having attained the upholding of all Buddhas, they practice that which is most supreme.
Possessing the unstained, wondrous Dharma-body, their eye of wisdom and ear are pure.
These are all entirely without obstruction; they are the practices of the unobstructed.
Having perfected all supernatural powers and being fully endowed with profound wisdom, their wisdom is most supreme—the practice of the wisdom of skillful means.
The mind is settled and never distracted; wisdom is immeasurable.
There is no realm that is not illumined, as all that is perceived is traversed.
Having reached the shore of merit, they deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Their minds are free from weariness, constantly practicing what they cultivate.
These beings of universal knowledge and vision are born into the family of all Buddhas;
throughout the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they are miraculously born within the Dharma.
Accomplished in the methods of speech, he subdues all disputants;
having perfected immeasurable practices, he enters the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Able to emit a single ray of light, it universally illumines immeasurable lands.
The great luminous brilliance of the world, which extinguishes all darkness,
manifests the body of the Tathāgata according to what is appropriate for beings to see,
in order to subdue the various classes of living beings and to purify all buddha-fields.
The practices of the Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, such that no one can know them all;
yet they manifest every kind of practice for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Immeasurable and beyond counting, they are equal in number to the realms of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.
Praising for incalculable eons, the virtues of the Bodhisattva are inexhaustible.
The virtues of the Bodhisattva are immeasurable; they perfect all virtues such that even all Buddhas, throughout immeasurable eons, would find no end to praising these virtues.
How much less could worldly people, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas ever reach the end of praising them, even throughout immeasurable kalpas? Chapter 18:

The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Bodhisattvas From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Bodhisattvas," Chapter Eighteen. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇakara again addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of treasuries of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, which have been expounded by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. What are these ten?

The treasury of faith, the treasury of ethical discipline, the treasury of self-respect, the treasury of moral dread, the treasury of learning, the treasury of generosity, the treasury of wisdom, the treasury of right mindfulness, the treasury of retention, and the treasury of eloquence.
These are the ten. What is the treasury of faith of a bodhisattva?

This bodhisattva has faith that all phenomena are empty and lack reality; faith that all phenomena are signless; faith that all phenomena are wishless; faith that all phenomena have no agent; faith that all phenomena are unreal; faith that all phenomena lack solidity; faith that all phenomena are immeasurable; faith that all phenomena are unsurpassed; faith that all phenomena are ungraspable; and faith that all phenomena are unborn.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes such conforming pure faith, they will not be startled or terrified upon hearing that the dharmas of all buddhas are inconceivable;
they will not be startled or terrified upon hearing that all buddhas are inconceivable;
and they will not be startled or terrified upon hearing that sentient beings are inconceivable.
Hearing that the dharma-realm is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified;
hearing that the space-realm is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified;
hearing that the nirvana-realm is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified.
Hearing that the past world is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified;
hearing that the future world is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified;
hearing that the present world is inconceivable, their minds are not startled or terrified.
Hearing that one enters all inconceivable eons, the mind is not startled or terrified.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva possesses unswerving and firm faith in all Buddhas that cannot be undermined; such is the Buddha’s knowledge of the inexhaustible and boundless wisdom of the Buddhas.

In all worlds throughout the ten directions, within each and every world, there appear in the world Buddhas—immeasurable and innumerable throughout the three periods of time—who perform buddha-activities and then enter parinirvāṇa.

The wisdom of those Buddhas neither increases nor decreases; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither exhausted nor departed, neither near nor far, and neither wise nor chaotic. When a Bodhisattva accomplishes such an infinite and inexhaustible treasury of faith, they are then able to mount the Tathāgata-vehicle.

When this bodhisattva accomplishes such immeasurable and boundless faith—faith that is non-retrogressive, undisturbed, indestructible, unattached, rooted, conforming to the sages, and the faith in the nature of the Tathāgata’s family—they are then able to protect and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, nurture all bodhisattva roots of goodness, and accord with the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas. Born from the skillful means of all Buddhas, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s inexhaustible treasury of faith.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this treasury of faith, they are able to hear and retain all the teachings of the Tathāgatas, and extensively expound them for the sake of all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s treasury of ethical discipline?"

This bodhisattva accomplishes the precept of benefiting others, the precept of non-acceptance, the precept of non-attachment, the precept of peaceful abiding, the precept of non-contention, the precept of non-harming, the precept of non-mixture, the precept of being free from wrong livelihood, the precept of being free from evil conduct, and the precept of purity.
What is the precept of benefiting others?
This bodhisattva first seeks to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
What is the precept of not receiving [precepts]?
This bodhisattva does not accept the precepts of external paths, but fully upholds the impartial pure precepts of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
What is meant by "unattached precepts"?
This bodhisattva is not attached to the precepts of the desire realm, not attached to the precepts of the form realm, and not attached to the precepts of the formless realm.
Why is this? Because it is not dedicated toward that [goal].
What is meant by abiding in ethical discipline?
This bodhisattva accomplishes the pure precepts free from doubt and regret;
why is this? Because the bodhisattva does not commit the five crimes of immediate retribution and never intentionally violates any precept.
What is the precept of non-contention?
This bodhisattva does not criticize what was previously established, nor does he innovate or establish new rules; his mind always accords with and inclines toward the precepts of nirvāṇa.

He maintains them all fully without any transgression, and he does not, by means of these precepts, disturb or vex sentient beings, nor engage in mutual conflict and contention. When a bodhisattva upholds the precepts, it is solely to benefit sentient beings and cause them to rejoice.
What is the precept of non-harming?
This bodhisattva does not, on account of maintaining the precepts, study various incantations or medicinal herbs to harm sentient beings. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva wishes to rescue and protect sentient beings, they uphold the pure precepts.
What constitutes the unadulterated precepts?

This bodhisattva, having abandoned the views of annihilationism and eternalism, does not uphold adulterated precepts; rather, by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they uphold the pure precepts.
What is the precept of being free from wrong livelihood?

This bodhisattva does not manifest the appearance of upholding pure precepts with the desire to make others know that he possesses no actual inner virtue, yet he displays the appearance of possessing actual virtue; he merely upholds pure precepts, seeking the Dharma exclusively and ultimately attaining sarvajñā (omniscience).
What is non-evil precept?

This bodhisattva does not become conceited, saying, "I uphold the precepts. When seeing those who violate the precepts, he does not treat them with contempt or revile them to cause them distress; rather, he unifies his mind and upholds the pure precepts.
What is pure ethical discipline?

This bodhisattva abandons killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, abusive speech, divisive speech, frivolous talk, covetousness, malice, and wrong views, fully maintaining the ten wholesome paths of action.
When this Bodhisattva maintains such pure precepts, he reflects thus:

"If there are sentient beings who violate the pure precepts, it is due to their various inverted afflictions. All Buddhas clearly discern that all these sentient beings, because of their various inversions, have transgressed the pure precepts.

Therefore, I shall single-mindedly seek the Buddha-way and ultimately realize unsurpassed Bodhi; I shall extensively expound the true Dharma for sentient beings to cause them to leave behind inversions, to purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, and to lead them all to ultimate unsurpassed Bodhi."
This is the second inexhaustible treasury of the bodhisattva mahāsattva: the treasury of ethical discipline.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s treasury of shame?"
This Bodhisattva recollects his past lives:

for countless ages, he has committed acts of shamelessness toward his six kin—whether through insolence and lack of propriety, or lewdness and lack of restraint, or through malice and lack of affection, or by raising armies to wage war; deluded and inverted, there was no evil he did not commit. This was due to the three poisons and false suspicions, which caused him to be entangled in hypocrisy, flattery, crookedness, and various unwholesome states.

All sentient beings are likewise thus, all having accumulated and habituated themselves to various acts of shamelessness; this is due to a lack of wisdom, up to and including flattery and crookedness.

The distinction between the honorable and the lowly was lost, and they failed to show mutual respect and obedience; unable to practice humility or revere the wise, they constantly harbored poisonous thoughts, their resentment grew ever more intense, and they slaughtered one another without the slightest sense of shame or fear.

Reflecting upon myself and all other sentient beings, those who throughout the past, future, and present have practiced the ways of shamelessness—the Buddhas of the three periods of time are without exception aware of and witness this; how could I still continue to practice shamelessness?
This is utterly unacceptable!

Therefore, I should cultivate the dharma of shame, attain ultimate bodhi, and extensively expound the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may forever leave behind all dharmas of shamelessness and achieve bodhi.
This is the third inexhaustible treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: the treasury of shame.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s treasury of remorse?"
This Bodhisattva reflects with self-reproach:

"In the past, I greedily sought after forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; wives, children, kinsmen, wealth, treasures, servants, and vehicles, my mind never knowing satisfaction. I ought not to have engaged in these various unrighteous acts, for they gave rise to and increased greed, anger, and delusion, even up to deceit and crookedness."
Again, he reflects:

"The conduct of sentient beings, characterized by a lack of shame, arises entirely from ignorance up to and including deceit and crookedness; because of these various unwholesome dharmas, they do not accord with one another, nor do they respect or make offerings to one another, but instead constantly harbor poisonous minds and mutually harm each other."

Throughout the past, future, and present, I and all sentient beings have cherished and greedily sought after this dharma, accumulating its practice. Because of this dharma, we undergo conception, birth, death, and immeasurable sufferings. All Buddhas of the three periods of time fully know and see this; yet if I still practice this shameless dharma, all Buddhas of the three periods will not be pleased.

I shall instead cultivate the dharma of shame, attain ultimate Bodhi, and extensively preach such a dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may abandon shamelessness and achieve the Buddha-way.
This is the fourth inexhaustible treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: the treasury of shame.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s treasury of extensive learning?"
This Bodhisattva is one of great learning, meaning:
he knows that because this exists, that exists; because this does not exist, that does not exist;
because this arises, that arises; and because this ceases, that ceases.
These are mundane dharmas; these are supramundane dharmas; these are conditioned dharmas; these are unconditioned dharmas; these are determinate dharmas; these are indeterminate dharmas.
"What is meant by 'because this exists, that exists'?
It is said: because ignorance exists, volitional formations exist."
What is it that, being absent, causes this other thing to be absent?
It is as follows:
because consciousness is absent, name-and-form are absent.
What is meant by "because this arises, that arises"? It is as follows:
because craving arises, suffering arises.
What is meant by "because this thing ceases, that thing ceases"?
It is as follows:
because existence ceases, birth-and-death ceases.
What are the worldly dharmas? They are:
form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What are the supramundane dharmas? They are:
the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
What are conditioned phenomena? They are:
the realm of desire, the realm of form, the realm of formlessness, and the realm of sentient beings.
What are the unconditioned dharmas?
They are: space, nirvāṇa, cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, the twelvefold dependent origination, and the dharma-realm.
What are the dharmas that are determinately explained? They are:

the Four Noble Truths, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, the four analytical knowledges, the four fearlessnesses, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
What are the indeterminate dharmas?
They are as follows:
the world is finite, the world is infinite, the world is both finite and infinite, and the world is neither finite nor infinite;
The world is eternal; the world is non-eternal; the world is both eternal and non-eternal; the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he exists; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he does not exist; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he both exists and does not exist; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he neither exists nor does not exist.

There is a self and there are sentient beings; there is no self and no sentient beings; there is both a self and no self; there are both sentient beings and no sentient beings; there is neither a self nor no self; there are neither sentient beings nor no sentient beings.

How many Tathāgatas have passed into parinirvāṇa in the past, and how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa? How many Tathāgatas, how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and how many sentient beings will arise in the future? How many Buddhas, how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas exist in the present?
Which Tathāgata was the first to appear in the world?

What are those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who first appear in the world? What are those sentient beings who are born first? What is the Tathāgata who last appears in the world? What are those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who last appear in the world? What are those sentient beings who are born last?
Which dharmas are at the very beginning? Which dharmas are at the very end?
From where does the world come, and to what place does it go? How many worlds are formed, and how many worlds are destroyed? From what source do worlds come, and to what destination do they go?
"What is the initial limit of birth and death? What is the final limit of birth and death?
These are called indeterminate dharmas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:

"Sentient beings have wandered through birth and death for a long night; these ignorant and ordinary folk do not know how to cultivate the Way. I shall, day and night, apply myself with diligence to study and inquiry, receive and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, ultimately achieve unsurpassed Bodhi, and extensively expound the true Dharma for sentient beings, universally causing all to attain the Unsurpassed Path."
"This is the fifth inexhaustible treasury of learning of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s treasury of giving?"
This Bodhisattva practices ten kinds of giving, namely: the giving of the Dharma;

the giving of the Dharma that is most difficult to give at the final moment; internal giving; external giving; internal-and-external giving; the giving of all things; giving in the past; giving in the future; giving in the present; and ultimate giving.
"What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the dharma of giving?

From the very beginning, this bodhisattva has practiced impartial giving; they do not harbor personal attachment to fine delicacies or delicious flavors, but bestow them upon all, and it is the same with all other things."
Only after giving away the remainder of what he has offered does he eat himself, thinking to himself:
"For the sake of the eighty thousand families of worms within my body, when my body is at peace and happy, they too are at peace and happy;
when my body suffers from hunger, they too suffer from hunger."
