His original vows are entirely fulfilled; he is endowed with pure wisdom and has reached the ultimate state of the Buddhas, the most excellent Sugatas. He has achieved the universal sovereignty of the Dharma King, is fully possessed of the gateway to all-knowledge, and has perfected the most supreme and pure Dharmakāya.
The merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are equal, and no one in all the worlds can provide a sufficient analogy for them;
their bodies are adorned with the primary and secondary marks and they are fully endowed with all powers, such that one never tires of beholding them;
and even if one were to praise the wisdom and merit of the Tathāgata throughout all kalpas, manifesting them with sovereign ease, they could never be exhausted.

All Bodhisattvas are unable to exhaustively fulfill the sun of wisdom for the sake of all sentient beings, extinguish the darkness of the three periods of time, attain the sovereign spiritual power of the Dharma King, and give birth to immeasurable pure merits.

At that time, after the King of the Tuṣita Heaven had prepared such various offerings for the Tathāgata, he, together with immeasurable, incalculable, and asāṃkhyeya sons of the Tuṣita Heaven, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
"Welcome, Perfectly Awakened One! We pray that you will take pity on us and dwell in this palace.

At that time, the World-Honored One adorned himself with the adornments of a Buddha; all sentient beings who saw him felt nothing but reverence and joy. He fulfilled the aspirations of all Bodhisattvas and caused the gods of Tuṣita Heaven to rejoice greatly. He caused all sentient beings everywhere to cultivate the realm of the Buddha and plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood, their merit being inexhaustible. They attained pure and indestructible faith, constantly making offerings to the Buddha with hearts free from weariness.

With a mind upright and pure, in order to inspire sentient beings to seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he accepted the invitation of the King of Tuṣita Heaven and immediately ascended the lion throne of the treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels within the palace adorned with all kinds of gems.

Just as in this world, in the four continents, and in the Tuṣita heaven palace, the Tathāgata accepted the invitation and ascended the lion throne of the treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels in the palace adorned with all kinds of gems;

so too it was in all the ten directions, in all the four continents, and in all the Tuṣita heaven palaces, in every palace adorned with all kinds of gems, upon every lion throne of the treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels.

At that time, the Palace Adorned with All Jewels was spontaneously and exceptionally magnificent, adorned with wondrous jewels surpassing all the adornments of the devas. A network of all kinds of jewels completely covered it above, raining down everywhere clouds of all manner of exquisite jewels, clouds of all jewel-adornments, clouds of all precious garments, clouds of all sandalwood, clouds of all solid fragrances, clouds of all various jewel-adornments, and inconceivable clouds of myriad flowers.
It spontaneously produced the sounds of inconceivable music and song, proclaiming the Tathāgata’s omniscience and his subtle, wondrous Dharma words.
All these articles of offering surpassed those offered by all the devas.
At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, for the sake of the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, all the music became silent and ceased its disturbances;
the Heavenly King, with right mindfulness, nurtured his roots of goodness, increased his great resolve, and became courageous, diligent, and exceedingly joyful.
With a mind upright and pure, he immediately gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta and maintained all dharma-gates through dhāraṇī without forgetting them.
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke in verse:
“The Unobstructed Tathāgata is like the full moon, The foremost among all that is auspicious.”
He has entered the Hall Adorned with Myriad Jewels; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The wisdom of the boundless Tathāgatas is profoundly deep; it is the foremost among all that is auspicious.
He has entered the Pure Golden Hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Universal Eye is most luminous and pure, The foremost among all that is auspicious;
Having entered the Jewel-Treasury Lotus Palace, This place is therefore most auspicious.
The Tathāgata’s color is as fresh and pure as coral, the foremost among all auspicious things;
having entered this pure treasury palace, this place is therefore most auspicious.
The Tathāgata, the supreme lion of debate, the foremost among all auspicious things, has entered this palace of Indra’s jewel mountain; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Pūrṇacandra possesses immeasurable virtues; He is the foremost among all that is auspicious.
Having entered this Hall of Wondrous Jewel-Flower Treasury, This place is therefore most auspicious.
The light of the immeasurable Tathāgatas is boundless; Foremost among all that is auspicious, it enters the palace adorned with jewel trees; Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Ratnaketu is free from doubt and confusion; he is the foremost among all that is auspicious.
Having entered this palace adorned with exquisite jewels, this place is therefore most auspicious.
The Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom, a lion among men, the foremost among all that is auspicious, has entered the Adorned Hall of Fragrant Mountain; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Guṇa has light that shines everywhere; he is the foremost among all auspicious things.
Having entered this Palace Adorned with Supreme Jewels, this place is therefore most auspicious.
Just as the King of Tuṣita Heaven in this world, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, recollected the past Perfectly Enlightened Ones and praised them with verses;

so too did the Kings of Tuṣita Heaven in all worlds throughout the ten directions each recollect the roots of goodness they had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and praise them with verses in the same manner.

At that time, the World-Honored One ascended the lion throne of the treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels within the Palace Adorned with All Jewels and sat cross-legged. His pure Dharma-body was characterized by the sovereign equality of the realms of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; he was utterly tranquil, adorned himself with the adornments of all Buddhas, and was joined by an immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable assembly of pure great Bodhisattvas who had gathered from worlds in other directions.

The Tathāgata knows the proper time and expounds the Dharma; the Dharma-body is non-dual and free from all attachment. That which is brought forth by all Buddhas, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, is detached from all conditioned activities.

At that time, in the Palace Adorned with All Jewels, there spontaneously appeared immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and asaṃkhyeya offerings—extraordinary, marvelous, and surpassing all those offered by the devas.

These included flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, precious robes, banners, canopies, silken streamers, various kinds of jewels, and music; with these they reverently made offerings and praised the Tathāgata.

Such inconceivable arrays of all manner of offering ornaments as were present in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace within the four continents of this world, and in the Palace Adorned with All Jewels upon the lion throne of the treasury of wish-fulfilling gems, were likewise found in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya Scripture, Scroll Ten-Three;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya Scripture, Scroll Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: The Assembly of Bodhisattvas in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace Praising the Buddha.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, there was a world named Solid Jewel (Dṛḍharatna).
Next is named Solid Joy;
next is named Solid Jewel King;
next is named Solid Gold.
Next is named Solid Maṇi; next is named Solid Vajra; next is named Solid Lotus.
Next is named Firm Blue Lotus;
next is named Firm Sandalwood;
next is named Firm Fragrance.
The Buddha there was named Endless Life Banner;
the next was named Wind Banner;
the next was named Pure White Banner.
Next is named Banner of Dignified Manner;
next is named Banner of the Auspicious Signs;
next is named Constant Banner.
Next was named Urdhvaketu;
next was named Īśvaraketu;
next was named Brahmaketu.
Next is the banner named Peaceful Stability.
All those bodhisattvas have identical names; they are called Vajradhvaja, followed by Dṛḍhadhvaja; and so forth.
Next is named Courageous Banner;
next is named Night-Light Banner;
next is named Wisdom Banner.
The next is named Ratnaketu;
the next is named Vīryaketu;
the next is named Vimalaketu.
The next was named True Banner;
the next was named Dharma Banner.
Those bodhisattvas each, in the presence of the Buddhas in their respective lands, purely cultivated the holy life.
Each of these bodhisattvas, accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-worlds, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and paid him homage.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, in each direction from which they had come, lion thrones made of wish-fulfilling jewel-treasuries were manifested, filling the ten directions;
upon these they sat cross-legged, their bodies covered by nets of pure white jewels.
Furthermore, he emits thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of light rays—stainless light, immeasurable light—which universally illuminate the ten directions;
with a straightforward mind, he embraces the Triple Gem and remains far removed from all evils.
The arising of the great vows of Bodhisattvas is such that all sentient beings never tire of beholding them;

those who see them do so not in vain, for there are none who are not thereby tamed. These vows manifest the sovereign pure dharmas of all Buddhas, serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings, and exhort and transform them to resolve upon the great vows of Bodhisattvas.
All these bodhisattvas have fully accomplished immeasurable Dharma-gates;
that is to say:
the Dharma-gate of supernormal power that travels unhindered throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions;
The Dharma-door of seeing the pure Dharma-body without attachment;
the Dharma-door of maintaining the wisdom-body and being able to manifest countless transformation-bodies to visit the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas;
and the Dharma-door of entering the inconceivable sovereign power of the Tathāgatas, which is infinite and boundless.
The dharma-door of immeasurable and boundless omniscience;
the dharma-door of fearless skillful means that universally illumines all phenomena with immeasurable light;
and the dharma-door of inexhaustible eloquence that, throughout all kalpas of the future, analytically expounds the treasury of all merits.
The Dharma-door of the Universal Illumination of the Wisdom Light of All Dhāraṇīs;
the Dharma-door of Accomplishing the Pure Eye of Wisdom to Universally Contemplate the Dharma-realm;
and the Dharma-door of the Sphere of Wisdom, which is immeasurable and boundless, free from bondage and attachment, ultimately like empty space.

As it is with this world, so it is with all the four continents of every world-system: the bodhisattvas who have gathered in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, the lands from which they came, and the names of the Buddhas there are likewise as described.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his two knees hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of rays of light, which universally illumined all worlds throughout the ten directions, including the Tuṣita palaces within the four continents of every world-system, as vast as space and the Dharma-realm; the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas were all clearly manifested therein.

Those bodhisattvas who have been able to witness the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual powers were all, during their practice of the bodhisattva path, spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to Vairocana Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while he was cultivating immeasurable dharma-gates.
These bodhisattvas always delight in the profound liberation, sovereign spiritual powers, and indestructible dharma-realm bodies of all Buddhas;
they attain unimpeded samādhi and behold inconceivable Buddhas with minds free from attachment;
with unimpeded minds, they pervade the entire dharma-realm.
With a jewel-heart free from defilement, they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
attaining the immeasurable power of the Buddhas' sustaining grace, they are certain to reach the ultimate further shore; with pure and right mindfulness, they swiftly achieve equal enlightenment;
and reaching the very source of the Tathāgatas' minds, they enter profound wisdom and attain mastery.
Having reached the ultimate further shore of profound wisdom, they possess the pure Dharma-body;
abiding where the Buddhas abide, they attain all-knowledge and become equal to the Tathāgatas;
arising from the jewel of wisdom, they are all born within the sublime realm of the Tathāgata, opening and developing the Dharma-gates of pure wisdom.

Having reached the ultimate other shore of great adamantine wisdom, they have accomplished the samādhi of adamantine skillful means; forever free from all the darkness of ignorance, they teach and bring to maturity immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable sentient beings.
They possess the absolute sovereignty of all Buddhas and have reached the ultimate other shore;
they do not cling to any numerical categories, yet they are well-versed in all numbers and have perfected the wisdom regarding all numbers.
Abiding well in the true Dharma, they have accomplished such immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, inexhaustible, and ineffable treasuries of merit as these.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, Nor is there any nirvāṇa;
Yet, through the power of his original great vows, He manifests the dharma of sovereign mastery.”
This Dharma is difficult to conceive; it is not the realm of the mind.
Only through the wisdom that reaches the ultimate further shore does one behold the realm of the Buddhas.
The physical body is not the Tathāgata, and the same is true of his voice.
Nor is it apart from form and sound that the Buddha’s power of mastery exists;
those of little wisdom cannot know the Buddha’s profoundly deep realm.
Only by perfecting the wisdom of one's fundamental practice can one reach the domain of all Buddhas.
The Buddhas have no place from which they come, nor do they go anywhere when they depart;
yet through the power of their sovereign manifestation, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body appears within immeasurable worlds, revealing the body of the Tathāgata.
He extensively expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, his mind free from all attachment.
With immeasurable and boundless wisdom, he encounters no obstacles regarding any phenomena;
entering the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), he manifests the power of mastery.
Sentient beings and all phenomena— Thoroughly comprehending them without obstruction,
He manifests immeasurable transformation bodies, Appearing universally in all lands.
Seeking omniscience, He spontaneously attains perfect enlightenment.
First, one should purify the mind and fully cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
Seeing the Tathāgata thus, with his immeasurable power of mastery,
one should eliminate doubt and always draw near to this unsurpassed spiritual friend.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Most Supreme, beyond whom there is none higher, Is profoundly deep and ineffable;
All modes of speech are severed, Pure as the void.”
Contemplate clearly the Lions among Men, Whose power of mastery is immeasurable;
The Buddhas are free from falsehood, Yet the world gives rise to delusive thoughts.
That which the Teacher has expounded— His Dharma is most profound and wondrous.
The pure body of the Tathāgata arises in accordance with causes and conditions;
such is the wisdom of the Mahāyāna, the realm of all Buddhas.
If one desires to seek this wisdom, one should always draw near to the Buddha.
Making offerings with a pure mind to all the Teachers,
With a heart never weary or satisfied, one shall ultimately attain the Buddha-way.
This inexhaustible treasury of merit increases the bodhicitta.
Far removed from all doubt, they gaze upon the Buddha without weariness.
Having realized the ultimate nature of all phenomena, these sons of the Buddha, born through the transformation of the Dharma,
are fully able to comprehend the sovereign powers of all Buddhas.
As taught by the King of Wisdom, desire is the root of all dharmas;
one should give rise to pure desire and resolve to seek the unsurpassed path.
If one can revere all Buddhas and know how to repay the grace of the Tathāgata, [one shall attain this].
That person has never been apart from all the Teachers;
thus they have seen and heard the Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma,
fulfilling pure vows and reaching the ultimate, unsurpassed Way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Valāgraketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"With eyes and the light of the sun, One can see even the most subtle forms;
By the power of the Most Victorious One, The pure mind beholds all Buddhas."
Through courageous and diligent application of skillful means, one can reach the very bottom of the ocean's source;
such is the power of wisdom that it ultimately fathoms the ocean of all Buddhas.
It is like a fertile and excellent field where whatever seeds are sown will surely flourish and multiply.
Thus, from this Ground of Pure Mind, all Buddha-dharmas are born.
Just as a poor person finding a treasure trove eliminates the suffering of hunger and cold,
so too does the Bodhisattva, having attained the Buddha-dharma, become free from defilement and pure in mind.
Just as the *gadhā* medicine can eliminate all poisons,
so too does the World-Honored One eradicate the poison of afflictions.
Through the causal condition of a spiritual friend, the mind that places faith in the Buddha grows and flourishes.
Through the causal condition of a spiritual friend, one is able to hear all the Buddha-dharmas.
Even if one were to constantly practice unsurpassed giving for immeasurable and incalculable eons,
if one can transform a single person, that merit would surpass the former.
The Tathāgata is adorned with the marks [of perfection], his merit inconceivable;
the treasury of the merits of all Buddhas is such that none can know it.
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not rise from a single seat.
They are able to pervade everywhere throughout the ten directions and all worlds.
Just as the nature of empty space is neither born nor extinguished, so too are the dharmas of all Buddhas; they likewise have no arising or ceasing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Night-Light Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“In all worlds throughout the ten directions, among every class of living beings,
all behold the Honored One of Gods and Humans, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body.”
Just as the power of a single mind can give rise to various kinds of minds,
so the Tathāgata’s single Dharmakāya gives birth to the bodies of all Buddhas.
Awakening is a non-dual reality, and it likewise possesses no intrinsic nature.
The non-dual, pure Dharmakāya manifests every adornment;
Ultimately like space, yet appearing like a magical illusion,
Its merits are inexhaustible— this is the realm of the Buddhas alone.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, Their Dharma-bodies are entirely pure;
According to those who should be transformed, They universally manifest wondrous form-bodies.
Without ever giving rise to the thought, "I am such a form," [they appear].
Far removed from all expectations, they respond spontaneously to sentient beings.
Without destroying the nature of all phenomena, nor clinging to the dharma-realm,
they manifest in various forms for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
The Dharma-body is not a transformation, nor is it not a transformation;
all phenomena are without transformation, yet they manifest as having transformation.
Perfect enlightenment is immeasurable, ultimately equal to the Dharma-realm.
Profound and vast, without limit or bottom, the path of speech is entirely cut off.
Regarding all dharmas of the various realms of existence, the Tathāgata knows their true meaning;
he travels through all lands without ever encountering any obstruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Entering into profound wisdom, Free from all obstructions,
With a mind that knows no limits, One cultivates the bodhisattva practices."
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, one constantly beholds all Buddhas;
yet those Buddhas have no fixed location, and the Dharma likewise has nothing to which it clings.
Each and every Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of mastery.
Even in inconceivable eons, one could speak of them without end.
One might know the total number of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time,
but the number of the treasures of merit within the Guide’s treasury can never be exhausted.
Non-dual and inconceivable, they manifest various bodies;
throughout the ten directions there is nowhere they are not seen, yet never is there any distinction.
Like the pure full moon, they appear universally in all waters.
Though reflections are immeasurable, the original moon has never been two.
So too, this unimpeded wisdom that achieves perfect enlightenment manifests in all lands;
yet the Buddha-body is from the beginning non-dual.
Neither one nor two, and yet not infinite either;
according to those who are to be transformed, he manifests infinite bodies.
The Buddha-body is not of the past, nor is it of the future.
In a single thought, he manifests birth, attains Buddhahood, and enters nirvana.
Like illusory forms, they neither arise nor cease;
the Buddha-body is likewise thus—tranquil, without arising or ceasing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, yet sentient beings perceive it as measurable;
according to those who are to be transformed, the Guide manifests his form.”
The Dharma-body has no location, yet it fills the worlds of the ten directions;
the Buddha-body is inconceivable, like space, without boundaries.
It is devoid of mind, thought, and consciousness, and likewise lacks the arising of mental conceptions.
The realm of all Buddhas is ultimately without arising or ceasing.
Just as a person without eyes does not perceive forms within or without,
when the Tathāgata has not appeared in the world, one does not see any phenomena.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Tathāgata appears in the world;
though sentient beings perceive his appearance, in reality he does not arise in the world.
The Buddha-field is not the Tathāgata, and day and night are likewise so.
From years down to a single thought-moment, none of these are the Perfectly Awakened One.
All sentient beings say, "The Buddha-Sun has appeared in the world," yet the Teacher who attained self-awakening— the Tathāgata— is not the pure sun.
Falsehoods are non-existent; the path of speech is entirely severed.
The Tathāgatas of the three times who appear in the world are likewise thus.
Just as the pure sun does not coexist with the dark night, so it is.
Yet they speak of the characteristics of day and night; all Buddhas are likewise thus.
All kalpas of the three periods of time do not coexist with the Tathāgata, yet they speak of the Buddhas of the three periods; such is the Dharma of the Guide.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The bodies of all the Teachers are identical, and their meanings are likewise so;
yet throughout the realms of the ten directions, they appear individually distinct according to what is appropriate.”
Observe the Honored Muni: his realm is profoundly subtle and wondrous, filling all dharma-realms without exception.
The Tathāgata’s pure dharma-body is not to be reckoned as an internal body.
The Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body is likewise not reckoned as an external body.
According to the conduct of those sentient beings and their various, immeasurable karmas,
they perceive the Tathāgata in each case as being entirely different.
The wondrous Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, Cannot be numbered by anyone;
Profound and inconceivable, It is the realm of the Buddha alone.
As for me, I am not his realm, Beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.
The Buddha’s Dharma-body is thus, such that none can fathom it.
As a world-system is inconceivable, yet one sees its pure adornments, so too is the Buddha’s body; his wondrous marks appear without exception.
Just as all phenomena arise from the harmony of causes and conditions, so too,
through the convergence of such causes and conditions, one beholds all the Tathāgatas.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, they completely satisfy the desires of all sentient beings.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: it can fulfill all aspirations.
Within immeasurable worlds, the Guides arise in the world;
by the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows, they universally respond throughout the realms of the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The light of the Buddhas’ wisdom Fills and purifies the world;
Having purified the world, It causes beings to enter the Buddha-dharma.”
Suppose there were someone who wished to see Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings;
though the Tathāgata would respond to them all, in reality, he has no place from which he comes.
By single-mindedly recollecting the realm of the Buddha, they give rise to an immeasurable mind.
The Tathāgatas whom they behold are as numerous as their own thoughts.
Endowed with pure and white dharmas, their fame fills the ten directions;
regarding all-knowledge, their minds remain unshakable.
The Teacher, for the sake of sentient beings, expounds the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
wherever there is a place suitable for them to see, he universally manifests his most supreme body.
The Buddha-body is not "mine," and the world is likewise so.
He teaches that the mind is not the self, awakening to the bodhi of non-self.
All those lions among men, possessing immeasurable powers of mastery,
manifest bodies of mindfulness and the like, adorned with various marks.
The world is this very body; the body is itself the most supreme.
To know the true nature of the body is the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha.
The one who possesses all-knowing vision universally illuminates all phenomena.
The Buddha-dharma and bodhi—when sought, neither can be found.
The Teacher has no coming or going, nor does he abide anywhere;
far removed from all inversions, he is the pure, perfectly awakened one.
At that time, the Bodhisattva True Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Perfectly Awakened One traverses the ten directions throughout all worlds;
without leaving a single realm, he manifests universally in all lands.”
By the Tathāgata’s power of mastery, he manifests all bodies:
attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering ultimate parinirvāṇa.
Who could fathom the Buddha?
Who is it that performs the inconceivable?
Who sees all the Tathāgatas?
Who is it that attains equal and perfect enlightenment?
All phenomena are suchness, and the realm of all Buddhas is likewise;
there is not even a single phenomenon within suchness that undergoes arising or ceasing.
Because sentient beings are deluded by falsehood, they perceive this Buddha and this world.
For one who understands reality, there is neither Buddha nor world.
To bring joy to all beings, the Tathāgata manifests before everyone;
yet this manifested body is ultimately unattainable.
Far removed from all obstacles, dwelling securely and without hindrance;
having eliminated all difficulties and impediments, they are fully endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
All the Tathāgatas possess sovereign power through their supernormal faculties.
Throughout all three periods of time, it cannot be found when sought.
Thus knowing consciousness, one clearly understands all phenomena;
such a person of universal knowledge and vision will swiftly achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
“The sovereign power of the Tathāgata Is merely a conventional expression;
The Buddhas and their sovereignty Transcend all words.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Rather than endure all manner of suffering for immeasurable eons,
I would never distance myself from the Tathāgata nor fail to behold his sovereign power.
Throughout immeasurable births and deaths, I have never yet resolved to seek the Way."
If one hears of or sees the Tathāgata, they shall be fully endowed with the Buddha’s bodhi.
O person of penetrating wisdom and clear insight, if you give rise to the mind of the One Vehicle,
do not harbor doubts or suspicions, thinking that you will not attain Buddhahood yourself.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, the bodhicitta is difficult to obtain;
yet if one can seek it with a single mind, one will ultimately attain the unsurpassed path.
Even if, in every moment of thought, one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, [the merit of seeking the bodhicitta would surpass this].
If one does not recognize this as a skillful means, that is still not true worship.
But if one hears such a Dharma— from which all Buddhas are born—
one will endure suffering for immeasurable eons, resolutely seeking awakening.
Upon hearing once of the Mahāyāna, the vehicle upon which all Buddhas ride,
one becomes a guide throughout the three periods of time within the entire dharma-realm.
Even if one were to exhaust all future kalpas across all Buddha-fields, [the merit of this remains unsurpassed].
Those who do not understand skillful means will never achieve awakening.
For immeasurable kalpas in the past, they have wandered through birth and death;
not knowing the true Dharma, they remain ignorant of the place from which the Tathāgata arises.
"All phenomena are indestructible, And there is no one who destroys them;
They illuminate all worlds, Manifesting the dharma of sovereign mastery.

*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one, Part One: The Ten Dedications of Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva.* At that time, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi of "Clear Wisdom" (*prajñā-vidyā-samādhi*).

Having entered meditative absorption, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, he saw Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten million buddha-fields;
all these Tathāgatas were named Vajradhvaja.
At that time, those Buddhas addressed the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to enter this bodhisattva samādhi of clear wisdom and meditative absorption. O Good Man!

Because the Buddhas of worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten million Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions empower you with their spiritual power, you are thus able to enter this samādhi of right reception.
Furthermore, it is due to the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha, the power of his majestic spiritual authority, the purity of your own wisdom,
and the power of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas; it is for the purpose of enabling bodhisattvas to attain pure fearlessness,
to attain unimpeded and uninterrupted eloquence, to enter the stage of unimpeded knowledge, and to enter the oneness of the Buddhas.
Because of the vast mind of all-knowledge; because of being fully endowed with inexhaustible roots of goodness; because of fulfilling unimpeded, pure, and white dharmas;
because of entering the Dharma-realm of universal gates; because of manifesting the supernatural transformations of the spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
because of purifying mindfulness so that the wisdom of the past limit remains uninterrupted; and because of discerning the abodes of all Buddhas.
Because they maintain the faculties; because they extensively teach the Dharma through immeasurable gateways; because they hear, retain, and comprehend immeasurable teachings;
because they fully expound the ten dedications; because they gather all the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas;
because they abide in supramundane dharmas; and because the knowledge of all modes is never interrupted.
Because they develop great vows; because they enter into the true meaning; because they know the dharma-realm;
because they cause all bodhisattvas to rejoice; because they cultivate the same roots of goodness as all buddhas; and because they protect and uphold the nature of all Tathāgatas.

“Good son! You should, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound this Dharma, because you abide in the household of the Buddhas; because you nurture all supramundane merits; because you enter the light of dhāraṇīs; because you enter the non-extinction dharma of all Buddhas; because you universally illumine the dharma-realm; because you accumulate pure and white virtues while remaining free from unwholesome dharmas; because you abide in the sphere of vast wisdom; and because you abide in the light of the unobstructed dharma.”

At that time, the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immeasurable wisdom; they bestowed upon him eloquence that distinguishes the bodies of phrases through skillful means without obstruction; they bestowed upon him the light of the Dharma that is free from hindrance; they bestowed upon him a body shared by all Tathāgatas; they bestowed upon him immeasurable and subtle voices; they bestowed upon him the inconceivable samādhis and skillful means of all Bodhisattvas; they bestowed upon him the wisdom of impartially dedicating roots of goodness; they bestowed upon him the observation of the arising of all dharmas and immeasurable skillful means; and they bestowed upon him the unceasing eloquence for preaching the Dharma in all places.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the roots of goodness of that samādhi.
At that time, each of the Buddhas extended his right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
Having rubbed the crown of his head, that bodhisattva immediately arose from meditative concentration and addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
These inconceivable great vows of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva universally rescue and protect all sentient beings."
Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established this vow, they practice and study the dedication of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
There are ten kinds of dedication by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
all of which have been expounded together by the Buddhas of the past, future,
and present. What are these ten?
First, dedication by rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being";
second, indestructible dedication;
third, dedication equal to that of all Buddhas.
Fourth, dedication reaching all places;
fifth, dedication to the inexhaustible treasury of merit;
sixth, dedication to roots of goodness that accord with equality;
Seventh, the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings;
eighth, the dedication according to the nature of reality (*tathatā*);
ninth, the dedication of liberation, which is neither bound nor attached.
Tenth is the dedication to the immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as expounded together by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the dedication of saving and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings?
In this regard, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);..."
Purifying the perfection of ethical discipline;
cultivating the perfection of patience;
practicing the perfection of vigor;
They enter the dhyāna-pāramitā;
they discern the prajñā-pāramitā;

and they cultivate and accumulate immeasurable roots of goodness, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), forbearance, and relinquishment.
Having cultivated these roots of goodness, they form this thought:
"May all the roots of goodness I have cultivated bring benefit to all sentient beings and lead them to ultimate purity;
by means of these cultivated roots of goodness, may all sentient beings completely eliminate the immeasurable sufferings of the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and King Yama."
He further thought: "I dedicate these roots of goodness to act as a shelter for all sentient beings, so that they may extinguish the aggregates of suffering;
to act as a protection for all sentient beings, so that they may be liberated from afflictions."
To act as a refuge for all sentient beings, so that they may be freed from fear;
to act as a destination for all sentient beings, so that they may reach the ground of omniscience;
to act as a source of peace for all sentient beings, so that they may attain the state of ultimate peace.
They act as a great illumination for all sentient beings, so that they may extinguish the darkness of delusion and attain the light of wisdom;
they act as a torch for all sentient beings, so that they may extinguish the gloom of ignorance;
they act as a lamp for all sentient beings, so that they may dwell securely in ultimate clarity and purity.
They act as guides for all sentient beings, leading them into the methods of skillful means;
they act as sovereign jewel-ministers for all sentient beings, enabling them to attain the body of unimpeded, pure wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
By dedicating such immeasurable roots of goodness as these, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva causes all sentient beings to ultimately attain all-knowledge."
“O Son of the Buddha!
For the sake of enemies and kin alike, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness without any distinction. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters into the contemplation of equality because there is neither enemy nor friend.
He always regards all sentient beings with eyes of love;
even if a sentient being harbors malice toward him and gives rise to thoughts of enmity and hostility toward the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for all sentient beings, extensively analyzing and expounding upon all profound and wondrous Dharmas.
Just as the great ocean cannot be destroyed by any poison, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:

all those who are immature, ignorant, and lacking wisdom; those who do not know how to repay kindness; those who are prone to anger and arrogance; those who violate the precepts and are like the blind from birth—none of these, nor their immeasurable faults and evils, can disturb or unsettle the Bodhisattva’s mind of enlightenment.
"It is, for example, like the sun deity emerging and illuminating the world everywhere;

it does not remain hidden and fail to appear because of the blind, nor does it remain hidden and fail to appear because of such immeasurable obstructions as the city of the gandharvas, the dust and mist of the four continents, the barriers of the asuras, the shade of the Jambū tree, or the obstructions of other mountains."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: always maintaining right mindfulness, never becoming distracted, profound, vast, serene, and certain, with a mind free from sorrow or distress;
he correctly contemplates with the intent to bring to ultimate completion the light of pure Dharma—the merit and wisdom that universally illumines the world;
he demonstrates the true meaning and purely cultivates the gates of knowledge regarding all phenomena, constantly cultivating roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings.
All sentient beings possess immeasurable evils;
yet the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not, because of these evil beings, harbor resentment or despondency, nor does he fail to practice dedication.
He does not, because of beings who are difficult to subdue, abandon his roots of goodness, nor does he fail to practice dedication.

Although there may be sentient beings who are defiled by wrong views and anger, their minds do not waver from the Great Adornment; they do not abandon their great vows, but rescue and protect all sentient beings.
If one sees sentient beings who are turbid, evil, and lacking faith, and who do not know how to repay kindness;
yet one cultivates bodhi without ever becoming weary or negligent.
Even when engaged in affairs with the ignorant and the deluded, the mind remains free from sorrow and affliction.
Why is this? Because I have appeared in the world as the sun of wisdom—luminous, pure, and perfect—to purify and subdue all sentient beings.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not resolve to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and dedicate the roots of goodness for the sake of a single sentient being alone.
It is not for the sake of adorning and purifying a single buddha-field;
it is not for the sake of placing faith in a single buddha;
it is not for the sake of beholding a single buddha.
It is not for the sake of hearing even a single teaching of the Buddha,
nor for the sake of fulfilling a single vow.
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas desire to rescue and protect all sentient beings, they dedicate their roots of goodness to fully adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
To have faith in all Buddhas;
to behold all Buddhas;
and to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas.
They hear the true Dharma taught by all Buddhas;
they fulfill all great vows;
and they dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"The jewel of the resolve for enlightenment is the power of the Tathāgata’s realm; it is vast and impartial, free from indolence;
throughout all kalpas, its cultivation and study are difficult to attain, and it is equal to that of all Buddhas."
“Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all roots of goodness, their faith becomes pure and they nurture great compassion;
they universally dedicate these roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings with a profound mind, not merely in words.”

Toward all sentient beings, they give rise to a mind of joy, a clear and pure mind, a supple mind, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of affectionate concern, a mind of gathering them in, a mind of benefit, a mind of peace and happiness, and a most excellent mind;
they dedicate all these roots of goodness.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate their various roots of goodness, they form this thought:

"If all the merit of my dedication causes all sentient beings to attain pure destinies and pure births, such that their merit is fulfilled and cannot be destroyed by anything in any world, being inexhaustible;
and if they always receive respect, their minds remain free from error, and they clearly discern and understand all realms of existence;"
He contemplates the Buddhas, who are fully adorned in their physical, verbal, and mental actions;
they are fully adorned with all meritorious qualities. He further reflects:
"By dedicating the merit of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings constantly behold all Buddhas;
may they attain indestructible faith in those Buddhas;
may they hear and receive the True Dharma from those Buddhas, become free from all doubt and confusion, remember and uphold it without forgetting, and practice according to the teachings."
In the presence of the Tathāgata, they attain a supple mind, purify their physical and verbal karma, and their minds constantly abide in supreme and wondrous roots of goodness;
they are forever free from the dharma of poverty, their seven riches are fulfilled;
they practice and study all that is learned by all Buddhas, attain all roots of goodness, and achieve the equal, pure, and wondrous liberation of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Toward all sentient beings, they attain the eye of loving-kindness;
their bodies are pure, adorned with the primary and secondary marks; they possess eloquence and wisdom in speech, and are fully endowed with merit;
they have subdued the sense faculties and accomplished the ten powers.
They initiate all that is wholesome, their minds abide in contentment, and they remain free from attachment;
they cause all sentient beings to possess the bliss of a Buddha, to attain immeasurable abodes, and to dwell where the Buddhas dwell.
"Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
'All sentient beings commit immeasurable unwholesome karmas;
because of these karmas, they undergo immeasurable suffering, failing to see the Tathāgata, hearing the True Dharma, or recognizing the pure Saṅgha.'"
"These sentient beings possess immeasurable and great evil karmic offenses and should undergo immeasurable and boundless suffering and torment.
I shall, within those three evil realms, fully take their place in undergoing such suffering so that they may attain liberation;

I shall take the place of receiving immeasurable afflictions, and because of this suffering, my mind shall not regress, nor shall I become terrified or indolent, nor shall I abandon these sentient beings."
Why is this? It is because for the sake of sentient beings, I bear their heavy burdens and fulfill my vow of impartiality;
I deliver all from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, affliction, and the immeasurable hardships of wandering through the cycle of birth and death.
All those with wrong views who have lost all wholesome dharmas, who are foolish and devoid of wisdom—I shall deliver them all, freeing them from these manifold sufferings.
Sentient beings are constantly entangled in the net of craving, shrouded by ignorance, and stained by attachment; driven by their desires, they lack self-mastery.
Bound in the prison of suffering, they follow the works of Māra and harbor doubts and suspicions toward the Buddhas.
“They cannot attain the supramundane path, nor do they see the place of peace; they constantly gallop through the immeasurable wilderness of birth and death, undergoing immeasurable suffering.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees those sentient beings submerged in the mud of birth and death and enduring manifold torments, he gives rise to great compassion, benefits sentient beings, enables them to obtain wholesome gains, and delivers them from suffering and hardship, dedicating his roots of goodness toward this end.
One should dedicate with the great dedication, dedicating in the manner that the bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have dedicated;
dedicating according to the Great Dedication Sūtra as taught by all the Buddhas;
so that all sentient beings may attain complete purity, be fully endowed with roots of goodness, and ultimately realize all-knowledge.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to attain the dwelling place of peace and stability of the King of Supreme Wisdom; it is not for my own deliverance alone.

Rather, I desire to enable them to emerge from the abyss of birth and death, to attain the mind of omniscience, to pull sentient beings out of the treacherous valleys of the evil realms, to rescue them from immeasurable suffering, and to ferry them across the flow of saṃsāra."
Again, he formed this thought:
"I shall undergo immeasurable suffering for the sake of all sentient beings,
so that all sentient beings may be completely enabled to escape the parching desert of birth and death."
For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall endure all sufferings within all hells across all lands, never abandoning them;
in each and every evil realm, throughout all future kalpas, I shall take upon myself the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings.
Why is this? It would be better for me alone to undergo all sufferings than to let sentient beings endure various torments;
I shall use my own body to ransom all beings in the evil realms and cause them to attain liberation.
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:
'I shall, for the sake of all sentient beings, become one who speaks with truthful words, free from a mind of affliction or harm, and never abandon sentient beings.'"
Why is this? It is because I have given rise to the bodhicitta for the sake of sentient beings in order to deliver them all;
I practice the path of the bodhisattva not seeking nobility, not seeking the five desires, and not seeking the various pleasures of the world.
Why is this? The five desires are worldly dharmas, the realm of all Māras, the conduct of fools, and are censured by all Buddhas;

they can give rise to all suffering and affliction—those of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the abode of King Yama—and all instances of anger, strife, and mutual litigation arise solely from the five desires.
By habitually indulging in the five desires, one distances oneself from all Buddhas; they can obstruct rebirth even in the heavens, let alone the unsurpassed path.
The Bodhisattva clearly perceives that the five desires possess such immeasurable faults and afflictions.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not cultivate the Bodhisattva practice for the sake of the five desires, but rather seeks to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings by resolving upon bodhicitta and seeking the unsurpassed path.
May all sentient beings attain every benefit, fulfill all great vows,
sever the hooks and bait of their afflictions, and be freed from immeasurable suffering.
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought:
'I shall dedicate all roots of goodness so that all sentient beings may attain various kinds of happiness:

ultimate happiness, beneficial happiness, uncommon happiness, tranquil happiness, undefiled happiness, unshakeable happiness, immeasurable happiness, the happiness of neither dying nor transmigrating, the happiness of non-extinction, and the happiness of omniscience.'"

I shall act as a tamer for all sentient beings, as a minister of the treasury, and as a great lamp of illumination; I shall show them the path to peace and security, cause them to leave behind all calamities, and enable them to understand all dharmas.
I shall cause them to comprehend all profound meanings;
I shall act as a vessel of omniscience to ferry them across the ocean of birth and death.
"I shall cause them to know the dedication of immeasurable roots of goodness;
I shall manifest the further shore for all.
By dedicating these immeasurable roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva protects and shelters all beings, crosses the ocean of birth and death, and causes all Tathāgatas to rejoice.
They shall attain all-knowledge, abandon all demons, distance themselves from evil associates, and draw near to Bodhisattvas as supreme spiritual friends;
they shall accomplish pure karma, exhaust and extinguish all evils, and fulfill all roots of goodness through the immeasurable vows and practices of a Bodhisattva.
“After the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has correctly dedicated all roots of goodness, he forms this thought:
‘The sun does not rise for the sake of each and every sentient being within the four continents;
rather, when the single sun rises in the world, it is able to illuminate the entirety of all the worlds.’”
Furthermore, sentient beings do not know day and night, nor do they travel, observe, or perform various karmic deeds by means of their own bodily radiance;
all these arise because the Sun Deva-son emerges and shines universally upon the world, so that for all sentient beings, no task fails to be accomplished.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: cultivating various roots of goodness and dedicating them for the sake of all sentient beings, he forms this thought:
"Those sentient beings lack the light of wisdom; they cannot even illuminate themselves, let alone others."
I alone, with a singular resolve and without companion, cultivate all roots of goodness and dedicate them, desiring to deliver all sentient beings;
to universally illumine all sentient beings;
and to discern all sentient beings.
To thoroughly understand all sentient beings;
to cause all sentient beings to enter the profound Dharma;
and to gather in and sustain all sentient beings.
Bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment;
gladdening all sentient beings;
making all sentient beings supple and gentle.
"I shall eliminate all doubts and delusions of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects:
"I shall practice and study so that, like the Sun Deity, I may universally illumine all things without seeking any reward for my kindness."
One does not abandon the great armor of adornment because of evil sentient beings;
nor, on account of even a single evil sentient being, does one forsake all others and fail to deliver them.

Rather, one diligently cultivates roots of goodness and dedicates them, desiring to cause all sentient beings to attain every happiness, and gathers even small roots of goodness to dedicate toward the vast.
If any roots of goodness cannot benefit sentient beings, I shall never dedicate those roots of goodness;
rather, I dedicate all roots of goodness by generating the aspiration to give them entirely to sentient beings.
I dedicate so that all sentient beings may not cling to any phenomena, dedicating through the nature of sentient beings, which reaches nowhere.
When a bodhisattva dedicates in this manner, they are likewise without attachment;
they do not grasp at the nature of anything, but abide securely in all roots of goodness;
they dedicate without grasping at signs, for karmic retribution is illusory, being non-existent and without any object of attachment.
One dedicates without grasping at the characteristics of the five aggregates, and dedicates without destroying the characteristics of the five aggregates;
one dedicates without grasping at illusory karma, seeks no retribution, and does not give rise to illusory causes and conditions;
it is unborn, unarisen, and non-abiding—not abiding in solid characteristics, not abiding in illusory dharmas, and not grasping at the characteristics of sentient beings.
They do not discriminate regarding worlds; they do not abide in the inversion of mind, the inversion of perception, or the inversion of views, nor do they cling to the path of language.
They desire only to cause sentient beings to understand the true Dharma, dedicating themselves toward observing the equality of all sentient beings;
they dedicate themselves to the seal of the Dharma-realm, sealing all roots of goodness.
One dedicates [merit] toward the dharmas of detachment and so forth, observing the roots of goodness;
one dedicates toward the understanding of all dharmas, becoming free from inversion, and attaining all roots of goodness;
and one dedicates by observing the dharma-realm through the dharma of non-duality.
That dedication does not give rise to any phenomena, nor does it extinguish any phenomena; dedicating roots of goodness in such a manner, one practices the pure dharmas of counteractive measures.

One dedicates by contemplating all roots of goodness as being entirely dedicated to supramundane dharmas, and regarding those roots of goodness, one does not conceive of them as dualistic characteristics.
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is not identical with karma, nor is it separate from karma;
dedicating oneself and observing all-knowledge is not identical with karma, nor is it separate from karma;
because the karma of the vow for attaining all-knowledge illuminates and is pure, its fruition (*vipāka*) is likewise illuminated and pure.
Because their retribution is luminously pure, omniscience (*sarvajñā*) is also luminously pure.
Having abandoned all agitation, discursive thought, pride, and negligence,
they dedicate their various roots of goodness in accordance with skillful wisdom.

May all sentient beings fully attain true and ultimate liberation, remaining unattached to the nature of phenomena; with immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness, they dedicate them toward all dharmas, such that they give rise to karmic retribution while being free from karmic retribution.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they are able to forever leave behind all evils; this is praised by the Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s first dedication of merit: rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a 'sentient being.

" At that time, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and the entire assembly; he contemplated the dharma-realm, entered into the profound flavor of its words and meanings, and his great compassion universally covered all sentient beings;
he protected and sustained the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods so that it would never be interrupted.
They enter the treasury of all the merits of all Buddhas;
they give birth to the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
and they are skillfully able to discern the minds of all sentient beings.
Knowing the proper time without fail for all roots of goodness planted in the past, he was fully endowed with the Dharma-body and skillfully manifested a pure form-body, speaking in verse:
“What has been practiced throughout inconceivable eons, Always for the benefit of all living beings;
With firm diligence and an unimpeded mind, He constantly sought the wondrous merits of all Buddhas.”
With a mind pure and free from anger, they reverently make offerings to the Tamer of Men;
deeply understanding all dharmas, they rescue sentient beings, and thus they are able to skillfully enter the treasury of dedication.
Endowed with the power of courageous diligence, The light of their wisdom shines with supreme purity;
With firm resolve and an unshakable mind, They are always able to rescue and protect all living beings.
With a mind dwelling in the peerless, leaping with joy and pure in intention,
the Bodhisattva’s power of patience is like the great earth, able to benefit all sentient beings.
Not seeking happiness for oneself through asceticism, but giving rise to immeasurable practices out of great compassion,
one who can constantly protect all living beings will swiftly enter the stage of non-obstruction.
All worlds throughout the ten directions, And all sentient beings therein, he gathers and embraces;
Always dwelling in peace for the sake of sentient beings, He practices and studies immeasurable dedications.
Practicing generosity with a joyful heart, Fully upholding the pure precepts,
With courageous diligence and firm resolve, One skillfully dedicates pure wisdom.
His mind is vast and immeasurable; with the power of patience firm and strong, he constantly dedicates his merit.
He purely cultivates all meditative concentrations, and his wisdom is profound, subtle, and inconceivable.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, They fully cultivate pure conduct;
With wisdom, they dedicate all merits To benefit all sentient beings with every form of happiness.
That person has accumulated a multitude of virtuous deeds, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable;
desiring to cause all sentient beings to fully practice and cultivate them, so that they may abide in inconceivable, profound, and wondrous wisdom.
For the sake of all sentient beings everywhere, The Bodhisattva dwells in the hells for inconceivable eons;
His mind is ever free from indolence, And his resolute merit is constantly dedicated.
Seeking neither form, sound, fragrance, nor taste, Nor hoping for any tactile sensations,
They constantly seek the unsurpassed, most supreme wisdom To deliver and liberate all living beings.
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom is pure like space; He universally practices the immeasurable conduct of a Great Being.
In the path of pure karma practiced by the Most Victorious One, He constantly cultivates practice with immeasurable renown.
The Bodhisattva wanders through all worlds, Always able to bring peace and security to all classes of living beings;
Causing everyone to be filled with joy, They cultivate the Bodhisattva practices without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Eliminating all defilements of the mind, one contemplates and cultivates unsurpassed wisdom;
not seeking peace and happiness for oneself alone, one constantly desires to benefit all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva dedicates [merit] to reach the other shore, Eliminating the immeasurable poisons of mental defilement;
Fully cultivating the Buddhas of the three periods of time, And all immeasurable, pure virtues.
The Bodhisattva is never stained by attachment to form, And so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
Not dwelling in any of the three realms, They dedicate all their merits toward enlightenment.
All classes of sentient beings known by the Buddhas, They gather them all without exception;
Ultimately delivering all living beings— This is called the sublime practice of a Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is entirely settled in peace; his awakening is vast and beyond measure.
Free from delusion and with right mindfulness, he subdues the sense faculties; his actions of body, speech, and mind are ever tranquil.
All phenomena, both internal and external, are entirely false and devoid of reality;
like the wind moving through space without obstruction, so too is the mental activity of the Bodhisattva.
The physical actions they initiate are ever pure, Causing all Buddhas to be completely delighted;
Their speech before the Most Victorious Ones is never false, And their minds are always single-mindedly directed toward the Tathāgatas.
To all the most excellent realms throughout the ten directions, he travels to them all;
there he beholds the Honored One of Great Compassion and is able to pay him complete reverence and offerings.
With a mind always far removed from all evils, They dwell amidst the great assembly without fear;
With a mind always securely established in the path of the Tathāgata, They are a pool of coolness for the three realms of existence.
Skillfully cultivating the analysis of all phenomena, Fully possessing thorough penetration of existence and non-existence,
Able to skillfully proceed toward the true nature of dharmas, They enter deeply into the supreme samādhi free from contention.
Cultivating the steadfast conduct of a bodhisattva, which no sentient being can destroy;
clearly studying and thoroughly comprehending the profound meaning, they remain unattached to the phenomena of the three periods of time.
Ultimately dedicating merit to reach the other shore, universally causing all sentient beings to be completely purified;
far removed from all defilements and attachments, the conduct of the bodhisattva is without dependence.
Regarding the linguistic conventions of all sentient beings, their wisdom encounters no obstruction;
their discourse is skillful and free from attachment, as their minds always abide peacefully in unimpeded dwelling.
When Bodhisattvas practice dedication in this way, their treasury of merit from immeasurable virtuous minds causes all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions to rejoice.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the second indestructible dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains indestructible faith in all the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present; all Buddhas are completely pleased with them.”
Toward all bodhisattvas, from the very first moment they give rise to even a single thought seeking the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva and omniscience,
one attains indestructible faith in those bodhisattvas; with a mind that is consistently upright and unshakeable regarding all the teachings of the Buddhas,
one attains indestructible faith in the instructions of all the Buddhas.
They protect the Dharma of all Tathāgatas and attain indestructible faith;
they always regard all beings with eyes of love, impartially;
and by dedicating their roots of goodness, they cause those sentient beings to obtain all manner of wholesome benefits and attain indestructible faith.
They attain indestructible faith in pure and wholesome roots.
Why is this? Because they have cultivated and accumulated all wholesome roots.
They attain indestructible faith in the dedications of all bodhisattvas, because they have attained liberation through a straightforward mind and fulfillment;
they attain indestructible faith in all Dharma-teachers who are bodhisattvas, because they fully conceive of them as Tathāgatas;
and they attain indestructible faith in the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas, because they truly believe in the inconceivability of the Buddhas.
"Because they attain indestructible faith in all the skillful means of bodhisattvas, thereby encompassing the various, immeasurable, and innumerable spheres of practice.
O Son of the Buddha!..."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus abide in indestructible faith, they plant various roots of goodness and distinguish those roots of goodness toward all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the true teaching of the Tathāgata, and all sentient beings—within such immeasurable spheres.
They nurture the bodhicitta and cultivate the roots of goodness born of great loving-kindness;
they extensively practice great compassion and observe with equanimity.
Learning that which is learned by the Buddhas, one accords with all Buddhas;

one gathers all pure roots of goodness, penetrates deeply into the true meaning, accumulates a treasury of merit, practices great giving, cultivates all virtues, and contemplates the three periods of time with equanimity.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates such roots of goodness and merits toward omniscience;
he constantly beholds all Buddhas and draws near to spiritual friends;
he is always in the company of immeasurable Bodhisattvas, mindfulness of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) remaining undisturbed in his mind.
Receiving the teachings of all Buddhas, they give rise to the resolve to protect the Dharma; they teach and mature all sentient beings, their minds never departing from the supramundane dedication;
they make offerings to and protect all Dharma masters, understand all phenomena, and cultivate and fulfill all great vows.

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently cultivates immeasurable roots of goodness, accumulates and nurtures these roots of goodness, contemplates with right mindfulness, and observes the true meaning of objects and so forth;
they pay respectful homage and offerings, maintain perfect deportment, and dedicate their roots of goodness.
“After the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has dedicated their roots of goodness, they form this thought:
‘By dedicating these roots of goodness, may the resulting fruits of reliance cause me, while practicing the bodhisattva path, to see all buddhas in every moment of thought;
and may those buddhas all be filled with joy.’”
Toward all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they made offerings as befits a Buddha:

with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, incalculable flowers, incalculable perfumes, incalculable ointments, incalculable garlands, incalculable robes, incalculable parasols, incalculable banners, incalculable pennants, incalculable ornaments, incalculable decorative implements, incalculable provisions, incalculable powdered incense, incalculable faith and joy, incalculable reverent mindfulness, and incalculable pure faith; they burned incalculable solid incenses;
and they offered incalculable foods of supreme flavor, incalculable acts of respect, and incalculable prostrations.
Asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of jewels, asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of flowers,
asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of incense, asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of garlands, asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of pure sandalwood,
asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of garments, and asaṃkhyeya seats made of all kinds of vajra.
Incalculable seats of all kinds of mani-jewels; incalculable seats of all kinds of precious silken fabrics;
incalculable seats of all kinds of precious colors; incalculable wheels of all kinds of jewels; incalculable wheels of all kinds of flowers;
incalculable wheels of all kinds of incense; and incalculable adornments of all kinds of garlands.
Wheels of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) robes made of all kinds of jewels, wheels of incalculable adornments made of all kinds of jewels,
wheels of incalculable canopies spread with all kinds of jeweled silks, and wheels of incalculable, lofty, and towering *tāla* trees made of all kinds of jewels were established.
There were incalculable wheels of railings made of all kinds of jewels and incalculable wheels of nets made of all kinds of jewels, which covered them from above;
there were incalculable palaces of all manner of exquisite jewels, magnificently adorned and surpassing those of the devas;

there were incalculable palaces of flowers, incalculable palaces of incense, incalculable palaces of jewel-garlands, incalculable palaces of sandalwood, incalculable palaces of solid fragrant treasuries, incalculable palaces of diamond, and incalculable palaces of maṇi-jewels—all of which were exceptionally wonderful and surpassed those of the devas.

There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) trees of various jewels, incalculable trees of diverse fragrances, incalculable trees of precious garments, incalculable trees of exquisite music, incalculable trees of wondrous sounds, incalculable trees of inexhaustible jewels, incalculable trees with hanging jeweled silken banners, and incalculable trees of jewel adornments; as well as incalculable trees of all kinds of flowers, all kinds of garlands, all kinds of incense, all kinds of unguents, all kinds of parasols, all kinds of standards, and all kinds of flags. Such wondrous jewel-trees, uniquely magnificent in their adornment, served to ornament countless palaces.

It was adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious railings, incalculable precious windows, incalculable precious side-pavilions, incalculable inner curtains, incalculable crescent-moon ornaments, incalculable multi-storied pavilions, and incalculable precious canopies; it was covered above by incalculable nets of white jewels.
Incalculable solid fragrances were being burned, and incalculable precious garments were spread upon its ground.
"By means of such various ornaments as these, they adorned countless palaces that surpassed those of all the devas.

"With such supreme and wondrous offerings, throughout immeasurable, innumerable, unspeakable, and unspeakably many kalpas, they disciplined their faculties and made offerings with a reverent heart to all Tathāgatas;
and after these most excellent ones entered parinirvāṇa, they made offerings to their śarīras."
I wish to cause all sentient beings to be entirely joyful and to gather in the roots of goodness of all sentient beings;
to cause all sentient beings to leave behind immeasurable suffering and resolve upon Bodhicitta;

and to cause all sentient beings to adorn themselves with great adornments, such that these immeasurable adornments transcend the realms of all other sentient beings, manifesting the Buddha-dharma which is difficult to encounter.
They fulfill the powers of incalculable Tathāgatas, purify their faith, make offerings to the Teachers, and receive, uphold, and protect all the Buddha-dharmas.
Thus they make offerings to the Buddhas of the present, and after their parinirvāṇa, they make offerings to their relics;
even if one were to describe these articles of offering for immeasurable incalculable eons, they could never be exhausted.
The Buddhas have accomplished immeasurable merit and transform, deliver, and liberate all sentient beings.
I constantly make offerings to those Tathāgatas with a mind that never regresses, without rest, and never indolent;
I harbor no distress or affliction, nor do I have any attachment, and I am free from the conceptualization of mental objects.
Amidst all phenomena, they remain unstained and without dependence, yet do not obscure their roots of goodness;
free from all attachments, they seal the gateway of karmic phenomena with the Seal of the True Dharma;
they give rise to all dharmas and abide where the Buddhas abide.
Contemplating the Dharma-seal of the realm of the nature of non-arising, one seals that initial resolve.
One upholds the Tathāgata’s pure dedication;
one observes the dedication to the equal nature of phenomena.
Entering the skillful means of non-action while giving rise to all modes of action; dedicating with a mind that relinquishes everything;
dedicating through immeasurable skillful means;
and dedicating by being detached from all existence.
Abiding in the skillful means of detachment from signs, one cultivates the roots of goodness of the Dharma-gate and dedicates them.
From the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, the Bodhisattva cultivates all manner of sublime roots of goodness and dedicates them all;
by means of these roots of goodness, they cannot be destroyed within the cycle of birth and death.
Seeking all-knowledge, their minds do not regress;
dwelling within all states of existence, they remain in tranquil concentration without distraction;
delivering all sentient beings, they do not cling to birth and death.
Having attained the gateway of unimpeded wisdom and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, those roots of goodness are inexhaustible and cannot be destroyed by any worldly phenomena;
they are fully endowed with the pure perfections and ultimately perfect the power of all-knowledge.

In this way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abandons the darkness of delusion and accomplishes the bodhicitta, universally illuminating all long-standing pure dharmas and dedicating their roots of goodness.
Endowed with all practices, possessing a pure and straightforward mind, they observe equality and penetrate deeply into all phenomena;

they know that karma is like an illusion, karmic retribution is like lightning, all conditioned activities are like transformations, dependently arisen dharmas are like echoes, and the conduct of a Bodhisattva is like a shadow.
Born from the Dharma-eye of non-attachment, it is without action or that which is acted upon;
its nature is quiescent, entering both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
regarding all phenomena, it thoroughly realizes their non-duality and understands their suchness.
They discern all aspects of a bodhisattva’s conduct without clinging to any signs;
they skillfully understand expedient means and engage in activities of common purpose, never abandoning any pure and wholesome dharmas;
they are free from all hindrances, being unobstructed and unattached.
They are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas and remain far removed from ignorance.
Thus, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish roots of goodness, give rise to wholesome dharmas, do not destroy karmic retribution, clearly perceive reality, and skillfully understand dedication;

through the power of skillful means, they bring forth karmic retribution, ultimately realize the dharma-nature, reach the other shore, and thoroughly comprehend all phenomena, dedicating all their actions and roots of goodness toward great wisdom.
Their minds are pure, and their conduct is without anything to be performed.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate roots of goodness in this manner, they desire to deliver all sentient beings, ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted, extinguish all evil karma and its retributions, and dedicate [the merit] to all sentient beings;
they attain immeasurable wisdom, accomplish all-knowledge, transcend worldly realms, extinguish all afflictions, reach ultimate purity, and achieve wisdom.
Entering deep skillful means, they abandon the suffering of birth and death and accomplish the immeasurable roots of goodness of all Buddhas;
they subdue the works of Māra, attain the seal of the equal Dharma, and by sealing all karmas, they accord with the unsurpassed bodhi of sarvajñā.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice such dedication of roots of goodness, those roots of goodness become bright and pure, universally illuminating all things, and they fully accomplish the vehicle of sarvajñā (omniscience).
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the second indestructible dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in this dedication, they behold immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas and fully attain immeasurable, pure, and wondrous Dharmas.”
They attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, abandon ignorance, and enter into all dharmas;
they obtain the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas, subdue all Māras, extinguish all demonic activities, and become fully endowed with the noble Bodhicitta born of high lineage;
they attain unimpeded wisdom, awakening through themselves rather than by another.
Regarding all phenomena, they perceive their true meaning;
regarding all buddha-fields, they are able to receive and uphold them, discerning their characteristics with perfected wisdom that universally illumines all sentient beings.
“By means of this indestructible power of dedication, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas gather all roots of goodness and dedicate them.
At that time, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“They cultivate immeasurable and innumerable deeds; The vehicle they ride is firm and indestructible.”
They are able to bring all Buddhas complete joy; this is called the dedication of the wise.
The Buddhas they worship are inconceivable; through generosity and upholding the precepts, they subdue their faculties.
For the sake of all beings, they practice dedication with immeasurable purity.
With all manner of exquisite flowers and fragrances, Countless and immeasurable robes of various jewels,
And diverse ornaments as well as precious canopies, I make offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
