they discern and know entirely.
With a mind always equanimous, they reverently make offerings to all the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions,
using various kinds of incense, diverse jeweled flowers, immeasurable precious robes, as well as banners and canopies.
Completely filling the immeasurable dharma-realm, they are used as offerings to all Buddhas.
Within a single pore, the Bodhisattva is able to see all Buddhas, their number beyond calculation.
They are universally able to make offerings to the Lamps of the World; whatever Dharma they hear, they are fully able to receive and uphold.
With reverence and prostration, they cast their five limbs to the ground and offer themselves in total refuge to all who are most supreme.
Throughout the limits of the future, across immeasurable kalpas, one praises all the Most Victorious Ones of the ten directions.
At the abode of each Buddha, with all manner of offerings, their number is equal to that of all classes of sentient beings.
Just as with the offerings presented before a single Buddha, so it is likewise before all Buddhas.
Throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas, the Bodhisattva reverently honors all Teachers.
Exhausting all immeasurable and infinite kalpas, they reverently make offerings without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Throughout all sentient beings and across immeasurable kalpas, within these very kalpas,
they cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
Reverently making offerings to each and every Tathāgata throughout the entirety of all kalpas, one never feels weary or satisfied.
As for the great kalpas spoken of by all the Most Victorious Ones, no one at all is able to measure or calculate them.
Throughout all those great eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
They are able to fully awaken to the entire dharma-realm, which is vast, boundless, and without limit.
Various exquisite jewel-flowers fill its interior; with these he makes offerings, treating all sentient beings as equal to the Buddha.
These exquisite jewel-flowers are complete in color and fragrance, pure and pristine, with immeasurable adornments.
Throughout all worlds, there is nothing that can serve as a simile for making offerings to the Most Victorious One.
Equal in number to all sentient beings, immeasurable Buddha-fields are filled with various exquisite jeweled canopies.
With all these canopies, one offers to a single Tathāgata; likewise, one makes offerings to all Buddhas in this same way.
Most subtle and supreme, this extraordinary ointment is peerless throughout the entire world.
With this fragrant ointment, throughout all kalpas of sentient beings, I offer it to all the Tathāgatas,
the Buddhas. Likewise, with powdered incense, various kinds of mixed flowers, subtle and exquisite perfumes,
and immeasurable precious robes.
With countless exquisite jewels and all manner of ornaments, they make offerings to the Tathāgatas without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Equal in number to all sentient beings, they all attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment.
With immeasurable verses, they praise and proclaim, reverently making offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Equal in number to all sentient beings, these world-illuminating sages perform unsurpassed and most excellent offerings to the Bodhisattvas.
Even if one were to praise the virtues of the Tathāgata for as many eons as there are sentient beings, one could never exhaust them.
By making such offerings to all Buddhas, one fully accomplishes the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata.
Abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva is able to behold all Buddhas;
as well as the immeasurable and innumerable roots of goodness manifested through their deeds.
Cultivating the conduct of Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva abides in the state of Samantabhadra.
May the Bodhisattva stages,
which are known by all Buddhas, and the various kinds of sentient beings, all be brought to fulfillment;
may their wisdom be clear and penetrating, just like that attained by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
As the Buddha has taught, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the Bodhisattva is able to fully cultivate them all.
Having dedicated them all to all sentient beings, he causes them universally to achieve the unsurpassed dedication.
Throughout all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they are able to awaken to and thoroughly comprehend their causes;
they cause all sentient beings, without exception, to become equal to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Accomplishing generosity, entirely as in the dedication of merit; fully endowed with ethical discipline, like the power of Samantabhadra;
courageous and diligent, never retreating; accomplishing patience, which cannot be thwarted or destroyed.
Skillfully entering the profound meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), they discern and fully understand all samādhis.
With pure wisdom, they thoroughly penetrate the three periods of time— something that all the worlds cannot know.
All physical, verbal, and mental actions, as well as sounds and speech, are entirely pure.
Having ultimately accomplished all the practices of a bodhisattva, they are equal to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

Just as suchness is, so too is the entire realm of phenomena: having abandoned pride and all distracted minds, with obstacles forever extinguished and being universally pure, may it cause all sentient beings to be likewise.
Such is this sublime and most excellent dedication, as proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas.
By dedicating these immeasurable roots of goodness, one fully accomplishes the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Without exception, the true children of all Buddhas universally practice this profound dharma of dedication.
They encompass the entire subtle and wondrous Dharma-realm and enter deeply to abide securely within the powers of all Sugatas.
If there are those who joyfully seek this supreme practice taught by the Tathāgata— so profound and vast—
all these sons of the Buddha dwell therein, fully accomplishing it just like Samantabhadra.
The number of all sentient beings may still be known; The minds of all those throughout the three periods of time may likewise be known.
But the merit and virtue of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva— Profound, vast, immeasurable, and boundless—cannot be fully comprehended.
The space of the ten directions could be measured by a single hair, and the atoms within all lands could all be counted;
yet the merit in which the supreme Great Sages and true sons of the Buddha dwell is beyond measure.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-two and Volume Twenty-three,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
22. Chapter on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi-parivarta*).

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Maṇi-jewel palace of the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and had gathered from various worlds in other directions.
These bodhisattvas have attained mastery over all spheres of wisdom and conduct of all bodhisattvas, and have entered all gateways of the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
they are skillfully able to teach and transform all worlds, universally manifesting supernatural powers and other such deeds in every thought-moment;
they are fully endowed with all the vows of bodhisattvas, and constantly cultivate all bodhisattva practices throughout all worlds, all eons, and all lands.
They are fully endowed with the merit and wisdom of a bodhisattva, which are inexhaustible;
they are able to bring benefit to all beings;
and they are able to reach the further shore of the wisdom and skillful means of all bodhisattvas.
They are able to cause sentient beings to turn their backs on the path of birth and death and head toward the gate of nirvana;
they do not sever any of the practices performed by bodhisattvas;
and they skillfully traverse all bodhisattva dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, supernormal powers, and clear wisdom, being well able to manifest all their various deeds.

They have fully attained all the effortless spiritual powers (*anabhisaṃskāra-ṛddhipāda*) of all bodhisattvas; in a single thought-moment, they can reach the great assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions to exhort them, inquire of them, and receive and uphold the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). They constantly make offerings to the Buddhas with a great mind and are always able to cultivate the deeds and practices of the great bodhisattvas.

Their bodies appear universally throughout immeasurable worlds, their voices are heard everywhere reaching all places, and their minds penetrate clearly, perceiving and fully cultivating all the merits of every bodhisattva throughout the three periods of time.
Thus, the merits of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable and boundless; they could not be fully exhausted even if explained for incalculable eons. Their names are:
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva, and Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva.
[Sāgaramudrā] Bodhisattva, Padmaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Candragarbha Bodhisattva,
Vimalacandragarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvalokadhātupratibhāsavyūhagarbha Bodhisattva, Jñānaprabhāsagarbha Bodhisattva,
Guṇaketurāja-garbha Bodhisattva, Candanaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, and Puṣpaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Utpalaguṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Devaguṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Puṇyagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Asaṅgapariśuddhajñānaguṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇaguṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Vigatamalamala-garbha.
The Bodhisattva Vicitrapratibhānālaṃkārakośa, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhājālakosa,
the Bodhisattva Viśuddhaprabhātejavikrāntarāja-kośa, the Bodhisattva Mahākanakaparvata-prabhātejavikrāntarāja-kośa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvalakṣaṇālaṃkāra-viśuddhaguṇakośa, and the Bodhisattva Vajrajvālāguṇalakṣaṇālaṃkārakośa.
The Bodhisattva Blazing Radiance Treasury, the Bodhisattva Constellation King Illuminating Radiance Treasury,
the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Sublime Sound Treasury of Space, the Bodhisattva Dharani Merit Sustainer of All Worldly Vows Treasury,
the Bodhisattva Ocean Adornment Treasury, the Bodhisattva Sumeru Virtue Treasury, and the Bodhisattva Purifier of All Merit Treasury.
The Bodhisattva, the Tathāgatagarbha Bodhisattva, the Buddhaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, and the Vimukticandra Bodhisattva—
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as these were immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and inexpressible, with Vajragarbha Bodhisattva as their leader.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.

Immediately, in each of the ten directions, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in a billion Buddha-lands, there appeared Buddhas equal in number to the atoms in ten billion Buddha-lands, all named Vajragarbha.
In every world throughout the ten directions, it was likewise so; they all spoke in unison, praising him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Vajragarbha!”

You are now able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Great Wisdom Radiance; likewise, all the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of dust, who share this same name, empower you with their majestic spiritual authority.
That is to say:
by virtue of the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha;
by virtue of his original majestic spiritual power;
Because you possess great wisdom;
because you wish to proclaim the light of all the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas of all bodhisattvas.
That is to say:
Because they have entered the stage of wisdom;
because they have gathered all roots of goodness;
and because they skillfully discern all Buddha-dharmas.
Because of the extensive knowledge of phenomena;
because of the definitive exposition of all dharmas;
and because of the skillful discernment of non-conceptual wisdom.
Because they cannot be defiled by any worldly dharmas;
because their supramundane roots of goodness are pure;
and because they have attained inconceivable power of wisdom.
Because they have attained the realm of the wisdom of those who possess all-knowledge;
that is to say,
because they explain, according to reality, the distinctions among the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
Because Bodhisattvas abide securely in the ten stages;
because they analytically expound the untainted dharmas;
and because they are well-adorned by the great light of wisdom through skillful discernment.
Because they enter the gateway of perfect wisdom;
because they teach in accordance with the proper sequence of abidings;
and because they have attained the light of unhindered eloquence.
Because they are fully endowed with the stage of great unimpeded wisdom;
because they do not forget the bodhisattva mind;
and because they teach, transform, and bring to maturity the entire realm of sentient beings.
Because one attains the definitive wisdom that reaches all places. "Vajragarbha!
You should now explain the distinctions of this Dharma-gate."
That is to say:
it is by virtue of the spiritual power of all Buddhas;
and because you are able to receive the wisdom and spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Because of the purification of one's own roots of goodness;
because of the purity of the dharma-realm;
and because of the benefit of sentient beings.
Because they enter the body of wisdom of the Dharma-body;
because they receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
and because they attain the exalted and sublime bodies of all worlds.
"Because he has transcended all worldly paths;
because he has purified supramundane roots of goodness.

At that moment, the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowed upon Vajragarbha the true and formless body, the unobstructed eloquence of joyful speech, the pure wisdom of skillful discernment, excellent mindfulness without forgetfulness, the wisdom of excellent determination, the attainment of the stage of omniscience, the indestructible power of all Buddhas, the fearlessness of all Buddhas, the unimpeded wisdom of all Buddhas for discerning all phenomena and skillfully opening the gates of Dharma, and the supreme, wondrous deeds of body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas.

Why is this? It is because they have attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom; because of the power of the Bodhisattvas' original vows; because their straightforward mind is pure; because their wisdom is clear and bright; because they have skillfully gathered the factors conducive to the Path; because they have skillfully cultivated their fundamental practices; because they maintain in mind and uphold immeasurable teachings; because they have faith and understanding in the pure and radiant Dharma; because they have skillfully attained the indestructible gates of dhāraṇī; and because they are well-sealed by the seal of wisdom regarding the Dharma-realm.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all extended their right hands and stroked the crown of the head of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva;
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva immediately arose from samādhi and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

The vows of these bodhisattvas are definitive, faultless, and indestructible; they are as vast as the dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, pervading all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions. They act to rescue and deliver all the world and are protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas of the past, and likewise enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas of the future and the present.
“What is the stage of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?

There are ten stages of wisdom for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, are being taught by those of the present, and will be taught by those of the future; it is for the sake of these stages that I speak thus.”

What are the ten? First is the Joyful; second, the Stainless; third, the Radiant; fourth, the Blazing; fifth, the Difficult to Conquer; sixth, the Manifest; seventh, the Far-Reaching; eighth, the Immovable; ninth, the Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Cloud of Dharma.
Regarding these ten stages, the Buddhas of the three periods of time have already taught, are now teaching, and will teach them; I do not see any buddha-field where these ten stages are not taught.
Why is this? These ten stages are the most supreme and wondrous path of the bodhisattvas, the most supreme and luminously pure dharma-gate; namely:
The Analysis of the Matters of the Ten Stages.
O Sons of the Buddha!
These matters are inconceivable, namely:
"Bodhisattvas accord with the wisdom of the various stages.
After Vajragarbha Bodhisattva had finished speaking the names of the ten bodhisattva stages, he remained silent and did not further elaborate.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas, having heard the names of the ten bodhisattva stages, were filled with longing and desired to hear their explanation; each of them thought to themselves:
"For what cause and for what reason does the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having finished explaining the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), remain silent?
At that time, among the assembly of great bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva named Vimukticandra. Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, he asked in verse:
"O person of pure mindfulness and wisdom, For what reason have you explained the bodhisattvas..."
Having already stated the names of the various stages, why do you remain silent and not explain them?
Now all these great Bodhisattvas harbor doubts in their hearts:
for what reason have you spoken these names, yet do not expound their meaning?
The bodhisattvas of great wisdom all desire to hear the meaning of these stages;
we pray that you will explain them in detail for us.
This assembly of bodhisattvas is pure and free from all blemish.
Abiding in the firm and solid, endowed with the merit of wisdom,
we all gaze upon you, O Benevolent One, with hearts full of reverence;
desiring to hear what you shall speak, we are like the thirsty longing for nectar.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to gladden the assembly, replied in verse:
“The conduct of all bodhisattvas Is foremost and inconceivable;
The differentiation of the ten stages Is the very root of all Buddhas.”
Subtle and extremely difficult to see, it is beyond the reach of the mind;
born from the Buddha’s wisdom, one who hears it would become lost in confusion.
Holding the mind like a vajra, one should have deep faith in the Buddha’s wisdom.
Regarding this as the foremost marvel, their minds are free from doubt or difficulty.
Having distanced themselves from the conceit of a self and the domains where the mind operates, such bodhisattvas are then able to hear it.
The wisdom of quiescent extinction and the outflow-free is exceedingly difficult to explain through conceptual analysis;
it is like painting in the void, or like grasping a swift wind.
As I contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom, it is the foremost in being inconceivable.
"Sentient beings have little faith; for this reason, I remain silent.
Having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra spoke to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."

This assembly of great bodhisattvas possesses a straightforward and pure mind; they have skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path, skillfully accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, and skillfully honored and made offerings to all Buddhas.

Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas, they have accomplished immeasurable and profound merits. Free from delusion, doubt, and regret, they are without attachment or any fetters and hindrances. With deep-seated faith and understanding, they abide immovably, and within this Dharma, they do not rely on the teachings of others.
"Therefore, Son of the Buddha!
You should, by virtue of the Buddha's power, expound this meaning; these bodhisattvas are all capable of realizing and knowing this profound Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Moon of Liberation, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Please teach the Dharma of peace and security, the supreme conduct of the Bodhisattvas,
and the differentiation of the stages, so that wisdom may be purified.
When all wisdom is pure and stainless, one dwells securely in profound faith and understanding.”
"Regarding all the immeasurable Buddhas, you have realized and known the meaning of the ten stages.
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

Although this great assembly is entirely pure and free from delusion, doubt, and regret, and does not rely on the teachings of others regarding this Dharma, there are others who delight in inferior teachings;
upon hearing these profound and inconceivable matters, they may give rise to doubt and regret, and such people will suffer various miseries and afflictions for a long night.
Out of compassion for them, I remain silent.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "Though this assembly is pure, With profound wisdom free from doubt and regret,
Their minds are already resolved, No longer following the teachings of others."
Unshakable like Mount Sumeru, undisturbed like the great ocean;
others are of short practice, their wisdom not yet clear.
Following consciousness rather than wisdom, they give rise to doubt and regret upon hearing [the teaching].
"He would fall into an evil realm; out of compassion for him, I did not speak.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."

May we, by the power of the Buddha, skillfully discern this inconceivable Dharma and the matters for which the Buddha provides protective mindfulness, so that they may be easily believed and understood. Why is this?
Because you have well explained the meaning of the ten stages, the Buddhas of the ten directions should protect and mind you in accordance with the Dharma;
all Bodhisattvas should protect this matter as well, and thus practice with diligent vigor. Why is this?
This is the supreme practice of the bodhisattva, for it leads to the attainment of all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as all written characters are subsumed within the primary radicals, with the primary radicals serving as the foundation such that there is not a single character that does not enter into them;
so it is, O Son of the Buddha!
The ten stages are the root of all Buddha-dharmas;
when Bodhisattvas fully practice these ten stages, they are able to attain all-encompassing wisdom.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

"I pray that you will explain this meaning; may all Buddhas protect and keep it in mind, and bestow their spiritual power upon it, so that people may believe and accept it, and it cannot be destroyed.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Excellent, O Son of Wisdom, Endowed with pure conduct,..."
I pray that you will explain the practices of the ten stages and the dharmas entered upon those ten stages,
so that one may be fully endowed with wisdom and thereby attain bodhi.
May all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the most supreme among the honored ones of humanity, [grant their blessing].
All together protect and keep you in mind as they explain the meaning of these ten stages.
The ten stages are the foundation; they are called the sphere of wise conduct and are also the ultimate path—the immeasurable mass of the Buddha’s teachings.
"Just as all written characters are contained within the initial chapter,
so too the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas have the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as their foundation.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas simultaneously addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha with a single voice in verse, saying:
“The person of supreme and wondrous wisdom, Whose eloquence in exposition is immeasurable,
Whose virtue is as weighty as the king of mountains, Out of compassion has spoken of the ten stages.
With purity of ethical discipline, mindfulness, and wisdom, He has explained the meaning of these ten stages.”
The root of the ten powers, the fundamental practice of unimpeded wisdom,
and the merits of precept, concentration, and wisdom— all are gathered within the heart of the Benevolent One.
Arrogance and all false views have been utterly extinguished.
This assembly is free from doubt; we only wish to hear your excellent teaching.
Like the sick longing for a skilled physician, or the hungry longing for delicious food, so too are we:
having heard the flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, [we are filled with joy].
"Therefore, O One of Vast Intention, I pray that you open the gate of the first stage, and even unto the tenth stage, explaining them to me in their proper sequence.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a light of Bodhisattva-power, with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays as its retinue. It shone universally throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, pervading them all without exception, so that the sufferings of the three evil realms were all brought to rest.
It illuminated the assemblies gathered for the Dharma-discourses of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgatas.

After this light had pervasively illumined the bodies of the Bodhisattvas in the assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, it formed a great cloud-palace of radiant light in the sky above.

The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise did so; from the white tufts of hair between their eyebrows, they simultaneously emitted the light of the power of Bodhisattvas, with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays as its retinue, universally manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgatas. It fully illuminated all the assemblies of all Buddhas, as well as the entire multitude of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world, along with Vajragarbha Bodhisattva and his lion throne.
Having shone forth, they formed a great cloud-palace of radiant light in the sky above.
Then, from within those great cloud-palaces of radiant light, through the spiritual power of all Buddhas, a verse was spoken:
"The peerless Buddhas, Whose merit is like space,"
Possessing the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, the most honored Lord of the World manifested this supernatural power before Śākyamuni Buddha;
through the Buddha’s power, he revealed the fearless treasury of the Dharma King.
Explaining the practices of the various stages and the distinctions in their meanings,
sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, there is none who can destroy it.
If a person hears this Dharma-treasure, they shall be protected by all Buddhas.
Gradually fulfilling all the stages, one shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
If there are those capable of hearing it, even if they are within the great ocean or amidst the fires at the end of an eon, they will surely hear this sutra.
If a person is deluded, doubtful, or regretful, they will ultimately be unable to hear it.
Therefore, the Son of the Buddha now explains the path of wisdom regarding the stages;
entering the dharma of contemplation on power, one should practice it in successive order.
"Having reached other stages, each has obtained their respective benefit;
for the sake of all the world, we pray that you will speak so that [the teaching] does not cease.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva surveyed the ten directions, wishing to increase the faith and reverence of the great assembly, and spoke in verse:
“The path of the Buddhas, the Holy Lords, is subtle and extremely difficult to understand;
it cannot be attained through discursive thought, but is the sphere of activity only for the wise.
Its nature, from the very beginning, is quiescent and without arising or ceasing.”
Empty from the very beginning, it eliminates all suffering and affliction.
It is far removed from the various realms of existence and is identical to the mark of nirvana.
It has neither middle nor end, and cannot be expressed by words.
Transcending the three periods of time, its characteristics are like empty space;
it is the sphere of action of all Buddhas, pure, profound, and quiescent.
It is difficult for speech to reach, and the practice of the stages is likewise so.
To speak of it is already difficult; how much more so to show it to others?
The wisdom of all Buddhas transcends the path of mental factors;
it is inconceivable and possesses no aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
It can only be known through wisdom, not reached by ordinary consciousness;
like the track of a bird in the sky, it is difficult to describe—how could its characteristics be shown?
Such is the meaning of the ten stages: they are not within the range of the mind or mental activity.
Although this matter is difficult, one should resolve to practice compassion.
Gradually perfecting the various stages (*bhūmi*) is within the reach of the wise;
yet such practices of the stages are subtle and extremely hard to perceive.
This cannot be known by the mind; it must be expounded through the power of the Buddha.
You all should be reverent and listen with one-pointed minds.
This is that which accords with wisdom: the practice of entering the characteristics of the various stages.
Even in immeasurable billions of eons, one could not exhaustively explain it.
Now I shall briefly explain it according to reality, with its meaning complete and without remainder;
wait with a single mind in reverent devotion, for now I speak by the power of the Buddha.
The great voice proclaims the teaching of causes; the meaning and the names do not contradict one another.
The Buddha’s spiritual power is immeasurable, and now it all resides within my own body.
What I have spoken is but a single drop from the great ocean.
After Vajragarbha Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If sentient beings have extensively accumulated roots of goodness, cultivated various virtuous deeds, well gathered the factors conducive to enlightenment, made offerings to the Buddhas, accumulated all pure dharmas, been protected by spiritual friends, entered into a profound and vast mind, have faith and delight in the Great Dharma, possess minds largely inclined toward compassion, and take pleasure in seeking the wisdom of the Buddha;
It is such beings as these who are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For the sake of attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), for the sake of attaining the ten powers (*daśabala*), for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharmas, for the sake of rescuing all the world, for the sake of purifying the mind of great compassion, for the sake of directing oneself toward the non-remainder and unobstructed wisdom of the ten directions, for the sake of purifying all Buddha-fields so that none remain, for the sake of knowing the events of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment, and for the sake of freely turning the great wheel of Dharma and extensively manifesting the spiritual power of a Buddha—thus do the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas generate such a mind.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This mind takes great compassion as its foremost quality, is preeminent in wisdom, and is protected by skillful means;
its straightforward mind and profound mind are pure and ultimate, equal in measure to the power of the Buddhas."
They possess well-determined power over sentient beings and the power of the Buddha; they advance toward unimpeded wisdom and accord with spontaneous wisdom;
they are able to receive all Buddha-dharmas through the teaching of wisdom—vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future.

When a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and enter the rank of bodhisattvas. Born into the family of the Buddhas, their lineage is noble and beyond reproach;
they transcend all mundane paths and enter the supramundane path.

Abiding within the bodhisattva-dharma, they are counted among the ranks of bodhisattvas and equally enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. They are destined to reach the ultimate realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas, it is called "abiding in the Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because of the quality of being unshakable.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they possess abundant joy, abundant faith, abundant purity, abundant exultation, abundant pliancy, and abundant receptivity; they do not delight in contention, do not delight in harassing sentient beings, and do not delight in anger or resentment."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to a heart of joy because they mindfully recollect all Buddhas;
they give rise to a heart of joy because they mindfully recollect all Buddha-dharmas."
They give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the practices performed by all bodhisattvas;
and they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the pure characteristics of all the pāramitās.
They give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting that all bodhisattvas possess qualities superior to those of the multitudes;
they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting that the power of all bodhisattvas is indestructible;
they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the teaching methods of all Tathāgatas.
One gives rise to a heart of joy by reflecting on how one can benefit sentient beings;
one gives rise to a heart of joy by reflecting on the gates of wisdom and skillful means entered by all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"I shall turn away from all worldly realms; I give rise to a heart of joy.
I shall enter into the equality of all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy."
He gives rise to a heart of joy in distancing himself from the stage of ordinary beings;
he gives rise to a heart of joy in drawing near to the stage of wisdom;
he gives rise to a heart of joy in severing all evil paths.
They give rise to a heart of joy by acting as a refuge for all sentient beings;
they give rise to a heart of joy by seeing all Buddhas in their presence;
they give rise to a heart of joy by entering the realm of all Buddhas.
"One enters the ranks of all bodhisattvas and gives rise to a heart of joy;
one is free from all terrors and gives rise to a heart of joy. Why is this so?
When this bodhisattva attains the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all fears are immediately and completely abandoned.

These are: the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of falling into the evil destinies, and the fear of the majesty of the great assembly; he is free from all such fears.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has abandoned the mark of self, he does not even crave his own body, much less the objects he uses;
therefore, the bodhisattva has no fear of being unable to make a living.

The mind does not desire honor or offerings; rather, [the Bodhisattva] thinks, "I should make offerings to sentient beings and provide them with their necessities. For this reason, the Bodhisattva has no fear of ill repute.
Because they have distanced themselves from the view of self and are free from the mark of a self, they have no fear of death.
Furthermore, he thinks:
"Once I have died, wherever I am born, I shall certainly see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, I have no fear of falling into the evil realms.
My aspirations and joys are peerless—how could there be anyone superior?"
"Therefore, there is no fear regarding the majesty and virtue of the great assembly.
In this way, the Bodhisattva is forever free from all matters of terror.
"O Sons of the Buddha!"

This bodhisattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, harbors no resentment toward any sentient being; with a straightforward mind that is firm and naturally pure, they further diligently cultivate all roots of goodness.
That is to say:
faith is predominant, and they frequently practice a pure mind;
their understanding is pure, and they mostly discern through faith.

Giving birth to great compassion and accomplishing great loving-kindness, their minds never weary or indolent; adorned with a sense of shame and remorse, they achieve patience and gentleness, reverently following the teachings of all Buddhas, and placing deep trust in spiritual friends;
day and night they constantly cultivate all roots of goodness, always delighting in the Dharma, seeking extensive learning without weariness;

regarding the Dharma as they have heard it, they observe it with right mindfulness, their minds free from greedy attachment; they seek neither fame nor reputation, nor profit, offerings, or the necessities of life, but always give rise to the mind of a jewel, never feeling satiated.

Delighting in the stage of omniscience, desiring to attain the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of all Buddhas, seeking assistance through the dharmas of the *pāramitās*, and being free from all guile and crookedness;

acting according to what one says, always practicing truthful speech, not defiling the family of the Buddhas, not forsaking the bodhisattva precepts, giving rise to the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), remaining as immovable as the king of mountains, taking no pleasure in worldly affairs, accomplishing supramundane roots of goodness, and gathering the wholesome factors that assist enlightenment without ever feeling satiated; constantly seeking the most excellent path among the excellent—when a bodhisattva accomplishes such dharmas of the pure stages, it is called "abiding in the Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
When a bodhisattva thus dwells securely in the Stage of Joy, they give rise to great vows and generate such a concentrated mind as this: "I shall,
with a pure mind, make offerings to all Buddhas without exception, providing every kind of offering implement according to their wishes."

They make such great vows as these: vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future, they shall make offerings to all Buddhas throughout every kalpa, with great articles of offering, without ceasing.

Furthermore, they receive and uphold all the sutras and teachings spoken by all Buddhas; they encompass the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas; they accord with all the methods of teaching and transformation employed by all Buddhas; and they are able to protect all the dharmas of all Buddhas. They give rise to such great vows—vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate as space—to protect all the Buddha-dharmas throughout every kalpa until the end of the future, without ever ceasing.

Furthermore, whenever all Buddhas in all worlds descend from Tuṣita Heaven, enter the womb, dwell in the womb, are born, renounce the world, and attain the Way of Buddhahood; when they are entreated to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma and manifest entry into Great Parinirvāṇa—at those times, I shall go to them all to make offerings. With the gathering of the Dharma as my primary concern, because I turn [the wheel] during the three periods, I have made such a great vow: vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, reaching to the end of the future and through all kalpas, I shall welcome and make offerings to all Buddhas without ceasing.

"Furthermore, all the practices of Bodhisattvas are vast and immeasurable, indestructible, and non-conceptual. They are encompassed by the various *pāramitās*, purified by the various stages (*bhūmis*), and give rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Whether characterized by general or specific marks, with marks or without marks, involving formation or destruction—all the paths and *pāramitās* practiced by Bodhisattvas, their fundamental conduct, teach and transform all beings, causing them to accept and practice these teachings so that their minds may increase in virtue. They make such great vows, as vast as the *dharmadhātu* and ultimate like space, continuing until the end of the future and throughout all kalpas, never ceasing to mature sentient beings through various means of transformation."

"Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings—whether with form or without form, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; bound to the three realms and entering all places of birth within the six destinies, encompassed by name-and-form—I shall teach and mature them, severing all worldly paths and causing them to abide in the Buddha-dharma and all-encompassing wisdom, leaving none remaining.
I make such a great vow, as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing until the end of the future and through all kalpas, teaching and transforming all sentient beings without rest."

Furthermore, regarding all worlds—whether vast, narrow, or intermediate; innumerable and immeasurable; indistinguishable, indestructible, immovable, and ineffable; coarse or subtle; upright, inverted, level, square, or circular—he enters into the wisdom that penetrates such worlds. Just as with the distinctions of Indra’s net, he directly knows the distinctions of the worlds of the ten directions. He gives rise to such great vows, vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing to the end of the future and throughout all kalpas, so that he may directly know all such worlds without ever ceasing.
Furthermore, all Buddha-lands enter into a single Buddha-land, and a single Buddha-land enters into all Buddha-lands;

each and every Buddha-land possesses immeasurable adornments, is free from all defilement, and is perfectly pure. Sentient beings of wisdom fill them entirely, and they always possess the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas, manifesting them according to the minds of sentient beings.
They make such great vows—vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space—to purify such lands without rest until the end of the future and throughout all kalpas.

Furthermore, all these bodhisattvas are of one mind and study together; they collectively accumulate all virtues without resentment or envy. Sharing the same realm and being united in equal minds, they are never separated from one another. According to what is appropriate, they can manifest the bodies of Buddhas; within their own minds, they are fully able to understand and know the realms of all Buddhas, as well as their powers of supernatural penetration and wisdom. They constantly attain supernatural powers at will, enabling them to travel through all lands and manifest their physical forms in all Buddha-assemblies. They are born universally in all places of birth, possessing such inconceivable great wisdom and being fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva.
They have made such great vows, as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, to practice this path of great wisdom without rest until the end of the future and throughout all kalpas.

"Furthermore, riding upon the wheel of non-retrogression and practicing the bodhisattva path, the actions performed through body, speech, and mind are not in vain; those sentient beings who see me shall immediately become fixed in the Buddha-dharma;
upon hearing my voice, they shall immediately attain true wisdom;
and those who behold me shall have their hearts filled with joy and be freed from all afflictions."
Like the king of medicinal trees, they practice the bodhisattva path in order to attain such a state;

they make such great vows, as vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate as space, extending to the end of the future and through all kalpas, practicing the non-retrogressive path so that their deeds are never in vain and never cease.

"Furthermore, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in all worlds; upon a single hair-tip, they manifest entering the womb, leaving home, sitting at the site of enlightenment, attaining the Buddha-way, turning the wheel of Dharma, delivering sentient beings, and demonstrating Great Nirvāṇa. They manifest the great power of the Tathāgatas' wisdom and strength, and in every thought-moment, they attain the Buddha-way according to those among all sentient beings who are ready to be delivered.
Knowing that all phenomena have the characteristic of Nirvāṇa, they cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy with a single voice;
they demonstrate Great Nirvāṇa while never ceasing the practices of a Bodhisattva."
They demonstrate to sentient beings the ground of great wisdom, causing them to know that all phenomena are merely provisional and false;
through the sovereign power of great wisdom and spiritual penetrations, they manifest transformations that fill the entire dharma-realm;

they make such great vows—vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space—that until the end of the future and throughout all kalpas, they shall accomplish the task of attaining the Buddha-way, seeking great wisdom, great spiritual penetrations, and so forth, without ever ceasing.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas dwell on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they produce millions of asaṃkhyeyas of such great vows, headed by ten primary vows;
they produce these vows by means of ten inexhaustible dharmas, and in order to fulfill these vows, they practice with diligent vigor."
What are the ten? First, sentient beings are inexhaustible;
second, worlds are inexhaustible.
Third, space is inexhaustible;
fourth, the dharma-realm is inexhaustible;
fifth, nirvāṇa is inexhaustible.
Sixth, the appearance of Buddhas in the world is inexhaustible;
seventh, the wisdom of all Buddhas is inexhaustible;
eighth, the objects perceived by the mind are inexhaustible.
Ninth, the arising of wisdom is inexhaustible;
tenth, the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are inexhaustible.
Only when sentient beings are exhausted shall my vow be exhausted.

If the worlds, space, the dharma-realm, nirvana, the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the wisdom of all Buddhas, the objects of the mind, the arising of knowledge, and the exhaustion of all transformations were to come to an end, then my vows would come to an end;

yet sentient beings are truly inexhaustible. Since the worlds, space, the dharma-realm, nirvana, the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the wisdom of all Buddhas, the objects of the mind, the arising of knowledge, and all transformations are truly inexhaustible, my roots of goodness for these vows are likewise inexhaustible.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas resolutely give rise to these great vows, they then attain a mind of benefit and peace, a supple mind, a compliant mind, a tranquil mind, a heedful mind, a mind of cessation, a straightforward mind, a harmonious and moistening mind, a non-angry mind, and a non-turbid mind.”
Thus, one becomes a person of faith, who delights in discerning merit through faith:

faith in the path originally practiced by all Buddhas; faith that by practicing the various *pāramitās*, they attain growth; faith in skillfully entering the various stages (*bhūmis*) to obtain supreme merit; faith in attaining the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha; faith in being fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); faith in the indestructible unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*); faith in the inconceivable nature of all Buddha-dharmas; faith in the immeasurable and boundless sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas; faith in the immeasurable gateways of practice of all Tathāgatas; and faith that the fruit of retribution is accomplished through causes and conditions.
To state the essentials:
believe that all bodhisattvas universally practice the merit, wisdom, and majestic spiritual power of all buddhas.
"O Children of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"The True Dharma of all Buddhas is thus profound, thus devoid of marks, thus quiescent, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, thus unstained, thus immeasurable, thus vast, and thus indestructible."

Yet, the minds of all ordinary beings fall into false views; shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and delusion, their eye of wisdom is obscured. They constantly raise the banner of arrogance and fall into the net of craving and thirst. Following along with flattery and crookedness, they harbor stinginess and jealousy, thereby creating the causes and conditions for future births.

Having accumulated much greed, hatred, and folly, they give rise to grave karmas. The fierce winds of resentment blow upon the fire of the sinful mind, causing it to burn perpetually. Whatever they do is entirely associated with perversion.

The flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of views, and the flow of ignorance continuously give rise to mind, intellect, and consciousness, sowing seeds in the soil of the three realms to produce the sprouts of suffering and affliction, namely:
Name-and-form;
from the growth of the combination of name-and-form come the six sense bases;
from the encounter between the sense faculties and their objects arises contact;
From contact, feeling arises;
from craving for pleasant feeling, clinging arises;
from the increase of clinging, grasping arises.
Due to the condition of grasping (*upādāna*), there arises renewed existence (*punarbhava*);
due to the condition of existence (*bhava*), there arise birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Thus, through these conditions, the entire mass of suffering accumulates, and one undergoes all manner of affliction.
Within this there is no self and nothing belonging to a self;
there is no agent, no experiencer, and no knower, being like grass, trees, tiles, and stones, and like shadows and echoes.
Ordinary beings are pitiable; unaware and unawakened, they undergo suffering and affliction.

When a Bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings cannot escape these various sufferings, they give rise to the wisdom of great compassion, thinking: "I must protect and deliver all these sentient beings, causing them to abide in the bliss of the ultimate Buddha-way. Thereupon, they give rise to the wisdom of great loving-kindness.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, conforming to such a dharma of great compassion, dwells in the first stage (*bhūmi*) with a profound and wondrous mind. Regarding all things, he has no greed or attachment; because he reveres the great and wondrous wisdom of the Buddhas, he practices the great giving (*mahādāna*). At that very moment, he is able to give away everything he possesses: gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, *śaṅkha* shells, *musāragalva*, *vaiḍūrya*, coral, amber, *kaṅka* shells, precious gems, necklaces, and ornaments for the body; as well as elephants, horses, palanquins, people, male and female slaves, kingdoms, cities, gardens, parks, pleasure groves, wives, concubines, sons, and daughters—giving away everything he holds dear.
Because they hold the Buddha in profound reverence, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not begrudge or cherish their heads, eyes, ears, noses, limbs, joints, hands, or feet;
dwelling in the first stage (prathamā bhūmiḥ), they are able to practice great giving.

Because this bodhisattva, with a heart of great compassion and a heart of great generosity, seeks diligently the worldly and supramundane benefits for the sake of rescuing all sentient beings without weariness of mind, they give rise to the merit of tirelessness. Because they are able to understand various scriptures and treatises by themselves, they give rise to the merit of knowing scriptures.

Having attained such wisdom that knows scriptures, they are well able to deliberate upon what should and should not be done, benefiting superior, middling, and inferior sentient beings as appropriate; thus, the bodhisattva gives rise to the merit of worldly knowledge.

Having attained the merit of worldly knowledge, they know the proper time and measure, are adorned with shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), and cultivate the path of self-benefit and the benefit of others; thus, they give rise to the merit of shame and remorse.
Practicing such merits with diligent effort and without mental slackness or retreat constitutes the merit of non-retrogressive diligence;
having attained this power of endurance, one zealously performs offerings to all Buddhas and practices according to what the Buddhas have taught.
O Sons of the Buddha!
These Bodhisattvas fully understand how to give rise to such dharmas of the pure stages, namely:

faith, loving-kindness, compassion, and generosity; being free from weariness; knowing all scriptures; skillfully understanding worldly dharmas; possessing a sense of shame and remorse; being capable of receiving [teachings]; making offerings to all Buddhas; and practicing according to what has been taught.

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), although they see few Buddhas by ordinary means, through the power of their vows, they see hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of Buddha-Bhagavats. Their mind is filled with great joy and deep-seated love and respect; they offer the finest articles of pleasure to all these Buddhas and the entire Sangha, and dedicate all such merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because this bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, the method for teaching and transforming sentient beings arises within them; they primarily gather in sentient beings through the two means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), namely:

Regarding the two latter methods of integration—generosity and kind speech—the Bodhisattva practices them through the power of faith and understanding, though they have not yet fully mastered them. Thus, as the Bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas and transforms sentient beings, they are able to receive and practice all the dharmas of the pure stages. All such merits are dedicated toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience), whereby they become increasingly manifest, clear, and capable of effective application.

For example, just as a goldsmith refines gold, making it pliable and workable through the application of fire and enhancing its luster and color, so too does a bodhisattva, by making offerings to the Buddhas, teaching and transforming sentient beings, and practicing the dharmas of the pure stages, dedicate all these merits toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), whereby they become increasingly radiant and available for use according to one's will.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

These Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, while practicing in the first stage (*bhūmi*), inquire of and receive instructions from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) regarding the dharmas for accomplishing the stage, never becoming weary or negligent.

While dwelling in the first stage, these Bodhisattvas inquire of and receive instructions from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics of the practices and fruits of the second stage, never feeling satiated."

In this way, throughout the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, regarding the characteristics of their practice and its fruits, they consult, receive instruction from, and question the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends concerning the dharmas that perfect the ten stages, never becoming weary or negligent.

This bodhisattva skillfully knows the remedial dharmas of all stages; skillfully knows the formation and destruction of all stages; skillfully knows the fruits of the practices of all stages; skillfully knows the analytical attainment of all stages; skillfully knows the pure conduct of all stages; skillfully knows the practice of proceeding from one stage to the next; skillfully knows what is possible and what is impossible regarding all stages; skillfully knows the transition of the dwelling places of all stages; skillfully knows the superior progress of the activities of all stages; skillfully knows the non-retrogression attained in all stages; and even skillfully knows all the pure stage-dharmas of bodhisattvas that enter the stage of Tathāgata wisdom.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Thus, these Bodhisattvas skillfully know the practices of all the stages; even before they have set out upon the first stage, they already know that there are no obstacles regarding the ten stages.
Having attained the light of wisdom of all the stages, they even come to know the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.
Just as a great caravan leader, leading many merchants, desires to reach a great city, first inquires about the dangers of retreating from the road and the risks and benefits along the way;

even before departing from the starting point, he knows where to stay for the night and thoroughly understands how to reach that city. Using wisdom to contemplate and deliberate, he provides all necessary provisions so that no one lacks anything, and leads the multitude directly to the great city, escaping all calamities on the perilous path so that neither himself nor the people suffer any distress.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), skillfully knows the remedial dharmas of all stages, up to skillfully knowing all the pure stage-dharmas of Bodhisattvas and entering the stage of Tathāgata-wisdom.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gathers the great provisions of merit and wisdom to act as a caravan leader for sentient beings, teaching and transforming them according to their needs. He leads them out of the perilous and evil places of birth-and-death, showing them the path of peace and security, and even causes them to dwell in the great city of omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñā*), free from all decline and affliction.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva should always maintain a mind free from weariness, diligently cultivating the fundamental practices of the stages (*bhūmi*) until he thoroughly understands how to enter the stage of Tathāgata-wisdom.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

This is a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s entry into the Stage of Joy; were it explained in detail, there would be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya matters.”

When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), he often becomes a sovereign king of Jambudvīpa, noble, powerful, and autonomous, constantly protecting the True Dharma. He is able to gather in sentient beings through great giving, skillfully removing the defilement of stinginess and greed from them. He constantly practices great giving without exhaustion, performing the various wholesome deeds of generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.

All these merits do not depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, nor from mindfulness of all fellow-practicing Bodhisattvas, nor from mindfulness of the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, nor from mindfulness of the *pāramitās*, nor from mindfulness of the ten stages (*bhūmis*), nor from mindfulness of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*), up to and including mindfulness of the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the commander, and the honored one; indeed, I shall become the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
If these Bodhisattvas wish to leave the household life and practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they are able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires.
Having gone forth, by practicing with diligent vigor, they attain one hundred samādhis in a mere moment."
One attains the vision of a hundred buddhas;
one knows the spiritual powers of a hundred buddhas;
and one is able to shake a hundred buddha-worlds.
They are able to fly across a hundred Buddha-worlds;
they are able to illumine a hundred Buddha-worlds;
they are able to teach and transform the sentient beings of a hundred worlds.
They are able to abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas;
they are able to know the events of a hundred kalpas each in the past and future worlds;
and they are able to skillfully enter a hundred dharma-gates.
He is able to transform his body into a hundred forms, and within each individual body, he can manifest a hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue.
If he manifests through the sovereign power of his vows, it exceeds these numbers, being beyond calculation even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If there are sentient beings who have extensively cultivated and accumulated roots of goodness,
who have perfected pure and wholesome dharmas, and who draw near to the Buddhas,"
Through the power of pure faith and aspiration, And by conforming to a heart of compassion,
Such a person is able to give rise to The immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas.
The all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas Is of immeasurable power and purity.
With enduring strength and firm resolve, they accomplish all Buddha-dharmas;
with a compassionate heart, they rescue the world, purify all Buddha-fields,
and proclaim the turning of the Wheel of Dharma— thus they make this unsurpassed vow.
In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, yet there is no differentiation;
the various distinctions of time are displayed for the sake of the world.
Briefly stated, this is the complete seeking of all the merits of the Buddhas.
Aroused from a vast mind, it is like the empty sky;
with compassion and wisdom as its head, practiced in union with skillful means,
deep, upright, and reaching the ultimate purity— its power is immeasurable.
With a mind directed toward non-obstruction, not following the teachings of others,
and being equal to all Buddhas, one gives rise to the Great Mind.
O sons of the Buddha, give birth to such a precious mind.
Thus one leaves the stage of ordinary beings and enters the sphere of the Buddhas' conduct.
One is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, beyond all reproach;
being thus equal to all Buddhas, one will surely attain the unsurpassed path.
When such a mind arises, one immediately attains the first stage (*bhūmi*);
that mind cannot be moved, like the king of great mountains.
Then, for this bodhisattva, the signs of great joy manifest.
Their minds are ever pure, capable of undertaking great matters.
Their hearts take no pleasure in strife or litigation; they do not delight in vexing sentient beings.
Free from anger and resentment, they rejoice in shame, remorse, and reverence.
Furthermore, one practices with a straightforward mind, guards the sense faculties, constantly keeps in mind the salvation of the world, and yearns for the wisdom of all Buddhas.
With a heart full of joy, one thinks: "I shall surely attain this."
Upon attaining the Stage of Joy, one immediately transcends the five fears:
fear of lacking a livelihood, fear of death, fear of ill repute, fear of the miserable realms, and fear of the majesty of others.
This is because one no longer clings to a self or to what belongs to a self.
These sons of the Buddhas have distanced themselves from all fears;
they constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, always possessing faith and reverence.
Fully endowed with the virtues of shame and remorse, they increase wholesome dharmas day and night.
One delights in the true benefit of meritorious qualities, not in various sensual desires.
Just as one has heard the Dharma, one is able to constantly contemplate it well;
free from conduct of greedy attachment, one severs the mind for gain and offerings.
Always delighting in bodhi, seeking the Buddha’s wisdom with a single mind,
practicing the various pāramitās, and remaining free from a deceitful or crooked heart;
acting in accordance with what one says, dwelling securely within truthful speech.
They do not defile the family of the Buddhas, nor do they abandon the training of a bodhisattva.
They distance themselves from worldly affairs and aspirations, delighting in transcending the world;
seeking the sublime Dharma without weariness, their diligence increases ever further.
In this way, all bodhisattvas delight in all meritorious qualities and give rise to great vows,
desiring to behold all Buddhas. Protecting the Dharma,
they go to the presence of the Buddhas and practice the sublime conduct of bodhisattvas.
Transforming all sentient beings, purifying all Buddha-lands;
within my Buddha-land, it shall be filled with great Bodhisattvas.
All these Bodhisattvas shall be of one mind, so that seeing or hearing them shall never be in vain.
Within every single atom, all Buddhas attain the Way of Buddhahood;
from these arise such vows, immeasurable and boundless.
These vows are inexhaustible, as vast as space and as infinite as sentient beings.
The Dharma-realm, the world, and nirvāṇa— From these, the Buddhas give rise to wisdom.
When the mind conditions the arising of wisdom and it transforms, I vow to abide thus;
having made such a great vow, My mind becomes supple, harmonious, and compliant.
Being able to believe in the Buddha’s merits and observing sentient beings, one knows they arise from causes and conditions; thus, the mind of compassion arises.
Thinking, "I shall deliver those sentient beings who suffer," one acts accordingly.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he practices various kinds of giving:
namely, exquisite lands, all manner of rare treasures,
elephants, horses, and vehicles, as well as retinues and subjects.
Giving away his head, eyes, hands, and feet, as well as his flesh and muscles, he felt no regret;
seeking various sūtras and scriptures, his mind never grew weary;
having attained understanding of their meaning and intent, he was able to act in accordance with the world.
Through the power of shame and remorse, one gradually causes these qualities to increase;
with a mind of reverence, one is able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
Thus, throughout day and night, the wise person constantly practices in this way.
The roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure, like refined gold.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they are able to fully comprehend the ten stages;
as they progress through their practice, they encounter no obstacles whatsoever.
Just as a caravan leader, wishing to benefit the merchants,
first inquires about the various dangers and hardships along the road;
so too the Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage thoroughly understands the practices of all the stages.
Being free from all obstructions, one is able to reach the stage of a Buddha.
Abiding in this first stage (bhūmi), one often becomes a king of Jambudvīpa;
skillfully knowing all dharmas, one constantly practices a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Transforming and guiding others in accordance with the Dharma, all come to have faith and respect;
they are exhorted to practice giving in order to seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
When a Bodhisattva renounces their kingdom and leaves the household life to enter the Buddha-dharma,
By diligently practicing vigor, one immediately attains a hundred samādhis;
one can see a hundred buddhas, shake a hundred lands,
and illuminate a hundred lands with light, and likewise travel through the air.
Transforming sentient beings in a hundred lands, Entering into a hundred dharma-gates,
Recalling and knowing the events of a hundred kalpas, And manifesting a hundred bodies;
Able to manifest a retinue Of a hundred bodhisattvas.
If one were to calculate by the power of their vows, they would exceed these numbers immeasurably.
Now, to clarify the meaning of the first stage, I shall explain it only in brief;
were I to explain it extensively, even ten million kalpas would not suffice.
This is the first stage of the Bodhisattva, named "The Joyous" (Pramuditā).
For those who benefit sentient beings, this has now been fully explained.
— *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, Fascicle Twenty-Three.
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Twenty-Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of Central India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Twenty Stages, Part Two.
All the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, having heard the teaching on the meaning of the higher stages,
their minds became pure and their joy was immeasurable. Each,
from their respective seats, leaped up and stayed suspended in mid-air.
With various supreme and exquisite flowers, they scattered them over Vajragarbha, and all together praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Vajragarbha! You of great wisdom and fearlessness have skillfully expounded the Bodhisattva stages."
The Mahāsattva Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure and desiring to hear the description of the characteristics of the practices of the second bhūmi,
immediately requested Vajragarbha: "O One of Great Wisdom, please explain it."
"Everyone wishes to hear the characteristics of the second stage.
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
'O Son of the Buddha!'"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already fulfilled the first stage and wishes to attain the second stage, they should give rise to ten kinds of straightforward mind. What are these ten?
1. A supple mind; 2. A harmonious mind; 3. A receptive mind.
4. A mind of non-negligence;
5. A mind of quiescence; 6. A true mind;
7. An undistracted mind; 8.
A mind free from greed and stinginess;
9. A superior mind;
10. The Great Mind. By means of these ten minds, the bodhisattva enters the second stage.

Abiding in the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the bodhisattva naturally and completely distances himself from all killing; he discards weapons and implements of violence, is free from malice and resentment, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, gives rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, and constantly seeks what is beneficial. He does not even harbor an evil thought to distress a sentient being, let alone inflict physical harm upon them.

He abstains from all forms of theft regarding the necessities of life and always knows contentment. If an object belongs to another or is being used by another, he does not take it when it is not given.
He abstains from sexual misconduct; satisfied with his own wife, he does not give rise to even a single thought toward the women of others.
He abstains from false speech, always speaking truthfully, accurately, and consistently; he does not speak falsely even in his dreams, much less intentionally.
Free from divisive speech, they harbor no intent to cause estrangement; among those who are quarreling or divided, they always delight in bringing about reconciliation.
Free from harsh speech, they entirely abandon all words that are coarse, cruel, or evil—such speech which destroys one’s own person and likewise destroys others.

Free from idle chatter, they constantly guard themselves; regarding whatever they may speak, whether it should be done or not, they always speak at the proper time, speak what is beneficial, speak in accordance with the Dharma, and speak with due deliberation. Even in jest, they do not commit an offense, let alone do so intentionally.
He does not covet the property of others; regarding things belonging to others or under their control, he does not think, "I shall take this.
Free from thoughts of anger and malice, he always maintains toward sentient beings a mind of affectionate kindness and a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
They abandon divination and physiognomy, practicing right view and developing firm, deep faith in the causal conditions of sin and merit;
they abandon flattery and crookedness, sincerely taking refuge in the Triple Gem and giving rise to a mind of certainty.
The bodhisattva thus constantly protects the wholesome paths, reflecting:
"All sentient beings who fall into the evil realms do so because of the ten unwholesome paths;
I shall abide myself in wholesome dharmas, and I shall also explain these various wholesome dharmas for others, showing them the place of right practice."
"Why is this? It is impossible for one who does not practice virtue themselves to cause others to abide in virtue by teaching them the Dharma.
Furthermore, he reflected deeply:
"If one practices the ten unwholesome paths of action, one will fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
if one practices the ten wholesome paths of action, one will be born among humans, up to the Peak of Existence."

Furthermore, when one practices these ten paths of wholesome action in conjunction with wisdom, if the mind is weak and inferior, delighting in meager merit, feeling weary of and fearful toward the triple world, and possessing little great compassion, one hears the Dharma from others and reaches the Śrāvaka vehicle.

If one practices these ten paths of wholesome action without hearing them from others, knowing them spontaneously, yet being unable to fully perfect the skillful means of great compassion, one can enter deeply into the dharma of various causes and conditions and reach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

If one practices these ten paths of wholesome action with complete purity, with a mind that is vast, immeasurable, and boundless; if one gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, possesses the power of skillful means, maintains firm resolve, does not abandon any sentient being, seeks the great wisdom of a Buddha, purifies the various bodhisattva stages, purifies the various pāramitās, and enters into profound and expansive conduct, then one will be able to attain the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great kindness and great compassion, and even become fully endowed with the knowledge of all modes, gathering all the Buddha-dharmas. Therefore, I should practice the ten paths of wholesome action to seek omniscience.
"Furthermore, this bodhisattva reflects as follows:
'These ten unwholesome paths—those of the highest degree are the causes and conditions for the hells;
those of the middle degree are the causes and conditions for the animal realm.'"
The lowest [rebirth] is that of the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Among these, the transgression of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, a short lifespan; second, [a meager supply of food].
Second, they suffer from many illnesses.
The sin of robbery and theft likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; [second, illness].
Second, one lacks mastery over shared wealth.
The sin of sexual misconduct also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their spouse is not chaste.
Second, one obtains a retinue that is not compliant with one's wishes.
The sin of lying also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are frequently subjected to slander.
Second, one is deceived by others.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they obtain wicked and malicious associates.
Second, one obtains discordant kinsmen.
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they constantly hear unpleasant sounds; [second, they have quarrelsome relatives].
Second, whatever they may speak is always accompanied by contention and dispute.
The fault of meaningless speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, no one will believe or accept their words.
Second, whatever they say cannot be clearly understood.
The sin of covetousness also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, having excessive desire.
Second, there is no sense of satiety.
The sin of anger and malice also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are constantly sought out for their faults by everyone.
Second, they are constantly afflicted and harmed by the multitude.
The sin of wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, being born into a family of wrong views; [second, ...]
Second, their minds are crooked and deceitful.
O Sons of the Buddha!
These ten unwholesome paths are all the causes and conditions for a great mass of suffering.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"For what reason do I not myself refrain from these ten unwholesome paths and practice the ten wholesome paths, and also cause others to practice these wholesome paths?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately abandons the ten unwholesome paths and dwells securely in the ten wholesome paths, while also causing others to abide in the wholesome paths.

At that time, toward all sentient beings, this bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of peace, a mind of joy, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of benefit, a mind of protection, a mind of a teacher, a mind of a great teacher, and a mind of regarding them as oneself.
He forms this thought:
"These sentient beings have fallen into wrong views; following their own perverted minds, they travel upon wrong and perilous paths and are truly to be pitied.
I should cause them to abide in the path of right view and within the Dharma of reality."
These sentient beings are constantly engaged in mutual strife and contention, discriminating between self and other;
I should cause them to abide in great loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
These sentient beings are constantly greedy for wealth and possessions, never knowing contentment, and always sustain themselves through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
I should cause them to abide in pure actions of body, speech, and mind.

These sentient beings follow after greed, hatred, and delusion, and are constantly scorched by the great fires of various afflictions; they are unable to resolve to seek the skillful means for transcendence.
I should cause them to extinguish the fires of affliction and place them in a state of cool serenity.
These sentient beings are constantly shrouded by ignorance and enter into great darkness;
