deprived of the light of wisdom, they enter the perilous path of birth and death, following after various immeasurable false views.

I should cause them to obtain the unobstructed, pure eye of wisdom; by means of this eye, they shall know the true mark of all phenomena as they really are, and attain the unobstructed, all-encompassing knowledge of reality that does not depend on others.

These sentient beings have fallen onto the path of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and are entering the net of false views. They are shrouded by the dense forest of various forms of ignorance, following the tracks of delusive and heterodox paths, and are perpetually blinded by folly. Having strayed from the Guide, they follow what is not the essential path to liberation, yet they claim it to be the way out;
they comply with the mind of Māra and distance themselves from the intent of the Buddha.

I should cause them to cross over the perilous and difficult road of birth and death and settle them securely, so that they may dwell in the great city of fearlessness belonging to those of all-knowledge, free from all decay and affliction.
These sentient beings are submerged by the turbulent waters of the various afflictions;
they are swept away by the four floods of desire, existence, views, and ignorance;
they follow the stream of birth and death, entering the great river of craving.
Devoured by the power of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they are unable to seek the essential path of liberation;
they are constantly harmed by the evil insects of sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of malice;

furthermore, seized by the *rākṣasa* of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the water, they enter the deep, swirling current of the five desires, are submerged in the mud of craving and attachment, and are withered upon the dry land of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), having no place of refuge or destination.
Within the hostile village of the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*), they are unable to escape;
they have not encountered a guide capable of leading them across correctly.

Toward them, I should give rise to great compassion and, by the power of my roots of goodness, rescue and deliver them, so that they may reach the place of peace and security, be freed from all terrors, and dwell upon the jewel-island of all-encompassing wisdom.

"These sentient beings are deeply attached in their hearts; they abound in sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, and calamity; they are bound by hatred and love, fettered by the shackles of desire, and have entered the dense forest of ignorance within the triple world.
I should cause them to distance themselves from all attachments to the triple world and establish them in the unimpeded nirvana that is free from signs."

These sentient beings are deeply attached to "self" and "what belongs to self," dwelling within the nest-like caverns of the five aggregates and unable to emerge from them. They constantly follow the four inversions, rely upon the empty village of the six sense bases, are afflicted by the venomous snakes of the four great elements, and are slain by the bandits of the various afflictions; thus they undergo all these immeasurable sufferings.
I should cause them to leave behind all such attachments and abide in tranquility—that is, in the peace of nirvana, which severs all obstacles.

These sentient beings possess narrow and inferior minds; they delight in minor teachings and remain far removed from the unsurpassed, all-encompassing wisdom. Clinging greedily to the Lesser Vehicle, they are unable to aspire toward the Great Vehicle that leads beyond [suffering].
I should cause them to abide in a vast mind regarding the immeasurable and boundless dharmas of the Buddhas' path—namely, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
By thus conforming to the power of upholding the precepts, this bodhisattva is well able to extensively give rise to great compassion.

Abiding in the Ground Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), this bodhisattva beholds hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and makes offerings to them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life."
Toward all Buddhas they give rise to a mind of reverence and further undertake the ten paths of wholesome action; until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never lose them midway.

Because these bodhisattvas have remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, greed, and broken precepts for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they purely cultivate the merits of giving and upholding the precepts.
It is like pure gold: when refined with fire, all impurities are exhausted, and it becomes even more brilliant and pure.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: dwelling in the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), for hundreds of thousands, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*, because they have distanced themselves from the defilements of stinginess and breaking the precepts, they purely cultivate the merits of generosity and ethical discipline.
At that time, among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), their kind speech (*priyavāditā*) is predominant;
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is most eminent.
The other perfections are also all cultivated and gathered, increasing in accordance with each stage.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the second stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Stage Free from Defilement."

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), acting as a great Dharma King who extensively attains the power of the Dharma. Accomplished in the seven treasures, possessing strength and sovereignty, they are able to remove the stains of stinginess and greed and the breaking of precepts from all sentient beings.
Through skillful means, they cause sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action; they practice great giving that is inexhaustible.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—all such merits never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, and even the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."
"O Son of the Buddha!
If this bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life and practices with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they are then able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires.

Having attained the state of a renunciant, through diligent and vigorous practice, in a mere moment they attain a thousand samādhis, behold a thousand Buddhas, know the spiritual powers of a thousand Buddhas, can shake a thousand Buddha-worlds, can fly across a thousand Buddha-worlds, can illuminate a thousand Buddha-worlds, can teach and transform sentient beings in a thousand worlds, can maintain a lifespan for a thousand kalpas, can know the events of a thousand kalpas each in the past and future ages, can skillfully enter a thousand Dharma-gates, and can manifest a thousand bodies; in each of these bodies, they can manifest a thousand bodhisattvas as their retinue."
"If manifested through the sovereign power of vows, it would exceed this number by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, beyond all calculation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When a Bodhisattva enters the second stage, Their mind becomes supple and harmonious;..."
Capable of receiving non-negligence, Tranquil, truly unmixed,
and likewise free from greed and stinginess, Possessing all these supreme and great qualities,
Having attained these ten mental states, One enters the second stage.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they accomplish all meritorious virtues:
they always abstain from taking life and do not harm or injure any being;
they always abstain from stealing and likewise have no sexual misconduct.
One should refrain from double-tongued speech and lying, from harsh words and meaningless talk;
one should not give rise to greedy attachment toward the wealth and possessions of others,
nor cause distress to sentient beings, but should practice with a straightforward mind and hold right view.
Free from pride and arrogance, and likewise devoid of deceitful intent,
gentle and heedful, they uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.
All intense sufferings and afflictions— those of the hells and the animal realm— [they endure].
The bodies of hungry ghosts are ablaze; all arise from an evil mind.
Now I have forever departed from such evil matters;
I walk the path of truth, the wholesome dharma of tranquility.
From the human realm up to the Peak of Existence, all places where happiness is experienced,
and the bliss of meditative concentration and the Three Vehicles— all arise from the ten wholesome actions.
Having reflected thus, one’s mind should always remain free from negligence.
One personally maintains pure precepts and also teaches others to maintain them.
Observing all sentient beings everywhere undergoing various forms of suffering and affliction,
and having thus felt compassion for them, one gives rise to a heart of profound pity.
Ordinary beings are truly pitiable; Falling into various false views, their minds harbor much resentment, And they constantly delight in inciting disputes.
Ever craving the five desires, They greedily seek them without ever reaching satiety.
Arising from the causes and conditions of the three poisons, I should deliver these beings.
Deeply shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, they fall into the perilous path of birth and death;
they enter the great net of false views and are cast into the cage of the world.
Constantly beset by the thieves of Māra and destroyed by the afflictions (kleśa), these beings are truly pitiable; I should deliver and liberate them.
Submerged in the deep waters of affliction and tossed about by the four currents, they wander in saṃsāra.
Fully experiencing the immeasurable poisons of suffering within the three realms,
Dwelling in the deep nest of the five aggregates, one gives rise to the mind of "I" and "mine.
To deliver myself from this suffering, I shall diligently practice the Path.
Abandoning the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha, they give rise to inferior states of mind;
to cause them to abide in the great wisdom of the Buddha, they exert immeasurable diligence.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they accumulate immeasurable merit.
Having encountered the various Buddhas, one serves and makes offerings to them.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one's roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure,
just as fine, genuine gold is refined by the power of fire.
The sons of the Buddha dwelling on this stage often become universal monarchs (cakravartin kings),
causing all sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, they cultivate and accumulate all manner of merit and virtue.
May he save the world, enabling it to attain the ten powers of a Buddha.
If he wishes to renounce his royal throne, leave the household life, and practice the Way,
may he apply himself with diligent effort and enter into a thousand samādhis.
They behold a thousand Buddhas, making offerings and listening to their teachings;
dwelling on this stage, Bodhisattvas are able to manifest such deeds.
If, by the power of their vows, they manifest various supernatural feats, they display these miraculous events.
Having delivered sentient beings beyond measureless numbers,
for those who always diligently seek what is beneficial throughout all worlds,
this complete exposition of the second bhūmi is now concluded.
When the bodhisattvas heard of these inconceivable practices,
their hearts were filled with great joy and they paid immeasurable respect. At that moment,
from the midst of the sky, a rain of various famous flowers and incense fell.
Descending like clouds, they made offerings to Vajragarbha.
They all praised him, saying: "Excellent!
Well-spoken by you, O Great Being, who protects and upholds the practice of pure precepts."
Toward all sentient beings, he possesses a heart of profound compassion;
he expounds and explains these characteristics of the second stage.
The subtle and wondrous conduct of the Bodhisattva is truly without any discrepancy.
For these bodhisattvas, who are perfected in pure conduct and always seek what is beneficial for all sentient beings,
I have already fully expounded the second stage, the Stainless.
O you who are revered by devas and humans, please explain the third stage;
reveal well the functions of wisdom and the conduct practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Please speak of the merit of the practice of giving performed by these great beings.
Observing the precepts and practicing patience, Exerting diligence and cultivating meditative concentration,
Possessing wisdom and skillful means, As well as a heart of loving-kindness and compassion—
How should one practice these dharmas To purify the conduct of all Buddhas?
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva enters the third stage, with what kind of mind should they do so?"
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have purified the second stage and wish to attain the third stage, they should do so by means of ten kinds of profound resolve."
What are the ten? First, a pure mind;
second, a fierce and sharp mind;
3. The mind of revulsion;
4. The mind of detachment from desire;
5. The non-retrogressive mind;
Sixth, the firm mind;
seventh, the radiant and flourishing mind;
eighth, the insatiable mind.
9. The superior mind; 10.
The great mind. By means of these ten minds, the bodhisattva enters the third stage.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Radiance, they are able to contemplate all conditioned phenomena according to their true nature;
that is to say:

as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; as soon to perish, untrustworthy in character, neither arising nor ceasing, not coming from the past, not going to the future, and not abiding in the present.

When a bodhisattva thus contemplates the true nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they know that all dharmas are without action, without arising, without coming, and without going; yet sentient beings are bound by grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, as well as by hatred and attachment. These states do not persist or accumulate, nor is there a fixed place of birth for them;

rather, they are ignited by the fires of greed, anger, and delusion, increasing a great mass of suffering and affliction in future lives, lacking any real nature and being like illusions or transformations.
Having seen this, they become even more weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and proceed toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
These Bodhisattvas know that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable and immeasurable;

it possesses great power such that none can surpass it, it is free from mixed characteristics, it is without decay or affliction, and it can reach the great city of fearless security, saving immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and distress.

Thus perceiving and knowing that the Buddha's wisdom is immeasurable, and seeing that conditioned phenomena involve immeasurable suffering and affliction, one gives rise toward all sentient beings to ten further distinguished states of mind.

What are these ten? Sentient beings are pitiable; they are solitary and without rescue, impoverished and without refuge. The fire of the three poisons blazes unceasingly within them; they are imprisoned in the solid jail of the three realms of existence (trisaṃsāra). They dwell constantly in the forest of thorns of various afflictions (kleśa) and lack the power of right contemplation. Their desire and delight for wholesome dharmas are meager; having lost the Buddha’s sublime Dharma, they constantly follow the current of birth and death and stand in fear of nirvana.

When this bodhisattva sees sentient beings thus afflicted and distressed, he arouses great diligence, thinking: "I should rescue these sentient beings; I should liberate them; I should cause them to become pure; I should cause them to attain liberation; I should establish them in a wholesome state; I should cause them to dwell in peace; I should cause them to rejoice; I should cause them to know what is appropriate; I should cause them to attain crossing-over; I should cause their suffering to be extinguished."

"When a bodhisattva thus becomes weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), deeply contemplates sentient beings, and perceives the immeasurable benefits of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they immediately desire to perfect the wisdom of a Buddha to rescue and deliver sentient beings, diligently practicing the bodhisattva path. They reflect:

'These sentient beings have fallen into the midst of great suffering and various afflictions (*kleśa*); by what skillful means (*upāya*) can I extract and deliver them, so that they may dwell forever in ultimate bliss? "

One who immediately knows that they abide within the wisdom of unimpeded liberation can attain this very wisdom of unimpeded liberation; it is the wisdom of non-action that does not depart from the penetrating knowledge of all phenomena as they truly are.
From what, then, is such luminous wisdom obtained?
"You should know that this does not depart from the wisdom of certainty derived from extensive learning. He then further thought:
"What is the foundation of all Buddha-dharmas?"
"Not being separated from hearing the Dharma is the foundation.

Having understood this, the bodhisattva seeks the Dharma in every way, becoming increasingly diligent, listening and receiving it day and night without ever feeling weary or satisfied. He delights in the Dharma, loves the Dharma, relies on the Dharma, accords with the Dharma, fulfills the Dharma, masters the Dharma, brings the Dharma to its ultimate conclusion, takes refuge in the Dharma, seeks salvation in the Dharma, and practices in accordance with the Dharma.

When a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma through such skillful means, they do not begrudge any precious treasures and do not conceive thoughts of difficulty regarding these things; rather, they conceive thoughts of the rarity of encountering those who preach the Dharma.

For the sake of seeking the Dharma, there were no internal or external things he could not relinquish: kingdoms and subjects, mani-jewels and the seven treasures, elephants and horses, carriages and litters, various gems, necklaces, ornaments for the body, wives and concubines, sons and daughters, and even his own limbs, hands, and feet; he gave away his entire body without any sense of attachment or regret.

Furthermore, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should serve, honor, and provide offerings to the teacher of the Dharma with all one's heart, breaking down arrogance, self-conceit, and great pride, and being able to endure all evil and suffering.
Because they seek the Dharma deeply, if they obtain even a single phrase of the Dharma never heard before, it is superior to obtaining precious jewels filling the three-thousandfold world system;
and to hear a single verse is superior to dwelling for immeasurable eons in the positions of a wheel-turning sage king, Śakra Devānām Indra, or Brahmā Sahāmpati.
If someone comes to this bodhisattva and says:
"I possess a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha that can purify the bodhisattva path; if you can now enter a great pit of fire and undergo great suffering, I shall give it to you."
This bodhisattva reflects thus:

"For the sake of receiving even a single phrase of the Dharma, were the great trichiliocosm filled with raging fires, I would still cast myself down from the Brahma Heaven, let alone into a small fire;
I should seek the Dharma even at the cost of undergoing all the sufferings of every hell, let alone the various minor pains and afflictions of the human realm."

"For the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should give rise to such a mind; furthermore, regarding the Dharma as it has been heard, the mind should always find joy in it and be able to contemplate it correctly.
Having heard these teachings, the Bodhisattva subdues his mind and, in a secluded place, reflects thus:
"Only by practicing according to what has been taught does one attain the Buddha-dharma; to do so through mere verbal recitation is impossible."

Thus, the bodhisattva, having become detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna;

with the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, inwardly pure and with the mind focused on a single point, without directed or sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters the second dhyāna;

being detached from joy, dwelling in equanimity, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy," he enters the third dhyāna.

Having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and consists of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

This bodhisattva, by transcending all perceptions of form, by the cessation of all perceptions of sensory resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceives infinite space and thus enters the formless meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
transcending all perceptions of space, he perceives infinite consciousness and thus enters the formless meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending all perceptions of consciousness, one knows there is nothing and thus enters the formless meditative state of nothingness;
transcending the sphere of nothingness, one knows the security of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and thus enters the formless meditative state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one follows the practice of all dharmas without attachment or delight.
This bodhisattva, with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast and immeasurable—free from malice and free from harm—pervades the ten directions through the power of faith and understanding;
the same is true for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

This bodhisattva possesses supernatural powers by which he can shake the great earth; he can manifest many bodies from one body and one body from many bodies; he appears and then vanishes, passing through stone walls as if traveling through empty space;
he moves cross-legged through the air like a flying bird; he walks upon water as if on land and enters the earth as if it were water;
and his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire.
With the majestic power of the sun and moon, he is able to touch and stroke them with his hand; his physical strength is sovereign, reaching even as far as the Brahma world.
This Bodhisattva possesses the purified divine ear, which surpasses that of gods and humans, hearing all sounds of humans and devas, whether distant or near.
With the knowledge of others' minds, this bodhisattva knows the minds of others as they truly are: he knows a mind of desire as a mind of desire;
he knows a mind free from desire as a mind free from desire;
and he knows a mind free from desire, a mind of hatred, and a mind free from hatred as they truly are.
A mind of delusion and a mind free from delusion;
a defiled mind and a mind free from defilement;
a narrow mind and a vast mind.
A broad mind and a narrow mind;
a distracted mind and an undistracted mind;
a concentrated mind and an unconcentrated mind;
The bound mind and the liberated mind;
the surpassable mind and the unsurpassable mind;
knowing as they truly are the surpassable mind and the unsurpassable mind.
This bodhisattva recollects and knows his past lives and all places of birth: one life, two lives, up to hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, and nayutas of lives;

one eon, two eons, up to hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, and nayutas of eons. Within those eons, he can fully recollect and know the immeasurable cycles of formation and destruction, as well as all the causes and conditions experienced throughout those eons: "I was born in that place, with such a lineage, such a name, such food and drink, such suffering and joy, and such a long duration of stay;
I died there and was born here."
Dying here and being born there—such various matters he is able to recollect and know.

This Bodhisattva’s divine eye is pure, surpassing the eyes of devas and humans; he sees all sentient beings dying here and being born there, their forms and colors as beautiful or ugly, their poverty or nobility, their wealth or status, and their departure for good or evil realms, receiving retribution according to their karma—all he knows exactly as it is.
That is to say:

these sentient beings, having accomplished evil karma of body, evil karma of speech, and evil karma of mind, having opposed the noble ones and accepted the teachings of false views, fall into the evil realms at the dissolution of the body after death due to the causes and conditions of the karmic offenses they have produced.

These sentient beings, having accomplished good karma of body, good karma of speech, and good karma of mind, not opposing the noble ones and faithfully accepting right view, are born in a favorable realm at the dissolution of the body after death due to the causes and conditions of the wholesome karma they have performed.
This bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis without being reborn in accordance with them;
yet, in places conducive to the factors of enlightenment,
they are able to be born therein by the power of their vows.

"This Bodhisattva, dwelling in the Stage of Radiance (Prabhākari-bhūmi), beholds hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; he reverently makes offerings to them, honoring and praising them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines; he draws near to these Buddhas, listens to and receives their teachings, and practices according to what has been taught."
This bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, existing only through the conjunction of various conditions;

throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, the accumulated bonds of desire, the bonds of existence, and the bonds of ignorance all become attenuated and are no longer further accumulated.
Because they are no longer accumulated, he cuts off wrong greed, wrong hatred, and wrong delusion.

Just as genuine gold, when refined and processed by a skilled smith, becomes increasingly exquisite and its radiance becomes doubly superior, so too is it with the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*):
because they do not accumulate the three fetters, they sever perverse greed, perverse hatred, and perverse delusion, and all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.

This bodhisattva’s mind of patience, his exquisite mind, his indestructible mind, his unshakable mind, his unpolluted mind, his mind free from pride and dejection, his mind that expects no reward for anything he does, his mind that gives rise to a sense of gratitude when others do even a small thing for him, his non-deceptive mind, and his unadulterated mind become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure.
At that time, among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the Bodhisattva’s loving speech (*priyavāditā*) and beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) are particularly predominant;

among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) are especially superior; and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) become increasingly clear and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattvas’ third stage, the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently manifest as Śakra Devendra; with sharp and keen wisdom, they employ skillful means to transform sentient beings, causing them to abandon sensual desire.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and so on, up to being never apart from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."
If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, they can, in a single moment, attain one hundred thousand samādhis, and even manifest a retinue of one hundred thousand bodhisattvas.

"If, by the power of vows and the mastery of supernormal powers, it were to exceed this number, it could not be calculated or known even in several hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva’s profound faith and resolve Can attain the third stage."
With a mind that is pure and sharp, Free from attachment and never regressing,
Firmly enduring and never weary, Fully endowed with these supreme qualities—
By means of such a mind, One attains entry into the third stage.
The wise one abiding on the Ground of Radiance contemplates conditioned phenomena as impure,
impermanent, and suffering; they possess the characteristics of selflessness and decay,
lacking any stable nature, and perish momentarily in every instant before long.
Reflecting thus, one knows that there is no characteristic of coming or going.
One sees all conditioned phenomena as like a disease, like an abscess or a wound;
bound by the fetters of affectionate craving, they give rise to all manner of sorrow, lamentation, and suffering.
But being burned by the fierce fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
from beginningless time until now, they have blazed forth without ceasing.
At that moment, he conceived a sense of weary detachment toward everything within the three realms.
Contemning conditioned phenomena, their minds have no attachment.
They seek only the wisdom of all Buddhas— immeasurable, boundless,
profound and inconceivable, pure and free from all suffering.
Having thus seen the Buddha’s wisdom and being free from all suffering and affliction,
he takes pity on all sentient beings who are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom;
their fires of the three poisons burn constantly, and they have no one to protect them.
Falling into the midst of hell, they are tormented by immeasurable suffering.
The heedless worldlings are submerged in the ocean of afflictions;
blind and dark, they see nothing and lose the jewels of the Buddha-dharma.
Constantly following the flow of birth and death, they fear what is not to be feared;
for these sentient beings, I shall diligently strive to deliver them.
With vigor I seek wisdom, acting as one who brings benefit to all.
Reflecting on what skillful means might provide protection and refuge, I saw that only the Tathāgatas possess profound, wondrous, and unimpeded wisdom.
What is the cause of this wisdom? It arises from the wisdom born of non-active cultivation.
Reflection is wisdom; it arises from extensive learning.
Having deliberated in this way, one should diligently seek the Dharma of extensive learning.
Constantly persevering day and night, one listens and receives it without weariness.
One should read, recite, and delight in the Dharma, holding the Dharma alone as most precious.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should give away all manner of rare jewels,
as well as beloved wives and children and all one's attendants at will.
Kingdoms and cities, the necessities of life and all manner of precious things,
he joyfully bestowed as gifts, his heart free from any attachment or regret.
His head, eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, his teeth, hands, and feet— [he gave them all].
To give away one’s limbs, joints, body, flesh, and blood, as well as the heart,
liver, marrow, and brain— to bestow such things upon others is not yet considered difficult;
but to hear the True Dharma is what is truly rare.
Suppose there were a person who said to this bodhisattva:
"If you can now enter this great mass of fierce fire,
then I shall give to you the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas."
Having heard this, they immediately rejoice and cast themselves down without any doubt.
Even if the three thousandfold world-system were filled with great fires,
from the summit of Mount Sumeru down to the Brahma-world, it would not be considered difficult.
If one seeks even a single phrase of the Dharma taught by all Buddhas to save beings from suffering and affliction, it is extremely difficult to obtain.
From the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of the Buddha-way, [it is not easy].
Throughout this entire interval, for as many kalpas as there are,
I have endured the sufferings of Avīci hell for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
how much more so, then, the minor sufferings and afflictions of the human world?
By means of the causal condition of listening to the Dharma, one is able to attain right mindfulness;
by means of the causal condition of right mindfulness, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations,
profound and wondrous samādhis, as well as the matters of the five supernormal powers.
They are all able to arise in succession, yet with mastery they do not follow along with their arising.
Abiding in this stage, the Bodhisattva, with a resolute mind,
is able to make extensive offerings to the Buddhas and listen to the teachings they proclaim.
Having severed wrong desire, hatred, and delusion, all fetters become thin and faint;
like refined and tempered gold, it is brought into perfect harmony.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the treasury of merit is filled to overflowing.
He frequently acted as the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, exercising sovereign power over sensual desires.
Out of love for the Buddha’s merit, he transformed and guided immeasurable multitudes,
enabling them all to abide within the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able, with a supple mind,
to practice diligence with vigor, thereby attaining hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
They behold hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, their bodies adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Their minds become increasingly fierce and sharp; their power of aspiration is preeminent.
For the sake of all sentient beings, those who diligently seek what is beneficial explain this in detail:
thus ends the third stage, the Luminous Ground (Prabhākārī-bhūmi).
When the sons of the Buddha heard this discourse on the meaning of the practices of these stages—
profound, wondrous, and immeasurable— their hearts were filled with great joy.
They scattered various famous flowers and incense as an offering to the Tathāgata.
The earth and the waters of the great ocean all shook violently;
the celestial maidens and their attendants, from the midst of the sky above,
together with subtle and wondrous voices, sang praises of this supreme Dharma.
The King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, having heard this, was filled with great joy;
he rained down mani jewels, scattering them over the Buddha,
and leaping for joy, he uttered words of praise:
“Excellent is the appearance of the Buddha in the world; the treasury of merit has been spread abroad, bringing benefit to us.
Now that we have heard this exposition on the meaning of the bodhisattva stages and practices—something difficult to hear even in hundreds of thousands of eons—we have finally heard it.”
"May you further explain the subsequent stages, benefiting all devas and humans;
they all rejoice and desire to hear the meaning of the practices for attaining these stages.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra.
He again entreated Vajragarbha:
"I pray that you will explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the practices leading up to the fourth stage.
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha then spoke to Bodhisattva Vimukticandra:
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have purified the third stage and wish to attain the fourth stage, they should do so by means of ten gateways of the light of Dharma (dharmāloka-mukha). What are these ten?
First, observing the realm of sentient beings;
second, observing the realm of phenomena;
third, observing the realm of worlds.
4. Contemplating the element of space;
5. Contemplating the element of consciousness;
6. Contemplating the realm of desire;
7. Contemplating the realm of form;
8. Contemplating the formless realm;
9. Contemplating the realm of superior faith and resolve;
10. Contemplating the Great Mind Realm.
By means of these ten gates of the illumination of dharmas (*dharmāloka-mukha*), the bodhisattva enters the fourth stage.

When the bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Blazing Flames (*arcismatī-bhūmi*), they gain increased power within the family of the Tathāgatas; because they have attained the internal dharma, they possess ten kinds of knowledge.
What are the ten? First, the mind does not regress;
second, one attains indestructible faith within the Three Jewels, which is pure and ultimate.
Third, practicing the contemplation of arising and ceasing;
fourth, practicing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
fifth, constantly practicing the contemplation of the formation and destruction of the world.
Sixth, birth arises due to the causal conditions of the cultivation of karma;
seventh, cultivating the distinctions between the gates of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through discernment;
eighth, cultivating the distinctions among the karmas of sentient beings.
Ninth, the cultivation of the distinctions between the prior limit and the posterior limit;
tenth, the cultivation of the practice of constant cessation and non-abiding in the present.
These ten wisdom-minds give rise to birth in the Buddha-family and result in the attainment of sovereign power.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this fourth stage, he contemplates the body internally as a body, practicing with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow;
he contemplates the body externally as a body, practicing with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow.”
One contemplates the body internally and externally, observing the body with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow;
one contemplates internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings;
and internal mind, external mind, and both internal and external mind.
Contemplating internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena according to the Dharma, he is diligent and single-minded, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
This Bodhisattva, for the sake of preventing the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, arouses his mind and exerts right effort with diligent vigor;
for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, he arouses his mind and exerts right effort with diligent vigor.
For the sake of producing all wholesome dharmas not yet produced, one exerts diligent effort, arouses the mind, and practices correctly;
for the sake of maintaining, not losing, cultivating to fulfillment, and increasing all wholesome dharmas already produced, one exerts diligent effort, arouses the mind, and practices correctly.
This bodhisattva practices the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): achieving the mental formation of abandonment through the concentration of desire, he cultivates the base of psychic power;
relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, he dedicates it toward *nirvāṇa*.
Achieving the mental formation of abandonment through the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of wisdom, he cultivates the base of psychic power.
Relying on revulsion, detachment, and cessation, they dedicate themselves toward nirvāṇa.

These bodhisattvas cultivate the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom, relying on revulsion, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating them toward nirvāṇa.

This bodhisattva cultivates the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom; relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, they dedicate these toward nirvana.

This bodhisattva cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; relying upon disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, they dedicate these toward nirvana.

This bodhisattva practices right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, they dedicate these toward nirvana.
This bodhisattva practices because they do not abandon the mind [set on] sentient beings, because they are aided by their original vows,
because great compassion is their foremost priority,
and because they practice in union with great loving-kindness.
To encompass all-knowledge;
to adorn the Buddha-lands;
and to be endowed with the Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.
They act for the sake of perfecting their voice;
for the sake of conforming to the Buddha’s profound liberation;
and for the sake of contemplating the skillful means of great wisdom.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas dwell on the Blazing Ground (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), they abandon all attachment to the view of a self-body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), as well as attachment to a self, attachment to a sentient being;
and attachment to a person, a life-sustainer, a knower, or a viewer."

That which arises from the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements—its bending and stretching, its contraction and expansion, its emergence and disappearance; the pursuit of the mind’s activities and attachments, the cherishing of what is seen, and that which serves as a refuge or an island—all these are utterly extinguished.

This bodhisattva becomes increasingly diligent; through the factors conducive to enlightenment born of wisdom and skillful means, as he practices them, his mind becomes increasingly supple, capable and useful, and free from weariness.
He seeks ever higher dharmas, increases his wisdom, rescues all the world, follows his teachers, respectfully receives their instructions, and acts according to what they have taught.
At that time, this bodhisattva knows kindness and knows how to repay it; his mind becomes increasingly harmonious and gentle, dwelling in peace and happiness with others;
he possesses a straightforward mind and a supple mind, free from all crookedness;
he practices the conduct of right concentration, devoid of arrogance.

Following the instructions and grasping the intention of the speaker, one thus becomes endowed with a virtuous mind, a gentle mind, a tranquil mind, and a patient mind; purifying all dharmas of the stages, one contemplates and practices them.

At that time, this bodhisattva accomplishes irreversible diligence, unrelenting diligence, unstained diligence, indestructible diligence, tireless diligence, vast diligence, boundless diligence, fierce and sharp diligence, diligence equal to the unequaled, and diligence that rescues all sentient beings.

As this bodhisattva cultivates such diligence, their straightforward mind becomes pure; they do not lose their profound resolve, and their faith and understanding become sharp and keen. Their roots of goodness increase, and they remain far removed from worldly defilements and lack of faith, all of which have been completely extinguished. Free from doubt and regret, these qualities are fully present before them.
Regarding the matters of great faith and understanding toward all Buddhas, they never grow weary or abandon them; they naturally delight in practice, and an immeasurable mind is constantly manifest.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in the fourth stage, the Radiant (*Arciṣmatī*), they are able to see hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, whom they honor, serve, revere, and praise. They provide them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines; they draw near to these Buddhas, listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion, and are able to faithfully accept, uphold, and practice it.

Having mostly gone forth from home to cultivate the Way in the presence of these Buddhas, this Bodhisattva’s joyful mind and profound mind become pure; their faith and understanding become impartial and increasingly clear. Abiding for many kalpas, their roots of goodness become ever more excellent throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
For example, just as ornaments made of the finest refined gold cannot be matched by other gold,
so too, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Radiance (*arcismatī*), their roots of goodness increase further, such that they cannot be equaled by bodhisattvas on the lower stages.

For example, just as a mani jewel has pure radiance that can illuminate the four directions, such that other jewels cannot equal it, and its light is not extinguished even when drenched by water or rain;
so too, when a bodhisattva dwells on the Stage of Blazing (Arciṣmatī), they cannot be equaled by bodhisattvas of the lower stages, and all māras and afflictions (kleśa) cannot destroy them.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the fourth stage of the bodhisattva, the Stage of Blazing Radiance (*Arciṣmatī*).
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently manifest as the King of the Suyāma Heaven to teach and transform sentient beings, thereby destroying the notion of a self.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."
If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, they can, in a mere moment, attain ten billion samādhis, and even manifest ten billion bodhisattvas as their retinue.
"If manifested through the sovereign power of vows, it exceeds this number by several hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of eons, such that it cannot be calculated or known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When all Bodhisattvas have fully perfected And cultivated the Stage of Radiance,..."
Observing all sentient beings, phenomena, and the world,
as well as space, consciousness, desire, and form, and through the superior faith and understanding of the formless realm—
because their great mind is pure— they attain entry into the fourth stage.
Thus, within the family of the Tathāgata, they increase and attain power;
they do not regress from the Buddha-way, and their faith in the Triple Gem is indestructible.
Contemplating the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, they see that all are originally empty.
Knowing the formation and destruction of the world arises from karma,
And that the differences among sentient beings' karma result in the distinction between birth-and-death and nirvāṇa;
Contemplating the prior and posterior limits of phenomena, One always extinguishes them and does not dwell in signs.
When the great bodhisattvas and others have attained such a Dharma as this,
out of compassion for all sentient beings, they practice the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—
the four foundations of mindfulness, both internal and external— relying upon wearying detachment.
Relying likewise upon tranquility, one dedicates oneself toward nirvāṇa.
By eliminating unwholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas increase;
practicing the four right efforts and cultivating the four bases of power.
Practicing the five faculties and cultivating the five powers,
Cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment and practicing the eightfold noble path—
By cultivating such dharmas as these, it is all for the sake of sentient beings.
Assisted by his original vows, with a heart of compassion as his foremost guide,
he strives to encompass all-encompassing wisdom and adorns the buddha-fields.
He brings to fulfillment the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
All sounds and speech, the profound and wondrous Dharma,
as well as unimpeded liberation and great wisdom and skillful means—
[these arise] from the view of a self as the foremost, along with the sixty-two views and the like.
Sentient beings, self, person, life-span, and the knower—
those objects of craving and attachment within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—
are all entirely extinguished and abandoned upon attaining this fourth stage.
Having severed all afflictions and karma, their minds become increasingly bright and pure;
whatever wholesome deeds they perform, they do them all for the sake of saving the world.
With a supple and gentle mind, the Bodhisattva is never heedless.
One should employ a straightforward mind to seek the welfare of sentient beings.
Such pursuits as these are all for the sake of the unsurpassed path and the station of great wisdom, in order to benefit the world.
With a profound mind, they honor and support their teachers; they delight in practicing according to the teachings;
being those who recognize kindness and repay it, they are easy to transform and free from resentment.
Without crooked or devious minds, they dwell together in harmony and joy.
Cultivating such dharmas with diligence and without regression,
the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, not losing their profound and upright mind.
With a pure mind and resolute faith, they cause all roots of goodness to increase.
All the defilements and turbidities of the world, such as lack of faith, doubt, and regret— all such dharmas are entirely eliminated.
The Bodhisattvas dwelling in this fourth stage, the Radiant Ground (Arciṣmatī), [attain these].
Having encountered immeasurable Buddhas, he receives and accepts the teachings they proclaim.
Under these Buddhas, his renunciation of the world is firm and cannot be thwarted;
like an ornament of pure gold, it cannot be matched by other metals.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their profound mind of all merits,
their wisdom, and their skillful means constitute the pure path of practice.
Even ten billion māras cannot destroy them.
Like a truly wondrous, bright pearl, which is not ruined by water or rain,
the Bodhisattva dwelling on this stage is honored by gods and humans;
often acting as a King of Yāma, he is able to overturn all false views.
All the various wholesome deeds performed are for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom;
their minds are always firm and steadfast, unable to be moved or turned aside.
If one practices with diligent vigor, one will attain ten billion samādhis.
One can see ten billion Buddhas, yet through the power of vows, it exceeds even this.
Thus, the fourth stage, pure and named "Blazing," for those possessed of immeasurable merit and wisdom, has now been fully explained.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-four;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
When the bodhisattvas heard this, the dharma-practices of the fourth stage,
their hearts were filled with joy, and they leaped for joy beyond measure.
A rain of various precious flowers fell, scattering like snow;
all praised him, saying, "Excellent! to the Great Being Vajragarbha.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, together with his retinue, [did likewise].
In the space above, their hearts were filled with great joy.
They emitted various wondrous radiances and performed all manner of celestial music,
singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues as well as those of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The various celestial maidens, each with a pure and wondrous voice,
praised the Buddha in unison, speaking these words: “World-Honored One,
after a long time has passed, you have fulfilled the vows sought through diligent toil.
The unsurpassed, true, and perfect path—only now has it finally been attained.
One who brings benefit to devas and humans has, after a long time, been encountered;
Śākyamuni Buddha has now arrived at the celestial palace.
Since time immemorial, the ocean-like signs have only now begun to stir;
after immeasurable eons since antiquity, he now emits this wondrous light.
Sentient beings, having wandered for a long time, have now finally attained peace and happiness.
Only after a long time have I finally been able to hear The virtuous voice of Great Compassion.
Having crossed to the shore of all merits, After a vast eon, I have now encountered it.
The Holy King is able to completely shatter My mind of pride and the like.
Peerless and worthy of veneration, you now receive this offering;
you can open the path to the heavens and enable one to attain all-knowledge.
The World-Honored One is utterly pure, as immeasurable as space.
Untainted by worldly dharmas, like a lotus in the water;
dwelling in the world most exalted, like Mount Sumeru, the great king of mountains,
in the midst of the vast ocean— for this reason, I joyfully prostrate.
Thus these goddesses, each with various wondrous voices,
having finished their reverent songs of praise, gazed upon the Buddha in silence.
Then Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"Please explain the causes and conditions for attaining the fifth stage and its characteristics.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva spoke to Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already fulfilled the fourth stage and wishes to attain the fifth stage, they should do so by means of ten kinds of impartial minds. What are these ten?
1. The equality of the Buddha-dharma of the past;
2. The equality of the Buddha-dharma of the future;
3. The equality of the Buddha-dharma of the present.
4. Equality of purity of ethical discipline;
5. Equality of purity of mind;
6. Equality of purity through the removal of views, doubt, and regret;
7. The equality of purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path;
8. The equality of purity regarding knowledge, conduct, and vision;
9. The equality of purity regarding the increasingly superior development of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
10. Purity of equality in transforming sentient beings.
By means of these ten kinds of equal mind, the bodhisattva enters the fifth stage.

Dwelling in the stage of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), because he skillfully cultivates the dharmas of enlightenment, because his profound mind is pure, and because he seeks the ever-surpassing path, he is then able to attain Buddhahood.

Because this bodhisattva has attained the power of great vows; because his heart of compassion does not abandon any being; because he has attained the power of the path of mindfulness and wisdom; because he practices merit and wisdom without ceasing; because he gives rise to skillful means; because he desires to attain the superior path and the clear contemplation of the higher stages; because he is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas; and because he has generated a mind of concentration that never regresses, he knows as they truly are the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

This bodhisattva skillfully knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), skillfully knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of distinctions (*viśeṣa-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of expression (*deśanā-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of origination (*utpatti-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of entering the path (*mārgapraveśa-satya*), and skillfully knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages and the arising of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Because the Bodhisattva causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their inclinations, he knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
because he has reached the ultimate culmination of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), he knows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
and because he discerns the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena, he knows the truth of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-satya).
Because all phenomena are distinct from one another, one knows the truth of differentiation;
because one discerns the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one knows the truth of designation;
and because of the suffering and affliction of body and mind, one knows the truth of suffering.
Because the continuity of birth in the various realms of existence is perceived, one knows the Truth of Origination;
because all afflictions are ultimately extinguished, one knows the Truth of Cessation;
and because one reaches the dharma of non-duality, one knows the Truth of the Path.
By means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one knows the truth of the Tathāgata’s wisdom because one understands the sequential accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages;
by the power of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), one knows that this is not the attainment of the wisdom of the inexhaustible truth.

In this way, by means of the knowledge of these truths, the bodhisattva knows all conditioned phenomena as they truly are: as false and deceptive, as merely persisting for a moment, and as deluding ordinary people;
at that time, the bodhisattva’s great compassion toward sentient beings becomes even more eminent, and the light of great loving-kindness arises.

Having attained such power of wisdom, they do not abandon any sentient beings and constantly seek the wisdom of the Buddha. They contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as they truly are, from their prior limit to their subsequent limit. They know that sentient beings arise from ignorance and craving regarding the prior limit, transmigrating through birth and death, unable to move or depart from the abode of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), thereby increasing the mass of suffering and affliction. Within this, there is no self, no mine, no sentient being, no person, no knower, and no life-principle; the same applies to the subsequent limit.
Although there is thus nothing at all, out of delusion and attachment, they do not know whether there is ultimately an exit or no exit.
Furthermore, he reflects:

"Ordinary worldlings and sentient beings are truly pitiable; because of ignorance and delusion, they possess immeasurable bodies that have perished, are now perishing, and will continue to perish. Despite such cycles of birth and death, they cannot conceive a sense of weary detachment toward the body, but instead further increase the wheel of suffering within the five realms of existence. Drifting on the waters of birth and death, they cannot find a way back;
taking refuge in the house of the five aggregates, they are unable to abandon them."

They do not know how to fear the four great poisonous snakes; they cannot extract the arrows of pride and false views; they cannot extinguish the fires of greed, anger, and delusion; they cannot shatter the darkness of ignorance and folly; they cannot dry up the great ocean of craving and attachment; they do not seek the Great Holy Guide endowed with the Ten Powers, but instead constantly follow the will of Māra within the city of saṃsāra, perpetually driven by various evil thoughts and discursive reflections.

For these sentient beings who are thus afflicted, destitute, and solitary—having no savior, no refuge, and no one to show them the ultimate path—I alone, without equal companion, shall cultivate and accumulate merit and wisdom; by means of these provisions, I shall cause these sentient beings to abide in ultimate purity, even until they attain the power of unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena.

Reflecting in this way, one generates the power of wisdom from right contemplation and makes a vow that all roots of goodness performed shall be for the sake of delivering all sentient beings; for the sake of seeking peace and happiness for all sentient beings; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; for the sake of liberating all sentient beings; for the sake of ensuring all sentient beings are free from suffering and affliction; for the sake of ensuring all sentient beings are free from harshness and evil; for the sake of purifying the minds of all sentient beings; for the sake of taming all sentient beings; and for the sake of extinguishing all the sorrows and sufferings of sentient beings and fulfilling their aspirations.
When this bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), because they do not forget any dharmas, they are called "one who possesses mindfulness";
because their wisdom is definitive, they are called "one who possesses knowledge";
and because they know the sequence of the meaning of the scriptures, they are called "one who possesses the Way."
Because they protect themselves and protect others, they are called those possessed of shame and remorse;
because they do not abandon the upholding of the precepts, they are called those of firm resolve;
because they skillfully contemplate what is possible and what is impossible, they are called awakened ones.
Because they do not follow others, they are called those who follow wisdom;
because they skillfully discern the meaning of the chapters and phrases of all dharmas, they are called those who follow insight;
because they skillfully cultivate meditative concentration, they are called those who have attained supernormal powers.
Because they act in accordance with worldly dharmas, they are called those who possess skillful means;
because they skillfully accumulate the provisions of merit, they are called those who are never satiated;
because they constantly seek the causes and conditions for wisdom, they are called those who do not abandon [their practice].
Because they have accumulated the causes and conditions of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they are called those who are untiring;
because they always maintain right mindfulness, they are called those who are far removed from breaking the precepts;
because they seek with a profound mind the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities, they are called those who constantly keep the Buddha-dharma in mind.
Because they constantly cause sentient beings to leave evil and cultivate goodness, they are called "those who adorn the Buddha-land";
because they plant various merits to adorn the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, they are called "those who perform various wholesome deeds";
because they seek to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind, they are called "those who always practice diligence."
Because he makes offerings to all Bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma, he is called "One Who Delights in Great Reverence";
because his mind is unimpeded within the skillful means of all Bodhisattvas, he is called "One Whose Mind is Unobstructed";
and because he constantly delights in teaching and transforming sentient beings, he is called "One Who Day and Night Remains Far Removed from Other Minds."

"When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they transform sentient beings through the giving of material gifts; they also transform sentient beings through kind words, beneficial actions, and cooperation.

Furthermore, they transform sentient beings by manifesting a physical body; they transform sentient beings by preaching the Dharma; they transform sentient beings by demonstrating the conduct of bodhisattvas; they transform sentient beings by demonstrating the great deeds of the Buddhas; they transform sentient beings by demonstrating the faults and evils of birth and death; and they transform sentient beings by demonstrating the benefits of the wisdom of all Buddhas."
The Bodhisattva practices in this way, employing great supernormal powers and various causes, conditions, and skillful means to transform sentient beings.

Although this Bodhisattva uses these various causes, conditions, and skillful means, their mind remains constantly fixed on the Buddha; they do not lose their roots of goodness and further constantly seek ever-superior dharmas for the benefit of sentient beings.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this bodhisattva understands all worldly scriptures, arts, literature, and mathematics;
the various natures of metals and stones; medical prescriptions for treating diseases such as consumption, leprosy, demonic possession, and sorcery;
and [the skills of] music, song, dance, comedy, entertainment, and the governance of kingdoms.
...cities, walls, villages, houses, gardens, groves, ponds, and pavilions;
flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, conch shell, and agate;
he displays various hoards of treasures, as well as the sun, the moon, the five planets, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and divines their auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Regarding earthquakes, ominous dreams, and various physical signs within the body: through generosity and ethical discipline, one subdues the mind;
through meditative concentration, supernormal powers, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments, one remains free from all disturbances.
Out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of establishing them in peace, such dharmas are manifested to lead them into [the path].
Regarding the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddha:

when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), they encounter hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, whom they honor, provide for, respect, and praise with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines; they draw near to hear the Dharma, and having heard the Dharma, they leave the household life to become Dharma-preachers, benefiting others through their preaching. They attain the Samādhi of Increasing Superiority in Learning, which remains unlost even after the passing of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, and all their merits and roots of goodness become increasingly brilliant and pure.
For example, when refined gold or mother-of-pearl is polished and burnished, its radiance becomes increasingly superior.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, by the power of skillful means and wisdom, their meritorious roots become increasingly pure, bright, and excellent, such that the lower stages cannot equal them.
Furthermore, it is like the sun, moon, stars, and the celestial palaces of the various devas, which the wind sustains and causes to move without ever losing their proper course.

Thus, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Difficult Victory (*sudurjayā*), because of their skillful contemplation, their roots of merit and goodness become increasingly bright and pure; yet they do not realize [the ultimate fruit], nor do they swiftly attain the unsurpassed path.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Difficult-to-Conquer Ground (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this ground, they frequently become a king of the Tuṣita Heaven, possessing sharp and keen faculties, capable of completely subduing all externalists and their activities. In their practice of giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation, they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and so on, up to never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."
"O Son of the Buddha!
If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, in a mere moment they will attain ten billion samādhis, and even be able to manifest ten billion bodhisattvas as their retinue."

"If, by means of the power of vows and sovereign supernormal abilities, one were to continue for even more than this number—several hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When the Bodhisattvas have fully perfected The practices and dharmas of the fourth stage,"
Contemplating the Buddhas of the three periods of time, purifying the mind through the precepts and removing doubt and regret,
knowing the path and what is not the path, and transforming sentient beings toward Bodhi—
through such impartial observation, one enters the fifth stage.
The four foundations of mindfulness are the bow; faith and the five faculties are the arrows;
the four right efforts are the horses; the four bases of power are the chariot;
and the five powers are the armor—thus one destroys the thieves of all afflictions.
Valiant and non-retrogressive, they enter directly into the fifth stage.
With shame and remorse as their stainless raiment, pure precepts as their incense,
the seven factors of enlightenment as their flower garlands, and meditative concentration as their unguent.
With wisdom and skillful means, adorned by various forms of mindfulness,
one thus gains entry into the grove of dhāraṇīs.
Taking the four bases of power as feet and right mindfulness as the head and neck,
With eyes of compassion, clarity, and purity, With wisdom as its sharp fangs,
Roaring the lion’s roar of emptiness and non-self, It destroys the thieves of all afflictions.
Such a lion among men can enter the fifth stage.
This Bodhisattva, having already attained and abiding in the fifth stage,
further cultivates the most excellent and pure dharmas; for the sake of the Buddha-way alone,
they constantly practice a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, never once feeling weary or fatigued.
Constantly practicing these, the dharmas of the fifth stage,
one deeply accumulates the two provisions of merit and wisdom;
through various powers of skillful means, one clearly contemplates the dharmas of the higher stages.
Constantly protected by the Buddha, one attains mindfulness and wisdom;
through successive skillful contemplation, one knows the truths as they truly are:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the foremost matters regarding the nature of the world.
Explaining the distinctions of arising, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is non-arising;
thus observing the truths, the mind becomes subtle and pure.
Although one has not yet attained unobstructed liberation, [one proceeds].
Because they possess wisdom and the power of faith, they surpass all the worldly forms of knowledge.
Thus observing the truths, they fully understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Deceptive and unreal, they possess not a single mark of solidity.
Yet, having attained a portion of the compassionate radiance of all Buddhas,
for the sake of all sentient beings, one seeks the Buddha-wisdom with single-minded devotion.
Knowing the sequence of conditioned phenomena, [he sees that] sentient beings are most pitiable;
fallen into the darkness of ignorance, they are bound by the causal conditions of craving.
This Bodhisattva is able to extinguish the suffering and affliction of the world.
Knowing that phenomena have no life-span, they are like grass, trees, and the like.
Sentient beings always [perceive] through duality;
due to the causes and conditions of afflictions, they come from past lives, and so it is for future lives as well.
Their continuity remains unbroken, and they cannot reach the end of suffering;
feeling compassion for them in this state, I shall deliver and liberate them.
Unable to emerge from the five aggregates, they do not fear the harm of the four great elements.
Not extracting the arrows of various perversions, not extinguishing the fires of the three poisons,
and not removing the darkness of ignorance, they fall into the great ocean of craving;
they lack the eye of wisdom because they have departed from the Great Teacher.
Having understood these matters, one increases one's diligent effort all the more;
whatever actions or undertakings one performs, they are all for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Constantly abiding in right mindfulness and wisdom, possessing the Path, and endowed with shame and remorse.
With a firm mind, awakening follows wisdom, Which further causes them to increase.
Cultivating merit and wisdom without weariness, Maintaining the precepts without weakness,
Seeking extensive learning without fatigue, One rightly cultivates the purification of Buddha-lands.
The various marks, signs, and voices, And the causes and conditions thereof, are never satiated;
All the various wholesome deeds performed Are solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
For the sake of benefiting the world, He composed scriptures and other works.
Metals and stones, medicinal formulas, songs, dances, and jesting;
halls, pavilions, and gardens; garments and various foods and drinks;
he displays these as diverse heaps of jewels to cause the multitude to rejoice.
Divining the sun, moon, five planets, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions;
the signs of earthquakes and their auspicious or inauspicious omens; dream books and various strange occurrences;
the practice of giving and pure precepts; and the cultivation of meditative concentration through detachment from desire.
With the four immeasurables and supernormal powers, For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world;
The Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom, Having attained this difficult-to-conquer stage,
Makes offerings to ten trillion Buddhas And listens to the Dharma from those Buddhas.
All the roots of goodness one has cultivated become entirely bright and pure,
just as a carnelian gem is polished with genuine gold. Like a precious palace,
it is sustained by the wind so that its nature is never lost.
Untainted by worldly dharmas, like a lotus in the water,
the Bodhisattva dwelling on this stage frequently becomes a King of Tuṣita;
his faculties become increasingly sharp and powerful, and he shatters the views of all non-Buddhists.
All the various wholesome deeds performed are for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom;
having attained the Buddha’s powers and fearlessness, they are able to deliver all sentient beings.
This Bodhisattva diligently cultivates this ever-surpassing power of diligence.
They are immediately able to attain ten billion profound and wondrous samādhis;
they make offerings to ten billion Buddhas and shake ten billion worlds.
According to the power of their vows, these numbers exceed the measure of the infinite.
Thus, the fifth stage, with its various skillful means,
has been fully explained according to the Dharma by the Great Being of supreme wisdom.
Having heard this exposition of the characteristics of the higher stages, the bodhisattvas [rejoiced].
Abiding in the midst of space, they rained down a multitude of wondrous jewels and emitted pure, radiant light as an offering to the World-Honored One;
all praised him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent, O Vajragarbha!"
Countless billions of devas, their hearts filled with great joy,
rained down various precious jewels from the void above;
their radiant forms intermingled in exquisite patterns, subtle and most delightful.
Incense, flowers, and various necklaces, along with banners and canopies, were scattered over the Buddha;
the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, together with his retinue,
rained down a multitude of wondrous treasures, falling in dense flakes like snow.
They sang praises and made offerings to the Buddha, extolling Vajragarbha;
all cried out in acclaim, "Excellent! You have well explained the practices of the stages.
Tens of millions of billions of celestial maidens, in the sky above, [uttered these words].
The celestial hosts performed music and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues, all saying these words:
"That which the Tathāgata has taught is subtle and immeasurable; it is able to extinguish all afflictions."
All phenomena are empty by their very nature, Without even the slightest trace of characteristics.
This emptiness is devoid of discrimination, Uniform like the expanse of space.
It has no marks of going or staying, Nor is there any conceptual proliferation.
Primordially and eternally pure, suchness is without discrimination.
If a person can thoroughly penetrate the nature of all phenomena,
their mind will not waver amidst existence or non-existence.
Yet, out of great compassion, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings,
they are called children of the Buddhas, born from the Dharma of the Buddha’s own mouth.
They constantly practice giving, benefiting all sentient beings.
Although originally pure, one maintains the precepts with a firm mind;
although the original mind is unimpaired, one practices patience;
although knowing that the nature of phenomena is detached, one practices diligence.
Although he has previously extinguished the afflictions, he enters into the various dhyānas;
although he has previously realized the emptiness of all phenomena, he discriminates among those very phenomena.
Although his wisdom of quiescence is vast, he seeks to benefit the world.
One who can extinguish all evils is called a Great Being.
After these celestial maidens had offered praise and song with hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite voices, they fell silent and gazed upon the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
