"By what characteristics of practice can the sixth stage be attained?
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already fulfilled the fifth stage and wishes to enter the sixth stage, they should do so by means of ten dharmas of equality. What are these ten?
First, all phenomena are equal because they lack intrinsic nature;
second, all phenomena are equal because they lack marks;
third, all phenomena are equal because they are unarisen.
4. Because they are unestablished, all phenomena are equal;
5. Because they are primordially pure, all phenomena are equal;
6. Because they are free from conceptual proliferation, all phenomena are equal.
7. All phenomena are equal because they are neither grasped nor rejected;
8. All phenomena are equal because they are detached;
9. All phenomena are equal because they are like illusions, dreams, reflections, and the moon in water.
Tenth: Because existence and non-existence are non-dual, all phenomena are equal.
By means of these ten dharmas of equality, the bodhisattva attains entry into the sixth stage.

When the bodhisattva contemplates the nature of all phenomena in this way and attains patient endurance (*kṣānti*), they accord with and enter the sixth stage. Although the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) has not yet manifested before them, their mind has already achieved a clear, sharp, and compliant patience.

This bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as having such characteristics; with great compassion as the foremost priority and in order to increase that great compassion, they contemplate the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the world.
They form this thought:
"All places in the world where bodies are received and births occur do so because of attachment to a self; if one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place of birth."

All ordinary beings constantly follow wrong thoughts and walk upon false and delusive paths; blinded by ignorance, they are greedily attached to a self. They habitually give rise to the three types of action—actions leading to misfortune, actions leading to merit, and imperturbable actions—and because of these actions, they produce the seeds of the outflowing mind. Because this mind is outflowing and characterized by grasping, it gives rise to the body of birth and death. That is to say:
karma is the earth, consciousness is the seed, ignorance covers and conceals it, the water of craving provides moisture, the mind of "I" irrigates it, and various views cause it to grow and flourish.

The sprout of name-and-form arises; because of name-and-form, the sense-faculties arise; through the conjunction of the sense-faculties, contact occurs; from contact, sensation arises; because of pleasant sensation, craving arises; because craving increases, grasping occurs; with grasping as a condition, becoming arises; the arising of the five-aggregate body within becoming is called birth; the transformation of the five aggregates is called aging; the cessation of the five aggregates is called death. With aging and death as conditions, there is a gathering of a multitude of sufferings, including grief, lamentation, feverish distress, and affliction.
These twelve links of dependent origination have no one who assembles them, nor anyone who disperses them; they exist when conditions conjoin, and they cease to exist when conditions disperse.

"In this way, within the sixth stage, the Bodhisattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with reality. Furthermore, he reflects: 'Because one does not know the ultimate truth as it is, there is ignorance (*avidyā*).

From ignorance, karma is produced; this is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Depending on volitional formations, there is initial consciousness (*vijñāna*). Simultaneously arising with consciousness are the four aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*). Depending on these aggregates of grasping, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). With the completion of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Due to the conjunction of the faculties and their objects, there is contact (*sparśa*). With contact as a condition, sensation (*vedanā*) arises. Craving for and delighting in sensation is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The intensification of craving is called grasping (*upādāna*). From grasping, karma is produced; this is called becoming (*bhava*). The five aggregates resulting from the retribution of karma are called birth (*jāti*). The transformation of the five aggregates is called old age (*jarā*). The disintegration of the five aggregates is called death (*maraṇa*); "
At the time of death and separation, the feverish state of mind characterized by craving is called *śoka* (sorrow);

the weeping and wailing that arise are *duḥkha* (suffering) when associated with the five sensory consciousnesses and *daurmanasya* (lamentation) when associated with the mental consciousness; the intensification of this lamentation and suffering is called *parideva* (despair).
In this way, there arises merely a great accumulation of suffering.

These twelve links of dependent origination are without self and without what belongs to a self; they have no agent and no instigator. If there were an agent, there would be an action; if there were no agent, there would be no action. In the ultimate sense, there is neither agent nor action.
"Furthermore, he reflects thus:
'The three realms are illusory and are made solely by the mind;
the twelve links of dependent origination all rely upon the mind. Why is this so?'"

Following an object, a desire-thought arises; this thought is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*). The object is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); because these formations deceive the mind, they are called ignorance (*avidyā*). The basis upon which consciousness relies is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of these three factors constitutes contact (*sparśa*). That which arises simultaneously with contact is sensation (*vedanā*). Attachment to what is sensed is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Not relinquishing that craving is called grasping (*upādāna*). Because of their conjunction, it is called becoming (*bhava*). The arising of what has become is called birth (*jāti*). The transformation of birth is called aging (*jarā*). The decay of aging is called death (*maraṇa*).
Furthermore, ignorance has two functions:
first, it is delusion regarding the objects of perception; second, it acts as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Volitional formations also have two functions:
First, it produces the retribution of future lives; second, it acts as the cause for consciousness.
Consciousness also has two functions:
first, it is able to undergo birth; second, it acts as the cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form also has two functions:
first, it causes consciousness to arise in a continuous succession; second, it acts as the cause for the six sense bases.
The six sense bases also have two functions:
First, it can take the six sense objects as its object; second, it can act as the cause for contact (*sparśa*).
Contact also has two functions:
first, it can contact the object; second, it can act as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*).
Feeling also has two functions:
first, it perceives objects of aversion and attraction; second, it acts as the cause for craving.
Craving also has two functions:
First, it gives rise to a mind of craving toward objects that provoke attachment; second, it acts as the cause for grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping also performs two functions:
first, it is able to increase afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it acts as the cause for becoming (*bhava*).
Existence (*bhava*) also has two functions:
first, it enables rebirth in other realms; second, it acts as the cause for birth (*jāti*).
Birth also has two functions:
First, it can give rise to the five aggregates; second, it acts as the cause for aging.
Aging also has two functions:
first, it causes the faculties to mature; second, it acts as the cause for death.
Death also has two functions:
first, it destroys the body of the five aggregates; second, because of the failure to perceive and know [the truth], it causes the continuity [of existence] to remain unbroken.
Furthermore, regarding "ignorance conditions volitional formations": ignorance causes volitional formations not to cease, as it assists in their formation.
Regarding "volitional formations condition consciousness": they cause consciousness not to cease, as they assist in its formation.
Regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form": they cause name-and-form not to cease, as they assist in its formation.
...up to "with birth as condition, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress," which cause death to continue without interruption by assisting in the formation of death;

because ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease, and so on, up to: because birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress cease. Because the cause ceases, the effect also ceases.

Furthermore, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the three links that perpetuate the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*); volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) constitute the two links that perpetuate the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); and the remaining links of dependent origination perpetuate the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*). Because they continue through the prior and subsequent limits [of past and future lives], these three paths remain uninterrupted. These three paths arise and cease while being devoid of a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).

Furthermore, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are matters of the past; consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are matters of the present; craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are matters of the future.

Thus, there is the turning of the three periods of time. Because ignorance ceases, all volitional formations cease; this is called the teaching on the severance of the continuity of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the twelve links of dependent origination are said to be the three types of suffering:

ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are termed the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); contact and feeling are termed the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); craving, grasping, becoming, birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair are termed the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Because ignorance ceases, the volitional formations cease, and so on until because birth ceases, aging and death cease; this is called the teaching on the severing of the continuity of the three types of suffering.

Furthermore, conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. Because the nature of volitional formations is empty, the same applies to the rest.

Volitional formations arise with ignorance as their condition—this is explained in terms of the bond of arising. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease—this is explained in terms of the bond of cessation. The same applies to the rest.

Furthermore, that "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" is taught in accordance with the contemplation of non-existence; that "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" is taught in accordance with the contemplation of exhaustion; and the same applies to the rest.
Thus, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in ten ways, both in direct and reverse order:

namely, the sequential order of the factors of dependent origination; their inclusion within the mind; the mutual assistance in the accomplishment of phenomena; their inseparability; their progression according to the three paths; the differentiation of the prior and subsequent limits; the distinctions among the three types of suffering; their arising from causes and conditions; their bondage through birth and cessation; and the contemplation of non-existence and exhaustion.

“When this bodhisattva follows the twelve links of dependent origination—seeing them as being without self, without person, without sentient beings, without a life-span, devoid of an agent or one who causes action, and without a master; seeing them as belonging to a multitude of causes and conditions—then, at the time of such contemplation, the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha) manifests before him.
Because he extinguishes these phenomena so that they do not continue in succession, the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣa-mukha) manifests before him.

Knowing these two types [of liberation], he no longer takes pleasure in existence; yet, out of great compassion alone, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, and thus the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha) manifests before him.”

The Bodhisattva practices the three gates of liberation, detaching from the marks of self and other, detaching from the marks of agent and recipient, and detaching from the marks of existence and non-existence. His compassionate heart increases further; by virtue of this compassion, he exerts diligent effort so that the dharmas of enlightenment which are not yet fulfilled may be brought to completion.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Conditioned phenomena increase through combination and decrease through separation;
they increase when conditions are complete and decrease when they are incomplete."
Because I know the faults of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), I should not bring them together by assembling all their causes and conditions;
yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, I do not ultimately extinguish conditioned phenomena.

When a bodhisattva thus knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are devoid of intrinsic nature, free from the mark of solidity, and are without arising or ceasing, they harmonize with great compassion and do not abandon sentient beings; thereby, the light of the unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā* manifests before them.
Having attained this wisdom in its fullness, they cultivate and accumulate the causes and conditions for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they do not dwell within conditioned phenomena.
They contemplate the quiescent nature of conditioned phenomena and likewise do not abide therein, because they desire to fulfill the dharmas of unsurpassed enlightenment.

"When the Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi), he attains the Samādhi of Supreme Emptiness, the Samādhi of Essential Emptiness, the Samādhi of Ultimate Emptiness, the Samādhi of Culminating Emptiness, the Samādhi of Great Emptiness, the Samādhi of Combined Emptiness, the Samādhi of Emptiness of Arising, the Samādhi of Emptiness that is Truly Free from Falsehood, the Samādhi of Brief Emptiness, and the Samādhi of Emptiness Free from Discrimination and Non-discrimination. Such as these, ten thousand gates of the Samādhi of Emptiness manifest before him; the Samādhis of Signlessness (Animitta) and Wishlessness (Apraṇihita) are likewise."

When this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), their deep mind, resolute mind, true mind, profoundly deep mind, non-reversing mind, non-abandoning mind, expansive mind, boundless mind, mind that delights in knowledge, and mind harmonized with wisdom and skillful means—such minds as these increase ever more excellently. They accord with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such that no teacher of treatises can shake them;
they enter the ground of wisdom, transcend the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are decisively directed toward Buddha-wisdom, remaining indestructible by any māras or afflictions.

Abiding securely within the luminosity of a bodhisattva’s wisdom, they cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and single-mindedly employ wisdom and skillful means to practice the dharmas that assist enlightenment.

When this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence, they excel particularly in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and attain the superior conformative patience (anulomikī kṣānti); by conforming to these dharmas, they are free from all opposition.

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi), they behold hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines. They draw near to these Buddhas and, in their presence, listen to and receive the True Dharma. Practicing according to what has been taught, they bring joy to the Buddhas. Such a person becomes increasingly superior, coming to know the treasury of the Buddha-dharma; even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, all their roots of goodness become ever more wondrous, luminous, and pure."
Just as genuine gold, when polished with lapis lazuli, becomes increasingly brilliant in its luster and color;

so too, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), through the power of wisdom and skillful means, all their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure, such that no other stage can surpass them.

For example, just as the bright moon can bring refreshing coolness to the bodies of sentient beings and cannot be obstructed or extinguished by the four winds, so too when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), their roots of goodness become increasingly superior; they can extinguish the fire of afflictions in sentient beings and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of Māras.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this ground, they frequently become a King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Vaśavartin*), possessing sharp and penetrating wisdom capable of shattering all forms of arrogance. They cannot be exhausted by the challenges and interrogations of Śrāvakas; whatever deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor for even a brief moment, they will attain hundreds of thousands of billions of samādhis, and will even be able to manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas as their retinue.
"If, by the power of their vows, they were able to pass through this number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, it would be impossible to calculate or know.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattvas have already attained The complete practice of the fifth stage."
Knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, They are signless and without arising or ceasing.
Primordially and eternally pure, Free from all conceptual proliferation;
All phenomena are eternally detached from signs, Neither grasped nor abandoned.
The nature of phenomena is empty like an illusion; free from duality and non-conceptual, by practicing in accordance with this, one enters the sixth stage.
Abiding in the sharp and penetrating compliant patience, through the power of wisdom, one attains entry.
Observing all things, one sees the marks of arising and ceasing in the world.
One fully knows that all worlds exist because of ignorance;
if ignorance were extinguished, then the world would not exist.
Contemplating the law of dependent origination, one accords with the ultimate truth;
yet without destroying the retribution of conditions, one sees that in all actions and conventional designations,
there is in reality no agent and likewise no recipient.
Thus one contemplates conditioned phenomena, which are like clouds, lacking any substantial reality.
Not knowing the meaning of the True Dharma is called ignorance;
from this arises volition, which results in the karmic actions of body and speech.
From volitional formations arises consciousness, which in turn gives rise to name-and-form;
thus, in this sequential order, there arises this mass of suffering and affliction that is birth and death.
To fully comprehend the three realms, one must realize they exist solely from a mind of craving.
To know the twelve links of dependent origination as residing within a single mind—
thus, birth and death arise solely from the mind;
if the mind is extinguished, then birth and death are likewise exhausted.
Ignorance performs two functions: conditioned by delusion, it produces karma, continuing even unto old age and death, whereby the aggregate of the five skandhas is broken and dispersed.
From this very point, the full emergence of suffering and affliction occurs.
If these things are exhausted, suffering and affliction likewise cease.
If ignorance is fully present, the continuity of existence does not cease;
if causes and conditions are exhausted, the continuity of existence is also severed.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the path of afflictions; volitional formations and existence constitute the path of karma;
the remaining factors constitute suffering. Ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past;
consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases [belong to the present].
Contact and feeling belong to the present; the rest belong to the future.
Ignorance, karma, consciousness, and name-and-form are the past; the six sense bases are called formations.
Contact and feeling are the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā); the remaining factors are the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā).
Delusion arises from a multitude of conditions; thus there are various bonds.
If those conditions are extinguished, then all bonds are severed as well.
From causes, effects arise; when the cause is extinguished, the effect is extinguished.
Observing all phenomena in this way, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty.
Following along with ignorance, there are the various worlds;
if one can refrain from following it, then existence is severed.
From this, that arises; when this is absent, that does not arise.
These ten modes of contemplation are the profound law of dependent origination.
Regarding the sequence of the factors of dependent origination throughout the past, future, and present—
Practicing with undistracted single-mindedness, one discerns the three paths.
Through the distinctions of the three kinds of suffering, there is arising and ceasing within the phenomena of bondage;
by means of non-existence and exhaustion, one is able to practice the contemplations of reversal and conformity.
When a bodhisattva enters into the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination in this way,
they know it to be empty like a dream or an illusion, with neither an agent nor an experiencer.
Observing dependent origination thus, the wise cultivate emptiness.
When phenomena cease and no longer continue, one enters into signless practice.
Knowing these two to be false and provisional, one has no further aspirations therein;
yet, out of a heart of great compassion, one pities and delivers sentient beings.
Thus these great beings cultivate the gates of liberation;
with compassionate hearts they love the Buddha and his immeasurable merits.
Knowing that all conditioned phenomena arise from a combination of causes, they understand them to be such.
Attaining the samādhi of the ten thousand emptinesses, The concentrations of signlessness and wishlessness,
Wisdom increases further and further, Entering into the supreme conformative patience,
And attaining the unimpeded wisdom and liberation Of all bodhisattvas.
Thus these roots of goodness become increasingly superior, sharp, and pure;
they make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and are praised by all those Buddhas.
In the presence of the Tathāgatas, they leave the household life to study the Buddha-way.
Entering the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, their roots of goodness increase ever further.
It is like using lapis lazuli gems to polish fine gold;
its radiance becomes increasingly pure, such that nothing else can surpass it.
Just as the moon travels through the void, its cool radiance pervading all,
such that even when buffeted by the four winds, it cannot be obstructed or extinguished;
so too the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom extinguishes the fires of all afflictions.
The four Māras cannot destroy it; its meaning is likewise thus.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he mostly becomes a benevolent transformation-king (Cakravartin);
his faculties are all sharp and keen, and he is able to shatter overweening pride.
All the various wholesome deeds they perform follow entirely from wisdom;
even the challenges posed by the śrāvakas cannot exhaust them.
If these sons of the Buddha desire to exert themselves with such diligent vigor, [they shall attain this].
In a mere moment, one can attain hundreds of billions of samādhis;
one beholds hundreds of billions of Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions,
like the bright and pure radiance of the moon during the cool season of autumn.
Thus the sixth stage, profound and subtle, difficult to know or see,
which the śrāvakas do not comprehend— the Great Being has finished explaining it in brief.
At that time, the hosts of devas, dwelling in the midst of the void, [paid homage].
Raining down fragrant flowers and precious jewels, they scattered like clouds over the Buddha.
Leaping for joy, they uttered sublime sounds, all praising him, saying:
"Excellent! Vajragarbha, you who well know the ultimate truth."
A mass of immeasurable merit, a lotus among men,
he speaks these sublime practices to benefit all worlds.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations rains down precious flower-blossoms of light.
With clouds of offerings falling thickly, those who have removed the afflictions of grief and turmoil—
the devas and the celestial kings— all uttered these words:
"If one hears the meaning of this ground, one shall attain great benefit."
At that time, hundreds of thousands of kinds of supreme and exquisite music were performed, and the celestial maidens offered praise by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power:
“The Buddhas are most profoundly quiescent; they are able to transform evil into good.”
All throughout the worlds, they are universally revered.
Though they have transcended the world, they manifest worldly dharmas;
knowing that the body is identical with the true mark (*dharmatā*), they manifest bodies of every variety.
Although they expound the Dharma of quiescence through various words and sounds,
they know that within language there is no characteristic of sound.
They are able to traverse hundreds of thousands of lands and present sublime offerings to all Buddhas.
Knowing that the body is the Buddha-land, one attains mastery of wisdom through the transcendence of signs.
Though teaching and transforming sentient beings, one harbors no notion of self or other;
having extensively gathered great merit, one does not give rise to attachment therein.
Because they perceive signs, the fires of the three poisons burn the world;
by not grasping at any signs, compassion gives rise to diligence.
The gods and goddesses joyfully present offerings.
Having offered such praise, he remained silent and gazed upon the Buddha.
Then, Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
“The great assembly is pure; may you please explain the practices of the seventh stage.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already fulfilled the sixth stage and wishes to enter the seventh stage, they give rise to ten sublime practices from skillful means and wisdom. What are these ten?
They skillfully cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet abide among sentient beings with a heart of compassion;
they follow the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, yet do not cease making offerings to the Buddhas;
they constantly delight in contemplating the gateway of wisdom regarding emptiness, yet extensively cultivate and accumulate the provisions of merit.
They remain far removed from the three realms, yet adorn the three realms;

they have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, yet for the sake of sentient beings, they give rise to the Dharma that extinguishes the flames of the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion;

they accord with all phenomena as being like illusions, like dreams, and like the moon reflected in water—non-dual in nature—yet they give rise to various discriminations of afflictions and do not lose the retribution of karmic fruits.
Knowing that all Buddha-lands are empty like space and entirely devoid of marks, yet they initiate practices to purify Buddha-lands;
knowing that all Buddhas are the Dharma-body and have no body, yet they manifest the physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
knowing that the voices of all Buddhas are ineffable and the mark of quiescent extinction, yet they produce various adorned sounds in accordance with all beings.

Knowing that all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, penetrate the three periods of time and realize various characteristics, various times, and various kalpas in attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and that they speak thus in accordance with the faith and understanding of sentient beings—this is called the ten sublime practices born from wisdom and skillful means.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates these sublime practices, because such skillful means and wisdom manifest before them, they are said to have "entered the seventh stage.
This Bodhisattva, dwelling in the seventh stage, enters the realms of immeasurable sentient beings;
enters the immeasurable methods by which all Buddhas teach and transform sentient beings; enters immeasurable worlds; and enters the immeasurable pure lands of all Buddhas.
They enter into the distinctions of immeasurable dharmas; they enter into the wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas to attain the Unsurpassed Way;
they enter into the enumeration of immeasurable eons; they enter into the immeasurable Buddhas who penetrate the three periods of time;

they enter into the distinctions of the desires and inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings; they enter into the differences of the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of immeasurable Buddhas; they enter into...
They measure the various intentions, conducts, and faculties of sentient beings as known by all Buddhas;

they enter into the immeasurable sounds and languages of all Buddhas to bring joy to sentient beings; they enter into the immeasurable distinctions of the minds and mental activities of sentient beings;
they enter into the immeasurable Buddhas’ conduct according to wisdom; and they enter into the demonstration of the immeasurable vehicles of the Śrāvakas for those with faith and understanding.
They enter the causes and conditions for the immeasurable teachings on the Way spoken by all Buddhas, causing sentient beings to have faith and understanding;
they enter the cultivation and perfection of the immeasurable wisdom of pratyekabuddhas; they enter that which is taught by the immeasurable, profoundly deep wisdom of all Buddhas;
they enter the immeasurable paths practiced by all bodhisattvas; and they enter the immeasurable Mahāyāna compendiums spoken by all Buddhas.
This enables sentient beings to enter [the path].
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"Such Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless great power; I should cultivate and accumulate such power myself, and having attained this power, I shall not engage in discrimination."
When a bodhisattva contemplates with such wisdom and cultivates the great wisdom of skillful means, they abide securely in the Buddha-wisdom by virtue of the dharma of immovability.

They constantly give rise to various paths for delivering sentient beings without any obstruction; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they are always able to initiate the dharmas that deliver sentient beings. Remaining free from all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and dwelling in all dignified postures (*iryāpatha*), they never depart from them.
With such mental attention, this bodhisattva fulfills the ten *pāramitās* and the practices of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in every single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because in every thought-moment, these bodhisattvas take great compassion as their foremost priority, cultivate the Buddha-dharma, and dedicate everything toward great wisdom.
Regarding the ten pāramitās: when a bodhisattva dedicates the roots of goodness cultivated in the pursuit of the Buddha-way to all sentient beings, this is the dāna-pāramitā;
being able to extinguish the heat of all afflictions is the śīla-pāramitā;
having compassion as the foremost priority and harboring no intent to harm any sentient being is the kṣānti-pāramitā.
Seeking roots of goodness without weariness is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
practicing the path with an undistracted mind, constantly directed toward omniscience, is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā);
enduring the non-arising gate of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Being able to give rise to immeasurable gateways of wisdom is the perfection of skillful means;
seeking ever-superior wisdom is the perfection of aspiration;
being unable to be thwarted or destroyed by any demons or non-Buddhists is the perfection of power.
To speak of the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
in this way, within every thought-moment, one fulfills the ten perfections.

When this bodhisattva fulfills the ten perfections, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and all dharmas that assist toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, are all fully perfected within every thought-moment.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment only in the seventh stage, or can they also fulfill them in all stages?"
Vajragarbha said: “O Son of the Buddha!

Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully possess all the factors conducive to enlightenment throughout all the stages, this stage is taught [specifically] because of its excellence as the ‘Far-Reaching’ (dūraṃgamā). Why is that?
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fulfill their meritorious practices within the seventh stage by entering the path of the superknowledges of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
Because Bodhisattvas in the first stage resolve to take all Buddha-dharmas as their object, they become fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the second stage, because the mental defilements are removed, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment;
in the third stage, because vows increase further and the light of the Dharma is attained, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment;
in the fourth stage, because one enters the Path, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment.
On the fifth stage, because one acts in accordance with worldly dharmas, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment;
on the sixth stage, because one enters the profound gateways of the Dharma, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment;
and on this seventh stage, because one gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Why is this? Because within this stage, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the path practiced by all wisdoms; by the power of this, the eighth stage is naturally accomplished.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like two worlds: one is utterly pure and the other is utterly defiled; the space between these two is difficult to traverse.
To wish to pass beyond this realm, one must rely upon supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the power of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).
The Bodhisattva is also like this: traveling upon a path of manifold difficulties, it is hard to pass through;
yet by means of the power of great vows, the power of great wisdom, and the power of great skillful means, he is then able to pass through.
Vimukticandra asked:
"Is the seventh-stage bodhisattva one who practices pure conduct, or one who practices defiled conduct?
Vajragarbha replied:
"From the practices of a Bodhisattva on the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) onward, all actions are free from sinful karma. Why is this?
Because they are dedicated toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; thus, whatever is practiced according to each stage is pure and cannot be called a transgression."
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, riding upon a great precious elephant, travels through the four continents. Seeing sentient beings impoverished, distressed, and afflicted, the king himself suffers no such hardship; yet he has not yet transcended the human state. If he were to relinquish his royal body and be born in the Brahma world, traveling through a thousand worlds and manifesting great majestic power, only then would he be said to have transcended the human body.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: from the first stage, they ride upon the vehicle of the various *pāramitās*, knowing the mental activities and the defilements of all sentient beings, yet they are not defiled by those afflictions.
Although they ride upon the path of goodness, it is not yet called "transcendence.

If they relinquish all cultivated meritorious practices and enter the eighth stage, at that time they are said to ride the pure vehicle; fully knowing all the defilements of affliction without being stained by them, this is what is truly called "transcendence."
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas dwell in the seventh stage, they have transcended the defilements of afflictions such as sensual desire; thus, in this seventh stage, they are neither said to possess afflictions nor said to be free from afflictions.
Why is this? Because all afflictions do not arise, they are not called "having afflictions";
yet because their aspiration for the Tathāgata’s wisdom has not yet been fulfilled, they are not called "without afflictions."

When a bodhisattva dwells in the seventh stage, they accomplish profoundly pure actions of body, speech, and mind. All unwholesome karma and secondary afflictions associated with them have been completely abandoned, while all wholesome karma is constantly cultivated and practiced.
Furthermore, as described regarding the fifth stage, they naturally master worldly scriptures and treatises; within the trichiliocosm, this is considered most rare.
He has become a great teacher; with the sole exception of the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, there is no sentient being whose profound resolve or sublime practice can equal his.

All the meditative concentrations, supernormal powers, liberations, and samādhis possessed by this Bodhisattva do not arise as a result of those concentrations, for he exercises mastery over them at will. Abiding in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*), in every thought-moment he fully cultivates and accumulates the power of skillful means and wisdom, as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment, which become increasingly superior and complete.

He was able to enter the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Subjugation, the Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation of Meaning, the Samādhi of Advancing Wisdom, the Samādhi of Discerning the Treasury of Meanings, the Samādhi of Discerning Dharmas According to Reality, the Samādhi of Firm and Stable Abiding, the Samādhi of Knowing the Gateways of Supernatural Powers, the Samādhi of Purifying the Dharma-realm, the Samādhi of Accordance with the Buddha’s Teachings, the Samādhi of Various Treasuries of Meanings, and the Samādhi of Turning Away from Birth-and-Death toward Nirvāṇa. Thus, he was fully endowed with one million samādhis, whereby he purified this stage.

Because this bodhisattva has attained these samādhis, due to the thorough purification of wisdom and skillful means, and because they have deeply attained the power of great compassion, they are said to have transcended the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to be proceeding toward the stage of buddha-wisdom.

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they practice immeasurable physical actions without signs, and immeasurable verbal and mental actions without signs; because these are the pure practices of this bodhisattva, they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas and illuminates all phenomena.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the first stage, they possess immeasurable physical actions and immeasurable verbal and mental actions, and have already been able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:

“Because it relies upon the Great Dharma, it transcends the power of non-practice; because it is the power of practice in the seventh stage, it cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
For example, one born into a royal family is superior to all.
Why is this? Because the status of the ground is noble, his body grows tall, and his wisdom is perfected; only then is he truly superior to all.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, he surpasses the followers of the two vehicles because he has made great vows and his profound resolve is pure; now, dwelling in this stage, by the power of wisdom, he surpasses the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the seventh stage, they attain the profound state of detachment characterized by non-active bodily, verbal, and mental karma; yet they continue to seek the supreme Dharma without abandoning it. Because their mind is ever more exalted, although they course within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not realize that limit of reality.
Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha!
From which stage does a bodhisattva come to be able to enter into cessation?"
Vajragarbha said: "From the sixth ground onward, one is able to enter into cessation.
Now, dwelling on this ground, one is able to enter into cessation in every thought-moment without, however, realizing cessation."
This Bodhisattva accomplishes inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind; they practice within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) yet do not realize it.

It is like a person who boards a ship to enter the ocean; being skilled in the methods of navigation and well-acquainted with the characteristics of the water, they are not submerged by the perils of the sea. In this same way, the Bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh stage boards the ship of the various *pāramitās* and is thus able to practice within the limit of reality without realizing it.

In this way, because of the power of their great vows, because they have attained the power of wisdom, and because they give rise to the power of great skillful means from meditative concentration and wisdom, although they deeply cherish *nirvāṇa*, they manifest within birth and death; although surrounded by a retinue of followers, their minds are always detached;
through the power of their vows, they take birth within the triple world yet are not defiled by worldly dharmas, for their minds are always well-peaceful;
and through the power of skillful means, they nevertheless blaze forth with vigor.
Following the Buddha’s wisdom, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
they enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma while manifesting within the realm of Māra, and though they have transcended the four Māras, they manifest the conduct of Māra;
though they manifest the practices of non-Buddhists, they do not abandon the Buddha’s salvation; and though they manifest throughout all worlds, their minds always abide in the supramundane Dharma.

All their various adornments surpassed those of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, and Brahmā-devaputra; yet they did not abandon their delight in the Dharma nor their love for the Dharma.

When a bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), they encounter hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas, whom they honor, serve, revere, and praise. They provide these buddhas with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites; they protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, and their resolve cannot be undermined by the inquiries or challenges of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas regarding wisdom.

Because this bodhisattva has compassion for sentient beings, their patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) becomes increasingly pure, and their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) become increasingly superior over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* eons.
For example, just as pure gold, when interspersed with various exquisite jewels, becomes even more brilliant and pure, such that other gold cannot compare to it;

so too is the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūramgamā bhūmi*). All their roots of goodness arise from skillful means and wisdom, becoming increasingly brilliant and pure, and nothing can destroy them.
For example, just as the light of the sun cannot be rivaled by the light of the stars or the moon, and can dry up all mud and water,

so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of Far-Going (dūraṃgamā) possess roots of goodness that become increasingly superior, such that they cannot be rivaled by any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, and can likewise dry up the muddy sludge of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Stage of Far-Reaching Travel (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), possessing sharp and keen faculties. They are able to inspire sentient beings toward the causes and conditions for awakening to the Way. Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial action (*arthacaryā*), or cooperation (*samānārthatā*)—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the possession of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice such diligent effort, they will, in a single moment, attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas as their retinue.
"If manifested through the sovereign power of vows, it exceeds this number by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, such that it cannot be calculated or known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"With deep wisdom and a concentrated mind, Having fully practiced the six stages,..."
At one time, generating skillful means, Wisdom enters the seventh stage.
Practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, While cultivating a heart of compassion,
Following the Buddha’s law of equality, One makes offerings to all Buddhas.
Though one contemplates emptiness with wisdom, one cultivates merit without weariness;
though able to adorn the three realms, the mind delights in seclusion;
though the mind is ever in cessation, one arises to extinguish unwholesome dharmas.
Practicing the non-dual characteristic of emptiness, yet exercising a mind of loving-kindness and compassion;
though they contemplate all lands as empty as space,
they are able to skillfully adorn and purify the buddha-fields.
Although they know that the bodies of all Buddhas are identical to the markless nature of dharmas,
they manifest the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs.
Although they know that the dharma of vocal sound has a nature that cannot be expressed in words, [they teach it].
They extol the Buddha’s voice, causing all beings to rejoice.
Although they know that all Buddhas attain enlightenment within a single thought-moment,
they manifest eons and lands to guide all sentient beings.
Knowing all phenomena in this way, one attains the illumination of the Dharma;
a bodhisattva who is thus enters the seventh stage.
Abiding in this stage, they are able to observe the immeasurable conduct of sentient beings.
They also know the Buddhas and their methods for teaching and transforming sentient beings;
they know the worlds and the number of kalpas, as well as the distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, they know the various desires and pleasures of all sentient beings.
Knowing how to expound the teachings of the Three Vehicles, I shall cause sentient beings to have faith and understanding;
I should practice transformation and edification so as to bring these sentient beings to fulfillment.
With such reflection, the union of skillful means and wisdom,
Amidst the four modes of conduct, one constantly practices this path.
Within each and every thought-moment, one is able to fulfill the qualities of enlightenment—
namely, the ten perfections, such as generosity, ethical discipline, and the rest.
The merit cultivated by such bodhisattvas, when shared with all sentient beings,
is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
when it extinguishes the defilements of the mind, it is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Not being harmed by the six sense objects is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
Being able to give rise to ever-superior dharmas is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
Remaining unmoved on this path is called the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
The illumination of the patience of non-arising is the perfection of wisdom;
dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-way is the perfection of skillful means;
seeking ever more excellent dharmas is called the perfection of aspiration.
That which cannot be destroyed is called the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*);
that which can explain and expound according to reality is called the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
These factors that assist awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are able to be gathered up in every single thought-moment.
Arising from vast vows, because they take the Great Dharma as their condition;
the merit within the first stage is called "complete," while the second stage is named for "removing all mental defilements and evils."
The third vow increases illumination; in the fourth stage, one enters the Path.
In the fifth, one acts in accordance with the world; in the sixth, one enters the profound Dharma and attains the portion of the mark of non-arising, which gradually increases.
The seventh stage gathers all things, Possessing the factors of enlightenment,
Able to give rise to all merits As well as all vows.
Such merits as these cause [the practitioner] to dwell Within the subsequent eighth stage.
All practices whatsoever naturally attain purity.
This stage of Far-reaching (Dūramgamā) is difficult to traverse; it is accessible only through the power of great wisdom.
It is like the space between two countries, which is difficult to cross over.
Abiding within the seventh stage, They remain unstained like a noble king;
Though dwelling upon this path, They are not said to have transcended all faults.
If they reach the eighth, The Bodhisattva’s Stage of Wisdom,
At that time, having transcended the realm of mind, one abides within the activity of wisdom.
Like the Brahma King observing the world, he cannot be called a mere human;
the Bodhisattva is unstained by faults, like a lotus flower in the water.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they have transcended all greed and desire;
thus they are not said to possess afflictions, yet they are not said to have extinguished them.
Having entered into this true path, they are free from all afflictions.
Because they seek the path of the Buddha, they cannot be called those who have reached the end [of learning].
Within all the worlds, regarding scriptures, arts and crafts, literature, verse,
incantations, and so forth, they are naturally able to understand them clearly.
Cultivating all meditative concentrations and supernormal powers,
they are able to give rise to these matters that benefit the world through immeasurable mental states.
At that time, this bodhisattva surpasses the practices of the two vehicles.
Abiding in the seventh stage, among all the practices of the bodhisattvas,
they were previously superior by virtue of the power of their great vows at the time of first generating the mind;
now, within this stage, they are superior through the power of their own wisdom.
Just as a prince, born with a noble lineage,
later achieves preeminence among all people through his meritorious deeds; so too,
abiding here, one attains profound wisdom and further develops supreme diligence.
Moment by moment they enter into quiescence, yet they do not realize [nirvana] therein.
Like a person skillfully riding a boat who enters the great ocean,
though they travel through deep and perilous waters, they are not harmed by them.
The Bodhisattva’s practice becomes increasingly superior through skillful means and wisdom;
with all merits fully perfected, it cannot be known by the world.
Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, his mind becomes ever more pure.
Like pure gold interspersed with various jewels, Adorned in alternating splendor;
Having attained the light of the Buddha’s wisdom, One dries up the moisture of craving,
Just as the radiance of the sun Evaporates the mud and floods.
Dwelling on this stage, one mostly acts as a King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations;
all faculties are sharp and keen, and one penetrates the fruits of all paths.
If one desires to exert diligent effort, one shall behold hundreds of thousands of billions [of Buddhas].
The vows of the nayutas of Buddhas exceed even this.
The wisdom of the seventh stage is so pure that it is not within the realm of humans, devas, or those of the two vehicles; now this brief exposition is concluded.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-two, Part Four: The Stage of the Fourth Ten Levels.
The King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, along with all the devas and bodhisattvas, upon hearing this account of supreme conduct, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
They rained down exquisite flowers and incense, banners, canopies, precious necklaces,
and truly wondrous maṇi jewels, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
In the sky, celestial maidens performed all manner of musical performances.
Making offerings to the Tathāgata, as well as to all the Bodhisattvas,
they together with subtle and wondrous voices sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues:
“The one possessed of all wisdom, the most honored among all sentient beings.”
Out of compassion for the world, they manifest various supernormal powers;
from flowers, incense, precious jewels, and the like, such sounds all emerge.
Within a single atom, each displays nayutas [of worlds].
Countless Buddhas preach the Dharma therein;
within a single mote of dust, one sees immeasurable Buddha-lands,
with Mount Sumeru and the Vajra Ring Mountains, yet the worlds are not cramped.
Within a single mote of dust, one sees the three evil realms,
Where devas, humans, and asuras each receive their karmic retribution.
One hears the wondrous voices of all Buddhas throughout the Buddha-lands.
They turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, responding in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Within the worlds of all Buddhas, the bodies of sentient beings are of various kinds;
according to the lands and the beings therein, they manifest various forms.
All the devas and humans dwell together therein;
having first observed them all, the Buddha then preaches the Dharma for them.
All sentient beings perceive and see within a single mote of dust the Buddha-lands.
They also behold vast lands through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
The Buddha manifests such various supernormal powers that even if he were to explain them for the sake of sentient beings, these matters could never be exhausted.
With these subtle and wondrous sounds, they praised the World-Honored One;
their hearts were filled with great joy, and they gazed upon the Buddha in silence.
Then the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
“Son of the Buddha, please expound upon the practice of entering the eighth stage.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
“Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having already practiced the subtle wisdom of the seventh stage, has purified the path of skillful means, well-accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, and is endowed with the power of great vows;

protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas and empowered by his own roots of goodness, he constantly contemplates and accords with the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas), as well as his straightforward mind, profound mind, and purity; he accomplishes merit and wisdom, great loving-kindness and great compassion, never abandons sentient beings, and cultivates the path of immeasurable knowledge.

Entering into the fact that all phenomena are from the beginning unborn, unarisen, signless, unformed, undestroyed, without coming, without going, without beginning, without middle, and without end; entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata, one has no attachment to any mental activity, thought, consciousness, recollection, or conceptual discrimination;
seeing that all phenomena have the nature of empty space—this is called a bodhisattva attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and entering the eighth stage.

Upon entering the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one is called a Bodhisattva of Profound Practice; they cannot be fathomed by any in the world, are free from all marks (*nimitta*), free from all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) and all attachments (*abhiniveśa*), and cannot be destroyed by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, as profound and great detachment manifests before them.

For example, it is like a bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over his mind, who enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) in successive stages, whereby all movement of the mind, recollections, and conceptual discriminations are entirely extinguished.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: when the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, all diligent applications of physical, vocal, and mental conduct are completely stilled and extinguished, as he abides in great seclusion.

It is like a person who, in a dream, desires to cross a deep body of water; they exert great diligence and employ great skillful means, yet before they have crossed, they suddenly awaken and abandon all those skillful means.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: from the very beginning, having aroused great vigor and extensively cultivated the practices of the path until reaching the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), he relinquishes everything, no longer acts with dualistic thoughts, and all recollections and conceptualizations no longer manifest before him.
For example, when one is born into the Brahma-world, the afflictions of the desire realm do not manifest before them.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: dwelling in the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), all mind, mentation, and consciousness do not manifest before them; even the Buddha-mind, the Bodhi-mind, and the Nirvana-mind do not manifest, let alone the various mundane minds that arise in the world.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva accords with this stage by the power of their original vows.
Furthermore, the Buddhas manifest their bodies for them, dwelling within the flow of the Dharma of the various stages, acting as the causal conditions for the wisdom of the Tathāgata.”
All the Buddhas spoke these words:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Good son! You have attained this foremost patience, which accords with all Buddha-dharmas.
“Good son! [he continued].

I possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas, which you have not yet attained; for the sake of attaining these, you must apply yourself with diligent vigor and never abandon this gate of patience.

"Good son! Although you have attained this foremost, most profound liberation of quiescence, all ordinary beings remain far from the dharma of quiescence and are constantly harmed by the afflictions of discursive thought and mental examination; you should therefore take pity upon all these sentient beings."
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should call to mind your original vow: the desire to benefit sentient beings and the desire to attain the inconceivable gate of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The nature and characteristics of all phenomena remain eternally constant and unchanging, whether a Buddha exists or not.
It is not because Tathāgatas have attained these phenomena that they are called Buddhas; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas likewise attain this quiescent, non-conceptual Dharma.

"Good son! Observe our immeasurable and pure physical forms, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable and pure buddha-lands, immeasurable skillful means, immeasurable circular halos, and immeasurable pure voices; you should now give rise to such things as these."
Furthermore, son of good family!

You have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma, namely that all phenomena are quiescent and without discrimination. That which we have attained is immeasurable and boundless; you should apply yourself with diligence to give rise to these various dharmas.

"Good son! The infinite lands, infinite sentient beings, and infinite distinctions among all phenomena in the ten directions—you should penetrate these matters as they truly are, and accord with such wisdom."

For this bodhisattva, the Buddhas provide such immeasurable and boundless causes and conditions for the arising of gates of wisdom; by means of these immeasurable gates, the bodhisattva is able to give rise to immeasurable activities of wisdom, all of which are fully accomplished.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If the Buddhas did not grant Bodhisattvas the gateway to the arising of wisdom, these Bodhisattvas would ultimately enter into *nirvāṇa* and abandon the benefit of all sentient beings. Because the Buddhas have granted this immeasurable and boundless gateway to the arising of wisdom, the wisdom produced in a single thought-moment is such that the wisdom attained from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage does not equal even one hundredth of it; it does not equal even an immeasurable, boundless, *asaṃkhyeya*-th part of it, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy. Why is this so?"

Having previously cultivated and accumulated merit with a single body, one now, within this stage, attains immeasurable bodies to practice the bodhisattva path; by means of immeasurable voices, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable birthplaces, immeasurable pure lands, and immeasurable ways of teaching and transforming sentient beings; by making offerings to and serving immeasurable Buddhas; by conforming to immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, immeasurable supernormal powers, immeasurable distinctions among great assemblies, and immeasurable actions of body, speech, and mind; and by collecting all the paths practiced by bodhisattvas, through the quality of immovability.

O Son of the Buddha! It is like a person who boards a ship wishing to cross the great ocean. Before reaching the great ocean, they must exert much effort and labor; once they have entered the sea and are driven by the wind, there is no further difficulty or obstruction. In a single day’s journey, they surpass all the effort previously expended, such that what could not be reached in hundreds of thousands of years is now attained.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: having accumulated many roots of goodness and boarded the ship of the Mahāyāna, they enter the ocean of great wisdom practiced by Bodhisattvas. Without exerting further effort, they can draw near to the wisdom of all Buddhas; compared to their former practice, whether for one kalpa or for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, this cannot be equaled.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches the eighth stage, born from the wisdom of great skillful means, they dwell upon the path of the Bodhisattvas with effortlessness, contemplating the power of the Buddhas’ wisdom. They know the arising of worlds, the cessation of worlds, the formation of worlds, and the destruction of worlds; they know by what causal conditions of karma worlds are formed, and by what causal conditions of karma worlds are destroyed.”

This bodhisattva knows the nature of earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as their small characteristics, medium characteristics, immeasurable characteristics, and differentiated characteristics. He knows the subtle characteristics of atoms and the differentiated characteristics of atoms; he is able to know all the differentiations of atoms within a single world-system, and he is able to know the various numbers of atoms of earth, water, fire, and wind that constitute this one world-system.

They thoroughly know the number of atoms in precious objects, the number of atoms in the bodies of sentient beings, and the distinctions between the atoms of all things within the world-systems; they discern that the great bodies and small bodies of sentient beings are composed of a certain number of atoms, that the bodies of those in the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts are composed of a certain number of atoms, and that the bodies of asuras and devas are likewise composed of a certain number of atoms—all of which they fully understand.

When this bodhisattva enters such wisdom that analyzes atoms, they know the destruction of the desire, form, and formless realms; they know the formation of the desire, form, and formless realms; they know the formation and destruction of the desire, form, and formless realms; they know the small, medium, and immeasurable characteristics of the desire, form, and formless realms; and they know the distinct characteristics of the desire, form, and formless realms. Knowing the three realms in this way is called the bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation of sentient beings.

The factor of wisdom-aiding illumination consists in skillfully discerning the bodies of sentient beings and skillfully observing the places where they are to be born; according to the birthplaces of sentient beings and according to their bodies, the Bodhisattva assumes a body. Thus, the Bodhisattva manifests bodies that pervade the trichiliocosm, each distinct according to the bodies of sentient beings.

It is like the sun and moon, which manifest their reflections in all waters; whether in two or three, or even in immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and ineffable trichiliocosms, their bodies pervade them all, assuming forms according to the differences in the bodies of sentient beings.
This bodhisattva, having accomplished such wisdom, remains with his body unmoving within a single world,

yet manifests his physical form in the great assemblies of Buddhas throughout unspeakably many Buddha-worlds, according to the bodies of sentient beings and according to what they believe and delight in;
if among śramaṇas, he manifests the appearance and form of a śramaṇa.
Among brahmins, he manifests the form and color of a brahmin; among kṣatriyas, he manifests the form and color of a kṣatriya;
among householders, he manifests the form and color of a householder; among the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Māra, and the Brahmās, he manifests the form and color of a Brahmā;
and even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he manifests [the form and color of] the Akaniṣṭha devas.
With a form and color like that of Kaṇiṭṭha, he manifests the form and color of a śrāvaka to those who are to be delivered by the Śrāvakayāna;

he manifests the form and color of a pratyekabuddha to those who are to be delivered by the Pratyekabuddhayāna; he manifests the form and color of a bodhisattva to those who are to be delivered by the Bodhisattvayāna;
and he manifests the form and color of a Buddha’s body to those who are to be delivered by the Buddha-body.

In all the unspeakably many Buddha-lands, he manifests the assumption of a body in accordance with the bodies of sentient beings and their differences in faith and inclination; yet in reality, he is far removed from the distinctions of bodily characteristics, eternally abiding in equanimity.

This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, knows the body of the land, knows the body of karmic retribution, knows the body of the śrāvaka, knows the body of the pratyekabuddha, knows the body of the bodhisattva, knows the body of the Tathāgata, knows the body of wisdom, knows the body of the Dharma, and knows the body of space; this bodhisattva thus knows the inclinations of the deep minds of sentient beings.

If one regards the body of a sentient being as one’s own body; or if one regards the body of a sentient being as the body of a land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, or the body of space;
or if one regards the body of a land as one’s own body, the body of karma...
From the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) up to the space-body (*ākāśakāya*): if one regards the karmic reward body as one's own body, or even as the space-body;

or if one regards one's own body as the body of sentient beings, the body of lands, the karmic reward body, the body of śrāvakas, the body of pratyekabuddhas, the body of bodhisattvas, the body of Tathāgatas, or the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*).
The Dharma-body and the space-body; these are the bodhisattvas’ knowledges of the sentient beings' body of accumulated karma,
the retribution-body, the affliction-body, the form-body, and the formless-body, as well as the buddha-lands with their small characteristics, medium characteristics, immeasurable characteristics,
defiled characteristics, pure characteristics, vast characteristics, inverted characteristics, and level characteristics.
Furthermore, they distinguish various characteristics, knowing the conventional designations for the bodies of karmic retribution,
the conventional designations for the bodies of śrāvakas, the conventional designations for the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, and the conventional designations for the bodies of bodhisattvas;

they know the body of the Tathāgata, the body of awakening, the body of vows, the transformation body, the sustaining body, the body adorned with marks and signs, the body of power, the body of sovereign will, the body of merit, the body of wisdom, and the dharma-body.

One knows the wisdom-body as being skillfully distinguished according to reality; one knows the dharma-body as having the characteristic of equality and indestructibility; and one knows the space-body as having the characteristics of being immeasurable, all-pervasive, and formless.

Because this bodhisattva skillfully knows how to manifest such bodies, they attain mastery over life, mastery over the mind, mastery over resources, mastery over karma, mastery over birth, mastery over vows, mastery over resolute belief and understanding, mastery over supernormal powers, mastery over wisdom, and mastery over the Dharma.
This bodhisattva attains ten masteries, becoming one of inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, vast wisdom, and indestructible wisdom.
Following such wisdom, the bodhisattva ultimately and constantly gives rise to faultless bodily, verbal, and mental actions;
their bodily actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, their verbal actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, and their mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom.

With the perfection of wisdom as supreme and great compassion as the foremost, they skillfully cultivate expedient means, skillfully give rise to various vows, and are well protected by the supernatural powers of all Buddhas; they never abandon the practice of the wisdom that benefits sentient beings, and fully know the diverse affairs within boundless worlds.
To state the essentials:
when a bodhisattva dwells in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), all actions of body, speech, and mind are capable of gathering all Buddha-dharmas.
Because this bodhisattva, dwelling in this ground, is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*), they dwell well in the power of the pure mind.
Because the mind never departs from the Way, one skillfully abides in the power of profound resolve;
because one does not abandon sentient beings, one skillfully abides in the power of great compassion;
because one rescues all the world, one skillfully abides in the power of great kindness.
Because they do not forget the Dharma they have heard, they are well-established in the power of dhāraṇī;
because they discern and contemplate all Buddha-dharmas, they are well-established in the power of eloquence;
because they traverse infinite and diverse worlds, they are well-established in the power of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā).
Because they do not abandon any of the practices of a bodhisattva, they are well-established in the power of their vows;
because they cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas, they are well-established in the power of the pāramitās;
and because they skillfully give rise to the knowledge of all modes, they are well-established in the power of the Tathāgata.
Having attained such power of wisdom, this Bodhisattva demonstrates that all actions performed are free from fault.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Because this stage of the Bodhisattva cannot be destroyed, it is named the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi)."
Because wisdom does not regress, it is called the Stage of Non-regression;
because all worlds cannot fathom it, it is called the Stage of Majestic Virtue;
because there is no desire for form, it is called the Stage of Youthful Truth.
Because one takes birth according to one's will, it is called the Stage of Mastery;
because there is no further activity to be performed, it is called the Stage of Accomplishment;
because of definitive knowledge, it is called the Ultimate Stage.
Because they skillfully give rise to great vows, it is called the Stage of Transformation;
because they cannot be destroyed, it is called the Stage of Sustenance;
because they have previously cultivated roots of goodness, it is called the Stage of Effortlessness.

When a bodhisattva attains such wisdom, it is called entering the realm of the Buddha, being illuminated by the merits of the Buddha, and practicing in accordance with the Buddha’s majestic deportment.

They shall advance toward the Buddha-dharma, always protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, always welcomed by the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, the various Brahmā kings, and others, and constantly attended and guarded by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.

They are skillfully able to give rise to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and samādhis; they can manifest immeasurable varieties of bodies, each possessing sovereign power. Having attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of great fruition, they achieve mastery over boundless samādhis and receive immeasurable prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*). According to the place where sentient beings are brought to maturity, they manifest the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When this Bodhisattva enters such great wisdom, they skillfully penetrate all dharmas and constantly radiate the light of great wisdom. They traverse the path of the unobstructed Dharma-realm, skillfully know the distinctions between the paths of worlds, and can manifest all merits with sovereign ease according to their will. Being well-versed in the past and future limits, they are able to enter the wisdom that transforms the path of Māra and enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice. Capable of practicing the Bodhisattva path in infinite worlds, because they possess the characteristic of non-retrogression, this stage is named "Immovable."

“O Son of the Buddha! Because the Bodhisattva in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) has well-generated the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they constantly see boundless Buddhas and never cease making offerings and providing for them. In each and every eon and in each and every world-system, this Bodhisattva reverently makes offerings to, honors, praises, and attends upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas. From these Buddhas, they receive the light of the Dharma (*dharmāloka*) regarding the distinctions between world-systems and other such teachings. This Bodhisattva enters ever more deeply into the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma (*tathāgatadharmagañja*) and inquires about the matters of the distinctions between world-systems; there is no one who can exhaust their questions, and even if one were to speak for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, it could not be fully told.”
Furthermore, all their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure.
It is like a necklace of genuine gold interspersed with various jewels, worn by a Wheel-Turning King, which no common person can ever take away.

The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), their roots of goodness become increasingly pure, such that they cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even bodhisattvas up to the seventh ground.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, by means of the gateway of skillful analytical wisdom, the radiance of their wisdom extinguishes all the afflictions and fevers of sentient beings.

It is like Mahābrahmā, the lord of a thousand worlds, who is able at a single moment to spread a mind of loving-kindness throughout the thousand worlds and also emit light that shines everywhere within them.
