The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), he is able to emit bodily radiance that illuminates worlds as numerous as the dust motes in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields, extinguishing the heat of the afflictions of sentient beings and causing them to attain refreshing coolness.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable billions of eons.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a Great Brahmā King, presiding over a thousand worlds. Their faculties are sharp and keen; they provide for all sentient beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas the path of the pāramitās without end. They explain the distinctions of the worlds such that none can refute them. Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
He constantly gives rise to this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom all sentient beings rely.

If such a bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, in a single moment he attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten million trichiliocosm worlds, and he is even able to manifest as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten million trichiliocosm worlds to serve as his retinue.

"If, by the power of their vows and the mastery of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*), they were able to pass beyond this number, it would remain incalculable even after hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage, Whose wisdom and skillful means are already purified,"
Having well accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, bound by the power of great vows,
and protected by the spiritual might of all Buddhas, their roots of goodness are fully perfected;
seeking supreme wisdom, they are able to enter the eighth stage.
Having well accumulated merit and wisdom, and possessing profound compassion, you have transcended all limited minds; your mind is equal to space.
Within the Dharma as it has been taught, your mind has attained the power of certainty.
Thus one attains quiescence, the subtle and wondrous patience of non-arising.
All phenomena from the very beginning are without birth and without origination;
they are without marks and without formation, nor do they possess the meaning of coming or going.
All phenomena, in their beginning, middle, and end, are non-different from suchness;
they are devoid of the activities of mind and intellect, being identical to empty space.
Having accomplished such patience, one is free from all conceptual proliferation.
Having attained this Immovable Ground, one practices the profound and tranquil conduct. All worlds are unable to fathom it;
all characteristics of the mind have been entirely extinguished.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the mind-consciousness is without discrimination;
like one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation, there is no further recollection or perception.
It is just as if a person in a dream, through skillful means, desires to cross a body of water.
Upon awakening, the mind becomes vast and open, bringing rest to all conditioned activities.
Having attained this profound patience (*kṣānti*), all conceptualizations cease;
like being born in the Brahma Heaven, one is free from the afflictions of the desire realm.
By the power of our original vows, and through the Buddha’s present exhortation,
this foremost patience is the rank of all Buddhas.
It is our profound power of wisdom, our fearlessness, and our unique qualities.
You do not yet possess this; you must apply yourself with diligent effort.
Although you have extinguished all the fires of affliction, you should observe that in all worlds, the fires of affliction are constantly blazing.
One should remember one's original vow, desiring to benefit all sentient beings;
to fully and universally know all phenomena, and to extensively deliver all.
The true nature and characteristics of all phenomena are eternally abiding and without change.
The followers of the two vehicles also attain this, yet they are not called Buddhas.
Only because they have attained unimpeded, profound,
and subtle wisdom that penetrates the three periods of time are they named Buddhas.
These peerless equals, revered by gods and humans,
open this gateway to the arising of wisdom, causing entry into all Buddha-dharmas.
They achieve boundless depths and immeasurable, wondrous wisdom.
All the dharmas practiced previously do not equal a single present thought-moment.
Such Bodhisattvas, having attained the ground of wondrous wisdom,
are able within a single thought-moment to have their bodies pervade the ten directions.
Entering this gateway of wisdom, one traverses the path swiftly and without obstruction,
like sailing upon the ocean aided by the power of a great wind.
Free from all efforts of the mind, one abides solely in the activity of wisdom.
Contemplating the worlds of the ten directions— Their formation, destruction, and abiding;
One can know that the four great elements are one, And also know their various distinctions:
The minute and the immeasurable, With all their diverse characteristics.
One can count and know the atoms within the three thousandfold great chiliocosm,
and likewise know the number of atoms in the four great elements of the bodies of sentient beings.
One also knows the distinctions in the number of atoms in the various jewels that constitute the bodies of the devas.
All things are thoroughly and universally understood, and others are likewise known in this way.
By reason of wisdom, the mind becomes transformed and attains pliancy;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, the body pervades all worlds.
Able to manifest within the bodies of sentient beings, As one's own body,
as well as the lands of all Buddhas, And various other kinds of bodies;
Just as the sun and moon abide in the sky, Their reflections appear in all waters.
The Bodhisattva is likewise, pervading the great trichiliocosm;
eternally abiding in the Dharma-body, serene and unmoving,
yet manifesting his physical form to sentient beings of pure mind, each according to their own kind.
In accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, they manifest birth;
within the assemblies of devas and humans, they reveal their bodies to all.
The Bodhisattva possesses mastery over the convergence of causes and conditions.
Even unto the ability to act at will, manifesting for others the body of a Buddha,
the bodies of sentient beings and their lands, the bodies of karmic retribution and of sages,
the wisdom-body, and the Dharma-body— know that they are all equal and identical.
By these causes and conditions, they attain the supernormal power of fulfilling wishes;
to bring joy to the world, they manifest various bodies.
They are able to obtain ten kinds of wondrous and great sovereign wisdoms.
Their actions follow the course of wisdom and accord with the mind of compassion.
They are able to skillfully cultivate all the dharmas of the Buddhas;
abiding within the three pure precepts, they are as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
One who is able to attain the ten powers possessed by the great Bodhisattvas cannot be turned back by any of the hosts of Māras;
they are constantly protected by all Buddhas and revered by Śakra and Brahmā.
The Guhyapāda Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and attends upon him.
When a Bodhisattva attains this stage, his merit is immeasurable;
even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, it could not be fully described.
Having approached countless Buddhas, they further increase all roots of goodness;
like pure gold interspersed with various jewels, they adorn themselves with royal necklaces.
When Bodhisattvas abide in this stage, they frequently become Great Brahma Kings.
He presides over a thousand lands, his merit being immeasurable.
Through the teachings of the Three Vehicles, he is inexhaustible;
the light of his compassionate heart shines everywhere, extinguishing the heat of all afflictions.
In a mere instant, one can attain as many samādhis as there are atoms in a million sets of three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems;
one can likewise see Buddhas of the ten directions in numbers equal to those.
If one were to describe it by the power of his vows, it would be immeasurable beyond this.
Now I have briefly explained the wondrous characteristics of the eighth stage;
were they to be expounded in detail, they would not be exhausted even in a thousand billion eons.
When the Son of the Buddha expounded this sublime meaning of the eighth stage,
by the spiritual power of the Buddha, immeasurable lands were shaken.
From the body of the All-Knowing One, immeasurable subtle and wondrous rays of light issued forth.
Illuminating the realms of the ten directions, may all sentient beings attain peace and happiness.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas dwell in the midst of the void,
presenting various wondrous offerings such as those never before possessed by the devas.
The sovereign Mahābrahmā and the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods joyfully prepared sublime offerings for the Buddha of Ocean-like Virtue.
Ten million celestial maidens all paid him reverent homage with great delight.
With voices equally subtle and wondrous, they sang praises of the Buddha’s merits;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they uttered these sublime teachings:
"The one who practices wholesome conduct and dwells in tranquility possesses no evil mind."
Each remaining in their respective places, they skillfully cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
For the sake of benefiting the world, they travel everywhere throughout the ten directions,
demonstrating the Buddha-way to all, with minds as unobstructed as space.
The supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas and their most sublime offerings surpass those of the humans and devas of the ten directions; these are brought about by the power of merit.
These sons of the Buddha, who delight in wisdom, display the power of the Buddha through these means.
Without moving from a single land, he manifests in all places.
He benefits the world like the full moon, pure and bright;
he extinguishes all sounds, as well as speech and all conceptual thoughts.
Yet with various sounds and voices, they preach the Dharma like an echo.
If sentient beings are inferior and their minds are weary or despondent,
they show them the path of the śrāvaka to enable them to emerge from all sufferings.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings whose faculties are slightly clear and sharp,
who delight in the Dharma of causes and conditions, for them one preaches the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
If a person’s faculties are clear and sharp, and they bring great benefit to sentient beings, [for them one preaches the Mahāyāna].
Possessing a heart of great compassion, he expounds the path of the bodhisattva.
To those who possess the unsurpassed mind and are resolutely delighted by the Great Matter,
he reveals the Buddha-body and teaches the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.
Just as a master of illusions displays various forms and colors,
so too these bodily characteristics are entirely devoid of substantial reality. In this way,
the sons of the Buddha, well-versed in the arts of wisdom, [manifest such appearances].
Able to demonstrate all modes of conduct, with a mind detached from existence and non-existence;
ten million celestial maidens, together with subtle and wondrous voices,
having thus sung praises, fell silent and gazed upon the Buddha.
Vimukticandra spoke again:
"Sons of the Buddha, this great assembly is pure; with single-minded aspiration, they wish to hear about the correct practice for entering the ninth stage.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:

“O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has thus skillfully observed the path of the Buddhas with such immeasurable wisdom, and desires to seek a further superior, tranquil liberation; desires to contemplate the Tathāgata’s wisdom even more excellently; desires to enter the profound and secret Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata; desires to observe inconceivable great wisdom; desires to observe all *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis* so as to make them doubly pure; desires to cause his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to become vast; desires to discern the distinctions between worlds; desires to cultivate the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddhas that cannot be destroyed; desires to follow and practice the power of the Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma; and desires not to abandon the great compassion and great vows he has undertaken—it is by contemplating in this way that the Bodhisattva enters the ninth stage.”

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they know, as they truly are, the activities of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; the activities of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas; the activities of mundane and supramundane dharmas; the activities of conceivable and inconceivable dharmas; the activities of determinate and indeterminate dharmas; the activities of the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the activities of the dharmas of the bodhisattva path; the activities of the dharmas of the Tathāgata stage; and the activities of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas.

In accordance with such wisdom, one knows that the conduct of the bodhicitta is difficult; one knows the difficulty of the afflictions, the difficulty of karma, the difficulty of the faculties, the difficulty of desires, the difficulty of natures, the difficulty of the straightforward mind, the difficulty of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the difficulty of birth, the difficulty of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the difficulty of the distinctions among the three groups.

He knows, as they truly are, the various distinctions among the minds of sentient beings: the characteristics of the world-adorning mind, the characteristics of the swiftly shifting mind, the characteristics of the disintegrating and non-disintegrating mind, the formless mind, the characteristics of the boundless and sovereign mind, the characteristics of the pure and differentiated mind, the defiled and undefiled mind, the bound and liberated mind, the deceitful-crooked and upright mind, and the mind that follows the Path. He knows all these exactly as they are.

This bodhisattva knows the deep and shallow characteristics of afflictions; knows the characteristics of the mind’s companions and its inseparable characteristics; knows the distinct characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); knows the characteristics of what is associated with and dissociated from this mind; knows the characteristics of obtaining retribution as these arise; knows the distinct characteristics within the three realms; knows the characteristics of craving, delusion, and views penetrating deeply like arrows; knows the characteristics of the heavy offenses of pride and delusion; knows the characteristics of the uninterrupted causal conditions of the three karmas; and even knows, according to reality, the distinct characteristics of the eighty-four thousand modes of affliction.

This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of all karmas—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; their distinguishable and undistinguishable characteristics; their characteristics as companions of the mind;
their characteristics of non-separation; their characteristics of natural exhaustion; their characteristics of exhaustion through the practice of the path;

their characteristics of various accumulations; their characteristics of not losing the retribution of results; their characteristics of succession; and their characteristics of having or lacking retribution.

The characteristics of retribution; the characteristic of black karma with black retribution; the characteristic of white karma with white retribution; the characteristic of black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution;

the characteristic of karma that is neither black nor white which can exhaust all karma; the characteristic of knowing the arising of karma; the characteristic of the distinctions among the dharmas of experiencing karma;
the characteristic of knowing the arising of karma through immeasurable causes and conditions; and the characteristic of knowing the distinction between mundane karma and supramundane karma.
The characteristics of signs, the characteristics of retribution in the present life, the characteristics of retribution in the next life, the characteristics of retribution in subsequent lives,

the characteristics of fixed destinies according to the various vehicles, the characteristics of non-fixed destinies, and even the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among all karmas, he knows them as they truly are.

This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of the distinctions among the faculties as weak, middling, and superior; knows the characteristics of the differences and non-differences between the prior and subsequent limits; knows the characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior; knows the characteristics of the companions of the afflictions and their inseparable nature; knows the characteristics of being fixed according to the various vehicles, the unfixed, the matured, and the immature; knows the characteristics of following the transformation of the faculties, the easily broken, the characteristics of deep grasping, the predominant, the indestructible, the turning and non-turning, the distinctions of the three periods of time, the distinctions of long-term co-arising, and even knows the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among the faculties as they truly are.
This bodhisattva knows the distinctions of the inferior, middling, and superior grades of all desires, even knowing as they truly are the eighty-four thousand distinctions among desires;
this bodhisattva knows the distinctions of the inferior, middling, and superior grades of all dispositions, even knowing as they truly are the eighty-four thousand distinctions among dispositions;

this bodhisattva knows the distinctions of the inferior, middling, and superior grades of the straightforward mind, even knowing as they truly are the eighty-four thousand distinctions among the straightforward mind.

This bodhisattva knows that the various latent tendencies (anuśaya) arise together with the mind or do not arise together with the mind; they are associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind; they are characteristics that have afflicted sentient beings since beginningless time; they are characteristics contrary to all meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), and supernormal powers (abhijñā); they are characteristics bound to the three realms; they are characteristics whereby immeasurable states of mind do not manifest; they are characteristics that open the door to afflictions; they are characteristics of ignorance regarding the antidotes; they are characteristics of non-existence; and they are characteristics that fail to open the Dharma-door of the Noble Path—all these he knows as they truly are.
This bodhisattva knows the various distinctions among births, namely:
those of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, devas, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the distinction between those with perception and those without perception.

Karma is the field, craving is the water, ignorance is the covering, consciousness is the seed, and the subsequent body is the sprout. Name-and-form arise together and are inseparable; delusion and craving continue in succession. Desiring to be born, desiring to act, and desiring to experience, one does not delight in nirvana. One understands as they truly are the characteristics of the continuous succession of the distinctions within the three realms.

This bodhisattva knows that various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have both arising and non-arising; he knows them as they truly are: there are habitual tendencies according to the place of birth, habitual tendencies according to the conduct of sentient beings, habitual tendencies according to karma and afflictions, habitual tendencies regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, habitual tendencies regarding the departure from desire, habitual tendencies regarding subsequent bodies, and habitual tendencies that follow the successive realms of existence. He knows that these maintain afflictions and karma uninterruptedly over vast periods of time, such that if they were abandoned, no phenomena would exist. All of this he knows in accordance with reality.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of sentient beings who are fixed, unfixed, and correctly fixed; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong, the characteristic of being fixed in right view, and the characteristic of being unfixed apart from these two; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong through each of the [five] heinous acts, the characteristic of being correctly fixed through the five faculties, and the characteristic of being unfixed apart from these two; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong state, the characteristic of being correctly fixed in the right state, and the characteristic of being unfixed apart from these two; the characteristic of being deeply settled in the mass of the wrong and difficult to turn back, the characteristic of cultivating the causes and conditions for the unsurpassed path, and the characteristic of protecting unfixed sentient beings. All of these he knows as they truly are.
“O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who accords with such wisdom is said to be ‘dwelling securely in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they know the various characteristics of the different modes of conduct of sentient beings, and according to their respective liberations, they provide them with the necessary causes and conditions.”

This Bodhisattva, knowing truly the methods for transforming sentient beings and the methods for delivering sentient beings, preaches the Dharma for them; knowing truly the characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Bodhisattva vehicle, and the stage of the Tathāgata, he preaches the Dharma according to the causes and conditions of sentient beings;

he preaches the Dharma according to their minds, their faculties, and the distinctions of their inclinations; furthermore, he preaches the Dharma according to their spheres of practice and according to the spheres of their wisdom; knowing all spheres of practice, he preaches the Dharma; he preaches the Dharma by entering deeply into difficult places according to the natures of sentient beings; he preaches the Dharma because of following their destinies, their births, their afflictions, and the turning of their habitual tendencies; and he preaches the Dharma in order to bring liberation through the vehicles.
When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they become a great Dharma teacher who guards the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and enters into profound and subtle meanings.

By means of immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, they preach the Dharma through the words of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); this bodhisattva constantly follows these four unimpeded knowledges, remaining indestructible.

What are the four? First, non-obstruction regarding phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid); second, non-obstruction regarding meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid); third, non-obstruction regarding expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid); and fourth, non-obstruction regarding eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
"This bodhisattva, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), knows the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), knows the differentiated phenomena;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), knows that the teaching of all phenomena is indestructible."
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one knows how to teach all dharmas in an uninterrupted sequence.
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all dharmas.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of dharma (dharmapratisaṃvid), one knows that all phenomena are provisional designations and teaches them through these uninterrupted provisional designations;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid), one knows how to follow these provisional designations and deliver infinite teachings without impairment.
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinct characteristics of all phenomena in the present;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinct characteristics of all phenomena in the past and future;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one knows that the explanations of all phenomena in the past, future, and present are indestructible.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one attains the exposition of boundless illumination of the Dharma in each and every world-age.
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between all phenomena;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the meanings of all phenomena.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with all languages and sounds;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with what beings delight in and how they understand.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) and through the skillful means of the knowledge of phenomena, one knows that the distinctions among all phenomena are indestructible;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) and through subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena as they truly are;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) and through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one explains the distinctions among all phenomena.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one knows how to skillfully expound the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and indestructible;

by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*satya*), and the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence and through his subtle and wondrous voice, he is the refuge for all the world;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of joyful exposition, his teachings become ever more excellent, enabling sentient beings to attain boundless illumination of the Dharma.
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that the ultimate One Vehicle subsumes all things without distinction;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the various vehicles;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one is able to explain that the various vehicles are without distinction.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), they expound infinite clarifications of the Dharma through a single dharma-gate.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), they are able to enter all bodhisattva practices, wisdom practices, dharma practices, and practices that accord with wisdom;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), they are able to analytically explain the distinctions among the meanings of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), he explains the indestructible path that accords with all stages;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of ready speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), he explains the boundless characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all Buddhas attain enlightenment within a single thought-moment;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between various times and various lands;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains according to the distinctions in the events of the Buddhas' attainment of the Way.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one may expound upon a single phrase of the Dharma for infinite eons without exhaustion.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows all the Buddha’s words, all the Buddhas’ powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), great loving-kindness and great compassion, the unimpeded knowledges, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the Tathāgata’s voice as it preaches the eighty-four thousand teachings according to the differences in the mental faculties, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence and with the voice of a Tathāgata, they proclaim that all conditioned phenomena are indestructible;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of inspired speech and through the power of the Buddhas' wisdom, they teach according to the voices preferred by sentient beings.
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who thus well know unimpeded wisdom abide in the ninth stage, which is called ‘Attaining the Treasury of the Buddha-dharma.

They become great Dharma-preachers, attaining the *dhāraṇī* of manifold meanings, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold dharmas, the *dhāraṇī* of arising wisdom, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold luminosities, the *dhāraṇī* of excellent intelligence, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold wealth, the *dhāraṇī* of renown, the *dhāraṇī* of majestic power, the *dhāraṇī* of non-obstruction, the *dhāraṇī* of boundless revolution, and the *dhāraṇī* of the treasury of diverse meanings. Having attained such millions of *asaṃkhyeya* *dhāraṇīs*, they preach the Dharma through immeasurable gateways of eloquence, speaking according to skillful means.”

This bodhisattva, having attained such immeasurable dharanī-gates, is able to hear the Dharma from immeasurable Buddhas; having heard it, they do not forget it, and according to the Dharma as heard, they are able to expound it for others through immeasurable methods of differentiation.

This bodhisattva, at the site of a single Buddha, receives and upholds the true Dharma through ten million *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs; as it is with one Buddha, so it is likewise with all other immeasurable Buddhas.

When this bodhisattva hears the illumination of the Dharma while paying homage to the Buddha, it is not something that even a highly learned śrāvaka possessing the power of dhāraṇī could receive and uphold throughout a hundred thousand kalpas.

This bodhisattva, having attained such power of dhāraṇī and the power of unimpeded wisdom and eloquence, sits upon the Dharma seat and teaches the Dharma according to their inclinations to all sentient beings filling the great trichiliocosm.
When this bodhisattva sits upon the Dharma seat—save for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have received their office—he is the most preeminent among all.
When this bodhisattva occupies the Dharma seat, if he wishes to cause everyone to understand through a single sound, they immediately attain understanding;
if he wishes to cause everyone to achieve individual realization through various sounds, they immediately achieve realization.
Sometimes, by remaining silent and merely emitting light, they cause all beings to each attain the realization of the Dharma, and they immediately attain that realization;
sometimes, the sounds of the Dharma issue forth from every single pore;
or sometimes, all material and immaterial things throughout the trichiliocosm emit the sounds of the Dharma.
Alternatively, with a single sound that pervades the entire Dharma-realm, he causes those who wish to attain understanding to do so; they all immediately attain understanding.
Thus, when all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm simultaneously pose difficult questions using immeasurable voices, each question being different from the others.

In a single thought-moment, this bodhisattva receives all such inquiries and answers them with a single voice, causing everyone to attain understanding. Whether there be two, three, a hundred, a thousand, or even as many beings as would fill unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosm worlds, he extensively expounds the Dharma for them.
Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, they are able to perform extensive Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings, exerting themselves with even greater diligence.

With such luminous wisdom, within a single atom there are great assemblies as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable worlds; the Buddha is present therein, preaching the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings, causing each and every sentient being to attain various immeasurable dharmas. As it is with one Buddha, so it is with all Buddhas;
as it is with one minute atom, so it is likewise throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
Within this, he generates a great power of mindfulness; in a single thought-moment, he receives the illumination of the Dharma from all Buddhas without losing a single word.

Just as in the aforementioned great assembly where sentient beings fill it entirely, he expounds the pure Dharma through the definitive illumination of the Dharma, causing that many sentient beings to attain realization and understanding in a single thought-moment—how much more so for the sentient beings within various world-systems!

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their roots of goodness become increasingly superior; they enter deeply into the sphere of activity of all Buddhas and constantly participate in the assemblies of all Buddhas.

They enter deeply into the liberations of bodhisattvas; following such wisdom, they constantly see all Buddhas. Within each and every eon, they offer more than immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of types of offerings to the Buddhas. At the abodes of the Buddhas, they pose various questions and challenges, attaining mastery over all dhāraṇīs, and all their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, brilliant, and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as refined gold, fully adorned, becomes a precious crown worn by a Wheel-Turning King that no minor king can seize;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*): all their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure, such that they cannot be destroyed by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the other stages.

The roots of goodness of this bodhisattva become increasingly luminous, able to illuminate the difficult places of sentient beings' afflictions, just as the Great Brahmā King can illuminate all difficult places throughout the three-thousandfold world system;

so too does the bodhisattva, dwelling in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), with roots of goodness bright and pure, illuminate the difficult places of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
If it were explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable and boundless eons."

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he frequently becomes a Great Brahmā King, presiding over a trichiliocosm. He is unsurpassed by anyone who understands the meaning as it truly is; he attains mastery within mastery and is skillfully able to proclaim the *pāramitās* of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. No one can exhaust him when questioned by sentient beings. All the wholesome deeds he performs—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, up to and including being never apart from mindfulness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He constantly gives rise to this thought: "I shall be the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice such diligent effort, in a single thought-moment they will attain as many samādhis as there are atoms in a million *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms, and even manifest as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a million *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms to serve as their retinue.

"If, by the power of their vows and the mastery of their supernormal powers, they were to exceed this number for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, it still could not be calculated or known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The bodhisattvas, in accordance with The power of their immeasurable and profound wisdom,"
Supremely subtle and foremost, difficult for all in the world to know,
those who benefit sentient beings can reach the ninth stage;
they shall enter the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
Having attained the subtle and supreme samādhi and dhāraṇī,
and possessing vast and great supernormal powers, they skillfully enter the characteristics of worlds;
with the certainty of the power of wisdom, they are able to contemplate all Buddha-dharmas.
With great vows and pure compassion, one attains entry into the ninth stage.
Proceeding in accordance with this higher stage, one upholds the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas and is able to penetrate all phenomena— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
With outflows and without outflows, mundane and supramundane—
these are conceivable dharmas, yet they are also inconceivable.
Knowing that dharmas are determinate or indeterminate, one possesses the complete characteristics of the Three Vehicles.
Contemplating and discerning these conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,
one gives rise to knowledge of such dharmas; extinguishing the darkness of all ignorance,
a mind that accords with this wisdom is the most supreme and wondrous.
He fully knows all difficulties, the various distinct characteristics of minds,
the ease with which he adorns the world, and his boundless, sovereign mind;
he knows the characteristics of the depth and shallowness of afflictions, and the characteristic of the mind’s companions never being separated from it.
Knowing the distinctions between the proclivities and entanglements, and how they persist in accordance with the continuity of existence;
knowing the various mixtures of karma and their respective distinct characteristics;
and that while causes perish, their fruits are not lost—one thoroughly penetrates such matters.
Furthermore, he knows among sentient beings the distinctions of their faculties—whether dull, middling, or sharp—and their vast differences;
he knows the characteristics of their past and future limits.
He knows the degrees of desire—dull, middling, or sharp—as well as the distinctions among their various natures.
Even unto the full knowledge of all eighty-four thousand kinds of afflictions and latent tendencies—
difficult to overcome, unextinguished since beginningless time,
always functioning in concert with the mind, and binding so as to be difficult to sever.
Know that all fetters and afflictions are merely false conceptualizations and discriminations;
they have no location or place, nor do they possess any fixed characteristics.
They are never separated from the body, yet they are difficult to perceive.
The power of meditative concentration can obstruct it; the diamond path can sever it.
Furthermore, one can know all births, entering the distinctions of the six realms:
moistened by craving and covered by ignorance, karma is the field and consciousness is the seed.
The sprout of the subsequent body arises, and name-and-form grow together;
from beginningless birth and death, they continue in succession within the three realms.
One knows that the destinies of gods and nāgas arise through afflictions, karma, and the mind.
If one is separated from this Dharma, there is nothing at all.
All sentient beings abide within the three realms of existence;
some are submerged in false views, while others dwell upon the path of wisdom.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they fully know the minds of sentient beings,
their faculties, their inclinations, and the various meanings of their diverse differences.
With deep resolve and skillful reflection, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Having attained unimpeded wisdom, they skillfully expound with eloquent speech.
As Dharma-preachers, these Bodhisattvas are like the lion king,
the bull king, and the king of jewel mountains, dwelling securely in fearlessness.
Throughout all worlds, they rain down the flavor of the Dharma’s nectar,
just as a great dragon king can rain down to fill the vast ocean.
These Bodhisattvas possess excellent knowledge of the unimpeded [mastery] of phenomena, meaning, phrasing, and eloquence.
Skillfully able to practice in accordance [with the Dharma], they possess the power of eloquence.
They are able to attain millions of asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇīs,
and can receive all the Buddha-dharmas, just as the ocean receives the rain from the dragons.
When a bodhisattva attains such profound, wondrous, and pure,
immeasurable dhāraṇīs through the power of various samādhis,
they are able, within a single thought-moment, to behold immeasurable buddhas.
Having heard [this], with a pure Brahma-voice, they proclaim the precious jewel of the sublime Dharma.
These Bodhisattvas may teach the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm according to their mental faculties and inclinations, preaching the Dharma so that they may rejoice.
In this way, throughout immeasurable trichiliocosm worlds,
they exert themselves with ever-deepening diligence and reflect thus:
within a single atom, immeasurable Buddhas are preaching the Dharma.
In accordance with the mental dispositions of sentient beings, they expound the wondrous meaning;
these Bodhisattvas receive it all, just as the earth receives all seeds.
They further make this vow: "Whatever exists throughout the ten directions..."
All sentient beings within the lands, gathered together as a single assembly,
I know the thoughts of them all within a single thought-moment;
preaching the Dharma with a single voice, I cause them all to sever the net of doubt.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in this stage is a Dharma King among humans and devas;
acting as a great Dharma teacher, he accords with the natures of sentient beings.
Constantly, throughout day and night, he meets together with all Buddhas.
Able to abide in the profound and wondrous, In the liberation of the wisdom of cessation;
Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure,
Like a wheel-turning monarch, Adorned with a crown of pure gold.
The light shines upon sentient beings in the difficult places of all afflictions,
just as the light of Brahmā King illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, throughout the three thousandfold world system,
He becomes the Great Brahmā King, with all faculties fully sharp and keen.
Skillfully using the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, he instructs and awakens all sentient beings;
all the various wholesome deeds he performs accord with right mindfulness.
Within a single thought-moment, one can attain immeasurable,
profound, and wondrous samādhis, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds;
one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma with subtle and wonderful voices.
Beholding the Buddha’s great supernormal power, they further give rise to immeasurable vows.
Thus ends this brief exposition of the ninth stage, the sphere of activity for those of great wisdom— profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-Six;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
In the twenty-second chapter, "The Fifty Stages," Part Five:
An exposition of the unsurpassed deeds performed by the great bodhisattvas,
[as witnessed by] countless nayutas of devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
In the space above, their hearts were filled with great joy;
with minds of profound reverence, they all made manifold and wondrous offerings to the Buddha.
Those nayutas of bodhisattvas were filled with immeasurable delight.
They burned various wondrous and marvelous incenses to extinguish all afflictions.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, together with the great assembly of devas, dwelt in the midst of the void; their hearts were filled with great joy.
With hearts full of reverence, they prepared various kinds of offerings;
each scattered many precious garments, which spun in circles through the air as they descended.
Countless billions of celestial maidens, their faculties filled with joy and delight, [participated].
In the space above, with reverent hearts they made offerings to the Buddha,
performing countless billions of *nayuta* musical performances;
from all the precious instruments, these sounds emerged:
"The Buddha sat in this place, pervading all things;
throughout the lands of the ten directions, Buddhas likewise appear.
With immeasurable billions of various marks and signs, their bodies are adorned with majesty."
Exquisite and beyond compare, it fills the entire world.
From within a single pore, immeasurable rays of light emerge,
extinguishing all the fires of affliction in the world.
The number of motes of dust in the ten directions may still be calculated,
But the light from a single pore cannot be exhausted.
Each beholds the Buddha-body, Adorned with the thirty-two marks.
Adorned with the eighty minor marks, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Some see the Buddha in his various forms, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes;
others see him in Tuṣita Heaven, transforming and teaching the devas.
Some see him descending from Tuṣita to enter the womb;
some see the time of his initial birth, or his departure by night;
some see him sitting at the site of enlightenment, accomplishing the unsurpassed path.
Sometimes they see him turning the wheel of Dharma, and sometimes they see him entering nirvana.
In immeasurable lands, he manifests in various ways;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, there are such occurrences as these.
Just as a skilled illusionist, well-versed in the arts of illusion,
displays to many sentient beings various and diverse bodily forms; so too,
within the wisdom of the Buddha, one is skillful in manifesting [all things].
He manifests all manner of bodies, pervading all worlds.
All phenomena are empty and quiescent; from the beginning, they have lacked intrinsic nature or characteristics.
Being identical to space, the Great Teacher is likewise so.
Having attained entry into the ultimate truth, the subtle nature and characteristics,
and in accordance with the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, they manifest the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas.
The nature of all Buddha-activities, as well as all dharmas and sentient beings—
All are equally signless, for all phenomena are empty.
If you wish to attain the Buddha-wisdom, you should abandon all conceptual thoughts.
Thoroughly penetrating both existence and non-existence, you will swiftly become a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The hosts of celestial maidens all produced such millions of kinds of wondrous sounds,
yet they remained silent as they gazed upon the Buddha.
When the Bodhisattva Moon of Liberation saw that the assembly was entirely silent, he spoke.
He addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"From the ninth stage up to the tenth, regarding all the great supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas,
I pray that you will now explain them briefly."
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses such immeasurable wisdom and skillfully practices the Buddha-way, up to the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), they skillfully accumulate pure and white dharmas and gather immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Protected by great merit and wisdom, they extensively practice great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), deeply understand the distinctions between various worlds, enter the difficult places where sentient beings dwell, and enter the spheres of activity of all Tathāgatas. They keep in mind the sphere of the Tathāgata’s quiescent conduct, incline toward the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of all Buddhas, and, firmly maintaining them without relinquishing, they reach the station of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice such wisdom and draw near to the stage of Buddhahood, they attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, which manifests before them; furthermore, there manifest before them a million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, such as: the Samādhi of Entering the Differentiations of the Dharma Realm; the Samādhi of Adorning the Site of Enlightenment; the Samādhi of Raining Down the Radiance of Flowers upon All Worlds; the Ocean-Treasury Samādhi; the Ocean-Seal Samādhi; the Samādhi of the Vastness of Space; the Samādhi of Contemplating the Nature of All Dharmas; the Samādhi of Following the Mental Activities of All Sentient Beings; the Samādhi of Knowing All Dharmas as They Truly Are; and the Samādhi of Attaining Faith in the Wisdom of the Tathāgata. All such samādhis thus manifest before them.
This bodhisattva enters all these samādhis and thoroughly understands the distinctions among their functional applications; the final samādhi is named "Advancing the Stage of All-Knowledge."

When this samādhi manifests before him, there immediately emerges a great king of precious lotuses. It is as vast in circumference as a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; it is adorned with every kind of jewel interspersed in such a way that it surpasses all that exists among humans and devas. It is produced by supramundane roots of goodness and is accomplished through the wisdom of emptiness that knows all phenomena to be like illusions and transformations.
Its radiance can illuminate all worlds. Lapis lazuli forms its stem, the king of sandalwood forms its calyx, agate forms its filaments, and Jāmbūnada gold forms its petals.

Within it are immeasurable lights and all manner of exquisite jewels; a net of jewels covers it from above, and it is surrounded by a retinue of lotuses as numerous as the atoms within thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body was exquisite and harmoniously proportioned to the flower throne;
by virtue of the power of the samādhi of attaining the stage of omniscience, his body sat upon the great lotus throne.

Immediately, upon the lotuses of his retinue, there were Bodhisattvas, each sitting upon a lotus, who instantly attained a million samādhis and all with single-minded reverence gazed up at the Great Bodhisattva."

When this bodhisattva ascends the lotus throne, all worlds currently existing in the ten directions tremble greatly; all evil realms are completely stilled; light universally illuminates the worlds of the ten directions; all worlds become entirely adorned and purified; and all are able to see and hear the great assemblies of the Buddhas.

Why is this? When this bodhisattva sits upon the great lotus flower, there immediately issue forth from beneath his feet a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which illuminate the Avīci hells and other realms throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings;
from his two knees, he emits various rays of light, which illuminate all animals throughout the ten directions, eliminating their suffering and affliction.
From his navel he emitted various rays of light, which illuminated all hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions, extinguishing their suffering and affliction;
from his left and right flanks he emitted various rays of light, which illuminated the people of the ten directions, bringing them peace, security, and happiness;
and from both hands he emitted various rays of light, which illuminated the palaces of the devas and asuras throughout the ten directions.
From his two shoulders he emitted various rays of light, illuminating the assembly of śrāvakas throughout the ten directions;
from his neck he emitted various rays of light, illuminating the pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions;
from his mouth he emitted various rays of light, illuminating the bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, including those dwelling in the ninth stage.

From his white curl between the eyebrows, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the bodhisattvas who had attained their positions throughout the ten directions, causing all the palaces of Māra to be obscured and vanish from view.
From the crown of his head, he emitted millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, illuminating the great assemblies of Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

After circling them ten times, the light remained suspended in space, forming a network of radiance—lofty, vast, brilliant, and pure—as an offering to all Buddhas. Such an offering surpassed by a hundredfold all the offerings made from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the ninth stage; indeed, it is beyond the reach of any calculation or analogy.

This great net of light surpasses all offerings of flowers, incense, powdered incense, ointments, robes, banners, canopies, various jewels, necklaces, and mani-gems found throughout the worlds of the ten directions;

for it is born from supramundane roots of goodness. At every great Dharma assembly of each Buddha, it rains down various jewels like a vast cloud. Any sentient beings who perceive this offering are all destined for the unsurpassed Great Way.
After these lights have rained down such great offerings, they circumambulate the great assembly ten times and enter beneath the feet of the Buddhas.

At that time, the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, knowing that a certain Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in a certain world was practicing such a path and had achieved the reception of office (*abhiṣeka*), immediately caused boundless Bodhisattvas from the ten directions—even those dwelling in the ninth stage—to come and surround him.
They established a great offering and paid homage with single-minded reverence; each attained ten thousand samādhis, and all received their office.

From the chest of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, adorned with vajras, there issued forth a great light named "Destroyer of Mara’s Thieves," with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of lights as its retinue. It illuminated the worlds of the ten directions and displayed immeasurable spiritual powers, then likewise entered the chest of this great Bodhisattva. Once this radiance had subsided, the Bodhisattva immediately attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great powers, supernatural faculties, and wisdom.

"At that time, all the Buddhas emitted from the white tuft between their eyebrows a light named 'Benefiting All Wisdom,' accompanied by an immeasurable and boundless retinue of radiance. It illuminated all worlds throughout the ten directions and circled them ten times, manifesting the great supernatural powers of all Buddhas. It exhorted and inspired immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas; the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, extinguishing the suffering and affliction of all evil realms. All the palaces of Māra were eclipsed and became invisible, while the places where all Buddhas attained the Way were revealed.
Furthermore, the magnificent arrays of the great assemblies of all Buddhas were displayed—vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space."

Having illuminated all worlds, [the light] gathered in the void and displayed the manifestations of great supernormal powers and adornments; it entered the crowns of this Bodhisattva and his retinue’s radiance.
It then entered the crowns of the Bodhisattvas upon the lotuses of the retinue, whereupon each immediately attained ten thousand samādhis never before obtained.
As this radiance entered the crown of this Bodhisattva like the light of a single Buddha, so too did the lights of all Buddhas do likewise.

When the light of all Buddhas of the ten directions enters the crown of this bodhisattva’s head, it is called "attaining office" and "entering the realm of all Buddhas"; he becomes endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha and is reckoned among the ranks of Buddhas.

O Son of the Buddha! It is like this: for example, when the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the marks of royalty, the Wheel-Turning Sage King places his son upon a throne of Jāmbūnada gold atop the precious white elephant; he takes water from the four great oceans and, with various adornments of banners, streamers, and music, holds a golden vessel of fragrant water and pours it over the son’s head. Thereupon, he is named the Great King of Consecration. Because he fully possesses and turns the ten paths of wholesome action, he is called a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: at the time of receiving his office, all Buddhas pour the water of wisdom upon the crown of this Bodhisattva’s head, naming him a consecrated Dharma King. Because he is fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, he is reckoned among the ranks of the Buddhas; this is called the stage of the great office of wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

By virtue of this office, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva undergoes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of ascetic practices and difficult tasks. Once this Bodhisattva has obtained this office, he dwells on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), where his immeasurable merits and wisdom continue to increase.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Dharma-Cloud Stage (dharmameghā-bhūmi), they know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the accumulation of the form realm (rūpadhātu), and the accumulation of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);

they know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the nature of the world, the accumulation of the nature of sentient beings, the accumulation of the nature of consciousness, the accumulation of the nature of the conditioned (saṃskṛta), the accumulation of the nature of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), the accumulation of the nature of space, the accumulation of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the accumulation of the nature of nirvāṇa, and the accumulation of the nature of false views and all afflictions (kleśa).”

They know, as it truly is, the arising and ceasing of all worldly phenomena; the accumulation of the path of the śrāvakas, the accumulation of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, and the accumulation of the path of the bodhisattvas;
the accumulation of the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of the Buddhas, as well as the accumulation of the form-body and the dharma-body;
the accumulation of omniscience, and the attainment of the Buddha-way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the manifestation of parinirvāṇa.
To state the essentials:
it is the thorough knowledge of the distinctions and accumulations of all phenomena as they truly are.

By means of such wisdom, this bodhisattva accords with the practice of enlightenment and knows, as they truly are, the transformation of sentient beings, the transformation of karma, the transformation of afflictions, the transformation of views, the transformation of worlds, the transformation of the dharma-realm, the transformation of śrāvakas, the transformation of pratyekabuddhas, the transformation of bodhisattvas, the transformation of tathāgatas, the transformation of all things, and the transformation of discrimination and non-discrimination.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the sustaining power of the Buddha, the sustaining power of the Dharma, the sustaining power of karma, the sustaining power of afflictions, the sustaining power of time, the sustaining power of vows, the sustaining power of past lives, the sustaining power of conduct, the sustaining power of the lifespan of an eon, and the sustaining power of wisdom.
When this bodhisattva dwells in the tenth stage, they know, exactly as they are, all the subtle wisdoms of the Buddhas, namely:

the subtle wisdom of conduct; the subtle wisdom of the end of life; the subtle wisdom of entering the womb; the subtle wisdom of birth; the subtle wisdom of renouncing the world; the subtle wisdom of attaining the Way; the subtle wisdom of mastery over supernormal powers; the subtle wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma; the subtle wisdom of sustaining the lifespan; the subtle wisdom of manifesting parinirvāṇa; and the subtle wisdom of the long endurance of the Dharma—all such subtle wisdoms they know in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, regarding the secret realms of all Buddhas—namely:

the secret of body, the secret of speech, the secret of mind, the secret of knowing the timely and the untimely, the secret of bestowing predictions upon bodhisattvas, the secret of gathering and subduing sentient beings, the secret of the distinctions between the various vehicles, the secret of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among faculties, the secret of actions performed according to reality, and the secret of attaining enlightenment through practice—they know all such secrets as they truly are.
This Bodhisattva possesses the wisdom of all Buddhas for entering into eons (*kalpa*), namely:
a single eon subsumes incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and incalculable eons subsume a single eon;
numbered eons subsume unnumbered eons, and unnumbered eons subsume numbered eons.
A single thought-moment encompasses an eon, and an eon encompasses a single thought-moment;
an eon encompasses that which is not an eon, and that which is not an eon encompasses an eon;
an eon in which a Buddha exists encompasses an eon in which no Buddha exists, and an eon in which no Buddha exists encompasses an eon in which a Buddha exists.
Past and future kalpas encompass the present kalpa, and the present kalpa encompasses past and future kalpas;
future and past kalpas encompass the present kalpa, and the present kalpa encompasses future and past kalpas;
long kalpas encompass short kalpas, and short kalpas encompass long kalpas.
He knows, as they truly are, the characteristics that encompass all kalpas.

This Bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the wisdom of entering atoms attained by all Buddhas; the wisdom of lands; the wisdom of the bodies and minds of sentient beings; the wisdom of sentient beings attaining the Way through their bodies and minds; the wisdom of the conduct of sentient beings; the wisdom that reaches all places; the wisdom of traversing the Buddha-way everywhere; the wisdom of conforming conduct; the wisdom of contrary conduct;
and inconceivable wisdom—all of which cannot be known by any in the world, nor by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas. He knows them all as they truly are.
O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of all Buddhas is vast and immeasurable; when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to enter into such wisdom.

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing according to this stage, attains the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation, unimpeded liberation, pure conduct liberation, universal-gate illumination liberation, Tathāgatagarbha liberation, liberation that follows unhindered discourse, liberation that enters the three periods of time, liberation of the Dharma-nature treasury, illumination liberation, and supreme advancement liberation.

With these ten liberations as the foremost, this bodhisattva likewise attains immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* liberations; hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis; hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs; and hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). It is just so.

This bodhisattva, having accomplished such wisdom and being in accord with bodhi, achieves immeasurable power of mindfulness; in a single moment of thought, they can reach the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas in the ten directions and receive and uphold immeasurable illumination of the Dharma and immeasurable rains of the Dharma.
For example, when the Dragon King Sāgara pours down great rain, nothing except the great ocean can receive it;

likewise, the subtle and secret rain of the Tathāgata and the rain of the Great Dharma cannot be received by any sentient beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even bodhisattvas up to the ninth stage (navamī-bhūmi). Only this bodhisattva dwelling on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi) is able to fully receive and uphold them.

For example, the great ocean can receive the rain-clouds raised by a single dragon king; it can likewise receive those raised by two, three, or even an infinite and boundless number of great dragon kings, all pouring down at once, and it can sustain them all.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they are able to receive the rain of the great Dharma-light from a single Buddha; from two Buddhas, three Buddhas, and even from unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, they are able to endure and receive it all within a single thought-moment. Because of these great Dharma-cloud rains from all such Buddhas, this ground is named the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha!
How much rain of the great Dharma-light can this bodhisattva endure and receive within a single thought-moment?"
He replied: "O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds throughout the ten directions; and suppose every sentient being in all those atom-sized worlds were to attain the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, becoming an attendant of a Buddha and a great śrāvaka foremost in extensive learning."

Suppose, for example, there were a bhikṣu named Suvinita under the Tathāgata Vajrapadmottama, and one sentient being were to achieve such power of extensive learning, while all others did likewise; such that what was received by one person would not need to be asked again by another, and in this way each individual’s experience was distinct from the others—what do you think?
"Is the power of all these sentient beings who uphold and preserve what they have heard great?
He replied, "It is exceedingly great, beyond measure or calculation."

“O Son of the Buddha! I shall now explain for you this Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). In a single thought-moment, at the presence of a single Buddha, they receive the great rain of the light of the Dharma—the treasury of teachings of the three periods of time. The power of the vast learning of all sentient beings combined cannot equal even one hundredth part of it; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

Just as at the presence of one Buddha, they can hear and uphold the great rain of the light of the Dharma from as many Buddhas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, so too can they hear and uphold even more than that—immeasurable and boundless—even within a single thought-moment. For this reason, it is called the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.”
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they give rise from the power of their vows to great compassion, merit, and wisdom, which serve as dense clouds;
they manifest various bodies, which serve as multicolored clouds.
Pervasive clarity and fearlessness serve as flashes of lightning;

thundering with the great sound of a dragon’s roar, they preach the Dharma to subdue Māras. In a single thought-moment and at a single time, they are able to pervade all the aforementioned worlds as numerous as motes of dust.

By raining down the nectar-like rain of the sublime Dharma, they extinguish the flames of affliction arising from ignorance that follow the inclinations of all sentient beings; for this reason, it is called the Ground of the Dharma Cloud (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Dharma-Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), within a single world-system—from descending from the Tuṣita Heaven until manifesting Great Parinirvāṇa—they display all Buddha-activities and supernatural powers according to the needs of those to be converted. This extends to two or three worlds, or even as many worlds as there are atoms;

furthermore, they descend from the Tuṣita Heaven, manifest Great Parinirvāṇa, and perform all Buddha-activities, displaying supernatural powers according to the needs of those to be converted throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya worlds.
When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they attain supreme mastery over wisdom; they may make a narrow land wide and a wide land narrow;
or they may make a defiled land pure and a pure land defiled.

Thus, they possess supernatural power over all such worlds. Furthermore, within a single minute atom, this bodhisattva can place the Mount Cakravāḍa mountains, rivers, and peaks of a trichiliocosm without causing any crowding or compression.
Whether two or three, or even as many as unspeakably unspeakable worlds, he demonstrates the entry of all their various adornments into a single atom;
or he demonstrates the adornments of a single world within unspeakably unspeakable worlds;
or he places the sentient beings of unspeakably unspeakable worlds within a single world without causing them any crowding.
Or they may place the sentient beings of a single world-system into unspeakably unspeakable numbers of world-systems;
or they may cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of world-systems to enter into a single atom without distressing the sentient beings;
or within a single atom, they may manifest the adornments of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas.
Or, within a single thought-moment, they manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds; within each body, they display immeasurable hands.

With each hand, they grasp lotus flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to scatter before all Buddhas, as well as various fragrances, powdered incense, banners, canopies, and precious objects—all such articles of adornment are held in their hands to make offerings to the Buddhas, and this is likewise done by every single body.

Furthermore, each individual body manifests as many heads as there are atoms in a speck of dust, and within each head are tongues as numerous as atoms. With such supernormal powers, they praise all Buddhas; such deeds fill the ten directions in every moment of thought.

In every moment of thought, by means of their supernormal powers, they manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and even Great Parinirvāṇa in immeasurable worlds.

Throughout the three periods of time, they manifest immeasurable bodies by supernormal power, and within their own bodies, they manifest immeasurable Buddhas and the adornments of immeasurable Buddha-lands; within their own bodies, they manifest the formation and destruction of all worlds.
Or, from a single pore, they may emit all winds without afflicting sentient beings;

or, they may take immeasurable and boundless worlds as a single ocean of water, within which they produce a great lotus flower whose color, form, and radiance pervade immeasurable and boundless worlds, therein manifesting the wondrous adornments of the Bodhi tree, up to and including the manifestation of the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);

or, within their own bodies, they may manifest the mani-jewels, suns, moons, stars, and all lights of a world-system in one direction, and likewise for all the lights existing throughout the ten directions.
Or they may exhale from their mouths such that immeasurable worlds in the ten directions are all greatly shaken, yet they cause sentient beings to have no thought of fear;

or they may manifest the exhaustion of the water kalpa, the wind kalpa, and the fire kalpa in the worlds of the ten directions, while the bodies of sentient beings remain adorned according to their wishes;

or they may manifest their own body as the body of a Tathāgata, the body of a Tathāgata as their own body, the body of a Tathāgata as their own Buddha-land, and their own Buddha-land as the body of a Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), their spiritual transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) are such as these; furthermore, they manifest other immeasurable sovereign powers (*vibhutva*).

At that time, the various bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā Devendra, Īśvara, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas within the assembly each had this thought:
"If the supernatural power and the power of wisdom of a bodhisattva are thus immeasurable and boundless, what then of a Buddha?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Now this great assembly, having heard of the power of this bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges and wisdom, has fallen into a net of doubt; you should now sever all their uncertainties and demonstrate the wondrous deeds of a bodhisattva’s supernormal adornments.

Then, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha immediately entered the samādhi of the Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands. At that time, the entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-devaputra, Īśvara-devaputra, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas—all perceived themselves entering into the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha. Within his body, they beheld the various adornments of the trichiliocosm, such that even if one were to describe them for an entire kalpa, they could not be exhausted.

Within that [palace], he saw the Bodhi tree of the Buddha’s site of enlightenment; its trunk was ten thousand three-thousandfold world systems in circumference and one million three-thousandfold world systems in height, covering three hundred billion three-thousandfold world systems. In proportion to the height and breadth of the tree, there was a lion throne.

Upon that throne sat a Buddha named Sarvajñatā-rāja Tathāgata. The entire great assembly clearly beheld the Buddha seated upon the throne; as for all the magnificent and sublime implements of offering therein, even if one were to describe them for an entire kalpa, they could not be fully exhausted.

After the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had manifested such great supernormal powers, he restored the great assembly to their respective places; the entire congregation, struck with a sense of wonder, remained silent and single-mindedly gazed upon Vajragarbha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This samādhi possesses great power and is most rare; what is the name by which this samādhi is known?"
He replied, "This samādhi is named 'The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands. He asked:
“What is the power and the scope of this samādhi? He replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully cultivates and accomplishes this power of samādhi, they can manifest within their own body as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are atoms in immeasurable Ganges-sands of worlds, and even more than that number.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmiḥ*), they attain such immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of great samādhis;
therefore, while dwelling in this stage, their body and bodily actions are difficult to fathom,
and their speech and verbal actions are difficult to fathom.
The mind and mental karma are difficult to fathom;
sovereign spiritual power is difficult to fathom;
the contemplation of phenomena across the three periods of time is difficult to fathom.
The practice of various samādhis and their entry [into them] is difficult to fathom;
the power of wisdom is difficult to fathom;
and the playful mastery of various liberations is difficult to fathom.
The transformations they perform, the feats of supernatural power they manifest, and the deeds they accomplish at will are difficult to fathom;
even the mere lifting and lowering of their feet cannot be measured by Bodhisattvas dwelling on the Stage of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī).
O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma is thus immeasurable; if it were to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in the course of immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha!

If such are the power of the sphere of activity and the power of the supernormal knowledges of a bodhisattva, then what are the power of the sphere of activity and the power of the supernormal knowledges of a Buddha like?"
He replied: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a person who, seeing a single clod of earth, speaks these words:"
"Is the nature of the ground of infinite worlds more numerous than this?
Regarding what you have asked, I say it is so;
