how can the immeasurable wisdom of a Tathāgata be sought to be measured by the wisdom of a bodhisattva?
O Son of the Buddha!

It is as if a person were to take a tiny fraction of the earth-element from among the four continents, while the remainder is exceedingly vast; even so, the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) can only be described over the course of immeasurable eons, let alone the stage of the Tathāgata. I shall now speak of it so that you may know it, with the Buddhas manifesting as witnesses.

Suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are atoms in the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, and these worlds were entirely filled with Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage; though these Bodhisattvas possess immeasurable and boundless karma, having cultivated the merit, wisdom, and meditative concentrations of a Bodhisattva, they do not equal even one hundredth part of the power of the Tathāgata’s merit, wisdom, and strength—not even one part in a hundred-thousand-million-billion, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
“O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva, following such wisdom and conforming to the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata, does not abandon the samādhis of all bodhisattvas. With a diligent mind, they make offerings to all Buddhas; in each and every kalpa, they offer all manner of requisites to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, fully receiving the spiritual powers of all those Buddhas so that they become increasingly bright and superior. Regarding the questioning and debating of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no one who can surpass this bodhisattva, even throughout immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.”
“O Son of the Buddha!

It is like celestial gold, interspersed with mani-jewels and various treasures, serving as an ornament for the body of the Sovereign King of Gods (Śakradevendra), which none of the other gods can equal and which no one can seize. Likewise, the wisdom and roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage cannot be equaled by those from the first through the ninth stages;
because this Bodhisattva dwelling in this stage attains the illumination of great wisdom and accords with all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), their wisdom cannot be destroyed by any other wisdom.”

For example, the radiance of Maheśvara, King of the Gods, can cause the bodies and minds of sentient beings to become cool and refreshing; yet this radiance cannot reach those beings in any place of birth.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma possesses the radiance of wisdom that no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can reach, nor even the Bodhisattvas of the nine lower grounds.
When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to cause immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the path of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the Buddhas of the ten directions expound for them the wisdom of the three periods of time, the wisdom of the dharma-realm, the wisdom of all worlds, the wisdom that universally illumines and sustains all worlds, and the wisdom of great kindness and great compassion that universally covers all sentient beings.
To state the essentials:
he fully expounds for them the path leading to all-knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the tenth stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the celestial king Maheśvara. Their wisdom is clear and penetrating; they skillfully expound upon the *pāramitās* of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas. Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), even when faced with those who pose difficult questions and challenges, no one is able to exhaust their discourse.

All the wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and so on, up to never being apart from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He constantly reflects:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming their refuge."

"If one wishes to practice such diligent effort, in a single thought-moment one shall attain samādhis as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds, and even manifest as many bodhisattvas as those atoms to serve as one's retinue."
If, through the power of vows and sovereign spiritual penetrations, they exceed even these numbers—namely:

by means of supreme and wondrous offerings for all practices, arising from the karma of faith and understanding; whether by body, speech, light, the sense faculties, the bases of psychic power, voice, or sphere of activity—even for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they remain beyond calculation.
O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva proceeds through the ten stages in successive order, tending toward all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is like the four rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta; they satisfy the four continents without exhaustion before finally entering the great ocean.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: from the Bodhisattva flow the waters of the roots of goodness and great vows; by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they satisfy sentient beings without exhaustion, until reaching all-knowledge.
“O Son of the Buddha!
These ten stages of the bodhisattva possess distinctions because of the Buddha’s wisdom, just as there are ten great mountain kings upon the vast earth. What are these ten?
They are as follows:

the King of Mountains Himavat, the King of Mountains Gandhamādana, the King of Mountains Kailāsa, the King of Mountains Ṛṣigiri, the King of Mountains Yugandhara, the King of Mountains Aśvakarṇa, the King of Mountains Nimindhara, the King of Mountains Cakravāḍa, the King of Mountains Pūrvavideha, and the King of Mountains Sumeru.
Just as all medicinal herbs gather within the King of Snowy Mountains and can never be exhausted;
so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling on the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) contain within him all the worldly scriptures, arts, poetry, and incantations, which are likewise inexhaustible.
Just as Mount Gandhamādana is the place where all fragrances gather and are inexhaustible, so too is the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (vimalā-bhūmi);
there, the observance of precepts, the dhūta practices, and the supportive dharmas of dignified conduct gather together without end.
Just as Mount Kailāsa, the king of mountains, is composed solely of jewels and gathers all manner of exquisite flowers that can never be exhausted;

so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Radiance gather all worldly meditative concentrations, supernormal powers, liberations, and samādhis, such that they can never be exhausted through inquiry.
Just as the King of Mountains of Seers and Sages is composed solely of jewels and contains an inexhaustible multitude of sages possessing the five supernatural powers,

so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Blazing Flames (Arciṣmatī) gather the causes and conditions for sentient beings to enter the Path, such that their various inquiries and challenges are inexhaustible.
Just as Mount Gandhamādana, being composed solely of jewels, gathers an inexhaustible multitude of great yakṣas;
so too does the bodhisattva dwelling on the Ground Difficult to Conquer gather all sovereign and spontaneous supernormal powers, which can never be fully described.
Just as Mount Aśvakarṇa, consisting solely of jewels, gathers a multitude of exquisite fruits that can never be exhausted;
so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Presence gather the profound dharma of causes and conditions, such that the explanation of the fruits of the Śrāvakas can never be exhausted.
Just as Mount Nimiṃdhara, the king of mountains, is composed solely of jewels and gathers all the most powerful nāgas and devas in inexhaustible numbers;
so too does the bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of Far-Going gather various skillful means and wisdoms, and in expounding the path of the pratyekabuddha, he is inexhaustible.
Just as Mount Cakravāḍa, the king of mountains, is composed solely of jewels, and the collection of the masteries of those who have attained mental sovereignty can never be exhausted;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi): the collection of all the paths of Bodhisattva mastery and the exposition of the nature of the world can never be exhausted.
Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is composed solely of jewels and gathers the great supernatural powers of the asuras without end;
so too does the bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Good Intelligence gather the wisdom that transforms the conduct of sentient beings and expound upon the characteristics of the world without end.
Just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is composed solely of jewels and gathers celestial deities without end, so too is the Bodhisattva:

dwelling on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), he gathers the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) of the Tathāgata, and his exposition of the Buddha-dharmas is inexhaustible.
These ten jewel mountains all exist within the great ocean, yet they possess distinct characteristics due to the waters of the great ocean;
likewise, the ten stages of a bodhisattva all reside within the Buddha’s wisdom, yet they possess distinct characteristics due to the nature of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, the great ocean is called the "great ocean" by virtue of ten characteristics, and none can destroy it. What are these ten?
First, it becomes progressively deeper;
second, it no longer receives corpses;
third, other waters lose their original names.
Fourth, the single flavor;
fifth, the many jewels;
sixth, the extremely deep and difficult to enter.
Seventh, vast and immeasurable;
eighth, possessing many large-bodied sentient beings;
ninth, the tides do not miss their appointed times.
Tenth, it is able to receive all great rains without overflowing.
The Bodhisattva stage is likewise; by means of ten causes and conditions, it cannot be destroyed. What are these ten?
In the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one gradually gives rise to firm vows;
in the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), one does not cohabit with those who break the precepts;
in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), one relinquishes all provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
In the Blazing Ground (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), one attains unshakable pure faith in the Buddha;
in the Difficult to Conquer Ground (Sudurjayā-bhūmi), one gives rise to immeasurable worldly skillful means and supernormal powers to engage in worldly affairs;
and in the Manifest Ground (Abhimukhī-bhūmi), one contemplates the profound law of dependent origination.
In the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*), one skillfully contemplates all phenomena with a vast and expansive mind;
in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one is able to manifest great adornments;
and in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), one attains profound liberation and penetrates worldly conduct, remaining in accordance with reality without error.
Within the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), one is able to receive the great rain of the Dharma-light from all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a great maṇi jewel that possesses ten qualities by which it can provide all manner of treasures to sentient beings. What are these ten?
First, it is taken from the great ocean;
second, it is refined by a skilled craftsman;
third, it is further polished to exquisite perfection.
Fourth, removing impurities;
fifth, refining and treating with fire;
sixth, adorning with various jewels.
Seventh, it was threaded with precious cords;
eighth, it was set upon tall pillars of lapis lazuli;
ninth, its radiance shone in the four directions.
10. Raining down various precious objects according to the king’s will.
The jewel of the Bodhisattva’s resolve for enlightenment also has ten aspects. What are these ten?
First, the initial resolve for enlightenment consists of practicing generosity and abandoning stinginess.
Second, practicing the ascetic dhūtas and austerities of the precepts;
third, causing them to become increasingly refined through various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis;
fourth, purifying them through the practice of the Path.
Fifth, it is refined by skillful means and supernormal powers;
sixth, it is adorned with the profound dharma of causes and conditions;
seventh, it is threaded together by various profound skillful means and wisdom.
Eighth, they are established upon the banner of mastery in the supernormal powers;
ninth, observing the conduct of sentient beings, they radiate the light of wisdom born of great learning;
tenth, the Buddhas confer upon them the office of knowledge, enabling them to perform the Buddha-work for all sentient beings and to be reckoned among the ranks of the Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This chapter on the Dharma-door of the Collection of All Wisdom and Meritorious Qualities practiced by these Bodhisattvas cannot be heard unless one has deeply planted roots of goodness.”
He asked: "O Son of the Buddha!
If one should hear this, how much merit would that person obtain?"

He replied: "In accordance with the power of the Buddha's wisdom, when one thus generates the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), the merit encompassed by that object of focus is such that the merit obtained by a person who hears this Dharma-gate is likewise the same."

Why is this? If one lacks the bodhicitta, even upon hearing this Dharma-gate, one cannot believe, understand, accept, or uphold it; how much less could one cultivate it with the body to accomplish its purpose? Therefore, you should know that such a person accords with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thus is able to hear, believe, understand, accept, uphold, and practice it.

When this chapter was being spoken, worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten billion Buddha-lands in the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners. Because the Dharma is thus through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the devas rained down flowers, powdered incense, necklaces, precious robes, banners, canopies, and ornaments for the body; they rained down celestial music and songs of praise, while great sounds further extolled the sublime matters of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).
Just as the Ten Stages were taught in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven within the four continents of this world, so it was in all worlds throughout the ten directions;

by the spiritual power of the Buddha, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields from worlds beyond ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions came to this world, filling the entirety of space, and all spoke these words: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! Vajragarbha, you have well explained the Dharma of the ten stages of the bodhisattvas.
"O Son of the Buddha!"

We are all named Vajragarbha; we have set out from the world-system Vajraguṇa, coming from the presence of the Buddha Vajradhvaja. In every place we have passed through, we have preached this sutra; the assemblies were like this, and the words and meanings were likewise so. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, we have come to bear witness to this matter. Just as we have arrived here, so too in the mani-jewel palaces of the kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven in all worlds throughout the ten directions, there are bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields who have come to serve as witnesses, and it is exactly the same in each case.

At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva surveyed the ten directions, surveyed the entire great assembly, and surveyed the dharma-realm. He praised the initial arousal of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), revealed the domain of the bodhisattvas, purified the power of bodhisattva conduct, and encompassed all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Speaking in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, he removed the defilements of all worlds, provided the causes and conditions for the all-aspect wisdom of sentient beings, and displayed the inconceivable adornment of wisdom. He extolled the distinct characteristics of the merits of all bodhisattvas;
wishing to cause the successive stages (*bhūmi*) to become increasingly superior and clearly manifest to sentient beings, he, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, spoke in verse:
“The conduct of all bodhisattvas delights in sublime tranquility;
their minds are without attachment, just like space.
Having removed the stains of greed, hatred, and delusion, they dwell securely in the wisdom of the Path.”
Such is the supreme practice; I pray that you will grant me the opportunity to hear it.
These bodhisattvas, throughout immeasurable eons, have constantly cultivated all roots of goodness with a diligent mind.
Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats,
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he gave rise to the bodhicitta.
With diligence he maintained the practice of the precepts, and through dhūta austerities he removed the defilements of sin.
Cultivating wholesome patience becomes sublime; with shame and remorse, one is full of majestic virtue.
By means of the causes and conditions of merit and wisdom, one’s superior mind is far-reaching, clear, and pure.
Deeply delighting in the Buddha’s knowledge, one gives birth to bodhi together with the Buddha.
Making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time,
causing all lands as vast as space to be entirely purified;
because they have thoroughly and skillfully attained mastery over the equality of all phenomena.
To deliver all sentient beings, they give rise to the bodhicitta.
All bodhisattvas, in this manner, generate this immeasurable mind;
reaching the Stage of Joy, they cease evil and delight in giving.
Having attained the power of all original vows, They expand and broaden their hearts of compassion;
Deeply practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, They are able to reach the Ground Free from Defilement.
Fully endowed with the merits of precepts and learning, With compassionate hearts, they pity the world.
Forever free from all defilements, with a profoundly pure mind,
he universally observes that throughout all worlds the fires of the three poisons blaze fiercely;
such a Great Being enters the Third Stage of Radiance.
Contemplate that the three realms are all empty; impermanence is like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound pierced by an arrow, with immeasurable suffering constantly present.
Seeing the faults of all conditioned things, one comes to delight in the virtues of the Buddha.
Attaining the radiant flame of the Buddha’s wisdom, one enters the fourth stage.
Accomplishing mindfulness and wisdom, one attains the knowledge of the Path;
making offerings here to hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas.
Constantly able to contemplate and recollect the immeasurable virtues of all Buddhas,
one attains entry into all the stages of the world that are difficult to conquer.
Through wisdom and skillful means, one is able to manifest in various ways.
Whatever deeds one performs, they benefit the world; Making offerings to all Buddhas and acting for the welfare of sentient beings,
With the dharma of non-arising before them, They enter the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī*).
Whatever deeds the Bodhisattvas perform, all the worlds know them;
they are always without a self-centered mind, being entirely free from both existence and non-existence.
All phenomena are primordially empty and quiescent, yet they proceed by way of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Thoroughly understanding this subtle and wondrous [truth], one enters the stage of Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā).
Practicing wisdom and skillful means in equal measure, one attains the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena.
Such a Great Being is difficult to know and difficult to reach.
Desiring to cause the world to attain sublime tranquility,
he again gives rise to the cultivation of various practices and all manner of meritorious deeds.
He enters universally into the various mental dispositions and spheres of activity of sentient beings.
Thus one is able to enter the immovable stage that is like space.
The bodhisattvas of great wisdom are fully capable of practicing all manner of various intellectual activities and attain the ten powers of mastery.
Able to manifest, throughout the realms of the ten directions, Infinite and boundless bodies by means of the immeasurable, They preach the sublime Dharma for all.
They have thoroughly mastered the worlds As well as the natures of all sentient beings.
With such great compassion, one is able to enter the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Possessing the foremost, wondrously pure wisdom, one skillfully observes all worlds,
the threads of afflictions and karma, and the profoundly deep and difficult places.
In order to deliver these beings, he has attained the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas;
he skillfully expounds the ultimate truth (paramārtha) without any contradiction or error.
Practicing in this successive order, he becomes fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Up to and including the ninth stage, one accumulates merit and wisdom.
Desiring to attain the powers of all Buddhas and the foremost, profound, and wondrous benefit,
one then receives the rank of the position of knowledge from all Buddhas.
First one attains countless concentrations, And the practice of wisdom becomes exceedingly vast;
Finally, one attains the indestructible Samādhi of the stage of all-knowledge.
If one can thus attain The samādhi of the stage of increasing wisdom,
Adorned with every kind of jewel, the Lotus King emerged;
the Bodhisattva named Padma manifested his body and sat upon it.
All the other Bodhisattvas of the various lotuses gazed at him with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the Great Bodhisattva emitted from his body immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light, extinguishing the sufferings of all worlds.
Thereafter, from the crown of his head, there issued forth hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light.
Universally illuminating the realms of the ten directions and the great assemblies of all Buddhas,
it transforms into a net of light within the space above;
having made offerings to all Buddhas, it enters beneath the feet of those Buddhas.
At that time, all the Tathāgatas and the various Great Beings each knew that a certain Bodhisattva had received the office of wisdom.
All these Buddhas then emitted light from between their eyebrows.
Named "Benefiting All-Knowledge," he enters this Bodhisattva-peak.
All the infinite Buddhas confer upon this Bodhisattva their office,
just as a Wheel-Turning King invests his crown prince with the throne.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions all shook violently;
even in the Avīci hell and other realms, all sufferings were extinguished.
The Bodhisattva, possessing all wisdom, attained this office.
Thus it is called reaching the ground of the Cloud of Dharma, unsurpassed.
Abiding within this ground, one’s wisdom is boundless;
skillfully knowing how to deliver all beings from the various causes and conditions of the world.
Entering into the dharmas of the form and formless realms, as well as the desire, form, and formless worlds,
they are able to know sentient beings, their lands, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, they can enter into both countable and uncountable dharmas.
Even unto the ability to observe The infinite nature of space;
Furthermore, this stage fully knows The transformative deeds of Bodhisattvas,
The majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, And the subtle, secret matters of wisdom.
Furthermore, they are able to fully penetrate and comprehend all the enumerations of kalpas,
observing all worlds within a single atom.
All Tathāgatas, upon this unsurpassed stage, [attain such mastery].
Birth and renunciation, attaining the Way and turning the wheel of Dharma,
manifesting entry into nirvana— all these accord with wisdom;
this wondrous liberation of tranquil extinction is fully attained upon this ground.
The great beings of this stage, by virtue of the power of their mindfulness,
are able to receive and uphold all the great Dharma rains of the Buddhas.
Just as the waters of the great ocean can sustain the rain of the dragon kings, so too do they sustain the Buddha's teachings.
The vast Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise received by the Bodhisattvas. If,
in the presence of a single Buddha, they hear and receive the Dharma at one time,
it reaches sentient beings as numerous as atoms throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions.
Though all have attained great learning and dhāraṇī, and perfected the Śrāvaka vehicle,
they cannot compare to such a Bodhisattva, who is beyond the reach of calculation.
By means of immeasurable wisdom and the power of their former great vows, [they surpass them all].
Able, within a single thought-moment, to pervade immeasurable lands;
raining down the nectar-like Dharma rain, extinguishing the fires of all afflictions—
for this reason, the Tathāgatas name this stage the Cloud of Dharma.
When the Great Being dwells in this stage, his offerings to all Buddhas surpass those of all the devas; he universally displays great supernormal powers.
He manifests to the assembly superior powers beyond measure.
If a person wishes to deliberate upon this, they will be bewildered and unable to understand it.
When one of great wisdom dwells in this stage, even the lifting and lowering of their feet is beyond the reach of all bodhisattvas, up to those on the ninth stage.
None are able to know this, let alone other sentient beings,
nor the śrāvakas of the three periods of time, nor the pratyekabuddhas.
Abiding here, all the Buddhas reveal the matters of all-encompassing wisdom.
They also cause others to attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the three periods of time;
they demonstrate the quiescence of the nature of phenomena,
yet also manifest various transformations throughout all worlds and among all classes of sentient beings.
All phenomena practiced, profound, subtle, hidden, and remote matters,
and all the merits of the Buddhas— these he demonstrates in sequence to bring about understanding.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he is able to employ great articles of offering.
Making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout all worlds—
this surpasses all other types of sentient beings in all the worlds; no other ritual implements can ever equal it.
The wise ones dwelling on this stage are able to shatter all the darkness of ignorance and reveal the path of the Buddha.
Like the Sovereign King of Gods, their light extinguishes the heat of all afflictions.
The light of wisdom of the Buddha’s heirs extinguishes evil in this same way.
Dwelling in this stage, they mostly become sovereign kings over the three realms;
they penetrate all forms of wisdom and skillfully transform beings through the three vehicles.
Within a single thought-moment, one can attain immeasurable samādhis;
one can see the Buddhas of the ten directions, their number being likewise infinite.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha to the great beings:
"I shall now briefly explain the sublime practices of the ten stages;
were they to be expounded in detail, they would not be exhausted even in a thousand billion kalpas.
These are called the pure stages of the great bodhisattvas."
For the sake of attaining the Buddha-wisdom, they dwell within the ten stages,
abiding securely and immovable like the king of great mountains.
In the first stage, they possess all scriptures and various arts and crafts.
Just as within the Snowy Mountains, a multitude of medicinal herbs are gathered;
so too do those who uphold the precepts and possess great learning abide upon these two stages.
Just as the King of Fragrant Mountains collects all manner of fragrant substances; so it is with them.
Just as Mount Kailāsa is piled high with various precious flowers,
so too is the Ground of Radiance (Prabhākārī-bhūmi), where the wisdom of hearing is gathered;
the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi) likewise amasses much, entering the dharmas of the Path without impairment.
Just as in the mountains of the seers and sages, where the Well-Quiescent One dwells and roams,
none among those with the supernatural powers of the fifth stage can equal him;
like Mount Yugandhara, he gathers a great multitude of yakṣas.
On the sixth stage, one skillfully discerns that all fruits are inexhaustible;
like Mount Aśvakarṇa, these wondrous fruits are immeasurable.
On the seventh stage, with the wisdom of skillful means, there is none who can equal it.
Like the Nimiṃdhara mountain, filled with various dragon kings;
dwelling within the eighth stage, their sovereign wisdom is immeasurable.
Like Mount Cakravāḍa, they are masters of many minds.
In the ninth stage, the mind is pure and one preaches the Dharma without obstruction;
like Mount Sumeru of ancient wisdom, it is the dwelling place of asuras.
In the tenth stage, there are the powers of all Buddhas, whose merits are inexhaustible.
Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, he gathers all the hosts of devas.
Furthermore, in the first bhūmi, he gives rise to vast vows;
in the second bhūmi, he maintains the category of ethical discipline (śīla); in the third bhūmi, he destroys conventional designations (prajñapti).
In the fourth stage, there is single-minded concentration; in the fifth, manifold wonders;
in the sixth, the profound characteristics; in the seventh, the vast mind;
in the eighth, various kinds of adornments through all supernormal powers.
On the ninth stage, one contemplates wondrous wisdom, capable of transcending all worlds;
on the tenth stage, one is able to receive and uphold the great Dharma rain of all Buddhas.
The ocean of the Bodhisattva’s practice is difficult to shake and inexhaustible.
Generating the mind for the supramundane, one enters the first stage;
In the second stage, one purely maintains the precepts; In the third stage, one cultivates various dhyānas;
In the fourth stage, the practice of the path is purified; In the fifth, one refines skillful means and wisdom.
Sixth, adorned with the six causes and conditions; seventh, possessing profound skillful means and wisdom;
eighth, reaching the lapis lazuli banner; ninth, observing all sentient beings in places of every peril and difficulty, the light of wisdom shines everywhere.
Upon attaining the office of wisdom in the tenth stage, it is like a jewel that follows the king’s will;
thus, through successive purifications, the wondrous jewel of the bodhicitta [shines forth].
Throughout all the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms they contain—
Within a single thought-moment, one could calculate their number;
with the tip of a single hair, one might count the reaches of empty space.
Yet the great merits of all Buddhas are immeasurable and inexhaustible.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-seven and Volume Twenty-eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Ten Clarities.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of clarity. What are these ten?
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, namely:

They fully discern and know all such immeasurable and diverse kinds of sentient beings' minds as: wholesome minds, unwholesome minds, indeterminate minds; expansive minds, narrow minds, evil minds, superior minds; minds that follow the cycle of birth and death, minds that turn away from the cycle of birth and death; the minds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the minds of those practicing the path of śrāvakas, the path of pratyekabuddhas, and the path of bodhisattvas; the minds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, beings in the realm of Yama, and beings in the various states of affliction. Thus, they thoroughly distinguish and know all such infinite varieties of sentient beings' minds.

In this way, they are able to discern and know the mental thoughts of all sentient beings in hundreds of worlds, thousands of worlds, hundreds of thousands of worlds, billions of worlds, hundreds of billions of worlds, trillions of worlds, hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, and even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds; and so on, as extensively described, up to as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the clear realization of the knowledge of others' minds.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fully knows all sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—how they die here and are born there;
their various destinies of good and evil;
and whether they are handsome or ugly.
Whether defiled or pure;
whether black or white—
such are the immeasurable varieties of sentient beings.

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, subtle beings, small beings, medium beings, great beings, superior beings—such immeasurable and diverse kinds of beings die here and are born there.

By means of their unobstructed, luminous, and pure divine eye, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to perceive clearly all the pleasure and pain experienced according to their karmic retributions; they can see all various karmas, various practices, various thoughts and vows, and various views, exactly as they are within the sphere of karma and exactly as they evolve.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second unimpeded light of wisdom of the divine eye of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva recollects past lives—whether his own or those of others—and is able to remember all the events of immeasurable, innumerable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas within worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, innumerable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
he fully understands such births, such names and clans, such food, and such experiences of suffering and joy.

Furthermore, I recall the names, retinues, parents, attendants, śrāvakas, and supreme pair of great disciples of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields in the past; I recall how they left their royal capitals to renounce the world and seek the Way, how they sat cross-legged beneath Bodhi trees and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, their dwelling places, their seats, their preaching of the Dharma, their transformations and deliverances, their lifespans, and how, after performing these Buddha-works, they entered nirvana without remainder, and how the True Dharma remained for such a long duration after the Buddhas had passed away.

They are able to recollect all Buddhas—numbering as many as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields from the past—their initial aspiration, the arising of their vows and practices, their respectful offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, their teaching and taming of all sentient beings, their assemblies and retinues, their turning of the pure wheel of Dharma, their manifestation of sovereign transformations through spiritual powers according to the duration of their lifespans, their entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder, the adornment of their stupas and temples, the nurturing of roots of goodness, and even until the end of the Dharma’s abiding.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third profound penetration of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the unimpeded wisdom-light of recollecting past lives throughout the kalpas of the past.
O Son of the Buddha!"

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter deeply into future kalpas, even unto worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable, incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, observing the future cycle of birth and death within the three realms of existence for all sentient beings.

He knows the karma of sentient beings and knows their retribution; he knows the wholesome of sentient beings and knows their unwholesome; he knows the emergence of sentient beings and knows their non-emergence; he knows the fixed nature of sentient beings and knows their unfixed nature; he knows the right-fixation of sentient beings and knows their wrong-fixation; he knows which sentient beings possess latent roots of goodness and knows which do not; he knows which sentient beings are endowed with roots of goodness and knows which are not; he knows which sentient beings embrace the wholesome and knows which embrace the unwholesome; he knows which sentient beings accumulate the wholesome and knows which accumulate the unwholesome; he knows which sentient beings accumulate unwholesome dharmas and knows which do not accumulate unwholesome dharmas.

I know the names of the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields in the future; I know their retinues, their fathers and mothers, their attendants, their śrāvakas, and their two most eminent great disciples; I know how they leave behind their royal capitals to renounce the world and seek the Way; I know how they sit cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree and attain supreme perfect enlightenment; I know their dwelling places, their seats, their preaching of the Dharma, their transformation and deliverance of beings, their lifespans, and how, having performed the works of a Buddha, they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and how, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remains for such a long duration.

They fully know the initial generation of the mind, the arising of vows and practices, the respectful making of offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, the teaching and taming of all sentient beings, the assemblies of retinues, the turning of the pure wheel of Dharma, the manifestation of sovereign transformations through spiritual powers according to their lifespans, the entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder, the adornment of stupas and temples, the nurturing of roots of goodness, and even the duration of the Dharma’s abiding—all belonging to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of future Buddha-fields.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth profound illumination of unimpeded wisdom of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding the kalpas extending to the limit of the future.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives birth to the unimpeded divine ear, which is pure, vast, and fully perfected; it is immeasurable, cultivated until realization is attained, purified and free from hindrances, and characterized by definitive penetration.

The Bodhisattva achieves the unimpeded divine ear; regarding all sounds, whether far or near, throughout the ten directions, they can hear whatever they wish to hear with complete mastery according to their will.

As for the teachings spoken, uttered, revealed, demonstrated, established, disciplined, converted, contemplated, analyzed, and taught by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—numbering as many as the atoms within immeasurable, innumerable, unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields in the eastern direction—including their profound and subtle skillful means, infinite and pure, all such things he is able to hear and retain.

They are able to hear and retain, without any forgetfulness, the excellent meaning, the excellent phrasing, that which accords with the assembly, accords with individuals, accords with sounds, accords with wisdom, accords with consciousness, accords with the merits obtained through those to be converted, accords with the objective realm, accords with the basis, and accords with the path of deliverance.
He extensively expounds the sublime Dharma to deliver all beings, not losing even a single phrase or a single flavor;
as it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in all the ten directions.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth unimpeded, pure celestial ear wisdom-illumination of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
O Son of the Buddha!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in the light of wisdom of fearless supernormal power, attaining mastery in the supernormal power of non-action, the supernormal power of equality, the supernormal power of vastness, the supernormal power of immeasurability, the supernormal power of non-reliance, the supernormal power of reaching through mindfulness, the supernormal power of non-retrogression, the supernormal power of non-regression, the supernormal power of inexhaustibility, the supernormal power of indestructibility, the supernormal power of nurturing growth, and the supernormal power of conforming conduct.

If one hears of all the present Buddhas in all worlds throughout the ten directions—immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, boundless worlds, limitless worlds, incalculable worlds, inconceivable worlds, immeasurable worlds, and even worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Having heard this, they were all able to go to the abodes of those Buddhas, where they paid respectful homage, offered praise and offerings, and deeply understood that the various adornments and various merits of the Tathāgatas' pure Buddha-fields, as well as their immeasurable virtues, were entirely filled with perfection.
They manifest immeasurable mastery and immeasurable realms, praising all Tathāgatas and reverently making offerings to them.

They manifest their bodies so as to be present at the abodes of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, yet without departing from this place; they fully understand for themselves that they have gone to those places, where they pay respectful homage, praise, and make offerings, inquire about the Bodhisattva teachings, and give rise to the wisdom of the Buddhas.

He beholds the various Buddha-fields, retinues, and emanations; he knows the characteristics of the preaching of the Dharma and the characteristics of the Buddha-fields, remaining entirely free from attachment.
He has brought all matters to ultimate completion, reaching the other shore, with his spiritual power unimpaired.
Swiftly pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions, there is no Buddha they do not see, no Dharma they do not hear, and no assembly they do not know.

They constantly hear the True Dharma without interruption; delighting in seeking the Buddha-Dharma, their supreme vows are fulfilled, and they fully cultivate the immeasurable practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth [stage] of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: abiding in the light of wisdom of fearless supernormal power.
O Son of the Buddha!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fully comprehend the sounds and languages of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. That is to say:

the languages of central lands, the languages of borderlands, the languages of devas, the languages of nāgas, the languages of yakṣas, the languages of gandharvas, the languages of asuras, the languages of garuḍas, the languages of kiṃnaras, the languages of mahoragas, the languages of humans, and the languages of non-humans. Regarding such unspeakably unspeakable varieties of differing voices among sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fully comprehend them, discerning them well, entering into all conventional designations, and deeply penetrating and understanding all worldly truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
They fully know all various modes of speech and sound; they discern and understand all modes of speech and sound, entering the great ocean of every kind of speech and sound.
Following their entry therein, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas travel through the worlds and are able to fully understand the natures of the sentient beings within those worlds;
having known their natures, they thoroughly comprehend all modes of speech and sound.
Just as the Sun Deity emerges to illuminate all forms, enabling those with eyes to see all visible phenomena;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who enters into all clouds of speech and sound, and skillfully understands the nature of all speech and sound.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which discriminates all speech and sounds.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows all form-dharmas:
they are not produced as form, they have no manifold forms, they have no illusory forms, and they have no shapes such as blue, yellow, red, or white.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the profound Dharma-realm and dwells in and sustains various manifested forms:
immeasurable colors, luminously pure colors, pristine colors, universally manifesting colors, colors resembling those [of others],
universally illuminating colors, attained colors, undefiled colors, colors endowed with all marks, and pure colors.
The color of marks, the color free from evil, the color of great power, the color of respectability, the inexhaustible color, the unending color, the variegated color,
the dignified color, the immeasurable color, the color of well-trained learning,
the color of well-nourished growth, the matured color, the color that accords with transformation and deliverance, the unobstructed color, and the translucent color.
The color of form, the stainless color, the translucent color, the upright-body color, the color of inconceivable skillful means, the indestructible color, the most excellent color,
the color free from obscurity, the color free from darkness, the firm and strong color, the well-blended color,
the color of the marks of merit, the color of graceful beauty, and the color of the Great Self.
The color of the objective realm, the well-tamed color, the pure and upright color, the superior color,
the excellent and vast color, the indestructible color, the color without dependence, the peerless color, the color that fills unspeakable Buddha-fields,
the nurturing color, the most firm and solid color, the victorious color, and the formidable color.
The color of supreme merit; the color that accords with aspiration; the color of pure nature; the color of eternal goodness;
the color of excellent determination; the unobstructed color; the color of the luminous purity of space; the color of pure cultivation;
the stainless color; the color free from dust; the color free from various kinds of dust; the color of skillful manifestation; the universal...
The manifested form, the form displayed according to the occasion, the form of tranquility, the form of detachment from desire,
the true form of merit and field of blessings, the form of peace and security, the form of impartial deportment free from fear,
the form of transcendent wisdom, the form of the unimpeded body, the form of the body that travels everywhere, and the form free from delusion.
The color arising from great loving-kindness; the color sustained by great compassion; the color of emerging toward the correct destination;
the color endowed with the power of merit; the color following right mindfulness; the color of immeasurable jewels;
the color of the luminous pure treasury; the color that causes all sentient beings to rejoice; the color of the gateway to omniscience; and the color of the joyful eye.
The color of incomparable adornment with all jewels; the color of a mind free from attachment; the color of non-solidity; the color of sovereign maintenance;
the color of sovereignty over various spiritual powers; the color of being born into the family of the Tathāgata;
the color of incomparability; the color of filling the Dharma-realm; the color of approaching according to sentient beings; and the color of manifold variety.
The color of perfect feet; the color of virtuous conduct; the color of ultimate transformation; the color that one never tires of beholding;
the color of immeasurable variegated light; the color of emitting immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* flames of light; the color of unspeakably various radiances;
the color of inconceivable fragrant light universally perfuming the three realms; and the color of immeasurable solar radiance.
The color of blazing light; the color of the image of the moon beyond measure; the color of clouds of flowers emitting immeasurable bliss;
the color of clouds adorned with various garlands of precious flowers; the color of all-world-surpassing fragrant flames that universally permeate;
the color of the treasury of merits produced by all Tathāgatas; and the color of extensively expounding a single [teaching] through immeasurable sounds.
All phenomena manifest as forms, and all modes of conduct are fully endowed with the form of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the formless realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), they maintain and manifest various transformed forms according to what is appropriate; that is to say:

They teach through vision, teaching through right mindfulness, teaching by turning the wheel of Dharma, teaching according to the occasion, teaching moment by moment, teaching through intimacy, teaching by following after, teaching through spiritual powers, teaching through various masteries, and teaching through inconceivable great supernormal transformations; in all these ways, they are able to deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth birth of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: the wisdom-light of the adornment of immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya physical bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully know that all phenomena have no names;
they know that all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature;
and they know that all phenomena neither come nor go.
He knows that all phenomena are distinct;
he knows that all phenomena are not distinct;
he knows that all phenomena are neither dual nor non-dual.
Knowing that all phenomena are without self;
knowing that all phenomena are peerless;
knowing that all phenomena are unarisen.
They know that all phenomena are not extinguished;
they know that all phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere;
they know that all phenomena are indestructible.
Knowing that all phenomena are unreal;
knowing that all phenomena are not unreal;
knowing that all phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the absence of characteristics.
Knowing that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent;
knowing that all phenomena are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas;
knowing that all phenomena are neither language nor non-language.
Knowing that all phenomena are not karma, and knowing that all phenomena are not non-karma;
knowing that all phenomena are not retribution, and knowing that all phenomena are not without retribution;
knowing that all phenomena are not created, and knowing that all phenomena are not uncreated.
He knows that all phenomena are not the ultimate truth;
he knows that all phenomena do not emerge, and he knows that all phenomena do not fail to emerge;
he knows that all phenomena are not finite, and he knows that all phenomena are not infinite.
Knowing that all phenomena are not of the world, yet knowing that all phenomena do not depart from the world;
knowing that all phenomena are not born of causes, yet knowing that all phenomena are not born without cause;
knowing that all phenomena are not fixed in form, yet knowing that all phenomena are not unfixed in form.
He knows that all dharmas are not endowed with form, yet he knows that all dharmas are not devoid of form;
he knows that all dharmas do not emerge from birth-and-death, yet he knows that all dharmas are not such as not to emerge from birth-and-death;
he knows that all dharmas are not false, yet he knows that all dharmas are not such as not to be false.
He knows that all dharmas are neither expedient means nor non-expedient means.
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows these various dharmas in this way, he does not cling to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) nor does he cling to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
he does not falsely grasp at dharmas, nor does he give rise to verbal designations; he accords with the nature of cessation (*śānta-dharmatā*), yet does not abandon any of his vows.
Perceiving the primary ultimate truth, they definitively know all phenomena; they raise immeasurable clouds of Dharma, universally raining down the nectar-like Dharma rain upon all.
They enter ineffable skillful means and transcend ineffable skillful means.

With inexhaustible eloquence, he extensively expounds the meaning of reality as it is, never contradicting the true Dharma; through skillful means, he teaches all dharmas with an inexhaustible eloquence.
Having accomplished great compassion, they abide in a realm beyond words, yet give rise to the meaning of words without destroying the nature of words.
They observe that all phenomena arise from conditions and remain free from any defilement or attachment.
They understand all modes of language and expression, providing guidance and instruction, praising and manifesting them with complete purity, and extinguishing the web of doubts for all beings.
They gather in sentient beings without abandoning the true Dharma, never falling back from the non-dual Dharma.
They are fully endowed with the subtle voice of the unimpeded dharma-gate, universally raining down the rain of Dharma without ever missing its proper time.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth light of true wisdom regarding all dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

“O Son of the Buddha! In every thought-moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the cessation of all phenomena and does not regress; yet he does not abandon the bodhisattva’s activities, nor does he abandon the mind of great compassion, nor does he abandon the various *pāramitās*. He is skillfully able to discern all Buddha-fields without ever becoming weary or satisfied; he does not abandon his great vows to deliver sentient beings, nor does he abandon the turning of the wheel of Dharma, nor does he abandon the teaching and taming of sentient beings. He does not abandon making offerings and paying respect to all Buddhas, nor does he abandon the dharma-gate of mastery over all dharmas. He does not abandon the constant vision of all Buddhas, nor does he abandon the constant hearing of the true Dharma of all Buddhas.”

They are able to give rise to all unimpeded dharmas; they know that all dharmas are entirely equal; they fully accomplish all the supreme dharmas and vows of all Buddhas; they enter deeply into all Buddha-fields; they reach the ultimate further shore of the lineage of all Buddhas; in all worlds, they are able to skillfully learn everything;

regarding all the characteristics of dharmas they have studied, they penetrate deeply into those characteristics; they skillfully know that all dharmas arise from conditions; and they understand that all dharmas lack any true reality.
Conforming to the linguistic conventions of the world, they remain unstained by and unattached to any phenomena;
according to what is appropriate, they skillfully expound all dharmas.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in the meditative absorption of the cessation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirodha-samāpatti*), may abide for one eon, or a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or a billion eons, or ten billion eons, or a hundred thousand billion eons, or a hundred trillion eons, or a quadrillion eons, or a quintillion eons, or a sextillion eons; or he may abide for immeasurable eons, or boundless eons, or incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, or inconceivable eons, or incomparable eons, or limitless eons, or unspeakably unspeakable eons.

They constantly abide in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that extinguishes all phenomena; their countenances remain unchanged, their bodies suffer no decay, and they are neither destroyed nor dispersed. They cannot be burned, cannot sink, cannot be lost, and cannot be exhausted.
Regarding both existence and non-existence, they perform no action, yet they are fully capable of accomplishing all the deeds of a bodhisattva.
He is extensively able to expound all dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings, never missing the proper time;

he nurtures all the dharmas of the Tathāgatas, fulfills all the practices of Bodhisattvas, and does not abandon the benefit of all sentient beings, manifesting transformations throughout the ten directions without ceasing for even a moment.
Without abandoning the universal illumination of all realms of existence, they remain tranquil and unmoving within the stage of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the knowledge of the extinction-concentration (*nirodha-samādhi*) regarding all phenomena.

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this illumination, it cannot be conceived by any devas or humans; it cannot be conceived by any in the world; it cannot be conceived by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it cannot be conceived by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages. Their physical, verbal, and mental karma are inconceivable; their mastery over all samādhis is inconceivable; and the realm of their wisdom is inconceivable."
Only the Tathāgata is able to expound the merits of such a person; no one else is capable of doing so.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of luminous wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"By abiding in this illumination of wisdom, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully attain the unimpeded illumination of wisdom regarding the three periods of time.
Chapter 24: The Ten Endurances (*Daśakṣānti*) At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra again addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of the Buddha!..."

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish ten kinds of patience, they are able to attain the stage of all-unobstructed patience, and further attain the inexhaustible and unobstructed dharmas of all Buddhas.
What are these ten?

They are: the patience of conforming to sounds, the patience of conformity, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, the patience that they are like illusions, the patience that they are like mirages, the patience that they are like dreams, the patience that they are like echoes, the patience that they are like lightning, the patience that they are like transformations, and the patience that they are like space.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of patience of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they have been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by all Buddhas of the future, and are being taught now by all Buddhas of the present.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience that accords with the sound [of the Dharma]?

It is when, upon hearing the true Dharma, one is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; one believes, understands, accepts, and upholds it, cherishing it, entering into it in accordance with it, cultivating it, and dwelling securely within it.”
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first patience of accord with sounds for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s acquiescence in accordance (*anulomikī kṣānti*)?
O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva accords with tranquility, contemplates the equality of all phenomena, maintains right mindfulness without contradicting any phenomena, accords with and deeply penetrates all phenomena, and discerns all phenomena with a pure and straightforward mind.
Cultivating the contemplation of equanimity, they enter deeply and become fully endowed with it.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second conformative patience of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma arising, nor does he perceive any dharma ceasing.
Why is this? Because that which does not arise does not cease.
If there is no cessation, then there is no exhaustion;
if there is no exhaustion, then there is freedom from defilement;
if there is freedom from defilement, then there is no destruction.
If there is no destruction, then there is no movement;
if there is no movement, then it is the stage of quiescence;
if it is the stage of quiescence, then there is freedom from desire.
If one is free from desire, there is no activity;
if there is no activity, that is the great vow;
if it is the great vow, one abides in adornment.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
O Son of the Buddha!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s acceptance that all things are like an illusion?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva deeply penetrates the fact that all phenomena are entirely like illusions, and contemplates the dharma of dependent origination.
Within a single dharma, they understand manifold dharmas; within manifold dharmas, they understand a single dharma.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas differentiate various lands within those dharmas;
they enter the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.
He contemplates the world with equanimity;
he contemplates the Buddha’s entering and emerging as non-dual—his entry, emergence, and abiding—as being like an illusion, not consisting of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, or infantry;
neither male nor female.
It is not a boy or a girl;
it is not a tree, nor leaves, nor flowers, nor fruit;
it is not earth, water, fire, or wind.
Neither day nor night;
neither half-month nor month;
neither year nor hundred years.
It is neither moon nor sun; it is neither the calculation of kalpas;
it is neither fixed nor chaotic.
Neither one nor different;
neither pure nor mixed;
neither good nor evil.
It is neither many nor few;
neither measurable nor immeasurable;
neither coarse nor subtle.
The various multitudes are not illusion, and illusion is not the various multitudes;
it is only because of illusion that the various forms and images are manifested.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, observing that all worlds are entirely like illusions, namely:

The world of karma, the world of afflictions, the world of buddha-fields, the world of dharmas, the world of the three periods of time, the world of saṃsāra, the world of formation, the world of destruction, and the world of conditioned activity.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all worlds as being entirely like illusions, they do not give rise to the notion of sentient beings, nor do they destroy the notion of sentient beings;
they do not give rise to the notion of lands, nor do they destroy the notion of lands;
they do not give rise to the notion of phenomena, nor do they destroy the notion of phenomena.
One does not grasp at the false marks of the past, nor does one construct the future;
one does not transform the future or the present, nor does one abide in them or have any attachment to them;
one does not observe bodhi, nor falsely grasp at bodhi.
One does not grasp at the appearance of a Buddha in the world, nor is there the nirvana of a Buddha;
one does not dwell in great vows;
one does not grasp at purity or the equality that transcends birth—there is neither emergence nor attachment.
They give birth to the adornment of pure Buddha-fields and definitively know the true Dharma;
they give birth to the realm of sentient beings and discerningly know those beings;
they definitively know the Dharma-realm and abide immovably in the True Dharma.
They enter equally into the three periods of time, yet do not contradict the differentiation of those three periods.
They give rise to the aggregates and sense bases while eliminating their underlying supports;
they deliver sentient beings, observing the dharma-realm with equality, without any distinction.
He knows that all phenomena are neither words nor speech, yet he does not abandon his profound and wondrous eloquence.
He turns the wheel of Dharma without attachment to the transformation of sentient beings; for the sake of sentient beings, he upholds great compassion to deliver them all.
He explains past causes and conditions, truly knowing all phenomena, yet there is nowhere to which they go.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth illusory-like patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding the mirage?
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva realizes that all worlds are entirely like a mirage; they are like a shimmering heat haze, having no fixed location or direction.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva definitively knows that all dharmas likewise have no location or direction:
they are neither internal nor external;
neither existent nor non-existent.
It is neither eternal nor annihilated.
One contemplates that all phenomena are entirely true as mere conventional designations; they are not a single form, nor are they manifold forms;
they are not the realm of formlessness, yet one fully realizes and knows all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth patience of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, known as "the Patience Like a Mirage.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding dreams?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva understands that all worlds are entirely like dreams.
For example, it is like a dream: neither mundane nor supramundane;
neither the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm;
neither birth nor death.
It is neither pure nor defiled;
it is neither clear nor turbid, yet it manifests appearances.

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all worlds are entirely like dreams—neither destroying the dream nor clinging to the dream—for the nature of the dream is quiescent, and the dream has no intrinsic nature.

One should uphold the realization that all phenomena are entirely like dreams; one does not destroy the dream, nor does one grasp at the dream as false, but awakens to the fact that all worlds are entirely like dreams.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth patience of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, known as "the patience like a dream.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience like an echo?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva gives rise to all dharmas, achieves mastery through skillful study, reaches the ultimate in the noble Dharma, and attains the further shore.
He knows that all phenomena are entirely like echoes;
he discerns all sounds as being like echoes, which have no point of origin.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands that the voice of the Tathāgata does not emerge from within, does not emerge from without, and does not emerge from both within and without.

Those who hear that sound do not find it within, nor without, nor both within and without; yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom of skillful means, understanding that sound is like an echo, arising entirely from conditions, while never undermining the gift of the Dharma.
They penetrate deeply into sounds and voices, remaining far removed from inversion, and skillfully study all things.
Just as the consort of Śakra produces a thousand wondrous sounds within a single sound, yet does not grasp at those illusory sounds.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise: entering the dharma-realm free from delusion, they produce the sounds of skillful means throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds, extensively turning the pure wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and delivering them all.

They uphold the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue, producing immeasurable and unobstructed sounds that fill all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to attain universal understanding and to give rise to roots of goodness;

yet these sounds do not shift and cannot be described. They know that sound is not speech, yet they accord with speech; furthermore, they are untainted by various sounds, awakening to and thoroughly understanding all sounds.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh patience of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, known as 'Patience Like an Echo.
O Son of the Buddha!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like lightning?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva is not born in the world, nor does he die in the world.
Neither within the world nor outside the world;
neither practicing in the world nor not practicing in the world;
neither destroying the world nor not destroying the world.
Not arising in the worldly realms, yet not departing from the worldly realms;
not equal to the world, nor unequal to the world;
neither the world, nor apart from the world.
They do not practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, yet they do not abandon their great vows;
they are neither real nor unreal.

Their practice is true and authentic, bringing to ultimate fulfillment all the true dharma of the Tathāgatas and being able to accomplish all worldly affairs. Yet they do not follow along with the flow of the world, nor do they undergo the flow of the true dharma.

It is like lightning, or the sun, or the moon, which can illuminate everything—mountains, trees, men, women, houses, walls, the great earth, flowing waters, and so forth—rendering them bright and clear.
Just as water, oil, the body, a precious jewel, and a bright mirror—all such pure forms—are able to illuminate all pure realms.
Lightning is not separate from clarity and purity, and clarity and purity are not separate from lightning; while lightning can illuminate afar, the lightning itself is neither distant nor near.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: he is able to illuminate all realms of self and others, yet his wisdom does not engage in discrimination as it illuminates and manifests all realms of self and others.
Just as within a seed there are no roots, sprouts, stalks, nodes, branches, or leaves, yet it can serve as a cause, so too is it with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
within the dharma of non-duality, they differentiate two aspects and cultivate the limit of non-obstruction.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth lightning-like patience (*vidyut-sama-kṣānti*) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, although they do not go to the presence of the various Tathāgatas, they manifest universally in all Buddha-fields; yet they do not arise from this world, nor do they arrive at any other world.

The Bodhisattva manifests his body pervading all worlds, appearing like a flash of lightning; he travels without obstruction, reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions, unimpeded by diamond mountains or any solid objects.
He fully accomplishes the pure actions of body, speech, and mind of the Buddha-family, and attains immeasurable, pure bodies of all forms.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the ninth patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the patience regarding the nature of transformations?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This Bodhisattva knows that all worlds are entirely like transformations (*nirmāṇa*), namely: the transformation of the karma of all sentient beings;

the transformation of the conduct of all sentient beings; the transformation of all falsehoods; the transformation of all perversions of suffering and pleasure; the transformation of all false grasping; the transformation of all unreal phenomena in the world; the transformation of all paths of speech; and the transformation of all afflictions, because they arise from various conceptions;
as well as the transformation for the purpose of taming sentient beings, because it is free from defilement and pure.
The transformation of non-retrogression throughout the three periods of time, because it is equal to the unborn;
the transformation of the bodhisattva’s vows, because it nurtures the bodhisattva practices;
the transformation of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, because it eradicates all the sufferings of sentient beings.
This is the transformation through the skillful means of the Dharma-wheel wisdom, because it gives birth to immeasurable fearlessness, wisdom, and eloquence.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understands the world and effects transformations that transcend the world, definitively knowing the vast, the immeasurable, the boundless, and so forth.
Knowing suchness, they fully accomplish immeasurable mastery;
they remain unshakable within reality, perceiving that all things lack inherent reality and thus do not disrupt their conduct.
For example, like a magical transformation, it does not arise from the mind, nor does it dwell within the mind as it is produced;
it does not arise through karma, nor does it undergo retribution;
it is neither born of the world, nor does it perish with the world.
It is encompassed by what is not Dharma, touched by what is not Dharma;
it does not abide for long, nor does it abide for even a moment;
it is neither worldly conduct nor is it apart from the world.
It does not wander through the various directions, nor is it contained within those directions;
it is neither measurable nor immeasurable;
it is neither weary nor unwearied.
Neither resting nor without rest;
neither ordinary nor holy;
neither pure nor defiled.
Neither born nor dead;
neither ignorant nor wise;
neither seeing nor losing.
It does not rely on the mundane world, nor is it subsumed within the dharma-realm;
it is neither wisdom nor ignorance;
it is neither blazing nor quiescent.
It is neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa;
it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the world and practices the bodhisattva path, upholding skillful means and observing that the entire world is like a magical transformation.
They do not cling to the world, nor do they cling to emanations;
they do not falsely grasp the world, nor do they grasp emanations;
they do not abide in the world, nor do they extinguish the world.
They do not abide in the true Dharma, nor do they follow what is contrary to the Dharma;
yet they do not abandon the teaching and transforming of sentient beings, maintaining constant right mindfulness and fulfilling all vows.
They do not adorn the dharmas, nor do they destroy the dharmas of adornment.
In all phenomena, there is nothing whatsoever; yet one can fully perfect all Buddha-dharmas. Just as a magical creation is neither existent nor non-existent, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
dwelling securely within the patience of being like a magical creation, they are able to fully perfect the enlightenment of all Buddhas and bring benefit to sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth acceptance of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the acceptance that all things are like transformations.
O Son of the Buddha!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, they have no dependence or attachment toward any buddha-field.
Just as a magical creation has no dependence or attachment toward any world, so too does he practice without falsehood regarding all Buddha-dharmas;
like a magical creation, he acts without acting, free from all perversions.
For example, like a magical creation, it is not a body, yet it manifests all bodies;
for example, like a magical creation, it does not rely on form, yet it manifests all forms;
for example, like a magical creation, it does not cling to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), being equally fulfilled in its own nature which is devoid of self-nature.
For example, like a magical emanation, though it is not a dharma of liberation, it can manifest all places of dharmas;
for example, like a magical emanation, it has no inherent location, nor is it subject to discipline, nor is it purified;
for example, like a magical emanation, though it is devoid of all supernatural powers, it proceeds to the abodes of all Tathāgatas.
For example, like a magical transformation, it is irreversible, neither arising nor ceasing, and entirely free from all obstructions; it cannot be hindered by any powers or by any mountains of vajra.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the tenth patience of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which is like space?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva understands that the entire dharma-realm is like empty space because it is devoid of intrinsic nature;
just as with empty space, so too are all worlds, for they understand that all buddha-fields are without arising;
just as with empty space, so too are all dharmas, for they understand the non-duality of phenomena.
Just as space is, so too are the practices of all sentient beings, for they understand that there is nothing to be practiced;
just as space is, so too are all Buddha-dharmas, for they understand them to be without discrimination;
just as space is, so too are all Buddha-powers, for they understand them to be without difference.
Just as space is, so too are all meditative concentrations, for they understand the three periods of time;
just as space is, so too are all teachings of the Dharma, for they understand that which is ineffable;
just as space is, so too are all Buddha-bodies, for they understand non-obstruction.
"Just as space pervades all places, so too do these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas understand all phenomena to be like space.
O Son of the Buddha!

Thus, because these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas understand all phenomena to be entirely like space, they attain the patient acceptance and wisdom equal to space; they attain a body equal to space, and they attain bodily actions equal to space."
They attain a mouth equal to space and attain vocal karma equal to space;
they attain a mind equal to space and attain mental karma equal to space.
Just as space is neither born nor dies, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: the entire Dharma-body is neither born nor dies.
Just as space cannot be destroyed, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; his wisdom and various powers cannot be destroyed.
Just as space is that upon which all worlds rely, yet relies on nothing, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; he is that upon which all dharmas rely, yet relies on nothing.

Just as space is neither born nor extinguished, yet serves as the basis for all birth and extinction, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; being neither directed toward nor accomplished, he causes all sentient beings to become entirely pure.

For example, just as space is neither spatial nor non-spatial, yet can manifest the boundaries of all oceans, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: neither karma nor the retribution of karma, yet able to expound the boundaries of the great ocean of all birth and death.
