They attain skillful means to enter the indestructible true Dharma of all Buddhas;
they attain skillful means to enter all the adorned dharmas of all Buddhas;
they attain skillful means to enter all Buddha-dharmas through a single means.
They attain skillful means, entering the Buddha’s immeasurable methods of skillful means;
they attain skillful means, achieving mastery of mind regarding all Buddha-dharmas and never regressing.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of skillful means.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should listen to and receive this Dharma with single-minded reverence. Why is this?
Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through minimal effort, becoming equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma,
worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakably many billions of nayutas of buddha-fields shook in six ways. There fell rains of clouds of flowers surpassing all those of the devas,
rains of clouds of exquisite incense, rains of clouds of powdered incense, and multitudes of clouds of robes, parasols, banners, and pennants.
Rains of clouds of precious ornaments, rains of clouds of music and song, rains of clouds of all bodhisattvas,
rains of clouds of unspeakable praises of the Buddhas, rains of clouds of unspeakable acclamations of "Excellent!",
rains of clouds of the Buddhas' voices filling the dharma-realm, rains of clouds of unspeakably pure worlds, and rains of clouds of unspeakable nurturing.
The Bodhisattvas’ clouds and rains of merit, unspeakable clouds and rains of light,
and unspeakable clouds and rains of various sovereign spiritual powers— just as in this world of four continents,
where the Buddha sits at the site of enlightenment and rains down such diverse clouds and rains to expound all dharmas, so it is likewise in the worlds of the ten directions.

It is so. At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the Dharma is thus, there came from beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of worlds, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds. They arrived in this land, filling the ten directions, and spoke these words: "Excellent! "
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!

You are able to expound such a profound Dharma of the great vows and predictions of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas. We, who share the same name, Samantabhadra, have come from the presence of the Tathāgatas named Samantadhvaja-viśeṣa in the various Samantavijaya worlds to this land. In all worlds, this Dharma is likewise taught; thus, these word-constituents (*pada-kāya*) and flavor-constituents (*rasa-kāya*), as well as all practices, neither increase nor decrease. For this reason, we have come here to bear witness for you.

In this manner, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-worlds have come here to bear witness; it is likewise so at the abodes of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of his own roots of goodness, surveyed the ten directions and all dharma-realms.

Desiring to clarify the practices of all bodhisattvas and the enlightenment of all Buddhas; desiring to proclaim the great vows; desiring to distinguish all kalpas of all worlds; desiring to clarify how Buddhas manifest their appearance in the world according to the times; desiring to cause all beings to receive transformation according to their faculties; desiring to clarify that all teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are without falsehood; desiring to show that the fruits and retributions of planted roots of goodness are never in vain; and desiring to clarify how the pure Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva emits wondrous sounds to awaken sentient beings and cause them to give rise to the bodhi-mind, he spoke in verse: "All beings are filled with joy, As they eliminate all veils and hindrances."
Listen with single-minded reverence to the vows and practices of the bodhisattvas.
Following the vows and practices undertaken by the bodhisattvas of the three periods of time,
I shall now explain in succession the supreme and wondrous Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
Throughout the reckonings of all kalpas, and the reckonings of worlds and karmas,
I declare that the Peerless One has appeared in the world through emanation.
Having beheld the Buddhas of the past, he made great vows therein.
Benefiting the multitudes of sentient beings, he eliminates all suffering.
This Bodhisattva, King of Treatise-Masters, whose conduct is never interrupted,
has attained the peerless Dharma, the realm of omniscience.
The Bodhisattva beholds all the Teachers of the past, Who emit great nets of light, Universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
He makes this great vow: "May I become a lamp for the world."
With a body adorned by merit and endowed with the wisdom of the ten powers,
I shall extinguish for all living beings the blazing fires of greed, hatred,
and delusion, as well as the immeasurable sufferings of the evil realms.
Having made such a vow, firm and non-retrogressive,
they fully cultivate the multitude of bodhisattva practices and ultimately attain unimpeded power.
Having thus made this vow, they do not turn back from their worldly conduct.
His conduct is free from falsehood, and he has reached the ultimate in expounding the King of Dharmas.
Within this single Bhadrakalpa, a thousand Buddhas appear in the world;
following their true Dharma, he explains it in successive detail.
As it is with the Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, so it is with those of immeasurable kalpas;
I shall now explain in succession the teachings of all future Buddhas.
As is the nature of a single buddha-field, so it is with immeasurable fields.
I shall explain in detail the nature of all Buddha-fields:
the successive appearance of the Buddhas in the world, their vows and their names,
the predictions they receive, and the duration of their lifespans.
According to the True Dharma they practice, they single-mindedly seek the unobstructed path;
according to the sentient beings they transform, the True Dharma abides in the world;
according to the Buddha-fields they purify, so too do sentient beings and the Wheel of Dharma.
Teaching the Dharma at the proper and improper times, he gradually purifies all sentient beings.
According to the conduct of those beings, their various karmic natures,
and the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, he transforms them according to what each should receive.
With such profound wisdom, the bodhisattva enters this practice,
cultivates the deeds of Samantabhadra, and becomes fully endowed with the wheel of wisdom.
Their physical actions are unimpeded, and their verbal actions are entirely pure.
Their mental karma is likewise unimpeded, Penetrating the phenomena of the three periods of time.
When Bodhisattvas practice in this way, They bring the path of Samantabhadra to ultimate fulfillment;
They give birth to the sun of pure wisdom, Universally illuminating all dharma realms.
Throughout unspeakable eons and across all buddha-fields,
the bodhisattva knows them in a single thought, yet remains unattached to them.
The practitioner enters such a wondrous and profoundly deep stage.
Within the sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, I shall now explain a small portion.
Their wisdom is boundless, reaching the ultimate realm of the Buddhas;
they skillfully enter all places and achieve non-retrogression.
Possessing the pure wisdom of Samantabhadra, Fulfilling the vows of Samantabhadra,
The ultimate practice of the Bodhisattvas, They enter deeply into peerless knowledge.
Within a single mote of dust, They contain all buddha-fields.
They behold those immeasurable Buddhas and hear them fully expound the Dharma;
as it is within a single mote of dust, so it is within all motes of dust.
To see the lands and the Buddhas therein is the inconceivable wisdom.
Within each and every atom, the phenomena of the three periods of time are universally manifested;
the paths of birth and death within the five realms of existence are all fully discerned and known.
Within each and every atom, there are immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Within one, they know the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, they know the one.
Thus, regarding the equality of the dharma-realm and all buddha-fields—whether of identical nature or diverse natures—they are able to understand them all completely.
Deeply entering subtle wisdom, they discern all worlds;
The formation and destruction of all kalpas, they can fully analyze and explain.
Knowing the long and short durations of all kalpas, They realize that the three periods of time are but a single thought-instant.
Whether traveling together or not traveling together, they know all distinctions completely.
They enter deeply into all worlds, both pure and impure;
within a single body are infinite lands, and within a single land are infinite bodies.
Throughout all the ten directions, In immeasurable world-systems,
With their various and countless natures, He is able to know them all.
Throughout all the three periods of time, In immeasurable Buddha-lands,
Possessing profound wisdom, they fully comprehend all success and failure.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, whether they are forming or decaying,
Samantabhadra penetrates them all and understands them completely.
With the eye of pure wisdom, they see immeasurable Buddha-fields;
discerning and knowing all karmas, they become purified through their practice.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully know the conduct of sentient beings.
Due to various evil karmas, one obtains an impure land;
though there are immeasurable and boundless lands, they are known as a single land.
Thus entering into all lands, no one at all can know it.
All worlds are made to enter into a single land;
the worlds do not accumulate, nor do they disperse.
Some are face-down, some are face-up; some are high, and others are low.
The characteristics of sentient beings in the worlds, the Bodhisattvas know them all.
Whether there are worlds that are overturned or inverted, or immeasurable Buddha-fields,
they know the many as one, and they know the one as many.
Samantabhadra, true son of the Buddha, with inconceivable wisdom,
knows lands that are difficult to conceive and fully comprehends their boundless limits.
He knows the transformations of all worlds, the transformations of lands, and the transformations of sentient beings.
Knowing all phenomena to be transformations, one realizes that the ultimate is the transformation of the Buddhas.
The profound dharmas of the world, the various matters of adornment,
and the immeasurable retributions of sentient beings— all are the adornments of mental karma.
True sons of the Buddha, well-trained in the profound and wondrous Dharma-realm,
possess sovereign spiritual powers that fill the lands of the ten directions.
Throughout kalpas equal in number to all sentient beings, they constantly expound the laws of the worlds.
None are able to know it, except for the Equally and Perfectly Awakened One.
Regarding the world and the Tathāgata’s various names and titles,
even if one were to expound them for immeasurable eons, one could still not reach their ultimate end.
How much more so the realm of the mind, And the teachings of all Buddhas of the three times?
The true and wondrous Dharma-realm, The ground of all Buddhas,
With pure and unimpeded mindfulness, Possessing unhindered wisdom.
He analytically expounds the Dharma-realm; with wisdom he reaches the other shore.
Such worlds as these are adorned by immeasurable karma.
In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva fully knows all lands of the three periods of time.
In those worlds, they practice the most supreme conduct;
having attained ultimate, perfect enlightenment, they manifest sovereign power.
Thus, in all worlds throughout the future ages, [they shall do the same].
The Buddhas who arise in succession throughout the world, The Bodhisattvas are able to know them all.
Their practice of various sublime vows, Their cultivation of merit within their respective realms,
And their attainment of perfect enlightenment according to the kalpas— The Bodhisattvas distinguish and know them all.
They also know their lifespan and the sentient beings to be transformed;
according to the gates of expedient means, they turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
When Bodhisattvas know this, they are endowed with the stages of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Having accomplished all-knowledge, they are equal to all Tathāgatas.
Throughout the present worlds of the ten directions and the immeasurable Buddha-fields,
they enter deeply into this world and penetrate all realms of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
In that world, there currently dwell countless Buddhas who are kings of mountains of unimpeded discourse, having attained ultimate mastery over the Dharma.
They know the pure lands and their assemblies, possessing the sovereign power of manifesting transformations as required.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, He has constantly contemplated this matter.
The World-Honored One, the Tamer of Men, Has accomplished the power of mastery;
The Bodhisattva’s ultimate deliverance Is a profound entry into the treasury of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva is fully endowed with birth, possessing unimpeded eyes,
ears, and body, and an unimpeded, broad, and long tongue that causes all beings to rejoice.
With the most supreme and unimpeded mind, it is immeasurably and universally pure.
With profound and unimpeded wisdom, they fully comprehend the phenomena of the three periods of time.
Having skillfully mastered all transformations— transformations of lands, transformations of sentient beings,
and the ability to transform the world— they have reached the ultimate shore of transformation.
Adorned with various karmas, they embellish all worlds;
they accomplish the Buddha’s wisdom and skillfully know all characteristics.
Each and every Tathāgata-body, through immeasurable skillful means, [manifests].
According to those who are to be transformed, they deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Deeply entering the realm of wisdom, as the sun of supramundane insight,
their conduct is non-retrogressive as they travel throughout all lands.
Deeply understanding all worlds to be like dreams and magical illusions,
they fully realize that the entire realm of sentient beings is like a flash of lightning;
they do not grasp at false eons nor at any worldly realms.
Skillfully understanding that which is not real, one has no attachment to it.
Within immeasurable and incalculable eons, one understands them as a single thought-moment;
knowing that the thought-moment is also not a thought-moment, one sees that there is no real thought-moment in the world.
Without moving from his original seat, in a single thought-moment he travels through the ten directions;
throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, he constantly transforms all sentient beings.
Inexpressible eons are, in truth, but a single moment of thought.
Nor does he shorten the eons, for he has mastered the dharma of the ultimate moment.
All worlds and the minds of all sentient beings—
neither one nor two— the Bodhisattva fully understands.
Sentient beings, worlds, and eons, The Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma— All are entirely like illusions and transformations; In the dharma-realm, there is no duality.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, They manifest infinite bodies.
Not grasping at the illusory body, one has no attachment to the dharma-realm.
From within non-dual wisdom, the Lion among Men is born;
yet he does not cling even to the dharma of non-duality, for he knows that neither "one" nor "two" exists.
The Bodhisattva knows all phenomena To be like a mirage, like a flash of lightning,
Like an echo and also like a dream, Like an illusion and like a magical transformation;
Entering accordingly in this way, They reach the realm of all Buddhas.
Having accomplished the wisdom of equality, they universally illumine the profound Dharma-realm.
With immeasurable great compassion, they observe all sentient beings;
free from a mind of defiled attachment, they view the world with purity.
With a vast, pure, and inexhaustible body, they enter deeply into the stages of skillful means.
The Bodhisattvas maintain constant right mindfulness as they discourse upon the lion-like sublime Dharma;
seeing the manifold sufferings and afflictions of the world, they give rise to immeasurable great vows.
All their practices are pure, pervading the entire realm of phenomena.
Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Buddha-dharma and the world,
the Bodhisattva’s skillful contemplation penetrates them all as being without distinction.
The treasury of the pure *dharmakāya* is all the worlds;
Regarding both the world and the *dharmakāya*, there is no attachment to either.
It is like seeing a reflection in clear water, Which, though perceived, has no substantial existence.
The Dharma-body reaches throughout the ten directions, yet it reaches nowhere at all.
Being thus unattached, this pure body of the world,
though a body, is not a body, for all phenomena are without arising.
Deeply entering the inexhaustible body, which is neither born nor extinguished,
neither permanent nor impermanent, it manifests throughout all worlds.
It eliminates evil and false views and brings about the perfection of right view.
Contemplating all phenomena with equanimity, one does not cling to a self or what belongs to a self.
Like a skilled illusionist who manifests various illusions—
neither having come from anywhere nor going anywhere at all.
Illusion is neither finite nor infinite; within that great assembly, it manifests both the finite and the infinite.
With this mind of quiescent extinction, one cultivates all roots of goodness.
The arising of all Buddha-dharmas is neither measurable nor immeasurable.
Whether measurable or immeasurable, all such states are but conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Discerning all realms of existence, one does not cling to either the measurable or the immeasurable.
The profound Dharma of all Buddhas is most peaceful, quiescent, and sublime;
with profound and immeasurable wisdom, they know the depths of all realms of existence.
The Bodhisattva is free from delusion, and his mind and intellect are pure and immeasurable.
Cultivating all roots of goodness, Fulfilling immeasurable vows;
Delivering immeasurable sentient beings, Causing them to reach the place of peace and security;
Contemplating the Dharma-realm with equanimity, Without attachment to anything therein.
Deeply understanding the limit of reality, All phenomena are non-existent;
Awakening all worlds, All phenomena are without arising or ceasing.
Thoroughly knowing all dharmas, He transforms sentient beings according to their needs.
Universally raining down the Dharma of ambrosia, It fills all the worlds.
Transforming immeasurable sentient beings, Causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta,
Without abandoning the Bodhisattva practices, They all attain the stage of non-retrogression.
In accordance with the Buddha’s True Dharma, they ultimately attain the Dharma-body;
they fully comprehend the worlds and the bodies of all sentient beings.
They discern all sentient beings as well as all Buddha-fields.
Deeply entering the ocean of wisdom, they penetrate the ocean of the ten directions.
Within the Tathāgata’s pure body, the bodies of all sentient beings are universally manifested;
with the clear and pure eyes of Bodhisattvas, they are all able to behold them.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, Praising the body of the Tathāgata,
Even if one were to exhaust all kalpas, One would still not reach the end.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
Able, in every moment of thought, to distribute all the relics;
thus, in future ages, those who seek the Buddha-way and possess immeasurable bodhicitta shall know this with certain wisdom.
Thus, throughout the three periods of time, all the Buddhas who appear in the world and abide in the practices of Samantabhadra— I know them all through such discerning knowledge.
Through such discerning knowledge, I know the infinite stages of all practices.
Having accomplished firm wisdom, they are able to turn the wheel of non-retrogression.
With immeasurable, profound wisdom, they reach the ultimate realm of the Tathāgata;
through the clear and pure wisdom of Samantabhadra, they enter deeply into non-retrogression.
The Most Victorious Honored One of all, Deeply entered the wondrous realm,
Ultimately non-retrogressive, Attained unsurpassed bodhi.
With immeasurable and boundless mind, Regarding all various kinds of karma,
Through the cultivation of various mental formations, one can know in a single thought-moment whether they are defiled or undefiled,
whether they belong to those in training or those beyond training;
within a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva awakens to immeasurable states of mind.
Knowing them to be neither one nor two, Neither defiled nor pure,
and likewise not accumulated, Arising entirely from causes and conditions—
Thus one discerns and knows The minds of all sentient beings.
All the Buddha-fields in the world are entirely illusory.
Through such wondrous skillful means, they enter deeply into the bodhisattva practices;
equal to Samantabhadra, they are born through the transformation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Among all classes of sentient beings, their perceptions of good and evil differ;
some are born in the heavens, while others fall into the various evil realms.
The Bodhisattva sees that the world arises entirely from the conditions of karma.
Constantly clinging to false and delusive thoughts, sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death.
All living beings throughout the ten directions are shrouded by the net of falsehood;
within a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to bring them liberation.
Thus, regarding these sense bases— the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—
and the mental activities of discernment and cognition, the perceptions of the world differ.
Within the objective domain of each individual eye, there arise immeasurable eyes.
Their various marks are diverse, immeasurable and without bound.
According to the conduct of sentient beings and all their wholesome or unwholesome karma,
they receive retributions therein, each of which is entirely different in its likeness.
Samantabhadra’s pure eyes, Deeply entering the power of all stages,
Within each and every realm of vision, Give rise to immeasurable wisdom.
Thus, all these worlds He is able to discern and know completely.
Having perfected all practices, they attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Whether spoken by Buddhas or spoken by Bodhisattvas, whether spoken by lands or spoken by sentient beings—
whatever is spoken throughout the three periods of time— the Bodhisattva discerns and knows it all.
The past is the future, and the future is the past;
what is manifest is both the gone and the coming—all this the Bodhisattva fully understands.
Thus, throughout immeasurable eons, he awakens to their differing characteristics.
"Having perfected the practice of skillful means, they are fully endowed with the wisdom of all Buddhas. Chapter 32: The Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata-Ratnarāja, Part One.

*The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-Two, Part One: "The Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata-Ratnarāja. At that time, from the white tuft of hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, he emitted a great radiance called "The Dharma of the Illuminating Tathāgata. It was accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays, which universally illumined all worlds in the ten directions. Circumambulating them ten times, it manifested the infinite sovereignty of the Tathāgata and awakened countless billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas.

All worlds shook in six ways; all sufferings of the evil realms were extinguished; and the radiance of all Māras was eclipsed like a mass of ink. The bodhi of all Tathāgatas was revealed, as were the ultimate adornments of the great assemblies of all Buddhas, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Having again circled all the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, [the light] entered the crown of the Tathāgata-gotra-samudgata-vimala-guṇa Bodhisattva.
At that time, the entire assembly was filled with great joy; their bodies and minds became supple, and they thought to themselves:
"How marvelous and rare!..."
"The Tathāgata now emits this great net of light; he must surely proclaim the profound, true Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-vyūha-śrī rose from his lotus seat, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee upon the lotus pedestal. With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms, faced the Tathāgata directly, and spoke in verse:
"The Perfectly Awakened One has realized all dharmas And reached the ultimate limit of all realms."
To the Great Sages of the three periods of time, I therefore pay respectful homage.
Having reached the ultimate realm of signlessness, their bodies are adorned with the marks and signs;
they universally radiate stainless light, extinguishing all demons.
Shaking the worlds of the ten directions and all Buddha-fields,
yet sentient beings feel no fear— this is the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Abiding peacefully like space, equal to the pure Dharma-realm.
Eliminating all evils, he causes the multitude to attain purity.
Through ascetic practices over immeasurable kalpas, he sought the Buddha-way with a single mind;
having attained unimpeded objective wisdom, he is equal to all Tathāgatas.
Universally emitting immeasurable light, Shaking all buddha-fields,
Manifesting the power of mastery, They enter into my body.
All bodhisattvas who have trained well Have now gathered here in this assembly.
Therefore, I have resolved my mind: there must be the work of a Dharma King.
The great assembly is entirely pure; having perfected the bodhisattva practices, their wisdom is free from attachment, and they have achieved fearlessness.
The Great Sage’s conduct is immeasurable; through the power of wisdom and diligence, he has opened up the Bodhisattva mind and the Tathāgata’s most profound Dharma.
Who is able to expound upon the subtle and wondrous meaning of Perfect Enlightenment?
"I now wish to ask a question; may the Buddha reveal it for me.

Having spoken this verse, at that time the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance from his mouth called "Unobstructed Fearlessness," with immeasurable billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays as its retinue.

It universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, circling them ten times to manifest the infinite sovereignty of the Tathāgata. It awakens countless billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, causes all worlds to quake in six ways, and extinguishes the sufferings of all evil realms. It eclipses the radiance of all māras as if they were a mass of ink, manifests the enlightenment of all Tathāgatas, and reveals the ultimate adornment of the great assemblies of all Buddhas, universally illuminating all worlds equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Having again circled all the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, they entered the mouth of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.

At that time, the body and lion throne of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra were a hundred times more sublime than the bodies and lion thrones of all the other bodhisattvas, with the sole exception of the seat occupied by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotrasamudgata-vimalaśrī asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This inconceivable and great majestic spiritual power manifested by the Buddha—what auspicious sign is this?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra replied to the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-samudgama-viśuddhamati:
"O Son of the Buddha!
As I reflect and as I perceive, the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who emitted great radiance, must have taught the True Dharma of the Manifestation of the Tathāgata-nature."
"Therefore, the Buddha now emits a great radiance and manifests his sovereign power; he will surely proclaim the True Dharma of the Tathāgata-gotra-udaya.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-udaya-viśeṣa-mati heard the name of the True Dharma of the Tathāgata-gotra-udaya, the entire earth shook in six ways, and immeasurable rays of light for debate and inquiry emerged.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-samudgata-viśeṣa-guṇa asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra:
"O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva know the true Dharma of the arising of the nature of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas?"
O Son of the Buddha!
There is an assembly of countless billions of nayutas of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, a pure multitude who have skillfully studied and practiced the purification of all karmas;
they have accomplished mindfulness and wisdom, adorned with the ornaments of all Buddhas, and have reached the ultimate other shore.

Abiding in the majestic deportment of a Buddha, they fulfill the practices of a Tathāgata; with right mindfulness toward all Buddhas, they never become distracted; with great compassion, they observe all sentient beings;
with decisive wisdom, they discern the various sublime spiritual powers of Bodhisattvas;
having attained the spiritual power of a Buddha, they dwell securely in all the merits of the Buddhas.
Having accomplished such immeasurable merits, all the great bodhisattvas have gathered here.

O Benevolent One, you have, in the presence of immeasurable billions of nayutas of Buddhas, reverently made offerings and planted various roots of goodness; you have perfected the unsurpassed, wondrous practices of a bodhisattva and attained mastery over all gateways of samādhi;
you have deeply penetrated the secrets of all Tathāgatas and eliminated all doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma.

They have entered deeply into the Buddha-dharma and skillfully know the faculties of all sentient beings; they preach the Dharma according to the dispositions of sentient beings, expound all Buddha-dharmas by discerning them in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom, and having reached the ultimate shore, they have accomplished such immeasurable merits as these.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
We pray that you will expound the True Dharma of the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotrasamudgata-viśeṣa-mati, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra in verse, saying:
“Excellent is your unimpeded wisdom, which awakens to all phenomena;
endowed with impartial insight, you proclaim the Buddha’s immeasurable realm.”
Having heard this, all the sons of the Buddhas were filled with great joy in their hearts;
they prayed that you would now expound for them the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising.
What is the body of the Tathāgata? And what is his pure and wondrous voice?
What is the mind of the Tathāgata, and what are his immeasurable spheres?
What are the practices of the Tathāgata, and what is the bodhi of all Buddhas?
By practicing what dharma can one swiftly achieve equal and perfect enlightenment?
How does one turn the wheel of the Dharma, The pure, wondrous, and supreme teaching?
I pray that you will explain it in detail, The Dharma of the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata;
Having heard it, the sons of the Buddha Will experience immeasurable joy in their hearts.
All classes of sentient beings in the ten directions Behold all the Kings of Dharma;
They revere and make offerings to the Buddhas, Thereby planting roots of goodness.
If there are those who behold the Buddhas And reverently plant roots of goodness,
The treasury of merit is immeasurable; I pray that you will explain it in detail for us.
Should anyone hear the names of all the Tathāgatas—those currently residing in the ten directions as well as those who have already entered parinirvāṇa—
Those who hear the name of the inexhaustible treasury of merit and rejoice—
what benefit do they obtain?
Out of compassion, please explain this in detail.
O pure and true son of the Buddha, we pray that you will extensively expound and analyze this profound realm, an ocean of immeasurable merit.
All the bodhisattvas here have with one mind joined their palms in reverence.
Reverently beholding the Sugata, looking upon you, O Benevolent One, as well as upon me—
with skillful speech and subtle tones, pray explain the true meaning.
Eradicate all doubts and delusions, becoming pure like the void.
Please explain for me the causes, conditions, and parables;
having heard them, immeasurable multitudes will all resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
All Tathāgatas possess bodies adorned with the primary and secondary marks.
Pervading the lands of the ten directions, they deliver sentient beings through skillful means;
emitting subtle and wondrous sounds, they expound immeasurable dharmas,
instructing and transforming according to individual capacities, revealing and awakening them to the Buddha’s bodhi.
Throughout all realms in the ten directions, within immeasurable Buddha-fields,
for unspeakable eons, an assembly such as this has been exceedingly difficult to behold.
Thus has this great multitude gathered.
O pure sons of the Buddha, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas,
this is difficult to see and difficult to hear;
therefore, you are true sons of the Buddha.
I pray that you will explain the subtle and wondrous meaning,
manifesting the vast and immeasurable Dharma of the Tathāgata-gotra-utpatti for all Bodhisattvas.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms in homage, thirsting for the Great Vehicle and praying,
"May the nectar of the Dharma rain down. At that time,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the assembly, including the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotra-vyūha-guṇa and the rest, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
The nature-arising True Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is inconceivable. Why is this?
It is not through minor causes and conditions that one attains Samyaksaṃbodhi and appears in the world.”
O Son of the Buddha!
Through ten kinds of immeasurable, innumerable, hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya causes and conditions, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment and appears in the world. What are these ten?
First, to give rise to the immeasurable mind of bodhicitta and not abandon any sentient being;
second, to cultivate all roots of goodness with a straightforward and profound mind throughout countless past kalpas.
Third, to rescue and protect sentient beings with immeasurable compassion.
Fourth, to practice immeasurable deeds without retreating from their great vows.
Fifth, to accumulate immeasurable merit without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Sixth, to reverently make offerings to and serve the infinite Buddhas who transform sentient beings;
seventh, to give rise to infinite skillful means and wisdom;
eighth, to accomplish the infinite treasuries of all meritorious virtues.
Ninth, they are endowed with immeasurable wisdom of adornment.
Tenth, they analytically expound the true meaning of immeasurable dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this way, ten such immeasurable, innumerable, hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya dharma-gates have been realized as perfect enlightenment and manifested in the world.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, the trichiliocosm is not formed by few causes and conditions; it is only through immeasurable causes and conditions that it can be established.
These are as follows: great clouds and rain arise, and because of this great rain, four wind-circles emerge. What are these four?
The first is named Holding, which can hold great waters.
The second is named Gradual Dissipation, which gradually dissipates great waters.
The third is named Arising, which gives rise to various locations.
The fourth is Adornment, which adorns the karmic retributions of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm.
These four types all arise from the karmic retributions of sentient beings and the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!

Through such immeasurable causes and conditions as these, the trichiliocosm is formed; for such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no creator and no one who brings it into being. It is the same with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he is not accomplished through few causes and conditions, but through immeasurable causes and conditions, he achieves perfect enlightenment and appears in the world.
That is to say:

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having in the past heard and received the great rain of the nectar of the True Dharma from immeasurable Buddhas, are thereby able to give rise to the four kinds of Tathāgata wisdom-wind wheels. What are these four?
First, the wind-wheel of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom of right mindfulness upholding dhāraṇīs, which never forgets or loses them and is able to sustain all the rain of the Tathāgata’s teachings.
Second, the wind-wheel of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā, which is able to completely extinguish all afflictions.
Third, the Tathāgata’s wind-circle of great wisdom of skillful dedication, which accomplishes all roots of merit and virtue.

Fourth, the Tathāgata’s wind-circle of great wisdom that gives birth to the various stainless ornaments of the Dharma, which causes the faculties of all sentient beings to be purified and adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; these are accomplished by the Tathāgata’s untainted roots of virtue, for such is the nature of phenomena: there is no agent, nor is there any one who brings them to completion.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first and most supreme Dharma-gate for the manifestation of the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment in the world; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know it thus.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, when the trichiliocosm is being formed, a great cloud sends down rain called 'the Great Pouring. No world can contain or sustain it, except for the trichiliocosm at the very moment of its initial formation. In the same way, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world and proclaims the rain of the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising (*tathāgatagotra-utpatti*), no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can receive or uphold it, except for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have perfected the various powers."
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second causal condition for the manifestation of a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
Just as the great clouds of karmic retribution for sentient beings bring down rain that comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
by the power of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas, he proclaims the rain of the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s nature-arising, which comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when a great cloud pours down rain, no sentient being within the trichiliocosm can know its measure; were one to attempt to calculate it, their mind would become deranged—save for Maheśvara, the Lord of the Trichiliocosm, who, by the power of the fruit of his original roots of goodness, knows not even a single drop.

In the same way, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world and proclaims the nectar-like Dharma rain of the Tathāgatagarbha, it cannot be known by any sentient beings, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas; were they to attempt to fathom it, their minds would become deranged—save for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Lords of all worlds, who, by the power of the stages cultivated under past Buddhas, can discern every single phrase and every single flavor.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, when a great cloud sends down rain, it is called "extinguishing the blazing," or "able to arise," or "able to destroy," or "forming jewels," or "discerning the great trichiliocosm.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world and rains the rain of the True Dharma; one such rain is called "Elimination," for it eliminates the raging fires of the afflictions of sentient beings;
there is another rain of Dharma called "Able to Arise," for it can give rise to all the roots of goodness in sentient beings.
There is a rain of Dharma called "The Destroyer," which can destroy the various evil and false views of sentient beings;
there is a rain of Dharma called "The Forming of Jewels," which can form the jewel of omniscience for all sentient beings;
there is a rain of Dharma called "Discernment," which discerns the mental activities and mental factors of sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, just as a great cloud rains water of a single flavor, yet there are differences according to where it falls;

so too is it with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who rains the Dharma-rain of the single flavor of great compassion, which differs in various ways according to those to be transformed.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the trichiliocosm is first formed, the palaces of the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are formed first; next, the palaces of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are formed; and finally, the human abodes and the dwellings of other sentient beings are formed.

In the same way, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he first gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of bodhisattvas; next, he gives rise to the roots of goodness of all pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and other sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a great cloud that rains water of a single flavor, yet according to the power of the roots of goodness of various sentient beings, it gives rise to various kinds of palaces. In the same way, the Dharma-water of the Tathāgata’s great compassion is of a single flavor, yet because the vessels and faculties of sentient beings differ, the rain of the Dharma manifests in diverse ways.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the world was first forming, there was a great wheel of water that filled the trichiliocosm. Once it had filled the world, a great lotus flower named "Arisen from the Tathāgata" emerged, adorned with the jewels of all merits; it completely covered the trichiliocosm, its light illuminating all lands throughout the ten directions.

At that time, Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others, having seen the lotuses, immediately and with certainty knew that as many Buddhas as there were lotuses would appear in the world.
O Son of the Buddha!
At that time, there arose a wind-circle named Pure Radiance, which was able to form the palaces of the various heavens of the Form Realm;
another wind-circle arose named Pure Adornment, which was able to form the palaces of the various heavens of the Desire Realm;
and yet another wind-circle arose named Indestructible, which was able to form the great and small surrounding mountains as well as the Diamond Mountains.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named Victorious Height (*Jaya-unnata*), which can form Sumeru, the King of Mountains;
and there is another wind-circle named Immovable (*Acala*), which can form ten kinds of great mountains.
What are the ten? They are:
Mount Plantain, Mount Rishi, Mount Subduer of Māra, Mount Great Subduer of Māra, Mount Sustainer of Kalpas, Mount Black, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, Mount Fragrant, and Mount Snowy.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named "Abiding" that can form the great earth;
another wind-circle named "Adornment" that can form the palaces of the Earth-devas and the palaces of the Gandharvas;
and another wind-circle named "Inexhaustible Treasury" that can form the ocean of the three-thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named "Luminous Pure Treasury" (Vimalagarbha), which can produce the precious jewels of the great trichiliocosm;
and there is another wind-circle named "Firm Root" (Dṛḍhamūla), which can produce all wish-fulfilling trees.
O Sons of the Buddha!

This is how the great cloud rains water of a single flavor; yet, by the power of the karmic fruition of the roots of goodness of sentient beings, and because such is the nature of phenomena, various wind-circles arise. Due to the differences among these wind-circles, the forms and types of the great trichiliocosm are not the same.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise thus: appearing in the world and endowed with all roots of goodness, he possesses a radiance called the "Inconceivable Wisdom Arising from the Uninterrupted Tathāgata-nature, the Supreme Great Wisdom," which universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions and bestows upon all bodhisattvas the prediction of becoming a Tathāgata, signifying their attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment and their appearance in the world.
Furthermore, they are able to skillfully know how many bodhisattvas have accomplished meritorious virtues under each and every Buddha.
There is another light, named "The Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata Free from Defilement and Purity," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s untainted and non-arising wisdom.
There is another light, named "The Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata Universal Illumination," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom of the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there is a light named Tathāgata Great Wisdom Sustaining the Buddha-nature, which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s immovable powers;
furthermore, there is a light named Tathāgata Great Wisdom Unbreakable Supreme, which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s wisdom of fearlessness;
furthermore, there is a light named Tathāgata Great Wisdom All-Illuminating, which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s firm and non-regressing all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, there is a light named "The Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Emanation of Birth," which enables those who see, hear, revere, and make offerings to all Tathāgatas to ensure that their roots of goodness are not in vain.

Furthermore, there is a light named "The Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Universal Accordance with the Ultimate," which can perfect the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible merit, wisdom, and pure Dharma-body, thereby benefiting sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is a light named "The Inexhaustible Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata," which can perfect the Tathāgata’s profoundly subtle and wondrous wisdom and ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.

Furthermore, there is a light named "The Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Various Adornments," which can perfect the marks and signs that adorn the body of a Tathāgata, causing all sentient beings to rejoice and attain all-knowledge.

Furthermore, there is a light named "The Indestructible Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata," which can perfect the Tathāgata’s supreme lifespan, equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, which is inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as the water of the Tathāgata’s great compassion is of a single flavor, yet through the power of the roots of goodness of the various bodhisattvas, the differences in the faculties of other beings, and because such is the nature of phenomena, the manifestations of the Tathāgata’s wisdom appear in diverse ways.
O Son of the Buddha!

The True Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising is produced by the light of the equal wisdom of all Tathāgatas; it is the single-flavored wisdom of all Tathāgatas that gives birth to immeasurable and boundless merits. Sentient beings think to themselves:
"These various merits were created by the Tathāgata."
"O Son of the Buddha!
This was not created by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!"

Even until a single bodhisattva attains the unsurpassed path, it is impossible to say that a Buddha is its creator; for all Buddhas act as spiritual friends to all sentient beings, and by relying on them, sentient beings attain great wisdom. There is no created phenomenon, nor is there a creator.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth causal condition for the manifestation of Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the world; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, there are four wind-circles that abide in space and are able to support the water-circle. What are these four?
They are: the Abiding, the Immovable, the Constantly Abiding, and the Firm; these are called the four that are able to support the water-circle.
The water wheel can sustain the great earth so that it does not disintegrate; therefore, it is said that the great earth relies upon the water wheel.
The water wheel relies upon the wind wheel, the wind wheel relies upon space, and space has no support. Although space has no support, it enables the trichiliocosm to abide securely.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: relying upon the Tathāgata, there arises the fourfold wind wheel of unimpeded great wisdom, which can sustain the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.
What are these four? They are:

the great wisdom wind-wheel that gathers all sentient beings and causes them to rejoice; the great wisdom wind-wheel that distinguishes all dharmas so that sentient beings joyfully seek great wisdom; the great wisdom wind-wheel that protects all the roots of goodness of sentient beings; and the great wisdom wind-wheel that definitively realizes the untainted realm of phenomena (*anāsrava-dharmadhātu*). These are called the four kinds of great wisdom wind-wheels.

Great compassion serves as the refuge for sentient beings; great pity delivers sentient beings; great compassion and great pity benefit sentient beings; great compassion and great pity rely upon the wisdom of skillful means; the wisdom of great skillful means relies upon the Tathāgata; and the Tathāgata has no dependence whatsoever, his light of unimpeded wisdom universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth causal condition for the manifestation of a Perfectly Awakened One in the world; a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

It is, for example, like when the great trichiliocosm has been formed, providing manifold benefits to immeasurable sentient beings: aquatic beings obtain the peace and happiness of water; terrestrial beings obtain the peace and happiness of land; beings who dwell in palaces obtain the peace and happiness of palaces; and beings who dwell in space obtain the peace and happiness of space.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; appearing in the world, he benefits all sentient beings in manifold ways. Those who see or hear the Tathāgata leap for joy and cultivate various roots of goodness. Those who abide in ethical discipline (*śīla*) obtain the bliss of the Buddha’s precepts; those who abide in the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables obtain the bliss of the noble, unsurpassed light of wisdom; those who abide in the Dharma-gates obtain the bliss of reality; and those who abide in illumination obtain the bliss of pure wisdom. In such ways, through immeasurable Dharma-gates, he benefits all sentient beings in manifold ways.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth causal condition for the manifestation of the attainment of perfect enlightenment in the world; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should know it thus.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddhāvatamsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Three.
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Part Two of the Thirty-Second Chapter: "The Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata, King of Jewels."
“O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the True Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising (tathāgatagotra-utpatti):
its merits are immeasurable, for its practices are immeasurable;”
It pervades the ten directions because it has no coming or going;
it is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing because it has no conditioned activity;
it is free from mind, thought, and consciousness because it has no body.
Its nature is like empty space because it is entirely equal;
all sentient beings are without self or what belongs to self because they are inexhaustible;
and all lands are inexhaustible because they do not undergo transformation.
It is uninterrupted until the end of the future, for there is no regression;
the Tathāgata’s wisdom is free from doubt and non-dual, for it impartially contemplates both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
having attained perfect enlightenment, he benefits sentient beings, for his original vows have been fulfilled through mastery in dedication.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Listen attentively, all you multitudes, To the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s ten powers;
Throughout all worlds, It is the most supreme and unsurpassed."
They are entirely equal to the peerless, and likewise equal to space;
their merit is without equal, and their realm is immeasurable.
All Tathāgatas possess merit that is beyond measure.
No other classes of sentient beings are able to conceive of it.
Regarding this single Dharma-door of the Tathāgata, all living beings,
even throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, could not exhaustively fathom it through reflection.
If one could take all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions and grind them all to atoms,
and there were someone capable of calculating and fully knowing their total number;
even if that person spent immeasurable eons counting all the Tathāgatas, [they would still not reach the end].
The merit of a single hair cannot be known even in its smallest fraction.
It is like a man who could measure the realm of space,
and a second man who, following his calculations, could know its numerical extent.
Though one might exhaust the measurement of space over countless billions of eons,
the virtues of the Tathāgata can never be fully exhausted.
It is as if there were a man who, within a single thought-moment, could...
One might count the sentient beings of the three periods of time, and the mental activities of each being;
even if one were to spend as many eons as there are such beings, that counting could still come to an end.
But the immeasurable virtues of the Tathāgata—those cannot be fully numbered.
Just as with the various dharma-realms, Their boundaries cannot be apprehended;
Everything is neither everything, Neither seen nor graspable.
In this way, the spheres of all Tathāgatas Are immeasurable.
All things are not all things; the dharma-realm is without end.
Like the nature of suchness, it is free from falsehood and is quiescent;
therein is neither that which arises nor that which ceases.
Thus all Tathāgatas, as well as all objective realms,
are likewise identical to the nature of suchness (tathatā), neither increasing nor decreasing.
Just as the future limit is boundless, so too is the limit of true reality (bhūtakoṭi) without limit.
The nature of the three periods of time is inherently detached; its reality cannot be apprehended.
Such is the Perfectly Awakened One, and his sphere of experience is likewise so;
throughout all three periods of time, he penetrates them without obstruction.
All phenomena are without change, for their nature is empty and unconditioned;
free from defilement and untainted, their nature is like space.
All Tathāgatas are likewise pure by nature.
All natures are natureless; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
The nature of the True Dharma is remote from all paths of language;
all states of going and not going are entirely of the nature of quiescence.
The realm of all Tathāgatas is likewise thus:
it is far removed from the path of language and cannot be illustrated by analogy.
The Dharma awakened to by the Buddhas is such that both its nature and its characteristics are utterly quiescent.
Just as when a bird flies through the sky, its tracks cannot be found; so too,
the fruit of immeasurable great vows brings about the accomplishment of a pure form-body,
endowed with the virtues of the ten powers, manifesting great supernormal transformations.
If there are those who wish to know the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata,
they should purify their minds so that they are like space.
They must remain far removed from false conceptualizations, as well as from wrong views and inversions.
By practicing the path of purity, one ultimately attains a purified mind.
Therefore, sons of the Buddhas, listen with single-minded attention as I shall speak briefly of the realm of all the Sugatas.
The merits of all those who possess the ten powers are beyond counting;
yet, for the sake of awakening all living beings, I shall now briefly proclaim them.
All the Teachers have initiated pure physical actions.
The karma of speech and the karma of mind— Their spheres are entirely pure.
The profound sphere of the Tathāgata, The pure and wondrous Wheel of Dharma,
And the various roots of goodness in Nirvāṇa— I shall now explain them in detail.
For example, when the great trichiliocosm was first formed,
it could not have been accomplished by a few causes and conditions; rather,
through the power of immeasurable skillful means, it arose from all manner of causes and conditions.
Throughout the trichiliocosm, all sentient beings are established therein.
Such supreme ones as these— the Dharma of the Tathāgata-nature’s arising,
a treasury of immeasurable merit— none are able to know it.
All the worlds of the ten directions, Were all ground into fine dust;
One might calculate the number of those atoms And know the minds of sentient beings.
Even the atoms and the minds of sentient beings Could still be known by their count.
The merits of all those who possess the ten powers are unknowable.
Just as from heavy clouds a great rain can pour down,
and from the arising of the four kinds of wind-wheels the trichiliocosm can be formed.
The various roots of goodness of sentient beings and the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit arise throughout the three thousandfold world-system to establish all classes of living beings.
The Tathāgata is likewise; from the causal conditions, the cloud of Dharma arises.
The great wind-circle of wisdom, with a stainless and pure mind,
cultivates all roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas;
dedicating these to all sentient beings, may they swiftly attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
For example, in the midst of space, when clouds and rain fall as a great deluge,
there is no one in any other world capable of receiving or sustaining it,
except for those in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system at the time of its initial formation.
The immovable wind-circle rests upon the realm of empty space;
so too is the Tathāgata: having first attained equal and perfect enlightenment, the rain from the Dharma-clouds falls throughout all realms of the ten directions.
The supreme Dharma-realm is filled, yet there is no one who can uphold it.
Only the great Bodhisattvas, who have accomplished immeasurable virtues, raise clouds and rain in the void; they act without effort and create nothing.
Originally they come from nowhere, and in departing they go nowhere.
The Tathāgata is also like this; he rains down the nectar of the Dharma-clouds, which originally comes from nowhere and in departing goes nowhere.
All the Bodhisattvas, practicing immeasurable deeds,
rain down the True Dharma for those who are ready to be transformed according to their needs.
Just as when a great cloud rains, there is no one able to count its drops.
Only Maheśvara is able to discern and know them all;
the Sugata is likewise so, raining down immeasurable dharma-rain that fills all Buddha-fields, such that no one can count it.
Only the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the Sovereign of all worlds, is able to discern and know everything as clearly as if gazing at a jewel in the palm of his hand.
That which should be extinguished he can cause to be extinguished; that which should be brought forth he can cause to arise.
Eliminating all false views, he nurtures the jewels of merit.
The Tathāgata rains down the True Dharma, eliminating all afflictions and giving birth to immeasurable, incalculable roots of goodness.
Cultivating right view, one remains far removed from all perversions;
all those who are most supreme deeply understand the jewel of merit.
Just as in the midst of space, rain falls everywhere with water of a single flavor.
The power of the karmic retribution of sentient beings causes the objects that arise to differ.
When the Tathāgata rains down the True Dharma— the water of great compassion of a single flavor—
he speaks in various distinct ways according to those who are to be transformed.
When the world was first formed, the palaces of the Form Realm arose first;
then, in the heavens of the Desire Realm, palaces arose in succession;
next, in the human realm, dwelling places were constructed one by one.
Thereafter, they arise in succession: the abodes of the *gandharvas* and the various *nāgas*.

So too is it with the Tathāgata: having first attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), he first initiates the practice of a bodhisattva; next, he accomplishes the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, having attained mastery over emanated minds, he first [instructs] all the śrāvakas,
and then causes sentient beings to cultivate various roots of goodness.
Seeing the pure lotus flowers, the devas know that a Buddha has appeared.
From rain, wind can arise; from wind, the world can arise.
So too, when the Tathāgata emits radiance, he distinguishes Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, gives rise to the wheel of wisdom, and attains mastery over all Buddha-dharmas.
The water rests upon the wind-circle; the earth rests upon the water-circle.
The various jewel-trees rest upon the earth, yet space has nothing upon which it rests.
The wheel of wisdom rests upon the Tathāgata; compassion rests upon wisdom.
Merit relies upon skillful means, while the Dharma-body has no basis.
Just as when the great earth arises, it benefits all sentient beings;
the various species of creatures on land and in water each obtain peace and happiness.
Just as those who dwell in space, The various devas of the desire and form realms,
And all beings with two or four legs— All are fully benefited;
So too is the Dharma King, Who appears within this world.
May all sentient beings Attain every benefit.
Those who see or hear [this], And those who pay respect and make offerings,
Shall eliminate all afflictions And deeply understand the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"The Dharma of the Tathāgata’s nature-arising is something the world cannot know;
I have spoken but a small portion of it for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva know and see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and sees the Tathāgata as being fully endowed with and accomplished in immeasurable merits.”
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not transform a single sentient being by means of a single dharma, a single practice, a single body, or a single land;

rather, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows and perceives the Tathāgata as fully accomplishing immeasurable dharmas, immeasurable practices, immeasurable bodies, and immeasurable lands, in order to impartially teach and transform all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like space, which reaches all places—both those with form and those without form—yet neither reaches nor does not reach them. Why is this?
Because space has no form or color, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise: it reaches all places, all lands, all phenomena, and all sentient beings, yet there is nowhere to which it goes.
Why is this? Because the bodies of all Tathāgatas are not physical bodies;
they manifest their bodies according to those who are to be transformed.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s initial entry into the gate of supreme practice, whereby they know and see the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
Just as space is all-pervasive and can accommodate all sentient beings without being stained or attached, so too is the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
it illuminates the worldly roots of goodness and the supramundane roots of goodness of all sentient beings, yet remains unstained and unattached.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata has completely severed all defiled attachments.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the rising of the sun in the world, which benefits sentient beings through immeasurable deeds, namely:
It dispels darkness and nurtures all mountain forests, medicinal herbs, the hundred grains, and various plants; it eliminates cold and dampness.
It illuminates space, benefiting sentient beings within the void;
it shines upon ponds, causing lotus flowers to bloom, and universally manifests all forms and images, so that all worldly endeavors reach their ultimate fulfillment.
Why is this? Because the sun can universally emit immeasurable light;
the sun that is the body of the Tathāgata is likewise, for through immeasurable deeds it is universally able to benefit all sentient beings, namely:
Benefiting through the extinction of evil, they nurture the wholesome dharmas;
benefiting through universal illumination, they eliminate the darkness and obscurity of all sentient beings;
benefiting through great compassion, they rescue and protect sentient beings.
The benefit of great compassion is to deliver and liberate all beings;
the benefit of the True Dharma is to nurture all faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment;
the benefit of firm faith is to remove the defilements and turbidity of the mind.
The benefit of seeing the Dharma is that it does not destroy causes and conditions;
the benefit of the divine eye is that it perceives all sentient beings dying here and being born there;
the benefit of non-harming is that it does not destroy any of the roots of goodness in sentient beings.
The light of wisdom brings benefit, causing the lotus-flowers of the minds of all sentient beings to bloom;
the arousal of the mind brings benefit, bringing to ultimate fulfillment all the practices of Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because the sun of the Tathāgata’s body universally radiates all light of wisdom, O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third supreme practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the rising sun: it first illuminates all the kings of great mountains, next it illuminates all the great mountains, then it illuminates the diamond jewel mountains, and finally it shines universally upon the entire earth."
The sun does not form this thought:
"I shall first illuminate the great kings of mountains, and then, in succession, illuminate the entire earth.
It is simply because those mountains and lands have elevations and depressions that the illumination occurs in a sequence of before and after.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: having accomplished the sun-disk of wisdom regarding the immeasurable and boundless *dharmadhātu*, he constantly emits the immeasurable and unimpeded light of wisdom. First, it illuminates the great mountain-kings such as the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; next, it illuminates the Pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates the Śrāvakas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings with determined roots of goodness who are ready to be transformed according to their capacity; and finally, it illuminates all sentient beings, even those fixed in the wrong path, acting as a cause and condition for their future benefit.
The sun-like light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom does not form this thought:
"I shall first illuminate the bodhisattvas, and so on, down to those of fixed wrongness.
It simply emits the great light of wisdom, universally illuminating all.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the sun and moon appear in the world and illuminate everywhere—even deep mountains and secluded valleys—without exception;
so too is the sun and moon of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which universally illumines all things, leaving nothing unclarified.
However, because the aspirations and roots of goodness of sentient beings differ, the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom manifests in various distinctions.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth supreme practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
For example, when the sun rises in the world, sentient beings who are blind from birth have never seen it. Why is this?
Because they lack physical eyes,
O Son of the Buddha!
Although these beings blind from birth do not see the sun, they are nonetheless benefited by its light.

Because of the sunlight, one obtains food, drink, and various necessities of life; it eliminates cold and dampness, making the body light and supple, and completely removes all ailments such as wind, cold, phlegm, and swelling, resulting in peace and happiness.

The appearance of the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom in the world is likewise: all sentient beings who hold wrong views, violate the precepts, lack wisdom, lead wrong livelihoods, and are born blind have never beheld the sunlight of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Why is this? Because they lack the eye of faith,
O Son of the Buddha!
Sentient beings born blind, though they do not see the sunlight of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, are nonetheless benefited by this sunlight of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
it extinguishes all sufferings of the four great elements, brings peace and happiness to their bodies, and cuts off the very root of all afflictions and poisonous pains.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata possesses a light named "Accumulation of All Meritorious Qualities";
furthermore, there is a radiance named "Universally Illuminating All."
Furthermore, there is a light named Pure Sovereign Universal Illumination;
furthermore, there is a light named Producing Great Sublime Sounds;
furthermore, there is a light named Universally Illuminating All Languages and Dharmas.
Furthermore, there is a light named "Sovereign Eradication of All Doubt and Confusion";
furthermore, there is a light named "Independent Universal Illumination";
furthermore, there is a light named "Sovereignty of Wisdom," which eradicates all delusions regarding objective realms.
There is another light named "Discerning All Vehicles," which, according to what is appropriate for each, emits great and wondrous sounds;
there is another light named "Perfect Sovereignty," whose resonance adorns all lands and causes all sentient beings to attain purity.
O Son of the Buddha!

From each and every pore of the Tathāgata, he emits thousands of such rays of light; five hundred rays universally illuminate the regions below, and five hundred rays universally illuminate the regions above.

In each of their respective lands, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having seen this light in the presence of the various Tathāgatas, immediately became fully endowed with purity: ten heads, ten eyes, ten ears, ten noses, ten tongues, ten bodies, ten hands, ten feet, ten stages, and ten knowledges. By means of the stages of bodhisattva practice, all the sense-bases attained by those bodhisattvas were completely purified, and they brought their roots of goodness to fulfillment.
All-encompassing wisdom, as well as the [attainments of] śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, are all completely extinguished;

all afflictions, meager wisdom, and sentient beings who are born blind have their bodies become supple, peaceful, blissful, stainless, and pure; their faculties are tamed, and they fully accomplish the dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness;

sentient beings in the hells, the hungry ghost realm, the animal realm, and other evil paths have all their manifold sufferings eliminated and attain peace and happiness; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among humans and devas.
Those sentient beings, unaware and unconscious, do not know by what causes and conditions or by what majestic spiritual power they have come to be born in this world.
Those who were born blind think only this:
"I am Brahmā; I am a transformation of Brahmā."
At that time, the Tathāgata, abiding in the Samādhi of Universal Sovereignty, produced eight kinds of the Tathāgata’s wondrous voices and addressed the sentient beings, saying:
"You sentient beings are not Brahmā, nor were you created by Brahmā;
it is because you have received the Buddha's spiritual power that you have been born here."

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, those sentient beings immediately recognized their past lives and the evil realms they had traversed before being reborn in this world; they were all filled with great joy.

Having rejoiced greatly, they each took up clouds of udumbara flowers, clouds of incense, clouds of musical entertainment, clouds of all kinds of garments, clouds of parasols, clouds of banners, clouds of powdered incense, clouds of exquisite jewels, clouds of lion-banners, clouds of crescent-moon pavilions, and clouds of ornaments for praise and adornment; they proceeded to where the Tathāgata was and presented them as offerings.

Why is this? Because, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, their eye of wisdom has been opened and clarified; the Tathāgata then bestows upon those sentient beings the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!

You should know that the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom benefits those sentient beings who are blind from birth, nourishing them until they are fully endowed with and bringing to fruition their roots of goodness.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like the full moon, which possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities."

What are these four? They are: eclipsing the light of all the stars; manifesting increase and decrease within Jambudvīpa; reflecting in all pure waters without exception; and appearing face-to-face to all sentient beings who behold it.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise; it possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities.
What are these four? They are:

eclipsing all the stars of the dharmas and merits of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, those in training, and those beyond training; manifesting lifespans of varying lengths according to what is appropriate;
the dharma-body remaining eternally constant without ever increasing or decreasing; and appearing as reflections in all worlds.

For sentient beings with pure minds, within the vessel of Bodhi, according to the Dharma they hear and the stage of liberation they attain, all those who are ready to be transformed perceive the Tathāgata as appearing before them;
yet in reality, the Dharmakāya is without distinction of self and other, ultimately fulfilling the Buddha-work.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, in a trichiliocosm, the Great Brahmā King, by means of a slight expedient, causes all sentient beings throughout that great trichiliocosm to each perceive the Brahmā King appearing before them; yet he does not divide his body, nor does he possess various bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata is also like this: he does not divide his body, nor does he have various bodies; yet, for all sentient beings, he manifests his body according to what is appropriate for their transformation.
He never gives rise to the thought of manifesting himself as this or that among various sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, it is like a great king of physicians who thoroughly understands the methods for counteracting diseases with various medicines and is fully proficient in all medical treatises. When all the medicinal herbs of Jambudvīpa appear before him, that great king of physicians can identify them all;
because that great king of physicians possesses the power of past roots of goodness and clearly understands all medical treatises, he is able to cure all manner of illnesses.
When that great king of physicians approaches the end of his life, he forms this thought:
"Once my life has ended, all sentient beings will have no one to rely upon; therefore, I must manifest skillful means.

At that time, the King of Physicians applied medicine to his body and sustained himself with incantations, so that after his death, his body would neither dry up nor decompose, yet he could still fully maintain the four dignified postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—and continue to perform the work of a physician, healing all manner of illnesses just as before, without any difference from his original state.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians, is also thus: he is perfectly able to understand all remedial methods and can completely eliminate the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings.
For immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, he cultivated roots of goodness and perfected the Prajñāpāramitā, reaching the other shore;

he skillfully mastered expedient means, applying medicinal ointments and reciting mantras. In the past, the Tathāgata first established himself securely within the stages of bodhisattva practice through the power of the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā and the efficacy of medicinal mantras, thereby sustaining his life-span.
By employing these few expedient means, the Tathāgata performs the work of a Buddha, protecting and delivering sentient beings, and eliminating their afflictions.
