O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, within the great ocean there is a mani-jewel named Universal Illumination Pure Treasury. When the light of this jewel touches the bodies of sentient beings, they all become of one color. If any see it, their eyes immediately become pure. Wherever that light shines, it rains down mukha-jewels until they completely fill the place, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.

The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is also like this: as a sovereign king of great jewels and an accumulation of merit, the Tathāgata possesses a treasury of great wisdom with a light called Jewel Body Wisdom.
If any sentient beings touch this light, they all attain a body of the same color as the Buddha’s body. If any sentient beings see this light, they all attain the pure Dharma-eye.

If there are sentient beings who come into contact with this light, they will be freed from the suffering of poverty and low status, and attain the honor, nobility, wealth, and joy, even up to the bliss of unsurpassed bodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!
One should know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is without distinction of self and other, yet it is fully capable of performing the Buddha-work for all sentient beings to their ultimate fulfillment.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the great ocean, which possesses a jewel called the Sovereign Wish-Fulfilling Mani Jewel Adorned with All the World’s Ornaments, which is fully endowed with and has accomplished one million merits."

Wherever that King of Jewels resides, all the sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings are extinguished, and their every wish is fully satisfied. This King of Maṇi Jewels cannot be seen by sentient beings with meager merit; likewise, it is with the Maṇi Jewel-King of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

If there are sentient beings who hear of or see it, they will all have the suffering of birth and death extinguished. If all sentient beings simultaneously focus their minds on desiring to see the Tathāgata, they shall all behold him; he causes them to rejoice, and all their wishes are fulfilled.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata cannot be seen by sentient beings of meager merit, except through the Buddha’s spiritual power, which manifests bodies according to what is appropriate for them.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the Tathāgata.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fully accomplishes immeasurable pure minds that pervade the ten directions, penetrate deeply into the Dharma-realm, and abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Being without birth or extinction, equal throughout the three periods of time, they are able to utterly eliminate all falsehoods.
Entering the future limit, the True Dharma fills all worlds, all dharma realms, and all Buddha-bodies with immeasurable adornments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just as the nature of space Reaches everywhere without exception,
So too throughout the worlds of the ten directions Are all the Buddha-fields."
The sphere of form and the sphere of non-form, all classes of sentient beings—
past, future, and present— are neither reached nor unreached.
All the Most Victorious Ones possess the pure and wondrous Dharma-body.
There is nowhere it does not reach, filling the entire realm of phenomena.
This most supreme and wondrous Dharma-body cannot be seen by anyone;
yet for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the Guide manifests it.
Just as the nature of space, which no one can grasp or hold, allows all sentient beings everywhere to perform various deeds without obstruction;
yet space has no such thought: "What am I doing now?"
How is it performed? For whom is it performed?
By means of such supreme ones, through this purification of bodily action, [one attains excellence].
May all classes of living beings universally accomplish the pure and white dharmas.
The Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body benefits immeasurable multitudes;
yet the Dharma-body is also without thought: "I shall benefit all sentient beings."
Just as the bright and pure sun, appearing over Jambudvīpa,
dispels all darkness and shines everywhere without exception—
upon all mountains of various jewels and all the flower ponds upon the great earth.
Nurturing beings according to their needs, he benefits all multitudes.
The most supreme Sun is likewise; benefiting all multitudes, he causes every class of living beings to nurture all roots of goodness.
Having accomplished the light of wisdom, They extinguish all darkness;
Beholding all the Teachers, They are endowed with every bliss.
Just as when the sun rises, It first illuminates the King of Great Mountains,
Furthermore, it shines in succession upon all the great mountains,
then upon the smaller mountains, and other lofty and prominent places;
only thereafter does it shine universally upon the great earth of the world-system.
The Sugata is likewise: the sun of pure wisdom-light first illuminates the bodhisattvas, those great mountain-kings of merit;
only then does it shine successively upon all the pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, it illuminates in succession the śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training;
thereafter, it illuminates in succession all sentient beings.
The Dharma-body has no such thought as, "I am that which illuminates."
Just as the bright and pure sun, appearing in the world,
Though those born blind cannot see it, it is still able to bring benefit:
It eliminates the afflictions of hunger and thirst, Causing the body to become supple and joyful.
One should know that the bright, pure sun benefits all things without exception;
the Buddha-sun is likewise, appearing in the world to bring benefit even to those who lack the eye of faith.
Some hear the voice of the Tathāgata, Others are touched by the light of the Guide;
With these as their causal conditions, they shall ultimately attain Bodhi,
Just as the full moon Outshines all the stars.
To all the multitudes he manifests, Whether increasing or decreasing;
In all waters, clear and pure, The moon’s reflection appears without exception.
All the various classes of living beings in the world Behold it directly before their very eyes.
The most supreme, pure full moon eclipses the two vehicles;
according to those who are to be transformed, he manifests a long or short lifespan,
appearing as a reflection to all humans and devas whose minds are pure vessels for bodhi.
Each and every one thinks to themselves: "I stand before the Honored One of Gods and Humans;
like the Great Brahmā King, dwelling securely in the Brahmā palace, I manifest the body of a Brahmā King throughout the entire great trichiliocosm."
Possessing the power of mastery, he manifests infinite bodies;

they are seen everywhere, yet his body remains undivided. The Teacher is likewise: possessing the power of mastery, he manifests infinite bodies; they are seen everywhere, yet his body remains undivided.
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, he universally manifests immeasurable bodies;
though these immeasurable bodies cannot be fully seen by anyone,
he appears everywhere in response to sentient beings, yet without ever dividing his body.
Just as a great king of physicians, who well understands the methods of remedial treatment,
so that whoever beholds him finds no illness left unremoved;
when he is about to pass away, he gives rise to this thought:
After my body has perished, there will be nothing for all beings to rely upon.
By applying medicine to this body and sustaining it with incantations,
may it remain as it was after my life ends, without any change.
Thus are these most excellent ones, the unsurpassed Great Physicians,
who have skillfully studied the wisdom of expedient means and are fully endowed with all-knowledge.
Through their immeasurable practices of the past, they manifest the pure Dharma-body.
If sentient beings behold him, they eliminate the affliction of their defilements.
Just as within the great ocean, the maṇi, king of all jewels,
produces immeasurable varieties of pure and wondrous radiance.
When sentient beings touch this light, they all become the color of jewels;
if anyone should behold it, their pure eyes are opened.
Such is the most supreme jewel, universally radiating the light of wisdom.
If anyone touches this light, they will all become the same color as the Buddha.
If sentient beings see it, they will be endowed with the five pure eyes;
having extinguished all darkness, they shall dwell securely on the stage of the Tathāgata.
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem, which fulfills all wishes according to one's needs, satisfying the intentions of whoever makes a request;
yet that king of jewels does not give rise to the thought: "I am benefiting the world."
Sentient beings with little merit do not see this King of Jewels;
the Sugata is likewise, for he fulfills all aspirations—
whosoever seeks a wish, they shall all attain its fulfillment.
"The Sugata does not give rise to the thought: 'I benefit sentient beings.
Those who harbor evil minds do not behold the body of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know and perceive the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and perceives that the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere; with the Tathāgata’s various subtle and wondrous voices, he causes all sentient beings to rejoice greatly, proclaiming the immeasurable true Dharma of all Buddhas.
According to those who are to be transformed, they all attain understanding; in teaching and transforming sentient beings, he never misses the proper time.
It causes the body to be cool and refreshing, and the mind to be settled and undisturbed. One observes with equanimity that there is neither arising nor ceasing.
It is like an echo, which has no master; yet from it, knowledge and vision arise, for they nourish all roots of goodness.
Knowledge and vision are profoundly deep, for they have no limit or bottom.
They possess upright knowledge and vision, because they have ultimately crossed over the dharma-realm;
they possess uninterrupted knowledge and vision, because they encompass the dharma-realm;
they possess indestructible knowledge and vision, because they have reached the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that the voice of the Tathāgata is neither measurable nor immeasurable;
it has neither a master nor no master; it is neither wisdom nor the absence of wisdom.
Why is this? It is because when the world is about to be destroyed, it is the nature of phenomena that four kinds of sounds spontaneously emerge. What are these four?
First, you should know that the bliss of the first dhyāna is free from desire and ill-will, and is far removed from the realm of desire;
having heard this, sentient beings will naturally all achieve the first dhyāna, cast off their bodies of the desire realm, and be reborn in the Brahma heavens.
The second is: "You should know that the bliss of the second dhyāna is free from applied and sustained thought; being without applied or sustained thought, one is far removed from the Brahma-body.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings will naturally all achieve the second dhyāna, cast off their bodies in the Brahma-world, and be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The third is: "You should all know that the bliss of the third dhyāna is free from both joy and attachment.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings will naturally all achieve the third dhyāna; they will cast off their bodies of Ābhāsvara Heaven and be reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
The fourth is: "You should know that the four dhyānas are peaceful and blissful, far removed from all suffering;
having heard this, sentient beings will naturally all achieve the four dhyānas, cast off their bodies in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and be reborn in the Bṛhatphala Heaven."
“O Son of the Buddha!

When this world is about to be destroyed, it is by the very nature of phenomena that these four kinds of sounds spontaneously arise. These sounds have no master and no creator; likewise, the wondrous voice of the Tathāgata is also without master or creator, yet it spontaneously produces four kinds of sublime sounds in accordance with the Buddha-dharma.”

What are the four? First, you should know that all conditioned phenomena are suffering: the suffering in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; the suffering of King Yama; the suffering of those who commit evil deeds; the suffering of lacking merit; and the suffering of attachment to a self and what belongs to a self. If you wish to be born among humans or devas, you must plant roots of goodness, cultivate various merits, and distance yourselves from the eight difficulties to become beings who dwell in a state free from such hardships.
Having heard this, abandon your inverted views, cultivate roots of goodness, and distance yourselves from the eight difficulties to be reborn among humans and devas.

The second is: "You should all know that all conditioned phenomena are suffering and are entirely ablaze, like a glowing iron ball; all conditioned activities are subject to total extinction. Nirvana is quiescent, far removed from this blazing, cool, and blissful.

Upon hearing this, sentient beings will all cultivate roots of goodness; having cultivated roots of goodness, they will attain the patience of sounds; having attained the patience of sounds, they will study the Śrāvaka Vehicle."

Third, you should know this: those who study the Śrāvaka-yāna study for the sake of limited wisdom and attain awakening through others. There is a superior vehicle called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, wherein awakening occurs without a teacher; you should study this.
If there are sentient beings who delight in the superior path, upon hearing these sounds, they shall study the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
Fourth, you should know that beyond the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is a further, superior path called the Mahāyāna;

by practicing the bodhisattva conduct, perfecting the six pāramitās, and fulfilling the bodhisattva practices, one attains non-retrogression, does not abandon the bodhicitta, forever leaves birth and death behind, and proceeds toward unsurpassed bodhi.

If there are sentient beings whose faculties are sharp and keen, who have cultivated immeasurable roots of goodness in the past, and who furthermore receive the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they shall hear this sound and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The subtle and wondrous voices of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not issue from the body nor from the mind, yet they are able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first supreme and wondrous practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: to know and see the subtle and sublime voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like an echo, which arises from a sound in the mountains; it has no accumulation and cannot be seen, yet it can respond to all various sounds, though in reality there is nothing that responds."

The sublime voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it has no fixed location, yet it issues forth sounds according to what is appropriate; these sounds are not real, they cannot be perceived, and they cannot be described in words.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, like a wondrous celestial voice that naturally issues forth from the midst of space, it is able to awaken all heedless devaputras and address them, saying:

"You should know that the five desires are impermanent, false, and inverted; they change and alter in an instant, like holding a torch against the wind. They are the practice of fools. Do not be heedless! If you are heedless, when your body perishes and your life ends, you will fall into the three evil realms."

Upon hearing these sounds, the heedless devas gave rise to a sense of dread; they grew weary of and detached from the five desires, each abandoning their palaces to proceed to the Hall of the True Dharma, where they cultivated wholesome dharmas and took delight in the Right Path.
O Son of the Buddha!
The sublime sounds of the devas likewise have no owner and no creator; they neither arise nor cease, yet they are able to benefit the heedless devas.
The sublime voice of the Tathāgata is also like this: for the sake of all heedless sentient beings, it universally produces immeasurable sounds of the True Dharma to awaken them.

That is to say, it was entirely filled with the sound of non-attachment, the sound of heedfulness, the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and the sound of tranquil extinction and nirvana.

Throughout the entire dharma-realm, according to what is appropriate for each, all are made to rejoice; each, according to their own inclination, practices and studies the various vehicles, giving rise to the sounds of immeasurable great wisdom, the sound of non-retrogression, the sounds of the fulfillment of all bodhisattva practices, and the sounds of the Tathāgata’s ground of all-encompassing wisdom.

Once sentient beings have heard these various sounds, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable beings cultivate wholesome dharmas—some studying the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and some studying the unsurpassed Mahāyāna vehicle.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous voice transcends all marks and is cut off from the path of speech.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the Heavenly King Vaśavartin has a celestial jewel-woman named Sukhāvatī.

From a single utterance, she produces hundreds of thousands of musical sounds for entertainment; from each of those individual sounds of entertainment, she further produces hundreds of thousands of musical sounds for entertainment.
O Son of the Buddha!
You should know that from a single sound of virtuous speech, immeasurable and subtle sounds are produced; the voice of the Tathāgata is likewise.
Within a single sound, he produces immeasurable voices, causing all beings to attain understanding according to their respective needs.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

It is, for example, like the Great Brahmā King who, amidst the assembly of Brahmās, utters a Brahmā-sound; there is no one among the great multitude who does not hear it, yet that Brahmā-sound does not go beyond the assembly.
At that time, each of the gods of the Brahma-body thinks:
"The Great Brahmā King speaks only to me, and does not address the other gods."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; he produces immeasurable, unsurpassed, wondrous sounds, which all those who are ready for transformation hear, yet these sounds do not issue outside the assembly.
Why is this? Because the faculties of those sentient beings have not yet matured, those who hear the Buddha’s voice each think to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata speaks only for me, and not for others."

The sounds produced by the Tathāgata likewise have no source of production; those who hear the Buddha’s voice likewise hear nothing. Yet, they are able to perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the nature of water is of a single flavor throughout; yet because it conforms to different vessels, its flavors appear to differ.
Water has no such thought:
"I am producing these various flavors."

The sublime voice of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it is entirely of one single flavor, namely the flavor of liberation; yet, according to the differences among sentient beings who receive transformation, there appear to be distinctions.
The voice of the Tathāgata does not form such knowledge, nor does it form such a thought:
"I produce various and distinct sounds.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata. "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the Dragon King Anavatapta, who raises great, heavy clouds that fill Jambudvīpa and brings down a universal rain of great deluges. The hundred grains, grasses, and trees all flourish; the rivers, streams, ponds, and springs are all filled to overflowing. Yet this great rain does not issue from the body or the mind of the Dragon King, and yet it benefits immeasurable sentient beings."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he raises the great cloud of compassion that pervades the world, universally raining down the supreme nectar of the True Dharma, causing all sentient beings to rejoice greatly, giving rise to roots of goodness, nurturing the True Dharma, and bringing the various vehicles to fulfillment.
The voice of the Tathāgata does not come from without, nor does it issue from within, yet it is able to benefit all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the Dragon King Manasvin, who, when he intends to send down rain, first raises heavy clouds that completely cover the void; these clouds remain suspended for seven days without raining, first causing sentient beings to bring their various karmic actions to completion."
Why is this? Because that Great Dragon King, out of a heart of compassion, after seven days have passed, gradually sends down a fine rain that universally moistens the great earth;

so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. When he is about to rain down the rain of Dharma, he first raises the clouds of Dharma to universally cover all sentient beings, yet he does not immediately rain down the ambrosial True Dharma. First, he causes the faculties of sentient beings to ripen; once their faculties are matured, he then gradually lets fall the ambrosial rain of Dharma.
If one were to preach the profound Dharma immediately, sentient beings would be terrified.
Therefore, the Tathāgata gradually lets fall a fine rain of the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma of all-knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, within the great ocean there is a great nāga king named Mahāvyūha (Great Adornment),
who may rain continuously for ten days, or twenty days, or a hundred days, or a thousand days, or even a hundred thousand days.
O Son of the Buddha!
Rain does not form this thought:
"I shall rain for ten days, or even for a hundred thousand days."
"However, because that Dragon King possesses inconceivable and sovereign power, he may rain for ten days, or even for a hundred thousand days;

likewise, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, likewise desires to rain down the subtle and wondrous nectar of the True Dharma, whether through ten kinds of sounds, or twenty, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or eighty-four thousand varieties of sounds, or even up to immeasurable billions of nayutas of sounds, expounding the Dharma in detail to cause all sentient beings to rejoice."
The sublime voice of the Tathāgata does not form the thought:
"I am able to expound various dharmas.
Furthermore, because the dharma-realm is pure and without differentiation, what is taught differs only for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the Dragon King Sāgara wishes to manifest the great sovereign power of a dragon king and desires to benefit the various classes of sentient beings, he raises great, heavy clouds from the four continents up to the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, completely covering the six heavens with clouds of various colors:

In some places, they were the color of Jāmbūnada gold; in some places, the color of lapis lazuli; in some places, the color of white silver; in some places, the color of crystal; in some places, the color of ruby; in some places, the color of agate; in some places, the color of a supreme treasure-store; in some places, the color of red pearls; in some places, the color of exquisite fragrance; in some places, the color of various garments; in some places, the color of pure water; and in some places, various mixed colors. Such immeasurable clouds of colors covered the four continents and extended even to the six heavens.
They emit various flashes of lightning, namely:
from clouds the color of Jambūnada gold, there issues lightning the color of lapis lazuli; from clouds the color of lapis lazuli, there issues lightning the color of Jambūnada gold;
from clouds the color of white silver, there issues lightning the color of crystal; from clouds the color of crystal, there issues lightning the color of white silver.
From clouds the color of silver, lightning the color of rose-gems issued forth; from clouds the color of rose-gems, lightning the color of agate issued forth;
from clouds the color of the *śreṣṭharatnanidhi*, lightning the color of red pearls issued forth;
from clouds the color of red pearls, lightning the color of the *śreṣṭharatnanidhi* issued forth; from clouds the color of exquisite fragrance, lightning the color of various garments issued forth.
Clouds of various clothing colors emit wondrous fragrant-colored lightning flashes; clouds of pure water color emit various mixed-colored lightning flashes;

clouds of various mixed colors emit pure water-colored lightning flashes; and so on, as extensively described, until clouds of a single color emit various colored lightning flashes, and clouds of various colors emit lightning flashes of a single color.
Furthermore, various great thunderous sounds were made to bring joy to sentient beings, namely: the singing voices of celestial maidens,

the music of celestial entertainments, the singing voices of nāga maidens, the singing voices of gandharva maidens, the singing voices of kinnara maidens, the sound of the great earth, the sound of the great ocean, the voice of the king of deer, or the various wondrous and extraordinary voices of diverse birds, or various songs.

At that time, the Dragon King raised various winds and sent down fine rain, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; from the four continents up to the sixth heaven, he rained down all manner of diverse and immeasurable rains everywhere.
That is to say:
within the great ocean, there falls a rain called "Vast Downpour," which never ceases;
in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, there universally falls a rain of the sounds of songs, praises, and music for entertainment.
In the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations, they universally rained down jewels of liberation that emit clear and pure light;
in the Tuṣita Heaven, they universally rained down divine moon-jewels from crests;
and in the Yāma Heaven, they universally rained down various kinds of ornaments.
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, a rain of exquisite incense fell everywhere;
in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings, a rain of precious robes fell everywhere;
and in the palaces of the Dragon Kings, a rain of crimson, luminous pearls fell everywhere.
In the realm of the asuras, he rains down weapons everywhere, named "Subduing the Enemy";
in Uttarakuru, he rains down various flowers;
thus it is extensively described that throughout the four continents, he rains down all manner of rain.
However, that dragon king’s mind is impartial, without distinction between self and other; it is only because the faculties of sentient beings differ that there are differences in the rain.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, is also like this: when he intends to manifest immeasurable great dharmas, he first uses clouds of pure bodies to universally cover the entire dharma-realm, manifesting clouds of bodies according to what is appropriate for each being.
There may be sentient beings who should see the cloud of the Tathāgata’s birth-body;
there may be sentient beings who should see the cloud of the Tathāgata’s body sustained by supernatural power;
there may be sentient beings who should see the cloud of the Tathāgata’s form-body.
There may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata as various clouds of bodies;
there may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata as clouds of bodies of merit;
there may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata as clouds of bodies of wisdom.
There may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata’s cloud of indestructible bodies;
there may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata’s cloud of fearless bodies;
and there may be sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata’s cloud of Dharma-realm bodies.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, with such immeasurable clouds of bodies, universally covers all worlds, manifesting the lightning-flashes of radiance according to what is appropriate for each.”
There may be sentient beings who behold the lightning-flash of the Tathāgata’s radiance, named "Reaching Everywhere.
There may be sentient beings who behold the lightning-flash of the Tathāgata’s radiance, named "Illuminating the Immeasurable and Boundless."
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-like radiance of the Tathāgata’s light, name it "Entering the Buddha’s Subtle and Secret Teaching.
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-like radiance of the Tathāgata’s light, name it "Brilliantly Pure Universal Illumination."
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-flash of the Tathāgata’s radiance, call it "Pure Illumination.
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-flash of the Tathāgata’s radiance, call it "The Dharani Door of Entering the Inexhaustible Treasury."
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-flash radiance of the Tathāgata, attain that which is named "undisturbed right mindfulness.
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-flash radiance of the Tathāgata, attain that which is named "non-retrogressive wisdom."
There are some sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-like radiance of the Tathāgata, name it "Entering Accordantly into All Realms of Existence.
There are other sentient beings who, upon seeing the lightning-like radiance of the Tathāgata, name it "Universally Causing Sentient Beings to Fulfill All Their Vows."
“O Son of the Buddha!

In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha universally manifests for all sentient beings the lightning-flash of the Tathāgata’s radiance. Having manifested this lightning-flash, he brings forth the thunderous sounds of immeasurable great samādhis.”

They are as follows: the thunderous sound of the samādhi of emerging from perfect enlightenment; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the stainless and tranquil ocean; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of mastery over all dharmas; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the vajra-perfection; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the banner of Sumeru, King of Mountains; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the ocean-seal; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the sun’s radiance; the thunderous sound of the samādhi that causes all sentient beings to rejoice; the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; and the thunderous sound of the samādhi of the indestructible liberation of the arhat.
"O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, from the clouds of his Buddha-body, brings forth the thunderous sounds of immeasurable and various samādhis."

Having emitted the sound of thunder, when he was about to proclaim the Dharma of Ambrosia, he first manifested the auspicious sign of the Tathāgata’s Great Wisdom Wind-wheel. Arising from unobstructed great compassion, this first caused the bodies and minds of all sentient beings and all bodhisattvas to become supple, so that they were all filled with great joy.

In this way, the Tathāgata, by means of clouds of the True Dharma, clouds of great compassion, and inconceivable clouds, causes the bodies and minds of all sentient beings to become supple; only then does he rain down the inconceivable great cloud-rain of the Dharma.
That is to say:
for all bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there falls a great rain-cloud of the indestructible Dharma-realm;
for bodhisattvas in their final birth, there falls a great rain-cloud of the Tathāgata’s secret teachings, the sovereign joy of bodhisattvas.
For Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood, there falls a great Dharma-cloud rain of pure and universal illumination;
for Bodhisattvas who have received their prediction, there falls a great Dharma-cloud rain of the Tathāgata’s adornments;

for Bodhisattvas who have attained patience, there falls a great Dharma-cloud rain of the uninterrupted Bodhisattva practice, consisting of the flowers of merit, jewels, and wisdom; and for Bodhisattvas who are directed toward practice, there falls [a corresponding rain].
Entering the gateway of non-retrogressive practice and the gateway of profound transformation, they never experience weariness or fatigue.

They rain down the great dharma-clouds of the Tathāgata’s meditative conduct, great loving-kindness, and great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings for the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.

For those who delight in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they rain down the great dharma-clouds of deep knowledge of dependent origination, which abandons the views of annihilationism and eternalism and brings about indestructible liberation.
The Dharma-cloud rain of the fruit falls for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka as the Dharma-cloud rain of the treasury of wisdom that subdues the enemies of afflictions;
it falls for sentient beings who cultivate and nurture their roots of goodness— whether their resolve is fixed or unfixed—
as the Dharma-cloud rain of various gates of joy.
“O Son of the Buddha!
It rains these ten kinds of immeasurable and boundless great clouds of Dharma, filling the entire Dharma-realm.
O Son of the Buddha!”
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses a mind of equanimity, free from the distinction of self and other;
yet, because the faculties of sentient beings differ, the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata appears to have distinctions.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Four.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Five,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
Part Three of the Thirty-Second Chapter, "The Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata, King of the Triple Jewel."
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know and see ten kinds of immeasurability in the voice of the Tathāgata. What are these ten?
That is to say:
knowing and seeing that space is immeasurable, because there is nowhere it does not reach;
knowing and seeing that the dharma-realm is immeasurable, because there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
They know and perceive the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, in order to cause all sentient beings to rejoice;
they know and perceive the immeasurable karmic actions, in order to extensively explain all retributions;
they know and perceive the immeasurable afflictions, in order to bring them to ultimate quiescence.
They know and see the infinite varieties of sounds and voices, for there is nothing that those to be transformed cannot hear according to their needs;
they know and see the infinite desires and inclinations, for they explain all forms of liberation through detailed analysis;
they know and see the infinite aspects of the three periods of time, for they are without boundaries.
Knowledge, vision, wisdom, and so forth are immeasurable, for they penetrate deeply into all phenomena;
knowledge and vision of the Buddha’s realm, non-retrogression, and so forth are immeasurable, for they accord with the *tathatā* dharma-realm.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives that the voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses ten such kinds of immeasurable and incalculable [qualities].”
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "When the world is about to be destroyed, In that empty space,
By the power of the merit and retribution of sentient beings, Four sounds naturally emerge."
Within those four dhyānas, there is tranquil bliss free from all suffering;
when sentient beings hear this, they grow weary of and renounce their bodies in the desire realm.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise, spontaneously emitting these four sounds:
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, there is nowhere it is not heard.
Through the power of the causes and conditions of sentient beings, the Buddha responds with four kinds of sounds.
Those who hear these sounds shall forever cross over the ocean of birth and death.
For example, as when a valley serves as the cause for the emergence of an echo, responding to all external sounds;
arising from various causes and conditions, those who hear it likewise differ.
The echo does not form this thought: "I produce various sounds.
Such is the voice of the Tathāgata; it gives rise to immeasurable sounds, which all those who are ready to be transformed hear, without exception.
Causing all to rejoice and taming all sentient beings,
my voice is likewise free from conceptual thought as I produce various sounds.
Like the wondrous voice of the gods, within that very void, it resounds.
Spontaneously it was proclaimed, awakening all the sons of gods.
Having heard this sublime sound of the True Dharma,
the sons of gods practiced with heedfulness and grew weary of the five desires.
The Ten Powers are likewise thus: they produce subtle and wondrous sounds, and the resonance of the Dharma-cloud fills all worlds.
They cause all sentient beings to awaken; yet those sounds are without arising or ceasing.
If there are those who hear it, they shall all realize bodhi.
Just as the Queen of Jewels named Suvaktrā, belonging to the Sovereign King of Devas,
produces hundreds of thousands of sounds from within a single voice.
Furthermore, from each and every sound, hundreds of thousands of voices are produced;
if the gods should hear them, they all find joy and delight.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise: within that single voice, [he produces myriad sounds].
According to their needs, at one time he utters sounds equal in number to all sentient beings.
Once sentient beings have heard these sounds, they eliminate all their afflictions;
yet the voice itself forms no thought, "I am able to effect this elimination."
Just as the Great Brahmā King utters a pure Brahmā-sound,
such that among all the hosts of Brahmā gods there is none who does not hear it;
each and every sound of his Brahmā-voice causes the Brahmā hosts to rejoice.
Pervading the assembly of Brahmā gods, yet the sound does not issue forth beyond;
the Great Brahmā King of Virtue, seated upon the Tathāgata’s throne,
utters a single wondrous voice that fills all dharma-realms.
According to those who are ready to be transformed, there is none who does not hear;
yet the sound does not issue outside the assembly because they lack faith.
Just as all waters, though diverse, are of one and the same taste.
Pure and free from defilement, Possessing the eight meritorious qualities;
Because the ground upon which they rest differs, And the various vessels are each distinct,
Due to those respective causes and conditions, The taste of the water varies accordingly.
Sons of the Buddha, you should know: The sounds of all-encompassing wisdom, The subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata, Are all identical in the flavor of liberation.
Because of the various differences In the actions performed by sentient beings,
The Sugata transforms beings according to their needs, so that what they hear differs for each;
Just as the sovereign great Nāga King Anavatapta Rises with clouds to cover the world, raining everywhere to moisten the great earth.
Nurturing all forests, the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and the like—the rain that falls from it does not issue from the body or mind.
So too is the Tathāgata: first, he raises the great cloud of Dharma.
Universally covering all dharma-realms, it rains down the great nectar of the Dharma.
It causes sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness and extinguishes the heat of afflictions;
yet that nectar-like Dharma does not emerge from body or mind.
Just as the great dragon king named Manasvin,
after raising heavy clouds for seven days, holds them still without letting rain fall,
so as to allow all beings to fully complete their various undertakings.
First a fine, subtle drizzle falls, and only then does the great rain descend.
So too, the One of Ten Powers raises the cloud of Dharma, universally covering all realms of phenomena;
he rains down the great nectar of the Dharma, bringing benefit to all living beings.
According to those who are ready to be transformed, he preaches the profound Dharma for them;
those who hear it are not terrified, and they ultimately achieve Bodhi.
It is like the Great Dragon King, named Mahāvyūha (Great Adornment).
First spreading dense and heavy clouds, he then lets fall a great rain.
Whether for ten or twenty days, or even for a hundred thousand days, the rainwater is of one and the same taste;
it is only because of sentient beings that they differ.
Ultimately reaching the Tathāgata, the further shore of great eloquence,
he may speak ten dharma-gates, or even hundreds of thousands;
he may speak eighty-four thousand, or even immeasurable practices.
The Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought: "I am discerning the Dharma-realm.
It is like the ocean dragon king named Sāgara, who first raises dense and heavy clouds that completely cover the four continents.
Raining universally upon all places, each and every one is distinct;
yet the dragon king’s mind is impartial, possessing neither hatred nor affection.
The Most Victorious One is likewise so: the supreme Dragon King of the Dharma.
Raising great clouds of compassion, they universally cover all beings.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas at the site of enlightenment, they rain down the Dharma of great ambrosia;
according to those who are to be transformed, the Tathāgata’s mind remains impartial.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know and perceive the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that the mind, intellect, and consciousness are not themselves the Tathāgata; rather, because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, his mind is also immeasurable.”
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as space is the support for all things, yet that space itself has no support;
so too is the wisdom of the Tathāgata: it is the support for all worldly wisdom and for wisdom that transcends the world, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata has no support.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: to know and see the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, just as the pure dharma-realm serves as the basis for the liberation of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, yet the pure dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases;

so too is the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which serves as the basis for all mundane and supramundane knowledge, including calculation, arts, and all forms of worldly wisdom, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, the waters of the four great oceans can thoroughly moisten the lands of the four continents and the eight billion small islands; if there are sentient beings who seek water in those various places through skillful means, there is nowhere they go that they do not obtain it, yet that great ocean does not form this thought:
"I am able to provide water for all sentient beings."

The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise; it can moisten and nourish the minds of all sentient beings, and those beings each cultivate roots of goodness within their respective Dharma gates, thereby attaining the light of wisdom. Yet the Tathāgata does not form this thought:
"I am able to bestow wisdom upon all sentient beings."
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is as if the great ocean possesses four kinds of precious jewels;
these four kinds of jewels are all produced within the ocean, and if these jewels were absent, all the other treasures in the ocean would utterly perish.

What are the four? First, named Accumulation of Various Jewels; second, named Inexhaustible Treasury of Jewels; third, named Far Removed from Blazing Heat; fourth, named Mass of All Adornments. These are the four jewels.
O Son of the Buddha!
These four kinds of jewels cannot be seen by any asuras, garuḍas, nāgas, or other spirits; why is this?
Because the Naga King Sagara has secretly deposited profound treasures therein, these four kinds of jewels are magnificent and perfectly square;

likewise, the ocean of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, also possesses four kinds of great wisdom-jewels, which give rise to all the wisdom of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, those in training, and those beyond training, as well as the great jewels of the wisdom of all bodhisattvas.

What are these four? First, the jewel of pure wisdom of unadulterated and skillful means; second, the jewel of pure wisdom that discriminates and expounds upon the conditioned and the unconditioned; third, the jewel of pure wisdom that discriminates and expounds upon all phenomena without violating the dharma-realm; fourth, the jewel of pure wisdom that responds to and transforms sentient beings without ever missing the opportune moment. These are the four kinds of jewels of pure wisdom of the Tathāgata’s great ocean.
O Son of the Buddha!
These four kinds of pure wisdom-jewels of the Tathāgata cannot be seen by any sentient beings. Why is this?

Because these four great treasures of wisdom are enshrined within the Tathāgata’s subtle and secret treasury of Dharma-jewels; thus, the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is majestic, sublime, and extraordinary.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the great ocean possesses four great jewels of blazing radiance; these four kinds of jewels are all capable of exhausting the boundless waters of the great ocean.
What are these four?

First, the Great Jewel named Sun-Treasury Radiance; second, the Great Jewel named Moisture-Free Radiance; third, the Great Jewel named Fire-Bead Radiance; fourth, the Great Jewel named Ultimate Remainderless Radiance.
O Son of the Buddha!

If these four jewels did not exist within the great ocean, the four continents of the world, the Diamond Ring Mountains, and even the realms up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception would all be submerged and swept away.
O Son of the Buddha!

This great jewel of the light of the Sun-Treasury can transform the waters of the ocean entirely into curd; the great jewel of the light of Separation-from-Moisture can transform the ocean of curd entirely into clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the great jewel of the light of the Fire-Ball can completely incandesce the ocean of clarified butter; and the great jewel of the Light of Ultimate Exhaustion without Remainder can completely consume the ocean of clarified butter until it is forever exhausted without remainder.

Likewise, the ocean of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses four kinds of great *maṇi* jewels of wisdom-light, which illuminate all Bodhisattvas as they fully cultivate all manner of practices, up to and including the attainment of the equalizing wisdom of Buddhahood.

What are the four? First, the great precious jewel of the light of wisdom that forever stills all waves of unwholesomeness; second, the great precious jewel of the light of wisdom that extinguishes craving for all phenomena; third, the great precious jewel of the light of wisdom of great intelligence; and fourth, the great precious jewel of the light of immeasurable wisdom equal to that of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!

When those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate and accumulate bodhi, immeasurable waves of unwholesome birth-and-death arise, which none among all the devas, asuras, and others can stop. The Tathāgata, by means of the great jewel of the light of wisdom that extinguishes all unwholesome waves, illuminates the unwholesome waves of the Bodhisattva, causing them to cease forever, so that they may firmly abide in unsurpassed samādhi;

and by means of the great jewel of the light of wisdom that eliminates all craving for dharmas conducive [to samsara], he extinguishes all attachment to the flavor of samādhi that is difficult to relinquish.
By means of the great jewel of the light of wisdom of great intelligence, one extinguishes all ignorance and attains the penetration of pure wisdom;
by means of the great jewel of the immeasurable light of wisdom equal to that of the Tathāgata, one gives birth to the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom through slight expedient means.
O Son of the Buddha!
If there were not the four kinds of great jewel-lights of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it would be impossible for even a single bodhisattva to attain the stage of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth supreme practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, from the limit of the water-circle up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception—all the trichiliocosm worlds—rest upon space; namely, the abodes of sentient beings in the formless realm, the abodes of sentient beings in the form realm, and the abodes of sentient beings in the desire realm.
All places within these three realms rely entirely upon empty space, yet that empty space is not constricted;

the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise so. All the wisdom of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), as well as their wisdom regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—all such wisdoms arise based upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata and abide based upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata. The wisdom of the Tathāgata is not constricted. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom reaches everywhere.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the King of Medicinal Trees on the summit of the Snowy Mountains, named 'Neither Born from Roots nor Not Born from Them. That King of Medicinal Trees grows from six million eight hundred thousand yojanas down, reaching as far as the adamantine ground at the limit of the water-circle."
O Son of the Buddha!
When this medicinal king tree produces its roots, all the trees of Jambudvīpa produce their roots;

when it produces its trunk, all the trees of Jambudvīpa produce trunks; and when it produces branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, all the trees of Jambudvīpa likewise produce branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
In this medicinal king tree, the root can produce the trunk, and the trunk can produce the root; therefore it is called "not produced from the root, yet not not produced from the root.
O Son of the Buddha!

This medicinal king tree grows in all places, with the exception of two: it cannot grow in the deep pits of hell nor within the water-circle, yet the great medicinal king tree does not abandon its nature of growth.

The great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it is born from the lineage of all Tathāgatas and has cultivated immeasurable and boundless merits such as great compassion throughout past lives.
Firmly and correctly established, it cannot be shaken.

The immeasurable roots of goodness and wisdom of the three periods of time universally cover all worlds, extinguishing all the hardships of the evil realms. With the stem of skillful means, the branches of the pure Dharma-realm, the leaves of the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations, the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, and the fruit of unsurpassed liberation, it is sustained by dhāraṇī from the very beginning, without increase or decrease.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Great King of Medicine Tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has another name, called ‘Root Firm and Indestructible. Why is this?
Because they do not abandon nor sever the various practices of the bodhisattva assembly, their faculties are called "indestructible.
When the great medicinal king tree of that Tathāgata’s wisdom first produces its roots, all bodhisattvas likewise produce the roots of great compassion, never forsaking any sentient being;
when it first produces its trunk, all bodhisattvas grow the trunk of a firm, vigorous, and upright mind.
When the branches first emerge, all Bodhisattvas cause the branches of all the *pāramitās* to grow;
when the leaves first emerge, all Bodhisattvas cause the leaves of the merits of pure precepts, dignified deportment, and *dhūta* practices to grow;
when the flowers first emerge, the flowers of the marks and signs adorned by the roots of goodness of all Bodhisattvas come into full bloom.
When the fruit first arises, all bodhisattvas attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena and receive the fruit of the Buddha's prediction.
Son of the Buddha!
The great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom cannot grow in two places; namely:

Although śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, nirvāṇa, hells, deep pits, those who violate the precepts, those with wrong views, those who are greedily attached, and those who are not fit vessels for the Dharma do not grow from it, the tree of the Tathāgata nevertheless does not fail to grow; all other beings who are ready to be transformed grow within it, yet the great medicinal king-tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom neither increases nor decreases.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh sublime practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the kalpa-ending fire arises, everything within the trichiliocosm—the entire great earth, grasses, trees, and even the diamond-encircled mountains—is completely incinerated and consumed without remainder.
Suppose there were a person who threw dry grass into that fire; could it possibly fail to burn?
He replied, "No, it would not fail to be completely consumed by the flames."
"O Son of the Buddha!
The grass thrown there might yet not be exhausted.
Yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings, all buddha-fields, all kalpas, and all dharmas without exception; that there should be anything he does not know is impossible."
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is indestructible and fully penetrates all things.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth supreme practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

For example, when the world is destroyed by the calamity of wind, a great wind arises called "Dissolution," which is capable of completely dissolving, grinding down, and annihilating all things within the Great Trichiliocosm, including the Diamond Ring Mountains.
At that time, outside the trichiliocosm, there arises another wind called the "Wind of Obstruction, Destruction, and Dispersion," which prevents the calamity of wind from reaching other regions.
O Son of the Buddha!
If this obstructing wind did not exist, the infinite, boundless, and incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya*) of the ten directions would not disperse and perish;

likewise, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess a great wind of wisdom called "Dispersing and Destroying All Afflictions," which is fully capable of dispersing and destroying all the afflictive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses the wind of skillful means wisdom, which is able to sustain all bodhisattvas, preventing them from reaching ultimate extinction by falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained the power of the wind of this skillful means wisdom, they are able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and reach the ultimate stage of a Buddha.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
The Tathāgata’s wisdom reaches everywhere. Why is this?
Because there is no sentient being, nor any body of a sentient being, to whom the Tathāgata’s wisdom does not fully apply.
However, sentient beings are deluded and do not know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is far removed from delusion, giving rise to all-encompassing wisdom, teacherless wisdom, and unimpeded wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, suppose there were a single scripture as large as a trichiliocosm, in which everything existing within that great trichiliocosm was recorded without exception;
or one as large as a dichiliocosm, in which all matters within that dichiliocosm were likewise recorded.
Regarding the small thousand-world systems and so forth, he fully records all matters within those small thousand-world systems.
Regarding the four continents and so forth, he fully records all matters of the four continents.
Regarding Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and so forth, he fully records all matters concerning Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains.
The palaces of the Earth-Devas and so forth all record the matters within the palaces of the Earth-Devas;
the palaces of the Desire-Heaven Devas and so forth all record the matters within the palaces of the heavens of the Desire Realm;
the palaces of the Form-Heaven Devas and so forth all record the matters within the palaces of the heavens of the Form Realm.
If there are celestial palaces of the formless heavens, he fully records all matters within those palaces of the formless realms.
A scroll of this Great Trichiliocosm and other worlds is contained within a single minute atom, and it is likewise with all atoms.

"At that time, there appeared in the world a person of great wisdom and discernment who had fully perfected the pure divine eye. Seeing this sutra scroll within a minute particle of dust, he thought to himself:
'How is it that such a vast sutra scroll remains within a minute particle of dust without benefiting sentient beings?'"
"I shall diligently employ skillful means to break apart those atoms and bring forth this sutra scroll to benefit sentient beings.
At that time, that person immediately employed skillful means, broke apart the atoms, brought forth this sutra scroll, and benefited sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata’s wisdom is signless, his wisdom is unimpeded, and his wisdom is fully perfected; it dwells within the bodies of sentient beings. Yet, because foolish sentient beings are shrouded by inverted perceptions, they do not know it, do not see it, and do not give rise to faith.
"At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure divine eye, observed all sentient beings.
Having observed them, he spoke these words:
'How marvelous!'"
How marvelous!
Why is it that although the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom is fully present within their bodies, they do not know or perceive it?

I shall instruct those sentient beings to awaken to the Noble Path, causing them all to forever leave behind the defilements and bonds of delusive thoughts and inversions, so that they may fully see the Tathāgata’s wisdom within their own bodies, no different from that of a Buddha.
The Tathāgata immediately instructed those sentient beings to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path and abandon false, inverted views;
having abandoned such inversions, they came to possess the wisdom of a Tathāgata, becoming equal to a Tathāgata, and brought benefit to sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth supreme practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: knowing and seeing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
O Son of the Buddha!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such immeasurable and innumerable supreme and wondrous modes of conduct, through which they know and perceive the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If you wish to know the mind of the Tathāgata, You should understand his supreme wisdom.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, And his supreme mind is likewise so."
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, All classes of sentient beings Rely entirely upon space, Yet space has nothing upon which it relies.
Within the entire realm of phenomena, The various pleasures of sentient beings—
The skillful means and clever arts arise from the most supreme wisdom.
All forms of wisdom depend entirely upon the wisdom of the Sugata;
yet the Tathāgata’s most supreme wisdom is tranquil and has no dependence.
The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, And the fruits of liberation and wisdom, All arise from the dharmadhātu; Yet the dharmadhātu neither increases nor decreases.
Supreme wisdom is thus: It can give rise to all-knowledge.
The wisdom of training and the wisdom beyond training, The wisdom that thoroughly realizes existence and non-existence—
The unsurpassed wisdom of the Sugata gives birth to all-knowledge;
Neither born nor unborn, it is entirely without increase or decrease.
Just as the waters of the great ocean Moisten and nourish all the earth, So too,
through the skillful means of sentient beings, There is no seeking for water that goes unfulfilled.
The great ocean has no thought That "I am giving water to sentient beings."
The great ocean neither increases nor decreases, yet through skillful means, all who seek from it find their fill.
Likewise, the ocean of the Sugata’s wisdom can moisten and nourish all the various classes of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Each diligently applying skillful means, To cultivate all dharma-gates,
All such practitioners Will swiftly attain the light of wisdom.
Just as the Dragon King Sāgara Possesses four wondrous precious jewels,
Deeply hidden is the profound treasure-store, which sentient beings are unable to see.
Majestic and upright, it eternally abides within the great ocean;
from these four maṇi-jewels, all treasures are produced.
The four supreme kinds of knowledge, immeasurable and beyond compare,
give birth to all beings and their immeasurable wisdoms.
Abiding in the treasury of the Mahāyāna, they are adorned with immeasurable virtues.
Except for bodhisattvas who have received the prediction of enlightenment, none can see it.
It is like four maṇi jewels within the great ocean,
whose radiant flames are so fiercely hot that they can evaporate the waters of the sea.
If these four jewels did not exist, the heavens and earth would all drift and submerge;
yet the great ocean neither increases nor decreases, and the four quarters remain securely established.
So too are the Tathāgata’s four kinds of wisdom—immeasurable and beyond praise.
They are able to stifle the waves of unwholesome roots within all Bodhisattvas.
Throughout all the three worlds— of desire, form, and formlessness—
they are free from "I" and "mine," dwelling securely in the void.
The wisdom of the Sugata is likewise the root of all-knowledge:
the wisdom of śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, as well as that of the pratyekabuddhas;
and the immeasurable, profound wisdom of the bodhisattvas who universally benefit others.
All rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom, yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no basis.
Like the summit of the Snowy Mountains, where there grows a great king of medicinal trees named "Not Born from a Root," yet it is not that it is not born from a root.
By reason of this medicinal king-tree’s growth and development,
all the forests and trees of Jambudvīpa come into being.
When its roots grow, the roots of all other trees grow as well.
The stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits— all are likewise so.
Pure and profound wisdom is born from within the Tathāgata-nature;
relying upon the Tathāgata-wisdom, the wisdom of practice is produced.
All the practices of Bodhisattvas, And immeasurable virtues,
Are born from the ground of equanimity Of the Tathāgata, the King of Wisdom Trees.
Just as at the end of an eon, A fierce and blazing great fire of calamity [arises],
Even if one were to cast dry grass into it, it might still not be entirely consumed by the fire;
yet the Sugata’s pure wisdom is immeasurable and boundless,
for he is able to discern and know all classes of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, he knows all kalpas and all buddha-fields;
such immeasurable dharmas as these, the Tathāgata fully understands them all.
It is like when the kalpa comes to an end, and the wind-disaster known as "Dissolution" arises.
It can destroy all great earths, As well as the vajra and Mount Sumeru.
Beyond the world-systems, winds arise, Named "Obstructing, Scattering, and Destroying.
If these winds did not exist, The ten directions would utterly perish.
The Ten Powers are likewise; the winds of immeasurable wisdom can entirely disperse and extinguish all the afflictions of the bodhisattvas.
Through the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means, he gathers and sustains all bodhisattvas.
Surpassing the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one dwells securely in the stage of the Tathāgata.
It is like a great scripture, equal in size to the trichiliocosm, existing within a single mote of dust, which is of no benefit to sentient beings.
At that time, there was a person who appeared in the world, who broke through the dust to bring forth the sutra scrolls and benefited all the world.
Such is the wisdom of the Tathāgata; all sentient beings possess it entirely.
Shrouded by inverted delusions, sentient beings do not know or see.
The Tathāgata teaches sentient beings to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path,
to eliminate all obstacles, and to ultimately achieve Bodhi.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva know and perceive the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes immeasurable, boundless, and unimpeded wisdom; knowing all sentient beings, this is the realm of the Tathāgata.”

The realm of all worlds, all lands, all phenomena, and the conduct of all sentient beings—the realm of suchness that is indestructible, the realm of the unimpeded dharma-realm, the realm of the limit of reality which is boundless, the realm of immeasurable space, and the realm that is no realm—this is the realm of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Because all sentient beings are immeasurable, the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable;
because all worlds are immeasurable, the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Furthermore, because that which is not an object of experience is immeasurable as an object of experience, the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable;
because that which is not an object of experience reaches all places yet reaches nowhere, the realm of the Tathāgata is likewise so.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that the sphere of the mind is the sphere of the Tathāgata.
Just as the sphere of the mind is immeasurable, so too is the sphere of the Tathāgata immeasurable.”
Why is this? As the mind is immeasurable, so too is the arising of wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Just as a great dragon sends down rain according to its will, yet the rain comes from neither within nor without;
so too is the realm of the Tathāgata: according to what the mind contemplates, within every moment of thought, it gives birth to immeasurable and inconceivable wisdom.
Those various wisdoms have no place from which they come.
O Son of the Buddha!
All the waters of the great oceans arise from the mental vows of the dragon kings.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise thus; it arises entirely from the power of great vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable and boundless, ineffable, and inconceivable.
I shall speak a brief parable; listen now with careful attention:
O Son of the Buddha!
Within this Jambudvīpa, two thousand five hundred rivers flow out and all enter the great ocean.
Within Aparagoyānī, five thousand river currents flow out and all enter the great ocean.
Within Pūrvavideha, eight thousand four hundred river currents flow out and all enter the great ocean.
From within Uttarakuru flow ten thousand rivers, all of which enter the great ocean.
O Son of the Buddha!
Within these four continents, there are twenty-five thousand nine hundred such rivers, all of which enter the great ocean.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Is this water much or little? He replied:
“Very much. “O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, there are ten Dragon Kings of Radiance who rain down into the great ocean, and their waters all exceed the water mentioned previously.”
The Dragon King Hundred Radiances rains upon the great ocean, exceeding all that came before;
the Dragon King Great Adornment rains upon the great ocean, again exceeding all that came before.
The Nāga King Manasvin rained upon the great ocean, exceeding all that came before;
the Great Thunder Nāga King rained upon the great ocean, again exceeding all that came before.
The dragon kings Nanda and Upananda rain down upon the great ocean, exceeding all that came before;
the dragon king Immeasurable Radiance rains down upon the great ocean, again exceeding all that came before.
The Dragon King Uninterrupted Flow pours rain into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
The Dragon King Great Victory pours rain into the great ocean, again exceeding all that came before.
The Dragon King Vajraprabha rains upon the great ocean, exceeding the former by even more.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this manner, these eighty billion dragon kings each rain upon the great ocean, each succeeding one exceeding the one before.
The crown prince of the Naga King Sagara is named Buddhajanman; the rain he pours down upon the great ocean exceeds even that of the former.
"O Son of the Buddha!
The deep pools where those ten Radiant Dragon Kings dwell flow into the great ocean, and they too exceed even that of the former."
The deep pools where the Dragon King Hundred Radiances dwells flow into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
The deep pools where the Dragon King Great Adornment dwells flow into the great ocean, likewise exceeding all that came before.
The deep pool where the Naga King Manasvin dwells flows into the great ocean, exceeding all previous ones.
The deep pool where the Naga King Mahāmegha dwells flows into the great ocean, exceeding all previous ones as well.
The deep pools where the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda dwell flow into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
The deep pools where the dragon king Amitaprabha dwells flow into the great ocean, again exceeding all that came before.
The deep pools where the Dragon King Uninterrupted Flow resides flow into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
The deep pools where the Dragon King Great Victory resides flow into the great ocean, likewise exceeding all that came before.
The deep pools where the Naga King Vajraprabha dwells flow into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
Thus it is explained in detail, even unto the deep pools where the crown prince of the Naga King Sagara dwells, which flow into the great ocean, exceeding all that came before.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as those ten dragon kings and eight billion dragon kings, even including the crown prince of the Sāgara Dragon King, rain down upon the great ocean and its deep pools, none of these can compare to the rain poured by the Sāgara Dragon King upon the great ocean;
the water that gushes forth from the deep pool where the Sāgara Dragon King dwells and flows into the great ocean exceeds all the former amounts.
That surging flowing water, the color of blue lapis lazuli, fills the great ocean; it surges forth at specific times.
For this reason, the tides of the ocean never miss their appointed time.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this way, the great ocean has immeasurable water, immeasurable precious jewels, immeasurable sentient beings, and immeasurable land.
Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Is that water of the great ocean not immeasurable?
He replied: "It is indeed so.
The depth and breadth of that water are beyond comparison."
“O Son of the Buddha!
Thus, although the ocean water is immeasurably deep and vast, it does not equal even one hundredth part of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable ocean of wisdom; indeed, no analogy can be made for it.
It is only in accordance with those who are to be transformed that it is used as a metaphor.”
O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows and perceives the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom as profound, vast, and immeasurable.

Because they have practiced the immeasurable conducts of a bodhisattva from the first generation of the mind until their cessation, they know and perceive the immeasurable jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the uninterrupted continuity of the Three Jewels. Because they cause immeasurable sentient beings to rejoice and nurture all *śrāvakas*, those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and *pratyekabuddhas*, they know and perceive the immeasurable stages (*bhūmi*), from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate stage of unimpeded wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!

This is how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know and perceive the realm of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, because they possess immeasurable wisdom that brings immeasurable benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
The pure realm free from defilement Is immeasurable and beyond praise;
By the power of supreme vows, All things are without limit.
Just as the realm of the mind Is immeasurable and boundless,
So too is the realm of all those with Ten Powers.
Just as a great dragon king Does not leave his original place,
By the power of the mind’s aspiration, the rain is immeasurable.
The rainwater comes from nowhere, nor does it have a place of departure;
by the power of the Dragon King’s aspiration, it rains immeasurably according to his will.
All the lands of the ten directions, and likewise the One of Ten Powers,
have originally nowhere from which they come, and nowhere to which they go.
All immeasurable realms arise entirely from the conditions of the mind.
All realms of phenomena enter entirely into the path of a single hair;
Just as the waters of the great ocean are immeasurable and boundless,
So too are sentient beings, precious treasures, and the great earth immeasurable.
The waters of the ocean are ever serene, All of them being of one single taste;
Yet according to the enjoyment of sentient beings, Their tastes appear each to be different.
The Most Victorious One is likewise so: The ocean of his wisdom is immeasurable.
Because the Three Jewels are most supreme, their treasures are immeasurable;
The śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, and the pratyekabuddhas are immeasurable;
Because they fully cultivate the unsurpassed path, it is said that their stages are immeasurable.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva know and perceive the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives the unimpeded conduct and the suchness-conduct of the Tathāgata; this conduct of the Tathāgata is suchness itself: it was not extinguished in the past, it does not arrive in the future, and it does not arise in the present. The conduct of the Tathāgata is likewise: it is not extinguished, it does not arrive, and it does not arise.”
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, the dharma-realm is immeasurable and unbound. Why is this?
Because the dharma-realm has no body,
the practice of the Tathāgata is likewise immeasurable and unbound. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata acts without a body, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a bird flying through space; the distance it has traveled over hundreds or thousands of years cannot be measured.
The places where it has not yet traveled are likewise immeasurable. Why is this?
Because space is without boundaries.

The practice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise so: even if someone were to analyze and explain the practice of the Tathāgata for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, that which has been explained would be immeasurable, and that which remains unexplained would also be immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s practice is without limit.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha abides in the Tathāgata-abiding because he has no abode;
yet he is able to universally manifest and guide all sentient beings in the practice of a Tathāgata, so that upon seeing him, sentient beings transcend all paths of obstruction.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda), who flies through the void and dwells in the void; with his pure eyes, he observes the palaces of the Dragon Kings in the great ocean.
