Rousing his fierce and heroic power, he strikes the waters of the sea with his left and right wings, causing them to part completely on both sides. He then perceives those among the male and female dragons whose life-span has ended and seizes them.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuḍa), likewise abides within the unobstructed void. With his pure eye, he observes all sentient beings within the various palaces of the Dharma-realm; if there are those whose roots of goodness have already matured, he exerts the ten powers with heroic vigor and spreads the two wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā to widely open the great ocean of the waters of craving in birth and death. According to what is appropriate for each, he brings them forth from the sea of birth and death, eliminates all false imaginings and inversions, and establishes them in the unobstructed conduct of a Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like the sun and moon as they traverse the void; they do not form the thought:
'As I travel through the void, from where have I come?'"
"To where does it go?

The Tathāgata is also like this: he travels everywhere without obstruction through liberation as vast as space, discerning the entire dharma-realm and benefiting all sentient beings, extensively performing the works of a Buddha; yet the Tathāgata does not form the thought:
"I have coming and going."
"O Son of the Buddha!
By means of such immeasurable and boundless superior practices, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows and perceives the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "Just as Suchness is inexhaustible, Neither arising nor ceasing,
And having no location or direction, It cannot be seen even when sought."
The Tathāgata is likewise: his sphere of activity is immeasurable, he is far removed from the three periods of time, and his nature is entirely suchness (tathatā).
Just as the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu) is neither a realm nor a non-realm, so too is the Tathāgata.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither measurable nor immeasurable;
such is the upholding of merit. His conduct is unfathomable, neither existent nor non-existent, for his body is fundamentally non-existent.
Just as a bird flies through the void, passing through hundreds or thousands of years,
the places it has traveled and those yet to be traversed are entirely immeasurable.
Even if one were to expound upon the conduct of the Tathāgata for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, [it would remain beyond measure].
What has been spoken and what remains unsaid are both entirely immeasurable.
Like the golden-winged bird dwelling securely in the void,
observing the palaces of the dragon kings and seizing their sons and daughters.
The Ten Powers are likewise so: abiding in the conduct of the Tathāgata, they cause those whose roots of goodness are fully matured to emerge from the ocean of afflictions.
Like the pure sun and moon, they traverse throughout the void of space.
Bringing peace and happiness to all beings, yet not thinking, "I am able to do this.
So too is the Tathāgata: traversing all realms of phenomena, he delivers all beings, yet does not think, "I am able to deliver them."
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know and perceive the awakening (*bodhi*) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and perceives awakening; he understands all meanings, eliminates doubt and confusion, and possesses non-dual perfect awakening. It is signless, without activity, without regression, immeasurable, boundless, without bondage, and without liberation; it is far removed from the two extremes and knows what is possible and what is impossible.”

They know all letters and all modes of speech; they know the mental activities and mental states of all sentient beings; they know all faculties, afflictions, and habitual tendencies; and within a single thought-moment, they fully know all phenomena of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, the great ocean is the seal of the forms and images of all sentient beings; therefore, the great ocean is called "the seal.

The bodhi of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: the mental activities and faculties of all sentient beings appear within bodhi, yet there is nothing that appears. Therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be "the Awakened One of All."
“O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhi of all Buddhas cannot be recorded by any written characters, cannot be expressed by any speech, and is beyond all analogy; yet, according to what is appropriate for each, the Tathāgata analyzes and expounds it for them.”
O Son of the Buddha!
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha attains Bodhi, he abides in the skillful means of a Buddha and attains a body equal to all sentient beings;
he attains a body equal to all dharmas.
One attains a body equal to all lands;
one attains a body equal to all three periods of time;
one attains a body equal to all Tathāgatas.
One attains a body equal to all Buddhas;
one attains a body equal to all speech;
one attains a body equal to the entire dharma-realm.
They attain bodies equal to the realm of empty space;
they attain bodies equal to the unimpeded dharma-realm;
they attain bodies that give birth to immeasurable realms.
They attain a body equal to the realm of all conditioned phenomena;
they attain a body equal to the realm of tranquil nirvana.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as one should understand the body obtained by the Tathāgata, so too should one know that his voice and unimpeded mind are likewise; the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these three kinds of infinite purity.
O Son of the Buddha!

Within the body of the Tathāgata, one sees all sentient beings generating the bodhicitta, practicing the bodhisattva path, and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment; even seeing all sentient beings enter the nirvana of quiescence is likewise so—all are of one single nature.
Because they are without intrinsic nature;
because they are signless, inexhaustible, unarisen, and unceasing;
and because they are the nature of both self and non-self.
Because sentient beings and non-sentient beings are of the same nature;
because awakening is without anything to be awakened to;
and because the dharma-realm has no self-nature.
Because the realm of empty space lacks intrinsic nature;

thus, through such awakening to the inexhaustible wisdom and spontaneous wisdom that all things lack intrinsic nature, all Tathāgatas, by means of their infinite great compassion, deliver sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
For example, just as in the realm of space, whether worlds are formed or destroyed, it never increases or decreases. Why is this?

Because space is without arising or ceasing, the bodhi of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—whether it has been realized or not—is eternally without increase or decrease; it is of a single nature that is non-existent, having abandoned all manifold natures.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Suppose there were a person who appeared in the world, capable of manifesting as many minds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

Each and every one of those minds could manifest as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—formless and shapeless—and thus continue to manifest them without ceasing for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.”
"What do you think?
Would those emanated Tathāgatas be numerous? He replied:
“I understand your intention; whether you transform them or not, there is no difference between the two.
“Excellent! Excellent!”
O Son of the Buddha!
It is exactly as you have said.
O Son of the Buddha!
Even if all sentient beings were to attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment, whether they have attained it or not, they are entirely equal. Why is this?
Because awakening is without intrinsic nature, it neither increases nor decreases; the awakening of all Tathāgatas is of a single nature, namely:
the absence of intrinsic nature.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and perceives the awakening of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
O Son of the Buddha!
When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had attained perfect enlightenment, he entered the samādhi named "Excellent Awakening" (Sujñāna).
Having entered this samādhi, he attained a body of awakening (bodhikāya) equal in number to the bodies of all sentient beings.
Just as it is with one samādhi, so it is with all samādhis and all dharma-gates.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows and perceives the body of awakening (bodhi-kāya) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
Within a single hair-pore, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fully knows that the bodies of all sentient beings are equal to the body of the Tathāgata;
as it is with one hair-pore, so it is with all hair-pores and throughout the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s body of awakening reaches everywhere and exists everywhere. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha originally sought awakening;

through diligent and arduous cultivation, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, sat upon the lion throne, and attained supreme perfect awakening, reaching the ultimate realization of bodhi.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows for himself that within his own body there is the bodhi of all Buddhas. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva’s mind does not depart from the enlightenment of all Tathāgatas,
it is likewise within the minds of all sentient beings— immeasurable, boundless, existing everywhere, indestructible, and inconceivable.
O Son of the Buddha!

By means of such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable gates of skillful means, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives the awakening (*bodhi*) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Bodhi is not a dualistic dharma; It is far removed from the two extremes.
Having eliminated all evils, It is the equal awakening to all phenomena."
Thoroughly comprehending all phenomena, They are entirely like space;
Neither self nor non-self— Thus they perfectly awaken to all phenomena.
Just as in the great oceans, All classes of sentient beings...
All forms and images are fully manifested; therefore, they are called all seals (*mudrā*).
Within the worlds of the ten directions, among all classes of sentient beings, there is no phenomenon within the ocean of unsurpassed *bodhi* that does not appear.
Just as the nature of space, when the world is formed or destroyed,
whether it has been formed or not yet formed, remains without increase or decrease;
so too is the Supreme One regarding the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Whether awakened or unawakened, they are of one nature and yet without nature.
Just as throughout immeasurable eons, Buddhas are manifested in every thought-moment—
whether manifested or not— they are all entirely equal and without distinction.
Even if all sentient beings were to simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment—
whether they have attained it or have not— the Bodhi remains without increase or decrease.
There is a supreme samādhi called "Excellent Awakening."
At the site of enlightenment, one attains this samādhi;
universally emitting immeasurable light, it extinguishes all darkness for all sentient beings alike, awakening the multitudes of living beings.
All kalpas of the three periods of time, all Buddha-fields and all phenomena,
all faculties, minds, and mental factors— all these illusory phenomena—
are entirely manifested within the body of a single Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that bodhi is immeasurable and boundless.
"O Son of the Buddha!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva know and see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha turning the wheel of Dharma?"

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows and perceives all the vows and all the dharmas of the Tathāgata; they involve no turning, for there is originally nothing that arises. These three turnings are perfected and entirely pure; he is able to remain far removed from all false views, transcending both the limit of desire and its absence.
All phenomena are like the limit of space and are ineffable, for all dharmas have the nature of quiescent nirvāṇa;
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows and sees all letters and all modes of speech as the turning of the wheel of Dharma, for the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere;
he knows and sees the wheel of Dharma as an echo, for it is the true nature of reality.
To know and see that all sounds are but a single sound—by this the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma; for the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma has no master.
To know and see that the turning of the wheel of Dharma is untainted and inexhaustible, because there is nothing internal or external.
“O Son of the Buddha!

Just as written characters could not be exhausted even if spoken for immeasurable and incalculable eons, so too is it with the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; all written characters and all languages cannot exhaust its description.”
The Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma enters entirely into all languages and scripts, yet abides nowhere.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the system of letters, which enters entirely into all numerical counts of characters, all numerical counts of phenomena, all numerical counts of languages, all numerical calculations, and all mundane and supramundane realms, yet abides nowhere.
The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it penetrates everywhere without exception, yet it abides in nothing—not in any sentient being, any phenomenon, any karma, any retribution, or any mind.
All the linguistic expressions of all sentient beings are encompassed by the sound of the Wheel of Dharma.
Why is this? Because no sound whatsoever is apart from the sound of the Wheel of Dharma.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and sees the Dharma-gate for the arising of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma."
What is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate for giving birth to the turning of the wheel of Dharma?
The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings by means of sounds that correspond to the mental activities and thoughts of every sentient being in every moment of thought.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a samādhi called "Ultimate Unimpeded Fearlessness"; it is by entering this samādhi that the Tathāgata turns the wheel of the Dharma.

Once the Tathāgata has entered this samādhi, he produces voices equal in number to all sentient beings; within each and every voice, he further produces voices equal in number to all sentient beings, thereby turning the wheel of Dharma and causing all sentient beings to experience great joy.
O Son of the Buddha!

If one knows the turning of the wheel of Dharma in this way, you should know that such a person is in accord with the family of all Buddhas; if one does not know it in this way, then they are not in accord with the families of the Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know and see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha turning the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma, reaching everywhere throughout the three periods of time;
yet that which is turned is nothing turned, for it cannot be found when sought.
It is like all written characters: though one speaks them, they can never be exhausted.”
The Ten Powers are likewise thus, turning the wheel of Dharma without end.
Just as written characters are entirely included within all numerical systems,
yet that which is included has no locus of inclusion, so too is the wheel of Dharma.
Universally entering all sounds, yet that which enters has nothing to enter;
it is itself devoid of intrinsic nature, yet can cause all beings to rejoice.
Transcending all numerical limits, it ultimately brings about the realization of Bodhi.
Desiring to proclaim the true meaning, he therefore enters samādhi.
By the power of that samādhi, he produces sublime sounds,
equal in number to all sentient beings, and turns the wheel of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, from each and every one of those sounds, there arise immeasurable voices—
the languages and modes of expression of all sentient beings.
Greatly sovereign and free from thought, I produce all those various sounds.
According to those who receive transformation, there is nothing that does not hear it.
Just as all written characters are neither internal nor external,
they are untainted and inexhaustible, and likewise without accumulation.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise; he turns the pure wheel of Dharma, which is untainted and inexhaustible—the great supernormal power of all Buddhas.
*Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Five.
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Six,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
Part Four of Chapter Thirty-Two, "The Nature-Arising of the Tathāgata, King of the Four Jewels."
“O Son of the Buddha!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know and see the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know and see the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he should know it thus: as suchness (tathatā) enters parinirvāṇa, so too does the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.”

Just as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*), the nature of reality (*tathatā*), the limit of detachment from desire (*vairāgyakoṭi*), the limit of signlessness (*animittakoṭi*), the limit of the nature of self (*ātmatākoṭi*), the limit of the nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanāmakoṭi*), and the limit of true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are nirvana, so too is the Great Parinirvana of the Tathagata.

Why is this? Nirvāṇa is not a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; if a phenomenon does not arise, one should know that it does not cease, and when it departs, there is nowhere to which it goes.
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not expound or manifest the ultimate parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata for the sake of bodhisattvas. Why is this?
It is because he desires that all bodhisattvas, within a single thought-moment, may universally behold all Buddhas of the three periods of time appearing before them.
They give rise to the sublime forms of all Tathāgatas, yet they do not give rise to the conceptualization of duality or non-duality. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are far removed from all conceptualizations and are free from attachment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is only because the Tathāgata wishes to cause sentient beings to rejoice that he appears in the world;
it is only because he wishes to cause sentient beings to feel sorrow, grief, and longing that he manifests parinirvāṇa.”
In reality, the Tathāgata neither appears in the world nor enters parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata eternally abides, being identical to the dharma-realm.
To transform sentient beings, he manifests nirvana.
"O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose the sun rises and illuminates the world, its perfect, bright, and pure radiance equaling the Dharma-realm; its reflection would appear without exception in every vessel of clear water throughout all worlds."
The sun has no such thought:
"I am able to universally manifest all pure waters.
O Son of the Buddha!
Suppose at that time there were a water vessel that was broken, so that the reflection of the sun did not appear.
What do you think?
Is it because of a fault in the sun that the reflection does not appear?
He replied: "No!
Because the water vessel is broken, the reflection of the sun does not appear."
“O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata’s wisdom is like the perfect, pure sun; appearing in a single thought-moment, it is able to illuminate all worlds, all dharma-realms, and all sentient beings. It eliminates defilements and turbidity, purifying the water-vessels of the mind so that no reflection fails to appear, always manifesting before them.

Yet, for those sentient beings whose vessels are broken and whose minds are turbid, they do not see the reflection of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, even though they ought to see Nirvāṇa and thereby attain deliverance.”
Therefore, although the Tathāgata manifests parinirvāṇa, in reality the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished, and is forever without passing away.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a great fire that, throughout all worlds, performs the function of fire; it burns up grasses and trees, leaving nothing unburnt.
At times, that fire reaches a city, town, or village where there is no grass or wood and extinguishes of its own accord.
What do you think?
Is every fire in the entire world extinguished thereby?
He replied, “No!

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; he performs buddha-works throughout all worlds, and when his work of transformation and deliverance in a single buddha-field is complete, he manifests parinirvāṇa.”
"What do you think?
Have all Tathāgatas in all worlds entered parinirvāṇa? He replied:
"No, it is not so! O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like a great master of illusion who is well-versed in illusory arts.
Dwelling securely in these arts, [he manifests] throughout the trichiliocosm, in all cities, towns, villages, and royal capitals;"
He universally manifests an illusory body and sustains this illusory body with inexhaustible life-span.
At that time, wherever this illusionist has completed his work—in those cities, villages, or the capital of a great king—he then casts off the illusory body.
"What do you think?
Has the illusory body of the trichiliocosm been entirely abandoned and extinguished? He replied:

"No, it is not so! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he possesses great wisdom in the art of illusion and is fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful means. He can universally manifest the illusory body of a Tathāgata throughout the entire Dharma-realm; he is eternally abiding like the Dharma-realm and ultimately like space. He teaches and liberates beings across all Buddha-fields, and when his work in those places is complete, he manifests parinirvāṇa.
You should know that it is not because he has manifested parinirvāṇa in a single Buddha-field that the Tathāgata has attained ultimate and final extinction."
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
When the Tathāgata manifests his parinirvāṇa, he first enters the *asaṃhārya-samādhi* (the immovable samādhi).
Having entered this samādhi, from each and every body he emits immeasurable billions of nayutas of great light rays;
from each and every light ray, there emerge immeasurable asaṃkhyeya wonderful jewel lotuses.
Each lotus flower has unspeakably unspeakable numbers of exquisite jewel stamens;
each stamen has a precious lion throne;
and upon each throne, a Tathāgata sits in the full lotus posture.
At that time, the bodies of all the Tathāgatas who appeared were equal in number to all sentient beings;
they were fully endowed with merit, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, and had brought their original vows to ultimate fulfillment.

At that time, those sentient beings whose roots of goodness were mature beheld the Tathāgata; their bodies and minds were all tamed, and they received his transformation through the Way. That body of the Tathāgata remained ultimately established until the end of the future, never missing the proper time to transform sentient beings according to their respective capacities for instruction.
That Tathāgata’s body has no fixed location; it is neither real nor unreal.
It is because the Tathāgata desires to bring to ultimate fulfillment all past great vows, and because he desires to cause sentient beings to nurture all roots of goodness.
He manifests his body as eternally abiding and indestructible.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows and perceives the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is immeasurable and boundless, the ultimate realm of reality (dharmadhātu) without obstruction; it is neither born nor extinguished, pure as space, abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and manifests itself according to what is appropriate for beings."
"Upheld by his original vow, he does not abandon any sentient beings, any buddha-fields, or any dharmas.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just like the perfect sun, Equal throughout the entire dharma-realm..."
Just as reflections appear in all waters, Except for those in broken vessels, The Most Victorious is likewise so: He appears everywhere throughout all worlds;
Yet to sentient beings who lack faith, It seems that the Buddha has entered nirvana.
Just as a fierce and blazing fire, Consuming all things, will naturally extinguish itself When there is no more grass, wood, or village;
So too is the Most Victorious One: Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, [he likewise passes away].
Having brought all the works of the Buddhas to completion, he manifests entry into nirvana.
Just as a great master of illusions manifests countless bodies,
so too does the Tathāgata universally manifest all bodies.
Having brought all the works of the Buddhas to completion, they manifest parinirvāṇa;
according to those who are ready to be transformed, they manifest in this way.
The Most Victorious One possesses a samādhi named "The Immovable."
Having completed all Buddha-works, he then enters this samādhi.
He brings to mind countless Buddhas and emits immeasurable rays of light;
within these lights are immeasurable flowers, and within each flower are immeasurable Buddhas.
The supreme, immeasurable body fills all dharma-realms;
for those who have accumulated merit, there is nothing they do not see.
The Sugata’s pure dharma-body is equal to the immeasurable dharma-realms.
The purity and adornment of his lifespan are fully perfected in every way.
Just as the nature of non-arising is, so too is the manifestation of the Tathāgata;
just as the nature of non-arising is, so too is nirvāṇa.
Completely transcending the path of language, beyond all analogy,
the Heaven-among-Heavens, the Invincible One, is fully endowed with all virtues.
"O Son of the Buddha!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know and see the roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, revering, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas?

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and sees that the roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, revering, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas are all entirely non-empty; their merit is inexhaustible.

Having abandoned all craving and attained ultimate liberation, their retribution is not in vain, and they fulfill all vows. Within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are inexhaustible, yet they are able to accord with unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*), giving rise to the wisdom of all Buddhas that reaches the ultimate limit of the future, fully possessing the stages of all Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a man who eats a small amount of diamond; it will never be digested but must pass through his body until it reaches the boundary of the diamond-wheel, whereupon it comes to rest.
Why is this? It is because that vajra is indestructible; it is thus, O Son of the Buddha!
By planting even a small root of goodness toward the Tathāgata, one is able to destroy all conditioned afflictions, until finally abiding in the ultimate wisdom of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the roots of goodness planted in the presence of the Tathāgata are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, if there were a great heap of dry grass as large as Mount Sumeru, and someone were to take a fire the size of a mustard seed, they would be able to burn it all away.
Why is this? Because the nature of fire is such that it can burn everything.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is likewise with even a small root of goodness planted before the Tathāgata: it is able to incinerate all afflictions without exception, leading to ultimate nirvana.
Why is this? Because the nature of all roots of goodness planted in the presence of the Tathāgata is ultimately perfected.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, on the Snowy Mountains there is a great king of medicines named Bhadraśrī; if anyone sees it, their eyes attain purity;
if anyone hears of it, their ears attain purity;
if anyone smells its fragrance, their nose attains purity.
If one tastes it, the tongue attains purity;
if one touches it, the body attains purity;
and if one takes up the earth from that ground, it can completely eliminate immeasurable illnesses, bringing peace, security, and happiness.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Medicine, is likewise; he constantly benefits sentient beings through all manner of skillful means.
If there are those who behold the physical body of the Tathāgata, their eyes shall attain purity;
if there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata, their ears shall attain purity;
if there are those who perceive the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts, their noses shall attain purity.

If there are those who obtain the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-flavor, their tongues become purified; they obtain the adamantine, broad, and long tongue-faculty, and are able to expound all speech and sounds.
If there are those who touch the light of the Tathāgata, those people immediately obtain a pure physical body and ultimately attain the unsurpassed Dharma-body.
If there are those who mindfully recollect the Tathāgata, they obtain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, such that right mindfulness remains undisturbed.

If there are those who obtain a copy of this sutra, or who pay homage and make offerings at a stupa or temple of the Tathāgata, those sentient beings will be fully endowed with roots of goodness, extinguish the afflictions of their distress, and attain the bliss of the noble ones.
O Son of the Buddha!

Even for those sentient beings of wrong views who lack faith, if they see or hear the Buddha, the roots of goodness they plant through that seeing and hearing will not be in vain; until they reach ultimate nirvana, they shall sever all evils and unwholesome roots and become fully endowed with roots of goodness.
O Son of the Buddha!
The roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, making offerings to, and revering the Tathāgata are ineffable and beyond all analogy. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is inconceivable, for he transcends all that can be conceived;
yet, in accordance with what is appropriate, the Buddha provides analogies.
O Son of the Buddha!
"This is how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know and see that which the Tathāgata sees and hears, and how they reverently make offerings and plant various roots of goodness.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
"O Son of the Buddha!"
This sutra is named "The Secret Dharma-Treasury of All Buddhas.
It is inconceivable to all the worlds; it is the seal of the Tathāgata, the light of great wisdom that reveals and manifests the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
it nurtures all the merits of bodhisattvas, and no one in all the worlds can destroy it.
They accord with the realm of all Tathāgatas, causing all sentient beings to become entirely pure;
they analytically expound the ultimate Dharma of the Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
This sutra is explained and analyzed solely for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle and seek awakening with single-minded devotion; it is not for others.
Why is this? This sutra does not fall into the hands of all sentient beings, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, regarding the seven treasures possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin rāja), it is because of these treasures that he practices the dharma of a Wheel-Turning King.

None among the Seven Treasures of the Sage King are capable of bearing [the burden of succession], except for the crown prince born of the first queen, who is fully endowed with and has perfected the marks of a Sage King.
O Son of the Buddha!

If a wheel-turning monarch did not have such a crown prince endowed with all these virtues, then after the king’s life had ended, these various jewels and treasures would naturally disperse and vanish.
O Son of the Buddha!
This sutra is likewise not to enter the hands of any sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King:
those born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas and who have planted the various roots of goodness that produce the marks of a Tathāgata.
If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this sutra would perish. Why is this?
It is impossible for any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to hear this sutra, let alone to receive, uphold, transcribe, or explain it.
Except for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are able to personally recite, uphold, and transcribe this sūtra.
Sons of the Buddha!
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear this sūtra, they shall rejoice with reverence, receive it upon the crown of their heads, and uphold it.
Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has faith and delight in this sutra, even if they employ few skillful means, they will certainly and decisively attain unexcelled bodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!

Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may practice the six pāramitās and cultivate the roots of goodness of the factors of enlightenment for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, if they have not heard this sutra, or if they have heard it but do not believe it, nor receive, uphold, or accord with it, such individuals are still merely nominal bodhisattvas; they are not born from the lineage of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva hears this sutra, and having heard it, believes in it, turns toward it, upholds it, and accords with it, you should know that such individuals are true sons of the Buddha; born from the family of the Buddha, they accord with the realm of all Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with all the true dharmas of Bodhisattvas, dwell securely in the realm of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), remain far removed from all worldly dharmas, give birth to and nurture the conduct of the Tathāgatas, reach the further shore of all Bodhisattva dharmas, possess no doubt or uncertainty regarding the sovereign true dharma of the Tathāgatas, ultimately abide in the stage of teacherlessness, and enter deeply into the realm of all Tathāgatas.
Sons of the Buddha!

Having heard this sutra, Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas should give rise to an impartial mind and practice immeasurable states of mind; they should distance themselves from all false conceptions and, with ultimate sincerity, face reality directly; they should maintain right mindfulness of all Tathagatas and cultivate equanimity and purity that is like space.

Discerning and observing that all the practices of Bodhisattvas are equal to the Dharma-realm, they fully accomplish the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), remain far removed from all worldly defilements, and give rise to a pure mind that fills all worlds of the ten directions. They enter deeply into all Bodhisattva dharma-gates and impartially observe all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Possessing the merit and wisdom of roots of goodness, they enter deeply into all these dharmas yet have no point of entry; they do not think of one dharma, nor do they think of two dharmas, but observe all immeasurable dharmas with total equanimity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such merits as these, they attain teacherless wisdom with little effort.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one sees or hears the Tathāgata, and with reverence makes offerings,
the roots of goodness thus planted are immeasurable and beyond compare.
Amidst all conditioned phenomena, they can never be exhausted."
All afflictions are stilled; Leaving suffering behind, one attains nirvana.
It is like a person who swallows a small amount of vajra;
Ultimately it cannot be digested, But descends all the way to the vajra-limit.

Thus, the merit of seeing, hearing, and making offerings to those who possess the ten powers is such that one becomes fully endowed with vajra-wisdom, and afflictions are extinguished without remainder.
It is like a heap of dry grass, even if it were as vast as Mount Sumeru.
Just as a mustard seed cast into fire is consumed entirely without remainder,
so too, if one plants even a small amount of merit in the presence of the Sugata,
all afflictions will be incinerated, and one will proceed directly to Nirvana.
Just as in the Snowy Mountains there is a great king of medicinal trees, such that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, or touching it eliminates all ailments;
so too is the One of Ten Powers: whoever sees or hears him [is likewise freed].
"By cultivating supreme virtues, one ultimately achieves Bodhi.
At that time, worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in the ten directions shook in six ways:

the east surged while the west subsided; the west surged while the east subsided; the south surged while the north subsided; the north surged while the south subsided; the periphery surged while the center subsided; and the center surged while the periphery subsided.
And there were eighteen kinds of movements, namely: shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere;

rising, rising everywhere, rising equally everywhere; awakening, awakening everywhere, awakening equally everywhere; quaking, quaking everywhere, quaking equally everywhere; roaring, roaring everywhere, roaring equally everywhere; surging, surging everywhere, surging equally everywhere.
At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the nature of phenomena is thus, clouds of various flowers rained down, surpassing those of all the devas;

clouds of precious robes, canopies, banners, pennants, incense, ointments, garlands, ornaments, various jewels, clouds of bodhisattvas’ praises, clouds of bodhisattva bodies, and clouds of *samyak-saṃbodhi* rained down, causing all inconceivable worlds to become entirely pure. Furthermore, clouds of the Tathāgata’s wondrous sounds rained down, filling the immeasurable and boundless *dharmadhātu*.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, all these bodhisattvas in the four continents were made to rejoice greatly; it was likewise so in all the ten directions.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds, all manifesting their bodies as if standing face-to-face nearby, all bearing the same name: Samantabhadra.
Having appeared, they all spoke these words:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, to accord with the profound Dharma and explain this inconceivable True Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Nature.
O Son of the Buddha!
We Buddhas also teach this Dharma, and all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions do likewise;

when this sutra is preached, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields attain all Bodhisattva clarities and all samādhis, and receive the prediction that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in one more lifetime.

Sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a single buddha-field have resolved their minds on awakening; we shall all bestow upon them the prediction that in a future age they shall attain the path of Buddhahood, all bearing the same name: Buddha Supreme Realm.
Therefore, for the sake of all future bodhisattvas, we shall universally protect and uphold this sutra so that it may long abide in the world.

Just as with the sentient beings to be saved within these four continents, so too shall it be for the sentient beings to be saved in all worlds throughout the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the unspeakably many, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and ineffable dharmadhātus and space-realms.

It is by virtue of the power of Vairocana Buddha’s original vows, because the nature of phenomena is thus, by the power of roots of goodness, by the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible wisdom, because the Tathāgata does not miss the proper time, in accordance with the bodhisattvas who are to be transformed, for the sake of extensively practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and to manifest all-knowledge.
At that time, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions,
there came ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas,
as numerous as the atoms in those buddha-fields, arriving in this land and filling the entire dharma-realm.
Manifesting the great and wondrous adornments of a bodhisattva, emitting a vast net of great light, shaking all worlds,
shattering all the palaces of Māras, eliminating all hardships of the evil realms,
illuminating the merits of all Tathāgatas, praising the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas, and raining down everywhere—
With clouds and rains of immeasurable and boundless offerings, they manifest infinite varieties of diverse bodies and manifest their own bodies;
they are vessels for these immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Buddhas.
At that time, those bodhisattvas, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, each spoke these words:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to speak of these indestructible dharmas of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
We are all named Samantabhadra, and we have purified our brahma-conduct in the presence of the Tathāgata Samantavijaya in the world Samantaprabhā;
in those various Buddha-fields as well, this sutra is preached with these same words, these same meanings, these same practices, and these same characteristics.
"O Son of the Buddha!
By virtue of our reception of the Buddha's spiritual power, and because the nature of phenomena is thus, we have come from that world to this land to bear witness for you."
"In all worlds throughout the ten directions, as far as the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, it is likewise so.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha's spiritual authority, surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas.

Desiring to further clarify the True Dharma of the Tathāgata’s nature-arising; desiring to proclaim the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata; desiring to demonstrate that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is indestructible; desiring to give birth to the immeasurable light of wisdom and Dharma of all Bodhisattvas; desiring to expound all the complete qualities of the Buddha-dharma; desiring to observe the minds of all classes of sentient beings; desiring to respond to those to be transformed without missing the proper time; desiring to distinguish all the immeasurable and boundless True Dharmas of the Bodhisattvas; desiring to manifest the sovereign adornments of the transformations of all Tathāgatas; desiring to clarify that the single body of all Tathāgatas is without difference;
and desiring to bring forth the immeasurable fundamental practices of all Bodhisattvas, he spoke in verse: “The majestic deportment Accomplished by all Tathāgatas...”
The entire world offers praise, yet none can provide a fitting analogy.
To benefit all sentient beings and cause them all to attain understanding,
he uses what is not a conventional analogy as an analogy to reveal the true meaning.
Such a subtle and secret Dharma is difficult to hear even in immeasurable eons.
Those who possess diligence and wisdom shall hear of the Tathāgatagarbha.
If there are those who hear this sutra and respond with joy and reverence,
they have already, in the past, made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
One should know that such a person is constantly praised by the devas;
all the Sugatas embrace and constantly protect them.
All the Sugatas, who are supreme in both this world and the world beyond—
This sūtra is the inner treasury for the most excellent assembly of joyful beings;
it can give birth to all immeasurable, pure, and white paths.
Therefore, free from negligence, always uphold it with a single-minded heart.

33. Chapter on Transcending the World, Part One. At that time, the Bhagavat was in the kingdom of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall, seated upon a precious lion throne of the Lotus Treasury, having attained equal and perfect enlightenment;
he maintained non-dual mindfulness, the signless mindfulness;
he dwelt where all Buddhas dwell, being equal to all Buddhas.

They have reached the unimpeded realm and attained the state of non-returning; dwelling in the unobstructed sphere, they abide in the inconceivable and remain far removed from the three periods of time.

They manifest their bodies universally throughout all worlds, knowing all dharmas and fully accomplishing all sublime practices. Having forever extinguished doubt and confusion, they are free from the illusory body and are able to bestow immeasurable wisdom upon all bodhisattvas. Abiding in the non-dual dharma of the Buddhas, they ultimately reach the other shore and are endowed with the Tathāgata’s indestructible dharma-gate of wisdom. They have perfected the infinite, boundless stages of the Tathāgatas, which are equal to empty space and the dharma-realm;
together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields...
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas were all destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single lifetime;
they had each come together from the worlds of the ten directions, fully accomplished all the skillful means and wisdom of Bodhisattvas,
and through their mastery of expedient means, they tamed sentient beings, causing them all to dwell securely in the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
They discern and understand all worlds; they observe and clearly penetrate the realm of liberation;
they have completely eliminated all falsehoods; they are fully accomplished in all sublime practices;
they skillfully gather in sentient beings and lead them deeply into the methods of immeasurable skillful means; they well know the karmic retributions of all sentient beings; they are skilled in...
They know the minds of all sentient beings and employ skillful means regarding the spheres of their faculties;
they skillfully hear, receive, and uphold the phrases, expressions, and meanings taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and explain them extensively for others;
they skillfully enter the infinite and boundless worlds while remaining detached from worldly dharmas.
They are skillfully able to understand that all conditioned phenomena are entirely non-dual;

in a single thought-moment, they attain the wisdom of all Buddhas, and in every thought-moment, they are skillfully able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, causing all sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta and achieve perfect enlightenment.

Entering the realm of a single sentient being, they skillfully know the realms of the minds of all sentient beings; they do not forsake the stage of the Tathāgata while manifesting the body of a bodhisattva, attaining the non-retrogressive stage of omniscience and never abandoning the bodhisattva practices. They enter deeply into the wisdom of non-action and, for the sake of all sentient beings, cultivate the bodhisattva practices throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons. Throughout those immeasurable and incalculable eons—during which the jewel of a bodhisattva is difficult to encounter—they turn the wheel of the true Dharma and subdue sentient beings, causing them all to attain the clear and pure Dharma-eye. They accomplish the pure dwellings, practices, and vows of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and are fully endowed with such immeasurable and boundless merits.
All Buddhas, throughout all future kalpas, could never exhaustively describe them; their names are:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantadharmasamyak Bodhisattva, Samantavikurvita Bodhisattva, Samantamati Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantavyavalokana Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Samantadhvaja Bodhisattva, and Samantabodhi Bodhisattva. Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable Buddha-fields—all fully possess the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

In accordance with the appearance of Buddhas in all worlds, they are able to go before them all and request the turning of the wheel of Dharma; they are able to receive and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas, ensuring that the lineage of all Buddhas is never interrupted; they are able to fully comprehend the sequential predictions of enlightenment made by all Buddhas; and wherever they attain equal and perfect enlightenment in various worlds, they turn the pure wheel of Dharma even in Buddha-less realms, manifesting as Buddhas appearing in the world to cause those who are defiled to become entirely pure, to eliminate all karmic obstacles of Bodhisattvas, and to enter the unimpeded Dharma-realm.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered a samādhi called Buddha-Flower Adornment (*Buddhāvatamsaka*).

Having entered this samādhi, all worlds in the ten directions shook in six ways and with eighteen aspects, emitting a subtle and wondrous sound that was heard by everyone throughout all worlds; thereafter, he calmly arose from samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantamati, knowing that the great assembly of bodhisattvas had gathered like clouds, asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:

"As you have just asked, I pray that you will explain this in full detail.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the Bodhisattvas, including Samantamati and the others, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of fruits of reliance.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
The fruit of relying on the bodhicitta is that one never ultimately forgets it;
the fruit of relying on spiritual friends is that one accords with and harmonizes with them;
the fruit of relying on roots of goodness is that one nurtures all roots of goodness.
The fruit of reliance upon the various pāramitās, because they constitute ultimate cultivation;
the fruit of reliance upon all dharmas, because one forever transcends birth and death;
the fruit of reliance upon all vows, because they nurture bodhi.
The fruit of reliance on all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is due to extensive cultivation;
the fruit of reliance for a bodhisattva is due to being in the stage of "one birth remaining" (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
and the fruit of reliance for making offerings to the Buddha is due to the non-destruction of faith.
The fruit of reliance of all Tathāgatas is the correct teaching, for it is free from inversion.
O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten kinds of fruits of reliance of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in these fruits of reliance, they will attain the fruit of reliance of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are one's own roots of goodness;
regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are seeds of bodhi.
Toward all sentient beings, one should conceive the thought that they are vessels for Bodhi;
toward all vows, one should conceive the thought that they are one's own vows;
toward all phenomena, one should conceive the thought that they transcend birth and death.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena, one should conceive of them as one's own practice;
regarding all dharmas, one should conceive of them as the Buddha-dharma;
regarding all speech, one should conceive of them as the path of language.
Toward all Buddhas, one should conceive the thought of them as compassionate fathers;
toward all Tathāgatas, one should conceive the thought of their non-duality.
O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these conceptions, they will attain unsurpassed and skillful means to transform all conceptions.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?

That is to say: causing all sentient beings to practice the exclusive pursuit of the True Dharma; the practice of bringing roots of goodness to full maturity; the practice of skillfully training in all precepts; the practice of nurturing all roots of goodness; the practice of cultivating samādhi with a single, undistracted mind; the practice of discerning all forms of wisdom; the practice of cultivating all that is to be practiced; the practice of adorning all worlds; the practice of reverently making offerings to spiritual friends; and the practice of reverently making offerings to all Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten kinds of practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in these practices, they will attain the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of spiritual friends for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?

They are: spiritual friends who can cause one to dwell securely in the bodhicitta; spiritual friends who can cause one to cultivate roots of goodness; spiritual friends who can cause one to bring all the pāramitās to ultimate fulfillment; spiritual friends who can cause one to analyze and explain all dharmas; spiritual friends who can cause one to dwell in the maturation of all sentient beings; spiritual friends who can cause one to possess eloquence such that one is able to answer whatever questions are asked; spiritual friends who can cause one to remain unattached to all of saṃsāra; spiritual friends who can cause one to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout all kalpas without weariness of mind; spiritual friends who can cause one to dwell in the conduct of Samantabhadra; and spiritual friends who can cause one to penetrate deeply into the wisdom of all Buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of spiritual friends of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of diligent cultivation of vigor.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

They diligently cultivate vigor to transform and guide all sentient beings; they diligently cultivate vigor to enter into all dharmas; they diligently cultivate vigor to purify all worlds; they diligently cultivate vigor to bring to ultimate completion all that Bodhisattvas study; they diligently cultivate vigor to cause all sentient beings to extinguish all evils; they diligently cultivate vigor to eliminate the sufferings of all hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama; they diligently cultivate vigor to subdue all Māras; they diligently cultivate vigor to act as the pure eye for all sentient beings; they diligently cultivate vigor to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas; and they diligently cultivate vigor to cause all Tathāgatas to be completely delighted.
O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten kinds of diligent cultivation of vigor by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this vigor, they will possess the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of right aspirations for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
dwelling oneself in the bodhicitta, and causing sentient beings to dwell in the bodhicitta with right aspiration;
being free from anger and strife oneself, and causing all sentient beings to be free from anger and strife with right aspiration.
Having personally departed from ignorance and dwelt securely in the Buddha-dharma, they also cause sentient beings to abandon ignorance and dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma;

this is their right aspiration. Having personally cultivated roots of goodness and sought exclusively for the True Dharma, they also cause sentient beings to cultivate roots of goodness and seek exclusively for the True Dharma; this is their right aspiration.

Having personally brought all the *pāramitās* to completion and reached the other shore, they also cause sentient beings to bring all the *pāramitās* to completion and reach the other shore; this is their right aspiration.
Having personally been born into the family of the Tathāgata lineage, they also cause sentient beings to give rise to the correct aspiration to be born into the family of the Tathāgata lineage;

having personally deeply entered into the contemplation of the inexhaustible nature of all phenomena, they also cause sentient beings to deeply enter into the contemplation of the inexhaustible nature of all phenomena with the correct aspiration;
and having personally not slandered any Buddha-dharma, they also cause sentient beings not to slander any Buddha-dharma with the correct aspiration.
Having fulfilled one's own vow for omniscience, one also causes sentient beings to fulfill their correct aspiration for the vow of omniscience;

having personally entered deeply into the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, one also causes sentient beings to enter deeply into the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, fulfilling their correct aspiration.
O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten kinds of right aspirations of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, equal, and great wisdom of right aspiration.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dharmas by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas bring sentient beings to maturity. What are these ten?

That is to say: they accomplish sentient beings through giving; they accomplish sentient beings through the majesty and dignity of their physical form; they accomplish sentient beings through preaching the Dharma; they accomplish sentient beings through harmony of mind; they accomplish sentient beings through freedom from defiled attachment; they accomplish sentient beings by extolling the conduct of Bodhisattvas; they accomplish sentient beings by manifesting the blazing splendor of all worlds; they accomplish sentient beings by extolling the merits of the Tathāgata; they accomplish sentient beings by manifesting sovereign spiritual powers; and they accomplish sentient beings through various skillful means and subtle, secret practices that accord with worldly ways.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas bring sentient beings to maturity; if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will be able to mature all sentient beings.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya Scripture,
Scroll Thirty-Six and Scroll Thirty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Part Two of the Thirty-third Chapter on Transcending the World:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of precepts."
What are the ten? They are:
the precept of not destroying the bodhicitta;
The precept of remaining detached from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the precept of benefiting all sentient beings through contemplation;
and the precept of causing all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma.
The precept of training in all the bodhisattva precepts;
the precept of non-appropriation of all things;
the precept of dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment.
They do not cling to the body or the precepts of any Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!

There are ten kinds of dharmas by which a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows for themselves that they have received the prediction [of enlightenment], enabling those Bodhisattvas to know for themselves that they have received the prediction.”
What are the ten? They are:
the prediction of enlightenment for bodhisattvas who have single-mindedly resolved upon bodhicitta;
The bodhisattva who does not weary of the bodhisattva practice receives the prediction;
the bodhisattva who cultivates all ascetic practices throughout all eons receives the prediction;
the bodhisattva who accords with all Buddha-dharmas receives the prediction.
The prediction of bodhisattvas who possess resolute faith and inclination toward all that is taught by the Tathāgatas;
the prediction of bodhisattvas who fully cultivate all roots of goodness;
and the prediction of bodhisattvas who cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in enlightenment.
The prediction of a bodhisattva who harmonizes with and accords with all spiritual friends;
the prediction of a bodhisattva who conceives of all spiritual friends as Tathāgatas;
and the prediction of a bodhisattva who guards the original vow for enlightenment.
"O Son of the Buddha!

These are the ten ways in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows for themselves that they have received the prediction [of enlightenment], causing those bodhisattvas to know for themselves that they have received the prediction.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of entry.
What are the ten? They are as follows:

Entering into vows, entering into practices, entering into accumulations, entering into perfections, entering into fulfillments, entering into the differentiation of vows, entering into natures, entering into the adornment of buddha-fields, entering into mastery of spiritual powers, and entering into the manifestation of birth.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of entries of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas;
they also enter into all that has been entered by all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas deeply penetrate the Tathāgata. What are these ten?
That is to say:
they penetrate deeply into the infinite and boundless bodhi of all buddhas;
they penetrate deeply into the infinite and boundless turning of the pure wheel of Dharma.
They penetrate deeply into immeasurable and boundless methods of skillful means;
they penetrate deeply into immeasurable and boundless subtle and wondrous sounds;
they penetrate deeply into immeasurable and boundless ways of taming sentient beings.
They have deeply entered the sovereign mastery of immeasurable and boundless spiritual powers;
they have deeply entered the manifestation of immeasurable and boundless diverse bodies;
and they have deeply entered immeasurable and boundless samādhis.
They penetrate deeply into the immeasurable and boundless powers and fearlessnesses;
they penetrate deeply into the immeasurable and boundless manifestations of nirvana.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas deeply enter into the Tathāgatas;
these ten modes of deep entry are likewise entered by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter into the mental activities of sentient beings. What are these ten?
That is to say:
entering into the mental activities of all sentient beings of the past;
entering into the mental activities of all sentient beings of the future;
They enter into the mental activities of all sentient beings in the present;
they enter into the activities of all sentient beings' roots of goodness;
and they enter into the activities of all sentient beings' unwholesome roots.
Entering into the mental activities of all sentient beings;
entering into the activities of the faculties of all sentient beings;
entering into the activities of the spiritual lineages of all sentient beings.
They enter into the conduct of the afflictions, latent tendencies, and habitual impulses of all sentient beings;
they enter into the conduct of disciplining all sentient beings at the proper time and the improper time.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways of entering the mental activities of sentient beings;
by means of these ten ways of entering the mental activities of sentient beings, one is able to universally enter the mental activities of all sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of entry into worlds for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:

entering impure worlds, entering pure worlds, entering small worlds, entering medium worlds, entering worlds of motes of dust, entering subtle worlds, entering inverted worlds, entering upright worlds, entering worlds where a Buddha is present, and entering worlds where no Buddha is present.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter worlds;
by means of these ten entries into worlds, they are able to universally enter all worlds.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of entry into eons for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?

That is to say: entering past eons; entering future eons; entering present eons; entering countable eons; entering uncountable eons; entering both countable and uncountable eons; entering both uncountable and countable eons; entering all eons as non-eons; entering non-eons as all eons; and entering all eons as being a single thought-moment.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter eons;
by means of these ten entries into eons, they are able to universally enter all eons.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas speak of the three periods of time. What are these ten?
That is to say:
speaking of the past life in terms of the past life;
speaking of the future life in terms of the past life;
Speaking of the present world in terms of the past world;
speaking of the past world in terms of the future world;
and speaking of the present world in terms of the future world.
They speak of the future world as inexhaustible;
they speak of the future world within the present world;
and they speak of the past world within the present world.
In the present age, one speaks of equality;
in the present age, one speaks of the three periods of time as being a single thought-moment.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas discourse on the three periods of time;
by means of these ten ways of discoursing on the three periods of time, they are able to universally discourse upon all things of the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of entry into the three periods of time for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:

entering the world, entering the path of language, entering nature, entering designations, entering perceptions, entering names, entering speech, entering the inexhaustible, entering the departure from desire, and entering cessation.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the three periods of time;
by means of these ten entries into the three periods of time, they are able to universally enter all worlds throughout the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of relinquishing sorrow and affliction by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have no weariness or regret in their minds.
What are these ten?
That is to say:
making offerings to all Buddhas while abandoning sorrow and affliction, with a mind free from weariness or regret;
drawing near to all spiritual friends while abandoning sorrow and affliction, with a mind free from weariness or regret.
Diligently seeking all dharmas, they abandon sorrow and affliction, their minds free from weariness or regret;
constantly hearing the true Dharma, they abandon sorrow and affliction, their minds free from weariness or regret;
constantly preaching the true Dharma, they abandon sorrow and affliction, their minds free from weariness or regret.
To teach and transform all sentient beings so that they abandon sorrow and affliction, with a mind free from weariness or regret;
to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in the Buddha-way, abandoning sorrow and affliction, with a mind free from weariness or regret;
and within each and every world, to practice unspeakably unspeakable bodhisattva practices, abandoning sorrow and affliction, with a mind free from weariness or regret.
They travel through all worlds to teach and transform sentient beings, abandoning sorrow and affliction with minds free from weariness or regret;
they bring forth all Buddha-dharmas, abandoning sorrow and affliction with minds free from weariness or regret.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abandon sorrow and affliction, so that their minds are free from weariness and regret;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata and forever be free from weariness and regret.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of indestructible wisdom possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
knowing that the wisdom regarding sentient beings is indestructible;
knowing that the wisdom regarding the faculties is indestructible;
The knowledge that knows the arising of sensation is indestructible;
the knowledge that knows the world-systems is indestructible;
the knowledge that knows the dharma-realm is indestructible.
Knowing that the wisdom of the Buddha is indestructible;
knowing that the wisdom of the Dharma is indestructible;
knowing that the wisdom of the Sangha is indestructible.
The wisdom that knows the three periods of time is indestructible;
the wisdom that knows all paths of language is indestructible.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of indestructible wisdom of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this wisdom, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, indestructible wisdom.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of dhāraṇīs. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, because it does not forget any dharma;
the dhāraṇī of upholding the true dharma, because it skillfully and expediently discerns all dharmas according to reality.
The dhāraṇī of the non-arising of all phenomena, because one awakens to the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
the dhāraṇī of the illumination of the Dharma, because it universally illumines the inconceivable qualities of all Buddhas;
the dhāraṇī of samādhi, because one hears the Dharma in the presence of all present Buddhas without distraction.
The dharani of perfect sound, because it brings ultimate understanding of inconceivable methods of language;
the dharani of the three periods of time, because it analytically explains the inconceivable teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and the dharani of various eloquences, because it analytically explains the infinite and boundless teachings of all Buddhas.
They give birth to the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded hearing, because they are able to hear all the teachings spoken by unspeakably many Buddhas;
they possess the *dhāraṇī* that upholds all Buddha-dharmas, because they dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of dhāraṇīs of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain these dharmas, they should diligently practice and study them.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know how to analytically explain ten kinds of Buddhas. What are these ten?

They are: the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha of Vows, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution, the Buddha of Sustenance, the Buddha of Transformation, the Buddha of the Dharma-realm, the Buddha of Mind, the Buddha of Samādhi, the Buddha of Nature, and the Buddha of Sovereign Power.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and distinguishes the ten kinds of Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of generating the mind of Samantabhadra.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
He gives rise to a mind of great kindness, for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings;
he gives rise to a mind of great compassion, for the sake of undergoing all bitter poisons of suffering on behalf of all sentient beings;
he gives rise to a mind that takes universal giving as its foremost priority, relinquishing everything that belongs to him.
They resolve upon a mind headed by right mindfulness for the sake of all-knowledge, because they joyfully seek all Buddha-dharmas;
they resolve upon a mind adorned with merit, because they study all the practices of bodhisattvas;
they resolve upon a vajra-like mind, because they do not forget or lose anything throughout all their births.
They resolve upon the mind of the great ocean, because all pure and white dharmas flow into it;
they resolve upon the mind of Sumeru, the king of mountains, because they are able to endure all slander and harsh words;
they resolve upon the mind of peace and security, because they bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
They give rise to the mind that reaches the further shore of ultimate *prajñāpāramitā*, because they skillfully discern that all phenomena are non-existent.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the universal mind of Samantabhadra.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind, then with minimal effort, they will fully possess the skillful wisdom of Samantabhadra’s expedient means.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of Samantabhadra’s methods of vow and practice. What are the ten?
They are as follows:
The method of the practice of the Bodhisattva conduct and the vows of Samantabhadra throughout all future kalpas;
the method of reverently making offerings to all Buddhas of the future through the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra;
and the method of establishing all sentient beings in the vows and conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra through the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra.
The Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for accumulating all roots of goodness;
the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for entering all perfections;
the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for fulfilling all bodhisattva vows and practices.
The Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for adorning all worlds;
the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for being reborn in the presence of all Buddhas;
and the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices for seeking all dharmas through skillful means.
In all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, they accomplish the Dharma of the supreme Bodhi and the practices of Samantabhadra’s vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vow-practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate these vows and practices, they will swiftly attain the full perfection of the vows and practices of Samantabhadra.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of great compassion with which they constantly observe sentient beings."
What are the ten? They are:
observing that sentient beings have no refuge and giving rise to great compassion;
He observes sentient beings following false paths and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings who are impoverished and lack roots of goodness and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings who sleep long in birth and death and gives rise to great compassion.
He observes sentient beings practicing unwholesome dharmas and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings bound by the fetters of desire and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death and gives rise to great compassion.
He gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings have suffered from chronic illness for a long time;
he gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings lack the wholesome dharmas of desirelessness;
he gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings have lost all the Buddha-dharmas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of great compassion of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, by which they constantly observe sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
The causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by teaching and maturing all sentient beings;
the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by eliminating the suffering of all sentient beings;
and the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by bestowing various kinds of happiness upon all sentient beings.
The causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by eliminating the ignorance and darkness of all sentient beings;
the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by bestowing the Buddha-wisdom upon all sentient beings;
and the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by reverently making offerings to all Buddhas.
The causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by following the Tathāgata’s teachings and causing the Buddha to rejoice;
the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta upon beholding the physical body and its marks and signs of the Buddha;
and the causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta by entering the wisdom of all Buddhas.
They manifest the power and fearlessness of the Buddhas as the causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten causes and conditions for the generation of the bodhicitta by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, they should reverently make offerings to and draw near to spiritual friends. Why is this?
Because they desire to swiftly awaken to all-knowledge.
