the practice of the four means of integration, because it teaches and brings all sentient beings to maturity.
The practice of birth and death, for the purpose of nurturing all roots of goodness;
the practice of the playful speech of all sentient beings, for the purpose of pulling sentient beings out [of suffering];
the practice of blazing greed, for the purpose of awakening the faculties of all sentient beings.
They practice skillful means in order to nurture the *prajñāpāramitā*;
they practice at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in order to awaken to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) while never ceasing their bodhisattva conduct.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these practices, they will attain the supreme, great wisdom-practice of all buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of observations for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
observing virtuous karma, because they clearly perceive even the most subtle forms;
and observing death here and birth there, because they do not cling to any sentient beings.
They observe the faculties of all sentient beings, because they definitively know the dharma of no-faculties;
they observe the sublime Dharma, because the dharma-realm is indestructible;
they observe that which is manifest before them in all Buddha-dharmas, because they cultivate the Buddha-eye.
They observe wisdom, because they preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings;
they observe the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because they will certainly attain the Buddha-dharma;
they observe the non-retrogressive stage of Buddhahood, because they eliminate all afflictions and transcend the three realms and the stages of the two vehicles.
He contemplates the ground of the nectar-consecration rite, because he has attained unshakable mastery over all Buddha-dharmas;
he contemplates the samādhi of the Buddhas, because he performs the buddha-work throughout all ten directions.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of observations of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, great wisdom-observation of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of universal observation for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
universally observing all who come seeking, one gives with a compassionate heart to fulfill their wishes;
universally observing all who violate the precepts, one establishes them in the pure precepts of the Tathāgata.
He universally observes sentient beings with harmful intent, establishing them in the Tathāgata’s power of forbearance;
he universally observes those who are indolent, causing those beings to diligently cultivate vigor so as to ultimately realize the Great Vehicle;
he universally observes sentient beings with distracted minds, removing their distraction and establishing them in the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
He universally observes foolish sentient beings in order to eliminate their doubts and all views of existence;
he universally observes spiritual friends in order to abide in the Buddha-dharma according to the Tathāgata’s teachings;
and he universally observes the Dharma as it is heard in order to fully accomplish the unsurpassed meaning.
They universally observe all sentient beings because they do not abandon great compassion;
they universally observe all Buddha-dharmas because they awaken to all-knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of universal observation of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, great wisdom of all Buddhas that universally observes everything.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of heroic strides of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the "mastery of form," because one manifests as the most supreme among all assemblies, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth;
and the "mastery of the elephant," because one demonstrates the precious mind of an elephant.

The dragon’s vigorous display, because it raises great clouds of Dharma to universally cover all, flashes the lightning of radiant liberation, thunders the roar of ultimate truth, and rains down the nectar of the Dharma—the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis;

the vigorous display of the great king of golden-winged birds, because it destroys the shell-films of the darkness of ignorance, dries up the waters of craving, and seizes the various evil dragons of affliction within the great ocean of suffering;
the vigorous display of the lion, because it dwells securely in fearlessness, dons the armor and weapons of impartial great wisdom, and subdues all Māras and externalists.
They possess the vigor of valor, for they are able to destroy all great enemies—the afflictions—within the great battle-array of birth and death;

they possess the vigor of wisdom, for they definitively understand the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination, manifesting the sovereign dharmas of all Buddhas;
they possess the vigor of *dhāraṇī*, for they hear and retain all teachings without ever forgetting them, extensively analyzing and explaining them for the sake of all living beings.

The prowess of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is such that one distinguishes all *padakāya* and *vyañjanakāya* without obstruction; responding immediately to every question, one causes all to rejoice because one’s words are not false.

The prowess of the Tathāgata is such that, seated upon the lion throne, he subdues all Māras, tames the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), fulfills all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and possesses the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*). Because he has fully awakened to and realized all that is attained, known, perceived, and accomplished, he has achieved unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of heroic strides of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, sovereign heroic strides of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of lion’s roars of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the thought "I shall certainly attain Buddhahood" is the lion’s roar of the bodhicitta;

to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings—vowing to deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, settle those not yet settled, and lead those not yet in nirvana to attain nirvana—is the lion’s roar of great compassion.
To protect, uphold, and never sever the nature of the Triple Gem is the lion’s roar of repaying the Buddha’s kindness;
to cause all buddha-fields to be completely purified is the ultimate lion’s roar of the great vow;
to eliminate all hardships in the evil realms is the lion’s roar of personally maintaining pure precepts.
To fulfill the marks and embellishments of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind is the lion’s roar of insatiable accumulation of merit;
to bring to completion the wisdom of all Buddhas is the lion’s roar of insatiable accumulation of the requisites of wisdom;
and to eliminate all demonic activities while single-mindedly seeking the true path is the lion’s roar of the eradication of afflictions.

To know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*) and without what belongs to a self (*anātmīya*), without a life-principle (*jīva*) and without a person (*pudgala*), and to be empty, signless, and wishless; to contemplate all phenomena as pure as space—this is the lion’s roar of attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) regarding all phenomena.

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) purifies and causes all Buddha-fields to tremble; Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all entreat him to descend from the divine realm and take birth. With the unobstructed eye of wisdom, he universally observes that among all sentient beings in the world there is none superior to himself, and manifests his birth and takes seven steps, uttering the great lion’s roar:

"I am the most supreme and foremost in the world; I have forever reached the ultimate end of the cycle of birth, old age, and death. This is the lion’s roar of practicing according to what has been taught.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of lion’s roars of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme Great Lion’s Roar of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure giving for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
giving with an impartial mind, because there are no sentient beings toward whom one feels aversion;
giving according to their wishes, because it fulfills all aspirations.
Giving with an undistracted mind, because it is non-retrogressive;
giving according to what is appropriate for the recipient, because one discerns and understands the *pudgala*;
giving without discrimination, because one does not seek karmic retribution.
Giving with single-minded devotion, because the mind has no attachment to any object;
giving all things internal and external, because it is ultimately pure;
giving dedicated toward enlightenment, because it is far removed from both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The gift of maturing sentient beings through transformation, because it is never abandoned until the site of enlightenment;
and the gift of the threefold perfection and purity, because the giver, the recipient, and the material object are equally pure like space.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure giving of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this giving, they will attain the unsurpassed, pure, great giving of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure precepts for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure precept of body, because it guards against the three evils of the body;
the pure precept of speech, because it distances oneself from the four faults of speech.
The pure precepts of the mind, because they are forever free from greed, anger, and all false views;
the complete purity of all precepts, because they are most supreme and wondrous among gods and humans;
the pure precepts that guard the bodhicitta, because one does not delight in inferior wisdom.
They guard the pure precepts taught by the Tathāgata because they feel great dread even toward the most subtle transgressions;
they maintain the subtle and secret pure precepts because they skillfully uproot sentient beings who have violated the precepts;
they observe the pure precepts of refraining from all evil because they accumulate all wholesome dharmas.
The pure precepts that remain far removed from all views of existence, because they are unattached to the precepts;
the pure precepts that protect all sentient beings, because they give rise to great compassion.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure precepts of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these precepts, they will attain the supreme pure precepts of all Buddhas, which are far removed from all evils.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure patience for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
if others revile or insult them, they are able to endure it all for the sake of protecting the other's mind;
if others inflict harm with blades or staves, they are also able to endure it for the sake of protecting both the other and themselves.
The patience that knows all forms of anger, because it is naturally unmoving;
the patience of abiding in mastery, because it can harm that which cannot be harmed;
the patience that is the refuge for sentient beings, because it does not begrudge body or life.
Patience in remaining far removed from the conceit of "I" because one does not disparage those who have not yet trained;
patience when having limbs and joints severed because one contemplates them as being like an illusion;
and patience toward all evil deeds because one is free from the notions of self and other.
The patience of afflictions, because it remains far removed from the sphere of afflictions;

the patience of conforming to the skillful means and wisdom of all bodhisattvas, because one attains the patience of non-arising and realizes the sphere of omniscience without depending on others for awakening.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this patience, they will attain the unsurpassed dharma-patience of all Buddhas, awakening to it without depending on others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure diligence for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
diligence in purifying the physical karma, because one reveres, makes offerings to, and serves all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, honoring the field of merit without ever regressing;

diligence in purifying the verbal karma, because one hears and upholds the true Dharma of all Buddhas without ever forgetting it, praises the Tathāgata, and extensively expounds the teachings as heard for the sake of others without weariness.

The diligence of purifying mental karma, because it continuously gives rise to the meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity through skillful means without ever regressing;
the diligence of purifying the straightforward mind,
because it remains ultimately non-regressive in all skillful means, being upright in all matters and far removed from flattery and crookedness.
They purify the vigor of the profound mind by constantly tending toward the supreme state, thereby accumulating the unsurpassed, pure, and white dharmas of wisdom;
they practice the vigor of non-falsity by embracing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, extensive learning, and heedfulness, never ceasing until reaching the site of enlightenment;

and they purify the vigor that subdues all Māras and adversaries by being able to utterly eliminate greed, hatred, delusion, afflictions, wrong views, and all entanglements, hindrances, and obscurations.

The pure diligence of fulfilling the light of wisdom consists in ensuring that all actions are preceded by thorough reflection, that there is no regret in the mind, and that one ultimately accomplishes all tasks by attaining the unique qualities of all Buddhas;

the pure diligence of non-attachment consists in departing from the realms of the mind and the characteristics of body, speech, and mind—whether characterized or uncharacterized—through the profound Dharma-gate of universally observing all realms to definitively realize true suchness;

and the pure diligence of fully accomplishing the illumination of the Dharma consists in successively entering all the stages (*bhūmi*), receiving the nectar-consecration from the Buddhas, receiving the prediction of a Dharma King with the untainted *dharmakāya*, manifesting the relinquishment of celestial life to descend into the world, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the pure wheel of Dharma, and entering great *nirvāṇa*, thereby ultimately perfecting the conduct of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure diligence of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, great, pure diligence of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure meditative concentration for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure meditation of always delighting in leaving the household life, because it abandons all existence;
the pure meditation of associating with spiritual friends, because one consults them and receives instruction in the path of the True Dharma for its cultivation.
Pure dhyāna that delights in forest retreats, because it is far removed from the dharmas of "I" and "mine";
pure dhyāna that avoids the clamor and distractions of idle talk, because it delights in cessation;
pure dhyāna with a supple mind, because the sense faculties are not distracted.
The pure dhyāna of wisdom and tranquility, because it cannot be disturbed by the thorns of all sounds or various meditative concentrations;
the pure dhyāna of the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path, because its wisdom is decisive regarding the realm of omniscience;
and the pure dhyāna free from the defilements of attachment to flavors and other afflictions, because it does not grasp at the desire realm.
The pure dhyāna of the various supernormal powers and clear insights is for the sake of definitively knowing the faculties of all sentient beings;
the pure dhyāna of manifesting and sporting in supernormal powers through slight means is for the sake of the immeasurability of the Tathāgata’s samādhis.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure dhyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these dhyānas, they will attain the supreme pure dhyāna of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure wisdom. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure wisdom that knows causes, because it does not destroy karmic retribution;
the pure wisdom that understands all conditions, because it does not destroy the harmony of the assemblage.
The pure wisdom that understands all phenomena as neither eternal nor annihilated, because it realizes the suchness of dependent origination;
the pure wisdom that uproots all false views, because it does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings;
the pure wisdom that understands the minds and mental activities of all sentient beings, because it contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions.
The pure wisdom of the supreme knowledge of all eloquences, because it is able to answer questions according to their inquiries without obstruction;
the pure wisdom that subdues all Māras and heterodox teachers and transcends Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, because it deeply penetrates the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means;

the pure wisdom that perceives the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas, perceives all sentient beings as entirely pure, perceives all phenomena as entirely quiescent, and perceives all worlds as entirely empty, because its wisdom regarding all marks is unimpeded.
They encompass all dhāraṇīs; they possess the pure wisdom of skillful means that distinguishes the various pāramitās, because they have attained all supreme knowledge;
they possess the vajra-wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, the pure wisdom that awakens to the equality of all phenomena, because they have fully accomplished unsurpassed knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this wisdom, they will attain the supreme, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure compassion for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure compassion of equanimity, because it does not discriminate among sentient beings;
the pure compassion of benefit, because it is able to accomplish whatever deeds are performed for all sentient beings.
The pure compassion that rescues and protects, because it ultimately delivers all sentient beings from the perils of birth and death;
the pure compassion of pity that does not abandon any sentient being, because it nurtures conditioned roots of goodness;
the pure compassion of liberation, because it extinguishes all the afflictions of all sentient beings.
The pure compassion that gives birth to bodhi, because it causes all sentient beings to joyfully seek bodhi;
the unimpeded pure compassion toward all sentient beings, because it emits immeasurable light that universally illumines all beings;
the pure compassion of empty space, because it rescues and protects all sentient beings.
The pure compassion with a focal object (*sālambana*) arises from awakening to the true Dharma;
the pure compassion without a focal object (*anālambana*) arises from realizing the Bodhisattva’s state beyond birth (*jātivyativṛtti*).
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure compassion of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in this compassion, they will attain the supreme, pure great compassion of all buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure compassion for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
it is the pure compassion that is uncommon, because it arises from great compassion;
it is the pure compassion that never tires, because it undergoes great suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.
The pure compassion that dwells in all evil realms, because it undergoes birth and death to deliver sentient beings;
the pure compassion that takes birth among all devas and humans, because it manifests that all phenomena are entirely impermanent;
and the pure compassion for those fixed in false views, because it does not abandon them through the adornment of great vows throughout immeasurable eons.
Pure compassion that does not cling to one's own happiness, because it bestows happiness upon all sentient beings;
pure compassion that seeks no reward, because one’s own mind is pure;
and pure compassion that eliminates the delusions and misconceptions of all sentient beings, because it proclaims the true Dharma.

Knowing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, empty, and non-existent, yet defiled by adventitious dust, the Bodhisattva gives rise to pure compassion for them because he teaches the Dharma of true purity;

understanding that all phenomena are like footprints in the sky, while sentient beings, obscured by ignorance, do not know reality, the Bodhisattva gives rise to pure compassion for them, desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to the Mahāyāna mind and ultimately attain nirvāṇa.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure compassion of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this compassion, they shall attain the supreme, pure great compassion of all Buddhas.
The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sutra, Scroll Forty-one and Scroll Forty-two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Seventh Section on Transcending the World.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure joy for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas."
What are these ten? They are:
the pure joy of generating the bodhicitta;
The pure joy of relinquishing all that one possesses;
the pure joy of not conceiving ill will toward those who violate the precepts, but instead teaching and transforming them to bring them to fulfillment;
and the pure joy of causing all sentient beings engaged in disputes to reach harmony and attain unsurpassed wisdom.
Pure joy in protecting the True Dharma without sparing one's own body or life;
pure joy in remaining far removed from the five desires and always delighting in the True Dharma;
and pure joy in causing all sentient beings to remain unattached to the necessities of life and always delight in the True Dharma.
They behold all Buddhas with reverence and make offerings to them without ever feeling weary or satisfied, yet they do not disrupt the pure joy of the *dharmadhātu*.
They cause all sentient beings to always delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and samādhi, thereby maintaining a continuous stream of pure joy.

They cause all sentient beings to single-mindedly seek tranquility, extinguish distracted thoughts to attain unsurpassed wisdom, remain far removed from false views, fulfill all vows, and ultimately achieve the pure joy of the bodhisattva’s ascetic practices.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure joy of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these joys, they will attain the supreme, pure great joy of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure relinquishment for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:

when all sentient beings show respect, honor, and provide offerings, one does not give rise to attachment; when all sentient beings treat one with contempt, insult, or humiliation, one does not give rise to anger, but maintains pure equanimity;
and while constantly moving through the world, one is not defiled by the eight worldly winds, maintaining pure equanimity.
Knowing the proper time regarding those who are vessels for the Dharma, one maintains pure equanimity by not giving rise to malice toward those who are not vessels;
one maintains pure equanimity by not seeking the states of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, those in training, or those beyond training;
and one maintains pure equanimity by remaining far removed from the five desires and all afflictions, such that not even a single thought of malice arises.
It is pure equanimity that does not praise the practice of the two vehicles nor harbor aversion toward birth and death;

it is pure equanimity that remains far removed from worldly speech, speech contrary to *nirvāṇa*, speech contrary to dispassion, frivolous speech, speech that distresses others, the speech of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and indeed all speech that obstructs bodhi;
it is pure equanimity when there are sentient beings who must wait for the right time before they can be transformed.
If there are sentient beings who should be transformed by the Buddha, the bodhisattva practices pure equanimity (*śuddha-upekṣā*).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva remains far removed from dualistic phenomena; being without superior or inferior, without grasping or relinquishing, and without falsehood or reality, they contemplate equality, abide securely in truth, and attain the purity of equanimity through patience (*kṣānti*).
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of pure relinquishment of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this relinquishment, they will attain the unsurpassed, pure great relinquishment of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of meanings for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the meaning of extensive learning, because of practicing according to what has been taught;
the meaning of the Dharma, because of skillfully analyzing and understanding through expedient means.
The meaning of emptiness is because it understands the foremost emptiness;
the meaning of quiescent extinction is because it causes all sentient beings to leave birth and death;
the meaning of ineffability is because there is no attachment to any speech or language.
The meaning of "as it is" (yathārtha), because all three periods of time are observed as equal;
the meaning of entering the Dharma, because everything is of a single flavor;
the meaning of the Tathāgata, because one accords with the Tathāgata.
The meaning of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) is the awakening to truth;
the meaning of *mahāparinirvāṇa* (great parinirvāṇa) is the extinction of all suffering while not severing the bodhisattva practices.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of meanings for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these meanings, they will attain the supreme meaning of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dharmas for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the Dharma of reality, because one practices according to what has been taught;
the Dharma of non-harming, because one is far removed from malice.
The dharma of non-contention, because it extinguishes all afflictions;
the dharma of quiescence, because it is free from burning fever;
the dharma of detachment from desire, because it is forever free from the defilements of desire and all afflictions.
The non-false dharma, because it is free from delusion;
the unarisen dharma, because all dharmas are entirely empty;
the unconditioned dharma, because it is free from the three marks.
The dharma of intrinsic purity is so called because it is naturally pure;

the dharma of the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) and the nirvāṇa without remainder through the extinction of afflictions is so called because one practices the bodhisattva path and maintains it without abandoning it.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed dharma of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of endowments of merit for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
exhorting sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta is an endowment of merit, because it ensures that the Three Jewels are never interrupted;
conforming to the ten kinds of dedication is an endowment of merit, because it severs all unwholesome dharmas and gathers all wholesome dharmas.
Wisdom and the correct teaching are the equipment of merit, for they are the most preeminent among all merits within the three realms;
a mind free from weariness is the equipment of merit, for it delivers all sentient beings to the further shore;
the complete relinquishment of all that is internal and external is the equipment of merit, for there is no attachment whatsoever toward any object.
The perfection of the primary and secondary marks and non-retrogression through diligence are the possession of merit, because they cause the mind to cease its wandering;
not disparaging the three grades of roots of goodness is the possession of merit, because of skillful means dedicated toward Bodhi;

not giving rise to contempt for sentient beings who are fixed in error or have violated the precepts, but rather increasing great compassion, is the possession of merit, because it manifests the dharma of a Great Being.

He reverently makes offerings to all Tathāgatas and regards all bodhisattvas as Tathāgatas; he brings his deeds toward all sentient beings to ultimate completion because he nurtures and protects an upright mind.

For incalculable eons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has fully cultivated all roots of goodness and is able to relinquish them all to a single sentient being without any grief or regret; as it is with one sentient being, so it is with all sentient beings. This is the tenth great endowment of merit, equal to the realm of empty space, because he has fully accomplished vast wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of endowments of merit for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, great endowment of merit of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of endowments of wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:

to draw near to true and learned spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and to revere, respect, prostrate to, make offerings to, serve, and follow them, never contravening their instructions—this is the first endowment of wisdom, because it is free from flattery and crookedness.

Free from pride and with a humble mind, one is without negligence; body, speech, and mind are all supple, free from frivolity, and the heart is constantly joyful. One upholds the pure precepts, maintains a serene countenance and loving speech, inquires after others with kindness, and stays far removed from the false and deceitful. This is the second endowment of wisdom, for it naturally brings about the attainment of a vessel for the Buddha-dharma.

Abiding securely in mindfulness and wisdom, not abandoning right enlightenment, eliminating distracted thoughts, cultivating the six recollections, practicing the six points of respectful harmony, and seeking no reward for them—this is the third endowment of wisdom, because it gives birth to and nurtures the ten kinds of wisdom.

Delighting in the Dharma and its meaning, diligently practicing the true Dharma, and studying without satiety; remaining far removed from worldly treatises and mundane speech, while delighting in hearing discourse that transcends the world; distancing oneself from the Hīnayāna and joyfully seeking the Mahāyāna—this is the fourth endowment of wisdom, for it consists in the cultivation of right mindfulness, which is inconceivable.

They correctly seek the six *pāramitās*, upholding and practicing them; they fully accomplish the four kinds of Brahma-dwellings; they accord with all dharmas of clarity and are able to question the wise;

they distance themselves from evil destinies and focus exclusively on auspicious destinies; they tame themselves with a mind of loving-kindness, remain free from reproach and criticism, and protect the minds of others—this is the fifth possession of wisdom, for they practice the true Dharma of the Buddhas as it has been taught.

One constantly delights in leaving the household life and does not delight in the triple world; one guards one’s own mind, stays far removed from the three types of deluded thoughts, and does not give rise to evil intentions. One’s body, speech, and mind are all supple and gentle, and one skillfully understands the nature of the mind. This is the sixth endowment of wisdom, for it causes the minds of both oneself and others to be pure.

One contemplates the aggregates as being like illusions, like realms of existence, like venomous snakes entering [the body], and like empty villages; one contemplates all phenomena as being like transformations, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like images in a mirror, like dreams, like lightning, like echoes, like whirling firebrands, like letters in the sky, like Indra’s army, and like the light of the sun and moon—neither permanent nor annihilated, without coming, without going, and without abiding. To have deep faith and understanding in this way, without giving rise to slander, is the possession of the seventh wisdom of non-arising, abiding, and ceasing, because it fully accomplishes the pure wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena.

There is no self, no sentient being, no *pudgala*, no thought, no meaning, no greed, hatred, or delusion; there is nothing possessed, no disparagement, no praise, no grasping, no abandoning, no master, and no activity—this is ultimate *nirvāṇa*. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound Dharma, can believe and understand it, eliminating all doubt and confusion, this is the eighth perfection of wisdom, because they have ultimately and fully attained profound liberation.
Through right skillful means, one contemplates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, subdues the sense faculties, and realizes that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without fabrication;

they are unarisen, unconditioned, and entirely quiescent. For those sentient beings who conceive of a self, there is ultimately nothing at all—neither bondage nor liberation, neither body, speech, or mind, nor even diligence. One observes all sentient beings, all phenomena, all minds, and all activities as being without before or after, entirely equal. This is the ninth perfection of wisdom, for it is the ultimate arrival at the other shore by remaining far removed from all marks (*nimitta*).
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas skillfully understand dependent origination, they perceive the purity of phenomena;
because they perceive the purity of phenomena, they perceive the purity of buddha-fields;
because they perceive the purity of buddha-fields, they perceive the purity of space.
Because one perceives the purity of space, one perceives the purity of the dharma-realm;
because one perceives the purity of the dharma-realm, one then perceives wisdom.
This is the perfection of the tenth wisdom, for it accumulates all-encompassing knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of endowments of wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
If Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, unimpeded, and pure great wisdom of all Buddhas regarding all dharmas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of sufficiency of clarity (*vidyā-pāda*). What are the ten?
That is to say:
being fully illuminated by profound knowledge of the Buddha-dharma;
and being fully illuminated by the removal of the darkness of ignorance regarding all phenomena.
The light-footedness of being far removed from wrong views;
the light-footedness of the pure radiance of wisdom universally illuminating all faculties;
and the light-footedness of diligently cultivating right effort through correct application.
They have deeply entered the true reality of the bodhisattvas and correctly proceed toward the light-footedness that is free from birth;
they have extinguished the karma of afflictions and accomplished the light-footedness of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
and they possess the light-footedness of the pure divine eye through the contemplation of pure wisdom.
With pure recollection, he is perfected in the clear knowledge of recollecting past lives;

being fully endowed with the purity of the ground and the purity of all clear knowledges, he has extinguished all outflows and is perfected in the clear knowledge of the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of sufficiency of illumination for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme great illumination within all dharmas of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas seek the Dharma. What are these ten?
That is to say:
seeking the Dharma with a straightforward mind, because of being free from a mind of flattery, crookedness, and hypocrisy;
seeking the Dharma with diligent effort, because of being free from indolence.
Seeking the Dharma single-mindedly because one does not begrudge body or life;
seeking the Dharma to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings because one does not seek the requisites for livelihood;
seeking the Dharma to benefit all sentient beings because one does not seek self-interest.
One seeks the Dharma to enter deeply into wisdom, because one does not disparage others;
one seeks the Dharma with the desire to keep the True Dharma eternally firm, because one takes no pleasure in the world;
one seeks the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings, because one does not abandon the bodhicitta.
They seek the Dharma in order to be able to answer whatever questions all sentient beings may ask, thereby completely eliminating all doubts and delusions;
they seek the Dharma in order to fully perfect the Buddha-dharma, taking no pleasure in other vehicles.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the Dharma;
if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, unobstructed wisdom within all the teachings of the Buddhas, awakening to it through no other.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of clearly understood dharmas for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the clear knowledge of phenomena that accords with the world, for the purpose of nurturing the roots of goodness of all worldly ordinary beings;
and the clear knowledge of unimpeded and indestructible faith, for the sake of those who practice through faith and understand the true nature of phenomena.
Abiding securely in the dharma-realm and clearly understanding the dharma, because they understand those who practice the dharma;
being far removed from the eightfold wrong paths and clearly understanding the dharma of the eightfold noble path, because they understand the eight types of persons;
eliminating all fetters and severing the outflows of birth and death, clearly understanding the dharma of seeing the true reality, because they understand the *srotāpanna*.
Contemplating that flavors are a source of affliction, one clearly understands the Dharma for returning to receive birth, thereby realizing the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*;

even for a moment not delighting in the three realms and not clinging to receiving birth, one single-mindedly seeks the exhaustion of outflows and clearly understands the Dharma, thereby realizing the stage of *anāgāmin*;

possessing mastery over the six supernormal powers, roaming through the eight liberations, and entering the nine successive meditative attainments at will, one clearly understands the Dharma of the various eloquences, thereby realizing the stage of *arhat*.

They always delight in tranquility; through external conditions, they understand contentment and fewness of affairs, awakening not by means of others but by accomplishing the clear realization of the Dharma of wisdom, for they understand the state of a pratyekabuddha.

They accomplish supreme knowledge, with faculties that are keen and sharp, and their minds are constantly liberated. They nurture immeasurable merit and wisdom, fulfilling the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of all Buddhas, and clearly realizing all Buddha-dharmas, for they understand the state of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of clearly understood dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these dharmas, they will attain the clearly understood dharma of the unsurpassed, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dharmas of orientation for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
turning toward the Dharma by following and honoring spiritual friends;
and turning toward the Dharma by awakening the devas.
One approaches the Dharma by always maintaining a sense of shame and remorse toward all Buddhas;
one approaches the Dharma by compassionately regarding sentient beings and not severing the cycle of birth and death;
one approaches the Dharma by bringing all matters to ultimate completion without giving rise to false thoughts.
They distance themselves from other vehicles and exclusively cultivate the Dharma that leads toward the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattvas;
they distance themselves from false paths and exclusively seek the Dharma that leads toward the true path;
they subdue all Māras and eliminate afflictions through the Dharma that leads toward [enlightenment].
Abiding in the stage of Buddhahood, they know the faculties of all sentient beings and extensively expound the Dharma toward them according to what each should hear;
they abide in the immeasurable and boundless pure dharma-realm, directed toward the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of dharmas of orientation for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed dharmas of orientation of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of māras for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the māra of the five aggregates, because of being greedily attached to the five aggregates;
the māra of afflictions, because of being defiled by afflictions;
The karma-māra, because it can create obstacles;
the mind-māra, because of one's own arrogance;
the death-māra, because of the departure from birth.
The celestial demon arises from the cultivation of arrogance and negligence;
the demon of lost roots of goodness arises from a lack of remorse in the mind;
the samādhi demon arises from attachment to its flavor.
The demon of spiritual friends arises from the mind of attachment toward them;
the demon of ignorance regarding the true Dharma of Bodhi arises from the inability to give birth to the great vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of māras for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
you should employ skillful means to swiftly distance yourselves from them.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of demonic activities (*māra-karman*). What are these ten?
They are as follows:
To cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is the work of Māra;
to give with a malicious mind and to harbor anger toward those who uphold the precepts is the work of Māra;
to abandon sentient beings who are of evil nature, indolent, or who are contemptuous, weary of, distracted, and lacking wisdom is the work of Māra.

To be stingy with the True Dharma and to revile those sentient beings who are vessels for it; to greedily seek gain and offerings while preaching the Dharma to others; and to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma to those who are not vessels—these are the works of Māra.

To not hear of the *pāramitās*; though hearing them, to fail to practice them; to give rise to a mind of indolence; and to not seek the profound, wondrous, and unsurpassed Bodhi—these are the works of Māra.

To distance oneself from virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and to associate with evil friends; to delight in seeking the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); and to give rise to a mind of detachment, tranquility, and cessation regarding the places where one takes birth—these are the works of Māra.

To give rise to a mind of anger toward a bodhisattva, to speak of their faults and evils, to cut off their offerings and support, to constantly seek out their transgressions, and to look upon them with an evil eye—these are the works of Māra.

To slander the True Dharma, not to hear the sūtras, or to fail to praise them when heard; if there is a Dharma teacher preaching the Dharma, to be unable to show respect, to humble one’s mind, or to practice self-effacement;

to say, "This meaning is mine, while that meaning is his"—these are the works of Māra. To study worldly treatises, to be clever with words, skilled in phrasing and style, and proficient in calligraphy and recitation; to delight in expounding the Two Vehicles while concealing the profound Dharma; to preach miscellaneous talk and explain the extremely profound Dharma to those who are not suitable vessels; to distance oneself from Bodhi and abide in false paths—these are the works of Māra.

To approach, revere, and make offerings to those who have already crossed over and attained peace, while never approaching, revering, or making offerings to those who have not yet crossed over or attained peace—and furthermore, failing to teach and transform them—is the work of Māra.

To fall into overweening pride (*adhimāna*), to increase various forms of conceit, to despise sentient beings, to seek neither the True Dharma nor authentic wisdom, and to have one’s faculties scattered so as to be difficult to transform and deliver—these are the works of Māra.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten types of demonic activities of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should swiftly distance themselves from them and correctly seek the activities of a Buddha.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of abandoning demonic activities for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
associating with virtuous friends and abandoning the deeds of Māra;
not exalting oneself and not praising oneself, thereby abandoning the deeds of Māra.
Believing in the profound Dharma of the Buddha and not giving rise to slander is to abandon the works of Māra;
never forgetting the mind of omniscience is to abandon the works of Māra;
abiding in heedfulness and cultivating the most profound Dharma is to abandon the works of Māra.
Abiding securely in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and correctly seeking all dharmas is to abandon the works of Māra;
constantly desiring to hear the Dharma and delighting in hearing profound meanings with a tireless mind is to abandon the works of Māra;
taking refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions is to abandon the works of Māra.
With faith and right mindfulness, one abandons the works of Māra regarding all the Bodhi trees of the Buddhas;
with the realization that all roots of goodness produced by all Bodhisattvas are non-dual, one abandons the works of Māra.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abandon the activities of Māra;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these practices, they will leave behind all paths of Māra’s activities.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of seeing the Buddha for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the Unattached Buddha, because he dwells peacefully in the world and attains perfect enlightenment;
the Vow Buddha, because he brings [beings] forth;
The Buddha of karmic retribution, because of faith;
the Buddha of upholding, because of compliance;
the Buddha of nirvana, because of eternal transcendence.
The Buddha of the Dharma-realm, because he reaches everywhere;
the Buddha of the mind, because he dwells in peace;
the Buddha of samādhi, because he is immeasurable and unattached.
The Buddha of Nature, because of certainty;
the Buddha of Will, because of universal coverage.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas behold the Buddha;
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these dharmas, they will be able to perceive the unsurpassed Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of buddha-activities of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
exhorting and transforming sentient beings is the first buddha-activity, because it accords with and nurtures all Buddha-dharmas;
seeing the Buddha in dreams is the second buddha-activity, because it gives rise to past roots of goodness.
Extensive learning is the third Buddha-activity, because it attains the definitive wisdom that is free from doubt;
skillfully employing expedient means to teach the Dharma of repentance to those entangled by the fetters of remorse is the fourth Buddha-activity, because it eliminates all doubts and regrets;

if there are sentient beings who give rise to a mind of stinginess, a mind lacking wisdom, the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha, a harmful mind, a doubting mind, or a mind of arrogance, [the Buddha] manifests the Tathāgata’s body adorned with the primary and secondary marks to transform such types—this is the fifth Buddha-activity, because it gives birth to and nurtures the various roots of goodness from the past.

In times when the True Dharma is difficult to encounter, he extensively expounds the pure and wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; once sentient beings have heard it, they immediately attain the perfection of *dhāraṇī*, wisdom, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting as appropriate to benefit sentient beings—this is the sixth Buddha-activity, due to the purity of the power of mind.

If demonic activities arise, he swiftly distances himself from them through various skillful means; using subtle and wonderful sounds equal to the realm of empty space, he does not disparage others, extinguishes all demonic deeds, and fulfills patience—this is the seventh Buddha-activity, due to his upright merit.

Practicing immeasurable deeds, one does not realize the fruits of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; for those who have departed from the noble practices of birth and whose faculties are not yet mature, one does not preach the fruit of liberation, but merely removes the root of craving—this is the eighth Buddha-activity, because it gives rise to original vows.

Severing all outflows (*āsrava*) and bonds of birth and death, as well as all fetters (*saṃyojana*), one gives rise to the Bodhisattva practice, nurtures great compassion toward all sentient beings, and with a profound mind of faith and understanding, practices what the Bodhisattvas do until reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*—this is the ninth Buddha-activity, because it ensures that the Bodhisattva practice is never interrupted.

For the sake of themselves and others, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the path to liberation without ever becoming weary; they remain detached from all conditioned activities and all phenomena, and harbor no attachment to the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata. With diligent and exclusive focus, they seek unimpeded wisdom, attaining realization not through another. They cause all Buddha-fields to be adorned and purified, yet they definitively know them all to be empty space. They teach and bring to maturity all sentient beings, yet do not abandon the nature of selflessness (*anātmatā*).

Abiding in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they possess mastery over the supernormal powers and fully accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet do not abandon the bodhisattva practices.
They turn the pure wheel of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to rejoice, and extensively expound the profound Dharma for the sake of all beings.
They manifest the immeasurable sovereignty of a Tathāgata without abandoning the body of a bodhisattva; they manifest great parinirvāṇa without relinquishing birth in all places.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give birth to such [qualities] as these, up to and including the samādhi of overturning; this is the tenth Buddha-activity.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of Buddha-activities of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this karma, they will attain the supreme, teacherless great karma of all Buddhas, awakening to it without depending on another.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of arrogant actions. What are the ten?
They are as follows:
To fail to show respect, reverence, and make offerings toward those who are fields of merit—such as preceptors, ācāryas, parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—is the karma of pride.

There are certain Dharma masters who have attained the supreme and wondrous vehicle of the Dharma; they have profound knowledge of the Mahāyāna, have emerged from the path of birth and death, and have obtained dhāraṇīs.

Having accomplished much learning and possessing the treasury of wisdom, they are well able to expound the Dharma, yet they do not believe, accept, revere, or make offerings [to others]. This constitutes the karma of arrogance.

When listening to and receiving the Dharma, if upon hearing profound teachings one gives rise to a mind of detachment and experiences immeasurable joy, yet fails to praise the Dharma teacher so as to cause the assembly to rejoice, this constitutes an act of pride.

To give rise to a mind of arrogance, exalting oneself and disparaging others, failing to examine one's own reality, and failing to discipline one's own mind—this constitutes the karma of pride (*māna*).

To give rise to a calculating mind of "I," such that when seeing those with merit and wisdom one does not praise their excellence, yet when seeing those without virtue one conversely speaks of their goodness;
or, upon hearing another praised, giving rise to a mind of jealousy toward that person—this constitutes the karma of pride.

If there is a Dharma teacher who knows that this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the truth, and this is the word of the Buddha, yet out of hatred and jealousy, he declares it to be non-Dharma, non-Vinaya, not the truth, and not the word of the Buddha, desiring to destroy the faith of others—this constitutes the karma of arrogance.
To personally arrange a high seat for oneself, acting as the Dharma teacher, while refusing to perform manual labor, refusing to show reverence, and refusing to make offerings to others;
yet expecting all those who practice the holy life, seniors, and those of virtue to instead revere and make offerings to oneself—this constitutes the karma of arrogance.
To distance oneself from frowning or looking upon others with malicious eyes;

to always maintain a serene countenance and regard all sentient beings with equanimity; to speak always with gentleness, free from coarseness or harshness, and to be devoid of resentment—yet to seek out the faults and evils of that Dharma teacher: this constitutes the karma of arrogance.
Out of a mind of self-conceit, one does not go to those who are learned to pay them respect, thereby creating obstacles to hearing the Dharma;
nor does one inquire as to what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what should be done and what should not be done, what kind of karma brings long-term benefit to all sentient beings,
or what kind of conduct fails to benefit sentient beings.
By performing what kind of actions does one pass from light into light?
By performing what kind of actions does one pass from darkness into darkness?
Such people as these are adrift and submerged by my mind; they are unable to perceive the right path that leads to liberation. This constitutes the karma of conceit.

Because they give rise to conceit, they fail to encounter the rare Dharma of the Buddhas and exhaust the roots of goodness planted in past lives. They speak what should not be spoken, harbor thoughts of reproach, and engage in mutual derision, abiding in such dharmas;

they ought to enter onto a wrong path. Yet, by the power of their bodhicitta, they do not permanently abandon the practices of a bodhisattva. Although they do not forsake the bodhisattva path, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas they do not even encounter a Buddha, let alone hear the Dharma—this is the karma of conceit.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten types of prideful actions of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are free from these prideful actions, they will attain the ten kinds of unsurpassed, pure mental actions of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of intellectual activities of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
to have faith and understanding in dependent origination and not to subvert cause and effect is the work of wisdom;
not to abandon the bodhicitta and to constantly keep all Buddhas in mind is the work of wisdom.
To draw near to all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), honoring and making offerings to them with a mind free from indolence—this is the work of wisdom.

To delight in the Dharma and its meaning, to be insatiable in hearing much, to seek exclusively the True Dharma, to distance oneself from wrong thoughts, and to cultivate right mindfulness—this is the work of wisdom.

To give rise to no sense of "self" toward any sentient being; to regard all bodhisattvas as Tathāgatas; to love and cherish bodhisattvas as one's own body; to hold the True Dharma dear as one's own life; to love and respect the Tathāgata as one protects one's own eyes; and to conceive the thought of all Buddhas toward those who uphold the precepts—this is the work of wisdom.

To distance oneself from all unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and to cultivate pure actions of body, speech, and mind; to praise the noble ones and accord with enlightenment—this is the work of wisdom.
To not contradict dependent origination, to be free from all false views, to eliminate the darkness of ignorance, and to illuminate all phenomena—this is the work of wisdom.

To conceive of the ten dedications as one’s compassionate mother, to conceive of the perfections as one’s compassionate father, and to conceive of skillful means as enlightenment—this is the work of wisdom.

To single-mindedly seek generosity, pure precepts, and extensive learning, as well as tranquility and insight, merit, and wisdom, with a mind free from weariness or fatigue—this is the work of wisdom.

Furthermore, if an action is praised by all Buddhas, capable of subduing the various Māras, extinguishing afflictions, fetters, and hindrances, teaching and transforming sentient beings, conforming to the discipline of wisdom, embracing the True Dharma, purifying Buddha-fields, and proceeding directly toward penetration and clarity—this is the work of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of intellectual activities of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these activities, they will attain the skillful, expedient, and unsurpassed intellectual activities that give rise to all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of demonic influences by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are possessed. What are these ten?

Namely: being possessed by the demon of indolence; being possessed by the demon of abandoning the Buddha’s true Dharma; being possessed by the demon of insatiable greed; being possessed by the demon of focusing solely on one's own liberation; being possessed by the demon of failing to make great vows; being possessed by the demon of distancing oneself from afflictions while constantly delighting in tranquility; being possessed by the demon of severing the outflows of birth and death; being possessed by the demon of abandoning the bodhisattva practices; being possessed by the demon of abandoning the mind that teaches and matures all sentient beings; and being possessed by the demon of giving rise to doubt within the true Dharma and slandering the Buddha’s teachings.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of demonic influences by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are possessed; they should be swiftly abandoned.
If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can relinquish these demonic possessions, they will attain the ten kinds of support provided by all Buddhas.
What are the ten? They are:
first, generating the bodhicitta because it is sustained by the Buddhas;
Because they are sustained by the Buddha, they never forget the bodhicitta throughout all successive births;
because they are sustained by the Buddha, they awaken to all demonic activities and are able to remain entirely free from them;
because they are sustained by the Buddha, they hear the six pāramitās and practice them according to the teachings.
Because they are sustained by the Buddha, they know the suffering of birth and death yet do not feel revulsion toward it;
because they are sustained by the Buddha, they contemplate the profound Dharma and attain the fruit of liberation;
because they are sustained by the Buddha, they preach the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and liberation for the sake of sentient beings, yet do not take pleasure in those vehicles.

Because the Buddha sustains them, they contemplate the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) yet their minds do not delight in dwelling therein; regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they do not give rise to dualistic marks.
Because the Buddha sustains them, they cause [the cycle] not to continue, yet attain the continuity of quiescence (*śānti*).
Because the Buddha sustains them, they attain mastery over all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), yet do not abandon the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) or the conduct of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the Buddhas;
if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these sustainments, they will obtain the sustenance of the ten powers of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dharmas by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained. What are these ten?
That is to say:
all conditioned phenomena are sustained by the nature of impermanence;
all conditioned phenomena are sustained by the nature of suffering;
All phenomena are sustained by the dharma of selflessness;
they are sustained by the dharma of quiescent nirvāṇa;
and they are sustained by the dharma that arises from conditions and does not arise in the absence of conditions.

Due to improper reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), there arise ignorance (*avidyā*) and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); through the cessation of improper reflection, ignorance ceases, and with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation [of the links] up to old age and death—this is what is upheld by the Dharma.
The three gates of liberation give rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle and are upheld by the Dharma of the definitive absence of contention;
the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) give rise to the Mahāyāna and are upheld by its Dharma.
To know all lands, all phenomena, all sentient beings, and all worlds is to be sustained by the dharmas within the Buddha’s sphere;
to sever all conceptualization and relinquish all grasping is to be sustained by the dharmas that accord with nirvāṇa, transcending both past and future.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten dharmas by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained;
if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these sustainments, they will attain the unsurpassed dharma-sustainment of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of activities for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven. What are these ten?
That is to say:

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva preaches the Dharma of detachment to the devas of the desire realm, teaching that indulgence and self-indulgence are entirely impermanent and that all pleasures are ultimately suffering; he exhorts and guides those sons of heaven to resolve upon Bodhicitta—this is the first task performed while dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven.

For the sake of the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva explains the continuity of the characteristics of the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. To those who, having given rise to those factors of dhyāna, become attached to their flavor (*āsvāda*), he explains the wisdom of reality because such attachment gives rise to the view of a self, false views, and the afflictions of ignorance. To those who give rise to perverted thoughts regarding all exquisite forms and grasp at them as pure through deluded conceptualization, he explains their impurity and instructs them to contemplate impermanence. He exhorts, inspires, and guides those sons of the gods to resolve upon bodhicitta; this is the second of the activities performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, he enters the samādhi named "Adornment of Radiance. From within his own body, he emits a great light that universally illumines all the trichiliocosms, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings through various sounds according to their needs.

Upon hearing this teaching, those beings are all filled with great joy and give rise to a mind of reverence; after their lives end, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. There, he again preaches the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta. This is the third of the activities performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
With unimpeded, pure eyes, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally beholds all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas in the Tuṣita heavens throughout the ten directions;
those Bodhisattvas likewise see this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, and having seen one another, they extensively expound the True Dharma for those Bodhisattvas, namely:

Descending into the mother’s womb, being born into the world, leaving home to seek the Way, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, adorning oneself with great adornments, initiating past practices, recollecting past deeds, and accomplishing merit—all these are manifested without ever leaving this seat;
such is the fourth of the activities performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, all the Bodhisattvas from the Tuṣita Heavens of the ten directions come to him in order to see, revere, make offerings to, and prostrate before this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

At that time, desiring to cause all those Bodhisattvas to rejoice and fulfill their aspirations, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva expounds the Great Dharma Gate; he explains it extensively and in full detail according to the respective stages where those Bodhisattvas dwell, and according to what they practice, what they have abandoned, what they cultivate, and what they realize.

Having heard this teaching of the Dharma, all those Bodhisattvas are greatly delighted and each returns to the palace in their own original land. This is the fifth activity performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven and expounds the True Dharma, Māra Pāpīyān, the lord of the desire realm, together with his retinue, approaches the Bodhisattva’s abode to disrupt and confound his preaching.

At that time, the Bodhisattva abides in the state of adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñāna*), employing the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Prajñāpāramitā to enter deeply into the gates of wisdom and preach the nectar-like Dharma. Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, he proclaims the Tathāgata’s teachings and completely subdues all those hosts of Māras.

When that host of Māras beholds such sovereign spiritual power of the Bodhisattva and hears the preaching of the Dharma, they all resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This is the sixth of the activities performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, he perceives that the devaputras of the desire realm do not recognize suffering and thus have no inclination to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva emits a great sound and addresses the devaputras:
"Today the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is departing with his inner retinue; those who wish to see him should quickly come here."
Upon hearing this sound, immeasurable billions of nayutas of devaputras all went to that place.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally manifested all his retinue within the palace, whom those devaputras had never before heard of or seen;
having seen them, they were all filled with great joy.
From among the musical instruments of this bodhisattva’s retinue, such a sound emerged, declaring:
"O sons of the gods!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are great suffering; all dharmas are selfless, quiescent, and nirvana."
Furthermore, he addressed them again, saying:
"You all should cultivate the bodhisattva practices, realize ultimate enlightenment, and possess all-encompassing wisdom.

At that time, having heard these words, the sons of the gods were filled with great trepidation and single-mindedly sought unsurpassed bodhi. This is the seventh activity performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, without abandoning his seat in Tuṣita, he is able to travel to the abodes of all Buddhas, where he beholds the Tathāgatas, pays them respectful homage, makes offerings, and listens to the Dharma.

At that time, the Buddhas teach the Bodhisattva the method of the nectar-consecration and the bestowal of prophecy, as well as all the vidyās and the stages of bodhisattva practice, desiring that the Bodhisattva, through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, may become fully endowed with all branches and all aspects, and penetrate deeply into omniscience. This is the eighth activity performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, they reverently make offerings to all Buddhas of all worlds with every kind of offering equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. When sentient beings behold these offerings, immeasurable and boundless numbers of them resolve to attain Bodhicitta; this is the ninth activity performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, they give rise to immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates and manifest throughout all worlds in various colors, various forms, various modes of conduct, and various skillful means, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each;
this is because they desire to cause all sentient beings to rejoice. This is the tenth of their activities while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten types of activities performed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is fully endowed with these activities, they will then be able to descend to be born among humans.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, there are ten kinds of manifested events. What are these ten?
That is to say:

when a Bodhisattva is in the Tuṣita Heaven and his life is about to end, he emits a great radiance from the wheel-mark on the sole of his foot called "Adorned with Peace and Bliss. It shines universally upon all sentient beings in the various difficulties and evil realms throughout the trichiliocosm. Those who come into contact with this light have all their sufferings extinguished and attain peace and bliss.
At that time, all those sentient beings think to themselves:
"Today, suddenly, a wondrous Great Being has appeared in the world.
This is the first matter manifested.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in the Tuṣita Heaven is about to end his life, he emits from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a light called "Awakening."
It universally illumined the trichiliocosm and touched the bodies of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had practiced together with him in past lives.
Having been touched, they all thought:
"That bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the Tuṣita Heaven is now about to pass away."

At that time, the bodhisattvas immediately manifested immeasurable and boundless articles of offering and proceeded swiftly to where those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were; this was the second matter demonstrated.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva approaches the end of his life, a great radiance called "Pure Realm" emerges from his right palm; it is capable of completely purifying and adorning the trichiliocosm.

Within this world-system, if there are any outflow-free Pratyekabuddhas who perceive this light, they immediately relinquish their life-span. If they do not perceive it, by the power of the radiance, they are transported to other world-systems. All Māras and various non-Buddhists, as well as sentient beings who behold them, are likewise transported to other world-systems, with the exception of those sentient beings sustained and transformed by the Tathāgata’s empowerment. This is the third manifested event.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva emitted from his two knees a great radiance called "Stainless, Pure, and Adorned," which universally illuminated the palaces of the lowest devas;
reaching upward to the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, there was nothing it did not clearly illuminate.
At that time, all the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"Now this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to relinquish his life-span in the Tuṣita Heaven.

At that time, the sons of the gods quickly prepared offerings—incense, flowers, necklaces, unguents, powdered incense, robes, parasols, banners, pennants, and various musical instruments—and went to where the Bodhisattva was to pay him respectful homage. We all followed and guarded him from the time he passed away from there until he manifested the Great Parinirvāṇa; this is the fourth matter manifested.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva was about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emitted a great radiance from his heart called "Vajra-Pure-Splendid-Adornment," which universally illuminated all the Vajrapāṇis throughout every world-system.
At that time, ten billion Vajrapāṇis all had this thought:
"This is because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven; he has manifested this sign to us, and we shall all attend upon and protect him."
"Up until the manifestation of the Great Parinirvāṇa—this is the fifth matter manifested.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great radiance from all his pores called 'Discerning All Sentient Beings. It shines universally upon the trichiliocosm and pervasively touches the bodies of all Bodhisattvas; having touched them, it further touches all devas and worldly people.
At that time, all the Bodhisattvas think thus:"
"We should go to him to pay respectful homage and offerings to the Tathāgata, and furthermore, to transform and guide those sentient beings.
This is the sixth matter manifested.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great light called "Well-Subdued" within the Hall of the True Dharma of the Maṇi Jewel Treasury.
This light shines universally upon the royal palace at the place where that Bodhisattva has descended to take birth. Thereupon, those Bodhisattvas each form this thought:

"In whatever place this Bodhisattva shall be born—whether in a household, a village, a city, or any place of birth within Jambudvīpa—I shall be born there as well, for the purpose of teaching and transforming all sentient beings."
This is the seventh manifested event.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great radiance from within the celestial palaces, called "Pure Adornment of All Palaces.

This light shines upon his mother who is to give birth to him; having shone upon her, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes peaceful, secure, and joyful, fully endowed with all merits. Within her body, there spontaneously appears a palace adorned with the seven treasures, intended for the Bodhisattva to dwell therein. This is the eighth manifested event.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to pass away from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a light from beneath his feet called "Abiding Securely.
Because of this light, those devaputras and Brahmās whose lives are about to end are all enabled to extend their lifespans so that they may make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
From the time he passes away from there until he manifests the Great Parinirvāṇa, this constitutes the ninth matter manifested.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva emits a great radiance from his minor marks called "Pure Sun-Eye," manifesting the various karmas of the Bodhisattvas.

At that time, among humans and devas, some may see the Bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven; some may see his passing away from life; some may see him dwelling in the womb; some may see his birth; some may see his renunciation of the home; some may see his attainment of Buddhahood; some may see him turning the wheel of Dharma; and some may see the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa. This is the tenth matter of manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha!

Whether at his seat, or in a multi-storied pavilion, or in a palace, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva emits millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light such as these. When he emits these rays, they manifest the immeasurable karmas of all bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are fully endowed with all such pure karmas, they descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born into the world.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas descend into their mothers’ wombs for ten reasons.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
In order to teach, transform, and bring to maturity sentient beings of limited capacity, he manifests dwelling in the womb;
he does so not to allow those of limited capacity to think:
"The Bodhisattva is born through spontaneous transformation, and his roots of goodness and wisdom were not obtained through practice."
This is the first reason for manifesting entry into the womb.

Furthermore, it is because he wishes to cause his parents, kinsmen, and elders to nurture the roots of goodness from past lives that they shared; this is the second reason for manifesting entry into the womb.
