"Just as water contained within a vessel made of diamond cannot be exhausted, so too is the bodhicitta:
when established in the supreme and wondrous roots of goodness dedicated toward awakening, even while entering the realms of birth and death, no unwholesome dharmas can exhaust it."
"Just as a diamond can support the great earth, preventing it from falling or sinking, so too is the bodhicitta;
it supports all the vows and practices of the bodhisattvas, preventing them from falling or sinking into the triple world."
"Just as a vajra remains in water for hundreds of thousands of kalpas without rotting or decaying, and undergoes no change, so too is the bodhicitta;
throughout immeasurable kalpas within the cycle of birth and death, it cannot be destroyed by any afflictions or karma, nor does it suffer any diminution."
"Just as a vajra cannot be burned or heated by any great fire, so too is the bodhicitta;
it cannot be burned or heated by any of the fires of birth-and-death, greed, anger, or delusion."
"Just as the adamantine seat of the bodhimaṇḍa can support a bodhisattva, enabling them to subdue all māras and attain equal and perfect enlightenment, while nothing else can support them."

The bodhicitta is likewise: it can sustain all the vows and practices of bodhisattvas, the various pāramitās, the various patiences, and the various stages; it sustains the dedication of merit, the reception of predictions of enlightenment, the cultivation of the path to awakening, the making of offerings to all Buddhas, and the hearing, receiving, and practicing of the Dharma—things that no other mind can sustain.
“Good son! The bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable merits;
if any sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta, they will likewise possess such immeasurable merits.”
Therefore, virtuous son!
You have gained a sublime benefit by resolving to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva, and becoming fully endowed with such immeasurable merits.
“Good son! Regarding what you previously asked:
‘How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?’”

"Now, you who have entered this Great Tower of Radiant Pure Adornment Treasury will be able to fully understand how to study the bodhisattva practices and cultivate the bodhisattva path, thereby accomplishing and perfecting immeasurable merits."
At that time, the youth Sudhana respectfully circumambulated Maitreya Bodhisattva, joined his palms, and said:
"I pray only that the Great Sage will open the door of this tower and allow me to enter."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva snapped his right finger, and the gate opened of its own accord; Sudhana entered immediately, and once he had entered, it closed again.
Then Sudhana observed the tower-palace: it was vast and immeasurable, like empty space, with a ground made of various jewels.

There were incalculable windows and balconies with defensive parapets, all fashioned from the seven treasures; they were adorned with incalculable banners, flags, and canopies, incalculable precious necklaces and hanging ribbons, and incalculable great lion-banners, crescent-moon jewels, and various precious silken streamers.

Furthermore, it was adorned with incalculable celestial crowns and precious robes, covered above by incalculable jeweled nets, and from incalculable golden bells, subtle and wondrous sounds spontaneously issued forth.

Furthermore, they rained down clouds of immeasurable precious flower garlands and clouds of exquisite fragrances; they rained down incalculable fine gold dust and emitted incalculable, most sublime rays of light that universally illumined all things.
There were incalculable birds of various species, uttering harmonious and elegant sounds.
An incalculable rain of *utpala*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers fell, and an incalculable radiance from *maṇi* jewels issued forth, universally illuminating all things.
Within that tower-pavilion, there were hundreds of thousands of exquisite pavilions, all existing without mutual obstruction, adorned and decorated as previously described.
At that time, Sudhana beheld the inconceivable and wondrous adornments of the pavilion; his heart was filled with great joy, and he leaped for immeasurable delight.

His mind became supple, free from all false conceptions, and having extinguished all darkness of ignorance and obscuration, he contemplated with right mindfulness, single-mindedly seeking the sublime path, and paid reverent homage with an unimpeded body.

Having completed the prostrations, by the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, they saw their own bodies within all the towers and pavilions, and further beheld immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers and inconceivable wonders.

Some see Maitreya according to his original lineage, lifespan, and associates, as he nurtures roots of goodness throughout various eons and worlds at the abodes of all Buddhas, together with his retinue; they see him, by virtue of his great vows, first resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
or they see him first attain the *maitrī-citta-samādhi*, and thus receive his name therefrom.

Or they may see Maitreya practicing the bodhisattva path, fulfilling all the pāramitās, the various patiences (kṣānti), and the stages (bhūmi); purifying buddha-fields; beholding all Tathāgatas; hearing and upholding the Dharma; protecting the true Dharma; acting as a great Dharma teacher; attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and knowing in which direction and at which place, under which Tathāgata, and after how many eons (kalpa), he will receive his prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Some see Maitreya as a Wheel-Turning King, transforming the world through the ten wholesome paths;
some see him as one of the Four Heavenly Kings, benefiting all sentient beings;
or some see him as Śakra, rebuking the five desires.
Sometimes he acts as the King of the Yāma Heaven, praising heedfulness;
sometimes he acts as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, extolling the merits of bodhisattvas in their final birth;
and sometimes he acts as the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, praising the dharma of mastery.
Sometimes he becomes a Mara King to preach the Dharma of impermanence;
sometimes he becomes a king of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations to praise the Bodhisattva’s adornment of transformation bodies;
and sometimes he becomes a Brahma King to praise the four immeasurable minds.
Sometimes he becomes an asura king, subduing his retinue and entering the great ocean of wisdom, thoroughly comprehending that all phenomena are entirely like illusions and transformations;
sometimes he becomes King Yama, emitting a great radiance that universally illumines the hells and extinguishes all suffering.
Or they may give various delicacies and food and drink as alms to the hungry ghosts;
or, taking on various forms as animals, they preach the Dharma for them to eliminate their ignorance and darkness;
or they preach the Dharma for the retinues of the Four Heavenly Kings, and even for the retinues of the Brahma Heavenly Kings.
Sometimes he preaches the Dharma for the retinues of various nāgas, and even for the retinues of humans, non-humans, and so forth;
sometimes he preaches the Dharma for the great assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
and sometimes he preaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, up to those on the tenth bhūmi.
In some instances, they see the praise of the merits of bodhisattvas from those who have first resolved for enlightenment up to those on the tenth stage;

or they see them fulfilling all the *pāramitās*, entering the gate of the patient acceptance of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-kṣānti*), the gate of the vast *samādhi*, and the gate of delighting in the profound Dharma; they see them practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), giving rise to supernormal powers and clear insights (*abhijñā-vidyā*), filling all things, performing the conduct of a bodhisattva, conforming to the world, and accomplishing great vows;
or they see them together with fellow-practicing bodhisattvas, benefiting sentient beings.
In some instances, he saw himself together with bodhisattvas bound to one more birth, as the various Buddhas appeared before them and bestowed upon them their predictions of enlightenment;
in others, he saw Maitreya for hundreds of thousands of kalpas tirelessly walking, reciting, and transcribing the sutras;
or he observed the gateways of the Dharma and contemplated their true meaning.
Some enter the various dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the liberations, samādhis, and the bases of totality;
some see the emergence of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and clear knowledges;
or they see the samādhi of transformation through correct reception, from each and every pore issuing clouds of emanation bodies, namely:

There were clouds of celestial bodies, clouds of the bodies of all nāgas, yakṣas, and even mahoragas; clouds of the bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings, and even clouds of the bodies of Brahmā kings; clouds of the bodies of universal monarchs, princes, ministers, elders, householders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas. Furthermore, from every single pore, he saw emerging clouds of transformation-bodies equal in number to all sentient beings.
Or they manifest bodhisattva dharma-gates, namely: the gate of praising the merits of the bodhicitta; the gate of the *dānapāramitā*, up to the gate of the *praṇidhānapāramitā*;

the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the samādhis, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the clear insights (*vidyā*), and the dhāraṇīs; the truths (*satya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), and liberation (*vimukti*); dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*); the practices of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattvas; the stages (*bhūmi*), the patiences (*kṣānti*), and the vows and practices of the bodhisattvas—manifesting all such dharma-gates as these.

Or, within the towers and pavilions, they see various Tathāgatas surrounded by great assemblies; furthermore, they know that the families of the Buddhas differ, as do their lineages, their physical dimensions, their lifespans, their eons, their lands, and the immeasurable Dharma-gates they teach, as well as the duration of their True Dharma remaining in the world—all of these they discern and understand to be entirely distinct.

At that time, among all the towers and pavilions, Sudhana saw one particular tower that was high, vast, and magnificently adorned, surpassing all others in its exquisite beauty; it encompassed a trichiliocosm, including ten billion Jambudvīpas and ten billion Tuṣita heavens.

When the Bodhisattva’s life ends, he descends in spirit, undergoes conception and birth, walks seven steps, surveys the ten directions, and lets out the great lion’s roar; Śakra and Brahmā respectfully attend him; he manifests as a youth within the palace, goes out to stroll in the gardens, and with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), leaves the home life and practices austerities; he manifests the acceptance of milk-rice, proceeds to the site of enlightenment, subdues the hosts of Māras, contemplates the Bodhi tree, turns the wheel of the true Dharma, ascends to the celestial palaces, and—in terms of lands, kalpas, retinues, lifespans, the practice of bodhisattva deeds, the fulfillment of great vows, the preaching of the true Dharma, the teaching and transformation of sentient beings, and the manifestation of the distribution of relics—all these are entirely different.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Fifty-nine;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Sixty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Part Seventeen of the Thirty-Fourth Chapter, "Entering the Dharma Realm.
At that time, Sudhana saw his own body before all the Buddhas and witnessed such extraordinary and marvelous events as these.
Furthermore, I heard inconceivable and subtle sounds emerging from the golden bells atop the towers, namely:
the sound of first generating the bodhicitta;
and the sounds of the vows and practices of the various perfections (pāramitās) performed by Bodhisattvas.
They reverently made offerings to the inconceivable sounds of the Buddhas;
the sound of purifying Buddha-fields;
and the sound of the clouds of the Buddha-dharma.
All the various ornaments likewise produced such subtle and wondrous sounds.

Furthermore, they heard the voices of certain bodhisattvas in certain worlds, during certain eons, as they were transformed by certain spiritual friends to dedicate their roots of goodness and give rise to great vows;
and they heard the sounds of them generating the bodhicitta amidst great assemblies in the presence of certain Buddhas.
Furthermore, one hears the sound of Bodhisattvas practicing various deeds throughout kalpas of varying lengths; the sound of their attaining perfect enlightenment in certain lands;
the sound of their names, the duration of their lifespans, their fulfillment of great vows, and their transformation of sentient beings;
and the sound of them manifesting parinirvāṇa and the duration of the Dharma’s abiding amidst the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.

Furthermore, I have heard that in a certain world, a bodhisattva is able to extensively practice the perfection of giving, purely maintain the prohibitive precepts, cultivate patience, exert diligence, enter various meditative concentrations, and practice in accordance with wisdom;
for the sake of seeking the Dharma, he relinquishes all precious treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, head, eyes, hands, and feet.

They protect the True Dharma as great Dharma-preachers, bestowing the pure Dharma, convening great Dharma assemblies, erecting the great Dharma banner, beating the Dharma drum, blowing the Dharma conch, raining down the Dharma rain, and establishing stupas and temples;
through various adornments, they bring peace and happiness to sentient beings and guard the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings.

Furthermore, one hears that a certain Buddha, in a certain world, during a certain kalpa, attained equal and perfect enlightenment; [one hears of] the size of his retinue, the length of his lifespan, the fulfillment of his great vows, and his teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
Hearing such inconceivable and subtle sounds, their bodies and minds became supple, and they experienced immeasurable joy;
they immediately attained countless gates of dhāraṇī, eloquence, patience, diligence, great vows, supernormal clarity, wisdom, liberation, pāramitās, and samādhi.
At that time, within the precious mirror, Sudhana saw all the Tathāgatas and their retinues;
the great Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;
and pure worlds, impure worlds, and mixed worlds.
In some worlds there are Buddhas, while in others there are no Buddhas; there are worlds that are superior, middling, or inferior;
there are worlds like Indra’s net;
and there are worlds that are inverted or upright.
Furthermore, he beheld the world of evenness and clearly discerned the distinctions between the five realms of existence.

He also saw immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great bodhisattvas walking for exercise, practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and investigating all phenomena; they gave rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*) to universally shelter all sentient beings, composing various treatises to elucidate the meanings and principles of the teachings, or transcribing volumes of scripture;
some were questioning and others were answering, or he saw them manifesting the three kinds of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and various great vows—he beheld all such matters as these.

Furthermore, I saw from within the various jeweled pillars the universal emission of immeasurable nets of light in blue, yellow, red, white, and pure crystal colors, as well as from *nīla* gems and Jāmbūnada gold;
I also saw from within pearl necklaces the emergence of fragrant water possessing the eight virtues,
and from within lapis lazuli gems the emergence of immeasurable radiance.
Furthermore, he saw within the *utpala*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses the growth of various exquisite flowers as large as chariot wheels;

within these flowers were seen men and women, the old and the young, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, nāgas, yakṣas, and even humans and non-humans, as well as elephants, horses, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all manner of sentient beings of diverse forms and types—all of whom were reverently paying homage to the Buddha with palms joined.
Furthermore, within the jeweled trees, there were seen bodies of various wondrous colors, namely:

the bodies of Tathāgatas, the bodies of Bodhisattvas, the bodies of the eight classes of beings such as devas and nāgas, the bodies of Śakra and Brahmā, the bodies of wheel-turning kings (cakravartins), and the bodies of the fourfold assembly;
each holding various articles of offering, honoring and praising [the Buddhas], and reverently prostrating.
Furthermore, I saw within the image of the half-moon the emission of the light of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) suns and moons.

I also saw Maitreya, in past lives, practicing the bodhisattva path, giving away his head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, limbs, and joints—all parts of his body—as well as kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and all manner of things, providing them entirely according to whatever was required.
Furthermore, he saw Maitreya praising and reverently making offerings to the Buddhas;
or acting as a King of Physicians to treat various ailments;
and showing the correct path to those who had lost their way.
Sometimes he acts as a great shipmaster, guiding beings to the island of jewels;
sometimes he acts as a horse-king, bearing up sentient beings and causing them to escape the perils of demons;
sometimes he acts as a master of treatises, composing various sutras and śāstras.
Sometimes they become wheel-turning kings, transforming the world through the ten wholesome deeds;
sometimes they see those who are filial and obedient toward their parents, associating with virtuous friends, and not contravening their instructions;
or they see the forms and colors of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Some act as Dharma masters, praising the Buddha-dharma, practicing meditation and recitation, and performing various meritorious deeds; they construct stupas and temples and fashion exquisite images, honoring and making offerings to them with incense, flowers, and garlands.

Others instruct sentient beings in the three refuges, the five precepts, the eightfold fast, and the ten wholesome paths; they encourage them to leave the household life to study the Way, to hear and uphold the Dharma, to contemplate with right mindfulness, and to abide in the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, he saw Maitreya practicing the six pāramitās over immeasurable kalpas and his deeds in transforming sentient beings;
he also saw the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) that Maitreya encountered throughout those immeasurable kalpas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Sudhana: "Welcome, youth!
Do you see the inconceivable power of mastery of these great bodhisattvas within the towers?"
“Yes, indeed, I have seen it.

It is, for example, like a person who, in a dream, beholds mountains, forests, rivers, ponds, the great ocean, Mount Sumeru, and the palaces of the various devas; having seen all such things within the four continents, they experience immeasurable joy.

At that time, Sudhana was likewise; by virtue of the great bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power, he became free from delusion and saw all phenomena of the three realms as being entirely like a dream.

He entered the bodhisattva’s unimpeded dharma-gate of wisdom, the dharma-gates of the bodhisattvas' adornments, and fully realized the inconceivable and wondrous skillful means of the bodhisattvas, manifesting the sovereign power of the bodhisattvas’ spiritual transformations.
For example, when a person is about to die, they see the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
that is to say,
those who have performed evil deeds see the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts, undergoing all manner of agonizing torments.
Some see King Yama holding various weapons, seizing and leading them away;
some see mountains of knives;
others see forests of swords.
Some see sentient beings being sliced and cut by sharp leaves;
some see sentient beings being boiled and cooked in cauldrons of boiling water;
and some hear various sounds of lamentation and suffering.
If one cultivates wholesome deeds, at the time of death, they will see all the celestial palaces of the devas;
or they may see celestial maidens, adorned in various ways, sporting and enjoying themselves in bliss.
Seeing such various wondrous and supreme matters, he was not even aware of them;
dying here and being born there, he saw only the inconceivable realms of karmic activity.
Sudhana the youth was likewise: within the towered pavilion, he beheld the inconceivable realms of the supreme deeds of all the bodhisattvas.
For example, it is like a person possessed by a non-human spirit who sees various forms and types; if questioned or challenged, they are able to respond to all of them.
Sudhana the youth was likewise: through the majestic spiritual power of the great bodhisattvas, he was able to discern and contemplate with right mindfulness all phenomena.
For example, it is as if someone were to enter a dragon palace and perceive seven days, half a month, a year, or a hundred years as but a mere moment;
so too it was with the youth Sudhana, who entered the palace of Maitreya Bodhisattva through his supernatural power and perceived hundreds of thousands of kalpas as but a moment.
Just as in the Brahma palace named Treasury of Adornments, one sees within it all the various forms and images of the three thousandfold world system;
so too did the youth Sudhana, within the pavilion, see all manner of unprecedented wonders.

For example, just as a bhikṣu who has attained the meditative absorption of the universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) perceives all objects of his focus manifest before him whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
so too it was with the youth Sudhana, for within the tower he discerned and knew all those objects of focus.
Just as a person beholding a city of Gandharvas encounters no obstruction, so too was it with the youth Sudhana; within the multi-storied pavilion, he perceived all phenomena without any hindrance.
It is like a person ascending a celestial palace who sees the dwellings of men without any obstruction;
it is like the great ocean, within which one sees the entire trichiliocosm and all its various categories of beings;
it is like a master illusionist, who can manifest every form and color.
The youth Sudhana was likewise;
within the towered pavilion, through the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, he beheld all these unprecedented events without any obstruction.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva withdrew his majestic spiritual power and, immediately snapping his fingers, addressed Sudhana, saying:
"O son of good family!
Arise from your meditative concentration."
Having arisen from meditative concentration, he addressed him, saying:

"Behold this Bodhisattva’s sovereign spiritual power, his great vows and merits, his adornment as a Bodhisattva resulting from the fruits of his practice, and his cultivation of extraordinary and profound, wondrous deeds;
behold his gateways to all dharmas for emerging from the path of birth and death, his immeasurable adornments, the great vows of all Buddhas, and the inconceivable Bodhisattva samādhis."
“Did you see all such things as these?
Sudhana replied, “Indeed, I have seen them.”
"It is by the power of the spiritual benefactor's majestic virtue. At that time, Sudhana said,
"O Great Sage!"
"What is this Dharma-gate? He replied,
"It is the Dharma-gate of the Adorned Treasury of Right Mindfulness and Contemplation that Enters the Wisdom of the Three Times."
"Good son! A bodhisattva in their final birth attains such unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-gates as these. "O Great Sage!"
"From where do these various extraordinary and wondrously adorned dharmas come? He replied,
"They are produced by the spiritual power of a bodhisattva, yet they do not abide within that spiritual power."
It neither comes nor goes, and has no place of accumulation.
It is like the rain from a dragon: it does not originate from the body or mind, but simply through the arising of the intention, when there is a desire to rain, it rains;
yet that realm is inconceivable.
"Good son! These various extraordinary and wondrously adorned dharmas are likewise so:
they come from nowhere, but are produced solely through the spiritual power of the bodhisattva."
Good son! It is like a magician who manifests various things; they have no place from which they come or to which they go;
it is merely through the power of illusion that he manifests these various things.
These various extraordinary and wondrously adorned phenomena are likewise thus:
they neither come nor go, neither abide nor cling, and neither arise nor cease; yet, solely through the power of the bodhisattva’s wisdom and vows, such things are manifested.
At that time, Sudhana said: "O Great Sage!
From where have you come?"

He replied: "O Son of the Buddha! The bodhisattva’s realm is one without coming; without the realm of moving or staying; without the realm of attachment; without the realm of birth or death; without the realm of departing or arriving; without the realm of separation or arising; without the realm of relinquishing or clinging; without the realm of karma or retribution; without the realm of origination or dependence; and without the realm of permanence or discontinuity."

Good son! A bodhisattva comes solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming, and for the protection and salvation of sentient beings; he comes from great compassion in order to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings;
and he comes from the path of the bodhisattva’s pure precepts in order to take birth with mastery according to his own inclinations.
They come from the path of the great vows of bodhisattvas, because they have originally resolved their minds [for enlightenment];
they come from the path of the supernormal powers of bodhisattvas, because they dwell where the Buddhas abide while extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings;
they come from the path of the bodhisattvas' non-increasing and non-decreasing progression, because they do not lose the various wholesome karmas of body and mind.
They come from the wisdom and skillful means of bodhisattvas, for they accord with all classes of sentient beings;
they come from the manifestations of bodhisattvas, for they are like lightning or reflections in a mirror.
"Good son! As for your question regarding where I have come from: I have come from my place of birth, the country of Mālava;
there is a village there called Lūgaṇa."
There was the son of a householder named Gopāla; I preached the Dharma for him and caused him to establish himself in Bodhi.
For all the sentient beings in my former place of birth, I preached the Dharma according to their respective capacities for transformation.
I also preached the Dharma to my parents and various relatives as appropriate, establishing them in the Mahāyāna, and have now come here.
Sudhana said, "Great Sage! What are the birthplaces of bodhisattvas?"
He replied: “Good son! There are ten places of birth for bodhisattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the bodhicitta is the birthplace of the bodhisattva, for it gives birth to the family of bodhisattvas;
the upright mind is the birthplace of the bodhisattva, for it gives birth to the family of spiritual friends.
Abiding in the various stages is the birthplace of Bodhisattvas, for they are born into the family of the *pāramitās*;
giving rise to great vows is the birthplace of Bodhisattvas, for they are born into the family of the Bodhisattva practices;
great compassion is the birthplace of Bodhisattvas, for they are born into the family of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The true contemplation of phenomena is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives birth to the family of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
the Mahāyāna is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives birth to the family of the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*;
and the teaching and transforming of sentient beings is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives birth to the family of *bodhi*.
Wisdom and skillful means are the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for they give birth to the family of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena;
conforming to all dharmas is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for they give birth to the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
“Good son! For the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the mother;
great skillful means (mahopāya) is the father.”
The perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is the milk;
the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) is the wet nurse;
the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is the ornaments.
The perfection of vigor is the nurturer;
the perfection of meditation is purification;
and virtuous friends are the teachers.
The factors of enlightenment are one's friends;
all roots of goodness are one's kinsmen;
and all bodhisattvas are one's brothers.
The bodhicitta is the family;
as it is said, spiritual practice is the family ground;
and the dwelling place of the bodhisattva is the family abode.
The bodhisattva’s dharma of patience is his noble lineage;
the generation of great vows is his vast wealth;
and the possession of bodhisattva conduct is his adherence to family tradition.
Praising the Mahāyāna as the succession to the family dharma;

the Bodhisattva who has received the consecration of ambrosia in a single lifetime is the crown prince, capable of purely cultivating and maintaining the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Thus, these bodhisattvas transcend the stage of ordinary beings and realize the dharma of non-arising;
they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, abide in the lineage of the Buddhas, and do not sever the Three Jewels.”

They protect the lineage of all bodhisattvas, purify their places of birth, and remain free from all evil realms; they are venerated and supported by all devas, humans, Śakras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, because they are born into the family of the Buddhas and fulfill the treasury of all great vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are born into such a family, they know that all phenomena are like flashes of lightning; they never grow weary of taking birth within any of the realms of existence.

They understand that these realms are like magical illusions, and though they manifest within them, they remain unattached. Realizing that all phenomena are entirely devoid of a self, their minds are free from sorrow or regret; through great compassion, they teach and transform sentient beings without ever becoming exhausted.
They thoroughly understand that birth and death are entirely like dreams, yet they practice the bodhisattva conduct throughout all kalpas without weariness or cessation;
they realize that the five aggregates are entirely like illusions and thus do not fear birth and death; they know all dharma-realms with minds free from attachment;
they understand all phenomena to be like mirages and do not give rise to delusions regarding any practices; they sport within illusory dharmas, transcending the realm of Māra.
Having attained the pure Dharma-body, free from afflictions and karma, one attains mastery within all realms of existence and is devoid of inverted delusions. Good son!
My pure Dharma-body fills the entire Dharma-realm and manifests in forms equal to those of all sentient beings.
The equal vocal sounds of all sentient beings;
the equal names and titles of all sentient beings;
the equal modes of deportment of all sentient beings.
They manifest as being equal to all sentient beings in accordance with the world;
they manifest as being equal to all sentient beings in taking birth;
they manifest as being equal to all sentient beings in the form of youths.
The thought of equality toward all sentient beings;
the birth of all bodhisattva great vows; manifesting as transformation bodies equal in number to sentient beings to fill the dharma realm.

Because I wish to cause those fellow practitioners who have lost the resolve for enlightenment to once again give rise to the bodhicitta, I was born into a family of the Brahmin caste in the village of Kauti within the country of Mālava, in the southern region of this Jambudvīpa; I took birth there for the purpose of extinguishing their prideful minds and for the sake of transforming and delivering my parents and kinsmen.
"Good son! In the southern direction, I manifest various forms according to the needs of sentient beings to transform and deliver them;
having ended my life here, I am born in the Tuṣita Heaven."

In order to transform and deliver those various devas, he manifested the merit of supreme and wondrous wisdom to extinguish their thirst for desire, causing them to know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and that the lifespan in the celestial realms, however flourishing it may be, must inevitably decline.

All Mahāyāna bodhisattvas in their final birth gathered like clouds; and in order to instruct his fellow practitioners and to open the lotus flower transformed by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, he manifested his rebirth there.
"Good son! When I pass away from that realm and descend to be born here, attaining perfect enlightenment, you and Mañjuśrī shall both behold me."

"Good son! You should now go to Mañjuśrī and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path, so as to fully accomplish all that is practiced by Samantabhadra?'"
He shall explain it in detail for you. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī has fulfilled the vows and practices of immeasurable billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, and he has constantly served as the mother of immeasurable billions of nayutas of buddhas.

Furthermore, he is the teacher of immeasurable billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas; courageous and diligent, he transforms sentient beings, and his fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

He constantly serves as a great Dharma master amidst the assemblies of all Buddhas, being praised by all those Buddhas. Abiding in the gateway of profound wisdom, he discerns and understands all dharma realms;
for immeasurable eons, he has cultivated various Dharma gateways, reaching the ultimate consummation of the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
"Good son! Mañjuśrī is your spiritual friend; he can cause you to be born into the family of the Tathāgata, nurture your roots of goodness, and accumulate a mass of merit.
He can show you and instruct you in all spiritual friends, fulfill your great vows, and manifest all the inconceivable merits of the bodhisattvas."
Therefore, son of good family,
you should with single-minded devotion show respect and pay homage by going to his place. Why is this?

All those spiritual friends whom you previously beheld—those who cultivate the bodhisattva practices, fulfill their great vows, and attain the various Dharma gates—all do so through the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated himself before Maitreya Bodhisattva, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to depart.

At that time, Sudhana had thus traveled through one hundred and ten cities until he reached the outskirts of the city of Samantamukha. There he stood, reflecting and dwelling in thought, surveying the ten directions:
"O Mañjuśrī, when shall I meet him and behold his compassionate countenance face to face?"
While he was thinking this, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar, reaching across one hundred and ten yojanas to the city of Samantamukha, where he touched Sudhana’s crown and said: “Excellent!
Excellent! Son of good family!
If one is separated from the root of faith, the mind will be submerged by regret and remorse; one's meritorious practices will be incomplete, and one will fall away from diligent effort.
They consider a small amount of merit to be sufficient;
they give rise to attachment toward a single root of goodness;
they do not skillfully initiate the vows and practices of a bodhisattva; they are not sustained and protected by spiritual friends, nor are they remembered by the Tathāgatas.
All of these are unable to fully comprehend such a nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such a principle (*naya*), such a practice (*caryā*), or such a dwelling (*vihāra*);

they are entirely incapable of knowing them exhaustively, knowing them in their various aspects, reaching their ultimate source, gradually entering into them, explaining them, analyzing them, realizing them, or attaining them.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, having instructed, exhorted, and admonished the youth Sudhana, comforted and encouraged him until he was filled with joy and exultation. He caused him to achieve countless dharma-gates and attain immeasurable light of great wisdom, immeasurable bodhisattva dhāraṇīs, immeasurable great vows, immeasurable samādhis, immeasurable supernormal powers, and immeasurable wisdom—all of which he had already perfected.
Furthermore, he enabled him to enter the interior of the site of practice (maṇḍala) traversed by Samantabhadra.

Having established Sudhana in his own dwelling, Mañjuśrī withdrew and became invisible. Thereupon, Sudhana beheld as many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm; he did not disregard their instructions, and his treasury of great compassion for omniscience (sarvajñatā) increased.
With the eye of pure wisdom, he universally observed all sentient beings, abided in the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of tranquility, and discerned and understood the spheres of all phenomena.

He entered the profound ocean of the Buddha’s great merit, perfected the path of liberation, nurtured diligence, cultivated an upright mind for the sake of omniscience, and entered the profound ocean of dharmas throughout the three periods of time.

In accordance with the pure wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas, they manifest entry into all realms of existence, cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all eons to fulfill their great vows;

with the light of clear and pure wisdom, they illumine the sphere of all-knowledge, purifying the roots of a bodhisattva, and using the light of pure wisdom to remove the cataracts of ignorance and illuminate all phenomena, thereby thoroughly comprehending the entire realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), all Buddha-fields, and all sentient beings;
they shatter the mountains of obstacles, abide in the unimpeded Dharma, fully accomplish the treasuries of Dharma of all stages, and cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

Having heard the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as well as his vows, merits, the specific qualities of each stage (*bhūmi*), the dharmas of the stages, the attainments of the stages, the sequence of the stages, the cultivation of the stages, the abiding in the stages, the spheres of the stages, the sustenance of the stages, the commonalities of the stages, and the right path of the stages, the youth Sudhana single-mindedly desired to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
At that time, Sudhana, with right mindfulness, gave rise to the mind of the Tathāgata’s Vajragarbha Bodhimanda, the mind of the lion throne within the treasury of all jewel lotuses,
a mind equal to the realm of space,
and a mind entirely free from attachment.
A mind that purifies all buddha-fields without obstruction;
a mind that is without obstruction regarding the spheres of all phenomena;
and a mind that pervades all ten directions.
The mind that attains the immeasurable state of omniscience;
the mind that adorns the site of enlightenment;
and the mind that deeply penetrates and discerns the ocean of dharmas.
The vast mind that brings all sentient beings to maturity through transformation;
and the mind that, throughout all kalpas, practices the conduct of a bodhisattva to ultimately perfect the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

At that time, as soon as Sudhana gave rise to this thought, by the power of his own roots of goodness, the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, and the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
he immediately beheld ten kinds of auspicious signs.
What are these ten? They are:
the awakening that perceives the adornments of all pure lands;
They saw that in all lands there were no evil realms;
they saw that all lands were as pure as lotus flowers;
and they saw that in all lands, the bodies and minds of all sentient beings were supple and gentle.
He beheld the infinite adornments of all lands;
he beheld all sentient beings in all lands, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks;
he beheld clouds of adornments covering all lands.
He saw all beings in all lands achieve a mind of loving-kindness;
he saw all lands adorned as sites of enlightenment;
and he saw all beings in all lands universally practicing the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
These are the ten. Furthermore, one sees ten kinds of radiant signs:
one sees the atoms of all worlds, and within each and every atom, there emanate clouds of networks of light from all Tathāgatas, equal in number to the atoms of all worlds.
Within each and every atom, they emit various colored lights of all Buddhas, equal in number to the atoms of all worlds, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm;
within each and every atom, they emit the radiant light of clouds of all jewels, equal in number to the atoms of all worlds, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm;
within each and every atom, they emit clouds of Tathāgata-flame wheels, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.

From within each and every atom, clouds of all fragrances emerge, universally perfuming the Dharma-realm and praising the various practices, great vows, and ocean of merits of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
from within each and every atom, clouds of the light of all suns and moons are emitted, radiating the radiance of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to universally illumine the Dharma-realm;

from within each and every atom, clouds of bodies equal in number to all sentient beings emerge, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, emitting the Buddha’s radiance to universally illumine the Dharma-realm.
From within each and every atom, clouds of the bodies of all bodhisattvas emerge, perfecting all practices and filling the Dharma-realm;
from within each and every atom, clouds of images made of all kinds of jewels emerge, filling all worlds throughout the ten directions;

from within each and every atom, clouds of the bodies of all Tathāgatas emerge, equal in number to the atoms of all worlds, universally raining down the nectar of the true Dharma and filling the Dharma-realm.
These are the ten.
At that time, having seen these ten kinds of auspicious signs, Sudhana thought to himself:
"I shall now certainly see the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, so that my roots of goodness may increase and I may bring to completion the sublime practices of a bodhisattva."
"Seeing all Buddhas is like seeing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
one attains the perception of omniscience and, with single-minded reverence, desires to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
At that moment, Sudhana saw Samantabhadra Bodhisattva at the Vajragarbha Dharma-assembly, before the Tathāgata, seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by a great multitude.
The mind is like space, free from defilement and attachment; it eliminates all obstacles and purifies all lands;
through unimpeded dharmas, it fills the ten directions, abides in omniscience, enters all dharma-realms, and transforms sentient beings;
throughout all kalpas, it practices the bodhisattva path, reverently making offerings to all Buddhas, with a mind that never regresses.
Among all sentient beings, they are the most excellent and supreme; none in any world can destroy them, and no bodhisattvas can fathom the realm of their wisdom.
Possessing inconceivable and wondrous merits, they universally contemplate the three periods of time as equal to all Tathāgatas.

At that time, Sudhana saw that from every single pore of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva there issued forth rays of light equal in number to the atoms of all worlds, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm, extinguishing the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings and fully nourishing the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas;
from every single pore there emerged clouds of various fragrances, universally perfuming all Tathāgatas and their retinues throughout the ten directions;
from every single pore there emerged clouds of flowers equal in number to the atoms of all worlds.
From every single pore, clouds of fragrant trees as numerous as the atoms of all worlds issued forth, emitting myriad exquisite scents that adorned the Dharma-realm;
from every single pore, clouds of wondrous jewel-garments as numerous as the atoms of all worlds issued forth, adorning the void;

from every single pore, various jewel-trees as numerous as the atoms of all worlds issued forth, filling the void to serve as adornment, raining down various jewels as offerings to the Buddha and the great assembly.
From each and every pore, there emerge bodies of gods of the form realm as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, filling the entire dharma-realm and the realms of all sentient beings, praising bodhi;
from each and every pore, there emerge clouds of bodies of Brahma kings, exhorting the Tathāgatas to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma;
from each and every pore, there emerge clouds of bodies of gods of the desire realm, all of whom protect and uphold the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.

From every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge Buddhas of the three periods of time as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, filling the void and acting as a refuge for sentient beings who have no refuge;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge pure Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, filled with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who teach and bring to maturity immeasurable sentient beings;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge pure and impure Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, filling the void and causing those who are defiled to become entirely pure.
From every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge as many impure and pure lands as there are atoms in all worlds, to subdue impure sentient beings;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of bodies of all sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, to accord with the world and teach and transform sentient beings;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of bodhisattva bodies as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, to praise all Buddhas and nurture the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.

From every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of bodies of bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, manifesting the initial arousal of the bodhicitta in all lands;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of bodhisattva bodies, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, in each and every land praising the ocean of merit and vows of all Buddhas and the sublime practices performed by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;

from every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge the practices of Samantabhadra, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, raining down the nectar-like Dharma to cause all sentient beings to cultivate omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
From every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within all worlds, having newly attained perfect enlightenment and appearing in the world.
At that time, Sudhana beheld such inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers;
having seen them, he leaped for joy with immeasurable delight.

He again observed each and every part of Samantabhadra’s body, each and every limb and joint, and within each and every pore, he clearly saw the wind-circles, water-circles, fire-circles, and earth-circles of the trichiliocosm; the great oceans, jewel mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and the Diamond Ring Mountains; all dwellings and exquisite palaces; all classes of sentient beings; all hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; the realm of King Yama; the various devas and Brahma kings, up to humans and non-humans; the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; all kalpas; and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teaching and transforming sentient beings—all such matters were fully manifested. It was likewise so for all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Just as the sovereign power manifested by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana in this Sahā world,
so too was the supernatural power manifested at the abode of the Buddha Bhadrāśva in the Lotus-Wondrous-Virtue world in the eastern direction.
Just as at the place of the Buddha Bhadramukha, so too did he manifest his spiritual power at the places of all Buddhas in all worlds throughout the eastern direction;

and just as in the east, so too did he manifest his spiritual power at the places of all Buddhas in all worlds throughout the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
In all worlds, within every single atom, he likewise manifests his sovereign power in this same manner.
At that time, upon seeing the inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Sudhana immediately attained ten indestructible dharma-gates of wisdom. What are these ten?
That is to say:
in every thought-moment, one is able to pervade all lands with a single body;
in every thought-moment, one goes to the abodes of all Buddhas.
In every thought-moment, they reverently make offerings to all Buddhas;
in every thought-moment, at the abodes of all Buddhas, they hear and uphold the True Dharma, attaining the gate of the perfection of wisdom regarding the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas;
they attain the gate of the perfection of wisdom regarding the inconceivable sovereignty of the Buddhas.
They attain the dharma-gate of inexhaustible eloquence and wisdom;
they attain the Prajñāpāramitā dharma-gate of contemplating all phenomena;
and they attain the dharma-gate of the great skillful means-pāramitā of the ocean of all dharma-realms.
He attained the gate of the perfection of wisdom that knows the inclinations and natures of all sentient beings;
he attained the gate of the perfection of wisdom practiced by Samantabhadra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra extended his right hand and stroked the crown of Sudhana’s head.
Having rubbed it, Sudhana further attained samādhi-doors as numerous as the atoms in all worlds;
each samādhi-door had as its retinue samādhis as numerous as the atoms in all worlds;

within each samādhi, he beheld oceans of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, who nurtured a multitude of virtues as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, gave birth to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), fulfilled the ocean of great vows, and dwelt securely in the right path.
Having brought all bodhisattva practices to ultimate fulfillment, he has aroused *sarvajñā* (omniscience) and exerts courageous diligence, being illuminated by the light of all Buddhas.

Just as at the place of Vairocana Buddha in this Sahā world, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rubbed Sudhana’s crown, causing him to attain all the gates of samādhi equal in number to the atoms of all worlds, as well as all sublime merits;
so too are the merits obtained when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in the presence of all Tathāgatas throughout all worlds in the ten directions, rubs Sudhana’s crown.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Sudhana, saying:
"Good man! Do you now see these extraordinary and marvelous deeds of my sovereign spiritual power?"
He replied: "Indeed, I have seen it.
This inconceivable matter, which cannot be fathomed, can be understood by none except the Tathāgata."
“Good son! In the past, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds, I cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, single-mindedly seeking enlightenment;
in each and every eon, I beheld as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds, and therein cultivated the bodhicitta.”
In each and every eon, throughout all worlds, he established unspeakably unspeakable great assemblies of giving, bestowing everything upon all:
he gave away his wives and children, cities, towns, and villages, as well as his head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, joints, flesh, and blood—all parts of his body;
not sparing even his own life, he sought single-mindedly after the knowledge of all modes.

In each and every eon, they reverently made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds; in the presence of those Buddhas, they left the household life to study the Way and upheld the True Dharma. They never gave rise to thoughts of greed, anger, or delusion; thoughts of "I" and "mine"; thoughts of attachment to the false reality of birth and death; thoughts of contempt for others; or any obstructive thoughts. They cultivated the indestructible bodhicitta of the Buddhas, never forgetting it for a moment.

"Good son! The various practices of a bodhisattva that I have cultivated—purifying buddha-fields, teaching and transforming sentient beings, nurturing great compassion, making offerings to all Buddhas and spiritual friends, upholding the true Dharma, relinquishing all internal and external things, practicing mundane and supramundane wisdom, causing all sentient beings to turn their backs on the suffering of birth and death, and praising the merits of all Buddhas—all such matters as these could be expounded for unspeakably unspeakable eons;
yet those eons might come to an end, but these merits can never be exhausted."

"Good son! I have attained such powers as the power of fully endowed merit, the power of all roots of goodness, the power of delighting in the supreme Dharma, the power of cultivating merit, the power of observing the nature of quiescence of all phenomena, the power of the pure eye of wisdom, the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the power of great vows, the power of great compassion, the power of pure supernormal clarity, and the power of spiritual friends. Because I have attained these powers, I have realized the inherently pure Dharma-body, which remains indestructible throughout the three periods of time;
furthermore, I have attained the unsurpassed, pure form-body, which transcends all worlds, and there are none among those to be transformed who do not behold it."
I travel through all lands, reaching every place without exception; manifesting the power of mastery, those who behold me never tire of the sight. Good son!
Observe my pure Dharma-body, which has been accomplished through the practice of Bodhisattva deeds throughout an ocean of immeasurable eons.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, it has been difficult to hear or see;
having planted only a small root of goodness, even śrāvakas and bodhisattvas cannot yet hear my name, let alone behold my body.
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who hear my name, they shall no longer regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they see me, touch me, escort me, follow me, behold my light, or witness the shaking of the worlds of the Buddhas; [in all these cases, they shall not regress]."
It is likewise for those who see or hear me even in their dreams.

Whether they contemplate and keep me in mind for one day and night, seven days and nights, half a month, one month, one year, a hundred years, one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or even for as many kalpas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds;
or whether they keep me in mind for one lifetime, a hundred lifetimes, or even for as many lifetimes as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds—it is all the same.

By means of such subtle skillful expedients, as numerous as the atoms within these worlds, he causes all sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who hear that I cultivate and purify a buddha-field, they will certainly attain rebirth in a pure world;
if there are sentient beings who see or hear my body, they will certainly be born within my pure body."
"Good son! You should further contemplate my pure Dharma-body.
At that time, within the marks, signs, limbs, and joints of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and from all his pores, Sudhana beheld unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds, filled with Buddhas.
Each and every Tathāgata has an assembly of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of great bodhisattvas as his retinue.
He beholds those oceans of lands of each and every Tathāgata, whose foundations differ and whose forms and colors vary;
he sees the Diamond Ring Mountains, the vast clouds that overspread them, and the wheels of Dharma turned by the Buddhas as they appear in the world.
All such matters were entirely different.

Furthermore, he saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, throughout the lands of the ten directions, manifesting as many transformation bodies of the Tathāgata as there are atoms in all worlds, teaching and transforming sentient beings and causing them to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the merit that the youth Sudhana had acquired by approaching as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a buddha-world did not equal even one hundredth part of the merit he acquired upon seeing the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra; it did not equal even one part in a hundred thousand million, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy. Why was this?
In every thought-moment, the youth Sudhana entered unspeakably unspeakable oceans of Buddha-worlds and attained treasuries of all manner of merits, as numerous as unspeakably unspeakable atoms;
he knew the oceans of Buddhas appearing in succession in the world,
and the oceans of Bodhisattva assemblies surrounded by their retinues.
Having understood the faculties of sentient beings, they manifest sovereign power to transform and deliver them.
They may practice the bodhisattva path within a single world for the duration of one kalpa;
or even for as many kalpas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, they practice the bodhisattva path.

Without passing away from this world and without being born in that world, they are able to teach and transform sentient beings in immeasurable and boundless worlds, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the youth Sudhana was able to bring to ultimate fulfillment the ocean of great vows practiced by Samantabhadra; before long, he would become equal to all Buddhas in his single body filling all world-systems, in his bodies, in his practices, in his perfect enlightenment, in his sovereign powers, in his turning of the wheel of Dharma, in his various eloquences, in his sublime voices, in his skillful means, in his power of fearlessness, in the abodes of the Buddhas, in his great compassion, and in his sovereign power over inconceivable dharma-gates.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“You who have left behind afflictions, Listen with a pure mind and with focused attention As I speak of all the practices of the Buddha, The true perfections.”
Transcending all worlds, the unsurpassed Tamer of Men,
Far removed from the defilements of affliction, pure as space.
The sun of perfected wisdom dispels the darkness of afflictions.
Universally illuminating all phenomena, Bringing peace and happiness to all living beings.
The Tathāgata appears in the world only once in immeasurable eons;
Like the udumbara flower, he is difficult to see and difficult to encounter.
For the sake of all living beings, he practiced austerities for immeasurable eons;
conforming to all worlds, his mind remained free from attachment.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, having heard the teaching of Samantabhadra, [proceeded].
Listen with a reverent mind to the Tathāgata’s sovereign and true meaning.
Samantabhadra, the true son of the Buddha, has perfected all practices;
he is constantly praised by the Buddhas, and his words are never false.
The Flower of Samantabhadra’s Merit, Unstained by the phenomena of the three realms,
Exhorts the great assembly to listen To this inexhaustible ocean of wisdom.
The subtle and wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas Is as pure as empty space.
Clearly understanding all conditioned phenomena, their minds are free from attachment.
In a single thought-moment, they fully comprehend all dharmas of the three periods of time;
skillfully knowing the faculties of sentient beings, they transform them according to what is appropriate for each.
The Tathāgata fully knows the afflictions in the minds of sentient beings, their various karmas—both wholesome and unwholesome—and all that they delight in; thus he preaches the True Dharma for them.
Or one may see the Tathāgata seated, filling the realms of the ten directions.
Obstructed by the sins of sentient beings, though near, they are not seen.
Or one may see those who have first resolved their minds, remaining far removed from all negligence,
practicing the bodhisattva path for immeasurable and incalculable eons.
Some hear the Most Victorious Ones Proclaiming the Dharma with wondrous voices;
Yet sentient beings burdened by the defilements of sin Do not hear the names of the Buddhas.
Or they see great Bodhisattvas Filling the three thousandfold world system.
The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for those who have perfected the conduct of Samantabhadra;
or one may see Vairocana, who throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas has purified this world and attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
In some, one sees the Buddha Bhadraśrī and the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
all such beings fill the wondrous realm of Padmaguṇa.
In others, one sees Amitābha and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the bestowal of empowerment and prediction: they fill the entire dharma-realm.
Some see the Buddha Akṣobhya and the great bodhisattva Gandhahastin;
all such beings fill the wondrous, blissful, adorned, and pure lands.
In some, one sees the Buddha Moon-Wisdom and the Great Bodhisattva Golden Banner;
these and others all fill the wondrous land of the Bright and Pure Mirror.
In others, one sees the Buddha Sun-Treasury and the Great Bodhisattva Wisdom Consecration.
All these realms of pure radiance are completely filled;
Or one may see throughout the worlds of the ten directions The various Buddhas emitting great light,
Turning the wheel of Dharma for the sake of all beings, To eliminate the darkness of ignorance.
Or one may see within a single pore unspeakable Buddha-fields,
where Buddhas with bodies adorned by all virtues are surrounded by hosts of Buddha-sons,
turning the wheel of the true Dharma to deliver and liberate all living beings.
Or within a single pore, they universally see all the sons of the Buddha,
practicing the bodhisattva conduct throughout countless billions of kalpas;
or within each and every atom, they see infinite lands.
Whether pure or defiled, arising from various karmic actions,
some behold Vairocana turning the wheel of Dharma there;
manifesting his sovereign power, he enters nirvana through skillful means.
Observing the various classes of sentient beings and all their karmic afflictions,
they manifest the power of mastery to transform them and bring them to liberation.
Such Kings of Dharma, throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
I shall now briefly describe a small portion of his sovereign power of manifestation:
some see Śākyamuni having first attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
benefiting all living beings— a state that none can fathom.
Some see them as bodhisattvas making offerings to all buddhas;
some see them dwelling in the stage of a youth, manifesting sovereign powers;
some see them practicing generosity and morality, patience, and diligent vigor.
Deeply entering various meditative concentrations, they abide on the stage of wisdom and skillful means.
Some are seen to dwell in the ultimate stage of all-encompassing knowledge;
through samādhis and dhāraṇīs, they give rise to the various supernormal powers and clarities.
Some see them practicing the bodhisattva conduct for immeasurable eons,
attaining the stage of non-retrogression and receiving the consecration of ambrosia;
some see them as Brahmā, Śakra, or the Four Heavenly Kings.
As Kṣatriyas and Brahmins, they manifest such bodies as these.
Some see them passing away from Tuṣita and descending in spirit to take birth;
others see them dwelling in palaces, renouncing desire to leave the home life.
Some see him sitting at the site of enlightenment, subduing Māra and attaining perfect awakening;
turning the pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma, and after his parinirvāṇa, having stupas erected for him.
Others see Amitāyus, the most supreme Honored One among devas and humans.
Bestowing upon him the prediction of empowerment, he becomes an unsurpassed guide.
Or one may see the Honored One of Ten Powers, who, having completed his work of teaching and transformation,
has entered parinirvāṇa for immeasurable and incalculable kalpas.
Some see the Moon-like Teacher dwelling in the palace of Brahmā,
appearing likewise in the palaces of Maheśvara and the King of Māras;
or they see him in the Tuṣita heaven, surrounded by the hosts of devas.
For their sake, he preaches the True Dharma, causing them all to rejoice greatly.
Or he is seen dwelling among the Yāma devas, Śakra, and the Four Great Kings,
within the palaces of the kings of the nāgas and yakṣas, and the abodes of the eight classes of beings.
In the presence of Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, he made offerings and received his prediction;
through such skillful means as these, he teaches and transforms all living beings.
His radiant body and lifespan, his pure wisdom and his retinue—
The sounds of their majestic demeanor in teaching and transforming beings are all beyond counting.
They appear as Buddhas identical to sentient beings; some have bodies like Mount Sumeru, while others manifest sitting in the full lotus posture, filling the worlds.
Some see light extending for one fathom, others for hundreds or thousands of yojanas;
some see it illuminating the entire dharma-realm, others illuminating all lands.
Some manifest a lifespan of a hundred years, others of hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of years.
Throughout immeasurable nayutas of inconceivable eons,
with unimpeded and pure wisdom, one knows the three periods of time in a single thought:
that all things arise from causes and conditions, yet in reality possess no self-nature.
Attaining perfect enlightenment in a single land, they universally manifest in all worlds;
they can manifest a single world as immeasurable lands, and manifest immeasurable lands as a single world.
Abiding securely in the unsurpassed path, Possessing the power of fearlessness,
He turns the twelvefold wheel of Dharma with unimpeded wisdom,
Knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, As well as the twelve links of dependent origination.
With the fourfold unimpeded wisdom, he expounds all phenomena:
they are without self and without what belongs to a self; they possess no intrinsic nature;
they are neither arising nor ceasing, and neither coming nor going.
All are entirely like space, yet they do not destroy various karmas.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata uses skillful means to analyze and explain them;
when he turns this wheel of Dharma, all lands tremble.
Like the great ocean and the Vajra Mountains, they possess no fear.
When the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice, each understands according to their own capacity;
all stains of affliction are extinguished, and they are led to abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
When the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice, some hear it as the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and patience;
diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts; the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers.
The path of awakening, the stillness of contemplation, And the various dharma-gates of supernormal powers—
When the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice, The eight classes of beings, humans and non-humans alike, Including Brahmā, Śakra,
and the Four Heavenly Kings, Each understands according to their own kind of sound.
Those with much greed, anger, and delusion, Bound by pride, stinginess, and envy—
For each of these eighty-four thousand defilements, They hear the corresponding methods of remedy.
Those who have not yet cultivated pure karma, Upon hearing the teaching of the ten paths of wholesome action,
Those who have already cultivated generosity and morality, upon hearing the teaching of parinirvāṇa,
will abandon their attachment to saṃsāra. When all beings who are indolent hear the teaching of the gateway to liberation, they shall extinguish the suffering of birth and death.
Those with few desires and contentment, who delight in dwelling in seclusion and tranquility—
such beings as these hear the sounds of the Two Vehicles being taught.
Or there are those who cultivate the vast mind and possess the treasury of all merits.
Those who draw near to the Buddhas hear the sound of the Mahāyāna being taught.
In some worlds, they hear the voice of the One Vehicle being taught;
in others, two, three, four, or five, even up to an infinite number of vehicles.
The practices of wisdom differ, yet liberation is without distinction;
like the nature of space, it possesses no manifold characteristics.
The subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata is likewise of such a nature.
According to those who are to be transformed, what they hear differs for each.
Through his past practices, the Buddha has attained a single, subtle, and wondrous voice;
though he has no thought of "self" or "other," he is able to respond to all.
From the Buddha’s mouth, he emits wondrous light, numbering eighty-four thousand;
it shines universally upon all worlds, extinguishing the manifold afflictions.
Endowed with the merit of wisdom, he accords with sentient beings in three ways.
Detached from the world like space, yet constantly manifesting within the world;
though appearing in accordance with the world, [free from] the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death,
or even manifesting as dwelling in a lifespan, its nature remains like space.
The Tathāgata discerns and knows all classes of sentient beings—
their faculties, dispositions, and inclinations— and causes them to abide in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
The Buddhas, the Honored Guides, manifest their entry into the great assemblies.
In accordance with those to be transformed, he manifests the dharma of excellent deportment.
For the sake of the śrāvakas, he manifests the dharma of the deportment of renunciation;
they constantly delight in cultivating tranquility and realize nirvana without remainder.
Among the assembly of brahmins, he manifests a frail and aged body;
with matted hair and practicing austerities, his discourses are inexhaustible.
He practices breath-control or fasting, and scorches his body with the five fires.
Thus manifesting ascetic practices, he subdued all the heterodox teachers.
Some observed the precepts of alien paths; others were skilled in calculation and various arts, such as astrology, the signs of earthquakes, and the diverse characteristics of living beings.
Deeply entering various meditative concentrations, samādhis, and liberations,
they manifest diverse playful displays to enable others to attain sarvajñā (omniscience).
They manifest delight in clothing and adorn their bodies with various ornaments.
Brave and skilled in the art of military strategy, he subdues the kṣatriyas;
manifesting knowledge of the governance of the True Dharma, the proper seasons,
and all matters of benefit, he wins over sentient beings with gentle speech and subdues the great ministers.
Sometimes he goes to the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings or the various classes of spirits and deities,
employing skillful means to preach the Dharma and causing them all to rejoice greatly.
Sometimes he manifests as Śakra, dwelling securely in the Hall of Good Dharma.
Surrounded by the hosts of devas, he expounds the Dharma for them;
whether in Yāma or Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati or Paranirmita-vaśavartin,
from the realm of Brahmā up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, he expounds the Dharma for them.
Thus manifesting countless varieties of majestic deportment and immeasurable powers of skillful means, he delivers all living beings.
Just as a master illusionist can manifest all manner of things, so does he appear in various forms.
The Buddha, in order to transform sentient beings, manifests various kinds of bodies.
Like the moon traveling through the void, those who behold it perceive it as waxing or waning;
yet its reflection appears in all rivers and ponds, outshining the light of flickering lamps.
The Tathāgata’s moon of pure wisdom appears to wax and wane,
yet when situated within the water of the straightforward mind, it outshines the light of the two vehicles.
It is like the deep great ocean, whose precious treasures can never be exhausted.
Within it all is clearly manifested: The forms and likenesses of sentient beings.
In the ocean of profound causes and conditions, Where the jewels of merit are inexhaustible, Within the pure Dharma-body, There is no form that does not appear.
Just as the bright, pure sun Shines away the darkness of the world,
So the sun of the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom Completely dispels the darkness of the three times.
Like a dragon raising auspicious clouds, It rains everywhere upon all things.
When rain falls upon body and mind, it removes heat and brings refreshing coolness.
So too is the Tathāgata: he raises the clouds of great compassion and rains down the nectar of the Dharma everywhere, extinguishing the fires of the three poisons.
This Dharma does not emerge from the body or mind of the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body is peerless throughout the three realms.
Transcending all worlds, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
In truth, it has no basis; it does not go, yet it reaches everywhere.
It is like what is seen in a dream, and also like a painting in the sky;
it is neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor without marks.
Neither existent nor non-existent, its nature is like space.
Like the maṇi jewel of the ocean, which can produce all kinds of treasures,
so too are the various radiances of sentient beings, yet those radiances have no inherent existence.
The Teacher is also like this: though he exists, he does not exist;
he does not accumulate the jewels of merit within any single location.
The Great Sage appears in the void, like the self-nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Nirvāṇa, freedom from desire, and cessation— All these are of one single nature.
The atoms within the minds of sentient beings, The drops of water in the oceans that could be counted,
And even the dimensions of space that could be measured— The virtues of the Buddha are inexhaustible when described.
"Those who hear this Dharma with joy, And possess faith without doubt, Shall swiftly accomplish the Unsurpassed Way, Becoming equal to all Tathāgatas.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvatamsaka Sūtra) consists of one hundred thousand verses in its Sanskrit original. Formerly, the practitioner Zhi Falin obtained these thirty-six thousand verses from the kingdom of Khotan. On the tenth day of the third month in the year of the Chunchu fire (418 CE), during the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, at Daochang Monastery established by Xie Shi, the Minister of Works of Yangzhou, he invited the Indian meditation master Buddhabhadra to translate the Sanskrit into Chinese. With Buddhabhadra holding the Sanskrit text in hand, the śramaṇa Shi Faye personally received the translation by dictation.

At that time, Meng Yi, the Interior Prefect of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, served as patrons (dānapati); the work was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yuanxi era.
